units.la: IAm dudum puduit me, Vir maxime, tot tantaque beneficia à te nactum, nihil hactenus gratitudinis publicè rependisse. Quintus jam agitur annus, quum, qui ad te, tantum ac in tam sublimi loco constitutum virum, literas non modo non dare, sed ne cogitare quidem fuissem ausus, primus ipsemet, quod exspectandum minime videbatur, humanissimis tuis ac doctissimis literis non tantum fui salutatus, sed &, quod omnem spem longè maximè superabat, amplissimo Pentateuchi Samaritani munere beatus. Quod quidem, initium tantum tuæ erat beneficentiæ, latius se in posterum diffusuræ. biennio enim fere post, codicem egregio characterē Syro exaratum, qui omnia N. T. Syriaci, quæ in prioribus deerant editionibus, ac præterea prolixum Ephremi de Amore Sapientiæ tractatum contineret, mittis. addito Psalterio Syriaco, & speciminis loco, Pentateuchi Arabico-Samaritani, cujus Genesin & Deuteronomium tantum habere te scribebas, quaternione. Quis non hic tantæ liberalitatis finem fore credidisset? Sed id flagrans tuus in promovendas literas amor haud permisit. Proximo enim anno, qui post millesimum sexcentesimum trigesimus erat secundus, discedente illinc ad nos nobilissimo Iuvene Dungarvania vicecomite, per Ephorum ejus D. Frejum, virum omni eruditionis genere perpolitum, mittit Pentateuchum Syriacum, elegantissima manu pictum, nunquam nostris hominibus visum thesaurum, quo majorem vel optare non licuisset. Et ne praeter liberalitatem tuam nihil in te miraremur, addis propriae diligentiae atque eruditionis praeclarum specimen, Praedestinatiana (quam Ecclesias nostras tantopere perturbasse, vere dicis) controversiae historiam, & veterum Epistolarum Hybernicarum syllogen, utramque manu tua emendatam, & nova editioni, ubi opportunum esset, adaptatam. & ne hic quidem benignitatis tuae fons exaruit. Sequens rursus annus novum adfert beneficium. Dixit enim quicquid Syriacorum Ephremi opusculorum Academia nostra haberet, descripsisse me intelligis, vocales addidisse, & Latine transtulisse, quin protinus tres codices elegantissimos, quibus omnia Ephremi, quae instructissima tua Orientalis Bibliotheca habet, continentur, admiranda quadam liberalitate transmittas. Stupebunt, sat scio, Lectores omnes, tam raram humanitatem, tam inauditam beneficentiam. omnia haec enim M. S. quae tutemet avidissimo animo, quum non haberes, desiderasti, quae magnis impensis comparasti, quae praeclarissima supellectilis tuae libraria κτημα, & maxima bibliotheca ornamenta habuisti, ea te in tam dissitas oras, per tot pericula, ad peregrinum hominem, dubius an unquam esses recepturus, transmisisse! Novum plane est & insolens, quod ante te fecit nemo, nec quisquam post facile imitetur. neque adeo in quenquam quadrare potest magis quam in te, quod eleganter satis dicunt Arabes, الستي قريب من الله قريب من الناس قريب من الجنة بعيد من النار, liberalis est vicinus Deo, vicinus hominum, vicinus paradisi, remotus ab igne. Quaeporro etiam offers, majora hisce, taceo, ne nimia beneficentia in me tua praedicatione famam mihi captare videar. Non nego, vir amplissime, me tot, tantorum, & a tanto viro profectorum munerum amplitudinem maximopere mihi gratulari, & jactare propemodum. per te accensus est mihi animus, per te accrevit eruditio, per te & pluribus prodesse possum & magis. Tu me doctis chariorem reddidisti, tu ad ordinem eorum affectandum adegisti, tu majora, quam unquam a me proficisci posse putaveram, cogitare coegisti. Ut enim, quod res est, libere dicam, & quod te in animum induxisse existimo, tu me orbi Christiano obstrinxisti, ut, ni quid munerum tuorum subsidiis dignum a me proficiscatur, indignus merito sim habendus, in quem tot tantaque beneficia literaria sint collata. nec tantum ego indignus sed & tu parum prudens, qui uti nescienti beneficia dederis. neque enim abit a vero Hebraorum sapientum dictum, כסיל הנותן לסי שאינו ראוי, stultus est qui dat indigno. Id serio deinceps meditari & agere, meum erit: & tibi tuorum beneficiorum fructum referre. quod dum molior, differendum diutius non fuit, in tantum ac tam largum benefactorem, grati animi qualecunq; νκμήμον. paratas habebam hasce in Acta Apostolorum observatiunculas, quas edi, & 4 Euangeliis antehac editis subnecti volebat Typographus. annuentem obstringit, ut qua in omnes Epistolas affecta a multis annis, sed nondum pralo apta habeo, quamprimum apparem. Non possum id non promittere. Sed quia moram id longiorem habet, quam animus ad gratitudinem properans patitur, opusculum hoc, etsi perexiguum & beneficiorum tuorum amplitudini longe impar, consecrare tibi malui, quam beneficentia tua oblitus videri. Nihil rependo, vir Amplissime. demens enim sim, qui me pro tantis benefactis, τὸ ἰκανὸν ποιεῖν posse existimem. hoc tantum ago, ut animo meo insitum scias, me quamplurimum tibi debere. Nec ulla tibi a me laudis accessio poterit fieri, quam totam a te ipso habes, & a liberalitate summam. Nisi falsum sit illud Hebraeorum scitum, מי שנקה מן הכולת יגיע אל הגדולה, qui immunis est ab avaritia, pertinget ad magna. Animum scribentis spectat, in quo longe plus latet gratitudinis, quam libellus hic queat prodere. Vis rursus audire ex Hebraeis, quae sit vera liberalitas? הנירות ההרשה טובה עם קבלת התשלומין, liberalitas est sensus bonus, cum acceptione occultorum. hoc igitur liberalissimis tuis beneficiis adde, ut de amico tuo, quem tanto favore es complexus, benefentias, & non tam publicum hoc opusculum, quam occultum ejus animum accipias. Audeo id mihi ab humanitate tua promittere, vir Amplissime, gratum fore, quantulumcunque fit, quod offero. tum quia qua offero sacra sunt, quorum tu ϑεοφύης es maximus, tum quia qua antehac in Euangelia sum commentatus, tanta es dignatus amplecti benevolentia, ut, pramissis quibusdam qua taceo, quia non mea merita, sed tuus isthac expressit amor, monere etiam voluerus, ut, si te audiam (verba tua sunt qua scribo) non prius conquiescam, quam pari diligentia & simili Commentationis genere, quod Novi T. est reliquum, illustravero. In ipsam certe peccem amicitiam, si de animo tam benevolo sinistri quid & adversi suspicer. מרות האדם מקראי לבו mores hominis sunt lectiones (vel scriptura) cordis ejus, inquiunt Hebraorum sapientes, id est, quid cor cujusque continet, mores ejus exprimunt, qui veluti scriptura quedam sunt, in quibus legi quasi possunt animi affectus. Indignentur mihi igitur merito omnes qui te norunt, si, cum mores tui nihil testentur nisi studia literarum, nihil loquantur nisi humanitatem, nihil spirent nisi humilitatem & benevolentiam, meos hosce qualescunque labores adversam mentem & infestum animum inventuros arbitror. De Commentationis genere nihil dicam. tale est, quale postulasti, nempe simile priori. nisi quod sapius hic quam in Euangelis examen nostrum subiit Cl. Beza, ob incongruam, quam secutus est, autore Iunio, Arabus versionem. Nolim, vir Clar. aut tibi aut doctorum ac piorum ulli Zoilus haberi, qui ex tanti viri diffamatione laudem quaram. Novi & laudo prudens illud ac pulchrum Arabum dictum, ﺍﻟﺠﻨﺔ ﻣﻐﻨﻢ ﻭﺍﻟﺬﻳﻦ ﻣﻐﺮﻡ, laudatio ditat, at diffamatio multat. Multandus sane sim omni in posterum laude atque honore, si ex tanti viri incommodo meum quasiero commodum. Hoc tantum ago, ut doctissimus ejus Commentarius, a lapsibus quibusdam, quorum alii, quos secutus est, Interpretes maximam partem sunt autores, repurgatus, Theologiae candidatos certius atque tutius deducat. Verba Scriptura ac phrafes examinare,collatisque variorum Interpretum sententiis,quod sequendum maxime videbatur, annotare, is fcopus erat & institutum.In quo Criticum agere vix poteram, quin, neglecta magnorum virorum autoritate,nunc hunc nunc illum notarem,& ut quidem videbatur, emendarem. non ut cuiquam quid detraherem, sed quanta poteram modestia atque aquanimitate, veritatem illustrarem. quod tamen ipsum, fi aut tibi, vir optime, aut aliis probis ac piis viris improbari videam,spondeo me deinceps ab eo fcriptionis genere abstenturum, & ejus quod commisi culpam fassurum. nec refugio, quin censores omnes, qui simili moderatione, parique candore mea volent & examinare & castigare, aequissimo feram animo. felices fore judico errores meos, fi cui inveftiganda penitius & indaganda veritatis occasionem dederint. Non ineptum est quod in Alcorano Afora 7. legimus, [Arabic] Pondus est veritas, & quorum librae sunt graves, illi sunt beati. Veritatis pondus quaro. cujus fi alterius libra plus contineat mea, palmam ei & felicitatis & laudis libenter tribuo. At fatis jam apud te, virum aequissimum & candidissimum, est excusatum. Restat ut me tuo amori, laboresque meos favori tuo commendem. Deumque Opt. Max. supplex venerer, ut te diu Ecclesiis Reipublicaque literaria sospitem ac incolumem confervet. Id opto, qui sum
units.tr: II have long been ashamed, most distinguished sir, that although I have received so many and such great kindnesses from you, I have so far made no public return of gratitude. It is now the fifth year since, though I would not have dared even to think of writing to a man of your rank and high position, you were the first to greet me, and that by your most courteous and learned letter, which was least of all to be expected. Beyond that, you blessed me with the magnificent gift of a Samaritan Pentateuch, which far exceeded all my hopes. That was only the beginning of your generosity, which was to spread more widely afterwards. About two years later you sent me a codex written in a fine Syriac hand, containing all the Syriac New Testament that was lacking in the earlier editions, together with a lengthy treatise of Ephrem on the Love of Wisdom. You added a Syriac Psalter and, as a specimen, a quire of the Arabic-Samaritan Pentateuch, of which you wrote that you had only the Genesis and Deuteronomy. Who would not have thought that this was the limit of such generosity? But your burning zeal for advancing learning did not allow it. For in the following year, which was 1632, when the most noble young Viscount Dungarvan was leaving us for home, you sent through his tutor, Mr. Frey, a man polished in every kind of learning, a Syriac Pentateuch painted with the most elegant hand, a treasure our people had never seen, and one greater than anyone could have wished for. And so that we should not wonder at anything in you apart from your generosity, you added a splendid specimen of your own diligence and learning: a history of the Predestinarian controversy (which, as you rightly say, has so greatly disturbed our churches), and a collection of the old Irish letters, both corrected by your own hand and adapted to the new edition where it was appropriate. Nor has the fountain of your kindness run dry even here. The next year brought yet another benefit. You understood that I had copied out whatever Syriac works of Ephrem our university possessed, had added vowel points, and had translated them into Latin. Then, with a wonderful generosity, you at once sent three most elegant codices containing all the works of Ephrem that your well-stocked Oriental library holds. All the readers will be astonished, I am sure, at such rare humanity and such unheard-of kindness. For you sent to a foreigner, through so many dangers and to so distant a shore, all these manuscripts which you yourself had longed for with the greatest eagerness when you did not have them, which you had acquired at great expense, and which were the most splendid possession of your library and the greatest ornaments of your collection, while you were uncertain whether you would ever receive them back! This is indeed something new and unusual, which no one before you has done, and which no one afterwards will easily imitate. The Arabs say of a generous man, very elegantly, that it applies to no one more than to you: al-sakhi qarib min Allah, qarib min al-nas, qarib min al-janna, baid min al-nar, "the generous man is near God, near men, near paradise, far from the fire." What you also offer besides, I pass over, lest by praising your great generosity I seem to be seeking glory for myself. I do not deny, most distinguished sir, that I rejoice greatly in the abundance of so many and such great gifts, coming from so great a man, and that I almost boast of them. Through you my spirit has been kindled, through you my learning has grown, and through you I can be of use to more people and to greater effect. You have made me dearer to scholars, you have driven me to strive for their rank, and you have compelled me to think of greater things than I had ever believed I could produce. To speak freely, as the matter stands, and as I think you intended, you have bound me to the Christian world, so that, unless something worthy of your gifts comes from me, I shall rightly be considered unworthy of having received such great literary benefits. And not only am I unworthy, but you too are not very wise, since you have bestowed benefits on one who does not know how to use them. Indeed, the saying of the Hebrew sages is not far from the truth: kesil ha-noten le-sheh she-eino ra'ui, "a fool is he who gives to one who is unworthy." It will be my task to consider and carry out this seriously from now on, and to render you the fruit of your benefits. While I was working on this, it was not right to delay any longer; so, to so great and so generous a benefactor, I offer, as a token of a grateful mind [μνήμων], these little observations on the Acts of the Apostles, which I had prepared and which the printer wished to publish as an appendix to the four Gospels already printed. He is insisting, and I am bound to comply, that I bring out as soon as possible the work on all the Epistles, which I have had in hand for many years but which is not yet ready for the press. I cannot refuse to promise this. But because that will take longer than my mind, hastening towards gratitude, can bear, I preferred to dedicate this little work to you, though it is very slight and far unequal to the magnitude of your benefits, rather than seem to have forgotten your kindness. I make no return, most distinguished sir. I would be mad to think that I could make a sufficient return [τὸ ἰκανὸν ποιεῖν] for such great services. I only aim to make known that the sense of how much I owe you is deeply fixed in my mind. Nor can any praise from me add anything to you, since you have all of it from yourself, and the sum of it from your generosity. Unless the Hebrew proverb is false, "He who is free from avarice will attain to greatness" [מי שנקה מן הכולת יגיע אל הגדולה]. Look rather to the spirit of the writer, in which there is far more gratitude than this little book can reveal. Do you want to hear again from the Hebrews what true liberality is? Nedavah ha-rashah tovah im kabbalat ha-teshlumin [הנירות ההרשה טובה עם קבלת התשלומין]: liberality is a good sense together with the acceptance of hidden things. So add this to your most generous benefits: receive, not so much this public little work, but the hidden feeling of your friend, whom you have embraced with such great favour, and whose good wishes you have... Indeed I dare to promise myself from your kindness, most distinguished sir, that what I offer, however small it may be, will be welcome. This is because what I offer is sacred, and you are its greatest lover of God [θεοφιλής], and also because you have deigned to embrace what I have written before on the Gospels with such kindness that, after certain things which I pass over (because it is not my merits but your love that has drawn them out), you wished me to be reminded that, if I listen to you (these are your own words, which I write), I shall not rest until I have explained, with equal diligence and a similar kind of commentary, what remains of the New Testament. I would certainly wrong that friendship if I were to suspect anything sinister or hostile in a mind so kind. "The character of a man is the reading (or writing) of his heart," say the Hebrew sages, that is, the manners of each man express what his heart contains; they are like a kind of writing in which the emotions of the mind can, as it were, be read. Therefore, all who know you will rightly be indignant with me if, since your manners bear witness to nothing but the pursuit of learning, speak of nothing but humanity, and breathe nothing but humility and goodwill, I suppose that my labours, such as they are, will find a hostile mind and an unfriendly spirit. I will say nothing about the kind of commentary. It is what you asked for, namely similar to the former, except that here our examination has more often than in the Gospels had to deal with the famous Beza, on account of the unsuitable Arabic version by Junius, which he followed. I would not wish, most distinguished sir, to be taken by you, or by any of the learned and pious, for a Zoilus, seeking praise from the defamation of so great a man. I know and praise the wise and fine Arabic saying, al-hamd maghnam wa-al-dhamm maghram, "praise enriches, but blame fines." I would surely deserve to be fined all praise and honour in future if I sought my own advantage from the misfortune of so great a man. I aim only that his most learned commentary, purged of certain slips (of which the translators he followed are for the most part the authors), should lead candidates for the ministry more surely and safely. My purpose and plan was to examine the words of Scripture and its phrasing, to compare the opinions of various interpreters, and to note what seemed most worth following. In this I could hardly act as a critic without, disregarding the authority of great men, noting now this one, now that one, and, as it seemed, correcting them. I did this not to detract from anyone, but to illuminate the truth with as much modesty and equanimity as I could. Yet, if I see that this very thing is disapproved by you, most excellent sir, or by other upright and pious men, I promise that I shall in future abstain from that kind of writing and confess the fault of what I have done. Nor do I shun the idea that all censors who wish to examine and correct my work with similar moderation and equal candour, I will bear with the fairest mind. I judge that my errors will be fortunate if they give anyone an occasion to investigate and search out the truth more deeply. It is not inappropriate what we read in the Quran, sura 7: al-wazn yawmaʾidhin al-haqq, fa-man thaqulat mawazinuhu fa-ulaʾika humu al-muflihun, "the weighing on that day is the truth; those whose scales are heavy, they are the blessed." I seek the weight of truth. If another's scale holds more of it than mine, I gladly grant him the palm of both happiness and praise. But enough has already been excused before you, a most fair and candid man. It remains for me to commend myself to your love and my labours to your favour. And I humbly beseech God, most good and most great, to keep you safe and unharmed for a long time for the churches and the republic of letters. This I wish, I who am

units.la: O'N μὲν πεῶτν λόγον ἐποιησάμην. Recte Beza, Primum quidem librum confeci. Syrus, Arabs & Æthiopicus similiter λόγον verterunt librum. Et Jer. 29. 29. הַסֵּפֶר אֶת־הִקְרָא, הַזֶּה, LXX, ἀνέγνω οὗτος λόγος τούτος. Sic apud Lucianum: ἀληθὴς ἱστορίας λόγος πρῶτος, vera historia liber primus.
units.tr: "The former account I made" [πρῶτον μὲν λόγον ἐποιησάμην]. Beza rightly renders this I have composed the first book. The Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic translators likewise render logos as book. Compare Jer. 29:29, where the Hebrew reads "read this book" and the Septuagint reads [ἀνέγνω οὗτος λόγος τούτος] "this word was read." So also Lucian: [ἀληθὴς ἱστορίας λόγος πρῶτος], true history, first book.

units.la: V E R S. 2. Ἐπ̔ειλάμβανο τῆς Ἀποστόλοις διὰ πνεύματος ἁγίου, ὡς ἐξελέξατο. Vult hic Cl. Beza, per trajectionem διὰ πνεύματος ἁγίου referri ad ἐξελέξατο. Ideoque vertit, quum mandata dedisset Apostolis, quos per Spir. S. elegerat. Fateor Syrum & Arabem trajectione usos esse, ut & Æthiopicum, sed eo tamen verborum situ, ut ob absentiam distinctionum, quo quidque retulerint, incertum sit. Si enim ipsorum verba sic distinguas, Postquam præcepisset Apostolis, quos elegerat, per Spir. Sanctum, vides, per Spiritum referri ad præcepisset. contra ad elegerat, si comma post istud verbum tollas. Malim absque trajectione retinere verborum situm, quem Græca exemplaria continent, quemque Vulgatus, Theophylactus, aliique sunt secuti. ut Christus dicatur præcepisse Apostolis per Spir. Sanctum. Neque tamen hic respici puto, aut primam illam Spiritus missionem in Apostolos, de qua Joan. 20. 22. respectu cujus, ἀλλ' πνεῦμα ἅγιον ab Erasmo vertitur, impertitus ad hoc ipsum Spiritum Sanctum. neque alteram illam die Pentecostis, respectu cujus vertieretur, impertiturus Spiritum Sanctum. Sed unctionem Spiritus, qua ipse Christus à patre unctus fuit, per quam factus est Christus, & authoritatem nactus vocandi Apostolos, & mandata eis dandi, quibus Ecclesia colligeretur & regeretur. Ait Christum in cælum ascendisse, postquam per Spiritum Sanctum, quo à Patre unctus, & in Christum principemque Ecclesiæ constitutus fuerat, mandata Apostolis dederat. ut hoc, non à Christo quatenus simpliciter Deo, sed quatenus per Spir. S. ad munus mediatorium ordinato, profectum esse sciamus.
units.tr: VERSE 2. [ἐντειλάμενος τοῖς ἀποστόλοις διὰ πνεύματος ἁγίου οὓς ἐξελέξατο]. Cl. Beza wishes to refer "through the Holy Spirit" to "chose," by a transposition, and so translates: when he had given commands to the apostles, whom he had chosen through the Holy Spirit. I grant that the Syriac and Arabic translators, and the Ethiopic too, used a transposition; but their word order is such that, with no punctuation to mark the connection, it is uncertain which verb they meant the phrase to modify. If you punctuate their words thus, after he had commanded the apostles, whom he had chosen, through the Holy Spirit, you see that through the Spirit is attached to commanded; but if you remove the comma after that word, it attaches to chosen. I would rather keep the order found in the Greek manuscripts, without transposition, which the Vulgate, Theophylact and others have followed, so that Christ is said to have commanded the apostles through the Holy Spirit. I do not think, however, that the reference is to the first sending of the Spirit upon the apostles, concerning which John 20:22 speaks, where Erasmus translates [ἀλλὰ πνεῦμα ἅγιον] as having breathed on them the Holy Spirit; nor to that other sending on the day of Pentecost, for which the sense would be about to bestow the Holy Spirit. Rather it means the anointing of the Spirit, by which Christ himself was anointed by the Father, through which he was made Christ, and obtained authority to call the apostles and to give them commands by which the Church would be gathered and governed. The author says that Christ ascended into heaven after he had given commands to the apostles through the Holy Spirit, by whom he had been anointed by the Father and appointed as Christ and head of the Church. So we know that this came not from Christ simply as God, but from Christ as ordained through the Holy Spirit to his mediatorial office.

units.la: VERS. 4.
units.tr: VERSE 4.

units.la: Καὶ συναλιζόμενος μετ' αὐτῶν. Ait Cl. Beza, sic illud μετ' αὐτῶν restituisse, quia in veteribus interpretationibus Syra, Arabica & Latina exprimitur, & in illo suo vetustissimo codice. Nos id unius tantum codicis fide addendum non putamus de Latina interpretatione, προσέγραμμα est, ea enim id non exprimit. Syra, Arabica, addo Æthiopicam, exprimunt quidem, non tamen quod μετ' αὐτῶν legerint, sed quia compositis verbis carentes, συναλιζόμενος non aliter vertere potuerunt, quam per ἀλιζόμενος συν αὐτῆς. De significatione vocis vide Camerarii & Bezæ notas. quibus tantum addimus, Æthiopicum etiam Interpretem, cum Syro, Arabe & Vulgato, accepisse convescendi significatione. vertit enim, & prandens cum ipsis. Exi-stimarunt, sicut ἀλιζόμενος usitatum est pro saliri, ita συναλιζόμενος posse accipi pro eodem sale vesci. unde & in Glossario, συναλ&, confalinens. Verum tamen est quod dicit Cl. Beza, apud idoneos scriptores non usurpari nisi pro congregari. Hezychius συν-αλιζόμφ⊙, συναλισθεὶς, συναχθὲὶς, συναθροισθεὶς collectus, coactus, congregatus.
units.tr: [καὶ συναλιζόμενος μετ' αὐτῶν]. Cl. Beza says he restored the words with them [μετ' αὐτῶν] because they are expressed in the old Syriac, Arabic and Latin translations, and in his very ancient codex. We do not think that this should be added on the authority of one manuscript alone, as far as the Latin translation is concerned, which has it only as a marginal addition [προσέγραμμα]; for that translation does not express it. The Syriac and Arabic (I add the Ethiopic) do express it, but not because they read [μετ' αὐτῶν]; rather, lacking a compound verb, they could not render [συναλιζόμενος] in any other way than by [ἀλιζόμενος σὺν αὐτῆς]. On the meaning of the word see the notes of Camerarius and Beza, to which I add only that the Ethiopic translator, like the Syriac, Arabic and Vulgate, took it in the sense of eating together; for he translates and eating with them. They thought that, just as [ἀλιζόμενος] is used for being salted, so [συναλιζόμενος] could be taken to mean eating of the same salt; hence also the glossary entry [συναλ], eating together. It is true, however, what Cl. Beza says, that among reliable writers the word is used only in the sense of being gathered together. Hesychius glosses [συναλισθεὶς]: [συναχθεὶς], [συναθροισθεὶς], collected, gathered, assembled.

units.la: VERS. 4. Ἡν ἡκούσατέ μου. Syrus & Arabs,quam audistis ex me. Vulgatus,per os meum. ἐκ τῆς στόματός μου. ut habebat vetustissimus Bezæ codex. Et sic quoque Æthiopicus.
units.tr: VERSE 4. [ἣν ἠκούσατέ μου], "which you heard from me." The Syriac and Arabic: which you heard from me. The Vulgate: through my mouth [ἐκ τοῦ στόματός μου], as the very old codex of Beza had it. The Ethiopic also has it this way.

units.la: VERS. 5. Οὐ μετὰ πολλὰς ταύτας ἡμέρας. Syrus & Arabs omiserunt ταύτας, quamvis nequaquam otiari videatur, sed quasi digito demonstrare dies istos pauculos, inter id tempus & imminentem Pentecosten intercessuros.
units.tr: VERSE 5. [οὐ μετὰ πολλὰς ταύτας ἡμέρας], "not many these days from now." The Syriac and Arabic omit these [ταύτας], though it does not seem to be idle there, but as if pointing with the finger at the few days that would intervene between that time and the coming Pentecost.

units.la: VERS. 8. Ἀλλὰ λήψεσθε δύναμιν ἐπελθόντος τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος ἐφ' ὑμᾶς. Vulgatus,sed accipietis virtutem supervenientis Spiritus S. in vos. Beza, sed recipietis virtutem Spiritus Sancti, postquam supervenerit in vos. Conjunxerunt δύναμιν Πνεύματος in regimine Genitivi. At Syrus, Arabs, & Æthiopicus sic distinxerunt, ἀλλὰ λήψεσθε δύναμιν, ἐπελθόντος τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος ἐφ' ὑμᾶς. & acceptis Genitivis istis absolute, verterunt,sed quum venerit Spiritus S. super vos,accipietis virtutem. Sic & Erasmus. Sequitur, & eritis mihi testes in Ierusalem, & in tota Iudea & Samaria. Syrus, [Syriac] . Trem. & Boder. & inter Samaritanos. verte, & Samaria. ad verbum, & domo Samaritanorum. domus locum & regionem significat. vide quæ observamus infra, cap. 2. 9.
units.tr: VERSE 8. [ἀλλὰ λήψεσθε δύναμιν ἐπελθόντος τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος ἐφ' ὑμᾶς]. The Vulgate: but you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. Beza: but you will receive the power of the Holy Spirit, after he has come upon you. They have joined power of the Spirit in a genitive construction. But the Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic punctuated it thus: [ἀλλὰ λήψεσθε δύναμιν, ἐπελθόντος τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος ἐφ' ὑμᾶς], and, taking those genitives absolutely, rendered it but when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, you will receive power. Erasmus does the same. There follows: and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria. The Syriac has [Syriac word] (in Tremellius and Boderianus) and among the Samaritans; render it and Samaria, literally and the house of the Samaritans. The word "house" signifies place and region. See what we note below, chapter 2, verse 9.

units.la: VERS. 9. Καὶ νεφέλη ὑπέλαβεν αὐτὸν ἀπὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν. Hebraice, [Hebrew], & nubes accepit (id est,abstulit) eum ab oculis eorum. idem est quod ἀνέλαβεν, ut infra v. 11. ὁ ἀναλημφθεὶς ἀφ' ὑμῶν, [Hebrew], qui ablatus est à vobis. sicut 2 Reg. 2. 9. πρὶν ἢ ἀναλημφθῶ με ἀπό σου, [Hebrew], antequam capiar, id est, auferar à te. Porro Syrus & Arabs v. 11. legerunt quoque ἵνας ἐλεύσεται, non ἐτ⊙.
units.tr: VERSE 9. [καὶ νεφέλη ὑπέλαβεν αὐτὸν ἀπὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν]. In Hebrew, the verb is and a cloud took (that is, carried off) him from their eyes, the same verb as [ἀνέλαβεν]. Compare verse 11: [ὁ ἀναλημφθεὶς ἀφ' ὑμῶν], who was taken up from you, in Hebrew who was taken from you; likewise 2 Kings 2:9: [πρὶν ἢ ἀναλημφθῶ με ἀπό σου], in Hebrew before I am taken, that is, carried off from you. Moreover, the Syriac and Arabic in verse 11 also read [ἵνα ἐλεύσεται] and not [ἐτ⊙].

units.la: VERS. 12. Ἀπὸ ὄρους τοῦ καλουμένου Ἐλαιῶν, ὃ ἐστιν ἐγγὺς ἸερουΪερυσαλὴμ, σταδίατ ἔχον ὁδόν. Facile hoc cum Josepho Antiq. l. 20. cap. 16. montem hunc quinque stadiis ab urbe distitum esse afferente, conciliant viri eruditi. Iter enim sabbathi bis mille cubitorum fuisse, quam longitudinem Hebraei מיל milliare vocant, ex eorum libris liquido constat. Stadium autem Graecis fuisse centum passuum, passum sex pedum, sive quatuor cubitorum, ex his Herodoti verbis lib. 2. liquet: αἱ δὲ ἰκανὴν ἐγγυαὶ ἀκαμαὶ αὐτοι σταδίου ἐξάπαξ ἐθέρον. ἐξαπόδε μὲν τὸ ἐγγυὴς μετρεομένης ἡ πηχαπηχέων. τὸ δὲ ὡσαὶ πηχαπηχαίων ἐντων, ἡ δὲ πήχεων ἐξάπαξ. Vides sesquipedem constituisse cubitum: sexcentos ergo pedes, qui faciebant stadium, quadringentos cubitos: quinque ergo stadia, bis mille cubitos. Sed quomodo id cum Syro quadret, qui pro itinere sabbathi habet quasi septem stadia, non adeo facile expediverunt eruditi. nos simpliciter statuimus, Syrum non Graecorum, sed Hebraeorum stadia in animo habuisse, quae ipsis מיל vel מיל dicuntur, quorum septem cum dimidio faciebant מיל sive iter sabbathi. vide Baal Aruch in voce מיל, ubi ex Talmude citatur אחר מו' ומחצה בתיל והו מיל, unum ex septem & dimidio in mil (id est septima milliaris pars cum dimidia) est מיל, stadium. vide & Mappam Judaicam Amstelodami ab Hebraeis editam, ubi septem מיל & dimidium faciunt מיל, ut quatuor מיל unum פרסה. Æthiopicus pro σταδίατ ἔχον ὁδόν habet, spatio cursus viri, quod est iter antiquum sabbathi. Porro, quum hic dicantur regressi Hierosolymam a monte Oliveti, Lucae autem c. 24. 50. dicantur educti fuisse a Christo ἕως εἰς Βηθανίαν, usque ad Bethaniam, conciliari id haud posse creditum est, nisi mons Oliveti & Bethania eodem in loco constituerentur. unde nova, eaque magna, &c, ut Cl. Beza loquitur, inexplicabilis pene difficultas oritur, quod nempe mons Oliveti dicatur hic itinere tantum sabbathi, id est, quinquinque stadiis, Johannis autem cap. 11. 18. Bethania quindecim stadiis distare Hierosolymis. quem scrupulum tolli aliter non posse vir summus existimavit, nisi Bethaniam totum aliquem montis Oliveti tractum esse, non autem certum aliquem vicum, assereret. quod tantum abest, ut ex Joan. 11. 1. probari possit, ut contra vicum Mariæ & Marthæ Bethaniam isthic dici res & constructio evincant. adde, quod hoc modo montis Oliveti longitudo nimium extendatur. Quum enim Bethania quindecim stadiis absuerit ab Hierûsalem, mons autem Oliveti quinque, habes jam ab initio montis ad initium tractus Bethaniæ decem stadia. necesse autem & tractui isti suam tribuere longitudinem, ad minimum stadii unius atque alterius. si itaque totus ille tractus fuit in monte Oliveti, habuerit mons longitudinem ad minimum duodecim stadiorum Græcorum. at in Mappa Judaica duorum circiter stadiorum, qua Bethaniam spectat, mensura ei tribuitur. κωμ ποα, Bethania autem aliquammultis à monte stadiis removetur. Adrichomius similiter ait, Bethaniam esse nobile castellum Mariæ & Marthæ sororum Lazari, & ædibus frequens, quod ultra montem Oliveti situm, 15 à Jerusalem stadiis distat, nec posse inde, ob interpositum Oliveti montem, Jerusalem videri. nec aliter in descriptione hujus loci Henricus Buntingus. Considerent itaque eruditi, an non facile tota difficultas expediatur, si ἀναστρέψαι ἀπὸ ὄρους Ἐλαιῶν vertamus, reversi sunt per montem Oliveti. ut ἀπὸ ὄρους interjectum montem inter agrum Bethaniæ, quo Christus suos eduxerat, & urbem significet, quem transire necesse habuerint, ut à Bethania Hierosolymam venirent. sicut Joan. 11. 18. dicitur Bethania fuisse ἐγγὺς τῆς Ἱερουσαλὴμ, ὡς ἀπὸ σταδίων δεκαπέντε: vicina Hierosolymæ fere per stadia quindecim. ἀπὸ significat interjecta quindecim stadia, quæ transire necesse est à Bethania Hierosolymam. Sic Apoc. 13. 20. exivit sanguis è torcutorculari ad frena equorum, ἐπὶ τὰ σεδίων χιλίων ἐξακοσίων, Vulgatus & Beza, per stadia mille sexcenta. recte. ἐπὶ enim interjacens spatium significat. Unde & Act. 13. 14. ἐπὶ δὲ τὴν Διαλθύλης ἐπὶ τ̄ Πέργης, Vulgatus vertit, illi vero pertransjeuntes Pergem. Ex quo sequeretur, Christum non ex monte Oliveti, quod tamen Hieronymus passim asserit, & hactenus fuit creditum ex conjectura loci Act. 1. 12. ubi id tamen Lucas non dicit, sed ex agro Bethaniae, quod in Euangelio satis aperte innuit, in caelos ascendisse. Apostolos autem ex agro Bethaniae, petiisse montem Oliveti, atque ex eo compendiosissima via reversos esse Hierosolymam. Quod si vero male in Mappa & ab Adrichomio situs loci designatus, omninoque monti adhaesisse dicendus est, quod Hieronymus sensisse videtur, quum in locis Hebraicis testatur, Bethaniam esse villam in latere montis Oliveti, conciliatio sic institui poterit, Reversos eos esse a monte, id est, a latere montis Oliveti extremo, ubi erat vicus Bethania, distante Hierosolymis quindecim stadiis, quum initium montis distaret secundum Josephum quinque stadiis. Et ne nimium longitudo sive latitudo montis protendatur, monemus intelligi Johannem posse de stadiis Judaicis, quum Josephus intelligendus sit de Graecis: atque ita Bethania in extremo montis latere sita non longius ab ejus initio distabit, quam hoc Hierosolymis. quum enim quinque stadia Graeca faciant, ut supra diximus, septem Judaica cum dimidio, duplicato isto numero exsurgunt quindecim stadia Judaica, sive decem Graeca, quae exacte faciunt ביתא דן duo milliaria Judaica, sive iteratum iter sabbathi. quo sensu accipi poterit illud Hieronymi de locis Hebraicis, Bethaniam esse villam in secundo ab Ælia milliario.
units.tr: VERSE 12. [ἀπὸ ὄρους τοῦ καλουμένου Ἐλαιῶν, ὃ ἐστιν ἐγγὺς Ἱερουσαλὴμ, σαββάτου ἔχον ὁδόν]. Learned men easily reconcile this with Josephus (Antiquities, book 20, chapter 16), who says that this mount was five stadia from the city. For it is clear from their books that the Sabbath journey was two thousand cubits, which length the Hebrews call mil, a mile. A Greek stadium was one hundred paces, a pace six feet or four cubits; this is clear from the words of Herodotus, book 2. You see that the cubit was one and a half feet; so six hundred feet, which made a stadium, were four hundred cubits. Five stadia therefore make two thousand cubits. But how this agrees with the Syriac, which for the Sabbath journey has about seven stadia, learned men have not found easy to explain. We simply hold that the Syriac had in mind not Greek but Hebrew stadia, which are called mil, of which seven and a half made the mil, that is, the Sabbath journey. See Baal Aruch under the word mil, where from the Talmud is cited: one of seven and a half in a mil (that is, the seventh part of a mile together with a half) is a stadium. See also the Jewish map published at Amsterdam by the Hebrews, where seven mil and a half make one mil, as four mil make one parasah. The Ethiopic, for [σαββάτου ἔχον ὁδόν], has the distance of a man's course, which is the ancient Sabbath journey. Further, since here it is said that they returned to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, while Luke 24:50 says that Christ led them out as far as Bethany [ἕως εἰς Βηθανίαν], it has been thought that this cannot be reconciled unless the Mount of Olives and Bethany were placed in the same spot. Hence arises a new and great difficulty, almost inexplicable, as Cl. Beza puts it: namely, that the Mount of Olives is said here to lie only a Sabbath journey, that is, five stadia, away, while John 11:18 says Bethany was fifteen stadia from Jerusalem. This snag, the great man thought, could not be removed unless he asserted that Bethany was an entire stretch of the Mount of Olives, not a particular village. Yet this is so far from being proved by John 11:1 that the context and construction rather prove that Bethany there means the village of Mary and Martha. Add that in this way the length of the Mount of Olives is extended too much. For since Bethany was fifteen stadia from Jerusalem and the mount five, you already have ten stadia from the beginning of the mount to the beginning of the stretch of Bethany. That stretch must also have its own length, at least one or two stadia. If, then, that whole stretch was on the Mount of Olives, the mount would have a length of at least twelve Greek stadia. But the Jewish map gives it a measure of about two stadia where it faces Bethany, and the village [κώμη] Bethany is removed from the mount by some considerable number of stadia. Adrichomius likewise says that Bethany is a noble village of Mary and Martha, the sisters of Lazarus, full of houses, which, situated beyond the Mount of Olives, is fifteen stadia from Jerusalem, and that Jerusalem cannot be seen from it because of the intervening Mount of Olives. Henry Bunting also describes the place in the same way. Let learned men consider, then, whether the whole difficulty is not easily resolved if we translate [ἀναστρέψαι ἀπὸ ὄρους Ἐλαιῶν] as they returned by way of the Mount of Olives. The phrase from the mount would then signify the mount lying between the field of Bethany, to which Christ had led his disciples, and the city, which they had to cross in order to come to Jerusalem from Bethany. Just so John 11:18 says that Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia off [ἐγγὺς τῆς Ἱερουσαλὴμ, ὡς ἀπὸ σταδίων δεκαπέντε]: close to Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia. The [ἀπὸ] signifies the fifteen intervening stadia that must be crossed from Bethany to Jerusalem. So also Revelation 14:20: blood came out of the winepress up to the horses' bridles, [ἐπὶ] for a thousand six hundred stadia; the Vulgate and Beza: for one thousand six hundred stadia, rightly. For [ἐπὶ] signifies an intervening space. Hence also Acts 13:14: [ἐπὶ δὲ τὴν Πέργης], the Vulgate renders but they passed through Perga. From this it would follow that Christ ascended not from the Mount of Olives, though Jerome asserts this everywhere and it has hitherto been believed from a conjecture based on Acts 1:12; but Luke does not say that there, rather he clearly hints in the Gospel that he ascended into heaven from the field of Bethany. The apostles then sought the Mount of Olives from the field of Bethany, and returned from it to Jerusalem by the shortest route. But if the place is wrongly marked on the map and by Adrichomius, and it must be said that it adhered wholly to the mount, as Jerome seems to have thought, when in the Hebrew places he testifies that Bethany is a village on the side of the Mount of Olives, the reconciliation can be set up thus: they returned from the mount, that is, from the far side of the Mount of Olives, where the village of Bethany was, fifteen stadia from Jerusalem, whereas the foot of the mount was, according to Josephus, five stadia away. And lest the length or breadth of the mount be stretched too far, we advise that John may be understood to speak of Jewish stadia, while Josephus is to be understood of Greek ones; and so Bethany, situated on the far side of the mount, will not be farther from its foot than this is from Jerusalem. For since five Greek stadia make, as we said above, seven and a half Jewish, the double of that number gives fifteen Jewish stadia, or ten Greek, which exactly make two Jewish miles, that is, a repeated Sabbath journey. In this sense Jerome's statement about the Hebrew places can be understood, that Bethany is a village at the second mile from Aelia.

units.la: V E R S. 13. Καὶ ὅτε εἰσῆλθον, & cum intrassent, scilicet in urbem, ανέβησαν εἰς τὸ ὑπερῷον, ascenderunt in coenaculum. sic Syrus quoque & Arabs legerunt. longe sane melius quam Vulgatus, & quum introissent in cœnaculum, ascenderunt. neque enim quum intrassent in cœnaculum, ascenderunt altius; sed ascenderunt ut essent in cœnaculo, quippe quod ὑπερῷον superior domus pars erat. Cujusmodi autem domus hæc fuerit, controvertitur. Nicephorus ex Euodio quodam prodidit, fuisse domum Johannis Euangelistæ Zebedæi filii. Cl. Beza divinaret potius, fuisse domum Mariæ matris Johannis cognomento Marci. Ego neutram fuisse autumo, sed ipsum templum, testante id eodem hoc autore Luca, Euang. c. 24. 52. 53. διέπτυσαν εἰς Ἱερουσαλὴμ, μετὰ χαρᾶς μεγάλης. Καὶ ἦσαν διὰπαντὸς ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ αἰνοῦντες καὶ εὐλογοῦντες τὸν Θεόν. Observa, dici hic ἦσαν διαπαντὸς, ibi vero ἦσαν καταμένοντες, quæ ut eadem sunt, ita nunquam conciliabis, si alibi quam in templo manserunt. Multumque id illustrat illustrem illum Spiritus S. de quo sequenti capite, illapsum in Apostolos, si eum in templo contigisse statuamus, ubi olim שכינה majestas Dei habitaverat, sed jam à captivitate Babylonica una cum amissa arca exulaverat: ut typicam illam & umbratilem Dei præsentiam ex animo deponentes, ad veram illam aspirarent, quam Deus jam, ibidem loci ubi adumbrata fuerat, præstitit. & sicut 1 Reg. 8. 10. nubes dicitur implevisse domum à Salomone structam ac dicatam, ita Act. 2. 2. ventus Spiritus Sancti implevit eandem domum, non ut deinceps domui isti affixi hærerent, sed ut vento isto pulsi gratiæ Euangelicæ aura totum mundum afflarent. atque ita verè lex exivit ex Sion. Quapropter Erasmus paraphrasi ad Act. 2. cœnaculum hoc in monte Sion constituit: conferens enim hunc locum, cum eo in quo olim Lex data, Vtrobique, ait, loci sublimitas. sed illic nihil aliud quam mons est, quem populus etiam attingere prohibetur, nimirum crassus & terrenus, nec capax rerum spiritualium. Hic in ipso monte domus est, ut agnoscas Ecclesiæ concordiam. Illic mons Sinai, qui conveniebat ferendæ legi, quæ multitudine præceptorum ceptorum cohercet rebellem populum. nam a praecepto Sina dicitur. Hic mons Sion, qui Hebraeis sonat speculam unde despiciuntur omnia terrena. Nec obstat, quod dicatur ventus implevisse οἶκον, domum, non ἱερὸν, templum. notum enim, templum Solomonis vocari בית ראשין domum primam, Zorobabelis autem בית שני, domum secundam. Pertinet huc praeclarus locus Haggaei c. 2. com. 7. 9. וּמִלֵּאתִי אֶת הַבַּיִת הַזֶּה כָּבוֹד וְהָיָה כָּבוֹד, & implebo domum hanc gloria: major erit gloria domus hujus posterioris quam prioris. Id vere impletum Pentecoste, quum רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ, Spiritus S. quo ornatum fuerat primum templum, orbatum autem, fatentibus Hebraeis, una cum arca, cum Urim & Thummim, cum igne perpetuo & שְׁכִינָה, praesentia majestatis, templum secundum, implevit templum illud coelesti vento, Apostolosque donis quae omnes nationes in admirationem rapuere. Sicut unus ille Spiritus deinceps & arcae,& Urim & Thummim, & ignis perpetui vicem praestiterit,umbrasque in veritatem convertens, majestatem Dei ubique terrarum Ecclesiae praesentem dederit. Nec obstat quod dicantur ascendisse εἰς ὑπερῷον לעליה, Syrus [Syriac], in coenaculum. Habuisse enim templum in ambitu plurima עליות, ὑπερῷα, liquet ex 1 Paral. 28. 11. & 2 Paral. 3. 9. item לשכת, cubicula, conclavia. quale erat לשכת גמריהו, conclave Gamaria, in quo Baruch legit librum Jeremiae in domo Domini, Jer. 36. 10. LXX. Καὶ ἀνεγίνωσκεν Βαρὺχ ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ λόγως Ἱερεμίᾳ ἐν οἴκῳ Κυρίου ἐν οἴκῳ Γαμαριά. Vbi simul obser-vandum, non modo templum vocari οἶκον, sed & נשכה, conclave verti οἶκον. nec ibi tantum, sed & infra verf. 12. 2c. 21. ut & cap. 35. v. 4. plane sicut ὑπερῷον, ubi Apostoli erant Act. 1. 13. vocatur οἰκῶ· Act. 2. 2. serviebant autem cubicula illa & coenacula, non tantum templi custodibus ac ministris, Sacerdotibus & Levitis, rebusque sacris asservandis, sed & religiosorum hominum conventui, ubi sacris vacabant. Hinc in conclavi Gamariæ legit Baruch librum Jeremiæ. In ejusmodi conclavibus convenisse, & à filiis Eli stupratas fuisse pias mulieres consentaneum est, quæ dicuntur הנשואות פתח [Hebrew] אהל מועד, castra habuisse ad ostium tentorii conventus. Talem locum oportuit & Annam prophetissam habuisse, ἥ οὐκ ἀφίστατο ἀπὸ τοῦ ἱεροῦ, νηστείαις & δεήσεσι λατρεύουσα νυκτὸς καὶ ἡμέρας, Luc. 2. 36. Nec dubium esse potest, quin talem sibi locum delegerint Apostoli, quum dicuntur Luc. 24.53. fuisse semper in templo, laudantes & benedicentes Deo. describit locum Lucas, Act. 1. 13. 14. nempe fuisse ἦσαν προσκαρτεροῦντες ὁμοθυμαδὸν τῇ προσευχῇ καὶ τῇ δεήσει. Unde simul constat, quomodo accipiendum illud, ἦσαν καταμένοντες. Vulgatus, ubi manebant. Erasmus, mansitabant. Beza, commorabantur. nos ad verbum, erant permanentes. ut idem fit quod in Euangelio, ἦσαν διατρίβοντες, erant indesinenter, nempe μὴ χωριζόμενοι ἀπὸ τοῦ ἱεροῦ, non discedentes à templo. Syrus simpliciter, sed non satis accuratè [Syriac], in quo erant, ὅπου ἦσαν, omisso καταμένοντες. quamvis fatear [Syriac] esse, interdum pro degere, & habitare accipi, ut Joan. 1. 39. 40. quamobrem & hic Tremel. in quo manserunt. Boder. in quo degebant. Porro personæ ibi dicuntur convenisse, ὁ τε Πέτρος, ὁ Ἰάκωβος, ὁ Ἰωάννης, καὶ Ἀνδρέας. Hunc ordinem Arabs quoque servat. at Syrus, Vulgatus, & Æthiopicus, Johannem ponunt ante Jacobum. Deinde Βαρθολομαῖος ὁ Ματθαῖος. sic & Vulgatus. At Syrus & Arabs Matthæum habent ante Bartolomæum, ut & Æthiopicus. Καὶ Ἰούδας Ἰακώβου, Arabs, & Judas frater Iacobi. ut & Beza. quod ex epistola Judæ v. 1. confirmatur. Syrus tamen & Æthiopicus, filius Iacobi.
units.tr: VERSE 13. Καὶ ὅτε εἰσῆλθον, and when they had entered, namely into the city, ανέβησαν εἰς τὸ ὑπερῷον, they went up into the upper room. The Syriac and the Arabic read it in the same way. This is certainly far better than the Vulgate, which has when they had entered the upper room, they went up. For it does not mean that after entering the upper room they went higher; it means that they went up so as to be in the upper room, since ὑπερῷον was the upper part of a house. What kind of house this was is disputed. Nicephorus reports from a certain Euodius that it was the house of John the Evangelist, the son of Zebedee. Beza would rather guess that it was the house of Mary, the mother of John surnamed Mark. I think it was neither, but the temple itself. Luke, the same author, testifies to this in Luke 24:52–53: διέπτυσαν εἰς Ἱερουσαλὴμ, μετὰ χαρᾶς μεγάλης [they returned to Jerusalem with great joy]. Καὶ ἦσαν διὰπαντὸς ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ αἰνοῦντες καὶ εὐλογοῦντες τὸν Θεόν [And they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God]. Notice that here it says ἦσαν διαπαντὸς [they were continually], and there ἦσαν καταμένοντες [they were remaining]. These are the same, and you will never reconcile them unless they stayed somewhere other than the temple. This also throws much light on the famous descent of the Holy Spirit on the Apostles, described in the next chapter. If we hold that it happened in the temple, where the majesty of God, שכינה, had once dwelt, but had since departed into exile with the lost ark at the Babylonian captivity, then the Apostles were laying aside the typical and shadowy presence of God and aspiring to the true presence, which God had now granted in the very place where it had been foreshadowed. And just as 1 Kings 8:10 says that a cloud filled the house built and dedicated by Solomon, so Acts 2:2 says that the wind of the Holy Spirit filled the same house. It did not do so that they might cling to that house, but that, driven by that wind, they might breathe the breath of the gospel grace over the whole world. And so the law truly went out from Zion. For this reason Erasmus, in his paraphrase on Acts 2, places this upper room on Mount Zion. Comparing this place with the one where the law was once given, he says: In both places there is loftiness. But there is only a mountain, which the people are forbidden even to touch, certainly coarse and earthly, and not able to receive spiritual things. Here there is a house on the mountain itself, so that you may recognize the harmony of the Church. There is Mount Sinai, which suited the bearing of the law, which by the multitude of its precepts restrains a rebellious people, for it is named from the precept, Sina. Here is Mount Zion, which in Hebrew means a watchtower from which all earthly things are looked down upon. Nor is it an objection that the wind is said to have filled οἶκον, a house, not ἱερὸν, a temple. It is well known that Solomon's temple was called בית ראשין, the first house, and Zerubbabel's בית שני, the second house. The striking passage of Haggai 2:7, 9 bears on this: וּמִלֵּאתִי אֶת הַבַּיִת הַזֶּה כָּבוֹד וְהָיָה כָּבוֹד, and I will fill this house with glory: the glory of this latter house will be greater than that of the former. This was truly fulfilled at Pentecost, when the רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ, Holy Spirit, with which the first temple had been adorned, but which, as the Hebrews admit, was taken away together with the ark, the Urim and Thummim, the perpetual fire and the שְׁכִינָה, the presence of majesty, filled the second temple with a heavenly wind and filled the Apostles with gifts that carried all nations into wonder. Thus that one Spirit then took the place of the ark, the Urim and Thummim, and the perpetual fire, turning the shadows into reality, and gave the majesty of God, present everywhere on earth, to the Church. Nor is it an objection that they are said to have gone up εἰς ὑπερῷον, לעליה, [the Syriac has] into the upper room. It is clear from 1 Chronicles 28:11 and 2 Chronicles 3:9 that the temple had many upper rooms, עליות, ὑπερῷα, in its precincts; likewise לשכת, chambers, rooms. Such was the לשכת גמריהו, chamber of Gamariah, where Baruch read the book of Jeremiah in the house of the Lord (Jer. 36:10, Septuagint): Καὶ ἀνεγίνωσκεν Βαρὺχ ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ λόγως Ἱερεμίᾳ ἐν οἴκῳ Κυρίου ἐν οἴκῳ Γαμαριά. Here it should also be observed that not only is the temple called οἶκον, but the לשכה, chamber, is also rendered οἶκον. This happens not only here but also below, in verse 12 and in chapter 35, verse 4; just as the ὑπερῷον where the Apostles were (Acts 1:13) is called οἰκῶ (Acts 2:2). These chambers and upper rooms served not only the guardians and ministers of the temple, the priests and Levites, and the safekeeping of sacred things, but also the gathering of religious people, who devoted themselves there to holy duties. Hence Baruch read the book of Jeremiah in the chamber of Gamariah. It is consistent that pious women, who are said to have been violated by the sons of Eli, gathered in such chambers; they are called הנשואות פתח [Hebrew], אהל מועד, those who had camped at the door of the tent of meeting. The prophetess Anna must also have had such a place, ἥ οὐκ ἀφίστατο ἀπὸ τοῦ ἱεροῦ, νηστείαις & δεήσεσι λατρεύουσα νυκτὸς καὶ ἡμέρας [who did not depart from the temple, but served night and day with fastings and prayers] (Luke 2:36). Nor can there be any doubt that the Apostles chose such a place for themselves, since Luke 24:53 says they were always in the temple, praising and blessing God. Luke describes the place in Acts 1:13–14: they were ἦσαν προσκαρτεροῦντες ὁμοθυμαδὸν τῇ προσευχῇ καὶ τῇ δεήσει [they were devoting themselves together with one mind to prayer and supplication]. From this it is also clear how ἦσαν καταμένοντες should be understood. The Vulgate has where they were staying. Erasmus has they were lodging. Beza has they were dwelling. We have, word for word, they were remaining. It is the same as in the Gospel, ἦσαν διατρίβοντες, they were constantly there, that is, not separating themselves from the temple, not departing from the temple. The Syriac has it simply, but not very accurately, as in which they were (ὅπου ἦσαν), leaving out καταμένοντες. Although I grant that the Syriac word sometimes means to spend or to dwell, as in John 1:39–40, for which reason Tremellius also has in which they remained, and Boder in which they were living. Further, the persons are said to have gathered there: ὁ τε Πέτρος, ὁ Ἰάκωβος, ὁ Ἰωάννης, καὶ Ἀνδρέας [Peter, James, John and Andrew]. The Arabic keeps this order too. But the Syriac, the Vulgate and the Ethiopic put John before James. Then comes Βαρθολομαῖος ὁ Ματθαῖος [Bartholomew and Matthew]; so also the Vulgate. But the Syriac and the Arabic have Matthew before Bartholomew, as does the Ethiopic. Καὶ Ἰούδας Ἰακώβου [and Judas of James]: the Arabic has and Judas the brother of James, as does Beza. This is confirmed by the epistle of Jude 1. The Syriac and the Ethiopic, however, have son of James.

units.la: VERS. 14. τῇ προσευχῇ καὶ τῇ δεήσει. Vulgatus, Syrus, Arabs, & Æthiopicus non legerunt καὶ τῇ δεήσει.
units.tr: VERSE 14. τῇ προσευχῇ καὶ τῇ δεήσει [with prayer and supplication]. The Vulgate, the Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic did not read καὶ τῇ δεήσει [and supplication].

units.la: VERS. 15. Hebrew and Greek phrases: ἡ ἐχλ ... erat autem turba nominum, id est personarum vel capitum, sicut Num. 1. Hebrew, LXX, κατ' ἀριθμὸν ὀνομάτων, juxta numerum nominum, id est personarum. Sic saepe ibidem. Sequitur, Hebrew ... Vulgatus recte, simul. At sequenti cap. v. 1. vertit, in eodem loco, ut & Beza hic atque illic. malim prius, quia LXX Interpretes ea phrasi passim explicant Hebraeum, etiam ubi tantum personarum, aut rerum conjunctarum, non ejusdem loci habetur ratio. ut Psal. 19. 10. τὰ κρίματα τοῦ Κυρίου ... judicia Domini justa sunt pariter. Psal. 37. 40. ἀσεβεῖς ... impii perdentur pariter. Psal. 49. 9. ... pariter insanus & demens peribunt. in his si vertas, eodem in loco, nihil dicis.
units.tr: VERSE 15. The Greek phrase ἡ ἐχλ … there was a crowd of names, that is, of persons or heads, as in Numbers 1. The Hebrew (יַחַד?) and the Septuagint κατ' ἀριθμὸν ὀνομάτων, according to the number of names, that is, of persons. This is often so in the same place. What follows is Hebrew … The Vulgate rightly has together [Hebrew יַחַד]. But in the next chapter, verse 1, it translates in the same place, as Beza also does here and there. I would prefer the former, because the Septuagint translators often express the Hebrew by this phrase even where only persons or things joined together are meant, and not the same place. For example, Psalm 19:10: τὰ κρίματα τοῦ Κυρίου … the judgments of the Lord are just together. Psalm 37:40: ἀσεβεῖς … the wicked will perish together. Psalm 49:9: … the fool and the senseless will perish together. If in these passages you translate in the same place, you say nothing.

units.la: VERS. 16. τὸ ἡγούμενον ἰδηγέ. Vulg. qui factus est dux. Beza, dux viae, quia praevixit caeteris. angustè nimis, si solummodo dux itineris intelligitur. rectè autem, si per viam more Hebraeorum metaphoricè intelliguntur etiam consilia & actiones. neque enim in itinere solum praevixit, & qua eundum esset ostendit, sed & signum dedit quo persona capienda cognosci posset, & consilio juvit, quum diceret, prehendite eum & abducite ἀσφαλῶς tuto, ne evadat. Rectè ergo Syrus Hebrew ... qui fuit dux, rector, gubernator, director. haec enim omnia significat Hebrew ..., à Hebrew quod non ducere tantum, sed & regere, moderari ac dirigere significat. exempla passim obvia. ut 1 Tim. 3. 5. & 5. 14. & alibi. Porro agitur hic de Juda, dicto in Euangeliis Iscariot. de quo agnomine egimus, in Comment. ad Matth. 10. 4. Vbi Junius annotat ;ad Syri Hebrew, Secarjut quibusdam appellari marsupium, & Secarjuta, ὁ ἔχων γλωσσόκομον. qua autoritate hujus inventi autor nitatur nescio. Sed in lingua Æthiopica reperio Hebrew pro marsupio. Sic enim τὸ γλωσσόκομον Interpres reddidit Joan. 12.6. & 13.29. hinc non incommodè derivari potest ״ךשכ, ὁ ἔχων γλωσσόκομον. ut hoc agnomine ab ipsis Apostolis distinctus fuerit ab altero Juda Apostolo.
units.tr: VERSE 16. τὸ ἡγούμενον ἰδηγέ [who became the guide]. The Vulgate: who was made leader. Beza: leader of the way, because he went before the others. That is too narrow if it is understood only of the leader of the journey. It is right if, in the Hebrew manner, way is taken metaphorically to include also counsels and actions. For he did not only go ahead and show the way they must go; he also gave a sign by which the man to be seized could be recognised, and helped with advice when he said: seize him and lead him away ἀσφαλῶς [safely], so that he does not escape. So the Syriac rightly has the Hebrew word meaning who was the guide, ruler, steerer, director. For the Hebrew word signifies not only to lead but also to rule, to govern and to direct. Examples are everywhere, such as 1 Timothy 3:5 and 5:14, and elsewhere. Further, the passage is about Judas, called Iscariot in the Gospels, whose surname I have discussed in the commentary on Matthew 10:4. There Junius notes that the Syriac Hebrew word, Secarjut, is by some called a money-bag, and Secarjuta, one who has a money-box [ὁ ἔχων γλωσσόκομον]. I do not know on what authority the author of this discovery relies. But I find in the Ethiopic language a Hebrew word for a money-bag. For the translator rendered τὸ γλωσσόκομον [the money-box] in John 12:6 and 13:29 this way. From this, the Hebrew name ״ךשכ may be fairly derived, meaning one who has a money-box. So by this surname he was distinguished by the Apostles themselves from the other Judas, the Apostle.

units.la: VERS. 17. ὅτι κατηριθμημένος ἦν, Quia annumeratus erat. huic lectioni Syrus & Arabs assentiuntur. mirum ergo Vulgatum habere, qui connumeratus erat, id est, ὃς.
units.tr: VERS. 17. Quia annumeratus erat. Syrus and the Arab agree with this reading. It is strange, then, that the Vulgate has qui connumeratus erat, which is the equivalent of ὃς.

units.la: VERS. 18. Hic emit sibi χωρίον, agrum. Æthiopicus exprimit cujusmodi ager fuerit, reddens ״שדה כרם״, agrum vini, vinetum. cui non repugnat, quod Matth. 27. 5. vocetur ager figuli. potuit enim fuisse vinetum figuli. neque pugnant, quod hîc ipse Judas dicatur eum emisse, ibi autem primarii Sacerdotes. Nam præterquam quod locum habere queat conciliatio, quam Cl. Beza adfert, nihil obstat, cur non & ipse proditor, triginta hosce argenteos, quos biduo fere ante, (ut ex Matth. 26. 2. 14. colligi potest) acceperat, agro emendo impendere voluerit, eaque de re cum figulo aliove hujus fundi domino transegerit. postmodum vero, quùm pœnitudine sceleris dućtus, eos sacerdotibus refunderet, iidem illi arcana quadam & admiranda Dei providentia eundem agrum iisdem argenteis coëmerint. Καὶ πρηνὴς γενόμενος. Quam male Vulgatus & Erasmus verterint, & suspensus, recte autem Beza, & præcipitatus. optimè vero Syrus, Æthiop. & Arabs, & cecidit super faciem suam in terram. nec repugnare illud Matth. 27. v. 5. quia ἀπήγξατο non vertendum, suspendit se, sed suffocatus est: supersedemus plura de eo dicere, quia aliquid ejus tetigimus in Commentario nostro ad quatuor Euangelia p.36. & 131. reliqua relinquimus incomparabili viro Dan. Heinsio, qui ejus sententiæ author est, doćtissimasque suas in universum N. Test. notas jam jam evulgare pollicetur. Quod additur, καὶ ἐξεχύθη πάντα τὰ σπλάγχνα αὐτοῦ, Syrus vertit ܘܐܫܬܦܟܘ ܠܟܠ ܡܥܝܢܘܗܝ quod male transtulit Trem. & effusum est universum corpus ejus. respexit Hebræorum corpus. verte ad verbum, universum interius ejus. est enim intrinsecum, interius, Hebræorum קרב, quod & pro מעים viscera passim ponitur. Æthiopicus dixit, quod & significatione & radice convenit cum Heb. מעים.
units.tr: VERS. 18. He bought for himself a field [χωρίον], that is, a plot of land. The Ethiopic indicates what sort of field it was, rendering it [שדה כרם], a vineyard field, a vineyard. This is not inconsistent with Matt. 27.5, where it is called the potter's field, for it could have been a potter's vineyard. Nor is there a conflict in the fact that here Judas himself is said to have bought it, but there the chief priests. Apart from the fact that the reconciliation offered by the famous Beza can hold, nothing prevents the traitor himself, about two days before (as can be gathered from Matt. 26.2, 14), from wishing to spend the thirty silver pieces he had received on buying a field, and from negotiating this matter with the potter or another owner of the estate. Afterwards, however, led by remorse for his crime, he gave the money back to the priests, and by some hidden and wonderful providence of God those same men bought the same field with the same silver. Καὶ πρηνὴς γενόμενος [and falling headlong]. How badly the Vulgate and Erasmus translated this, and hanged, but Beza rightly, and falling headlong. The Syriac, Ethiopic and Arabic best of all, and fell upon his face on the ground. Nor does Matt. 27.5 contradict this, since ἀπήγξατο should not be rendered he hanged himself, but he was suffocated. We refrain from saying more about this, since we touched on part of it in our Commentary on the four Gospels, pp. 36 and 131. The rest we leave to the incomparable Dan. Heinsius, who is the author of this opinion and promises soon to publish his most learned notes on the whole New Testament. As for the added words, καὶ ἐξεχύθη πάντα τὰ σπλάγχνα αὐτοῦ [and all his bowels gushed out], the Syriac renders them [wa-ishtapkhu l-kull ma'eynohi], which Tremellius translated badly as and the whole body of him was poured out. The Syriac had in mind the Hebrew body; translate word for word, his whole inward parts. For it means inward, interior, which in Hebrew is קרב, and which is also commonly used for מעים bowels. The Ethiopic rendered it with a word that agrees both in meaning and in root with the Hebrew מעים.

units.la: VERS. 19. Ἀκελδαμά, omnino Syriacum est, ܚܩܠ ܕܡܐ. ubi nemo mirari debet, pathach sub p efferri per ɛ. id enim, ut Arabibus, ita & Syris usitatum est, quoties sequitur consona quiescens, id est, quæ per scheva quiescens jungitur præcedenti. præterquam quod notum sit, segol vocari Hebræis pathach parvum, ob affinitatem pronunciationis quam cum pathach habet. quod autem ܝ efferatur per ܕܐ, id est, scheva per ܐ, id quoque usitatissimum. ut ܚܠܝܬܐ, Ταλιθά, puella. ܥܙܝܐ, Ταϐιθὰ δοςκάς, caprea. pergit autem Syrus, atque interpretaturus quid sit ἀκελδαμά, ait valere ܩܕܡ ܐܓܪ, ager sanguinis. ubi solummodo Syriacæ linguæ studiosos monemus, ܐܓܪ, esse formæ constructæ à ܐܓܪ, ager, cujus plurale ܐܓܪܐ, quæ sunt anomala.
units.tr: VERSE 19. Akeldama [Ἀκελδαμά] is wholly Syriac, ḥaqel dema. Nobody should be surprised that the pathach under the p is pronounced as ɛ. This is the usual practice in Syriac, as it is in Arabic, whenever a quiescent consonant follows, that is, one joined to the preceding letter by a quiescent scheva. Moreover, the Hebrews call the segol the small pathach, because of the similarity of its pronunciation to that of the pathach. That the yod is rendered by aleph, that is, the scheva by aleph, is also very common, as in talitha [Ταλιθά], girl, and ʿazya [Ταβιθὰ δορκάς], roe. The Syriac goes on, and in explaining what Akeldama means, he says it signifies qadam agar, field of blood. Here we only remind students of the Syriac language that agar is the construct form of agra, field, whose plural is agre, and these are irregular.

units.la: VERS. 25. Ἐξ ἧς παρέδωκεν Ἰούδας. Vulgatus, de quo prævaricatus est Iudas. Erafmus, prævaricatus excidit. Merito neutrum secutus est doctiss. Beza, qui vertit, à quo aberravit Iudas. malim, recessit. utuntur enim Hellenistæ pro Hebraeo סור. ut Exod. 32. 8. סרו מהר מן הדרך, παρέκλιναν ταχὺ ἐκ τῆς ὁδοῦ, recesserunt celeriter à via: sic Deut. 9. 12. 16. & alibi sæpe. Optimè Syrus ܐܬܦܪܫ, Trem. & Boder. in Parisiensi edit. à quo separavit se. verte, recessit. id enim est ܐܬܦܪܫ. [illegible, ~12 letters] ut 2 Tim. 2. 19. [Hebrew and Greek] ἀπὸ ἀδικίας, recedat ab iniquitate.
units.tr: VERSE 25. "From which Judas fell away" [Ἐξ ἧς παρέδωκεν Ἰούδας]. The Vulgate has "concerning which Judas transgressed." Erasmus has "transgressing, he fell." The learned Beza rightly followed neither, and he renders it "from which Judas strayed." I would prefer "withdrew," for the Hellenists use [the Greek verb] for the Hebrew סור, as at Exodus 32:8, סרו מהר מן הדרך [suru meher min haderek], "they turned aside quickly from the way" [παρέκλιναν ταχὺ ἐκ τῆς ὁδοῦ], "they withdrew quickly from the way," and so also at Deuteronomy 9:12, 16, and often elsewhere. The Syriac has very well itpārash, as in the Trem. and Boder. Parisian edition, "from which he separated himself." Render it "withdrew," for that is the sense of itpārash. [illegible] as at 2 Timothy 2:19, "let him depart from iniquity" [ἀπὸ ἀδικίας].

units.la: VERS. 26. Cum undecim Apostolis. Vocat eos alibi passim Interpres Arabs [Arabic], quasi missos. hic vocat, ut & alibi saepe, & in Alcorano passim, [Arabic]. Quod id ab [Hebrew], candidum esse, usitata Hebraeis Syrisque significatione deductum velint, quasi candidis vestibus induti fuerint Apostoli, frivolum est. dicuntur & ab Aethiopico Interprete ubique [Ethiopic], proculdubio ab [Ethiopic] usitato ipsis verbo pro πρέσβευσαν, ire, proficisci. quia munus eorum ferebat, nusquam sedem figere, sed quaquaversum proficisci. sic & legatus quivis [Hebrew] dicitur Joh. 13. 16.
units.tr: VERS. 26. Cum undecim Apostolis. Elsewhere the Arabic translator everywhere calls them by a word that means, as it were, "those sent," and here, as often elsewhere and throughout the Qur'an, he does the same. That they are said to be derived from the Hebrew word meaning "to be white," in the sense commonly used by Hebrews and Syrians, as if the Apostles were clothed in white garments, is trivial. The Ethiopic translator likewise uses everywhere a word which doubtless comes from the verb customary among them for πρέσβευσαν, "to act as envoys, to go on a mission." This is because their office required them never to settle in one place, but to go out in every direction. So too any envoy is called שליח in John 13:16.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: VERS. 1. Καὶ ἐν τῷ συμπληροῦσθαι τὴν ἡμέραν τῆς πεντηκοστῆς. Vulgatus, Syrus & Arabs legerunt τὰς ἡμέρας. utrovis modo legatur, sensus nec est, quum primus dies pentecostes, nec quum omnes ejus dies essent exacti, sed quum numerus dierum à pascha ad pentecosten esset exactus. de quo vide doctissimas Bezae in hunc locum notas: & nostras ad Marc. 8. 31. Quod autem vir Doct. ἐν τῷ συμπληροῦσθαι positum velit pro μὴ τὰ συμπληρωθῆναι, nihil necesse videtur. numerus enim quinquaginta dierum, proprie loquendo, non erat completus, ineunte primo pentecostes, sed currente eo complebatur. erat enim ipse quinquagesimus. sensus est: quum tempus quinquaginta dierum, quod incidebat in diem pentecostes, compleretur, currente adhuc eo die quo complebatur, venit Spiritus S. Testatur autem Hieron. in Dan. quum tres fuerint precandi horae Judaeis, tertia, sexta & nona, hora tertia Spiritum S. descendisse in Apostolos. Sequitur, [Greek] ὁμοθυμαδὸν [Greek] τὸ αὐτό. Erasmus arbitratur Vulgatum legisse pro ὁμοθυμαδὸν, ὁμαδόν, quia vertit pariter. quod
units.tr: VERSE 1. And when the day of Pentecost was fully come [Καὶ ἐν τῷ συμπληροῦσθαι τὴν ἡμέραν τῆς πεντηκοστῆς]. The Vulgate, the Syriac and the Arabic read the days [τὰς ἡμέρας]. Whichever reading is adopted, the sense is neither when the first day of Pentecost nor when all its days were past, but when the number of days from Passover to Pentecost was complete. On this see Beza's most learned notes on this passage, and ours on Mark 8. 31. But that the learned man wishes in the being fulfilled [ἐν τῷ συμπληροῦσθαι] to stand for not yet fulfilled [μὴ τὰ συμπληρωθῆναι] seems quite unnecessary. For the number of fifty days, properly speaking, was not complete at the beginning of the first day of Pentecost, but was completed as that day ran its course, since it was itself the fiftieth. The sense is this: when the period of fifty days, which fell on the day of Pentecost, was complete, while that same day on which it was completed was still running, the Holy Spirit came. Jerome, in his commentary on Daniel, testifies that since the Jews had three hours of prayer, the third, sixth and ninth, the Holy Spirit descended on the Apostles at the third hour. There follows together [ὁμοθυμαδὸν] the same [τὸ αὐτό]. Erasmus thinks the Vulgate read ὁμαδόν instead of ὁμοθυμαδὸν, because he translates it equally, together.

units.la: magis etiam dicas, si videas Syrum pro ἡσαν ὁμοθυμαδὸν simpliciter dicere ꝏꝯ ... congregati erant. & eodem sensu Arabem ... At obscervandum, ὁμοθυμαδὸν saepe usurpari Hellenistis pro simplici ἁμα, simul, etiam ubi nullus animorum consensus locum habet: ut
units.tr: You would say this even more if you saw that the Syriac simply renders were together [ἡσαν ὁμοθυμαδὸν] as were gathered together, and the Arabic in the same sense. But it must be observed that homothymadon is often used by the Hellenists for the plain hama, at the same time, simul, even where there is no agreement of minds, as

units.la: 1 Paral. 10. 6. καὶ ὁ ἁλῶς ὁ οἶκος αὐτοῦ ὁμοθυμαδὸν ἀπέθανεν, & tota domus ejus simul mortua est. Job. 34. 15. Τελευτήσει πᾶσα σὰρξ ὁμοθυμαδόν, morietur omnis caro pariter. sic alibi saepe, adeo ut etiam inanimatis tribuatur, Thren. 2. 8. ἠ τεῖχος ὁμοθυμαδὸν ἠδύνησεν, & murus pariter debilitatus est. Laudo tamen Bezam, qui propria vocis significatione retenta vertit concorditer, Erasmus unanimiter. ut & Syrus praecedenti c. 1. v. 14. pro eo dixit ..., una anima. similiter ibi & Arabs, debuerant & hic.
units.tr: 1 Chron. 10. 6: And his whole house died together [καὶ ὁ ὅλος οἶκος αὐτοῦ ὁμοθυμαδὸν ἀπέθανεν]. Job 34. 15: All flesh shall perish together [Τελευτήσει πᾶσα σὰρξ ὁμοθυμαδόν]. So elsewhere often, so that it is even attributed to inanimate things, Lam. 2. 8: the wall also was weakened together [ἦ τεῖχος ὁμοθυμαδὸν ἠδύνησεν]. Yet I commend Beza, who, keeping the proper meaning of the word, translates concorditer, in harmony, while Erasmus has unanimiter, unanimously. So also the Syriac in the preceding chapter, 1. 14, renders it one soul; the Arabic likewise there, and they ought to have done so here too.

units.la: VERS. 2. Ἠχος φερομένης πνοῆς βιαίας. Syrus & Arabs non legunt φερομένης. Πνοὴ vertitur à Vulgato Spiritus, ut & à Syro ... & Arabe ... quae tamen ventum etiam significant, proprie πνοή, flatus, ut recte hic vertit doctissimus Interpres. vel spiratio. Unde LXX Interpretes, qui interdum πνέω dixerunt pro רוּחַ, saepius utuntur pro ... de quo illustris locus Job. 32. 8. ... πνοὴ δὲ πνευματικοῦ ἡ διδάσκουσα, spiratio autem omnipotentis est quae docet. Id Spiritui S. vere convenit, qui festo Pentecostes illapsus est in Apostolos, tanquam πνοὴ ἐκ πνευματικοῦ ἡ διδάξασα αὐτούς, spiratio omnipotentis edoctura ipsos.
units.tr: VERSE 2. And there came a sound from heaven like the rushing of a mighty wind [Ἠχος φερομένης πνοῆς βιαίας]. The Syriac and the Arabic do not read rushing [φερομένης]. Pnoē is translated by the Vulgate as Spirit, as also by the Syriac and the Arabic; yet it also means wind, properly breath [πνοή], blast, as the most learned translator here rightly renders it, or breathing. Hence the Seventy, who sometimes used pneō for the Hebrew ruach, use it more often for breath, as in the famous passage Job 32. 8: but the breath of the Almighty is that which teaches [πνοὴ δὲ πνευματικοῦ ἡ διδάσκουσα]. This truly befits the Holy Spirit, who came down on the Apostles at the feast of Pentecost, as a breath from the Almighty, teaching them [πνοὴ ἐκ πνευματικοῦ ἡ διδάξασα αὐτούς].

units.la: VERS. 3. Et conspectae sunt ipsis divisae lingua ὡσεὶ πυρός. Vulgatus, tanquam ignis. ubi quum ignis tam in recto quam in gignendi casu accipi possit, incommodum illud vitari, nec à Graecis deflecti exististimat Cl. Beza, si vertatur instar ignis. at vero Genitivus πυρὸς non regitur ab ὡσεί, sed à γλῶσσαι. Genitivus autem ignis ab instar, ideoque ambiguitatem guitatem habet longè maximam: quia instar ignis referri posset ad divisa, quasi sensus esset, divisæ instar ignis, id est, sicut ignis dividitur. ut ergo ambiguitas tollatur, omnino necesse est vertere cum Erasmo, tanquam igneæ. nam γλῶσ- σαι πυρὸς, linguæ ignis sunt igneæ. Syrus habet [Syriac], tanquam ignis, in Nominativo. Nam in Genitivo dicendum fuerat [Syriac]. Sequitur, ἐκάθισε η &c. Et sedit, nempe πῦρ, ignis. Syrus & Arabs, & sederunt, nempe linguæ. quia autem & sedit non convenit cum lingua ignea, necesse omnino videtur, Latinè supplere constructionem, hoc modo: divisa linguæ sicut linguæ ignis, & sedit, scilicet iste ignis. quo supplemento Græca Belgicaque lingua opus non habent, quia Genitivus ibi à Nomin. facile discernitur.
units.tr: VERSE 3. And there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire [ὡσεὶ πυρός]. The Vulgate has as fire. Here, since fire can be taken either in the nominative or in the genitive case, the famous Beza thinks the awkwardness can be avoided, without departing from the Greek, by translating like fire. But the genitive pyros is not governed by hōsei but by glōssai. The genitive of fire after like, however, carries by far the greatest ambiguity, because like fire could be referred to divided, as if the sense were divided like fire, that is, as fire is divided. So to remove the ambiguity it is absolutely necessary to translate, with Erasmus, like fiery tongues, for tongues of fire are fiery. The Syriac has as fire in the nominative; in the genitive it should have said otherwise. Next comes and it sat [ἐκάθισεν], namely fire. The Syriac and the Arabic have and they sat, namely the tongues. Since and it sat does not agree with fiery tongues, it seems absolutely necessary to supply the construction in Latin thus: divided tongues, like tongues of fire, and it sat, namely that fire. Greek and Dutch have no need of this supplement, because there the genitive is easily distinguished from the nominative.

units.la: VERS. 4. Et coeperunt loqui ἑτέραις γλώσσαις, Erasmus & Beza rectè aliis linguis. Vulgatus tamen habet variis linguis, ut & Syrus [Syriac], lingua lingua, quasi legissent γλώσσαις γλώσσαις, sic & Arabs. Sequitur καθὼς τὸ πνεῦμα ἐδίδου, sicut Spiritus dabat. Vulgatus & Æthiopicus addunt Sanctus. Syrus & Arabs id non agnoscunt.
units.tr: VERSE 4. And they began to speak with other tongues [ἑτέραις γλώσσαις]. Erasmus and Beza rightly have other tongues. The Vulgate, however, has various tongues, and the Syriac has tongue tongue, as if they had read tongues tongues; so also the Arabic. There follows as the Spirit gave them utterance [καθὼς τὸ πνεῦμα ἐδίδου]. The Vulgate and the Ethiopic add Holy. The Syriac and the Arabic do not recognise this.

units.la: VERS. 5. Ἦσαν δὲ ἐν Ἱερουσαλὴμ κατοικοῦντες Ἰουδαῖοι, ἄνδρες εὐλαβεῖς, ἀπὸ παντὸς ἔθνους τῶν ὑπὸ τὸν οὐρανόν. Hæc lectio vult, omnes istos ex omni gente fuisse Judæos. quod clarius etiam expressit Syrus, quum immutato paululum situ dixit: erant autem viri habitantes Hierosolyma, timentes Deum, Iudei ex omnibus gentibus quæ sub cælo sunt. Tum sub Judæis necesse est etiam proselytos completi, ex v. 10. Arabs autem Judæos à reliquis gentibus distinxit, inquiens [Arabic], Iudei, & ex omnibus gentibus. prior lectio receptior & melior.
units.tr: VERSE 5. Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men, from every nation under heaven [Ἦσαν δὲ ἐν Ἱερουσαλὴμ κατοικοῦντες Ἰουδαῖοι, ἄνδρες εὐλαβεῖς, ἀπὸ παντὸς ἔθνους τῶν ὑπὸ τὸν οὐρανόν]. This reading means that all these were Jews from every nation. The Syriac expressed this even more clearly, when, with a slight change of order, it said: there were men dwelling in Jerusalem, fearing God, Jews from all the nations that are under heaven. Then, among the Jews, the proselytes must necessarily be included as well, from v. 10. The Arabic, however, distinguished the Jews from the other nations, saying Jews, and from all nations. The former reading is more widely received and better.

units.la: VERS. 6. Γινομένης δὲ τῆς φωνῆς τούτης. Vulgatus ad verbum, Facta autem voce hac. ut & Syrus per ܟܠܦ expressit. Eraf. is rumor quum increbruisset. Beza, orto autem hoc rumore. Quaerenti diligenter, an uspiam aut קול Hebraeis, aut φωνή Hellenistis pro rumore sumatur, nusquam occurrit, sed semper pro voce, aut sonitu, aut tonitru. pro speciali autem sonitu qui rumor dicitur, nunquam, nisi forte Jer. 10. 22. קול שמועה הנה באה, φωνὴ ἀκοῆς ἰδὺ ἐρχεται. ubi tamen non φωνή sed ἀκοή, rumorem, φωνή autem ejus sonitum designat, quo innotescit & pervagatur. dubito an non φωνή hic accipi posset pro Hebraeorum דבר, quod LXX nunc per λόγον, nunc per ῥῆμα, nunc per φωνῶ interpretantur. & sicut דבר, λόγος & ῥῆμα saepe usurpantur pro re & negocio, ita & φωνή eodem modo sumi queat, ac verti, Facta autem re hac, id est, quum haec res ita contigisset. videtur certe φωνή, & Hebraeorum קול quoque ita accipiendum Exod. 4. 8. אם לא ישמעו לקל הראשון, והאמינו לקל האות האחרון, ἐὰν μὴ ἀκούσωσι φωνῆς τ̈ σημείου τῶν πρώτων, πιστεύσουσι τῇ φωνῇς τ̈ σημείου δεύτερου. quid hic vox signi, nisi negocium & ipsa res signi?
units.tr: VERSE 6. And when this voice was made [Γινομένης δὲ τῆς φωνῆς τούτης]. The Vulgate has, word for word, and when this voice was made, and the Syriac also expresses it in the same way. Erasmus has when this rumour had spread; Beza, and this rumour arising. On searching carefully whether anywhere either the Hebrew qol or the Hellenists' phōnē is taken for rumour, no instance occurs; it is always used for voice, or sound, or thunder. For a special sound which is called a rumour, never, unless perhaps Jer. 10. 22 (qol shemu'ah hinneh ba'ah [קול שמועה הנה באה]; Greek phōnē akoēs idou erchetai), where, however, it is not phōnē but akoē that means rumour, while phōnē designates the sound by which it becomes known and spreads. I doubt whether phōnē here could not be taken for the Hebrew dabar [דבר], which the Seventy translate now by logos, now by rhēma, now by phōnē. And just as dabar, logos and rhēma are often used for thing and affair, so phōnē too can be taken and translated in the same way: when this affair was done, that is, when this thing had so happened. Certainly phōnē and the Hebrew qol are to be understood in this way at Exod. 4. 8 (im lo yishme'u leqol harishon [אם לא ישמעו לקל הראשון]; Greek ean mē akousōsi phōnēs tou sēmeiou tōn prōtōn). What is the voice of the sign here, unless the matter itself and the very thing of the sign?

units.la: Sequitur, convenit multitudo, ἡ συνεχύθη. Vulgatus, & mente confusa est. Erasmus & Beza recte omittunt mente, referri tamen ad mentis conturbationem iidem volunt. Arabs vertit commoti sunt, ut & Syrus commotus est. quae non modo ad mentis conturbationem, sed vel maxime ad tumultuarium perplexumque populi concursum referri possunt, ubi sine ordine cum confusione alium alium impellit, alter alterius cursum retardat. id mihi hic est συνεχύθη. plane ut Act. 19. 29. Καὶ ἐπλήσθη ἡ πόλις ὅλη συγχύσεως, ὁ ὁρμησαν ὁμοθυμαδὸν εἰς τὸ θέατρον. ubi Syrus eodem verbo dixit ܐܬܬܒܠܠܬ, & conturbata est tota civitas, vel potius tumultuata est. & v. 32. ἡ γὰρ ἐκκλησία συγκεχυμένη, erat enim congregatio confusa. Syrus ܓܢܒܐ οὐδὲ ... turba admodum commota erant, nempe per modum tumultus.
units.tr: There follows the multitude came together [ἡ συνεχύθη]. The Vulgate has and the mind was confused. Erasmus and Beza rightly omit mind, though they wish it to be referred to a confusion of mind. The Arabic translates they were moved, as also the Syriac was moved. These can be referred not only to confusion of mind but most of all to a tumultuous and tangled crowding of the people, where without order and in confusion one pushes another, and one holds back the other's course.
