This, to me, is the synechythē here, just as in Acts 19. 29: And the whole city was filled with confusion, and they rushed with one accord into the theatre [Καὶ ἐπλήσθη ἡ πόλις ὅλη συγχύσεως, ὥρμησαν ὁμοθυμαδὸν εἰς τὸ θέατρον]. There the Syriac used the same verb: and the whole city was confused, or rather was in tumult. And at v. 32: for the assembly was confused [ἡ γὰρ ἐκκλησία συγκεχυμένη]. The Syriac has the crowd was greatly moved, namely in the manner of a tumult.

units.la: VERS. 7. Λέγοντες πρὸς ἀλλήλους. Vulgatus non habet πρὸς ἀλλήλους. Syrus & Arabs habent. VERS. 8. Καὶ πῶς ἡμεῖς ἀκούομεν ἕκαστος τῇ ἰδίᾳ διαλέκτῳ. Eras. & Beza, Quomodo igitur nos audimus eos sua quisque lingua, interferuerunt eos, ut τῇ ἰδίᾳ διαλέκτῳ per Ablati- vum commodè exponerent. at Vulgatus, & quomodo nos audimus unusquisque linguam suam, quasi τῶν ἰδίων διαλέκτων legisset. sic quoque Syrus & Arabs. VERS. 9. Ἐλαμῖται. Syrus [Syriac word], Alanai. ad quod sic Junius, id est Persa ανεκδοχικῶς, ut ostendit locorum ordo: nam ab Oriente ad Occidentem populos enumerat. quod autem Elamaeos appellat Syrus, vitiosum puto. nam Elanei ad Arabiam Petraam pertinent: & Graecus textus verior est. ha- ctenus ille. ubi recte docet, Elanaeos ad Arabiam Petraeam pertinere. est enim Alane aut Elane urbs ad mare rubrum sita, testibus Strabone & Ptolemaeo. Arabes [Arabic word], Aila vel Eila vocant; eamque Syriae initium faciunt, & ad Judaeos pertinuisse afferunt, ut est apud Abulfedam. Et apud Jo- sephum lib. 8. Antiq. c. 2. ubi Salomonem classem nava- lem ibi struxisse ait in sinu Aegyptiaco, in loco quodam ma- ris rubri, cui Esiongaber, alias Bernice nomen est, ἡ πόλις ἐλαυτῆς, ἡ χώρα τῶν Ἰουδαίων, non procul a civitate Eilane, quae regio olim Judaeorum fuit. Hos Alanaeos intelligi apud Lucam non posse, recte asserit vir do- ctissimus. Sed quidni intelligi possint, quos Benjamin in Itiner. pag. 73. edit. Leydensis, juxta Mesoporamiam & Ar- meniam collocat? Verba ejus sunt, [Hebrew text] Alania est regio montibus cincta, nec ullum habet exitum praeter portas ferreas quas Alexander fecit, ubi populus degit qui Alan
units.tr: VERSE 7. Saying to one another [Λέγοντες πρὸς ἀλλήλους]. The Vulgate does not have πρὸς ἀλλήλους, but the Syriac and the Arabic do. VERSE 8. And how do we hear each in our own language [Καὶ πῶς ἡμεῖς ἀκούομεν ἕκαστος τῇ ἰδίᾳ διαλέκτῳ]. Erasmus and Beza render it How then do we hear them, each in his own tongue, supplying them, so that they can neatly explain τῇ ἰδίᾳ διαλέκτῳ as an ablative. But the Vulgate has and how do we hear, each of us, his own tongue, as if it had read τῶν ἰδίων διαλέκτων. So too the Syriac and the Arabic. VERSE 9. Elamites [Ἐλαμῖται]. The Syriac has Alanai. On this Junius says that is, Persians, by synecdoche, as the order of the places shows, since the list runs from East to West. But I think the Syriac is wrong to call them Elamites. The Elaneans belong to Arabia Petraea, and the Greek text is more accurate. So far he. He rightly teaches that the Elaneans belong to Arabia Petraea. For Alane or Elane is a city on the Red Sea, according to the witness of Strabo and Ptolemy. The Arabs call it Aila or Eila, and they make it the beginning of Syria, and they state that it belonged to the Jews, as is found in Abulfeda. And in Josephus, Antiquities book 8, chapter 2, where he says that Solomon built a naval fleet there in the Egyptian gulf, in a certain place on the Red Sea called Esiongaber, otherwise Berenice, the city of Elath, the country of the Jews, not far from the city of Eilane, which region was once the Jews'. That these Alanaeans cannot be meant in Luke, the very learned man rightly asserts. But why should they not be understood to be those whom Benjamin, in his Itinerary, page 73 of the Leiden edition, places near Mesopotamia and Armenia? His words are: Alania is a region surrounded by mountains, which has no exit except the iron gates that Alexander made, where dwells a people called Alan.

units.la: dicitur. Recte hoc cum Syro noftro convenit, qui poft Parthos & Medos, Alanaeos conftituit,deinde incolas Mefopotamiae. Hos Alanaeos Perfarum gentem quandam fuiffe, fuspicari non immerito ex fitu licet. atque ita iidem effe poffint, quos Ἐλαμίτας vocavit Lucas, qui ab עילם, Elam, primogenito filio Semi originem traxere, de quo Josephus I. 1. Antiq. c. 7. Ἐλυμος Ἐλυμαῖος Πέρσαι ... Elymus Elimaos, ex quibus Perfa originem traxerunt, reliquit. Unde 1 Machab. 6. 1. Rex Antiochus dicitur au-diviffe, ὅτι Ἐλυμαΐς ... Elymaida effe Perfidis civitatem, divitiis auro & argento celebrem. Paulo aliter Plinius lib. 6. c. 35. Perfidis, inquit, initium ad flumen Oroatum, quo dividitur ab Elymaide. & c. 27. Infra Eulaum Elymais eft, in ora juncta Perfidi. cum quo confentit Stephanus de urbibus, Ἐλύμη, Ἀσυρίων ... Σωσίδ ... οἱ οἰκοῦντες Ἐλυμαῖοι. Elyma, regio eft Affyriorum juxta Perfidem, Sufiana vicina, cujus incola funt Elymaei. Parum refert: five in Perfide five propè eam fuerint Elamitae aut Elymaei, iidem effe poffunt, quos Elanaeos dixit Syrus, quofque Benjamin inter Perfidem, Chorefanem, Mefopotamiam & Armeniam locat. Porro pro ܥܝܠܡܝܐ ... Syrus habet ܐܠܝܡ ܥܝܠܡ ... Tremel. & Boder. & qui habitant inter fluvios. non exiftimo ܐܠܝܡ hic significare inter, fed valere idem quod ܥܝܠ, locus,regio. ficut ܐܠܝܡ ... Samaria, non urbs, quae dicitur, fed regio. etfi non negem בית etiam urbibus tribui poffe. ut apud Arab. בית אלמקדס, domus fanctificata eft Jerufalem. Itaque ܐܠܝܡ ..., eft regio duorum fluviorum, Mefopotamia, quae Hebr. ארם נהרים, Syria duorum fluviorum. & ponitur Δ_ ... pro Δ ... ex more. raro enim hæc præpositio huic dictioni præfigitur. nec arbitror ... hîc esse plurale, quod significet fluvios, id enim Syri efferunt terminatione fœminina ... sed esse duale. & non scribendum, ut faciunt Boder. & Ferrarius, ..., sed ..., ab Hebræo ... sicut ... à ..., ducenti. ... Ægyptus. ... à ..., duo. ... à ..., duæ. ..., revelati, pro Chald. ...
units.tr: called. This agrees well with our Syrian, who after the Parthians and Medes places the Alanaeans, and then the inhabitants of Mesopotamia. It is not unreasonable to suspect, from their location, that these Alanaeans were some people of the Persians. And so they could be the same as those whom Luke called Elamites, who drew their origin from עילם [Elam], the firstborn son of Shem. Of him Josephus, Antiquities book 1, chapter 7, says: Elymus left the Elymaeans, from whom the Persians derived their origin. Hence at 1 Maccabees 6:1 King Antiochus is said to have heard that Elymais was a city of Persia, famous for its riches of gold and silver. Pliny speaks rather differently, book 6, chapter 35: Persia, he says, begins at the river Oroatis, by which it is divided from Elymais. And chapter 27: Below Eulaeus is Elymais, on the coast joined to Persia. Stephanus, in his work on cities, agrees with this: Elyme is a region of the Assyrians beside Persia, near Susiana, whose inhabitants are the Elymaeans. It makes little difference whether the Elamites or Elymaeans were in Persia or near it; they can be the same as those the Syriac calls Elanaeans, and whom Benjamin places between Persia, Khorasan, Mesopotamia and Armenia. Moreover, where the Syriac has Alam Alam [the Syriac words], Tremellius and Bode have and those who dwell between the rivers. I do not think that the Syriac word here means between, but that it has the same sense as the word for place, region, just as the Syriac word for Samaria means not a city, as is said, but a region. Though I do not deny that the word for house can also be applied to cities, as in Arabic, where the sanctified house is Jerusalem. So the Syriac is the region of the two rivers, Mesopotamia, which in Hebrew is ארם נהרים [Aram Naharaim], Syria of the two rivers. The preposition is put for the other one as is usual, for this preposition is rarely prefixed to this word. Nor do I think that the plural is here meant to signify rivers; the Syrians express that with a feminine ending, but it is the dual. And it should not be written, as Bode and Ferrarius write it, but derived from the Hebrew, as the Syriac for two hundred is from the Hebrew, the Syriac for Egypt is from the Hebrew, the Syriac for two is from the Hebrew, the Syriac for two (feminine) is from the Hebrew, and revealed, in place of the Chaldee.

units.la: VERS. 18. Καὶ γε ... δἀλως μου &c. Vulgatus & Beza emphasin particulæ γε recte expresserunt, & quidem super servos meos. Syrus & Arabs non satis congruè omiserunt. Fecerunt fortassis, quia non satis congruam particulam habent qua id enarrent. Æthiopicus, potius quam omitteret, egregia periphrasi explicuit, Et amplius dicit, super servos meos &c.
units.tr: VERSE 18. And indeed upon my servants, etc. [Καὶ γε ... δούλους μου &c.]. The Vulgate and Beza rightly expressed the emphasis of the particle γε: and indeed upon my servants. The Syriac and the Arabic omitted it, not very fittingly. Perhaps they did so because they do not have a suitable particle to express it. The Ethiopic, rather than omit it, explained it by an excellent periphrasis: And he says further, upon my servants, etc.

units.la: VERS. 20. Priusquam veniat dies ille Domini magnus καὶ ἐπιφανὴς. Vulgat. & manifestus. Beza, & illustris. Syrus ... Arabs ..., terribilis. rectè. Nam Joëlis 2.31. unde hic locus petitus, extat ..., dies terribilis, pro quo LXX ἡμέραν ἐπιφανῆ. ut & v. 11. sic Jud. 13. 6. ..., & aspectus ejus terribilis valde. LXX ἡ ἰδέα αὐτοῦ ἐπιφανὴς σφόδρα. vide etiam 1 Paral. 17.21. Hab. 1.7. Malach. 1. 14. Nec dubium, quin inde truculentus ille Antiochus dictus sit ἐπιφανὴς, terribilis potius quam illustris.
units.tr: VERSE 20. Before that great and notable day of the Lord comes [καὶ ἐπιφανὴς]. The Vulgate has and manifest; Beza has and illustrious. The Syriac and the Arabic have terrible, and rightly so. For in Joel 2:31, from which this passage is taken, stands a terrible day, for which the Septuagint has ἡμέραν ἐπιφανῆ, as also at verse 11. So at Judith 13:6, and his appearance is exceedingly terrible; the Septuagint has ἡ ἰδέα αὐτοῦ ἐπιφανὴς σφόδρα. See also 1 Chronicles 17:21, Habakkuk 1:7, Malachi 1:14. There is no doubt that the savage Antiochus was called ἐπιφανὴς from this, meaning terrible rather than illustrious.

units.la: VERS. 22. Ἄνδρα ἀποδεδειγμένον εἰς ὑμᾶς. Hebraicè dico, ..., virum demonstratum vobis à Deo. est enim ... Hebraeis non tantum redarguere, sed & arguere, certisque atque indubitatis argumentis demonstrare, probare & confirmare. idem quod Χαοδακνύψ Græcis. sic accipimus Gen. 24.14.
units.tr: VERSE 22. A man demonstrated to you [Ἄνδρα ἀποδεδειγμένον εἰς ὑμᾶς]. In Hebrew I say [the Hebrew word], a man demonstrated to you by God. For the Hebrews have this word not only in the sense of to refute but also to prove, and to demonstrate, prove and confirm by certain and indubitable arguments. It is the same as the Greek ἀποδείκνυμι. So we take it at Genesis 24:14.

units.la: VERS. 23. Syrus hîc habet, [Syriac] [Syriac] [Syriac]. Trem. hunc qui segregatus erat ad hoc. Boder. in Parif. qui electus erat. in Reg. qui expositus erat. verto hunc qui determinatus erat ad hoc. alibi antehac diximus [Syriac] frequenter sumi pro ὁρίζειν, determinare, definire, certo statuere. ita & hoc loco, expressurus quid sit, τὴν τῇ ὡρισμένῃ βυλῇ ἐ προγνώσει ἡ Θεὸς ἐκδόσει λαζόντες, dixit, hunc qui determinatus erat ad hoc, per præscientiam & per voluntatem Dei tradidistis.
units.tr: VERSE 23. The Syriac here has [Syriac words]. Tremellius: him who was set apart for this. Bode in Paris: who was chosen. In the Regius: who was set forth. I translate: him who was determined for this. Elsewhere before now we have said that the Syriac word is frequently taken for ὁρίζειν, to determine, define, decide firmly. So also here, when he is about to say what it is, he has rendered τῇ ὡρισμένῃ βουλῇ καὶ προγνώσει τοῦ θεοῦ ἔκδοτον λαβόντες [Acts 2:23, delivered up by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God] as: him who was determined for this, you have handed over by the foreknowledge and will of God.

units.la: VERS. 25. David enim dicit εἰς αὐτὸν de eo. recte sic vertit Eraf. & Cl. Beza. ut & Eph. 5. 32. εἰς Χριστὸν ἐ εἰς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν, de Christo & de ecclesia. εἰς pro εἰς, sicut apud Hebræos sæpe ל pro ב, ut Pf. 91. 11. יצוה, pracipiet de te, εἰς σε, Matt. 4. 6. sic Gen. 20. 31. & 26. 7. 2 Sam. 11. 7. Est. 3. 2. itaque recte Syrus [Syriac], de eo. Addit, [Syriac] [Syriac] Λόγοι. Trem. & Boder. in Parif. ab initio fui spectans Dominum meum. melius quam in Reg. coram me prospiciebam dominum meum. illud coram me non est apud Syrum. quod enim in Græco est ἐνώπιόν μου omisit. verto, prævidebam dominum meum. προοράω τ κύριον. quum enim componere nequeant, quod Latini faciunt per pra, Græci per προ, illi faciunt per verbum [Syriac]. ut [Syriac] [Syriac], προγίνωσκε. [Syriac] [Syriac], προώρισε. & similia. ad verbum, pramisfit cognovit, pramisfit determinavit, id est, præcognovit, prædeterminavit. Sic hoc loco, pramittebam videbam dominum meum, id est, prævidebam. hæc in gratiam Φιλοσόφων.
units.tr: VERSE 25. For David says εἰς αὐτὸν, concerning him. Erasmus and Beza rightly translate it so, as also at Ephesians 5:32, εἰς Χριστὸν ἢ εἰς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν, concerning Christ and concerning the Church. εἰς is put for περί, just as in Hebrew ל is often put for ב, as at Psalm 91:11, he will command concerning you [יצוה], εἰς σε, Matthew 4:6. So at Genesis 20:31, 26:7, 2 Samuel 11:7, Esther 3:2. Thus the Syriac rightly has concerning him. It adds [Syriac words], which Tremellius and Bode in Paris render from the beginning looking to my Lord, better than the Regius: I was looking ahead at my lord before me. The words before me are not in the Syriac; it has omitted what in the Greek is ἐνώπιόν μου. I translate: I foresaw the Lord. For since they cannot compose the word as the Latins do with prae or the Greeks with προ, they use the verb [Syriac word], as in [Syriac word] for προγινώσκω and [Syriac word] for προώρισε, and similar forms. Literally, he sent ahead, he knew; he sent ahead, he determined, that is, foreknew, predetermined. So here, he sent ahead, saw my lord, that is, foresaw. These remarks are for the benefit of the philosophers.

units.la: VERS. 26. Et exultavit, ἡ γλῶσσά μου, lingua mea. Sic Vulgat. quoq; & Arabs legerunt. at Syrus ܐܠܗܐ, gloria mea. secutus textum Hebraeum, ubi est כְּבוֹדִי. quod hoc quidem loco LXX verterunt per ἡ γλῶσσά μου. quomodo & accipi posset Pf. 30. v. ult. לְמַעַן יְזַמֶּרְךָ כָבוֹד, ut canat tibi gloria, id est, lingua. ibi autem LXX ad verbum verterunt. Hebraei utroque in loco per כבד intelligunt הנשמה aut הנפש, animam. quomodo procul dubio accipiendum Gen. 49.6. Coetui eorum ne uniatur כְּבוֹדִי, gloria mea, id est, anima.
units.tr: VERSE 26. And my tongue exulted, ἡ γλῶσσά μου, my tongue. So the Vulgate and the Arabic read. But the Syriac has my glory, following the Hebrew text, where it is כְּבוֹדִי. The Septuagint indeed translated it in this passage as ἡ γλῶσσά μου, as also Psalm 30, last verse, לְמַעַן יְזַמֶּרְךָ כָבוֹד, that glory may sing to you, could be taken, that is, the tongue. But there the Septuagint translated it word for word. The Hebrews in both places understand כבד [kabod] to mean הנשמה or הנפש, the soul. This is without doubt how it must be taken at Genesis 49:6, Let not my glory be united to their assembly [כְּבוֹדִי], that is, my soul.

units.la: Additur, Insuper & caro mea requiescet ἐπ' ἐλπίδι, Vulg. in spe. Beza cum spe. nihil refert. modo attendatur, phrasin illam non esse ex lingua Latina, aut puriori Graeca aestimandam, ubi ἐλπίς, spes est exspectatio boni futuri, sed ex lingua Hellenistica, quae pro Hebraeo לִבְטַח, in fiducia, id est securè, tuto, dixit ἐπ' ἐλπίδι, etiam ubi spes proprie dicta, id est expectatio futuri boni nullum prorsus locum habet. ut Jud. 18.7. viderunt populum, יוֹשֵׁבֶת לָבֶטַח, habitantem securè, ἐγκαθήμενον ἐπ' ἐλπίδι. שָׁקֵט וּבֹטֵחַ, quiescentem & confidentem, ἡσυχάζοντας ἐν ἐλπίδι. sic Prov. 1.33. Qui auscultat mihi, יִשְׁכָּן בֶּטַח, habitabit confidenter, aut securè, κατασκηνώσει ἐπ' ἐλπίδι. sic Pf. 4.10. & 78.58. Esa. 32.9. Ezech. 28.26. Ofeae 2.18. Zophon. 3.1. & alibi passim. Sic ergo & hoc loco sensus est, Caro mea, יִשְׁכֹּן לָבֶטַח, κατασκηνώσει ἐπ' ἐλπίδι, habitabit secura, id est, tuta ab omni malo. Vbi non possum praeterire commentarium Davidis Kimchi in hunc locum, cujus haec sunt verba, בעודני בחיים ישכון לבטח שתצילני מכל נוק וברדש אשר מיתה כלמר, שלא שלטה בו רמה ותולעת, id est, si sensum literalem spectes mens est, dum adhuc sum in vivis, habitabit caro mea securè, quia liberabis me ab omni damno. at mysticè post mortem, perinde est ac si doceat,non dominaturam ei corruptionem & vermem. Lubens à verpo hanc interpretationem amplector, ut sensus sit, Habitabit post mortem caro mea tuta à vermibus in sepulchro, quia non derelinques in eo animam meam, nec permittes Sanctum tuum videre corruptionem.
units.tr: It is added, "Moreover my flesh also shall rest in hope" [ἐπ' ἐλπίδι]. The Vulgate has "in spe" and Beza "with hope"; it makes no difference. Only let it be noted that this phrase is not to be judged by Latin usage or by purer Greek, where ἐλπίς, "hope", means the expectation of a future good. It should be judged by Hellenistic usage, which rendered the Hebrew לִבְטַח [livtach], "in confidence", that is, securely or safely, as ἐπ' ἐλπίδι, even where there is no room at all for hope properly so called, that is, the expectation of a future good. Compare Judges 18:7, where "they saw the people" יוֹשֵׁבֶת לָבֶטַח [yoshevet lavetach], "dwelling securely", is rendered ἐγκαθήμενον ἐπ' ἐλπίδι [enkathēmenon ep' elpidi]; and where שָׁקֵט וּבֹטֵחַ [shaqet uvotēach], "quiet and confident", is rendered ἡσυχάζοντας ἐν ἐλπίδι [hēsychazontas en elpidi]. So Proverbs 1:33, "he who listens to me" יִשְׁכָּן בֶּטַח [yishkon betach], "will dwell in confidence" or securely, is rendered κατασκηνώσει ἐπ' ἐλπίδι [kataskēnōsei ep' elpidi]. So also Psalms 4:10 and 78:58, Isaiah 32:9, Ezekiel 28:26, Hosea 2:18, Zephaniah 3:1, and everywhere else. So here too the sense is: "my flesh" יִשְׁכֹּן לָבֶטַח [yishkon lavetach], κατασκηνώσει ἐπ' ἐλπίδι, "will dwell secure", that is, safe from every evil. Here I cannot pass over the commentary of David Kimchi on this passage, whose words are: בעודני בחיים ישכון לבטח שתצילני מכל נוק וברדש אשר מיתה כלמר, שלא שלטה בו רמה ותולעת. That is: "If you look at the literal sense, the meaning is that while I am still alive my flesh will dwell securely, because you will deliver me from every harm. But mystically, after death, it is as if he taught that corruption and the worm will not have dominion over it." I gladly embrace this interpretation from the Hebrew, so that the sense is: after death my flesh will dwell in the grave, safe from the worms, because you will not leave my soul there, nor will you permit your Holy One to see corruption.

units.la: VERS. 27. Οὐ δώσεις τ ὅσιόν σου ἰδεῖν ἀλαφϑρεγὶν. ὅσιον@ est Hebraeorum הסיד, pius. pro quo Syri abjecto ד dicunt [Syriac], unde est Graecum ὅσιον. ἀλαφθρεγὶν Syrus dixit [Syriac], חבלא, Arabs [Arabic], חבל, corruptionem. miror ergo, unde Cl. Beza habeat, Syrum & Arabem usurpasse vocem Hebraeam חלה, chalah quae consumtionem declarat.
units.tr: VERSE 27. "Thou wilt not give thy holy one to see corruption" [Οὐ δώσεις τὸν ὅσιόν σου ἰδεῖν ἀλαφθρεγὶν]. ὅσιον [hosion] is the Hebrew חסיד [chasid], "pious". The Syriac, dropping the ד, say ḥasyā, whence the Greek ὅσιον comes. The Syriac rendered ἀλαφθρεγὶν [corruption] as ḥabla, and the Arabic as ḥabal, both meaning "corruption". I am surprised, then, where the most distinguished Beza got the idea that the Syriac and Arabic had used the Hebrew word חלה [chalah], which denotes consumption.

units.la: VERS. 31. ὅτι οὐ καταλείφθη ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτοῦ εἰς ᾅδην. Non derelictam esse animam suam in inferno. Vulgatus, quia neque derelictus est in inferno. sic quoque Syrus & Arabs. nisi quod Arabs pro ὅτι videatur legisse ὅς, qui. non videntur legisse ἡ ψυχὴ. ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτὸς. aut certe interpretari voluerunt, animam hic ipsam personam denotare, & sensum esse, quod non derelicta est persona ejus, id est, ipse.
units.tr: VERSE 31. "That his soul was not left in hell" [ὅτι οὐ καταλείφθη ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτοῦ εἰς ᾅδην]. The Vulgate: "for neither was he left in hell". The Syriac and Arabic do the same, except that the Arabic seems to have read ὅς, "who", for ὅτι, "that". They do not seem to have read ἡ ψυχὴ [hē psychē] but αὐτός [autos]. Or at least they meant to render it so that "soul" here denotes the person himself, and the sense is "that his person was not left", that is, he himself.

units.la: VERS. 33. Τῇ δεξιᾷ οὖν ϑεοῦ ὑψωθείς. Dextrâ igitur Dei exaltatus. Arabs ﻊ ﺮ, ad dextram, quod ἐν δεξιᾷ, ἐν δεξιοῖς, ἐκ δεξιῶν dici solet. At cap. 5. 31. ὕψωσε τῇ δεξιᾷ αὐτῷ, bene vertit ﻊ, extulit eum dextra sua.
units.tr: VERSE 33. "Therefore being by the right hand of God exalted" [Τῇ δεξιᾷ οὖν θεοῦ ὑψωθείς]. The Arabic has ʿalā yamīn, "on the right", which is how ἐν δεξιᾷ, ἐν δεξιοῖς, or ἐκ δεξιῶν is usually expressed. But in chapter 5:31, ὕψωσε τῇ δεξιᾷ αὐτοῦ, the Arabic translates well: "he exalted him with his right hand".

units.la: VERS. 34. Λέγει ὁ αὐτός. dicit autem ipse. Syrus & Arabs, quia dicit ipse. nolim tamen afferere, aliter cos legisse quam δι. est enim & alibi ea particula causalis, pro enim. ut Rom. 8. 11. εἰ δὲ τὸ πνεῦμα, si enim spiritus &c. 1 Cor. 10. 11. ἐγράφη δὲ πρὸς νουθεσίαν ἡμῶν, scripta enim sunt ad monitionem nostram. & alibi passim.
units.tr: VERSE 34. "For David is not ascended into the heavens; but he saith himself" [Λέγει ὁ αὐτός, "he himself says"]. The Syriac and Arabic have "because he himself says". I would not, however, claim that they read anything other than δέ [de]. For that particle is elsewhere causal, meaning "for", as in Romans 8:11, εἰ δὲ τὸ πνεῦμα, "for if the Spirit", etc.; 1 Corinthians 10:11, ἐγράφη δὲ πρὸς νουθεσίαν ἡμῶν, "for they were written for our admonition"; and everywhere else.

units.la: VERS. 35. Donec ponam inimicos tuos ὑποπόδιον, scabellum pedum tuorum. Arabs ﻊ, sub scabellum pedum tuorum. Sic & Matth. 22. 24. & Hebr. 1. 13. At Marc. 12. 36. & Luc. 20. 43. tantum habet, sub pedibus tuis. Video & Æthiopicum Interpretem ubique in hac phrasi adhibere nnn, sub, expressa etiam voce scabelli. imo Luc. 17. 16. ubi Samaritanus dicitur cecidisse in faciem suam παρὰ τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ, ad pedes ejus, Æthiop. habet sub pedibus ejus, similiter Act. 4. 35. nam ad pedes ejus significat in terram quae erat sub pedibus ejus. sic capioillud Jacobi 2. 3. καθὼς ἔδει ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν μου, sede hic sub scabello meo, id est, in terra quae est sub scabello meo.
units.tr: VERSE 35. "Until I make thy foes thy footstool" [ὑποπόδιον, "footstool", and "the footstool of your feet"]. The Arabic has taḥta, "under the footstool of your feet". So also Matthew 22:44 and Hebrews 1:13. But Mark 12:36 and Luke 20:43 have only "under your feet". I see that the Ethiopic translator everywhere uses for this phrase the word taḥta, "under", and also expresses the word "footstool". Indeed in Luke 17:16, where the Samaritan is said to have fallen on his face παρὰ τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ, "at his feet", the Ethiopic has "under his feet"; similarly Acts 4:35, for "at his feet" means "in the ground that was under his feet". So I take the passage in James 2:3, καθὼς ἔδει ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν μου, "sit here under my footstool", to mean "in the ground that is under my footstool".

units.la: VERS. 37. Ἀκούσαντες ἡ καταγγελία. Eras. & Vulg. His autem auditis. Syr. & Arabs, Quum autem haec audivissent. malim sane, quam quod Cl. Beza dixit, Qui vero haec audiverunt. pro οἱ ἀκούσαντες. quod ei subintelligere, & hic & Act. 19. 5. durum est.
units.tr: VERSE 37. Ἀκούσαντες ἡ καταγγελία [Having heard the proclamation]. Erasmus and the Vulgate read, "But when these things were heard." The Syriac and Arabic read, "Now when they had heard these things." I certainly prefer this to what the illustrious Beza said, "Those who heard these things," rendering οἱ ἀκούσαντες. To supply the article in this way, both here and at Acts 19:5, is harsh.

units.la: VERS. 38. Καὶ λήψεσθε, & accipietis. Syrus & Arabs, ut accipiatis. Hebraeorum saepe pro ut.
units.tr: VERSE 38. Καὶ λήψεσθε [and you shall receive]. The Syriac and Arabic read, "that you may receive," as the Hebrews often use the word for "that."

units.la: VERS. 39. Καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς εἰς μακρὰν. Nescio quid viderit Arabs, quum verteret (Arabic) & omnibus qui sunt respipiscentes, vel convertentes se. Vulgatus & Erasmus, & omnibus qui longè sunt. Syrus (Syriac), qui longinqui sunt. Hebraicè (Hebrew). idem ipsis fuit atque τοῖς μακρὰν. qui opponuntur passim τοῖς ἐξ ἔθνους, gentiles nempe Judæis. At Cl. Beza, ob particulam εἰς expositum, & omnibus longè post futuris. Judæis nempe, in multas deinceps generationes convertendis. De Ethnicis enim id minus rectè accipi arbitratur, quia Gentium vocationis arcanum Petrus nondum norat. quod dictum, salva magni viri pace, ægrè admodum admitto. qui enim Apostolus, Scripturarum peritissimus, & jam Spiritu S. illuminatus, vocationem gentium futuram aliquando ignoraverit, quam Prophetæ, non unus, sed ferme omnes, non obscuris sed clarissimis verbis, non uno sed infinitis pene locis prædixerunt, quamque ipsimet, etsi gentibus infensissimi, hodierni Judæi futuram tempore Messiæ sui agnoscunt? videatur Kimchius in Esa. 19. 25. & alibi. Nec obstat quæ Act. 10. de Petro ad Cornelium mittendo extat historia. Inde enim aliud colligi nequit, quam ignorasse Petrum, quo tempore vocandæ essent Gentes, exististimasseque, dum incircumcisæ essent & à fœdere Dei alienæ, pro pollutis esse habendas, cum quibus nullum Judæo commercium intercedere deberet. ἀφέμπτης, inquit, ἐπὶ ἀνδρὶ Ἰουδαίῳ κοινωνίαν ἔχειν, ἀλλοφύλῳ. Sciebat nempe vocandas esse aliquando Gentes. quando, ignorabat. quumque hactenus vocatæ non essent, detrectavit iis agglutinari. cognita autem Dei voluntate, qua de jam jam vocandis constabat, morem gessit. Non gravatè itaque magnis viris assentior, qui τοῖς εἰς μακρὰν ad gentes, tum à fœdere gratiæ remotas, sed aliquando adducendas, referunt. nec repugno, quod
units.tr: VERS. 39. [Καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς εἰς μακρὰν] I do not know what the Arab saw when he rendered this as to all who are repentant, or who turn themselves around. The Vulgate and Erasmus have to all who are far off. The Syriac has who are far away. In Hebrew the phrase was the same as τοῖς μακρὰν, which is often set over against τοῖς ἐξ ἔθνους, that is, the Gentiles, in contrast to the Jews. But the learned Beza, taking the particle εἰς as meaningful, explained it as to all who are far off in time, that is, the Jews who were to be converted in many generations to come. He thinks this should not be understood of the Gentiles, because Peter did not yet know the mystery of the calling of the Gentiles. With all respect to so great a man, I find this statement very hard to accept. How could an apostle, most skilled in the Scriptures and already enlightened by the Holy Spirit, have been ignorant that the calling of the Gentiles was to come, when the Prophets, not just one but almost all of them, foretold it in the clearest words and in almost countless passages? Even today's Jews, most hostile as they are to the Gentiles, acknowledge that it will come in the time of their Messiah. See Kimchi on Isaiah 19:25 and elsewhere. Nor does the story in Acts 10 about Peter being sent to Cornelius stand in the way. From that story one can conclude only that Peter did not know when the Gentiles were to be called, and thought that, as long as they were uncircumcised and alien to God's covenant, they were to be regarded as unclean, so that a Jew ought to have no dealings with them. He says: [ἀθέμιτον ἐστιν ἀνδρὶ Ἰουδαίῳ κοινωνίαν ἔχειν ἢ προσέρχεσθαι ἀλλοφύλῳ], it is unlawful for a Jew to have fellowship with, or approach, a foreigner. So he knew that the Gentiles would at some time be called, but not when; and since they had not yet been called, he shrank from joining himself to them. Yet once he knew the will of God, which made clear that they were about to be called, he complied. I therefore do not hesitate to agree with great men who refer τοῖς εἰς μακρὰν to the Gentiles, who were then far from the covenant of grace but were to be brought in at some point. Nor do I object to their view that τὰς εἰς Μακεδονίαν means the same as τῆς Μακεδονίας.

units.la: τὰς εἰς μαχεδὼν idem esse velint quod τῆς μαχεδών. constat enim praepositionem εἰς ejusmodi adverbiis adjunctam saepe vacare. talia sunt εἰς τὸ παραχρῆμα, statim, subito. εἰς αὔριον, cras. εἰσέτι, adhuc, amplius. εἰς ἅπαξ, semel. εἰς τρίς, ter. & similia. nec aliter accepit Chrysostomus, qui inde vim argumenti Apostolici sic nectit, εἰ τῆς εἰς μαχεδὼν, πολλῷ μᾶλλον ὑμῖν τῆς ἐγγύς, si iis qui longe sunt facta est promissio, multo magis vobis qui prope estis. Additur, ὅσους ἂν προσκαλέσηται Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, quoscunque advocaverit Dominus Deus noster. Nemo hic aliter legit, praeter Æthiopicum, qui habet, & omnibus qui longe sunt, & invocabunt Dominum Deum nostrum. Quis hic non audacissimam impudentissimi alicujus Pelagiani manum deprehendat, qui laudem divinae gratiae non ferens, eam in humanos conatus transtulit?
units.tr: It is established that the preposition εἰς, when joined to adverbs of this kind, is often redundant. Examples are εἰς τὸ παραχρῆμα, immediately, at once; εἰς αὔριον, tomorrow; εἰσέτι, still, further; εἰς ἅπαξ, once; εἰς τρίς, three times; and similar phrases. Chrysostom also understood it this way, and he draws the force of the apostle's argument from it: [εἰ τοῖς εἰς μακρὰν ἐπηγγέλη, πολλῷ μᾶλλον ὑμῖν τοῖς ἐγγύς], if the promise was made to those who are far off, much more to you who are near. The text continues: [ὅσους ἂν προσκαλέσηται Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν], as many as the Lord our God shall call. No one reads it otherwise except the Ethiopic, which has: to all who are far off, and they shall call upon the Lord our God. Who here would not detect the boldest hand of some most shameless Pelagian, who, unable to bear the praise of divine grace, transferred it to human efforts?

units.la: VERS. 41. οἱ μὲν οὖν ἀσπάσως ὑποδεξάμενοι τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ.
units.tr: VERS. 41. Those then who gladly received his word [οἱ μὲν οὖν ἀσπάσως ὑποδεξάμενοι τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ].

units.la: Syrus & Arabs addiderunt, & crediderunt. Vulgatus non legit ἀσπάσως. Syrus & Arabs verterunt promte, parate, ܐܚܕܘ ܒܬܫܘܒܬܐ, nec praetereundum, οἱ μὲν οὖν verti a Syro ܐܟܘܬܘ ܕܐܝܢ, & quidam eorum, similiter ab Arabe. quod nequaquam rejiciendum. ut idem hic sit οἱ μὲν, quod οἱ δὲ Matth. 28. 17. οἱ δὲ ἐδίστασαν, quidam haesitabant.
units.tr: The Syriac and Arabic add "and believed." The Vulgate does not read ἀσπάσως. The Syriac and Arabic render it "promptly, readily," "(Syriac)" and "(Arabic)." It should also not be passed over that the Syriac rendered οἱ μὲν οὖν as "and some of them," "(Syriac)," and the Arabic does likewise. This is by no means to be rejected, so that here οἱ μὲν means the same as οἱ δὲ in Matthew 28:17, οἱ δὲ ἐδίστασαν [but some doubted].

units.la: IBID. Addita sunt die illo animae quasi τρισχίλιοι, ter mille.
units.tr: IBID. On that day there were added souls, about τρισχίλιοι, three thousand.

units.la: consentiunt lectiones omnes. Æthiopicus tamen habet ܡܐܬ ܬܠܬܡܐܐ, trecenta. In quo cum errorem deprehenderet incomparabilis vir Josephus Scaliger, notavit in margine pro ܡܐܬ legendum ܬܠܬܝܢ. nos potius mendum esse putamus (est enim mendosissima editio Æthiopica) in ܬܠܬ, tres, & pro eo legendum ܬܠܬܝܢ, triginta, ac vertendum, anima circiter trigesies centum, id est ter mille. quod ideo libentius annotavimus, ut errorem nostrum fateremur, quem in Appendice nostro ad Mar. 14. 21. commisimus. quum enim apud Æthiopicum pro ὥσπερ πνεῦμα λεγeremus, מאת חמש מאות, & ad Scaligeri emendationem, qui rursus in margine pro מאת substituerat אלף, magis quam ad rationem constructionis Æthiopicæ attenderemus, lapsum Interpreti impegimus, qui pro quinquies mille quingentos tantum dedisset, quum vertendus sit, quasi quinquagesies centum, id est, quinquies mille. alterum enim מאת חמשים dicendum fuerat. similiter Matt.15.38. מאת ארבע verteramus quadringentos, quum vertendum esset quadragesies centum, id est, quater mille. alterum enim מאת ארבעים dicendum. Sic infra Act. 4.4. & factus est numerus virorum qui crediderunt, quasi מאת חמש, quinquagesies centum, id est, quinquies mille.
units.tr: All the readings agree. The Ethiopic, however, has "(Ethiopic: mĕʾat salasa)," that is, trecenta, three hundred. When the incomparable Joseph Scaliger detected this error, he noted in the margin that "(Ethiopic: mĕʾat)" should be read as "thirty" (Ethiopic: sələtin). I think rather that the fault lies in the "three" (Ethiopic: salasa), since the Ethiopic edition is very faulty, and that "thirty" should be read in its place, so that it is to be rendered "about thirty hundred souls," that is, three thousand. I have noted this more willingly so that I may confess my own error, which I made in our Appendix on Mark 14:21. When, in the Ethiopic corresponding to ὥσπερ πνεῦμα [as a spirit], I had written מאת חמש מאות [meʾat ḥamesh meʾot], and paid more attention to Scaliger's emendation (who again in the margin had substituted אלף [elef, a thousand] for מאת) than to the construction of the Ethiopic idiom, I attributed to the translator a slip, since he had given only "five thousand five hundred," when it ought to be rendered "as fifty hundred," that is, five thousand. The phrase should have been מאת חמשים [meʾat ḥamishim]. Similarly at Matthew 15:38 I had rendered מאת ארבע [meʾat arbaʿ] as "four hundred," when it should have been rendered "forty hundred," that is, four thousand, for the phrase should have been מאת ארבעים [meʾat arbaʿim]. So below, at Acts 4:4, "and the number of men who believed was," as though מאת חמש [meʾat ḥamesh], "fifty hundred," that is, five thousand.

units.la: VERS. 42. Καὶ τῇ κοινωνίᾳ, ἐν τῇ κλάσει τοῦ ἄρτου, καὶ ταῖς προσευχαῖς.
units.tr: Vers. 42. And they continued in the fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and in the prayers. [Καὶ τῇ κοινωνίᾳ, ἐν τῇ κλάσει τοῦ ἄρτου, καὶ ταῖς προσευχαῖς.]

units.la: Vulgatus, & communicatione fractionis panis. unde tamen non colligo, variasse hujus loci Scripturam. sed explicuisse Interpretem, quomodo constructionem Græcam intelligendam arbitraretur. nempe τῇ κοινωνίᾳ ἐν τῇ κλάσει, communione & fractione, poni pro τῇ κοινωνίᾳ τῆς κλάσεως, communione fractionis, id est, communi fractione. sicut patera libabat & auro, id est, patera auri vel aurea. Idem de Syro & Arabe Interpretibus judico. nisi quod hi, mutato situ, preces dixerint ante fractionem. Nec sequitur Syrum pro ἄρτου legisse ܩܘܪܒܢܐ, quia apud ipsum extat ܠܚܡܐ ܕܩܘܪܒܢܐ, in fractione Eucharistia. Interpretatur potius, panem de quo hic agitur, non esse communem, sed S. Cœnæ, quæ in Ecclesiis Græcis, atque inde in Syriacis ܩܘܪܒܢܐ vulgo dicebatur.
units.tr: The Vulgate has and the communion of the breaking of bread. I do not conclude from this that the reading of the text varied. Rather, the translator explained how he thought the Greek construction should be understood. Namely, τῇ κοινωνίᾳ ἐν τῇ κλάσει [by the communion in the breaking] stands for τῇ κοινωνίᾳ τῆς κλάσεως [by the communion of the breaking], that is, common breaking, just as he poured a libation from a dish and of gold means a dish of gold, or a golden dish. I judge the same of the Syriac and Arabic translators, except that they, with the order changed, have put the prayers before the breaking. Nor does it follow that the Syriac read ἄρτου as qurbana, because in that version stands in the breaking of the Eucharist, lḥma dqurbana. Rather, it interprets the bread spoken of here as not common bread but the bread of the holy Supper, which in the Greek churches, and from them in the Syriac, was commonly called qurbana.

units.la: VERS. 43. Ἐγίνετο δὲ πάσῃ ψυχῇ φόβος. πολλὰ τε τέρατα καὶ σημεῖα διὰ τῶν ἀποστόλων ἐγίνετο.
units.tr: Vers. 43. And fear came upon every soul. And many wonders and signs were done through the apostles. [Ἐγίνετο δὲ πάσῃ ψυχῇ φόβος. πολλὰ τε τέρατα καὶ σημεῖα διὰ τῶν ἀποστόλων ἐγίνετο.]

units.la: Vulgatus, Fiebat autem omni anima timor. multa quoque prodigia & signa per Apostolos in Ierusalem fiebant: & metus erat magnus in universis. Cum qua lectione conferatur Arabs, qui sic habet, & fiebat timor in omni omni anima. fiebatque metus magnus super omnes, & signa multa fiebant per manus Apostolorum in Ierusalem. Syrus à recepta Græcorum exemplarium lectione quam & Chrysostomus expressit, nihil variat, nisi quod addiderit quoque in Ierusalem.
units.tr: The Vulgate has Fiebat autem omni anima timor. multa quoque prodigia & signa per Apostolos in Ierusalem fiebant: & metus erat magnus in universis. With this reading let the Arabic be compared, which runs thus: and fear came upon every soul. And great fear came upon all, and many signs were done by the hands of the Apostles in Jerusalem. The Syriac, from the received reading of the Greek copies, which Chrysostom also expressed, differs in nothing, except that it has also added in Jerusalem.

units.la: V e r s. 45. Καὶ τὰ κτήματα, ἡ πρᾶσις ὑπῆρχον ... Syrus, & quibus erat possessio, vendebant eam. quod annotavimus supra ad v. 42. hic rursus locum habet, Syrum nempe τὰ κτήματα ἡ πρᾶσις accepisse pro τὰ κτήματα τῶν πράσεων, quod jam tantundem valet atque καὶ οἷς τὰ κτήματα ὑπῆρχον, ὑπῆρχον αὐτῷ. atque ita Syrus vertit. possessio collective valet τὰ κτήματα. itaque non assentior Cl. Bezæ, affirmanti Syrum non legisse ἡ πρᾶσις. multo minus, Arabem non legisse, qui distinctè habet & agros suos, & quod erat ipsis. Vbi simul observandum, τὰ κτήματα Arabi esse bona immobilia, qualia sunt fundi, agri, prædia. τῆς πράσεως vero reliqua omnia bona. Certè pro שדה, ager, LXX κτῆμα dixerunt, Prov. 23.10. nec aliter usurpatur à Syracide c. 28. 27. ἀφίεσεν τὸ κτῆμα σου ἀλλότριος, sepi agrum tuum spinis. & c. 36. 25. ὁ οἶκος ... ὁ ἀγρὸς κτῆμα, ubi non est sepes, diripietur ager. quin & speciatim כרם, vineta, LXX dixerunt κτήματα, Prov. 31.16. Ofeæ 2.15. Joël 1.11. hinc est quod κτῆμα & χωρίον pro eodem sumantur Act. 5.1.8.
units.tr: Vers. 45. And their possessions and goods they sold [Καὶ τὰ κτήματα, ἡ πρᾶσις ὑπῆρχον ...]. The Syriac has and those to whom there was possession, sold it. What we noted above at v. 42 applies here again: the Syriac took τὰ κτήματα, ἡ πρᾶσις [ta ktēmata, hē prasis] as τὰ κτήματα τῶν πράσεων [ta ktēmata tōn praseōn], which already amounts to the same as καὶ οἷς τὰ κτήματα ὑπῆρχον, ὑπῆρχον αὐτῷ [kai hois ta ktēmata hyparchon, hyparchon autō], and so the Syriac translates. Possession taken collectively means τὰ κτήματα. Therefore I do not agree with the learned Beza, who affirms that the Syriac did not read ἡ πρᾶσις. Much less that the Arabic did not read it, which distinctly has and his fields, and what was his. Here one must observe that for the Arab τὰ κτήματα are immovable goods, such as estates, fields and farms, while τῆς πράσεως [tēs praseōs] means all the remaining goods. Certainly for the Hebrew שדה [sadeh], field, the Seventy said κτῆμα [ktēma], Prov. 23.10. The Son of Sirach uses it no differently in c. 28.27: ἀφίεσεν τὸ κτῆμα σου ἀλλότριος [aphiesen to ktēma sou allotrios], a stranger has let your field go, [and] you hedge your field with thorns. And c. 36.25: ὁ οἶκος ... ὁ ἀγρὸς κτῆμα [ho oikos ... ho agros ktēma], where there is no hedge, the field will be plundered. Indeed, specifically for כרם [kerem], vineyards, the Seventy said κτήματα [ktēmata], Prov. 31.16, Hos. 2.15, Joel 1.11. Hence it is that κτῆμα and χωρίον [chōrion] are taken for the same thing at Acts 5.1, 8.

units.la: V e r s. 46. Κλῶντες τε κατ' οἶκον ἄρτον. Arabs ... quod aliter verti nequit quam, & frangebant domi panem. البيت enim opponitur ipsis loco publico. ut si quærenti, ubi sit pater, respondeas esse في البيت, sensus est, domi esse. Ita & Syrus simpliciter vertit ... & domi frangebant panem. non existimarunt, sensum esse, eos per varias domos, nunc hîc nunc illic simul congregatos cibum sumpsisse, quod volunt qui vertunt domatim, sed κατ' οἶκον opponi τῷ ἱερῷ, ut sensus sit, eos quotidie in templo convenisse ad Deum colendum, domi vero cibum sumentes, id fecisse cum exultatione & simplicitate cordis. ita ut κατ' οἶκον simpliciter sit privatim. sic c. 5. v. 42. Πᾶσάν τε ἡμέραν ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ καὶ κατ' οἶκον οὐκ ἐπαύοντο διδάσκοντες, Quotidie autem in templo & privatim non cessabant docere. Porro pro κλῶντς ἄρτν Syrus habet [Syriac] oooi [Syriac], Trem. frangebant portionem. Boder. munus benedictum. Ferrarius, [Syriac] panis, placenta. est etiam, inquit, panis consecrationis: quem procul dubio intellexit Boder. per munus benedictum. Sacram enim Coenam, & Pontificii suam Missam, quam Sacramentum altaris indigetant, vocant [Syriac], Arabice الفديس الزبان, munus sanctum, interpretantes sic illud Mal. 1. 12. מנחה טהורה, munus mundum.
units.tr: Verse 46. Κλῶντες τε κατ' οἶκον ἄρτον [and breaking bread at home]. The Arabic ... cannot be translated otherwise than and they broke bread at home. For al-bayt is set against a public place: if, when someone asks where the father is, you answer that he is fi al-bayt, the sense is he is at home. So too the Syriac simply renders ... and at home they broke bread. They did not think the sense is that they gathered by turns in various houses, now here, now there, to take their food together, as those do who translate from house to house. Rather, κατ' οἶκον is opposed to τῷ ἱερῷ [the temple], so that the sense is that they met daily in the temple to worship God, but took their food at home, and did so with exultation and simplicity of heart. Thus κατ' οἶκον simply means privately. So in chapter 5, verse 42: Πᾶσάν τε ἡμέραν ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ καὶ κατ' οἶκον οὐκ ἐπαύοντο διδάσκοντες [And every day, in the temple and at home, they did not cease teaching], Quotidie autem in templo & privatim non cessabant docere. Further, for κλῶντες ἄρτον the Syriac has a word which Tremellius renders they broke a portion, and Bodecker a blessed gift. Ferrarius gives the Syriac word as bread, cake, and says it also means bread of consecration, which Bodecker undoubtedly understood by a blessed gift. For the Papists call the Lord's Supper, and their own Mass, which they name the Sacrament of the altar, by the Arabic al-qurbān al-quds, a holy offering, interpreting in this way the passage in Malachi 1:12, מנחה טהורה [minchah tehorah], a pure offering, as munus mundum.

units.la: Sequitur, ἢ μεταλαμβανων τροφῆς ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει ἐκ ἀφελότητι καρδίας. Sic etiam distinxerunt Vulgatus & Arabs. At Syrus illud καὶ ἀφελότητι καρδίας differpsit à praecedentibus, ac conjunxit cum sequentibus, & in simplicitate cordis sui laudabant Deum. Hebraicè dicitur בתם הלב, Syrus [Syriac] [Syriac], in puritate cordis sui.
units.tr: There follows: ἢ μεταλαμβανων τροφῆς ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει ἐκ ἀφελότητι καρδίας [ē metalambanōn trophēs en agalliasei ek aphelotēti kardias], and took food with exultation and simplicity of heart. The Vulgate and the Arabic also divided the sentence in this way. But the Syriac separated καὶ ἀφελότητι καρδίας [kai aphelotēti kardias] from what precedes and joined it with what follows: and in the simplicity of their heart they praised God. In Hebrew it is said betom ha-lev [בתם הלב], and the Syriac [Syriac] [Syriac], in the integrity of their heart.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: VERS. 1. Ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ ἐπὶ τὸ συνάγειν. De tribus precandi horis, tertia, sexta, & nona vide ad hunc locum Drusium in Praeteritis. Mahomedani autem quinquies in die precantur. 1. [Arabic], in diluculo. 2. [Arabic], oriente sole. 3. [Arabic], meridie. 4. [Arabic], inter meridiem & vesperam. 5. [Arabic], occidente sole. Et haec quidem sunt instítu-
units.tr: VERSE 1. Together, at the same place [Ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ]. On the three hours of prayer, the third, sixth and ninth, see Drusius on this passage in his Praeterita. The Mohammedans, however, pray five times a day: (1) at dawn [al-fajr]; (2) at sunrise [al-shurūq]; (3) at midday [al-ẓuhr]; (4) between midday and evening [al-ʿaṣr]; (5) at sunset [al-maghrib]. These are the prescribed observances of the Mohammedan institution, and so of necessary law.

units.la: institutionis Mahomedicæ, adeoque juris necessarii. Quibus accedere duæ aliæ precationes, 1. لاَ الْحُضْر, in vespera, nempe 1½ hora post occasum solis. 2. الْعِشَاء, circa mediam noctem. hæc sunt السُّنَّة, traditionis seu consuetudinis, adeoque liberæ observationis. quæ tamen ad imitationem Mahomedis ac primorum ejus assectarum à devotis observantur.
units.tr: To these are added two other prayers: (1) al-ḥuḍr, in the evening, namely an hour and a half after sunset; (2) al-ʿishāʾ, about midnight. These are the sunna, that is, of tradition or custom, and so of free observance, yet the devout keep them in imitation of Mohammed and his first followers.

units.la: VERS. 2. Quidam autem vir claudus ab utero matris sua portabatur: quem ponebant καθ' ἡμέραν, quotidie ad portam templi &c.
units.tr: VERSE 2. And a certain man, lame from his mother's womb, was carried, whom they laid daily [καθ' ἡμέραν] at the gate of the temple, etc.

units.la: Syrus, Ecce, virum quendam claudum ab utero matris sua portabant quidam, qui soliti erant adferre & ponere eum in porta templi. non expressit quidem ad verbum illud καθ' ἡμέραν. rem tamen dixit. nam pro qui ponebant eum quotidie, dixit, qui soliti erant eum ponere. Syrum secutus est verbotenus Arabs. quod non aliam ob causam attuli, quam ne variæ lectiones fingantur, ubi nihil necesse est.
units.tr: The Syriac: "Behold, certain men were carrying a certain lame man from his mother's womb, who were accustomed to bring him and set him at the gate of the temple." It does not express the words καθ' ἡμέραν verbatim, yet it conveys the sense: instead of "who laid him daily," it says "who were accustomed to lay him." The Arab follows the Syriac word for word. I mention this only so that variant readings are not invented where there is no need.

units.la: VERS. 11. Κεράτιν⁠... ἡ ἴσχυς αὐτοῦ χωλὸς τῆς πίστεως ἐπὶ ἰωάννου.
units.tr: VERSE 11. Holding on to Peter and John [κρατοῦντος ... ἐπὶ Ἰωάννου], the lame man of faith [χωλὸς τῆς πίστεως] ...

units.la: Syrus & Arabs non legerunt τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ χωλὰς. ut nec Vulgatus, qui præterea vertit quum tenerent κεράτιν ἐπὶ ἰωάννου. quod procul dubio mendosum, etsi & in Æthiopico candem lectionem reperiam. quomodo enim populus dici potest tenuisse Petrum & Johannem, quum sequatur demum, eos accurrisse ad ipsos?
units.tr: The Syriac and the Arab did not read "his strength, lame" [τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ χωλὰς], nor did the Vulgate, which further translates "when they held on to [κρατεῖν] John." This is undoubtedly corrupt, although I find the same reading in the Ethiopic. For how can the people be said to have held Peter and John, when it follows only afterwards that they ran up to them?

units.la: VERS. 13. Κεράτιν ἐκάνυ ἀποδοῦναι. Syrus ... quod nec Trem. nec Boder. in Parisiensi recte verterunt, sed recte in Regiis, quum ipse æquum judicaret eum esse absolvendum.nam in prima Conjug. ... est decet, convenit, justum & æquum est. in secunda ergo ... est pro re decenti, convenienti, justa & æqua habere. alibi tamen est justificare, ubi ad personam refertur & casum persónæ post se habet. Arabs eodem modo, idque supra (vel contra) quod ipse conveniens judicasset dimittere eum, id est, reclamante judicis sententia, qui eum dimittendum judicavit.
units.tr: VERSE 13. Having judged it right to release him [κρίναντος ἐκείνου ἀπολῦσαι]. The Syriac ... This Tremellius and Beza did not translate correctly in the Paris edition, but they did correctly in the Royal one: "when he himself judged that he ought to be acquitted." For in the first conjugation the verb means "to be fitting, suitable, just and equitable." In the second conjugation, then, it means "to hold as fitting, suitable, just and equal." Elsewhere, however, it means "to justify," where it is referred to a person and governs the case of the person after it. The Arab likewise has it: "and that against (or contrary to) what he himself had judged fitting, to dismiss him," that is, the judge's sentence being contrary, he who judged that he was to be dismissed.

units.la: VERS. 19. 20. Οπως αν ἐλθωσι καιροὶ ἀναψύξεως &c. καὶ ἀποστείλῃ τὸ προκεκηρυγμένον ὑμῖν Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν. Vulgatus & Eras. ut cum venerint tempora refrigerationis, &c. & miserit, &c. Beza, postquam venerint, &c. & miserit, &c. Exististimarunt nempe ad primum Christi adventum esse referenda, quae hic dicuntur. At Syrus & Arabs existimarunt, continuari hic promissionem inchoatam in praecedenti εἰς τὴν ἐξαλειφθῆναι ὑμῶν τὰς ἁμαρτίας, & ὅπως ἂν tantum copulare secundam promissionem primæ: quapropter per copulam & transtulerunt, & veniant vobis tempora quietis a conspectu Domini, & mittat vobis eum, qui paratus erat vobis, Iesum Christum. nempe ad secundum Christi adventum, quo mittendus denuo e coelis exspectatur, quaque adventus vere dabit refrigerii tempora Ecclesiae, haec retulerunt. Aethiopicus similiter. Nec video cur non id sequamur, quum usus construtioque postulent, ὅπως ἂν ἐλθωσι verti, ut veniant. nec obstat, quod ὅπως ἂν futurum dicat, ἐλθωσι autem & ἀποστείλῃ sint aoristi. solet enim passim cum aoristis eo sensu construi. ut Matt. 6. 5. ὅπως ἂν φανῶσι, ut appareant. Luc. 2. 35. ὅπως ἂν ἀποκαλυφθῶσιν, ut revelentur. Act. 15. 17. ὅπως ἂν ἐκζητήσωσι, ut requirant. Rom. 3. 4. ὅπως ἂν δικαιωθῇς, ut justisiceris. & passim alibi. Nam ὅπως ἂν valere postquam, nondum inducor ut credam. statuere autem hic ἀναπόδοτον, quod Erasmus volebat, durum est, nec necessarium, quum res ipsa interpretationem, quam verba praeferunt, facile admittat. Syrus porro, quem sequitur Arabs, pro προκεκηρυγμένον habet ... eum qui praparatus erat vobis. legit procul dubio προκεχειρισμένον. ἐχσπιλμένον, prout omnes veteres Græci codices, quos Beza legisse ait, scriptum habent, & Chrysostomus legit, qui & ὅπως αὐτὸ ἔλθωσι interpretatur sicut nos. ait enim Apostolum iis verbis κέρδος ἐπάγει, lucrum addere, quod facturi sint, si respiscant. quinque præcedenti concione resurrectionem & ascensionem Christi in cœlum innuerat, jam hic τῶν ἐμφανῆ παρουσίαν illustrem ejus adventum exponere, quum addit ἐκ Ἁπτελῆ &c. Æthiopicus tempora refrigerii explicat per tempus misericordiæ, & τὸ ἀνεκλείψιμον, quod procul dubio cum Syro & Arabe legit, vertit quem præunxit. nisi forte legerit, τὸν ἀνεκλείψιμον.
units.tr: VERSES 19, 20. So that times of refreshing may come [ὅπως ἂν ἔλθωσι καιροὶ ἀναψύξεως] &c., and he may send the Jesus Christ who has been preached to you [καὶ ἀποστείλῃ τὸ προκεκηρυγμένον ὑμῖν Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν]. The Vulgate and Erasmus render: "when the times of refreshing shall have come," &c., "and he shall send," &c. Beza: "after the times of refreshing shall have come," &c., "and he shall send," &c. They judged, that is, that what is said here refers to the first coming of Christ. But the Syriac and the Arab judged that the promise begun in the preceding words, "for the blotting out of your sins" [εἰς τὸ ἐξαλειφθῆναι ὑμῶν τὰς ἁμαρτίας], continues here, and that ὅπως ἂν merely links the second promise to the first. Therefore by the conjunction "and" they translated: "and there may come to you times of rest from the presence of the Lord, and he may send to you him who was prepared for you, Jesus Christ." That is, they referred these things to the second coming of Christ, when he is awaited to be sent again from heaven, and when that coming will truly bring times of refreshing to the Church. The Ethiopic likewise. Nor do I see why we should not follow this, since usage and construction require that ὅπως ἂν ἔλθωσι be rendered "that they may come." Nor is it an objection that ὅπως ἂν takes the future, while ἔλθωσι and ἀποστείλῃ are aorists, for it is often construed with aorists in that sense: as Matt. 6.5, ὅπως ἂν φανῶσι, "that they may appear"; Luke 2.35, ὅπως ἂν ἀποκαλυφθῶσιν, "that they may be revealed"; Acts 15.17, ὅπως ἂν ἐκζητήσωσι, "that they may seek"; Rom. 3.4, ὅπως ἂν δικαιωθῇς, "that you may be justified"; and passim elsewhere. For I am not yet persuaded to believe that ὅπως ἂν means "after." To posit here an ἀναπόδοτον, as Erasmus wished, is harsh and unnecessary, since the matter itself readily admits the interpretation that the words themselves suggest. Further, the Syriac, which the Arab follows, has for προκεκηρυγμένον "him who was prepared for you" [eum qui praeparatus erat vobis]. It undoubtedly read προκεχειρισμένον, not προκεκηρυγμένον, as all the ancient Greek codices, which Beza says he read, have it; and Chrysostom read it so too, and he interprets ὅπως αὐτὸ ἔλθωσι as we do. For he says that the Apostle by these words adds gain [κέρδος ἐπάγει], that is, the benefit they will receive if they repent. In the preceding sermon he had hinted at Christ's resurrection and ascension into heaven; now he sets forth his manifest presence, his illustrious coming, when he adds "from the ..." [ἐκ ...] &c. The Ethiopic explains "times of refreshing" as "time of mercy," and it renders τὸ ἀνεκλείψιμον, which it doubtless read with the Syriac and the Arab, as "whom he has anticipated." Unless perhaps it read τὸν ἀνεκλείψιμον.

units.la: V E R S. 22. Μωσῆς γὰρ ἔφη πρὸς αὐτὸν πατέρας ἡμῶν. Concordant Arabs & Æthiopicus. at Vulgatus & Syrus non legerunt πρὸς αὐτὸν πατέρας.
units.tr: VERSE 22. For Moses said to them [πρὸς αὐτὸν] "our fathers." The Arab and the Ethiopic agree. But the Vulgate and the Syriac did not read πρὸς αὐτὸν πατέρας.

units.la: V E R S. 26. Misit eum, qui benediceret vobis, ἐν τῷ ἀποστρέφειν ἕκαστον ἀπὸ τῶν πονηριῶν ὑμῶν, Vulg. ut convertat se unusquisque a nequitia sua. id est, εἰς τὸ ἀποστρέφειν. Beza, avertente se unoquoque, id est, ἀποστρέφοντα ἕκαστον. Etsi ἀποστρέφειν in N. Test. intransitive pro converti, aut convertere se non usurpetur, fateor tamen apud LXX Interpretes usurpari non raro pro שׁוּב, reverti, & pro הָשִׁיב, converti. quapropter Syrus quoque & Arabs eo sensu hic acceperunt. sed nihil videtur impedire, quominus transitiva, eâque usitatiori significatione vertamus, avertendo unumquemque a pravitatibus vestris, בְּשׁוּבְכֶם מִדְּרָכֵיכֶם, ut ad Christum referatur, & modus indicetur quo benedicturus ipsis missus erat, nempe avertendo ipsos a pravitatibus. id enim muneris Christi esse, docet Paulus Tit. 2. 14. & passim.
units.tr: VERSE 26. He sent him to bless you, in turning each one of you away from your wickedness [ἐν τῷ ἀποστρέφειν ἕκαστον ἀπὸ τῶν πονηριῶν ὑμῶν]. The Vulgate: "that he may convert each one of you from his wickedness," that is, reading εἰς τὸ ἀποστρέφειν. Beza: "each one turning himself away," that is, reading ἀποστρέφοντα ἕκαστον. I grant that in the New Testament ἀποστρέφειν is not used intransitively to mean "to be converted" or "to convert oneself." Yet I admit that among the Septuagint interpreters it is often used for שׁוּב, "to return," and for הָשִׁיב, "to convert." Therefore the Syriac and the Arab also took it in that sense here. But nothing seems to prevent us from rendering it transitively, in its more common meaning: "by turning each one of you away from your wickedness," בְּשׁוּבְכֶם מִדְּרָכֵיכֶם, so that it refers to Christ, and the manner is indicated in which he was sent to bless them, namely by turning them away from their wickednesses. For Paul teaches that this is the office of Christ, Titus 2.14, and elsewhere.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: V E R S. 1. Καὶ ὁ στρατηγὸς ἱερεύς. Beza, & præfectus templo. Vulg. & Erasmus, & magistratus templi. puto eos magistratus plur. num. accepisse. quasi legissent οἱ στρατηγοί.
units.tr: VERSE 1. "And the captain of the temple" [ὁ στρατηγὸς ἱερεύς]. Beza translates "and the prefect of the temple"; the Vulgate and Erasmus translate "and the magistrates of the temple." I think they took the word as plural, as if they had read οἱ στρατηγοί.

units.la: Syrus certe, Arabs & Æthiopicus plurali num. verterunt, ille ⟨Syriac⟩, ἄρχοντες, prefecti, magistratus. iste ⟨Syriac⟩, capita, supremi. hic ⟨Syriac⟩, prefecti. Ϝ πρεσβύτεροι ⟨Greek⟩ mentio fit Luc. 22. 52. porro de usu vocis πρεσβύτερος nihil annotamus, quia fusè satis id fecit Drusius in Præteritis.
units.tr: The Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic certainly rendered it in the plural. The first has the Syriac word for rulers, which he renders prefects, magistrates. The second has the Syriac word for heads, rendered heads, chief men. The third has the Syriac word rendered prefects. The elders [πρεσβύτεροι] are mentioned at Luke 22:52. As for the use of the word πρεσβύτερος, I make no note, since Drusius has treated it quite fully in his Praeteritis.

units.la: VERS. 3. Ἡ ἐπιστήμη ... Syrus ⟨Syriac⟩ ⟨Syriac⟩. Tremel. quia prope erat vespera. verto, quia appropinquaverat vespera. aliud est, appropinquaverat, aliud appropinquabat. sensus est, jam erat vespera. vide Comment. nostrum ad Euangelistas p. 112. 113.
units.tr: VERSE 3. "Now the evening" [ἡ ἑσπέρα]. The Syriac has two words for this. Tremellius: because evening was near. I translate: because evening had drawn near. One is had drawn near, the other was drawing near. The sense is that evening had already come. See our commentary on the Evangelists, pp. 112–113.

units.la: VERS. 5. Καὶ γραμματεῖς εἰς Ἱερουσαλήμ. Hæc apud Arabem editionis Erpenianæ non desunt. in exemplari, quod Fr. Junius transtulit, videntur abfuisse. apud Syrum deest εἰς Ἱερουσαλήμ. apud Æthiopicum nihil horum deest.
units.tr: VERSE 5. "And the scribes in Jerusalem" [Καὶ γραμματεῖς εἰς Ἱερουσαλήμ]. These words are not lacking in the Arabic of the Erpenius edition. In the copy that Francis Junius translated they seem to have been absent. In the Syriac the words "into Jerusalem" are lacking. In the Ethiopic none of these is lacking.

units.la: VERS. 8. Israëlis. Syrus, Arabs & Æthiopicus addunt ἀκούσατε, audite. Nec dubium, quin optima veteris Interpretis exemplaria idem legerint. monent enim Correctiones Romanæ, non facile omittendum esse verbum audite.
units.tr: VERSE 8. "Israelites." The Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic add ἀκούσατε, "hear." There is no doubt that the best copies of the old translator read the same, for the Roman Corrections warn that the word "hear" should not easily be omitted.

units.la: VERS. 9. Ἐν τίνι ἔτῳ σέσωσται. Erasm. qua ratione ista salvus factus sit. Beza, quo modo. quasi ἐν τίνι τρόπῳ. Arabs ⟨Arabic⟩, ad quid, quorsum. non satis appositè. Syrus melius, ⟨Syriac⟩, per quid. id est, qua virtute. Vulgatus, In quo, relicta ambiguitate quæ est in Græco. potest enim ad rem referri, vel ad personam, ut sensus sit, vel per quid, vel per quem. quæsiverant enim γʹ. 7. ἐν ποίᾳ δυνάμει, qua virtute. ei respondere hic potest, per quid. quæsiverant porro ἐν τίνι ὀνόματι, in quo nomine, id est, in cujus personæ nomine: ei respondere hic potest, per quem. hoc sane Petrus responsione sua præcipuè tangit, quum in nomine Jesu Christi Nazareni id factum ait.
units.tr: VERSE 9. "By what means has this man been made whole" [ἐν τίνι σέσωσται]. Erasmus: by what means this man has been made whole. Beza: in what way, as if it were ἐν τίνι τρόπῳ. The Arabic has to what, whither, which is not very apt. The Syriac is better: by what, that is, by what power. The Vulgate has In quo, leaving the ambiguity that is in the Greek. For it can refer to the thing or to the person, so that the sense is either by what or by whom. For at verse 7 they had asked "by what power" [ἐν ποίᾳ δυνάμει], by what power, to which the answer here can be by what. Again, they had asked "in what name" [ἐν τίνι ὀνόματι], in what name, that is, in whose name, to which the answer here can be by whom. Peter certainly touches especially on this in his answer, when he says that it was done in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth.

units.la: E
units.tr: E

units.la: VERS. 14. Οὐδὲν ἀχος ἀντιπαρ. Arabs فلم يطيقوا ان يذولوا ... nõn potuerunt dicere quicquam mali contra eos.
units.tr: VERSE 14. "They had nothing to say against it" [Οὐδὲν εἶχον ἀντειπεῖν]. The Arabic: they could not bring themselves to say anything evil against them.

units.la: Doct. vir Fr. Junius, qui & Arabica, quod tunc multum erat, degustaverat, transtulit, non inveniebant quid dicerent, ut autoritate abuterentur in illos. quum scilicet ambigeret, quid عربيبus esset, derivavit perperam ab Hebr. דמה, dominari, autoritate uti. quum malum significet. Non quod animus nobis sit universam viri maximi translationem ad trutinam revocare, sed in iis solummodo locis, ubi notæ Cl. Bezæ, quæ in omnium manibus versantur, autoritate summi viri falluntur, aliosque in errorem inducere possent, lectorem monere.
units.tr: The learned man Francis Junius, who had also tasted Arabic, which was then much in vogue, translated: they did not find what to say, so that they might abuse their authority against them. Since he was unsure what the Arabic word meant, he wrongly derived it from the Hebrew [דמה], to rule, to exercise authority, although the word signifies harm. It is not that we intend to call the whole translation of that great man into question, but only to warn the reader in those places where the notes of the renowned Beza, which are in everyone's hands, are misled by the authority of so great a man and could lead others into error.

units.la: VERS. 20. Non enim possumus, quæ vidimus & audivimus, non loqui.
units.tr: VERSE 20. For we cannot but speak what we have seen and heard.

units.la: Arabs alio sensu, لا ... nam non possumus loqui, nisi quod vidimus & audivimus. repugnant huic lectioni exemplaria Græca, Chrysostomus, Syrus, Vulgatus, & res ipsa. Negant enim licere sibi mandato Synedrii morem gerere, quia divino mandato tenentur, quæ viderunt & audiverunt, loqui.
units.tr: The Arabic has a different sense: for we cannot speak except what we have seen and heard. The Greek copies, Chrysostom, the Syriac, the Vulgate and the thing itself are against this reading. For they deny that it is lawful for them to obey the order of the Sanhedrin, since they are bound by a divine command to speak what they have seen and heard.

units.la: VERS. 21. ο᾽ν πάντες ιδόξαζον τ θεὸν ἐπὶ τῷ γεγονότι. Sic Chrysostomus, Syrus, Arabs & Æthiopicus quoque legerunt. Mirum ergo unde Vulgatus, quia omnes clarificabant id quod factum fuerat, in eo quod acciderat. VERS. 25. Διὰ φύματ@. Ἀαβίδ ... Vulg. per os patris nostri David pueri tui. sic Arabs quoque & Æthiopicus inseruerunt patris nostri. παιδὸς autem verterunt servi. VERS. 36. Βαρνάβας ὁ ἐπι μεθερμηνευόμενος, υἱὸς παρακλήσεως. Syrus scripsit ..., בר נחמא. Drusius suspicatur, id usurpatum fuisse pro בר נחמא, & hoc per syncopen pro בר נחמא, filius consolationis. quod mihi valde alienum videtur. Beza mavult ab Hebr. נבא, prophetare deducere, quia prophetandi munus exhortationem & consolationem complectitur, quod utrumque nomine ⲥⲁⲣⲁⲕⲗⲏⲥⲱⲥ declaratur. At quamvis munus prophetæ utraque ista functione constet, neutram tamen Hebræorum גנב significat, adeoque cum interpretatione Apostoli non convenit, apud Arabes גנב est annunciare, indicare, narrare. hinc esset, filius annunciationis. propius accedit Arabum נבה, hortari. ut נחמה sit υἱὸς παρακλήσεως, filius adhortationis. Sed quia prior compositionis vox est Syriaca (נב enim non est Arabicum, ubi filius בר dicitur) præstat & alteram vocem à Syris arcessere. Junius vult consolationem Syris dici Nabba: à verbo παρακαλῶ anomalo beja consolari. agnoscimus Syrorum ܢܚܡܐ, נחמא, consolatus est. at נחמא nabba non agnoscimus, quippe quod à præcedenti verbo nec formatur, nec formari potest. consolationem ܢܚܡܬܐ, נחמתא dicunt. Nos ab eodem verbo sic deducimus. à נחם, futurum tertiæ personæ est ינחם. ut autem apud Arabes plerumque, ita & non raro apud Hebræos & Syros futurum habet vim participii præsentis. hinc ergo ינחם, & compendii causa בן נחם, filius consolans. hoc amplectemur, donec quis melius suggesserit.
units.tr: VERSE 21. "Because all glorified God for what had happened" [ὅτι πάντες ἐδόξαζον τὸν θεὸν ἐπὶ τῷ γεγονότι]. So Chrysostom, the Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic also read. It is strange, then, where the Vulgate gets because all were glorifying what had been done, in that which had happened. VERSE 25. "Through the mouth of David our father, your servant" [Διὰ στόματος Δαβὶδ παιδός σου]. The Vulgate: by the mouth of our father David, your servant. So the Arabic and the Ethiopic also inserted our father, but they rendered παιδός as servant. VERSE 36. "Barnabas, who is called by interpretation, son of consolation" [Βαρνάβας ὁ ἐπιμεθερμηνευόμενος υἱὸς παρακλήσεως]. The Syriac has written [בר נחמא]. Drusius suspects that this was used for [בר נחמא], and that this, by syncope, stood for [בר נחמא], son of consolation, which seems to me quite foreign. Beza prefers to derive it from the Hebrew [נבא], to prophesy, because the office of prophesying embraces exhortation and consolation, both of which are expressed by the word [παράκλησις]. Yet although the office of prophet consists of both these functions, neither of them is what the Hebrew [גנב] signifies, and so it does not agree with the Apostle's interpretation. Among the Arabs [גנב] means to announce, to indicate, to narrate; hence it would be son of announcement. Closer is the Arabic [נבה], to exhort, so that [נחמה] would be son of exhortation. But since the first element of the compound is Syriac (for [נב] is not Arabic, where "son" is [בר]), it is better to draw the second word from the Syriac too. Junius wants the Syriac word for consolation to be Nabba, from the irregular verb parakaleō, to console [beja]. We recognise the Syriac (nḥmʾ), [נחמא], he consoled. But we do not recognise nabba [נחמא], since it is neither formed from the preceding verb nor can be formed from it. They say consolation (nḥmtʾ), [נחמתא]. We deduce it from the same verb as follows. From [נחם], the future of the third person is [ינחם]. As among the Arabs for the most part, so also not rarely among the Hebrews and the Syrians, the future has the force of a present participle. Hence [ינחם], and for brevity [בן נחם], son consoling. We shall embrace this until someone suggests something better.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: VERS. 1. Ἀναγίας. Hebraice חנה, gratia Domini, aut gratiosus Domini. Σαπφείρη Syriacè ܥܦܪܐ, quod Hebraicè dagesch habet יפה, pulchra. κῆπος rectè Vulgatus vertit agrum. ut & Syrus atque Arabs כרם. vide supra ad c. 2. ψ. 45. Æthiopicus specialius כרם, vineam, quomodo supra ἀμπελών verterat c. 1. 18. & infra ἀμπελῶνα vertet v. 8. quia nempe prædia terræ Canaan fere erant vineta. Sic & pro כרמים, vineis, LXX Interpretes dixerunt κήπους, Prov. 31. 16. Osee 2. 15. Joël 1. 11. & χωρίον 1 Paral. 27. 27.
units.tr: VERS. 1. Ananias: in Hebrew חנה [Chanah], "grace of the Lord" or "gracious to the Lord." Sapphira: in Syriac 'pirā, which in Hebrew has a dagesh, יפה [yafeh], "beautiful." The Vulgate rightly renders κῆπος [kēpos] as "field," as the Syrian and the Arab also do with כרם [karem], "vineyard." See above on chapter 2, verse 45. The Ethiopic translator, more specifically, uses karem, "vineyard," as he rendered ἀμπελών [ampelōn] in chapter 1, verse 18, and as he will render ἀμπελῶνα [ampelōna] in verse 8, because the estates in the land of Canaan were mostly vineyards. So too, for כרמים [karmim], "vineyards," the Seventy translated κήπους [kēpous], "gardens" (Prov. 31:16; Hos. 2:15; Joel 1:11), and χωρίον [chōrion] (1 Chron. 27:27).

units.la: VERS. 2. Καὶ ἐνεσφίαν ἐπὶ τῆς πηγῆς. Syrus & Arabs, cum uno verbo commodè non possent, duobus id expresferunt, & cepit aliquid de pretio & occultavit, id est, clam surripuit.
units.tr: VERS. 2. And kept back part of the price: the Syrian and the Arab, since they could not conveniently express this in one word, used two, "took something of the price and hid it," that is, secretly stole it.

units.la: VERS. 3. Διὰ τὶ ἐπλήρωσεν ὁ Σατανᾶς τὴν καρδίαν σου. Vulgatus non recte, cur tentavit Satanas cor tuum. Erasmus, Beza & Arabs recte ad verbum, cur implevit cor tuum. Syrus, implevit in corde tuo. quae phrasis quid apud Syrum valeat, vide in Comment. nostro ad Euangelia, p. 463. 464. 465. Beza implevit accipit pro prorsus occupavit. nobis implere cor alterius est audacem eum reddere. implere cor suum, audacem fieri. Huc pertinet illud Regis Assueri, Esth 7. 5. מִי הוּא זֶה אֲשֶׁר מְלֵא לִבּוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת כֵּן, quis hic est, qui implevit cor suum (vel quem implevit cor ejus) ad faciendum sic? id est, qui tam audacis animi sit, ut hoc facere sustineat. recte Graeci, τίς ἀτὸς ἐς ἐπλήρωσεν τὴν καρδίαν... talis est illud Eccles. 8. 11. Quia non fit sententia de opere malo celeriter, עַל כֵּן מָלֵא לֵב בְּנֵי הָאָדָם לַעֲשׂוֹת רָע, propterea impletur cor filiorum hominis ad faciendum malum, id est audax fit cor. audacia enim implet cor turgidumque reddit fervidis spiritibus, qui extrorsum prorumpentes, membra exteriora, praesertim linguam & manus ad quaevis audenda impellunt. nihil enim metuit cor, spiritibus plenum. unde recte Vulgatus mentem Ecclesiastis expressit, cum vertit, absque timore ullo filii hominum perpetrant mala. Optime autem LXX, Διὰ τῆν ἐπληροφορίαν καρδία ὑῶν & ἀνθρώπων ἐν αὐτῆς & τοιῆσαι τὰ πνηρά. recte κὸ verterunt ἐπληροφορήθη. duplex enim est πληροφορία, plenitudo. una τῆς πίστεως, fidei, qua cor fidelium, sanctis spiritibus ex firmissimis Dei promissionibus repletum, fideliter atque intrepide quaevis adversa contemnit. altera τῆς θρασύτητος, audacia, qua cor prophanorum, temerariis spiritibus ex vana incolumitatis spe repletum, sine metu mala audet. Eo in loco hic erat Ananias, cujus cor diabolus temerariis istis audaciae spiritibus ita repleverat, ut fideliter admodum & sine metu vel Spiritui S. mentiri auderet. ἐπληρώθη itaque idem hic quod
units.tr: VERS. 3. Why has Satan filled your heart? The Vulgate, not rightly, has "why has Satan tempted your heart." Erasmus, Beza and the Arab rightly render it literally, "why has he filled your heart." The Syriac has "filled in your heart." What this phrase means in Syriac, see our commentary on the Gospels, pp. 463–465. Beza takes "filled" to mean "utterly occupied." For us, to fill another's heart is to make him bold, and to fill one's own heart is to become bold. To this belongs the saying of King Ahasuerus, Esth. 7:5: מִי הוּא זֶה אֲשֶׁר מְלֵא לִבּוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת כֵּן [mi hu zeh asher mele libo la'asot ken], "who is he, who has filled his heart to do so?" That is, who has a spirit so bold that he dares to do this. The Greeks rightly say τίς ... ἐπλήρωσεν τὴν καρδίαν [tis ... eplērōsen tēn kardian], "who has filled the heart." Similar is Eccles. 8:11: "Because sentence is not executed speedily against an evil work," עַל כֵּן מָלֵא לֵב בְּנֵי הָאָדָם לַעֲשׂוֹת רָע [al ken male lev benei ha'adam la'asot ra], "therefore the heart of the sons of men is filled to do evil," that is, the heart becomes bold. For boldness fills the heart and makes it swollen and hot with spirits, which, breaking outward, drive the outer members, especially the tongue and hands, to dare anything. A heart full of spirits fears nothing. Hence the Vulgate rightly expressed the mind of the Preacher when it rendered: "without any fear the sons of men commit evil." The Seventy render very well: Διὰ τὴν ἐπληροφορίαν καρδίας ... [dia tēn eplērophorian kardias], "through the full assurance of the heart," and they rightly translated the Hebrew verb by ἐπληροφορήθη [eplērophorēthē]. For πληροφορία [plērophoria], "fullness," is twofold. One is of faith (τῆς πίστεως [tēs pisteōs]), by which the heart of believers, filled with holy spirits from the most certain promises of God, faithfully and fearlessly despises all adversities. The other is of audacity (τῆς θρασύτητος [tēs thrasutētos]), by which the heart of the profane, filled with rash spirits from a vain hope of safety, dares evil without fear. In that place was Ananias, whose heart the devil had so filled with these rash spirits of audacity that he dared to lie, quite confidently and without fear, even to the Holy Spirit. Therefore ἐπληρώθη [eplērōthē] here means the same as

units.la: {y} ... quod ἐπληροφόρηςε, fidens reddidit. habet enim utique θρασύτης, audacia fidentiam. neque aliud est θρασύς, audax, nisi ὁ ἐν τῷ παρρησίᾳ ὑπερεξεχυκὼς, qui in fidendo excedit. ut docet Arist. Ethic. l. 2. Sequitur, ψεύσασθαι σε τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον. ψεύσασθαι cum Accusativo. at ÿf. seq. cum Dativo, eodem sensu. Sic LXX, Esa. 57. 11. ἐψεύσω με, mentita es mihi. 2 Reg. 4. 16. μὴ ἀψεύσῃ τῷ δούλῳ σου, ne mentiaris ancillæ tuæ. vides cum Accusativo. accipe cum Dativo, Pf. 89. 35. ἐν τῷ Δαυὶδ ψεύσονται, si Davidi mentiar. Pf. 78. 40. γλῶσσα αὐτῶν ἐψεύσαντο αὐτῷ, lingua sua mentiti sunt ei.
units.tr: {y} ... what ἐπληροφόρησε [eplērophorēse] means: "made confident." For θρασύτης [thrasutēs], "audacity," certainly gives confidence. Nor does θρασύς [thrasus], "bold," mean anything else than one who "exceeds in confidence" (ὁ ἐν τῷ παρρησίᾳ ὑπερεξεχυκώς [ho en tō parrēsia hyperexechykōs]), as Aristotle teaches in Ethics, book 2. It follows: ψεύσασθαι σε τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον [pseusasthai se to pneuma to hagion], "to lie to the Holy Spirit." ψεύσασθαι [pseusasthai] takes the accusative, but in the following verse it takes the dative, with the same meaning. So the Seventy, Isa. 57:11: ἐψεύσω με [epseusō me], "you have lied to me." 2 Kings 4:16: μὴ ἀψεύσῃ τῷ δούλῳ σου [mē apseusē tō doulō sou], "do not lie to your servant," where you see the accusative. Take it with the dative: Ps. 89:35, ἐν τῷ Δαυὶδ ψεύσονται [en tō Dauid pseusontai], "if I lie to David"; Ps. 78:40, γλῶσσα αὐτῶν ἐψεύσαντο αὐτῷ [glōssa autōn epseusanto autō], "their tongue lied to him."

units.la: VERS. 4.
units.tr: VERS. 4.

units.la: Οὐχὶ μένον, σοὶ ἔμενε; ἓ ωραλῆν ἐν τῇ σῇ ἐξουσίᾳ ὑπῆρχε; Sensum valde bene expressit Syrus, An non tuus erat, antequam venderetur? & postquam venditus esset, tu potestatem habebas in pretium ejus? Non videtur hic sacrilegii pariter & mendacii Ananias argui, sed mendacii tantum, quod enim voto jam ante totum agrum Deo consecraverit, votoque isto violato sacrilegus evaserit, ex textu colligi non videtur. sed tantum, quod cum per ambitionem totius pretium donasse videri voluerit, partem ejus suppresserit. quod hypocriseos fuit & mendacii. Auget hoc peccatum Apostolus, eo quod nihil necesse fuerit simulationem istam adhibere. Nam, inquit, & antequam venderetur, in tua potestate erat non vendere. & venditi pretium in tua potestate erat, ut aut nihil de eo, aut quantum velles, dares. utrumque dictum sine exceptione intelligo, quæ statuenda est, si votum statuas. Nam & reliquos pios possessionum suarum divenditarum pretia in commune contulisse arbitror ex mera liberalitate & fraterna charitate. de voto, ne verbum. Æthiopicus sic reddidit, Nonne tuum manssiset, si manssiset? & cum vendidisti, voluntate tua vendidisti? nova hæc est lectio, nec fulcrum habet, cui innitatur.
units.tr: Did it not remain yours? And when it was sold, was it not in your power? The Syriac has expressed the sense very well: "Was it not yours before it was sold? And after it was sold, did you have power over its price?" Here Ananias does not seem to be charged with sacrilege as well as lying. That he had consecrated the whole field to God by a vow beforehand, and by breaking that vow became guilty of sacrilege, does not seem to be gathered from the text. Rather, he is charged only with this: wanting through ambition to seem to have given the whole price, he kept back part of it. That was hypocrisy and lying. The Apostle increases this sin by pointing out that there was no need to pretend at all. For, he says, even before it was sold it was in your power not to sell it, and once sold, the price was in your power, so that you could give either nothing of it or as much as you wished. I understand both statements without exception, which would have to be qualified only if you had made a vow. For I think the other pious believers also brought the prices of their sold possessions into the common fund out of pure generosity and brotherly love, and not from any vow. Of a vow, not a word. The Ethiopic renders it thus: "Would it not have remained yours, if it had remained? And when you sold it, did you sell it by your own will?" This is a new reading, and it has no support to lean upon.

units.la: VERS. 6.
units.tr: VERSE 6.

units.la: Σπεῖραλλαν αὐτὸν. Vulg. & Eras. amoverunt eum. Beza, subtraxerunt. Arabs ..., involucris involverunt eum. est enim cadaver linteis involvere, quod fit ἐν τῷ ἐνταφιασμῷ, in praeparatione ad sepulturam. Syrus שמאלה ־ ־ ־, collegerunt eum. eo sensu fortassis,quo quæ humi jacent colligi dicuntur, quum humo levantur & attolluntur,atque ita versus attollentem colliguntur & contrahuntur. Belgicè opnemen. quod huic loco non male congruit.Sed est cur opiner, Syrum idem voluisse quod Arabem , collegerunt eum , nempe in involucra. Nam infra ℵ ℵ ℵ 10. de Sapphira utitur verbo ℵ ℵ ℵ. Trem. & impositam in capulum deferentes sepelierunt eam. Boder. & collectam in feretrum efferentes &c.non necesse videtur addi illud in capulum,vel in feretrum. Ferrarius collegit, reposuit, strinxit, contraxit. summa rei, quum tota res quasi in summam colligitur & contrahitur. hinc sæpe in Euang. horreum, locus collectionis in quem colliguntur & reponuntur fruges.verto ergo ad verbū, & collegerunt, seu constrinxerunt.ibi quidem nihil est in Græco quod respondeat τῷ at cap.8. 2. ponitur pro συνεχόμενον. quod non dubito quin idem sit quod præcedens συνέσφαλκαν. Vult autem Doctiss. Fullerus lib. Miscell. 6. cap. 18. συνέστελλαν & Syriacum ܣܘܢܬܘܪܐ intelligi de fasciis funeralibus quibus membra mortui colliguntur & arctè constringuntur ad sepulturam. mirè id placet. nec aliter accipiendum censeo illud συνεχόμενον, quam de comportatione membrorum in vincula & fasciás ad sepeliendum. quod recte Syrus dixit ℵ ℵ ℵ. id enim, ut ex Ferrario attulimus, non tantum colligere, sed & stringere, contrahere significat.Nec aliud voluerunt Vulgatus & Erasmus, quum verterunt, curave-
units.tr: Σπεῖραλλαν αὐτὸν [Σπεῖραλλαν αὐτὸν]: the Vulgate and Erasmus have removed him, Beza carried him off, and the Arabic wrapped him in shrouds, since a corpse is wrapped in linen when it is prepared for burial [ἐν τῷ ἐνταφιασμῷ], in preparation for the tomb. The Syriac has gathered him together, perhaps in the sense in which things lying on the ground are said to be gathered up when they are lifted from the earth and raised, and so are drawn together and contracted as they are lifted. The Dutch opnemen (take up) fits this place well enough. But I have reason to think the Syriac meant what the Arabic meant, gathered him together, namely into wrappings. For below, at verse 10, about Sapphira, he uses the same verb, and Tremellius has laid her on a bier and carried her out and buried her, and Boderianus gathered her up and carried her out on a bier; there seems no need to add onto a bier or into a bier. Ferrarius gives gathered, put away, bound, drew together; the sense is summed up, since the whole matter is, as it were, gathered and drawn into a sum. Hence in the Gospels barn (horreum) is a place of gathering, where fruits are gathered and stored. I therefore translate literally and they gathered, or bound together. Admittedly there is nothing in the Greek that answers to the article here, but at chapter 8 verse 2 the word is used for συνεχόμενον [συνεχόμενον], which I do not doubt is the same as the preceding συνέσφαλκαν [συνέσφαλκαν]. The most learned Fuller, in his Miscellanies, book 6, chapter 18, holds that συνέστελλαν [συνέστελλαν] and the Syriac word are to be understood of the funeral bands by which the limbs of the dead are gathered and tightly bound for burial.
