I like this very much, and I think συνεχόμενον must be taken in the same way, of the bringing together of the limbs in bands and wrappings for burial, which the Syriac rightly rendered by a word meaning, as I have shown from Ferrarius, not only to gather but also to bind and to draw together. The Vulgate and Erasmus, when they rendered it pious men took care of [curaverunt] Stephen, meant nothing different

units.la: runt autem Stephanum viri timorati.longè sanè melius,quam extulerunt autem Stephanum, ut habet D. Beza. Nam, ut apud H.Stephanū est,συγκομίζειν νεκρόν est componere mortuum ad sepulturam. Sophocles in Ajace, ἐτ@· σὶ φωνῶ. τὶνδὶ τ νεκρὸν χεροῖν μὴ συγκομίζειν, ἀλλ' ἐᾶν ὅπως ἔχ{·}. iftum mortuum manibus ne componito. Sic vero & Æfchyli Scholiaftes in Trag. quæ ἐπὶ ἀδῆ Θήβας inscribitur, tradit de mortuis dici συγκομίζειν, ἐκκομίζειν, & ἀνακομίζειν. eam autem differentiam inter hæc tria constituit, ut συγκομιδὴ fit ἡ ἀπὸ τ πόλεως πάσου ἀπημίλια. ἐκκομιδὴ autem, ἡ ἀπὸ τ πόλεον ἀπαγωγή. at ἀνακομιδή, ἡ ἐκ πόλεως εἰς πόλεον μεταβάσις. Hæc Stephanus. Arabs eodem prorsus modo intellexit. nam συνεκόμισαν vertit , id est, conftrinxerunt. σωίσηλαν vero , id est, quæ ad funus pertinebant curaverunt, præsertim fasciis & linteaminibus eum involvendo.nam & sunt linteamina. Addo Æthiopicum, qui συνείςλαν vertit , involverunt eum. idem verbum est quo Marc. 15. 46. & Luc. 23. 53. utitur de Christi corpore, cum id involucris involveretur.
units.tr: runt autem Stephanum viri timorati: this is far better than and they carried Stephen out, as Beza has it. For, as in H. Stephanus, συγκομίζειν νεκρόν [συγκομίζειν νεκρόν] means to lay out a corpse for burial. Sophocles in Ajax says: do not gather up this corpse with your hands, but leave it as it is [μὴ συγκομίζειν ... ἀλλ' ἐᾶν ὅπως ἔχει]. So too the scholiast on Aeschylus' tragedy inscribed Seven against Thebes says that of the dead one speaks of συγκομίζειν, ἐκκομίζειν and ἀνακομίζειν [συγκομίζειν, ἐκκομίζειν, ἀνακομίζειν], and he distinguishes the three thus: συγκομιδή [συγκομιδή] is the gathering of the dead from the whole city; ἐκκομιδή [ἐκκομιδή] is the carrying out from the city; but ἀνακομιδή [ἀνακομιδή] is the transfer from one city to another. So Stephanus. The Arabic understood it in exactly the same way: he renders συνεκόμισαν [συνεκόμισαν] as bound together, and συνέστειλαν [συνέστειλαν], that is, those who attended to the funeral, especially by wrapping him in bands and linen cloths. For there are linen cloths. I add the Ethiopic, which renders συνείλησαν [συνείλησαν] as wrapped him up. It is the same verb that Mark 15:46 and Luke 23:53 use of Christ's body, when it was wrapped in cloths.

units.la: V E R S. 9. Τί ὅτι πειράζητε ὑμῖν, &c. Syrus & Arabs non legerunt τί. ideoque omisla interrogatione verterunt, propterea quod convenit inter vos tentare Spiritum S. ecce pedes &c. Malè Trem. Syrum verterat, quid pares facti estis in tentando? Bene id correxit Junius, Quoniam pares fuistis. proprie, quoniam pariter feciftis tentando.
units.tr: VERSE 9. Τί ὅτι πειράζητε ὑμῖν [Τί ὅτι πειράζητε ὑμῖν], etc. The Syriac and Arabic did not read τί [τί]. So, dropping the question, they rendered it: because it was agreed among you to tempt the Holy Spirit; behold the feet, etc. Tremellius wrongly rendered the Syriac as why have you become equals in tempting? Junius corrected this well: since you were equal; properly, since you together did it by tempting.

units.la: V E R S. 12. Ἐν τῇ στοᾷ Σολομῶνος, In porticu Salomonis. Hæc quæ esset nesciremus, nisi Josephus id doceret Antiq. l. 20. c. 8. his verbis, Ἐπεὶ τ βασιλεὺς τῶν ἀναπλικῶ φαν ἀνεγεραμ. ὣ ἡ στὰ ἐξω ἐξωθεν ἱερῆς, καμίνη ἡ ἐν φάραγγι βαθεῖα πτεράσων πηγῶν σὺν πίχυς ἴχυσα, ἐκ λίθων ἡ πτεραγωνῶν κατωσκάσι, ἡ λαξευῶν πάνυ. τὸ μὲν μῆκος ἐκάτη λίθε, πηχυς ἕκαστ, τὸ δ' ὕψος ἐξ. ἐχεν Σολομῶνος βασιλεὺς. Suafit (populus) Regi Regi (Agrippæ) orientalem instauraret porticum. erat autem porticus exteriorûs templi, profunda valli imminens, proinde subnixa muris quadringentorum cubitorum, saxis quadratis constructa valde candidis. longitudo autem cujusque saxi erat cubitorum viginti, altitudo vero sex. opus Solomonis regis. Cujus loci explicationem si quis velit, adeat doctissimum viri maximi Const. l'Empereur Commentarium in Middoth p. 53.
units.tr: VERSE 12. Ἐν τῇ στοᾷ Σολομῶνος [Ἐν τῇ στοᾷ Σολομῶνος], in the porch of Solomon. We would not know what this was unless Josephus taught us, in Antiquities book 20, chapter 8, in these words: the people asked King Agrippa to rebuild the eastern porch. This porch was on the outer side of the temple, overhanging a deep valley, and was supported by walls four hundred cubits high, built of square stones, very white. The length of each stone was twenty cubits, the height six. It was the work of King Solomon [Ἐπεὶ ... βασιλεὺς]. If anyone wishes an explanation of this place, let him consult the most learned Constantin l'Empereur's commentary on the Middoth, p. 53.

units.la: VERS. 13. Caeterorum autem nemo audebat κολλᾶσθαι αὐτοῖς. Vulgatus, conjungere se illis. Malim certe, quam appropinquare ipsis. præsertim si id sumatur pro congredi cum illis, quod vult Doctiss. Interpres. nec juvatur ab Arabe, qui habet ﻳﺠﺘﻤﻊ (?) quod Junius male vertit certare cum ipsis, metaphora desumta à luctatoribus. spectavit Hebræorum רִיב, litigare, certare, contendere. At radix Arabica est ﻗﺮﺐ vel קרב, quod nihil aliud est quam appropinquare, accedere. Sensus est, Horrendum illud Ananiæ Sapphiræque supplicium tanto omnes terrore perculisse, ut eorum, qui fidem Christi nondum amplexi essent, nemo Apostolorum consortio adjungere se auderet. Obortus quidem etiam timor toti Ecclesiæ, ♆ f. 11. at hi tamen non desiterunt κολλᾶσθαι adhærere Apostolis. erant enim unanimiter omnes in porticu Salomonis, ♆. 11. cæteri id non fuere ausi. sufficiebat plebi, quippe simpliciori integriorique (primores enim & Pharisæi etiam calumniabantur) extollere eos laudibus, sed agglutinari Apostolis, iisque familiariter uti non sunt ausi. Nec repugnat, quod ♆ f. 14. dicantur magis magisque additi fuisse qui crederent, quos adeo auditores Apostolorum fuisse necesse est. auditores enim esse possunt, qui tamen non sunt κεκολλημένοι, agglutinati. vetro ergo κολλᾶσθαι, arctè adhærere. Ad hostes certe Apostolorum, quorum nemo congredi cum illis, eosque adoriri ausus fuerit, aptè referri non videtur, quia mox ♆ f. 17. 18. ausi fuerunt manus in eos injicere & carceri tradere.
units.tr: VERSE 13. Caeterorum autem nemo audebat κολλᾶσθαι αὐτοῖς [κολλᾶσθαι αὐτοῖς]. The Vulgate has to join themselves to them. I would certainly prefer that to to approach them, especially if it is taken to mean to engage with them, as the most learned interpreter wants. Nor is he helped by the Arabic, which has a word (?) that Junius wrongly rendered to contend with them, a metaphor taken from wrestlers. He had in view the Hebrew רִיב [רִיב], to dispute, contend, strive. But the Arabic root is qrb, that is קרב [קרב], which means nothing other than to approach, draw near. The sense is this: the horrible punishment of Ananias and Sapphira struck all with such terror that none of those who had not yet embraced the faith of Christ dared to join themselves to the company of the apostles. Indeed fear also arose through the whole Church, verse 11; but these men nonetheless did not cease to cling to the apostles [κολλᾶσθαι, to adhere closely]. For they were all unanimously in the porch of Solomon, verse 11; the others did not dare. It was enough for the common people, who were simpler and more upright (for the leaders and Pharisees even slandered them), to extol the apostles with praises, but they did not dare to attach themselves to them or to use them familiarly. Nor does it conflict with verse 14, where it says that more and more were added who believed, who must have been hearers of the apostles. For there can be hearers who are nonetheless not joined [κεκολλημένοι]. So I render κολλᾶσθαι [κολλᾶσθαι] as to cling closely. It does not seem aptly applied to the enemies of the apostles, none of whom dared to engage with them and attack them, since immediately afterwards, at verses 17 and 18, they dared to lay hands on them and hand them over to prison.

units.la: VERS. 14. Μᾶλλον ἢ προσετίθεντο &c. Beza, imo vero adjiciebantur &c. At Vulgatus, magis autem, Syrus & Arabs & magis adjiciebantur. Hi μᾶλλον construxerunt cum προστίθεντο. quod praefero, quia post μᾶλλον δὲ non est distinctio, quae necessario ponenda, si accipiatur pro imo vero, vel potius autem. Sensus est; quamvis caeterorum nemo familiarem se pro eo tempore Apostolis reddere audebat, ob recentem adhuc ex prodigioso Ananiae interitu metum, id tamen progressui Euangelii non obfuit. Sed & plebs majori in pretio eos habuit, & plures magis magisque adjiciebantur credentium numero.
units.tr: VERSE 14. Μᾶλλον ἢ προσετίθεντο &c. [Μᾶλλον ἢ προσετίθεντο]. Beza has nay rather, they were added, etc. But the Vulgate has moreover, and the Syriac and Arabic and more were added. These construe μᾶλλον [μᾶλλον] with προστίθεντο [προστίθεντο], which I prefer, because after μᾶλλον δὲ there is no punctuation, which would necessarily be placed if it were taken as nay rather or rather. The sense is this: although none of the others at that time dared to make themselves familiar with the apostles, because of the fear still fresh from the dreadful death of Ananias, this did not hinder the progress of the gospel. Moreover, the people held the apostles in greater esteem, and more and more were added to the number of believers.

units.la: VERS. 15. Ὥστε καὶ εἰς τὰς πλατείας ἐκφέρειν τοὺς ἀσθενεῖς. Vulgatus, ita ut in plateas ejicerent infirmos. Syrus dixit ܐܝܟ ܕ quod tam ejicerent quam efferrent verti potest. sic enim passim usurpatur. ut & in Kal pro exire & ejici. id non raro Hellenistae imitantes, utuntur ἐκπορεύεσθαι, exire pro ejici. ut Marc. 7. 19. ita & ἐκφέρειν, efferre pro ejicere. sic Esdr. 1. 19. & dederunt manum suam, τὰς ἐξενίγκας γυναῖκας ἑαυτῶν, ut ejicerent uxores suas. Rectius tamen, ni fallor, Erasmus exportarent, & Beza efferrent. Sed quod κατὰ τὰς πλατείας verterunt in plateas, εἰς τὰς πλατείας, malim per plateas. ut κατὰ feriem & distributionem aliquam significet, ac sensus sit, eos non simpliciter eduxisse aegros foras in plateas, sed factum illud hic illic per varias plateas. eâdem phrasi, qua Act. 21. 21. Paulus dicitur docuisse τοὺς κατὰ τὰ ἔθνη πάντας Ἰουδαίους, omnes Iudaos qui per gentes hac illac dispersi erant. & cap. 22. 19. idem dicitur fuisse διὰ τὰς συναγωγὰς κατὰ πρὸς τὰς οἰκίας, cadens hic illic per synagogas credentes.
units.tr: VERSE 15. Ὥστε καὶ εἰς τὰς πλατείας ἐκφέρειν τοὺς ἀσθενεῖς [Ὥστε καὶ εἰς τὰς πλατείας ἐκφέρειν τοὺς ἀσθενεῖς]. The Vulgate has so that they would cast the sick into the streets. The Syriac word can be rendered either cast out or carry out, as it is used everywhere, and likewise in the Kal stem for go out and be cast out. The Hellenists, often imitating this, use ἐκπορεύεσθαι [ἐκπορεύεσθαι], go out, for be cast out, as at Mark 7:19; so too ἐκφέρειν [ἐκφέρειν], carry out, for cast out. So Esdras 1:19, and they gave their hand, τὰς ἐξενέγκας γυναῖκας ἑαυτῶν [τὰς ἐξενέγκας γυναῖκας ἑαυτῶν], that they might cast out their wives. Yet carry out (Erasmus, exportarent) and bring out (Beza, efferrent) are, I think, more correct. But I would prefer through the streets to into the streets for κατὰ τὰς πλατείας [κατὰ τὰς πλατείας], to render εἰς τὰς πλατείας [εἰς τὰς πλατείας]. The preposition κατά [κατά] signifies a distribution, and the sense is that they did not simply carry the sick out into the streets, but did this here and there, through various streets. It is the same phrase as at Acts 21:21, where Paul is said to have taught all the Jews who were among the nations, τοὺς κατὰ τὰ ἔθνη πάντας Ἰουδαίους [τοὺς κατὰ τὰ ἔθνη πάντας Ἰουδαίους], who were dispersed here and there; and at chapter 22 verse 19, where the same is said of the believers who fell here and there through the synagogues, διὰ τὰς συναγωγὰς κατὰ [διὰ τὰς συναγωγὰς κατὰ], here and there.

units.la: IBID. Ἡ σχιὰ Πέτρου ἐπισκιάσῃ αὐτῶν. Syrus ܐܝܟ ܕ Trem. umbra ejus tegeret illos. Bod-er. operiret illos. respexerunt Hebraicam significationem, ubi μ valet tegere. at apud Syros ⟨Syriac⟩ est supervenire, descendere, illabi. deinde morari, habitare. priori sensu construi solet cum ⟨Syriac⟩, poniturque pro προσκαρτερέω, hic & Luc. 1. 3. pro προσπίπτειν, Act. 10. 44. & 11. 15. pro προσκλυσιν, 2 Cor. 12. 9. Posteriori sensu cum ⟨Syriac⟩, poniturque pro σκηνοῦν, Ioh. 1. 14. & καταςκηνοῦν, Act. 2. 26. idem est quod Arabum ⟨Arabic⟩, quod iisdem constructionibus idem significat, & hic ab Interprete adhibetur.
units.tr: IBID. Let the shadow of Peter overshadow them [Ἡ σχιὰ Πέτρου ἐπισκιάσῃ αὐτῶν]. The Syriac and Tremellius render this: his shadow would cover them. The Bod-er. version has would overshadow them. They followed the Hebrew sense, in which the verb means to cover. But in Syriac it means to come upon, to descend, to alight, and then to remain, to dwell. In the former sense it is usually construed with the Syriac preposition, and it is used for "to persevere" [προσκαρτερέω], here and at Luke 1.3, and for "to fall upon" [προσπίπτειν], Acts 10.44 and 11.15, and for "to rush upon" [προσκλυσιν], 2 Cor. 12.9. In the latter sense it is construed with the Syriac preposition and is used for "to dwell" [σκηνοῦν], John 1.14, and "to dwell down" [καταςκηνοῦν], Acts 2.26. The Arabic word has the same meaning with the same constructions, and the translator uses it here.

units.la: VERS. 16. Συνῆγχθο ἡ δὲ πᾶσα ἡ πλῆθος τῶν πολέων εἰς Ἱερουσαλήμ.
units.tr: VERS. 16. And the multitude also of the cities round about came together into Jerusalem [Συνῆγχθο ἡ δὲ πᾶσα ἡ πλῆθος τῶν πολέων εἰς Ἱερουσαλήμ].

units.la: Vulg. Eras. & Beza, Conveniebat autem & multitudo vicinarum civitatum Ierusalem. Nisi quod Beza pro multitudo dixit vulgus: Syrus, veniebant autem ad eos multi ex civitatibus aliis quae erant ⟨Syriac⟩ circum Ierusalem. Recte intellexit, multitudinem civitatum non esse hic multas civitates, sed multos ex civitatibus. deinde τ πλῆθος πόλεων non esse vicinas sed circumjacentes urbes. neque enim idem est quod τ ἐγγὺς, sed τ κύκλῳ πόλεων. Hezychius σύνεγγυς, κύκλῳ. sic & Arabs vertit, & Æthiopicus.
units.tr: The Vulgate, Erasmus and Beza: And there came also a multitude of the neighbouring cities to Jerusalem. Except that Beza put the common people for multitude. The Syriac: many came to them from the other cities which were around Jerusalem. He understood rightly that a multitude of cities here means not many cities but many people from cities. Next, "a multitude of cities" [τὸ πλῆθος πόλεων] means not neighbouring but surrounding towns, for it is not the same as "near" [ἐγγὺς] but as "round about" [κύκλῳ]. Hesychius glosses near [σύνεγγυς] as round about [κύκλῳ]. The Arabic and the Ethiopic also translate it so.

units.la: VERS. 17. Ἀναςὰς δὲ ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς καὶ πάντες οἱ σὺν αὐτῷ &c. ἐπλήσθησαν ζῆλος. Syrus & Arabs, & impleti sunt invidia principes Sacerdotum & omnes qui cum eo erant. non verterunt illud ἀναςὰς. an ergo non legerunt? arbitror potius, consulto praeteriisse, ut vacare hic indicarent. ut enim ⟨Hebrew⟩ Hebraeis, sic Hellenistis ἀνίςημι non semper situm personae indicat, quae sedens antea jacensve stare incipit, id est, surgit, sed saepe novae actionis initium & primordium, & tum, non aliter quam verbum ἀρχέσθαι, Luc. 3. 8. Act. 1. 1. & alibi, vacat. sic Act. 6. 9. ἀνέστησαν δὲ τινες συζητοῦντες, surrexerunt disputantes, id est, incoeperunt disputare, disputarunt. Iosue 6. 9. maledictus vir, ὅς ἀναςὰς καὶ οἰκοδομῶν, qui surget & aedificabit civitatem illam Iericho, id est, simpliciter, qui aedificabit, vel aedificare ficare incipiet. Esr. 10. ς. dicitur Esras, qui ℣ζ. 1. in faciem pronus oraverat in templo, surrexisse, & principes, qui ad se in domum Dei venerant adjurasse, ut alienigenas uxores dimitterent. ibi proprie surgendi vox intelligitur. at v. sequenti rursus dicitur, ἡ ἀνίςη ἱσδρας ὑπὸ τοῦ σωτῆρ οἴκε ἔ Θεῦ, ἕ ἐπορεύθη εἰς προζοφυλάκιον. An ergo bis continuo surrexit? an potius, surrexit & ivit, hic simpliciter est ivit? Id sane constructio indicat, וַיָּקָם עֶזְרָא מִלִּפְנֵי בֵּית הָאֱלֹהִים הָלַךְ לִשְׁכַּת יְהוֹחָנָן & surrexit Esdras ab ante domum Dei & abiit in conclave Iohannis, id est, & abiit ab ante domum Dei in conclave. vide & Exod. 32. 1. Deut. 32. 38. & alibi, ubi surgere jubentur, quos non necesse est tum sedisse aut jacuisse, sed initium solummodo actionis injungitur. habent ita & Arabes duo verba ﻗﺎﻡ & ﺫﻫﺐ, quae aliis verbis praepositia initium actionis denotant, & simpliciter redundant. Nolim itaque hic multum culpare Syrum & Arabem, qui surgens autem Pontifex maximus & omnes qui cum eo erant, repleti sunt invidia, verterunt simpliciter, repleti sunt invidia, quasi sensus sit, coeperunt autem pontifex &c. repleri invidia. Beza, insurgens autem pontifex &c. quod magis arrideret, si adderetur ἐπ' αὐτὸς, in eos. nunc malim cum Erasmo & Vulgato, exurgens.
units.tr: VERS. 17. "And the high priest rose up, and all who were with him, etc., and were filled with envy" [Ἀναςὰς δὲ ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς καὶ πάντες οἱ σὺν αὐτῷ ἐπλήσθησαν ζῆλος]. The Syriac and the Arabic have: and the chief priests and all who were with him were filled with envy. They do not translate the word ἀναςὰς. Did they then not read it? I think rather that they deliberately passed it over, to show that it is superfluous here. For just as with the Hebrews, so with the Hellenists, ἀνίςημι does not always indicate the posture of a person who, having been sitting or lying, begins to stand, that is, rises. It often marks the beginning and first stage of a new action, and then it is superfluous, no differently from the verb ἀρχέσθαι (Luke 3.8; Acts 1.1, and elsewhere). So in Acts 6.9, ἀνέστησαν δὲ τινες συζητοῦντες, "some rose up disputing," means that they began to dispute, that is, they disputed. In Joshua 6.26 the words "cursed be the man who rises up and builds" [ארור האיש אשר יקום ובנה] mean simply "who will build," or "who will begin to build." In Ezra 10.1 Ezra is said to have risen, who in verse 1 had prayed prostrate in the temple, and the leaders who had come to him in the house of God to make them swear to put away their foreign wives. Here the word for rising is to be taken in its proper sense. But in the following verse it is said again: "Ezra rose up from before the house of God and went into the chamber of Johanan." Did he then rise twice in a row? Or rather, is surrexit & ivit, "he rose and went," here simply ivit, "he went"? The construction certainly indicates this: wayyaqam ʿEzraʾ millifnei bet ha-ʾelohim halakh liskhat Yehohanan [וַיָּקָם עֶזְרָא מִלִּפְנֵי בֵּית הָאֱלֹהִים הָלַךְ לִשְׁכַּת יְהוֹחָנָן], that is, "and he went from before the house of God into the chamber." See also Exodus 32.1 and Deuteronomy 32.38, and elsewhere, where people are bidden to rise who need not have been sitting or lying, but only the beginning of the action is enjoined. The Arabs too have two verbs, qāma and dhahaba, which when placed before other verbs denote the beginning of an action and are simply redundant. I would not therefore blame the Syriac and the Arabic too much for translating "the high priest rising and all who were with him were filled with envy" simply as "were filled with envy," as if the sense were "the high priest and the others began to be filled with envy." Beza has insurgens autem pontifex, which would please more if ἐπ' αὐτοὺς, "against them," were added. For my part I prefer, with Erasmus and the Vulgate, exurgens.

units.la: VERS. 24. Syrus, Vulgatus & Æthiopicus non legerunt ὁ, πι ἱερεύς. Arabs legit: aut certe, quod quidam Graeci codices habent, ὁ ἀρχιερεύς. vertit enim ﺍﻟﻜﺎﻫﻦ ﺍﻻﻋﻈﻢ, maximus Sacerdotum. quod autem sequitur, & Syrus Vulgatusque legerunt ἕ οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς, non legit. Sequitur, ἀπήγγειλαν αὐτῷ, τί ἂν γένοιτο τοῦτο. Arabs ﻓﺎﺭﺗﺎﺑﻮﺍ ﻓﻲ ﺍﻣﺮﻫﻢ ﻭﺍﺑﺘﺪﺃﻭﺍ ﺍﻟﺘﻔﻜﺮ, dubitarunt de negocio eorum, & coeperunt cogitare, quid hoc esset. ﺃﺧﺬ est hoc verbum, quod v. 17. diximus, redundare apud Arabes. itaque ﺍﺑﺘﺪﺃﻭﺍ ﺍﻟﺘﻔﻜﺮ, coeperunt cogitare, est id ipsum quod explicationis gratia interseruit
units.tr: VERSE 24. The Syriac, the Vulgate and the Ethiopic did not read ὁ before ἱερεύς. The Arabic reads it, or certainly, as some Greek manuscripts have, ὁ ἀρχιερεύς, for it translates al-kāhin al-aʿẓam, "the greatest of the priests." What follows, "and the chief priests," which the Syriac and the Vulgate read (ἕ οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς), the Arabic does not read. Then comes ἀπήγγειλαν αὐτῷ, τί ἂν γένοιτο τοῦτο. The Arabic has: they doubted in their affair and began to think what this might be. The word akhadha, which I noted at verse 17, is redundant in Arabic. So ibtadaʾū al-tafakkur, "they began to think," is the very thing that he inserted for the sake of explanation.

units.la: ἱσδρας, ἔ ἐπορεύθη: Ioan. 3. terseruit Syrus [illegible, ~8 letters] cogitabant. quod ergo vertit Junius, & colloquentes rogabant, quasi legisset Arabs, [Greek?] [illegible, ~6 letters], aut ut habet Beza, [Greek?] [illegible, ~5 letters], non est apud Arabem.
units.tr: Ioan. 3. ... The Syriac inserted they thought [illegible]. So what Junius rendered as "conferring they asked," as if the Arabic had read something else, is not in the Arabic at all. The same holds for what Beza has.

units.la: VERS. 31. Τὴν ὁ Θεὸς ἀρχηγὸν [?] σωτῆρα ὕψωσεν. Vulg. & Eraf. Hunc principem & salvatorem Deus evexit. Beza rectius, Hunc Deus dextra sua evectum constituit principem ac servatorem. evexit pro evectum constituit, ex antecedenti intelligitur consequens, more Hebraeorum, ut יָסַף accepit, pro acceptum adduxit. Vel Accusativus ἀρχηγὸν finem designat, ponitypque pro εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἀρχηγὸν Ὁ σωτῆρα.. quod Interpres doctiss. recte etiam annotavit, nos exemplis firmabimus. tale est Jacobi 2. 5. nonne Deus elegit pauperes hujus mundi, πλουσίους ἐν πίστει, pro εἰς τὸ εἶναι πλουσίους, ut sint divites? Adde Act. 7. 35. Τὴν ὁ Θεὸς ἀρχηγὸν καὶ Λυτρωτὴν ἀπέστειλε, pro εἰς ἀρχηγὸν, in principem, qui esset princeps & liberator.
units.tr: VERSE 31. "This one God exalted as Prince and Saviour" [Τὴν ὁ Θεὸς ἀρχηγὸν σωτῆρα ὕψωσεν]. The Vulgate and Erasmus: Hunc principem & salvatorem Deus evexit, "God exalted this one as Prince and Saviour." Beza more correctly: Hunc Deus dextra sua evectum constituit principem ac servatorem, "God, having raised him by his right hand, appointed him Prince and Saviour." Evexit stands for evectum constituit: the consequence is understood from the preceding, in the manner of the Hebrews, as yasaph, "he received," means "he received and brought." Or the accusative ἀρχηγὸν marks the purpose, and stands for εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἀρχηγὸν καὶ σωτῆρα, "to be Prince and Saviour." The most learned interpreter also noted this rightly, and we shall confirm it with examples. James 2.5 is such: "Has not God chosen the poor of this world, πλουσίους ἐν πίστει," for εἰς τὸ εἶναι πλουσίους, "that they might be rich"? Add Acts 7.35: Τὴν ὁ Θεὸς ἀρχηγὸν καὶ Λυτρωτὴν ἀπέστειλε, for εἰς ἀρχηγὸν, "as a prince, who should be prince and liberator."

units.la: VERS. 32. Καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐσμὲν μάρτυρες τῶν ῥημάτων τούτων. Vulg. Syr. Arabs & Æthiopicus non legerunt αὐτὸ.
units.tr: VERSE 32. "And we are witnesses of these words" [Καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐσμὲν μάρτυρες τῶν ῥημάτων τούτων]. The Vulgate, the Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic did not read αὐτὸ.

units.la: VERS. 33. Διεσχίζοντο. Vulg.& Eraf.disseccabantur. Beza, frendebant. Syrus [Syriac, illegible, ~6 letters], Trem. dissecabantur ira. Boder. corripiebantur ira. verte inflammabantur ira. est enim [Syriac, illegible, ~3 letters], inflammari, exardescere. de qua voce qui plura vult, videat notas nostras ad 2 Thess.1.8. Arabs similiter [Arabic, illegible, ~5 letters], caeperunt inflammari ira. ubi obiter nota alterum illud verbum,quod v. 17. redundare passim apud Arabes diximus. doctissimè autem Cl. Beza Διεσχίζοντο eorum gestum declarare tradit, qui prae rabie dentibus stridebant, veluti si quis serra, trahat. hinc recte Æthiopicus [Ethiopic, illegible], stridebant dentibus suis.
units.tr: VERSE 33. Διεσχίζοντο, "they were cut to the heart." The Vulgate and Erasmus: disseccabantur. Beza: frendebant, "gnashed." The Syriac, Tremellius: dissecabantur ira. Boderianus: corripiebantur ira, "were seized with anger." Render it "were inflamed with anger," for the Syriac word means to be inflamed, to blaze up. Whoever wants more on this word may see my notes on 2 Thessalonians 1.8. The Arabic similarly has bādaʾū yatalahhabūna ghaḍaban, "began to be inflamed with anger," where I note in passing that other verb, which I said at verse 17 is often redundant in Arabic. Most learned Beza reports that Διεσχίζοντο describes their gesture, of those who in rage gnashed their teeth, as if one were sawing with a saw. Hence the Ethiopic rightly has they gnashed their teeth.

units.la: VERS. 40. Ἐπείσθησαν δὲ αὐτῷ. Vulg. consenserunt autem tem illi. Beza, assensi sunt illi. Syrus [Syriac], & paruerunt ei. Arabs [Arabic], Junius, & crediderunt voci ejus. ad verbum, & responderunt ad vocem ejus, id est, assensi sunt verbis ejus. sic quum quis alteri petitionem largitur, dicere solent [Arabic]; & respondit ei ad hoc, id est, consensit ei hac in re, annuit ei hanc rem.
units.tr: VERSE 40. Ἐπείσθησαν δὲ αὐτῷ, "they were persuaded by him." The Vulgate: consenserunt autem tem illi, "they agreed with him." Beza: assensi sunt illi, "they assented to him." The Syriac: "and they obeyed him." The Arabic, and Junius: "and they believed his voice." Word for word it is "and they answered to his voice," that is, they assented to his words. So when someone grants another's request, they customarily say, "and he answered him in this," that is, he agreed with him in this matter, he nodded assent to him in this.

units.la: VERS. 41. [Greek] [Greek]. Syrus & Arabs non legerunt [Greek]. vertunt enim simpliciter, quod pro nomine digni fuissent ignominia affici. Nomen absolute pro Deo, usitatissimum est Hebraeis. sic dicunt [Hebrew], ob sanctificationem nominis, ob profanationem nominis, id est Dei. Causam denominationis dat Elias in Thisbi, [Hebrew], quia vetitum est vel unum ex nominibus ejus in vanum usurpare. Addit autem, non usurpari pro Deo nisi cum [Hebrew], He emphatico [Hebrew]. Secus tamen est Levit. 24. 16. [Hebrew], quum blasphemaverit nomen, id est Deum, morietur. Æthiopicus legit [Greek].
units.tr: VERSE 41. ὑπὲρ τοῦ ὀνόματος ἀτιμασθῆναι, "to be dishonoured for the name." The Syriac and the Arabic do not read τοῦ ὀνόματος. They simply translate "because they were worthy to be treated with contempt." The absolute use of "Name" for God is very common among the Hebrews. Thus they say "for the sanctification of the Name, for the profanation of the Name," that is, of God. Elias of Tishbi gives the reason for this name: because it is forbidden to take in vain even one of his names. He adds, however, that it is not used for God except with the emphatic He. It is otherwise in Leviticus 24.16: "when he has blasphemed the Name," that is, God, "he shall die." The Ethiopic reads τοῦ ὀνόματος.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: VERS. 1. [Greek] quos intellexerit Beza, vide in ipsius notis, quem merito rejicit Drusius in Præteritis, ubi vide. Quod autem sequitur, [Greek], Æthiopicus transtulit, quod viderent viduas suas ministrare quotidie. videtur contemtum viduarum Græcarum in eo constituisse, quod quotidianus administrandorum pauperum labor ipsis imponeretur. Eo sensu [Greek] sumeretur pro [Greek].
units.tr: VERS. 1. [Greek] Whom Beza understood, see in his notes. Drusius rightly rejects him in the Praeterita, where you should look. As for what follows, [Greek], the Ethiopic translated it that they saw their widows being served daily. It seems to have placed the contempt for the Greek widows in this, that the daily labour of ministering to the poor was imposed on them. In that sense [Greek] would be taken for [Greek].

units.la: VERS. 2. [Greek]. Vulg. & Beza, non est æquum. Eras. non est placitum. Arabs [Arabic], non est in bono, id est, bonum. phrasi usitata, qua dicunt, Deus est [Arabic], in poin potente, id est, potens. sic & Syrus [Hebrew], non est bonum, pulchrum: recte. omne enim bonum placet. itaque [Greek] est [Greek]. Deut. 12. 18. [Hebrew], LXX [Greek] ubi tamen alia exemplaria, mutato situ, legunt [Greek].
units.tr: VERS. 2. [Greek]. The Vulgate and Beza have it is not right. Erasmus has it is not pleasing. The Arabic has it is not in the good, that is, it is not good, by a common idiom in which they say God is [Arabic], powerful in power, that is, powerful. So also the Syriac [Hebrew], it is not good, fair, rightly, for every good thing pleases. Thus [Greek] is [Greek]. Deut. 12. 18. [Hebrew]; the Septuagint [Greek], though other copies, with the order changed, read [Greek].

units.la: VERS. 3. [Greek]. Vulgatus, confiderate viros septem. Eras. circumspicite. Beza, dispicite. Hebraismus est, quo ex antecedenti intelligitur consequens, pro considerantes eligite. ideo Syrus [Hebrew], considerate & eligite. sic & Arabs. Æthiopicus simpliciter eligite. Dicitur autem [Greek], quae Arabs ita conjunxit, quasi legeretur, [Greek] vertit enim, de quibus testimonium perhibetur quod sint pleni Spiritu. [Greek], Vulgat. vertit, boni testimonii. Eras. spectata probitatis. Beza, idoneo testimonio ornatos. sufficit cum Syro simpliciter dicere, de quibus testimonium est, die getupgenifie hebben. ies enim de qua agitur satis docet, de bono, honesto & idoneo testimonio sermonem esse.
units.tr: VERS. 3. [Greek]. The Vulgate: look out seven men. Erasmus: look about you. Beza: look out. It is a Hebraism, by which the consequent is understood from the antecedent, meaning consider and then choose. Therefore the Syriac has [Hebrew], consider and choose, and so also the Arabic. The Ethiopic simply has choose. But the words [Greek] are joined by the Arabic as if it read [Greek]; for he renders it of whom testimony is borne that they are full of the Spirit. The Vulgate renders [Greek] as of good testimony; Erasmus as of proven integrity; Beza as adorned with a suitable testimony. It is enough, with the Syriac, simply to say of whom there is testimony, die getupgenifie hebben (have a good testimony). For the context itself sufficiently shows that the discussion is of a good, honourable and suitable testimony.

units.la: VERS. 5. [Greek]. Hebraice id sonat, [Hebrew]. Illud [Hebrew], LXX interdum per [Greek], interdum per [Greek] vertunt. prioris exemplafunt Gen. 34.18. & 41. 37: posterioris Deut. 1.23.
units.tr: VERS. 5. [Greek]. In Hebrew this sounds like [Hebrew]. The Septuagint render that word sometimes by [Greek], sometimes by [Greek]. Examples of the former are Gen. 34. 18 and 41. 37; of the latter, Deut. 1. 23.

units.la: 2 Sam. 3.36. est & ubi ad verbum vertunt per [Greek]. ut 1 Sam. 18.5. & alibi.
units.tr: 2 Sam. 3. 36. There is also a place where they render it word for word by [Greek], as in 1 Sam. 18. 5, and elsewhere.

units.la: VERS. 7. [Greek]. Ait Junius, defuisse [Greek] in suo exemplari. non decet sane in eo quod Erpenius edidit. Syrus pro eo habet, Iudaeorum. quam lectionem veram quidem esse non affirmo, improbandam tamen prorsus non sentio. Quod enim Vir doctis, inepte hic Judaeos nominari censeat, quum solis adhuc Judaeis promulgaretur Euangelium, largirer, si per Judaeos intelligantur omnes Hebraei. At Syrus procul dubio intellexit Judaeos proprie sic dictos, Hebraeos nempe Judaeam incolentes, qui opponebantur τῇ Ἀλεξανδρέων ... Βαβυλῶνι ... ἐν τῇ Ἀλεξανδρέων ἑτέρων, Hebraeis per Babyloniam Asiamve dispersis, itemque per Graecorum insulas. Sic sensus esset, crevisse vehementer discipulorum multitudinem Hierosolymae, non tantum ex Asiaticis Europaeisque, sed & ex Palaestinis Hebraeis. vel Judaei opponuntur proselytis, ut Act. 2. 10. qui cum ad gentem Judaicam pertinerent, licet ex ea oriundi non essent, praedicationis quoque Euangelii participes erant. At nihil causae est, cur recepta τῶν ἑπτὰ lectio, quam praeter Graeca exemplaria omnia, & Chrysostomum, Vulgatus, Arabs & Aethiopicus comprobant, suspecta sit. Cur enim ex plebe sola, non autem ex ductoribus quosdam Euangelii sui luce & gratia donarit Deus? nec est quod exiguum sacerdotalis generis numerum supponas, quum Esdr. 2. v. 36. 37. 38. 39. quatuor millia, ducentos & octoginta novem ex captivitate reduces propheta recenseat; quos multum deinde auctos facile est opinari. Ex his si insignem aliquam multitudinem conversam dicamus, non est quod offendamur, si πολὺς ὄχλος multa turba eorum dicatur fidei morem gessisse.
units.tr: VERS. 7. [Greek]. Junius says that [Greek] was missing from his copy. Certainly this is not appropriate in what Erpenius published. The Syriac has of the Jews in its place. I do not affirm that this reading is true, but I do not think it should be utterly rejected. For that learned man judges it foolish to name the Jews here, since the gospel was still being proclaimed only to Jews; I would grant that if by Jews are meant all Hebrews. But the Syriac no doubt understood Jews properly so called, namely the Hebrews dwelling in Judaea, who were opposed to those dispersed in Babylon or Asia, and likewise to those on the islands of the Greeks, to Hebrews scattered through Babylonia or Asia. The sense would then be that the number of disciples in Jerusalem had grown greatly, not only from Asians and Europeans but also from Palestinian Hebrews. Or Jews are opposed to proselytes, as in Acts 2. 10, who, though they belonged to the Jewish nation, though not born of it, were also partakers of the preaching of the gospel. But there is no reason why the accepted reading [Greek], which all Greek copies, Chrysostom, the Vulgate, the Arabic and the Ethiopic confirm, should be suspected. For why should God have bestowed the light and grace of his gospel on the common people only, and not on some of the leaders? Nor is there any reason to suppose a small number of priestly stock, since the prophet in Ezra 2. 36–39 lists four thousand two hundred and eighty-nine returning from captivity; and it is easy to suppose that they increased greatly afterwards. If we say that a considerable multitude from among these was converted, there is no reason to be offended if a [Greek], a great crowd of them, is said to have obeyed the faith.

units.la: VERS. 8.
units.tr: VERS. 8.

units.la: πλήρης πίστεως καὶ δυνάμεως, pro πίστεως in 4 codicibus invenit Beza χάριτος. Sic Vulgatus, Erasmus, Syrus & Arabs legerunt. Aethiopicus plenus gratia Dei & potentia.
units.tr: full of faith and power: for faith Beza found grace in four codices. So the Vulgate, Erasmus, the Syriac and the Arabic read. The Ethiopic has full of the grace of God and power.

units.la: VERS. 9. Ἀλεξανδρέων.
units.tr: VERS. 9. Alexandrians.

units.la: Syrus [Syriac word] & ad hujus imitationem Arabs eodem modo. Errat autem doctiss. Interpres, quod Syrum & Arabem exi-stimet, singulari numero vertisse ἡ Synagoga Libertini. est enim plurale, quamvis peregrinae terminationis, quia peregrina vox est. a singulari [Syriac word], quod & ipsum peregrinæ terminationis est. sic Aposal. 2. 6. pro τῶν Νικολαϊτῶν est apud Syrum ܥܠܝܐ quod plurale itidem est, à ܕܢܝܐ. videntur autem omnino Libertini dici, Judæi qui pro mancipiis divenditi, deinde emancipati, & Latina voce Libertini dicti, peculiare collegium Hierosolymæ habuerint. Porro textus noster sic habet, Ἀνέστησαν δέ τινες τῶν ἐκ τῆς συναγωγῆς τῆς λεγομένης Λιβερτίνων, ἐ Κυρηναίων &c. Illud καὶ Vulgatus quoq; & Arabs noster (Junii enim aut non habuit, aut à Junio est neglectum) legerunt ut & Æthiopicus. videturque omnino varias synagogas innuere, quarum prima fuerit Libertinorum, altera Cyrenæorum, tertia Alexandrinorum &c. Cum enim copula ista Libertinos ab Alexandrinis, Cyrenæis, reliquisque distinguat, quid attinebat illos cum hisce non Libertinis in idem collegium compingere? Apud Syrum vero, qui καὶ aut non legit, aut omisit, res plana est. Vertit enim, surrexerunt quidam è synagoga quæ vocatur Libertinorum, Cyrenai & Alexandrini &c. Sic unum indigetatur collegium Libertinis Judæis consecratum, cujuscunque tandem gentis essent, sive Cyrenæi, sive Alexandrini, sive Cilices, sive Asiatici, quod valde nobis arrideret, si lectio comprobaretur.
units.tr: The Syriac, and in imitation of it the Arabic, has the same form (the Syriac word). The learned interpreter errs, however, in thinking that the Syriac and Arabic rendered the synagogue of the Libertines in the singular. It is a plural, though of a foreign ending, because the word itself is foreign. It comes from the singular (the Syriac word), which is itself of a foreign ending. So too in Acts 2. 6, where the Greek has of the Nicolaitans, the Syriac has a word which is likewise plural, from a singular. It seems that the Libertines were called such, namely Jews who had been sold as slaves, then freed, and called Libertines by a Latin name, and that they had a special congregation in Jerusalem. Moreover, our text reads: [Greek], that is, some arose from the synagogue called that of the Libertines, of the Cyrenians, etc. The Vulgate too, and our Arabic (for Junius either did not have it or neglected it), read that kai, as does the Ethiopic. And it seems altogether to indicate various synagogues, the first of Libertines, the second of Cyrenians, a third of Alexandrians, and so on. For since that conjunction distinguishes the Libertines from the Alexandrians, Cyrenians and the rest, why would one gather them into the same congregation with those who were not Libertines? But in the Syriac, which either did not read or omitted the kai, the matter is plain. For it renders: some arose from the synagogue which is called that of the Libertines, Cyrenians and Alexandrians, etc. Thus one congregation is indicated, consecrated to Jewish Libertines, of whatever nation they might be, whether Cyrenians, Alexandrians, Cilicians or Asians. This would please us greatly, if that reading were confirmed.

units.la: VERS. 10. ὁ ἰλαλῆ. Beza, per quem loquebatur. rectè annotavit vir doctiss. phrasin Græcam non aliam admittere interpretationem. Vulgatus, qui loquebatur. ὁ ἰλαλῆ. Syrus & Arabs plenius, qui loquebatur in eo. quod idem est, atque per quem loquebatur. Æthiopicus hic ut alibi sæpe paraphrasten egit, non potuerunt resistere ei, quia insapientia & Spiritu sancto alloquebatur eos.
units.tr: VERS. 10. to whom he spoke. Beza: through whom he spoke. The learned man rightly noted that Greek idiom admits no other interpretation. The Vulgate: who spoke. The Syriac and the Arabic, more fully: who spoke in him, which is the same as through whom he spoke. Here, as often elsewhere, the Ethiopic played the paraphrast: they could not withstand him, because he spoke to them in wisdom and by the Holy Spirit.

units.la: VERS. 11. Τότε ἐξαπέστειλαν ἄνδρας λέγοντας. Optimè mentem expresserunt Syrus & Arabs, Tunc miserunt quosdam & docuerunt eos ut dicerent.
units.tr: VERS. 11. Then they suborned men who said. The Syriac and the Arabic express the sense very well: Then they sent certain men and taught them to say.

units.la: C A P. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII

units.la: VERS. 2. Visus est patri nostro Abrahæ quum esset in Mesopotamia. at \u05e4 f. 4. dicitur Abraham exiisse è terra Chaldæorum. an ergo Chaldæa pertinet ad Mesopotamiam ? Sic etiamnum censent Arabes. Geographus enim Nubiensis sexta parte climatis quarti, ubi [Arabic], Mesopotamiam describit, dicit eò pertinere regiones quasdam [Arabic], Parthia, & inter eas [Arabic], Bagdad, quæ hodierna Babylonia est, Chaldææ metropolis. cujus provinciam Benjamin in Itiner. pag. 75. edit. Leydensis, constituit [Arabic], in terra Sinear, quæ est Chaldæa.
units.tr: VERS. 2. He appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia. But at vers. 4 it is said that Abraham came out of the land of the Chaldeans. Does Chaldaea then belong to Mesopotamia? The Arabs still think so. For the Nubian geographer, in the sixth part of the fourth climate, where he describes Mesopotamia, says that certain regions belong to it, Parthia among them, and among these Baghdad, which is today's Babylonia and the metropolis of Chaldaea. Benjamin, in his Itinerary (p. 75, Leiden edition), assigns its province to the land of Shinar, which is Chaldaea.

units.la: VERS. 4. Τότε ἐξελθὼν ἐκ γῆς Χαλδαίων, κατῳκησεν ἐν Χαρ-ράν. κἀκεῖθεν, μὴ πὰ ἀποθανεῖν τὸ πατέρα αὐτοῦ, μετῳκισεν αὐτὸν εἰς τὴν γῆν ταύτην εἰς ἣν ὑμεῖς νῦν κατοικεῖτε. Exercuit multùm eruditos, quod Abrahamum dicatur Deus transtulisse è Charran in terram Canaan, mortuo patre ejus Tharè. quum Gen. 12. 4. dicatur Abrahamus profectus è Charran, ætatis anno 75. natus autem fuit ætatis Tharæ anno 70. ut ex Gen. 11. 26. colligendum videtur. exivit ergo è Charran, ætatis Tharæ anno 145. qui vixit annos 205. Gen. 11. 32. supervixit ergo ab egressu Abrahami ex Charran, annos 60. Solvi hunc nodum docet Cl. Mercerus, si Abraham negetur fuisse primogenitus, sed natus statuatur ætatis Tharæ anno 130. quibus si addas annos 75, quæ ætas erat Abrahami, quum Charran defecerat, incidet in verum annum mortis Tharæ. Aliam adfert solutionem Eucherii, qui eum quidem ante mortem Tharæ excessisse è Charran voluerit, sed sexaginta demum post annis, mortuo patre, collocatum verè fuisse in terra Canaan, & quasi inquilinum factum, ubi agrum in ea emisset, atque id Stephanum innuere voce κατοικιαν. Sed monemus, quod Cl. Mercerus non animadvertit, πξωπμάτητος non dixisse κατοικίαν, sed μετοικίζειν αὐτὴν. Vulgatus transtulit eum. Syrus eodem sensu ܐܬܐ . & Arabs ܘܐܠ. verum ubi de habitatione ejus in Charran agitur, dicitur, κατοίκησεν ἐν Χαρράν. Considerent eruditi & nostram conjecturam. Dicit Stephanus translatum fuisse Abrahamum ἐκ τῆς γῆς τοῦ γένους, εἰς τὴν γῆν ὑμῶν τὴν καναὰν. quibus verbis non videtur innui terra Canaan universim, sed speciatim determinari ea pars, quae tribui Judae cesserat, in qua Judaei, quos Hierosolymis alloquebatur Stephanus, tum habitabant. adeoque respici habitationem ejus in Mamre, & quidem postquam empto ibi prope Hebron in medio tribus Judae agro firmam sedem ibi fixit. quod non nisi mortuo patre Thare contigisse ex historia colligi potest. Digressus enim à Charran aetatis anno 75. venit Sichemum, inde juxta Bethel, inde Ægyptum petiit. reversus contendit ad priorem locum juxta Bethel exinde quidem consedit in planitie Mamre, ibique per annos aliquot haesit, non tamen firma fede. eversa enim Sodoma profectus est Gerarem in terram Philistaeorum, ubi natus est Isaac, anno Abrahami 100. diciturque peregrinatus in regione Philistaeorum diebus multis, Gen.21.34. perrexit certe habitare Beersebae non procul à Gerare, etiam post tentatam Isaaci oblationem. Tandem vero contulit se Hebronem, ubi mortua est Sara. in cujus sepulturam agrum isthic loci emit è regione Mamre, in medio tribus Judae, ubi sepulta Sara. ubi exinde tanquam in propria possessione vixit ad mortem usque Abrahamus, ibidemque sepultus est. adeo ut ad id usque tempus vagatus fuerit, ac tum demum fixum domicilium, idque in ea terrae parte, in qua tempore Stephani tribus Judae habitabat, natus fuisse recte dicatur. quando autem id contigerit, sic colligi poteft. Mortua est Sara, annos nata 127. Gen. 23. 1. tum Abrahamus annos habuit 136. quippe novem annis major Sarâ. hæc enim 90. erat annorum, quum promissio ei de concipiendo Isaaco fieret, Gen. 17. 17. ille autem 99. Ibid. ⁊f. 24. Separentur jam à 136, anni 75, quæ ætas erat Abrahami, quum è Charran discederet, restant anni 61, qui inter egressum è Charran, emptumque agrum ac firmatam in tribu Judæ sedem intercesserunt, annoque uno mortem Tharæ excesserunt. Videtur autem non sine prudenti Dei consilio factum, quod cum per sexaginta annos huc illuc per terram Canaan vagatus esset Abraham, tandem in ea terræ parte, quæ Judæ attribuenda, regnoque & sacris destinata erat, firmam usque ad vitæ finem sedem invenerit, nec dubium, quin se Judæ posteri eo nomine digniores aliis tribubus felicioresque gloriarentur. non est, inquit, Stephanus, quod ea in re felicitatem collocetis. nam ne pater quidem vester Abrahamus inde fuit felicior. Etsi enim eum è Charran eductum, post multas peregrinationes tandem patre ejus mortuo, Deus in hanc eandem terram transtulerit, in qua vos Judæ posteri nunc habitatis, hæreditatem tamen ei in ea non dedit, ne quidem vestigii pedis. quod faciendum sane fuerat, si ad felicitatem conferre ea quicquam poterat. Etsi enim agrum in ea sibi comparasset, quia tamen ad sepulturam tantum, non ad præsentis vitæ usum spectabat, pro hæreditate haberi non poterat. præsertim non pro eâ, quam Deus promiserat, quæ pecuniâ nequaquam emi, sed solius Dei donatione haberi debebat. At vero inquit, Deus in hac ipsa terra, quam vos jam nunc incolitis, & in quam Abrahamum quoque transtulerat, ne vestigium quidem pedis ipsi dederat. itaque aliunde pendebat Abrahami felicitas, aliunde pendet & vestra. Porro, quia in Charran habitavit Abraham, sacer is locus, etiam Benjaminis tempore, fuit Muhammedanis. sic enim is Itinerarii pag. 69. edit. Leydensis,
units.tr: VERS. 4. Then he went out of the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran. And from there, after his father died, God moved him into this land, in which you now live [Τότε ἐξελθὼν ἐκ γῆς Χαλδαίων, κατῳκησεν ἐν Χαρράν. κἀκεῖθεν, μετὰ τὸ ἀποθανεῖν τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῦ, μετῴκισεν αὐτὸν εἰς τὴν γῆν ταύτην εἰς ἣν ὑμεῖς νῦν κατοικεῖτε]. Many learned men have been troubled that God is said to have transferred Abraham from Haran into the land of Canaan after his father Terah died. For at Gen. 12.4 Abraham is said to have set out from Haran in his seventy-fifth year, and Terah's age at Abraham's birth was seventy, as seems to be gathered from Gen. 11.26. So he left Haran when Terah was 145, and Terah lived 205 years (Gen. 11.32). Terah therefore outlived Abraham's departure from Haran by 60 years. Mercer, the distinguished scholar, teaches how to untie this knot: if Abraham is denied to have been the firstborn, but is held to have been born in Terah's 130th year, then if you add 75, Abraham's age when he left Haran, you arrive at the true year of Terah's death. Eucherius offers another solution: he holds that Abraham did leave Haran before his father's death, but only sixty years later, after his father's death, did he truly settle in the land of Canaan, becoming as it were a sojourner, when he bought a field there; and that Stephen hints at this by the word "settlement" [κατοικίαν]. But we point out, what Mercer did not notice, that Stephen did not say κατοικίαν but μετοικίζειν αὐτὴν [moved him]. The Vulgate translates "transferred him." The Syriac uses the same sense, and the Arab likewise. But where his dwelling in Haran is spoken of, the text says κατῴκησεν ἐν Χαρράν [he settled in Haran]. Let the learned also consider our own conjecture. Stephen says that Abraham was transferred "out of the land of his kindred" into "your land, the land of Canaan." By these words it does not seem that the land of Canaan in general is meant, but that a particular part is specified, namely that which had fallen to the tribe of Judah, where the Jews whom Stephen was addressing in Jerusalem then lived. And so his dwelling in Mamre is referred to, and indeed after he bought a field there near Hebron, in the middle of the tribe of Judah, and fixed a firm seat there. History shows that this could not have happened until after his father Terah's death. For after leaving Haran in his seventy-fifth year he came to Shechem, then near Bethel, then sought Egypt. Returning, he went back to the former place near Bethel, and from there settled in the plain of Mamre, and stayed there for some years, but without a firm seat. For after Sodom was overthrown he moved to Gerar in the land of the Philistines, where Isaac was born in Abraham's 100th year; and it is said that he sojourned in the land of the Philistines for many days (Gen. 21.34). He certainly went on living at Beersheba, not far from Gerar, even after the attempted sacrifice of Isaac. At last, however, he went to Hebron, where Sarah died; and for her burial he bought a field there, opposite Mamre, in the middle of the tribe of Judah, where Sarah was buried. From then on, as in his own possession, Abraham lived there until his death, and was buried there. So it is rightly said that he wandered until that time, and then at last fixed his home, and that in that part of the land where the tribe of Judah lived at the time of Stephen. When this happened may be gathered thus. Sarah died aged 127 (Gen. 23.1), and Abraham was then 136, being nine years older than Sarah; for she was ninety when the promise of Isaac's conception was made to him (Gen. 17.17), while he was ninety-nine (ibid. v. 24). Now subtract from 136 the seventy-five years, Abraham's age when he left Haran; 61 years remain, which passed between his departure from Haran and his buying the field and fixing a firm seat in the tribe of Judah, and these fell one year short of Terah's death. It seems that it was not without the prudent counsel of God that, though Abraham had wandered here and there through the land of Canaan for sixty years, he at last found a firm seat until the end of his life in that part of the land which was to be assigned to Judah and destined for kingship and worship; and there is no doubt that the descendants of Judah gloried in this above the other tribes as more worthy and more fortunate. "There is no reason," says Stephen, "for you to place your happiness in this. For not even your father Abraham was made happier by it. Although God transferred him, after many wanderings, when his father was dead, into this same land in which you descendants of Judah now live, yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's breadth. This surely ought to have been done, if it could contribute anything to happiness. For though he had acquired a field there for himself, since it looked only to burial and not to the use of the present life, it could not be regarded as an inheritance, especially not as that which God had promised, which could by no means be bought with money but had to be held by the sole gift of God. But, he says, God did not even give him a foot's breadth in this very land which you now inhabit, and into which he had also transferred Abraham. So Abraham's happiness depended on something else, and yours depends on something else too." Moreover, because Abraham lived in Haran, that place was holy to the Muslims even in Benjamin's time. For so the Itinerary says (p. 69, Leiden edition):

units.la: יהודים ושם כנסת עורא ובאותו מקום שהיה שם בית של אברהם אביהם אין עליו ,בנין וישבעאלים סבבים אותו מקום ובאים שם להתפלל In antiqua Haran sunt 20. ferme Iudai, & synagoga Esra. quo vero loco aedes Abrahami patris nostri quondam fuere, nullum extat aedificium. & Ismaelita locum eum venerantes, proficiscuntur eo precandi gratia.
units.tr: יהודים ושם כנסת עורא ובאותו מקום שהיה שם בית של אברהם אביהם אין עליו בנין וישבעאלים סבבים אותו מקום ובאים שם להתפלל. In old Haran there are about twenty Jews and the synagogue of Ezra. But at the place where there once was the house of Abraham our father there is no building standing. And the Ishmaelites surround that place, venerating it, and go there to pray.

units.la: VERS. 5. Nec dedit ei possessionem in ea, ne vestigium quidem pedis. καὶ ἐπηγγείλατο &c. Vulg. & Erasm. & repromisit, illud re iterationis non est in Graeco. Arabs [Arabic] sed promisit ei. Beza, quamvis pollicitus esset. καὶ pro καίπερ hic accipit, ut & Matth. 5,19. & 15,5. At nihil necesse mihi videtur, in ullo horum locorum ita accipere. & quod ad hunc locum attinet, non videtur adversativa particula quamvis hic habere locum, ob ea quae versum finiunt, ὃτε οὐτῷ τίκνα, quum non haberet filium, id est, quamvis non haberet filium. non ergo hoc mirari videtur Stephanus, quod Deus ne vestigium quidem pedis Abrahamo haereditarium dederit in Cananaea, licet ipsi eam promisisset: sed quod eam ipsi feminique ejus promiserit, licet filium haeredem non haberet. Itaque ᾧ ἐπηγγείλαλο verto ut sonat, & promisit. vel ut Syrus [Syriac] enim, junctum verbo praeterito, plusquamperfectum format. Duo mihi hic Protomartyr contribulibus suis in patriarcha Abrahamo consideranda proponere videtur, quibus fidem ejus Deus vehementer exercuerit. Primum, quod in terram Canaan & in Judaeam eum transtulerit, nec tamen ullam possessionem, ne vestigii quidem pedis ei dederit. Alterum, quod hanc terram ipsi & femini ejus obtinendam promiserit, quum semen non haberet. τέκνον, filium melius, meo judicio, verterunt Vulgatus, Erasmus, Syrus & Arabs, quam Beza prolem. de quo etiam ad Matth. 22.24. antehac diximus. & hoc quidem loco generali nomine opus non est Interpreti, tum quod hæredes terræ promissæ filii essent, non filiæ. tum quod pro בְּנֵי, filio, υἱῷ dicere, usitatissimum est lxx interpretibus. exemplo sic locus huic nostro parallelus, Gen. 17. 16. תֵּן נְתִי לְךָ מִמֶּנָּה בֵּן, etiam dabo tibi ex ea filium. lxx, Ἐ δώσω σοι ἐξ αὐτῆς υἱόν.
units.tr: VERS. 5. Nor did he give him possession in it, not even a foot's breadth. [καὶ ἐπηγγείλατο, etc.] The Vulgate and Erasmus have "and he promised" (repromisit); the word for repetition is not in the Greek. The Arabic has "he promised him." Beza has "although he had promised." Beza takes καὶ here in the sense of καίπερ, as also at Matt. 5.19 and 15.5. But it seems to me there is no need to take it so in any of these places. And as far as this passage is concerned, the concessive particle does not seem to apply here, given the words that end the verse, ὅτε οὐκ ἦν αὐτῷ τέκνον [when he had no child], that is, although he had no child. So Stephen does not seem to marvel that God gave Abraham not even a foot's breadth of inheritance in Canaan, though he had promised it to him; rather that he promised it to him and to his seed, although he had no heir. Therefore I translate the verb ἐπηγγείλατο as it sounds, "and he promised," or as the Syriac does, joining it with the preterite verb to form a pluperfect. Here the first martyr seems to set before his fellow tribesmen two things to consider in the patriarch Abraham, by which God severely tested his faith. First, that he transferred him into the land of Canaan and into Judaea, and yet gave him no possession, not even a foot's breadth. Second, that he promised him and his seed to possess this land when he had no seed. In my judgement Vulgate, Erasmus, the Syriac and the Arabic translate τέκνον better as "son" than Beza does as "offspring" [τέκνον]. I have already spoken of this at Matt. 22.24. Nor is the translator required here to use a general term, both because the heirs of the promised land were sons, not daughters, and because to say υἱῷ for בְּנֵי [son] is very usual with the Seventy. An example of a parallel passage is Gen. 17.16: תֵּן נְתִי לְךָ מִמֶּנָּה בֵּן, "I will also give you a son by her." The Seventy: καὶ δώσω σοι ἐξ αὐτῆς υἱόν [and I will give you a son by her].

units.la: VERS. 6. Ἐ λάλησεν αὐτῇ ὁ Θεός. pro αὐτῇ Syrus quoque & Arabs videntur legisse αὐτῷ. verterunt enim, & locutus est Deus cum eo, dicens ei. nisi forte αὐτὴ expositerint per dicens, quæ vera ejus est expositio. ὅτι ἔχει τὸ σπέρμα αὐτοῦ παροικον. Syrus & Arabs pro αὐτῷ legerunt σα. aut certè perspicuitatis gratia tertiam personam in secundam mutarunt, quod & Beza fecit, ut Deum potius loquentem, quam Lucam narrantem introducerent. Et male tractabunt, ἐπὶ πεξαχόσια, annos quadringentos. in hoc numero conveniunt quoque Syrus, Arabs, & Æthiopicus. Invenitur autem à nato Isaaco hoc modo. Isaacus, anno ætatis Abrahami 100 natus, suscepit Jacobum ætatis suæ anno 60. Jacobus natus annos 130 venit in Ægyptum. Exinde usque ad liberationem fluxerunt anni 210. habes 400. quibus si addas 25 annos Abrahami, ex quo ex Haran profectus est, (discesserat inde enim anno ætatis 75) rursus 5 annos, quibus derelicta Chaldæa Harane habitavit, habes 430 annos, de quibus Exod. 12. 41. & Gal. 3. 17.
units.tr: VERS. 6. ἐλάλησεν αὐτῇ ὁ Θεός [ἐλάλησεν αὐτῇ ὁ Θεός]. The Syriac and the Arabic seem to have read αὐτῷ, "to him," in place of αὐτῇ, "to her," for they translate: and God spoke with him, saying to him. Unless perhaps they took αὐτὴ as "saying," which is indeed the correct sense of it. ὅτι ἔσται τὸ σπέρμα αὐτοῦ πάροικον [ὅτι ἔσται τὸ σπέρμα αὐτοῦ πάροικον]. The Syriac and Arabic read a word for "to him" here. Either way, for clarity they changed the third person into the second, as Beza also did, so that God is introduced as speaking rather than Luke as narrating. And they will ill-treat them for four hundred years, [ἐπὶ τετρακόσια]. The Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic agree on this number. It is reckoned from the birth of Isaac as follows. Isaac was born when Abraham was 100 years old, and he begot Jacob in his sixtieth year. Jacob, aged 130, came into Egypt. From then until the deliverance there passed 210 years. You have 400. If you add the 25 years of Abraham from the time he set out from Haran (for he had left it at the age of 75), and again the 5 years during which he lived in Haran after leaving Chaldea, you have 430 years, concerning which see Exod. 12. 41 and Gal. 3. 17.

units.la: VERS. 8. Et dedit ei fœdus circumcisionis, ἐ ὑτως ἐγέννησε τὸν Ἰσαὰκ, & sic genuit Isaacum. Syrus, Arabs, & Æthiopicus, & tunc genuit. similiter ὅτως per tunc vertunt, Act. 20. 11. vide quæ annotavimus ad Joan 4. 6. ubi ὅτως pro particula illativa interdum usurpari docemus.
units.tr: VERS. 8. And he gave him the covenant of circumcision, οὕτως ἐγέννησε τὸν Ἰσαάκ [οὕτως ἐγέννησε τὸν Ἰσαάκ], and so he begot Isaac. The Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic have and then he begot. Similarly they render οὕτως by then, as at Acts 20. 11. See what I have noted on John 4. 6, where I show that οὕτως is sometimes used as an inferential particle.

units.la: VERS. 10. Et eruit eum ex omnibus, τῶν θλίψεων αὐτοῦ, afflictionibus ipsius. Syrus [Syriac text], oppressoribus ejus. quod moneo, quia Trem. male vertit angustiis suis. & Boder. oppressionibus ejus. id Syriacè dicitur [Syriac text].
units.tr: VERS. 10. And he rescued him from all his afflictions, τῶν θλίψεων αὐτοῦ [τῶν θλίψεων αὐτοῦ], his afflictions. The Syriac has his oppressors. I point this out because Tremellius mistranslates it as his straits, and Bodere as his oppressions. In Syriac the word is used for oppressors.

units.la: G 3 altera illa vox concreta est, non abstracta. estque nomen actoris. Arabs receptam lectionem sequitur.
units.tr: That other word is concrete, not abstract, and it is the name of the agent. The Arabic follows the received reading.

units.la: VERS. 13. A'νηγγελθη ἱωσὴφ τῆς ἀδελφὰς αὐτῶ. Vulg. Eraf. & Beza, agnitus est Iofeph à fratribus suis. id est, ἐφανερώθη τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς αὐτοῦ. malim ad verbum, notificatus est Ioseph fratribus suis. neque enim hîc actio fratrum indigetatur, quâ ipsi Iosephum agnoverint, sed Iosephi potius, qui se ipsis aperuit. quod quum recte animadverterent Syrus & Arabs, verterunt, notum fecit Ioseph seipsum fratribus suis.
units.tr: VERS. 13. Ἀνεγνωρίσθη Ἰωσὴφ τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς αὐτοῦ [ἀνεγνωρίσθη Ἰωσὴφ τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς αὐτοῦ]. The Vulgate, Erasmus and Beza have Joseph was recognised by his brothers. That is, Joseph was made known to his brothers, ἐφανερώθη τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς αὐτοῦ. I would prefer a word-for-word rendering: Joseph was made known to his brothers. For the action here is not that of the brothers recognising him, but rather that of Joseph, who revealed himself to them. The Syriac and the Arabic noticed this correctly and rendered it: Joseph made himself known to his brothers.

units.la: VERS. 14. E'v ἱσδομήκοντα τὴν ψυχὰς. Multum torsit Interpretes conciliatio hujus loci cum illo Gen. 46. 27. ubi septuaginta solum animas domus Jacobi, quæ intrarunt in Ægyptum, commemorat Moses. At difficultatis parum est, si dicamus, non esse loca parallela. Moses enim catalogum instituit, in quo una cum Jacobo soli ejus posteri, & quidem ex femore ejus egressi, exceptis diserte filiorum uxoribus, ᵻf. 26. comprehenduntur. ob quam causam, non ii solum qui cum ipso Ægyptum adtu sunt ingressi, sed & Joseph cum duobus filiis Ephraim & Manasse, in septuagenario numero continentur, etsi jam ante in Ægypto essent. quia & ex femore Jacobi nati, & è terra Canaan orti, peregrini in Ægypto degerent, adeoque merito haberentur quasi cum Jacobo in Ægyptum introiissent. Specialisque in eo catalogo rationis est, quod Judæ duo nepotes ex Phares, Hezron scilicet & Hamul, etsi nondum tum, ut ex serie temporis liquido colligitur, sed postmodum in Ægypto nati, in numerum istum ᵻf. 11. referantur: ut nempe duorum filiorum Judæ Er & Onan jam defunctorum locum supplerent. Ob quam causam & Num. 26. 21. quum in reliquis tribubus, veluti Rubenis, Simeonis &c. non nepotes, sed soli filii constituant principes familiarum, in sola tribu Judæ, non modo filii ejus Selah, Phares & Zerah, sed & nepotes Hezron & Hamul principes familiarum Judæ constituuntur, quasi filiis ejus accensiti. Nihil autem horum in oratione Stephani locum habet. non enim genealogia Jacobi instituitur, sed quosnam Josephus è terra Canaan in Ægyptum advocaverit, docetur. verba sunt, Ὑπο-στείλας ἡ Ἰωσὴφ μετακαλέσατο τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῦ Ἰακὼβ, ἐν πᾶσι τῷ συγγενείᾳ αὐτοῦ ἐν ἐβδομήκοντα πέντε ψυχαῖς. plures, quam è femore Jacobi ortos, accersivit. neque omnes è femore Jacobi ortos accersivit. Excludendi ibi sunt, primo duo nepotes Judæ, deinde ipse Joseph cum duobus filiis. illos enim, quippe nondum natos, se suosque filios, quippe jam in Ægypto degentes, accersere non potuit. Separatis istis quinque, deinde & patre Jacobo, qui seorsim à Stephano commemoratur, restant ex septuagenario Mosis numero sexaginta quatuor, nempe undecim fratres, una soror Dina, & 52 fratrum filii. quibus si adjungas undecim fratrum undecim uxores, quasque necessario Josephus una cum maritis accersivit, quæque ad τὸν συγγενῶν pertinebant, habes πάντα τὸν συγγενῶν αὐτοῦ ἐν ἐβδομήκοντα πέντε ψυχαῖς. Æthiopicus vertit, & Joseph postquam cognovisset illud, jussit ut vocarent patrem suum, & totam cognationem suam. & venerunt ad eum 75 animæ. quæ quidem versio excludit Josephum ejusque liberos, quippe qui venisse ad eum dici nequeunt. sed in eo peccat, quod Jacobum etiam includat numero 75 animarum, quippe qui cum reliquis venit ad Josephum. soli autem cognationi competit iste numerus. Nec obstat dictis, quod decem filiorum Benjaminis, qui in numero 52 nepotum Jacobi à Mose censentur Gen. 21. aut nullos aut paucos tum temporis fuisse natos plerique existiment, ideoque nec accersitos recte à Josepho dici posse. Respondere enim liceret, recte ejus filios, etsi postmodum natos, in catalogum referri, ne solus inter omnes fratres sine liberis censeatur. At nil opus eo recurrere, quum ætas ejus omnes istos filios ferat. Joseph enim erat trigenarius, quum primum sisteretur Pharaoni. Gen. 41. 46. inter quod tempus & ingressum Jacobi in Ægyptum intercesserunt 7 anni fertilitatis, & duo sterilitatis, Gen. 45. 6. Nato autem Josepho 39 annos, potuit Benjamin esse annorum 37. qua ætate, præsertim ubi polygamia locum habebat, cur non 10 filiorum pater esse potuerit? Hinc jam colligi potest, nec textui Mosaico ex verbis Stephani, nec verbis Stephani ex textu Mosaico ullum mendum esse ascribendum. Sed pro diverso instituto optimè dixisse ambos. Unde simul consequitur, corruptum esse textum lxx Interpretum, qui Gen. 46. 27. pro 70 habent 75. quod omnino à Christianis ortum videtur, qui quum locum Stephani cum verbis Mosis conciliare non possent, & Stephano fidem omnino habendam esse crederent, textum Græcum Mosis emendarunt aut verius corruperunt, ut demonstrari saltem possit, unde hæc S. Stephanus hauserit. Corruptionis manifesta sunt indicia. Primum enim, omnia exemplaria Hebraea, Josephus 2. lib. Antiq. c. 4. & Vetus Interpres Latinus non legunt nisi 70. 2. Ipsi lxx Interpretes Deut. 10. 22. ubi haec historia repetitur, consentiunt cum Hebraeo, & non enumerant nisi 70. 3. Ut cum specie aliqua veritatis interpolarent versum, quem diximus 27, corruperunt etiam ¥f. 20. ubi contra fidem omnium exemplarium Hebraeorum, & Samaritani, & Veteris Latini, quinque alios addiderunt ex posteris Josephi, nempe Machir filium Manassis ex concubina Syra, & Machiris filium, Manassis nepotem, Galaad. Deinde Ephraimi filios duos, Sutalaam & Taam, filiumque Sutalaami unum, Ephraimi nepotem, Edem. Pro Taam autem Augustinus de Civitat. Dei l. 16. c. 40. habet Bareth, ex 1 Paral. 7. in quo simul capite observandum, nec Taami, nec Edemi fieri mentionem, & Manassis, Machiris, atque Ephraimi plures recenseri filios quam quinque. Cur ergo apud Moisen quinque tantum ex his excerpserunt? quia pluribus opus non habebant, qui numerum Stephani supplere apud Mosen voluerunt. At iidem illi, sibi nequaquam constantes, ✡ 27. Manassi & Ephraimo cum quinque eorum filiis ac nepotibus addiderunt, etsi innominatos, duos alios. Nam pro, quod apud Mosen est, & filii Ioseph, qui nati erant ei in Aegypto sunt ⲯⲏ ⲯⲏ, anima dua, LXX habent, ψυχαὶ ἑννέα, anima novem. unde colligendum postmodum erat numerus animarum 47. adeo ut omnia ibi sint corruptissima, nec ulla fide digna. nec absurdius quicquam tribui S. Stephano potest, quam Iosephum ad se accersivisse non se tantum & duos filios sibi praesentes, sed & tres nepotes ac duos pronepotes, longe post demum natos.
units.tr: VERS. 14. [ἐν ἑβδομήκοντα πέντε ψυχαῖς]. The reconciliation of this passage with Gen. 46. 27 has greatly troubled the interpreters, where Moses mentions only the seventy souls of Jacob's house who entered Egypt. But the difficulty is slight if we say that these are not parallel passages. For Moses drew up a list in which, along with Jacob, only his descendants, and indeed those descended from his thigh, are included, the wives of the sons being expressly excluded (v. 26). For this reason not only those who came into Egypt with him, but also Joseph with his two sons Ephraim and Manasseh, are counted in the number of seventy, although they were already in Egypt before. This is because they were born of Jacob's stock and had come from the land of Canaan, living as strangers in Egypt, and so were rightly regarded as having entered Egypt along with Jacob. There is a special reason in that list for the fact that the two grandsons of Judah through Perez, namely Hezron and Hamul, are included in that number at v. 12 (v. 11 in some editions), although, as is clear from the order of time, they were not yet born then, but were born later in Egypt. They are included so as to fill the places of Judah's two sons Er and Onan, who had already died. For this reason too, at Num. 26. 21, while in the other tribes, such as Reuben, Simeon and so on, only the sons, not the grandsons, are the heads of families, in the tribe of Judah not only his sons Shelah, Perez and Zerah, but also the grandsons Hezron and Hamul are constituted heads of families of Judah, as if they had been reckoned among his sons. None of this, however, has any place in Stephen's speech. For it does not set out Jacob's genealogy, but teaches whom Joseph summoned from the land of Canaan into Egypt. The words are: Ἀποστείλας δὲ Ἰωσὴφ μετεκαλέσατο τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῦ Ἰακὼβ ἐν πάσῃ τῇ συγγενείᾳ ἐν ἑβδομήκοντα πέντε ψυχαῖς [Ἀποστείλας δὲ Ἰωσὴφ μετεκαλέσατο τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῦ Ἰακὼβ ἐν πάσῃ τῇ συγγενείᾳ ἐν ἑβδομήκοντα πέντε ψυχαῖς]. He summoned more than those descended from Jacob's thigh, and not all of those descended from Jacob's thigh. Here we must exclude, first, the two grandsons of Judah, and then Joseph himself with his two sons. For since they were not yet born, he could not summon them, and his sons, who were already living in Egypt, could not be summoned by him either. With those five set aside, and also the father Jacob, who is mentioned separately by Stephen, there remain sixty-four of Moses' seventy: namely, eleven brothers, one sister Dinah, and fifty-two sons of the brothers. If you add to these the eleven wives of the eleven brothers, whom Joseph necessarily summoned along with their husbands, and who belonged to the kinsfolk, you have all his kinsfolk in seventy-five souls. [πάντα τὸν συγγενῶν αὐτοῦ ἐν ἑβδομήκοντα πέντε ψυχαῖς]. The Ethiopic renders it: And Joseph, after he had learned of it, ordered them to call his father and all his kinsfolk, and there came to him seventy-five souls. This version does exclude Joseph and his children, since they cannot be said to have come to him. But it errs in that it includes Jacob too in the number of seventy-five souls, since he came to Joseph with the rest. Yet that number suits only the kindred. Nor is it an objection that many think that the ten sons of Benjamin, who are counted by Moses among the fifty-two grandsons of Jacob (Gen. 46. 21), were either none or few born at that time, and so could not rightly be said to have been summoned by Joseph. For one could answer that his sons, although born later, are rightly included in the list, so that he should not be counted alone among all the brothers as without children. But there is no need to have recourse to that, since his age allows for all those sons. For Joseph was thirty years old when he was first presented to Pharaoh (Gen. 41. 46). Between that time and Jacob's entry into Egypt there passed seven years of plenty and two of famine (Gen. 45. 6). Since Joseph was thirty-nine years old when Benjamin was born, Benjamin could have been thirty-seven years old at that time. At that age, especially where polygamy was practised, why could he not have been the father of ten sons? From this it can now be inferred that no error should be ascribed either to the Mosaic text from the words of Stephen, or to the words of Stephen from the Mosaic text. Rather, both spoke very well according to their different purposes. From this it also follows that the text of the Septuagint is corrupt, since at Gen. 46. 27 it has seventy-five in place of seventy. This seems to have arisen entirely among Christians, who, unable to reconcile Stephen's passage with the words of Moses, and believing that Stephen is entirely to be trusted, emended the Greek text of Moses, or rather corrupted it, so that at least it could be shown whence St Stephen drew these things. The signs of corruption are clear. First, all the Hebrew manuscripts, Josephus in the second book of the Antiquities, chapter 4, and the old Latin translator read only seventy. Second, the Septuagint itself at Deut. 10. 22, where this history is repeated, agrees with the Hebrew and counts only seventy. Third, in order to interpolate the verse I mentioned, under a show of truth, they also corrupted v. 20, contrary to the testimony of all the Hebrew manuscripts, of the Samaritan, and of the old Latin, by adding five other descendants of Joseph: Machir, son of Manasseh by a Syrian concubine, and Machir's son Gilead, grandson of Manasseh. Then, two sons of Ephraim, Shuthelah and Tahath, and one son of Shuthelah, Ephraim's grandson, Eran. Augustine, in De Civitate Dei book 16, chapter 40, has Bered in place of Tahath, from 1 Chron. 7. On this chapter it should be observed that no mention is made either of Tahath or of Eran, and that more than five sons are listed for Manasseh, Machir and Ephraim. Why then did they select only five of these in Moses? Because they had no need of more, since they wished to fill out Stephen's number from Moses. But these same men, by no means consistent with themselves, added two others, unnamed, to Manasseh and Ephraim with their five sons and grandsons, at v. 27. For where Moses has and the sons of Joseph who were born to him in Egypt, the Hebrew reads nephesh shenayim, two souls, while the LXX have ψυχαὶ ἐννέα, nine souls. From this one would afterwards have had to deduce a total of forty-seven souls, so that everything there is most corrupt and worthy of no trust. Nor can anything more absurd be attributed to St Stephen than that Joseph summoned to himself not only the two sons who were with him, but also three grandsons and two great-grandsons, who were born much later.

units.la: VERS. 15. 16. Καταβὰς δ' Ἰακὼβ εἰς Αἴγυπτον· καὶ ἐτελεύτησεν αὐτὸς καὶ οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν. Καὶ μετετέθησαν εἰς Συχέμ, καὶ ἐτέθησαν ἐν τῷ μνημείῳ, ὃ ὠνήσατο Ἀβραὰμ πρὸς ἀργυρίου τιμῆς παρὰ τῶν υἱῶν Ἐμμὼρ τοῦ Συχέμ. Variis aliorum in difficillimum hunc locum conjecturis, quas hic lubens praetereo, meam quoque adjungere non verebor. ὁ ὠνήσατο Ἀβραὰμ verti solet, quod emerat Abrahamus, ὁ Ἀβραάμ. quod inexplicabilem peperit difficultatem, quum ex sacra historia constet, non Abrahamum, sed Jacobum eum agrum emisse. at quum articulus non exprimatur, tam Dativus subintelligi potest quam Nominativus, ut sensus sit ὁ ὠνήσατο τῷ Ἀβραάμ, quod emerat (scilicet Jacob, de quo com. praecedenti) Abrahamo. Etsi enim jam tum Abrahamus diem suum obiisset, ipsi tamen dici potest emtus iste ager, ad designandum scopum, quem in agri emtione habuit Jacob, qui non fuit duntaxat, ut eo pro sepulchreto uteretur: neminem enim isthic Jacobus inhumavit, nec ipse ibi inhumatus est. Sed vel maxime, ut primitiae quaedam essent terrae Canaan, cujus totius haereditatem Abrahamo Deus & semini ejus promiserat. non semini, inquam, ejus tantum, sed & ipsi Abrahamo, Gen. 13. 15. quippe cui primo facta est promissio, ut haeres mundi esset; Rom. 4. 13. vere ergo Abrahamo emtus est iltg ager, quippe qui jam promissione divina hæres ejus esset. Atque ibi simul causa latet, cur non tantum Josephus, sed (quod hic à S. Stephano didicimus) reliqui etiam Patriarchæ à posteris, hæreditatem terræ promissæ jam capientibus, Sichemum sint translati, atque in ejus agro sepulti; nempe quia ager iste emtus erat Abrahamo, tanquam pignus hæreditatis totius terræ Abrahamo promissæ. Id & simplicissimum videtur, & totum negocium extricare. Fateor tamen, huic sententiæ repugnare Josephum, qui eos non Sichemi, sed Hebrone sepultos ait. Verba ejus adscribam, quæ habentur Archajol. l. 2. c. 4. πλὰ τῶν ἢ αὐτὸ ἐ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ ζηταῦς ἐδαιμόνως ἐκ τ Αἰγύπτῳ. καὶ τοῦτο ἐμὲ τὰ σώματα κομίσαντες μὴ γένοι αὐτῶν οἱ ἀνήγεντοι ἐ οἱ παῖδες, ἐθαψαν ἐν Χιλέρων. τὰ ἡ Ιωσὴφ ἐξ τοῦ ἑκτωρ ὅτι μετάσπεσαντ ἐκ τ Αἰγύπτῳ οἱ Ἑβραῖοι ὡς τὴν Χαναάν ἐκόμισαν. Moriuntur vero & fratres ejus quum feliciter in Aegypto vixissent, quorum quidem corpora post tempus a'iquod posteri eorum & filii Hebrone sepeliverunt. Josephi autem ossa postmodum, quum ex Aegypto migrarunt Hebrai, in Cananeam transportarunt. Unde colligitur, undecim Patriarcharum corpora Hebrone, & quidem ante migrationem ex Ægypto, fuisse humata. Josephi autem ossa serius, migrantibus ipsis, in Cananæam translata. Etsi enim undecim Patriarcharum corpora non statim ab ipsorum morte, sed μετὰ χρόνον, interjecto tempore sepulta dicat: Josephi tamen ossa solius, dicit translata esse ὕστερον, postea, cum ex Ægypto migrassent. priorum ergo inhumatio contigit ante migrationem. quod & ipsa series narrationis à Stephano institutæ arguere videtur. quum enim primum de Jacobi morte egisset, deinde de Patriarcharum morte, translatione & sepelitione, subjicit, appropinquasse deinde tempus promissionis Abrahamo factæ, adeoque auctum magno numero populum incurrisse regis odium, & à Mose post tristissimas calamitates ex Ægypto eductum. quæ sane sic narrantur, ut post Patriarcharum sepelitionem contigisse videantur. Quod si ita est, sic statuendum videtur, Patriarcharum filios transtulisse ipsorum corpora Sichemum primò, ad filios Emmor patris Sichem, tanquam ad amicos, in quorum regione agrum sibi avita hæreditate vindicabant. inde Hebronem transportasse, & in sepulchro, quod Abrahamus emerat, condidisse, operâ & adjumento filiorum Emmor patris Sichem. quum enim rerum adhuc in Cananæa potientibus peregrinis populis inhumatio ea contigerit, adeoque periculum Hebræis, patrum suorum cadavera inhumaturis, creari à Cananæis incolis potuisset, prudenter admodum Sichemum se primum contulerunt, filiorumque Emmor non modo opem postularunt, sed &, quo tutius perageretur, rem totam ipsis commiserunt, ut negocium hoc tanquam suum conficerent. ita οὐ τ' ὑμῖν Ἐμμὼρ ἡ Συχέμ non erit construendum cum ἀνήρ, sed cum ἰτίφ quam sententiam, ob Iosephi authoritatem, fateor apud me potiorem esse.
units.tr: VERS. 15, 16. Jacob went down into Egypt, and died there, he and our fathers. And they were carried over to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Emmor the father of Shechem [Καταβὰς δ' Ἰακὼβ εἰς Αἴγυπτον· καὶ ἐτελεύτησεν αὐτὸς καὶ οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν. Καὶ μετετέθησαν εἰς Συχέμ, καὶ ἐτέθησαν ἐν τῷ μνημείῳ, ὃ ὠνήσατο Ἀβραὰμ πρὸς ἀργυρίου τιμῆς παρὰ τῶν υἱῶν Ἐμμὼρ τοῦ Συχέμ]. Since others have offered various conjectures on this very difficult passage, which I gladly pass over here, I shall not hesitate to add my own. The phrase "ho ōnēsato Abraam" [ὁ ὠνήσατο Ἀβραὰμ] is commonly rendered "which Abraham had bought," taking Abraam as the subject. That produces an insoluble difficulty, since sacred history makes clear that it was not Abraham but Jacob who bought that field. But because the article is not expressed, the dative can be understood just as well as the nominative, so that the sense is "which (Jacob) had bought for Abraham" (the subject being Jacob, from the preceding context). For although Abraham had by then already died, the field could still be said to have been bought for him, to mark the purpose Jacob had in buying it. It was not merely to serve as a burial place, for Jacob buried no one there, nor was he himself buried there. Rather it was, above all, so that it would be a kind of first fruits of the land of Canaan, the whole inheritance of which God had promised to Abraham and to his seed (Gen. 13. 15). I say promised not only to his seed but to Abraham himself, to whom the promise was first made that he would be heir of the world (Rom. 4. 13). Truly, then, that field was bought for Abraham, since by divine promise it was already his inheritance. Here too lies the reason why not only Joseph but also (as we learn here from St Stephen) the other patriarchs were carried over to Shechem by their descendants, who were already taking possession of the inheritance of the promised land, and were buried in its field. The reason is that this field had been bought for Abraham, as a pledge of the whole land promised to him. This seems both the simplest explanation and one that untangles the whole matter. I admit, however, that Josephus stands against this view, for he says they were buried not at Shechem but at Hebron. I shall quote his words, which are found in Antiquities, book 2, chapter 4: "Their brothers, when they had lived happily in Egypt, died; and their descendants and sons later buried their bodies, after carrying them out of Egypt, at Hebron. Joseph's bones, however, when the Hebrews later left Egypt, they carried to Canaan." Hence it is gathered that the bodies of the eleven patriarchs were buried at Hebron, and indeed before the departure from Egypt, while the bones of Joseph alone were carried across later, when the people themselves had migrated. For although he says the bodies of the eleven were not buried immediately after their death but "after a time" [μετὰ χρόνον], with an interval, he says only of Joseph's bones that they were carried across "later" [ὕστερον], after they had left Egypt. So the burial of the first group took place before the departure. The very order of the narrative set out by Stephen seems to show this too. For after he had first spoken of Jacob's death, then of the death, transfer and burial of the patriarchs, he adds that the time of the promise made to Abraham then drew near, and that the people, greatly increased in number, incurred the hatred of the king and were led out of Egypt by Moses after most grievous calamities. These events are certainly related in such a way that they seem to have happened after the burial of the patriarchs.
