If this is so, it seems necessary to conclude that the sons of the patriarchs first carried their fathers' bodies to Shechem, to the sons of Emmor, father of Shechem, as to friends, in whose region they claimed for themselves by ancestral inheritance a field. From there they conveyed them to Hebron and placed them in the tomb that Abraham had bought, with the labour and help of the sons of Emmor, father of Shechem. For since this burial took place while foreign peoples still held power in Canaan, and so danger could arise from the Canaanite inhabitants for the Hebrews who were to bury their fathers' corpses, they very wisely went first to Shechem and sought not only the help of the sons of Emmor but also, to make the business safer, entrusted the whole affair to them, so that they might carry it out as their own. Thus "the sons of Emmor, the father of Shechem" [οὐ τ' ὑμῖν Ἐμμὼρ ἡ Συχέμ] should not be construed with "man" but with "price." I admit that, on account of Joseph's authority, I hold this opinion as the more probable.

units.la: VERS. 19. οὗτος καταφιλιύμενος τὸ γένος ἡμῶν. Vulg. & Eraf. hic circumveniens genus nostrum. Beza, hic adversus genus nostrum ingeniosus. Syrus optimè, [Syriac], quod non rectè Tremel. composuit se adversus generationem nostram. Melius Boder. dolosè egit. Nos, astutia usus est. Syris enim [Syriac], astutus, callidus, versutus, vafer. [Syriac], astutia, versutia, calliditas. [Syriac], ars, astutia. Nec aliter accipiendum illud Exod. 1. 9. [Hebrew], LXX. δεῦτε οὖν καταφιλιώμεθα αὐτούς. verto, agite, astutè nos geramus in eos. [Hebrew] enim non sapientia tantum, sed & astutia. Porro, quod in eodem versu sequitur, ἵνα μὴ ζωογονήσωσιν, Syrus vertit & Arabs, ut non viverent. Vulg. ut non vivificarentur. Eraf. ne vitales essent. ad puerulos referunt, qui in aquas abjiciebantur. quod etsi Beza perperam factum dicat, qui ad parentes referens vertit, ut non sobolesceren t, illud tamen præferimus. vide quæ de voce ζωογονεῖσθαι ad Luc. 17. 33. annotavimus.
units.tr: VERS. 19. "This man, dealing craftily with our race" [οὗτος καταφιλιούμενος τὸ γένος ἡμῶν]. The Vulgate and Erasmus have "this man, circumventing our race." Beza has "this man, cunning against our race." The Syriac renders it well, though Tremellius does not, when he has "he arranged himself against our generation." Bodé has the better version: "he acted deceitfully." We have "he used craft." For in Syriac the words mean "crafty, cunning, sly, wily," and "craft, guile, cunning," and "art, cunning." The same sense must be given to Exodus 1. 9, where the Septuagint has "Come, let us deal craftily with them" [δεῦτε οὖν καταφιλιώμεθα αὐτούς]. I translate it, "Come, let us act cunningly against them." For the Hebrew word means not only "wisdom" but also "cunning." Further, what follows in the same verse, "lest they should bring forth life" [ἵνα μὴ ζωογονήσωσιν], the Syriac and the Arabic render as "that they might not live." The Vulgate has "that they might not be made alive," and Erasmus "lest they be vital." They refer this to the little boys who were cast into the waters. Although Beza says this was wrongly done, since he refers it to the parents and renders "that they might not bear children," we nonetheless prefer the former. See what I noted on the word zōogoneisthai at Luke 17. 33.

units.la: VERS. 20. Καὶ λῶ ἀγαθῷ τῷ Θεῷ. Non pigebit hic adscribere, quæ de venustate ejus tradit Iosephus Antiq. l. 2. c. 9. Πρὸς κάλλος, inquit, ἴδιας ἀφιλοῦμητ.
units.tr: VERS. 20. "And he was fair to God" [καὶ ἦν ἀστεῖος τῷ Θεῷ]. It will not be tiresome to set down here what Josephus, Antiquities, book 2, chapter 9, says of his beauty. "For beauty," he says, "...".

units.la: Πρὸς κάλλος, inquit, ἴδιας ἀφιλοῦμηντ ῳ λῷ ἴτως, ὡς Μωϋσῆν θαυμάζῳ μὴ ἐκπληγῶσαι τὸ ἄμορφίας. πλοῖς τε συνέβαινε καθ' ὁδὸν ἐφεροῦ ὠν γὰν ... id est, nemo erat tam negligens formarum spectator, qui conspecta Mosis pulchritudine non stupesceret: multisque ei per viam portato occurrentibus contigit, ut non solum ob pueri faciem respicerent, sed & negociis relictis, conspectu ejus sese pascerent. tanta enim erat pueri gratia, ut intuentes in se detinerent. Laudo hic præ Vulgato, Erasmo, Syro, Arabe, & Æthiopico, Cl. Bezam, qui ἀγαθῷ τῷ Θεῷ vertit; divinitus venustus, vel divine, excellenter. videatur doctus ejus commentarius.
units.tr: "For beauty," he says, "...". (The Greek of this passage is so garbled in the transcription that it cannot be fully reconstructed; the sense, as given in the Latin version, is:) No one was so careless an observer of form that, having seen the beauty of Moses, he would not be astonished; and many who met him as he was carried along the way happened to turn round, not only because of the boy's face, but, leaving their business aside, to feast their eyes upon him. For the boy's charm was so great that it held those who looked at him. Here, before the Vulgate, Erasmus, the Syriac and the Arabic and Ethiopic, I commend the learned Beza, who renders "fair to God" [ἀγαθῷ τῷ Θεῷ] as "divinely lovely," or "divine, surpassingly." His learned commentary may be consulted.

units.la: VERS. 22. Ἡ γ δυναμίς ἐν λόγοις ἐν ἔργοις. Erat autem potens in dictis & in factis. Syrus ... dives. Arabs ... promtus, paratus. Æthiopicus autem ... potens.
units.tr: VERS. 22. "For he was mighty in words and in works" [Ἦν γὰρ δυνατὸς ἐν λόγοις ἐν ἔργοις]. "He was mighty in words and deeds," the Vulgate has. The Syriac has "rich." The Arabic has "ready, prepared." The Ethiopic has "powerful."

units.la: VERS. 26. Visus est ipsis μαχομάχοις. Vulgatus, Eraf. Syrus & Arabs, litigantibus. rectè. μάχεσθαι enim sæpe de verbis tantum dicitur. ut annotavimus ad Iohan. 6. 52. & in Hebræo Exod. 2. 13. est רֵעִים, litigantes, contendentes. Vbi tamen LXX habent διαμαχομένοις, dimicantes. nec malè. etsi enim רוב, ut apud Syros, sic & apud Hebræos ad verba proprie pertineat, extenditur tamen etiam ad verbera. unde 2 Sam. 14. 6, do duobus fratribus, quorum alter alterum occidit, dicitur םַשְׁהּ בְּנֵי הַיְּשָׁ, LXX καὶ ἀπέμαχοῦντο ἀμφότεροι ἐν τῷ ἀγρῷ, & pugnabant ambo in agro. Itaque & hoc loco non male Beza, visus est ipsis pugnantibus. additur, ὁ σωτὴρ λαὸν αὐτὸς ὡς ἁπλῶς. Arabs [Arabic text], quod non verto, & graviter exhortatus est eos ut quiete agerent, sed & cepit orare eos ut pacem inirent. Syrus [Syriac text] , & hortabatur vel orabat eos. [Syriac text], est persuadere, & incipere persuadere, id est, orare, exhortari, incitare. Insignis emphasis est in verbo συνάλλαγειν. quam non satis expressit Vulgatus, quum dixit, reconciliabat eos in pace. nec Erasmus, redegit eos in pacem. at recte Beza, compulit.
units.tr: VERS. 26. "He appeared to them as they were fighting" [ὤφθη αὐτοῖς μαχομένοις]. The Vulgate, Erasmus, the Syriac and the Arabic have "quarrelling." This is right, for the verb to fight [μάχεσθαι] is often used only of words, as I noted on John 6. 52. In the Hebrew of Exodus 2. 13 the word is "quarrelling, contending" [רֵעִים]. Yet the Septuagint has "fighting against each other" [διαμαχομένοις], which is not wrong either. For although the word for strife [רוב], both in Syriac and in Hebrew, refers properly to words, it also extends to blows. Hence in 2 Samuel 14. 6, where it is said of two brothers, one of whom killed the other, the Septuagint has "and they both fought in the field," and the Hebrew means "and they struck each other in the field." So here Beza is not wrong to render it, "he appeared to them while they were fighting." To this is added: "the Saviour, who approached them, earnestly exhorted them" [ὁ σωτὴρ λαὸν αὐτὸς ὡς ἁπλῶς]. The Arabic says he earnestly exhorted them to live quietly, and began to beg them to make peace; I do not translate it word for word. The Syriac has "he exhorted or begged them." The Syriac verb means "to persuade," and "to begin to persuade," that is, to beg, to exhort, to urge. There is a striking emphasis in the verb "to reconcile" [συνάλλαγειν], which the Vulgate has not expressed well when it says "he reconciled them in peace," nor Erasmus, "he brought them back into peace." Beza rightly renders it "he compelled them."

units.la: VERS. 35. Τὸν δὲ Θεὸς ἄρχοντα καὶ λυτρωτὴν ἀπέστειλεν, id est, ὡς ἄρχοντα καὶ λυτρωτήν, in principem & redemtorem misit, id est, qui princeps & redemtor esset. similem phrasin vide supra Act. 5. 31. λυτρωτὴς est גֹּאֵל, redemtor, quomodo hic Vulg. & Eras. verterunt. Beza maluit liberatorem. At non fugio redemtoris nomen, quod qui Mosi tribuit, non magis in Redemtorem Christum injurius est, quam qui eum μεσίτην, mediatorem vocaverit cum Apost. Gal. 3. 19. Utrumque ei typicè rectè convenit. & λυτρωτὴς quidem dicitur, quatenus post multa magnaque in Ægypto patrata miracula, interemptis tandem ab Angelo exterminatore Ægyptiorum primogenitis, populum Dei per sanguinem agni immunem incolumemque eduxit ac servavit. atque ita typum exhibuit veri istius lytri, veraeque redemtionis, quam per mortem primogeniti omnium creaturarum, & in sanguine agni immaculati Christi, acquisitam sibi gaudent fideles. Additur, ἐν χειρὶ ἀγίᾳ ἐν ἰφῷ... αὐτῷ ἐν τῇ βάτῳ. Vulg. cum manu. Eras. per manuum. Syrus, per manus. Beza, ductu. Sed habet hic, nescio quam emphasin vox manus, ut omittenda non videatur. sensus enim est, Deum, quum Mosen mitteret principem & redemtorem, & Mosis & redemtionis per eum praestandae regimen universum commisisse manibus hujus Angeli. unde liquido constat, Angelum istum, qui Exod. 3. apparuit Mosi in rubo, quinque ibi aliquoties Jehova ac Deus patrum nuncupatur, ac qui isthic Mosen mittit & instruit, non fuisse creatum angelum, sed ipsum filium Dei, אשר בידו [?] per cujus manum Stephanus ait Deum, nempe Patrem, misisse Mosen. qui Angelus vocatur, quia in hac actione, ut & in tota populi liberatione subserviit patri. est ille מלאך פניו [?], angelus faciei ejus, de quo Esa. 63. 9. מלאך הברית [?], angelus foederis, quem Mosi in deserto comitem fuisse, eumque in monte Sinai esse allocutum, Stephanus infra testatur †f. 38. vere ergo princeps foederis, qui populo Israelis tanquam suo legem tulit in monte Sinai, qui se שר צבא יהוה [?], principem exercitus Domini merito vocavit Jos. 5.14. ideoque non angelus modo foederis, sed & האדון [?], ipse Dominus jure vocatur, Malac. 3.1. hic Angelus eduxit populum ex Aegypto, Num. 20.16. & duxit per desertum, Exod. 23.20. & 33.2. in quo capite observandum, quod v.2. dicit Deus ושלחתי לפניך מלאך, & mittam ante te Angelum, idem esse cum v.14. פני ילכו והנחתי לך, facies mea ibit, & ducam vos. Angelus enim ille est Angelus faciei Domini, ipsa facies Dei, quam qui videt, patrem videt, Joh. 14.9. quippe est ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ, splendor gloriae & character personae ejus. Itaque gratulamur nobis testimonium ipsorum Judaeorum, qui in Haggadah paschatis, ubi referunt verba Deuter. 6. 21. in ea sic commentantur: ויוציאנו י' ממצרים לא על ידי מלאך ולא על ידי שרף ולא על ידי שליח אלא הקב"ה בכבודו שנאמר ועברתי בארץ מצרים בלילה הזה והכיתי כל בכור בארץ מצרים מאדם ועד בהמה ובכל אלהי מצרים אני י' & eduxit nos Iehova ex Aegypto, non per manus Angeli, neque per manus Seraphi, neque per manus legati, sed Deus gloria sua. sic enim legitur, Exod.12.12. Transibo per terram Aegypti nocte hac, & percutiam omnem primogenitum genitum genitum in terra Ægypti ab homine ad brutum, & in omnes Deos Ægypti exercebo judicia : ego Iehova. Habentur hæc apud Maimonidem in tractatu de נסי פתן, in מנתן נסו. Negant ab Angelo se eductos. quod tamen affirmat Moses Num. 20. 16. Rectè negant de Angelo creato. rectè affirmat Moses de increato, de quo Deus, Exod. 23. 21. cave tibi ab eo & ausculta voci ejus, neque irrita ipsum : nam non condonabit transgressioni vestrae: כי שמי בקרבו, quia nomen meum est in medio ejus. quem Christum fuisse, testatur Apostolus 1 Cor. 10. 9. Hic quum eduxit Israelitas ex Ægypto, ipse Jehovah eos eduxit במצרים, ipsissimâ sua gloria. Rectè quoque Legato, id est Mosi, hanc gloriam derogant. Etsi enim id ei passim tanquam instrumento tribuatur, quia tamen Angelum Dei visibiliter semper tanquam ducem rectoremque præsentem habuit, rectè Stephanus totam hanc redemptionem principaliter τῇ χειρὶ ἀγγέλου manui Angeli, id est, ut loquuntur Judæi, ipsius Dei tribuit.
units.tr: VERS. 35. "God sent him as ruler and redeemer" (Τὸν δὲ Θεὸς ἄρχοντα καὶ λυτρωτὴν ἀπέστειλεν), that is, as ruler and redeemer, sent as prince and redeemer, that is, one who would be prince and redeemer. For a similar phrase see above, Acts 5:31. λυτρωτὴς is גֹּאֵל, redeemer, as the Vulgate and Erasmus translate it here. Beza preferred liberator. But I do not shy from the name "redeemer." Whoever applies it to Moses does no more wrong to Christ the Redeemer than whoever calls him μεσίτης, mediator, together with the Apostle in Galatians 3:19. Both titles fit him rightly as type. He is called λυτρωτής in the sense that, after many great miracles in Egypt, when the Angel who destroys the Egyptians had at last slain the firstborn, he led out and saved God's people, who were spared by the blood of the lamb. In this way he displayed the type of that true ransom and true redemption which the faithful rejoice to have been won for them through the death of the firstborn of all creatures and through the blood of the spotless Lamb, Christ. Next comes ἐν χειρὶ ἀγίᾳ ἐν ἰφῷ... αὐτῷ ἐν τῇ βάτῳ, "by the hand of the holy angel in the bush." The Vulgate has with the hand, Erasmus by the hand, the Syriac by the hands, and Beza by the guidance. But the word "hand" carries a certain emphasis here that seems not to be omitted. The sense is that God, when he sent Moses as prince and redeemer, committed the whole direction both of Moses and of the redemption to be accomplished through him into the hands of this Angel. From this it is clear that the Angel who appeared to Moses in the bush at Exodus 3, where Jehovah and the God of the fathers is named several times, and who there sends and instructs Moses, was not a created angel but the Son of God himself, whose hand (אשר בידו [?]), through whom Stephen says God, namely the Father, sent Moses. He is called an Angel because in this action, as in the whole liberation of the people, he served the Father. He is the angel of his face (מלאך פניו [?]), of whom Isaiah 63:9 speaks; the angel of the covenant (מלאך הברית [?]), angel of the covenant, who, as Stephen testifies below at verse 38, accompanied Moses in the wilderness and spoke to him on Mount Sinai. Truly, then, he is the prince of the covenant, who gave the law on Mount Sinai to the people of Israel as his own, and who rightly called himself prince of the army of the Lord (שר צבא יהוה [?]) at Joshua 5:14. For this reason he is rightly called not only angel of the covenant but also the Lord himself (האדון [?]), the Lord himself, at Malachi 3:1. This Angel led the people out of Egypt (Num. 20:16) and guided them through the wilderness (Exod. 23:20; 33:2). In this chapter it should be noted that at verse 2 God says, "and I will send an angel before you" (ושלחתי לפניך מלאך), which is the same as verse 14, "my face will go, and I will give you rest" (פני ילכו והנחתי לך), "my face will go, and I will lead you." For that Angel is the Angel of the face of the Lord, the very face of God, and whoever sees him sees the Father (John 14:9), for he is ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ, the brightness of glory and the express image of his person. Therefore we rejoice in the testimony of the Jews themselves, who in the Haggadah of the Passover, where they quote the words of Deuteronomy 6:21, comment on them thus: ויוציאנו י' ממצרים לא על ידי מלאך ולא על ידי שרף ולא על ידי שליח אלא הקב"ה בכבודו, "And the Lord brought us out of Egypt, not by the hand of an angel, nor by the hand of a seraph, nor by the hand of a messenger, but the Holy One, blessed be he, in his glory himself. For thus it is written, I will pass through the land of Egypt this night, and I will strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from man to beast, and I will execute judgments on all the gods of Egypt: I am Iehova" (Exod. 12:12). These things are found in Maimonides in the treatise on the miracles of the Passover, in the section on the miracles of the Passover. They deny that they were led out by an Angel, which Moses nevertheless affirms at Num. 20:16. They rightly deny it of a created angel; Moses rightly affirms it of the uncreated one, of whom God says at Exod. 23:21: beware of him and obey his voice, and do not provoke him, for he will not pardon your transgression: for my name is in the midst of him (כי שמי בקרבו), "for my name is in him." That this was Christ the Apostle testifies at 1 Cor. 10:9. When he led the Israelites out of Egypt, Jehovah himself led them out of Egypt (במצרים) in his very own glory. Rightly, too, this glory is denied to the legate, that is, to Moses. For although it is ascribed to him everywhere as to an instrument, nevertheless, since he always had the Angel of God visibly present as leader and guide, Stephen rightly attributes this whole redemption chiefly to the hand of the Angel (τῇ χειρὶ ἀγγέλου), that is, as the Jews put it, to God himself.

units.la: VERS. 36. Καὶ ἐξήγαγεν αὐτοὺς. Et in mari rubro.
units.tr: VERS. 36. And he led them out [Καὶ ἐξήγαγεν αὐτοὺς]. In the Red Sea.

units.la: Hebraeis dicitur ים סוף. ut & Syrus hic ܝܡܐ ܕܣܘܦ, At Arabs البحر الأحمر, in mari Colsuma. Vrbs est ad extremitatem maris rubri, prope Isthmum Ægypti. unde sinus iste, quem mare rubrum dicimus, mare Colsumæ dictus est. Vrbis hujus meminit Chronologus Arabum Elmacinus in vita Omari, cujus jussu ait factam esse الخليج, fossam sive stagnum, quo annona veheretur من الفسطاط الى القلزم, القلزم ومن القلزم الى المدينة في البحر الذي, Fustata (quae alias nunc Alcairo dicitur) usque ad Colsumam, inde Medinam per mare salsum. Vbi simul notandum, mare salsum idem esse quod rubrum. Sic enim Arabibus dicitur, quia aqua ejus salsa, quippe ex Oceano Persico profluens. atque eo epitheto distinguitur sinus iste à Nilo, qui البحر الحلو, mare dulce dicitur. omnis enim aquarum collectio, sive salsarum sive dulcium, sive in Oceano, sive in sinu, sive in fluvio, sive in stagno lacuque שׁ, mare Arabibus dicitur. Aliud itaque est הלה הים, mare salsum aut salsum, de quo passim apud Mosen. per hoc enim mare mortuum seu lacus Asphaltites intelligitur, qui in agro Sodomitico erat, מזרח seu ממה ad Orientem terrae Sanctae. quum mare rubrum fuerit ad Zephyrum, sive eum tractum qui est inter Meridiem & Occidentem. Porro, quod sequitur, ἐξ ἐρήμου, ἐν ποταμῷ, non videtur praecisum dicendi genus continere, quasi sensus sit, ubi versatus est annos 40. commodè enim refertur ad miracula quae Moses edidit, non modo in Ægypto, & mari rubro, sed & in deserto, idque per 40 annos. iter enim illud 40 annorum, ab initio ad finem plenum fuit miraculorum.
units.tr: The Hebrews call it [ים סוף] Yam Suph, as the Syriac here does (yamma d-Suph), and the Arabs call it al-bahr al-ahmar, "in the Sea of Colsuma." Colsuma is a city at the end of the Red Sea, near the isthmus of Egypt. For this reason the gulf that we call the Red Sea was also called the Sea of Colsuma. The Arab chronicler Elmacinus mentions this city in his life of Omar, by whose order, he says, a canal or pool (al-khalij) was made, by which the grain was carried from al-Fustat (now otherwise called Cairo) as far as Colsuma, and from Colsuma to Medina by the salt sea (al-bahr al-malih). Here it should be noted that the salt sea is the same as the Red Sea. The Arabs call it this because its water is salt, since it flows from the Persian Ocean. By this epithet the gulf is distinguished from the Nile, which is called the sweet sea (al-bahr al-hulw). For the Arabs call any collection of water, whether salt or fresh, whether in the ocean, in a gulf, in a river, or in a pool or lake, a "sea." So the [ha-yam ha-melach] or "salt sea," which appears often in Moses, is something different. It means the Dead Sea, or the Lake Asphaltites, which lay in the land of Sodom, to the east [mizrach] of the Holy Land, whereas the Red Sea lay to the south-west, that is, in the region between the south and the west. Further, the words that follow, [ἐξ ἐρήμου, ἐν ποταμῷ], do not seem to contain a precise indication of the place, as if the sense were "where he lived for forty years." They refer more fittingly to the miracles that Moses performed, not only in Egypt and at the Red Sea but also in the desert, and that over forty years. For that whole journey of forty years was full of miracles from beginning to end.

units.la: VERS. 38. Λόγια ζῶντα.
units.tr: VERS. 38. Living oracles [Λόγια ζῶντα].

units.la: Vulgatus, verba vita, quasi λόγια ζωῆς. ut & Syrum vertit Tremellius. sed male. scribitur enim verba viva. non verba vivi. Arabs λόγιον ζῶν (ut quaedam exemplaria Graeca legere testatur D.Beza) sermonem vivum, non vitae, ut habet Junius.
units.tr: The Vulgate has "verba vitae" [words of life], as if it were "λόγια ζωῆς," and Tremellius also renders the Syriac this way, but wrongly. For the text is "verba viva" [living words], not "verba vivi." The Arab has "λόγιον ζῶν" [a living oracle] (as D. Beza testifies some Greek copies read), "living speech," not "of life," as Junius has it.

units.la: VERS. 39. Καὶ ἐσπάφησαν ταῖς καρδίαις αὐτῶν εἰς Αἴγυπτον.
units.tr: VERS. 39. And they turned back in their hearts to Egypt [Καὶ ἐσπάφησαν ταῖς καρδίαις αὐτῶν εἰς Αἴγυπτον].

units.la: Vulg. Eraf. & Beza, & aversi sunt cordibus suis. Syrus & Arabs, & reversi sunt. quod rectum putamus. sensus enim est, Quum Deus eos, non è terra modo, sed vel maximè ex idololatria Ægypti eruisset, hi corporibus ab Ægypto jam absentes, cordibus suis eò sunt reversi, quippe qui mentes suas reflecterent ad idola Ægypti, dicentes Aaroni, Fac nobis Deos &c. Vel simpliciter, versi sunt cordibus suis. Æthiopicus, verterunt corda sua ad terram Aegypti.
units.tr: The Vulgate, Erasmus and Beza have "and they turned away in their hearts." The Syriac and the Arab have "and they turned back," which we think is right. For the sense is this: when God had rescued them not only from the land but, above all, from the idolatry of Egypt, they, though their bodies were already absent from Egypt, turned back in their hearts, since they directed their minds back to the idols of Egypt, saying to Aaron, "Make us gods," etc. Or simply, "they turned in their hearts." The Ethiopic has "they turned their hearts to the land of Egypt."

units.la: VERS. 41. Καὶ ἐμαςτοποίησεν.
units.tr: VERS. 41. And they made [Καὶ ἐμαςτοποίησεν].

units.la: num. plur. Consentiunt Vulg. Arabs, & Æthiopicus At Syrus, & fecit ipsis vitulum, nempe Aaron. Καὶ ἀνήγαγον ϑυσίαν τῷ εἰδώλῳ, Vulg. & obtulerunt hostiam simulacro. Syrus & Arabs simulacris. Videntur τῷ εἰδώλῳ accepisse collectivè, non pro singulari vituli simulacro. non satis rectè.
units.tr: The number is plural. The Vulgate, the Arab and the Ethiopic agree. The Syriac, however, has "and he made for them a calf," namely Aaron. "Καὶ ἀνήγαγον ϑυσίαν τῷ εἰδώλῳ" [and they offered sacrifice to the idol]: the Vulgate has "and they offered a victim to the image." The Syriac and the Arab have "to the images." They seem to have taken "τῷ εἰδώλῳ" collectively, not as the single image of the calf. Not quite correctly.

units.la: quatenus divinæ mentis virtus è cœlo proveniens, in omnia se diffundit, continetque universam omnium rerum lucem & providentiam, quæ ad ordinem & vitam & mutationes omnium fortunarum pertineat. Nec omittendum, quod de Saturno Dionysius Halicarnassæus lib. 1. tradit, Antiquos existimasse τὴν τ δαίμονα πάσης δὲ δαιμονίας δοτῆρα καὶ πληρωτὴν ἀνθρώποις, ἐπὶ χρόνον αὐτὴν δὲ καλὲν, ὡς Ἕλληνες ἀξιῶσιν, ἐπὶ χρόνου ὡς Ῥωμαῖοι, πάσων ἡ σωσιληφότα τὸ ξ κόσμου φύσιν, ὁποτέρου ἄνλης ὀνομάσαι. Hunc Daemonem omnis felicitatis datorem esse & completorem, sive Tempus ipsum vocare oporteat, secundum Graecos, sive Saturnum, secundum Romanos. eumque, quocunque tandem nomine vocaveris, universam mundi naturam complexum esse. Hinc jam non difficile videtur causam reddere, cur Saturnus Orientalibus dictus sit. Nam enim in Kal Hebraicè est aptari, disponi. Arabicè & Syriacè fieri. in Piel & Hiphil Hebraicè disponere, aptare. Arabicè in Piel, Syriacè in Hiphil, facere exístere, generare, naturam indere. natura, Syris. Hinc est ea virtus quæ existentiam, naturam, aptitudinem & dispositionem omnibus rebus tribuit. proprie naturatio. forma est Hebraeis usitatissima. qualia sunt confirmatio, condemnatio, speculatio. & sexcenta alia, quæ ex Piel deducta, actionem fere significant. atque ita adaptatio, vel ut barbarè dicam essentificatio proprie id ipsum exprimit, quod Saturno Antiqui tribuerunt. Jam vero videndum quid sit ῥημφάν, vel ῥωμφᾶ, vel ῥεφᾶ, vel ῥεφάν, vel ῥαφάν, vel ῥαμφάν. has omnes enim formas exemplaria exhibent. Syrus antepenultimam, Arabs penultimam habet. Æthiopicus ῥεφάμ. dicimus autem Arabicam esse dictionem, ejusdem omnino notionis cum Hebraeo. nam verbum movere, agitare, & proprie alas, quod faciunt aves incubantes ovis, ut pullos excludant. quod enim Gen. 1. 2. de Spiritu Dei dicitur, quod מְרַחֶפֶת agitabat se in su-perficie aquarum ad foecundandas eas, id Arabibus est ‭﻿ يَرِفُّ‬.
units.tr: insofar as the power of the divine mind, coming from heaven, spreads itself into all things and holds the universal light and providence of all things, which pertains to the order and life and changes of all fortunes. Nor should we omit what Dionysius of Halicarnassus says about Saturn in book 1: the ancients thought that this daemon, the giver and fulfiller of all happiness to men, should be called Time itself, as the Greeks think fit, or Saturn, as the Romans do. And whatever name you finally give it, it embraces the whole nature of the world. [τὴν τ δαίμονα πάσης δὲ δαιμονίας δοτῆρα καὶ πληρωτὴν ἀνθρώποις]. From this it now seems not difficult to give the reason why Saturn was called by the Orientals what he was called. For in Hebrew the Kal form means "to be fitted, to be arranged," and in Arabic and Syriac "to become." In the Piel and Hiphil forms in Hebrew it means "to arrange, to fit." In Arabic Piel, and in Syriac Hiphil, it means "to make exist, to generate, to implant a nature." "Nature" is [natura] in Syriac. Hence comes that power which gives existence, nature, fitness and arrangement to all things, properly "natural constitution." This form is very common in Hebrew, such as "confirmation," "condemnation," "speculation," and countless others, which, derived from the Piel, mostly signify an action. And so "adaptation," or, to speak barbarously, "essentification," expresses exactly what the ancients attributed to Saturn. Now we must consider what [Ῥεμφάν], or [ῥωμφᾶ], or [ῥεφᾶ], or [ῥεφάν], or [ῥαφάν], or [ῥαμφάν] is, for the manuscripts show all these forms. The Syriac has the antepenultimate, the Arabic the penultimate. The Ethiopic has [ῥεφάμ]. We say that the Arabic word has exactly the same meaning as the Hebrew. For the verb means "to move, to stir," and properly of wings, as birds do when they brood over their eggs to hatch their young. For what is said in Genesis 1.2 of the Spirit of God, that [מְרַחֶפֶת] "was moving over the surface of the waters," to make them fruitful, is in Arabic [yarifu].

units.la: Lex. Arab. cui nomen Camus, الْجَاحِظ ‭ يَضْرِبُ ‬ agitavit columba super ova sua & expandit alas suas. & talis actio etiam dicitur ‭﻿ يَرِفُّ‬, ψιφ, terminatione autem Graeca; ψιφᾶ, & addito ν ψιφάν. (saepe etenim ea litera peregrinis dictionibus affigitur, ut pro ταλῶμ, σαλωμών ut & μ, qualia sunt pro שלום, ψιφαλαμ. pro שלום, σαλωμ. praesertim autem in Arabicis dictionibus non debet insolens videri affixio τῆ ν in fine. quia omnia fere nomina, etsi in nun non terminentur, sed alia quavis consonâ, pronunciatione tamen nunnantur in fine, efferturque Nominativus per on, Genit. Dat. & Abl. per in, Accus. per an. sic ut ψιφ vel ψιφὸν, in Accus. faciat ψιφᾶ. At unde ψιμφᾶ & ψιμφᾶν cum μ in medio? ne hoc quidem in mendo habendum. μ est pro ν euphoniae causa ex more, quia sequitur φ. ν autem est pro dagesch, sicut pro נש, tu, Syri dicunt נש. pro נמור, fortis, נמר. pro כמש, LXX μαμφάμ, Gen. 46. 21. & infinita alia. sic pro ψιφφᾶ, ψιμφᾶ. est enim ‭﻿ يَرِفُّ‬ ex verbis surdis, sive ut loquuntur Hebraei, ex duplicantibus secundam radicalem. Sed unde ψαφάν & ψαμφάν? Quia, etsi Arabes ‭﻿ يَرِفُّ‬ pronuncient ψιφ, vocalis tamen litera Resch est pathach, quae recte etiam scribitur ψάφ. Est ergo ψιφᾶ seu ψιφάν ea virtus, quae movendo se & agitando super omnes res, eas quasi excludit & existere facit. idem ergo prorsus quod πν. & utrumque idem quod Saturnus, ὁ ἀπελαυνῶν ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἀμμὼν φύσιν, ut dixit Halicarnassaeus. At nec tacere debemus, jam memoratum Lex. Arab. ‭﻿ يَرِفُّ‬, ψιφ etiam vertere per ‭﻿ مُلْتِي اِفْسُوْنِم‬, multi-efsionem, seu voracitatem. quod ipsum
units.tr: The Arabic lexicon called the Camus gives, under the entry for the verb meaning "he struck" (yaḍribu), the sense: "the dove brooded over her eggs and spread her wings." Such an action is also called [yarifu], which is psiph, and with a Greek ending psiphā, and with a nu added, psiphān. (That letter is often attached to foreign words, as in salōmōn for talōm and salōm for shalom, with a mu as well, as in psiphalam for shalom. Indeed a final nu should not seem unusual in Arabic words, since nearly all nouns, even when they do not end in nun but in some other consonant, are pronounced with a nasal at the end. The nominative is given as -on, the genitive, dative and ablative as -in, and the accusative as -an. So psiph or psiphon becomes psiphā in the accusative.) But whence psimphā and psimphān, with mu in the middle? Not even this need be counted an error. Mu stands for nu for the sake of euphony, as is customary, because phi follows. Nu stands for the dagesh, as the Syrians say nesh for "you" (tu), and for [nimor], "strong," they say [nemar]. For [kemesh], the Seventy have [mampham] at Genesis 46:21, and there are countless other examples. So psiphphā becomes psimphā, since [yarifu] comes from verbs with doubled letters, or, as the Hebrews call them, from verbs that double the second radical. But whence psaphān and psamphān? Although the Arabs pronounce [yarifu] as psiph, the vowel of the letter resh is pathach, and it is correctly written psaph. So psiphā or psiphān is that power which, by moving and stirring itself over all things, as it were hatches them and makes them exist. It is therefore exactly the same as [pneuma], and each is the same as Saturn, "he who drives away from the earth the sand of nature," as the Halicarnassian said. Nor should we keep silent that the Arabic lexicon already mentioned also renders [yarifu], psiph, by [multi-efsionem], that is, "great devouring" or "voracity." This very thing

units.la: Saturno etiam optimè convenit, cui tantam voracitatem tribuit Antiquitas, ut & liberos suos deglutiverit sicut enim omnia tempore oriuntur, ita & tempore intereunt omnia. quumque generatio unius sit corruptio alterius, eadem vis naturæ, quæ unum producit, alterum corrumpit. idem Saturnus, qui ortus causa, idem & interitus. Hæc quum ita lusissemus, & conjecturis, non tamen omnino frustra, omnia tentassemus, Cl. vir, omni literaturæ genere excultissimus, & in diffusa eruditione Ægyptiacæ etiam linguæ peritissimus Claudius Salmasius uno verbo nos expedivit. In ea enim lingua ϸιϕάν, Saturnum significare affirmavit. utque dicto fidem faceret, Alphabetum Ægyptiacum, Roma ad se missum ostendit, ubi nomina septem planetarum, hoc ordine scripta simul & explicata continerentur. ΠΙΡΗ, Sol.
units.tr: agrees very well with Saturn, to whom antiquity ascribed such voracity that he even swallowed his own children. For just as all things arise in time, so all things perish in time. And since the generation of one thing is the corruption of another, the same power of nature that produces one also corrupts another. The same Saturn is the cause both of origin and of destruction. While we were playing with these things and trying every conjecture, though not altogether in vain, the distinguished man, most accomplished in every kind of learning and most skilled in the wide scholarship of the Egyptian language as well, Claudius Salmasius, settled the matter for us in a single word. For he affirmed that in that language psiphān means Saturn. To confirm his statement he showed us an Egyptian alphabet sent to him from Rome, in which the names of the seven planets were written and explained together, in this order:

units.la: ΠΙΙΟ, Luna. ΡΗΦΧΠ, Saturnus. ΠΙΖΕΥC, Iupiter. ΧΛΟΧΟΧ, Mars. COYPOT, Venus. ΠΙΕΡΛΗC, Mercurius. Characteres fere Græci sunt, sic legendi πιρη. πηα. ρηφων. πιζευς. μολοχ. σουρον. πιρρης. Jam cecidit recepta illa apud omnes fere eruditos sententia, ϸιϕάν apud LXX Interpretes corruptum esse ex Hebræo ϒ, pro quo ϒ legerint, inde ϸιϕάν. Laudandi jam doctissimi prudentissimique interpretes, quod cum in Ægypto, in Ægyptiorum gratiam, à Philadelpho Ægyptiorum Rege vocati, Biblia in Græcam linguam transferrent, ignotum Ægyptiis Hebræorum ϒ, in notissimum ipsis ϸιϕάν tranmutarint. Quod si scrupulum cuipiam moveat, quod Saturnum in deserto coluisse Israelitas queratur Deus, quum in historia Mosis solius vituli vel bovis (David enim ϒ vocat Ps. 106. 20.) fiat mentio: Resp. bovem, arationis præcipuum adorem, retulisse Deum agriculturæ authorem & præsidem. eum autem antiquis gentilibus fuisse Saturnum. Is enim fuisse
units.tr: PIRH, Sun. PIIO, Moon. RHPHChP, Saturn. PIZEUS, Jupiter. ChLOChOCh, Mars. COUPOT, Venus. PIERChLC, Mercury. The characters are almost Greek and are to be read thus: pirē, pēa, rēphōn, pizeus, moloch, sourōn, pirrēs. Now that opinion, received by almost all learned men, has fallen, namely that psiphān in the Seventy was corrupted from the Hebrew [kiyyun], for which they read [kiyyun], and from this came psiphān. Most learned and prudent translators deserve praise, because when they had been summoned to Egypt by Ptolemy Philadelphus, king of the Egyptians, to translate the Bible into Greek for the sake of the Egyptians, they changed the Hebrew [kiyyun], unknown to the Egyptians, into psiphān, which was perfectly familiar to them. If anyone is troubled by the fact that God complains that Israel worshipped Saturn in the desert, since in the history of Moses mention is made only of the calf or ox (for David calls it [eglah], Psalm 106:20), the answer is this: the ox, the chief animal of ploughing, was referred by God to agriculture, its author and patron. And among the ancient Gentiles, this was Saturn. For he is said to have been

units.la: Hebraeorum ϒ ... fuisse fertur, qui in Italia Janum vivendi rationem & agrorum cultum docuit, cui pro accepta ista disciplina dimidium regni sui dederit. atque eo nomine cum conjuge sua Rhea pro Deo fuisse habitum, quod in Italia plantationes, & insitiones & educationes omnium arborum, omniumque fructiferarum rerum culturam docuerit. Restat ut verba Amosi interpretemur, & cum verbis Stephani conferamus. Prophetam sic interpretamur, & portasti tabernaculum Molochi vestri, & Saturnum imagines vestras, stellam Dei vestri, quae fecistis vobis. Cur םיִמֶלַצ, imagines vestras, dixit in plurali? quia תֹכּוֹס, tabernaculum, non tantum locus erat & receptaculum, in quo inclusus Moloch gestabatur aut circumferebatur, sed & ipsummet idolum erat, quippe imago caeli, in quo Sol sive Moloch, magnus ille astrorum rex & rerum sublunarium praeses, tanquam in tabernaculo continetur. unde Psaltes Ps. 19. 5. שֶׁמַּשׁ בָּהֶם לְאֹהֶל, Soli posuit tabernaculum in illis, שָׁמַיִם, coelis. exprobrat ergo, quod & tabernaculum Molochi & Saturnum pro imaginibus circumferrent. quis autem iste Saturnus? stella inquit Dei vestri. id est, quam vos pro Deo habetis & colitis, sicut stellam Saturni dicimus, quae est ipse Saturnus. stellam Jovis, quae est ipse Jupiter. כּוֹכַב אֱלֹהֵיכֶם; fluvius Euphratis, qui est ipse Euphrates. Unde liquet, vos portastis Saturnum, stellam Dei vestri, idem esse atque, vos portastis stellam Dei vestri Saturni. quod ipsissimum illud Lucae est, ἀνελάβετε τὸ ἄστρον τοῦ θεοῦ ὑμῶν Ῥεμφάν. Porro quod in Hebraeo sequitur אֲשֶׁר עֲשִׂיתֶם לָכֶם, quae fecistis vobis, refero ad duas jam memoratas imagines, nempe tabernaculum Molochi, & Saturni stellam. atque ita, quum dixit Lucas, ἀνέλαβετε ἃς ἐποιήσατε, optime elucidavit mentem Prophetae, quasi situs verborum fuisset, וְנִשָּׂאתֶם אֶת־סִכּוּת מַלְכְּכֶם וְאֶת־כִּיּוּן צַלְמֵיכֶם כּוֹכַב אֱלֹהֵיכֶם אֲשֶׁר עֲשִׂיתֶם לָכֶם quod Graece ad verbum est, καὶ ἀνελάβετε τὸν σκηνὸν τοῦ Μόλοχ ὑμῶν, ἐ Ῥεμφάν (idem enim hoc quod בִּיּוּן) τὸ ἄστρον τοῦ θεοῦ ὑμῶν ὑμῶν (quod idem atque ἡ τὰ ἀςτρον ἡ Θεᾶ ὑμῶν Ρεμφάν) τύπως ἂς ἐποιησάτε. Confer hæc cum verbis Lucæ, aut LXX Interpretum, & vide an prudenter satis locutus sit qui dixit, Græcam versionem in hoc testimonio ab Ebraica veritate plurimum variare. Quin & fateor, me multum dubitare, an illud Lucæ ῥεμφάν conveniat Genitivo casu cum Θεῶν, an potius Accusativo cum τὸ ἀςτρον. nam præterquam quod terminatio Arabica, ut diximus, id innuat, eadem tum erit constructio in Græco quæ in Hebræo, etsi situs dictionum variet. Nec est quod turbet quempiam, quod supra Saturnum cum Molocho confuderimus: Propheta autem & Lucas hos Deos distinguant, & plurali numero imagines vocent. Tanta enim fuit priscorum ad augendum Deorum numerum propensio, ut sola nominis imaginisve variatio ad unum eundemque Deum Deamve in plures discerpendum sufficeret. Isis, Lucina, Diana, Trivia, Hecate, variæ erant Deæ, quum tamen unius Lunæ diversa solum essent nomina. De quo qui plura vult, videat de Diis Syris Prolegomenon caput tertium Cl. Seldeni. At, quod tandem illud Tabernaculum Molochi, quod portarint in deserto, quum in historia Mosaica non alterius quam Mosaici fiat mentio? Illud ipsum, inquam, intelligitur Tabernaculum, & per τύπως ἂς ἐποιησάτε; figuras quas fecistis, non aliæ quam quas jussu Dei Bezaleel ejusque socii efformarunt: sed quibus infideles illi idololatræ, de quibus hic agitur, mirum in modum sunt abusi. Neque enim, quod in Epist. ad Hebr. disputat Apostolus, Tabernaculum eoque contenta crediderunt esse umbram & exemplaria futurorum bonorum in Christo præstandorum, sed mundi ac naturæ delineationem & compendium. πρὸς μίμησιν τῆς τοῦ ὅλου φύσεως συνέβαινεν ἀπαγ, commensurationem Tabernaculi ad imitationem Universitatis naturæ esse contigit, ait Josephus Antiq. l. 3. c. 5. & R. D. Kimchi ad
units.tr: Hebrew [kiyyun] ... he is said to have been the one who taught Janus in Italy the manner of living and the cultivation of the fields, and for receiving this teaching he gave him half his kingdom. For this reason, together with his wife Rhea, he was regarded as a god, because in Italy he taught the planting, grafting and rearing of all trees and the cultivation of all fruitful things. It remains for us to interpret the words of Amos and to compare them with the words of Stephen. We interpret the prophet thus: "You bore the tabernacle of your Moloch and Saturn, your images, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves." Why does he say "your images" in the plural, [tselemeikhem]? Because the tabernacle [sikkut] was not merely a place and receptacle in which Moloch, enclosed, was carried or paraded about, but was itself the idol, namely an image of the heavens, in which the Sun or Moloch, that great king of the stars and governor of sublunary things, is contained as in a tent. Hence the Psalmist, Psalm 19:5, says of the sun that [in them he set a tent for the sun], "in the heavens." So he reproaches them for carrying about both the tabernacle of Moloch and Saturn as images. But who is this Saturn? "The star of your god," that is, the star which you hold and worship as a god, just as we speak of the star of Saturn, which is Saturn himself, and the star of Jupiter, which is Jupiter himself, [kokhav elohekhem], as the river Euphrates, which is the Euphrates itself. Hence it is clear that "you carried Saturn, the star of your god," is the same as "you carried the star of your god Saturn." This is precisely the wording of Luke: [aneläbete to astron tou theou hymōn Remphan]. As for what follows in the Hebrew, [asher asitem lakhem], "which you made for yourselves," I refer it to the two images already mentioned, namely the tabernacle of Moloch and the star of Saturn. And so, when Luke said [aneläbete has epoiēsate], he cleared up the prophet's meaning admirably, as if the order of the words had been: "and you took up the tabernacle of your king and the [kiyyun] of your images, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves," which in Greek word for word is: "and you took up the tent of your Moloch, [Remphan] (for this is the same as [kiyyun]), the star of your god, [tou theou hymōn] (which is the same as the star of your god Remphan), the figures which you made." Compare these words with Luke's, or with the Seventy's, and see whether he spoke prudently enough who said that the Greek version in this testimony differs greatly from the Hebrew truth. Indeed I confess that I have much doubt whether Luke's [Remphan] agrees in case with [theōn] in the genitive, or rather with [to astron] in the accusative. For apart from the fact that the Arabic termination, as we said, suggests this, the construction in Greek would then be the same as in Hebrew, though the order of the words differs. Nor should it trouble anyone that above I have confused Saturn with Moloch. The prophet and Luke distinguish these gods and call the images by the plural number. For the ancients were so inclined to multiply the number of gods that a mere variation of name or image was enough to split one and the same god or goddess into many. Isis, Lucina, Diana, Trivia, Hecate were different goddesses, though they were only different names of the one Moon. Whoever wants more on this should consult the third chapter of the Prolegomena of the distinguished Selden, On the Syrian Gods. But what of that tabernacle of Moloch which they carried in the desert, since in the Mosaic history mention is made of no tabernacle other than the Mosaic one? That very tabernacle, I say, is understood, and by [tupous has epoiēsate], "the figures which you made," are meant none other than those which Bezalel and his companions fashioned by God's command, but which those unfaithful idolaters, of whom this passage speaks, abused in a remarkable way. For the Apostle in the Epistle to the Hebrews does not argue that the Tabernacle and its contents were believed to be a shadow and copies of the good things to be bestowed in Christ, but rather a outline and summary of the world and of nature. Josephus says, Antiquities book 3, chapter 5, that "the measurement of the Tabernacle was made in imitation of the universe of nature," and Rabbi David Kimchi, when about to expound on Psalm 19:8 why the testimony of God is said to give wisdom to the simple, gives this reason, [ki kol ha-...].

units.la: Psal. 19. v. 8. expositurus cur testimonium Dei dicatur sa-pientiam dare simplicibus, hanc causam allegat, כי כל הנרי
units.tr: Psalm 19:8, where the author explains why the testimony of God is said to give wisdom to the simple, and gives this reason: [כי כל המשכן חכמה נפלאה] "for all the Tabernacle is marvellous wisdom."

units.la: המשכן חכמה נפלאה כי לא רבר רק הנעדה המוזנחות והידיעת וכן כל הרוברים כלם מורים על חכמה עך שיקראו אותו החכמים עולם האמצעי שהוא רמות העולם העליון ודמות העולם הקטן וכן שמירת השבת היא חכמה נחלה שיחוק האדם בגללה על חדש העולם וכל מעשה בראשית והיא חכמת הטבע id est,
units.tr: The Tabernacle is marvellous wisdom, because it speaks not only of the things that are made and known, and all the things it speaks of point to wisdom. So the wise call it the intermediate world, which is the image of the upper world and the likeness of the small world. Likewise the keeping of the Sabbath is a great wisdom, for which man is to study the beginning of the world and all the works of creation, and this is the wisdom of nature [id est, "that is"]. [הנעשה המוזכר והידוע, המשכן חכמה נפלאה, ועולם האמצעי, דמות העולם העליון ודמות העולם הקטן, שמירת השבת, חכמת הטבע]

units.la: omnes enim res Tabernaculi miranda sunt sapientia. neque enim inane quid sunt candelabrum, altaria, cortina, & reliqua. sed omnia tantam docent sapientiam, ut sapientes eam vocarint Mundum intermedium, qui similitudo sit & supremi mundi, & parvi. similiter observatio Sabbathi magnam quandam sapientiam comprehendit, cujus gratia scrutari debet quisque ortum mundi, & res creatas. qua quidem sapientia Physica est. Vides non Tabernaculum tantum, sed & Sabbathum ad naturalem scientiam referri. Sancta sanctorum volebant significare mundum intelleCtualem seu Angelicum. Sancta, mundum cælorum visibilium. Atrium, orbem terrarum. Mensam cum duodecim propositionum panibus, senario numero sibi oppositis, firmamentum cum duodecim signis Zodiaci, quorum sex septentrionalia, sex istis opposita meridionalia. Candelabrum septem lampadibus ita adornatum, ut è media, tanquam rami è stipite, tres utrinque orirentur, septem planetas, quorum medius Sol reliquis sex lucem præbet. Quatuor cortinarum colores quatuor mundi Elementa ipsis denotabant, nempe byssus sive linum Terram, ex qua nascitur. Purpura aquam, unde provenit. Hyacinthus aërem, cui puritate similis est. Crocus ignem, ob ruborem. de quibus partim apud Josephum 1. 3. Antiq. c. 5. & 6. partim apud Hieron. tom.3. sol. 61. Quum ergo universam mundi naturam Tabernaculo comprehendi existimarent, mirum ne cuipiam videatur, si idololatræ ex Dei Tabernaculo Saturni Tabernaculum fecerint, τῆ πάσῃ μεγαλη-φόρῳ τῶ ὲ κόσμῳ φύσει, universam comprehendentis mundi naturam, ut antea ex Halicarnassæo produximus? Neque hic leviter prætereundum, quod Sabbatho etiam arcana scientiæ Physicæ, id est Saturni arcana contineri Kimchius dixerit. Sabbatho enim magis quam cæteris diebus liberis operam dare solent Hebræi, quia benedicto isto die corporibus & animabus vires restaurari credunt Judæi. Quum Deus Gen.2.2.dicitur benedixisse diei septimo, quid ibi est ברכה benedictio? Est, inquit ibi Aben Esra, תוספת טובה, additamentum boni. quodnam vero illud additamentum? ביום הזה התחדש בנשמת רוח בתולת ובנשמת כח הכר והשכל , die illo innovatur in corporibus species quædam virium in generatione, & in animabus vires cognoscendi & intelligendi. Id vero in Saturni, qui septimi diei præses est, ideoque à Sabbatho Hebræis dicitur, honorem redundare, eoque à Judæis referri, liquet ex R. Isaac Caro, qui planetæ Saturni virtutes prædicans, Is eam, inquit, habet facultatem, ut in corporibus robur naturæ supra cæteros dies renovet, ac in portione ejus est vis cogitandi, intelligendi & sciendi mysteria & cultus Domini, est stella seu sydus Israëlis, ut dicunt omnes Astrologi, & in portione ejus est itidem anima rationalis, & ex partibus terræ domus sanctuarii, & ex linguis lingua Hebraica, & inter leges Lex Israëlis. Habes hic commentarium in verba S. Stephani. Si enim Saturnus est sidus Israëlis, si ab eo & generandi & intelligendi vires habent Judæi, si ad eum & domus sanctuarii, & lingua Hebraea, & lex Israëlis referenda, merito stellam Saturni nuncupavit Stephanus stellam Dei vestri, & merito domum illam sanctuarii vocavit Tabernaculum Molochi. Additur autem, & transferam vos ὑπέκεινα Βαβυλῶνος, Vulg. trans, Erasm. ultra Babylonem. Sic Syrus quoque & Arabs. At Beza, ad Babylonis fines. ὑπέκεινα proprie & usitate est ultra. & hic ponitur pro מֵהֵלָּאָה, qua voce Propheta usus est, quæ ut per ad fines vertatur, non satis est conveniens, neque ipsa res id facile admittit. neque enim hic de tribu Judæ agitur, quæ à Rege Babylonis in Babyloniam transportata, intra ejus fines fere constitit, sed de decem tribubus Israël, quarum propheta, Amos fuit, c. 1. 1. quas alloquitur c. 5. v. 4. 5. quæque per Salmanassarem Assyriæ regem ultra Babyloniam in Chalacho, Chabore, Nehargozane, & civitatibus Mediæ collocatæ fuere, 2 Reg. 17. 6. Cur autem Stephanus dixit, ultra Babyloniam, quum Propheta Amos c. 5. 26. dixerit, ultra Damascum? quia Amos peculiarem suo tempore causam habebat, cur longinquam populi migrationem designaturus, ultra Damascum diceret. magnis enim jam cladibus Hasaël Rex Damasci terram decem tribuum afflecerat. plurimos interemerat, plurimos in Syriam captivos abduxerat. nec tamen id animos improbi populi domuerat, ut resipiscerent. pergit itaque majorem Propheta calamitatem denunciare, fore ut brevi ultra Damascum longius deportentur, quam longè autem ultra Damascum, res ipsa postmodum demonstravit, quando in fines Mediæ & Armeniæ ultra Babylonem transportati fuere. Stephanus itaque neglecta circumstantia quam spectavit Amosus, rem dicere maluit, quam intendebat Propheta.
units.tr: For all the things of the Tabernacle are marvellous in wisdom. The candlestick, the altars, the curtains and the rest are not empty things, but all of them teach such wisdom that the wise have called it the intermediate world, which is the likeness both of the highest world and of the small world. Likewise the observance of the Sabbath contains a certain great wisdom, for the sake of which each person ought to examine the origin of the world and created things. This wisdom is physical. You see that not only the Tabernacle but also the Sabbath is referred to natural knowledge. They wished the Holy of Holies to signify the intellectual or angelic world; the Holy Place, the world of the visible heavens; the Court, the globe of the earth. The table with the twelve loaves of the showbread, a number of six paired opposite each other, signifies the firmament with the twelve signs of the zodiac, six of them northern and six southern, opposite to those. The candlestick, adorned with seven lamps so that three branches arise on either side from the middle, as branches from a trunk, signifies the seven planets, of which the middle one, the Sun, gives light to the other six. The colours of the four curtains signified to them the four elements of the world: the fine linen, the earth from which it grows; the purple, water, from which it comes; the hyacinth, air, to which it is similar in purity; the crimson, fire, because of its redness. Concerning these things, partly in Josephus, Antiquities book 3, chapters 5 and 6, and partly in Jerome, vol. 3, p. 61. Since therefore they thought the whole nature of the world was comprehended in the Tabernacle, should it seem strange to anyone that idolaters made from God's Tabernacle the Tabernacle of Saturn, comprehending the whole nature of the world, as we brought forward earlier from the Halicarnassian? Nor is it to be passed over here lightly that Kimchi said the secrets of physical knowledge, that is, the secrets of Saturn, are contained in the Sabbath too. For the Hebrews are accustomed to devote themselves to labour on the Sabbath more than on other days, because the Jews believe that on that blessed day strength is restored to both bodies and souls. When God is said in Genesis 2:2 to have blessed the seventh day, what is the blessing [ברכה] there? It is, says Aben Ezra there, an addition of good [תוספת טובה], an additional good. But what is that addition? "On that day there is renewed in bodies a certain power of generation, and in souls the power of knowing and understanding." That this honour redounds to Saturn, who presides over the seventh day and is therefore called by the Hebrews after the Sabbath, and that it is referred by the Jews to him, is clear from R. Isaac Caro, who, extolling the powers of the planet Saturn, says: "He has this faculty, that he renews the strength of nature in bodies above the other days; and in his portion is the power of thinking, understanding and knowing the mysteries and worship of the Lord. He is the star or constellation of Israel, as all the astrologers say; and in his portion is likewise the rational soul; and from the parts of the earth the house of the sanctuary, and from the languages the Hebrew tongue, and among the laws the law of Israel." You have here a commentary on the words of St Stephen. For if Saturn is the constellation of Israel, if from him the Jews have both the powers of generating and of understanding, if the house of the sanctuary, the Hebrew tongue and the law of Israel are to be referred to him, then Stephen rightly called the star of Saturn "the star of your god," and rightly called that house of the sanctuary "the Tabernacle of Moloch." But there is added, "and I will carry you beyond [ὑπέκεινα] Babylon," the Vulgate "trans," Erasmus "beyond Babylon." So also the Syriac and the Arabic. But Beza, "to the borders of Babylon." ὑπέκεινα properly and commonly means "beyond," and here it stands for the Hebrew מֵהֵלָּאָה, the word the prophet used. To translate this as "to the borders" is not sufficiently fitting, and the matter itself does not readily admit it. For here it is not concerned with the tribe of Judah, which was carried by the king of Babylon into Babylonia and remained almost within its borders, but with the ten tribes of Israel, whose prophet was Amos, chapter 1 verse 1, whom he addresses in chapter 5 verses 4 and 5, and who were settled by Shalmaneser, king of Assyria, beyond Babylon, in Halah, Habor, Gozan, and the cities of the Medes, 2 Kings 17:6. But why did Stephen say "beyond Babylon," when the prophet Amos, chapter 5 verse 27, said "beyond Damascus"? Because Amos at his own time had a special reason, when he was to designate a distant deportation of the people, for saying "beyond Damascus." For Hazael, king of Damascus, had already by great slaughters afflicted the land of the ten tribes; he had killed very many and led very many away captive into Syria; yet this had not subdued the minds of the wicked people so that they repented. Therefore the prophet goes on to announce a greater calamity, that before long they would be carried away much further beyond Damascus. How far beyond Damascus, the event itself afterwards showed, when they were transported beyond Babylon into the regions of Media and Armenia. Stephen, therefore, neglecting the circumstance which Amos had regarded, preferred to say the thing that the prophet intended.

units.la: VERS. 44. ἡ σκηνὴ τοῦ μαρτυρίου, tabernaculum testimonii.
units.tr: VERS. 44. ἡ σκηνὴ τοῦ μαρτυρίου, the tabernacle of testimony.

units.la: Rectè docet Cl. Beza, sic solere Græcos Interpretes exprimere quod Hebr. dicitur אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד, id est, tabernaculum conditionis, seu tentorium conventus. Addimus, alibi vocari אֹהֶל הָעֵדוּת, tabernaculum testimonii, Num. 9. 15. & 17. 23. item מִשְׁכַּן הָעֵדוּת, habitaculum testimonii, Exod. 38. 21. Num. 1. 50. & alibi. Voluerunt ergo LXX Interpretes, idem esse ibi מוֹעֵד & עדות, quod non usque adeo est incongruum. nam sicut עֵדָה valet cœtum, conventum à יָעַד, & testimonium ab עוּד, ita & מוֹעֵד utrumque significare potest. Sæpe enim verba quiescentia prima jod, & media vau significationes permutant. sic הוֹרִיד significat arefacere, à יָבֵשׁ, & pudefacere, à בּוּשׁ, הוֹרִיד, possefpossessione expellere, à יֵרֵש, & depauperare, à רוש. aliaque similia. nec aliter intellexit Vetus interpres, quum vertit, tabernaculum fœderis. idem enim, fœdus & testimonium. sicut arca eodem sensu appellatur arca fœderis, & arca testimonii, vel testimonium absolutè. Conciliari autem possunt qui vertunt tabernaculum conventus, cum iis qui tabernaculum testimonii aut fœderis. si dicantur, non tam populum respicere, qui isthic ad Deum convenerit, quam ipsum Deum, qui testimoniorum ac fœderis sui declaratione ibi populo patefiebat, & cum eo quasi conveniebat. Sic enim ipse Deus id explicat Exod. 29. 42. 43. ubi causa datur, cur vocetur אוהל מועד, quia אועד לכם שמה לדבר אליך שם conveniam vobis eo, ut alloquar te isthic. vides Deum convenire, ut alloquatur. & quidem, ut alloquar te, inquit, Moses nempe. quod fieri poterat sine ullo populi conventu. neque datum est tabernaculo hoc nomen propter האוהל, vestibulum, qui locus erat conventus populi. sed propter הדביר, adytum, ubi erat arca testimonii, ubi Deus Moses & summum sacerdotem conveniebat. unde Exod. 25. 22. ויועדתי, & conveniam tibi illic, nempe ad arcam, & loquar tecum è propitiatorio.
units.tr: Clarissimus Beza rightly teaches that the Greek interpreters usually render the Hebrew אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד [ohel mo'ed], that is, tabernacle of appointment or tent of meeting. I add that elsewhere it is called אֹהֶל הָעֵדוּת [ohel ha'edut], tabernacle of testimony, Num. 9. 15. and 17. 23.; likewise מִשְׁכַּן הָעֵדוּת [mishkan ha'edut], dwelling of testimony, Exod. 38. 21., Num. 1. 50., and elsewhere. The Seventy therefore intended that מוֹעֵד and עדות mean the same thing there, which is not so very incongruous. For just as עֵדָה [edah] means assembly, congregation, from יָעַד [ya'ad], and testimony from עוּד [ud], so מוֹעֵד can signify either. Verbs whose first radical is yod and whose middle radical is vav often change their meanings in this way. Thus הוֹרִיד [horid] means to dry up, from יָבֵשׁ [yavesh], and to shame, from בּוּשׁ [bush]; הוֹרִיד also means to drive out of a possession, from יֵרֵשׁ [yeresh], and to impoverish, from רוש [rush]; and there are many similar cases. The Old Interpreter (the Vulgate translator) understood it no differently when he rendered tabernacle of covenant, for covenant and testimony are the same thing, just as the ark is called in the same sense the ark of the covenant and the ark of testimony, or simply the testimony. Those who translate tabernacle of assembly can also be reconciled with those who say tabernacle of testimony or of covenant, if we consider not so much the people who there assembled before God as God himself, who there revealed himself to the people by the declaration of his testimonies and covenant, and who as it were met with them there. For God himself explains this in Exod. 29. 42. 43., where the reason is given why it is called אוהל מועד [ohel mo'ed]: אועד לכם שמה לדבר אליך שם [e'ved lakhem shamah ledabber elekha sham], I will meet with you there, to speak with you there. You see that God meets in order to speak. And indeed he says to speak with you, namely with Moses, which could be done without any assembly of the people. The tabernacle did not receive this name because of the האוהל [ha'ohel], the vestibule, which was the place of the people's assembly, but because of the הדביר [ha-debir], the inner sanctuary, where the ark of testimony was, and where God met with Moses and the high priest. Hence Exod. 25. 22.: ויועדתי [ve-ye'adti], and I will meet with you there, namely at the ark, and I will speak with you from the mercy seat.

units.la: Sequitur, ὧ ἐν τῇς πατρῶν ἡμῶν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ. Vulg. Eras. & Beza, fuit patribus nostris, id est, τῆς πατρῶν. quomodo legit exemplar per Thomam Platerum Basileæ impressum anno 1543. At ibidem impressum ex officina Joh. Oporini, 1552. ut & exemplaria quæ Beza expressit habent, ἐν τῆς πατρῶν, inter patres nostros. quomodo & Æthiopicus legit. Syrus & Arabs non videntur ἐν legisse. verterunt enim, Ecce tabernaculum testimonii patrum nostrorum fuit in deserto. sensus ubique idem est.
units.tr: There follows ὧ ἐν τῇς πατρῶν ἡμῶν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ [hō en tēs patrōn hēmōn en tē erēmō]. The Vulgate, Erasmus and Beza read which was among our fathers, that is, τῆς πατρῶν [tēs patrōn], as the copy printed at Basel by Thomas Platter in 1543 reads. But the copy printed in the same place by the workshop of Johannes Oporinus in 1552, and the copies Beza followed, have ἐν τῆς πατρῶν [en tēs patrōn], among our fathers, as the Ethiopic also reads. The Syriac and the Arab do not seem to have read ἐν [en]. For they translate: Behold, the tabernacle of testimony of our fathers was in the desert. The sense is the same everywhere.

units.la: VERS. 45. ἡν δὲ εἰσῆγαγον διαδεξάμενοι οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν.
units.tr: VERS. 45. ἡν δὲ εἰσῆγαγον διαδεξάμενοι οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν.

units.la: Laudo Bezam, quum vertit, quod etiam acceptum introduxerunt patres nostri. Sic Arabs, ... quum accepiffent illud patres nostri, nempe ex manibus Mosis, Aaronis, aliorumque seniorum qui in deserto occubuerunt. Erasmus, qui successerunt. fateor ἀλαδιχέσθαι non aliter quam pro excipere, id est, succedere usurpari apud LXX Interpretes, & qui Apocryphos libros scripserunt Hellenistas. nec dubitarem, quin hoc loco ita esset interpretandum, si legeretur οἱ ἀλαδεξάμενοι πατρὶς ἡμῶν. sic enim ad Erasmi sententiam exprimendam dicere debuit, qui Græcè loqui voluit. Jam vero constructio arguit, ἀλαδεξάμενοι non esse personarum, sed actionis determinationem. Sequitur ἐν τῇ καταχτίσει τῶν ἐθνῶν, Vulg. & Eras. in possessionem gentium. Beza in ipsa occupatione gentium, id est, quum inciperent obtinere gentes. κατάσχεσις tamen apud LXX Interpretes usurpatur pro אחזה, ירושה & נחלה, & potius ipsam terram quæ obtinetur aut possidetur, quam ejus occupationem aut acquisitionem significat. unde Syrus paraphrasticè vertit ܠܐܪܥܐ ܕܝܗܒ ܠܗܘܢ ... in terram quam dedit ipsis Deus possessionem ex gentibus. Et nisi sic interpreteris, subaudienda erit terra Sancta, in quam tabernaculum introduxerunt, cum occuparent gentes. simplicius itaque est ἐν pro εἰς hic accipere ut & apud Græcos interp. ἐν κατάσχεσι & εἰς κατάσχεσιν promiscuè usurpantur. confer Num. 32. 5. & 22. cum Deut. 32. 51. & alibi. atque ipsa constructio id hic satis innuit, quum dixit Lucas εισήγαγεν ἐν τῇ καταχτίσει. influit enim præcedens εἰς in sequens ἐν.
units.tr: I commend Beza, who translates which our fathers also brought in, having received it. So the Arab: when our fathers had received it, namely from the hands of Moses, Aaron and the other elders who died in the desert. Erasmus has who succeeded. I admit that ἀποδέχεσθαι [apodechesthai] is used in the Seventy and in the Hellenistic writers of the Apocryphal books only in the sense of receive, that is, succeed. I would not doubt that this passage should be so interpreted if the text read οἱ ἀποδεξάμενοι πατέρες ἡμῶν [hoi apodexamenoi pateres hēmōn]. For to express Erasmus's meaning, the one who wished to speak Greek ought to have written it that way. But the construction shows that ἀποδεξάμενοι [apodexamenoi] does not name persons but determines the action. There follows ἐν τῇ καταχτίσει τῶν ἐθνῶν [en tē katachtisei tōn ethnōn], which the Vulgate and Erasmus render into the possession of the nations, and Beza in the very occupation of the nations, that is, when the nations were beginning to hold it. Yet κατάσχεσις [kataschesis] in the Seventy is used for אחזה [achuzzah], ירושה [yerushah] and נחלה [nachalah], and signifies the land itself which is held or possessed rather than its occupation or acquisition. Hence the Syriac paraphrases freely: into the land which God gave them as a possession from the nations (la-ar'a d-yahab lehon, into the land that he gave them). And unless you interpret it so, one would have to supply the Holy Land as the place into which they brought in the tabernacle when the nations occupied it. It is therefore simpler to take ἐν [en] here for εἰς [eis], as among the Greek interpreters ἐν κατάσχεσι [en kataschesi] and εἰς κατάσχεσιν [eis kataschesin] are used interchangeably. Compare Num. 32. 5. and 22. with Deut. 32. 51., and elsewhere. The construction itself hints at this here, since Luke wrote εἰσῆγαγεν ἐν τῇ καταχτίσει, for the preceding εἰς [eis] flows into the following ἐν [en].

units.la: VERS. 46.
units.tr: VERS. 46.

units.la: Καὶ ἡτήσατο εὑρεῖν σκήνωμα τῷ Θεῷ Ἰακὼβ. petita phrasis ex Pf. 132. 5. donec invenero locum Domino. quid in utroque loco est invenire? Optimè hic Arabs ... & petiit facere habitaculum. Ipse David sic interpretatur 2 Paral. 28. 2. cum corde meo est ædificare &c. Invenire ergo est facere. ex more enim linguarum Orientalium ... est invenire, consequi, & incipere consequi, id est parare & facere ut habeas. Talia sunt, Esa. 58. 14. ne invenias, id est, facias, voluntatem tuam. Ofea 12. 8. inveni, id est, paravi, divitias mihi. Prov. 3. 13. Beatus vir qui invenit, id est, paravit sibi, sapientiam. sic accipi potest illud Pf. 36. 1. inveniendo, id est, faciendo, iniquitatem suam ad odium, sive odiosam. non aliter quam apud Arabes accipere, usurpatur pro facere, quod est incipere accipere. ut hoc ipso cap. 43. imagines quas fecistis.
units.tr: Καὶ ἡτήσατο εὑρεῖν σκήνωμα τῷ Θεῷ Ἰακὼβ [Kai ētēsato heurein skēnōma tō Theō Iakōb]. The phrase is taken from Ps. 132. 5., until I find a place for the Lord. What does to find mean in both places? The Arab renders this very well: and he asked to make a dwelling. David himself explains it this way in 2 Chron. 28. 2., it was in my heart to build, and so on. To find therefore means to make. For in the manner of the Oriental languages, to find and to obtain, and to begin to obtain, mean to prepare and to make so that you have something. Such is Isa. 58. 14., you shall not find, that is, you shall not make, your will. Hosea 12. 8., I have found, that is, I have prepared, riches for myself. Prov. 3. 13., Blessed is the man who finds, that is, who prepares for himself, wisdom. So too Ps. 36. 1. may be understood: in finding, that is, in making, his iniquity hateful, or odious. This is no different from the Arabic usage of to receive for to make, which means to begin to receive, as in this same chapter, 43: the images which you made.

units.la: VERS. 51. Ὡς εἰ πατρὸς ὑμῶν, ἐ ὑμεῖς. Illud καὶ ὑμᾶς, Syrus etiam & Arabs, nec non Æthiopicus legerunt, nec redundat.
units.tr: VERS. 51. Ὡς οἱ πατέρες ὑμῶν, καὶ ὑμεῖς [Hōs hoi pateres hymōn, kai hymeis]. The Syriac, the Arab and also the Ethiopic read the words καὶ ὑμᾶς [kai hymas], and it is not superfluous.

units.la: VERS. 53. Qui accepistis legem, εἰς ἀγγέλων. Vulg. in dispositione Angelorum. Beza per dispositionem, singul. numero. Eraf. per dispositiones, plur. num. Syrus & Arabs per mandatum. Nos quoque διαταγὴ pro mandato, ordinatione & sanctione accipimus. sicut Rom. 13. 2. τῇ διαταγῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ, Dei sanctioni aut mandato restitit. Etsi enim Angeli sint Ecclesiae διάκονοι, ministri, Hebr. 1. 14. ut tamen διαταγὴ sit hic idem quod διαταγία, non facile affirmem. Habent enim & ministri Dei suam mandandi authoritatem, licet ὑπηρετικῶ, non διακονικῶ. Porro εἰς respondet Hebraeorum Lamed, quod quia aliquando pro ב in, per usurpatur, hinc alii in dispositione, alii per dispositionem. nos, servatâ propriâ particulae significatione, ad ordinationes Angelorum. quo sensu dicitur filius facere ad nutum patris. quomodo & ל usurpatur Num. 16. 34. לקול, fugerunt ad clamorem eorum, id est, clamantibus ipsis. Sic, accepistis legem ad ordinationes Angelorum, id est, ordinantibus angelis. vel, secundum, juxta ordinationes. id enim Hebraeorum ל valet in לצבאותם, secundum speciem suam, Gen. 1. 21. juxta exercitus suos, לפשׂחוּם, fecundum familias suas, Num. 1. sæpe. Syrus & Arabs quoque legerunt in plur. ἀγγέλων. ille enim habet ﻟﻠﻤﻼﺋﻜﺔ, hic ﻣﻼﺋﻜﺔ. male ergo Syrum Tremel. & Arabem Junius interpretati sunt. nisi forte codices eorum aut variaverint, aut mendum habuerint. Huic autem loco parallela sunt, ad Gal. 3. 19. ὁ νόμος δι' ἀγγέλων. & Hebr. 2. 2. ὁ δι' ἀγγέλων λαληθεὶς λόγος. Horum dictorum hæc videtur esse ratio & veritas. S. Stephanus supra v. 39. dixit Angelum locutum esse cum Mose in monte Sina, eundem nempe qui in rubo ipsi apparuerat, v. 35. qui quamvis in se Deus, hic tamen κατ' οἰκονομίαν tanquam Angelus Dei, cæterorumque Angelorum præfectus confideratus, e medio Angelorum, qui eum undique stipabant, legem in monte Mosi dedit. cujus rei figuram expressit Sanctuarium, ubi inter Cherubim sedens Deus, e medio Cherubim oracula dabat. Eodem enim modo in monte fuisse actum, inde colligitur, quod tabernaculum struere jussus fuerit ad formam quam in monte viderat. Hinc Psal. 68. 8. quum dixisset, Currum Dei esse viginti millia, iterata millia Angelorum, in quorum medio sit Deus, addit סִינַי בְּקֹדֶשׁ, Sinai est in sanctuario. ut doceret, sicut olim in Sinai Deus myriadibus Angelorum cinctus, iisque tanquam curribus vectus legem dedit, ita adhuc eandem montis Sinai rationem in Sanctuario obtinere, ubi Deus vehitur curru Cherubim. quandoquidem ergo Lex prodiit e senatu Angelorum, cujus præses erat summus ille Angelus Jehovah, merito dixit Apostolus, prolatam esse & ordinatam per Angelos, Stephanus, acceptam esse a populo ad ordinationes Angelorum. idem hic est διαταγὴ ἀγγέλων, quod Dan. 4. 14. עִיר קַדִּישׁ, decretum vigilum, פִּתְגָּם קְרִישׁ, & mandatum sanctorum. intelligitur decretum mandatumque senatus Angelici, cui præerat summus Dei filius, respectu cujus idem illud decretum dicitur ϒf. 21. גְּזֵרַת עֶלְיוֹן, decretum Altissimi. Atque inde colligi potest causa, cur Apostolus Hebr. 2. 2. 3. Legi Euangelium tantopere anteferat. Etsi enim utriusque autor & promulgator fuerit idem Dei Filius, quia tamen legem tulit in forma Angeli, e senatu Angelico, & velatus gloria Angelorum, (quamobrem & inter Cherubim sedens conspicuus non erat) tandem vero caro factus & in carne manifestatus, gloriam præfe ferens, non Angelorum, sed unigeniti filii Dei, Euangelium ipsemet, humanâ voce, habitans inter homines prædicavit, merito Lex Angelorum sermo, Euangelium autem solius filii Dei dicitur.
units.tr: VERS. 53. Who received the law [εἰς ἀγγέλων]. The Vulgate has in the disposition of angels. Beza has by disposition in the singular. Erasmus has by dispositions in the plural. The Syrian and the Arab have by command. We too take διαταγὴ to mean command, ordinance and decree, as in Rom. 13. 2, where τῇ διαταγῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ is resisted the ordinance or command of God. For although angels are the Church's διάκονοι, ministers (Heb. 1. 14), I would not readily affirm that διαταγὴ here means the same as διαταγία. The ministers of God also have their own authority to command, though it is ὑπηρετικῶ [serving], not διακονικῶ [ministering]. Moreover εἰς corresponds to the Hebrew Lamed, which is sometimes used for ב, in or by. Hence some render in the disposition, others by the disposition. I, keeping the proper sense of the particle, render to the ordinances of angels. In this sense a son is said to act at the nod of his father. So too ל is used in Num. 16. 34, לקול [lekol], they fled at their cry, that is, while they were crying out. So you received the law at the ordinances of angels means while the angels ordained it. Or it may mean according to, in accordance with the ordinances. For the Hebrew ל has this force in לצבאותם [letsiba'otam], according to their kind (Gen. 1. 21), according to their hosts, לפשׂחוּם [lemishpeḥotam], according to their families (Num. 1), and often elsewhere. The Syrian and the Arab also read angels in the plural. The Syrian has lilmalā'ikah and the Arab malā'ikah. So Tremellius translated the Syrian, and Junius the Arab, badly, unless perhaps their manuscripts differ or are corrupt. Parallel to this passage are Gal. 3. 19, the law was ordained through angels [ὁ νόμος δι' ἀγγέλων], and Heb. 2. 2, the word spoken through angels [ὁ δι' ἀγγέλων λαληθεὶς λόγος]. The reason and truth of these sayings seems to be this. St. Stephen said above, v. 39, that the Angel spoke with Moses on Mount Sinai, the same who had appeared to him in the bush (v. 35). Although he is God in himself, here he is viewed economically, as the Angel of God and the prefect over the other angels, and from the midst of the angels who surrounded him on every side he gave the law on Moses' mountain. The Sanctuary expressed the figure of this matter, where God, sitting among the cherubim, gave oracles from the midst of the cherubim. That the same thing was done on the mountain is inferred from the fact that Moses was commanded to build the tabernacle according to the pattern he had seen on the mountain. Hence Psalm 68. 8, having said that the chariot of God is twenty thousand, even thousands of angels, in the midst of whom is God, adds סִינַי בְּקֹדֶשׁ [Sinai is in the sanctuary]. This teaches that, just as formerly on Sinai God, surrounded by myriads of angels and borne on them as on chariots, gave the law, so even now the same condition of Sinai obtains in the Sanctuary, where God is carried on the chariot of the cherubim. Since therefore the Law came forth from the council of angels, over which presided that highest Angel, Jehovah, the Apostle, Stephen, rightly said that it was spoken and ordained through angels, and received by the people at the ordinances of angels. This is the same as διαταγὴ ἀγγέλων [the ordinance of angels], which in Dan. 4. 14 is עִיר קַדִּישׁ [a decree of the watchers] and פִּתְגָּם קְרִישׁ [and a command of the holy ones]. It is understood as the decree and command of the angelic council, over which the Son of God presided. With respect to that council the same decree is called, in Dan. 4. 21, גְּזֵרַת עֶלְיוֹן [the decree of the Most High]. From this one can gather why the Apostle, in Heb. 2. 2–3, so greatly prefers the Gospel to the Law. For although the same Son of God was the author and proclaimer of both, yet because he gave the Law in the form of an Angel, from the angelic council, and veiled in the glory of angels (for which reason he was not visible even when sitting among the cherubim), but at last was made flesh and manifested in the flesh, bearing a glory not of angels but of the only-begotten Son of God, he himself preached the Gospel with a human voice, dwelling among men. Rightly, therefore, the Law is called the word of angels, but the Gospel the word of the Son of God alone.

units.la: VERS. 55. Quum autem plenus effet Spiritu Sancto. Syrus, quem sequitur Arabs, fide & Spiritu S.
units.tr: VERSE 55. But when he was full of the Holy Spirit. The Syriac, which the Arab follows, has in faith and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: VERS. 57. Σωίχον τὰ ὦτα αὐτῶν. Vulg. & Beza, continuerunt aures suas. Syrus ꞎ ꞎ ..., obstruxerunt, obturarunt: five digitum ingerendo in aures, five ipsam auriculam, infimam dico & mollem auris partem, quæ אלה, cauda Hebræis dicitur, de qua illi sic אחן ספני מה כלה קשה אלה שלה רכה שאם ישמע quare auris tota dura est, caudicula vero ejus mollis? ut fi quis verbum indecorum audiat, inflectat caudiculam intra aurem.
units.tr: VERSE 57. Σωίχον τὰ ὦτα αὐτῶν [ἔσχον τὰ ὦτα αὐτῶν]. The Vulgate and Beza have they held their ears. The Syriac has they stopped up, they blocked, whether by thrusting a finger into the ears or by pressing the ear itself, meaning the lowest and softest part of the ear, which the Hebrews call cauda [אלה]. Of this they say: Why is the whole ear hard but its little tail soft? So that if a man hears an indecent word, he folds the little tail into the ear. [מה כלה קשה אלה שלה רכה שאם ישמע]

units.la: VERS. 58. Et ejectum eum extra urbem lapidabant: testes autem deponebant pallia &c. Libet hîc ritum Lapidationis ex Rabbi Mikotfi ad præcept. affirmativum 99 paucis aponere אומרים חכמים שהאיש נסקל ערום ולא האישה מבית הסקילה ארבע id est, Ajunt sapientes, virum lapidatum fuisse nudum, non fæminam. eique quatuor à lapidationis loco cubitis distanti extraCtas fuisse vestes, teCtis solummodo ab anteriori pudendis. Locus lapidationis altitudinem dinem dinem habebat duarum statuarum, ad quem reus vinctis manibus adscendebat. illum alter testium ad lumbos pulsatum praecipitem dabat in terram, ex qua impulsione si extinctus non esset, elevabant testes lapidem ibidem collocatum, pendere duorum hominum, quem alter testium super eum projiciebat. quod si nesic quidem expirasset, accessit totus Israël & lapidavit eum.
units.tr: VERSE 58. And they cast him out of the city and stoned him; and the witnesses laid down their garments, etc. Here I think it worth setting out briefly the rite of stoning from Rabbi Mikotfi on the affirmative precept 99. The wise men say that the man was stoned naked, but not the woman. At a distance of four cubits from the place of stoning, the garments were taken off, covering only the private parts in front. The place of stoning had the height of two men, and the condemned man ascended it with his hands bound. One of the witnesses struck him at the loins and threw him headlong to the ground. If he was not killed by this fall, the witnesses lifted a stone, placed there, which weighed two men, and the other witness threw it upon him. If he had not yet expired even so, all Israel came and stoned him. [אומרים חכמים שהאיש נסקל ערום ולא האישה]

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: VERS. 1. Σαῶλ δὲ ἦν συνευδοκῶν τῇ ἀναιρέσει αὐτοῦ. Vulgatus, Saulus autem erat consentiens neci ejus. Eraf. consenserat. Beza, ultro consenserat. Syrus ܫܐܘܠ ܗܘܐ ܕܡܬܪܥܐ ܒܩܛܠܗ, quae verto, Saul autem delectabatur & participabat in cade ejus. nempe quum compositum verbum non haberet, duobus expressit, quod uno dixit Lucas συνευδοκῶν. sic & Arabs erat amans & particeps. Nihil ergo apud hos Interpretes est, cur Cl. Beza συνευδοκῶν verteret, ultro consenserat. Ego Syrum secutus verto, una delectabatur cade ejus. Συνευδοκῶν est delectari. σὺν significat, eum una cum aliis, de quibus cap. praecedenti, fuisse delectatum.
units.tr: Verse 1. "Now Saul was consenting to his death" [Σαῶλ δὲ ἦν συνευδοκῶν τῇ ἀναιρέσει αὐτοῦ]. The Vulgate has "Saul was consenting to his death." Erasmus has "had consented." Beza has "had readily consented." The Syriac, Shaul hawa d-mitr'a b-qtaleh, which I render "Saul was delighting in and sharing in his slaughter," has no compound verb, so it expresses with two words what Luke expresses with one, συνευδοκῶν. The Arabic likewise says "was loving and participating." Nothing in these interpreters, then, explains why the illustrious Beza translated συνευδοκῶν as "readily consented." Following the Syriac, I translate it "was delighting together with his slaughter." Συνευδοκῶν means "to be delighted," and the σύν signifies that he was delighted together with others, those mentioned in the preceding chapter.

units.la: VERS. 2. Συνευδόμενοι δὲ τὴν Ἐπαφρῶν. vide quae observavimus supra, ad cap. 5. Ψ. 6. Addimus hic solummodo הלוית הפת, deductionem mortui ad sepulchrum referri ab Hebraeis inter opera, שאום אבל מפרוטיהם בעולם הזה הקרן קימת לו בעולם הבא, quorum fructus homo edit in hoc saeculo, fors autem ipsi manet in futuro. Sequitur, & fecerunt planctum magnum super eum. quomodo lugere mortuos soleant Hebraei, videat, qui avidus est, apud Schickardum de jur. reg. Hebr. c.6. & apud Joh. Cochum in Sanhedr. c. 6.
units.tr: VERSE 2. Συνευδόμενοι δὲ τὸν Στέφανον [Devout men then buried Stephen]. See what I noted above on chapter 5, verse 6. I add here only that the Hebrews list among the works of mercy the conveying of the dead to the grave: Whose fruit a man eats in this world, while the principal remains for him in the world to come [הקרן קימת לו בעולם הבא]. The text continues: and they made great lamentation over him. Whoever is eager to know how the Hebrews customarily mourn their dead may consult Schickard, De jure regio Hebraeorum, chapter 6, and John Coch on Sanhedrin, chapter 6.

units.la: VERS. 4, At illi qui dispersi erant, διῆλθον. Vulgat. pertransibant. Eraf. peragrabant. Beza, peragrabant regionem. Hebraicè dicas מִלָּה vel דָּבָר. Syrus & Arabs circuibant. nam & διέρχεσθαι apud lxx Interpretes usurpatur pro סבב & שוט circuire. Additur, Διαγγελιζόμενοι τ λόγον, Vulg. Annunciantes verbum. Beza, Euangelizantes sermonem Dei. Syrus quoque & Arabs addiderunt Dei. etsi non fit necessarium. ὁ λόγ⁠ος enim passim absolutè verbum Dei κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν significat. talia sunt Matth. 13. 20. ὁ ἀκούων τ λόγον. & sf. 21. διωγμὸς διὰ τ λόγον. & sf. 22. συμπνίγει τ λόγον. In quibus locis etiam verbum dicere malo quam sermonem. est enim λόγος Hebraeorum דָּבָר, quod proprie verbum significat. sermo enim sive oratio מִלָּה potius ipsis dicitur. differunt ut apud Belgas tooojt ende reden. hinc alibi pro λόγος est ῥῆμα. ut ἐγγύς σε τ ῥῆμα ἐστίν. Rom. 10. 8. τὸ ῥῆμα τ πίστως. sf. 9. ἡ ὁ ἀκοὴ διὰ ῥημάτ⁠ων Θεοῦ. sf. 17. & alibi saepe. & ut λόγος, ita & ῥῆμα absolutè pro verbo Dei. ut Eph. 5. 26. καθαρίσας τῷ λουτρῷ ἐν ὕδατι ἐν ῥήματι.
