units.tr: VERSE 4. Those who were scattered abroad, διῆλθον [went through]. The Vulgate: passed through. Erasmus: wandered about. Beza: went through the region. In Hebrew one would say מִלָּה or דָּבָר. The Syriac and Arab have went about, for διέρχεσθαι in the Septuagint is also used for סבב and שוט, to go about. There is added, Διαγγελιζόμενοι τὸν λόγον [preaching the word]; the Vulgate: announcing the word; Beza: proclaiming the word of God. The Syriac and Arab also added of God, though this is not necessary, for ὁ λόγος everywhere, used absolutely, means the word of God, κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν. Such are Matthew 13:20, ὁ ἀκούων τὸν λόγον [he who hears the word], and verse 21, διωγμὸς διὰ τὸν λόγον [persecution because of the word], and verse 22, συμπνίγει τὸν λόγον [chokes the word]. In these places I prefer to say word rather than speech, for the Hebrew λόγος is דָּבָר, which properly means word; the Hebrews call speech or discourse מִלָּה. They differ as the Dutch woord and rede. Hence elsewhere ῥῆμα is used for λόγος, as in Romans 10:8, ἐγγύς σου τὸ ῥῆμά ἐστιν [the word is near you], and in verse 8 τὸ ῥῆμα τῆς πίστεως [the word of faith], and verse 9, ἡ ἀκοὴ διὰ ῥημάτων Θεοῦ [hearing through the words of God], and verse 17, and often elsewhere. And as λόγος, so ῥῆμα is used absolutely for the word of God, as in Ephesians 5:26, καθαρίσας τῷ λουτρῷ ἐν ὕδατι ἐν ῥήματι [cleansing it by the washing of water with the word].

units.la: VERS. 5. Philippus autem quum devenisset in urbem Samaria.
units.tr: VERSE 5. Then Philip went down to the city of Samaria.

units.la: Samaria & regionis & urbis nomen est. hic urbs ipsa intelligitur, totius regionis metropolis, ut ex sf. 8. liquet. regni Israelitici olim sedes, ab Omri מְשָׁמְרִין rege Israelitarum in monte structa, quem à quodam, שֶׁמֶר Semer dicto, emerat, indeque urbem שֹׁמְרוֹן, Somron, alias Samaria, vocavit, ibique regni sedem fixit, quae antea Thirsae erat.
units.tr: Samaria is the name both of a region and of a city. Here the city itself is meant, the metropolis of the whole region, as is clear from chapter 8. It was once the seat of the kingdom of Israel. Omri, king of the Israelites, built it on a mountain [מְשָׁמְרִין] which he had bought from a certain man named Shemer [שֶׁמֶר]. From him he called the city Shomron [שֹׁמְרוֹן], otherwise Samaria, and there fixed the seat of the kingdom, which had previously been at Tirzah.

units.la: 1 Reg. 16. 23. alludens autem ad radicem ejus שָׁמַר, custodivit Hieron. ad cap. 4. Amos, dicit Samariam à custodia esse dictam, non quod custodiant sermones Domini, sed quia custodes praeceptorum ejus se esse jactent. quo pertinent etiam, etsi frivola, verba Epiphanii l. 1. de haeres. ἐμβλωσκούλαι ἡ Σαμαρῖτ⁠αι φύλακες, διὰ τὸ ἐν τῇ φυλάκων πληχθῆναι ἐν τῇ γῇ. ἡ ἀπὸ ἐν φύλαξ αὐτὸς εἶναι τ ἰς τ νόμου Μωϋσέως διαξέως. Vocantur autem Samaritae, si interpreteris, custodes, propterea quod custodum locum in terra obtinebant, aut quod custodes erant constitutionis secundum legem Mosis. Vrbem hanc occupavit, decem L tribus abduxit, aliisque coloniis territorium Samariæ instruxit Salmanassar Assyriorum rex. 2Reg. 17. Funditus autem deletam esse vult ab Assyrio Rabbi D. Kimchi ad
units.tr: 1 Kings 16.23. Jerome, on Amos chapter 4, alluding to its root שָׁמַר, "to keep," says that Samaria was so named "from custody, not because they keep the words of the Lord, but because they boast that they are the guardians of his precepts." To this also belong, though they are trivial, the words of Epiphanius in book 1 of Against Heresies: "The Samaritans are called guardians, if you interpret the name, because they held the place of guards in the land, or because they were guardians of the constitution according to the law of Moses." [ἐμβλωσκούλαι ἡ Σαμαρῖται φύλακες, διὰ τὸ ἐν τῇ φυλάκων πληχθῆναι ἐν τῇ γῇ, ἢ ἀπὸ ἐν φύλαξ αὐτὸς εἶναι τῆς τοῦ νόμου Μωϋσέως διαταξέως.] This city was taken by Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, who carried off the ten tribes and furnished the territory of Samaria with other colonies. 2 Kings 17. Rabbi D. Kimchi, however, holds that it was utterly destroyed by the Assyrian, on Micah chapter 1 verse 6 ... "I will make Samaria as a heap of the field." Yet the words he comments on seem to contradict this, for they say that the colonists possessed Samaria and inhabited its cities. [Note: the commentary on 2 Kings 17.24 is cited by Dieu.] However that may be, Epiphanius is very gravely mistaken, since in book 1 of On Heresies he attributes to Shalmaneser what must be ascribed to the king of the Assyrians, namely Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians, who lived long afterwards. And more absurdly still, he says that at that time Ezra the scribe was sent to teach the Assyrians, whom lions were devouring, the law in Samaria.

units.la: 2 Reg. 17. v. 24. secundum prædictionem Michæ c. 1. v. 6. Ponam Samariam in cumulum agri. repugnare autem videntur ipsa verba ad quæ commentatur. dicuntur enim colonix posseđisse Samariam,& habitasse urbes ejus.ut ut se habeat, gravissimè hallucinatur Epiphanius, qui l. 1. de hæresibus, quod regi Assyriorum tribuendum erat Salmanassari, Babyloniorum regi Nabuchodonosori, qui dudum post vixit, tribuit. & fœdius etiam, quod eo tempore Efram scribam missum dicat, qui Assyrios, quos leones devorabant, legem in Samaria doceret. Hanc urbem ab Hyrcano fuisse funditus deletam, docet Josephus Antiq. l. 13. c. 18. verba ejus sunt, τ'ςχάν&ῳ τὼ πόλιν ἱλὼν, ἐκιαυπ̀ ἁπολιορκήσας, ἐπηρχιέδη μόνῳ τῶτῳ, ἀλλὰ ἐ πᾶσα ἀυτὼ ἡφάνισεν, ἐπῆκλυσεν τὴς χαμάρρεις πολήσας. Ἀλαπαλῶσ δ᾽ ἀυτὼ, ὡς εἰς χαρίδρας μεταπίσῶν, τὰ σημαῖα δ᾽ ἡμίσυ πῇ πόλιν ἀυτὼ ἀφέλαρ. Hyrcano non suffecit, urbem, post annalem obsidionem, cepisse, sed & torrentibus inundatam totam funditus delevit. effossam enim eam in alveos torrentis injecit, ut indicia etiam urbis penitus sublata essent. Eam restituit, vehementerque ornavit, atque in honorem Augusti sive τῇ σεβαστῇ Sebasten appellavit Herodes, l.1. de bell. Jud. c. 16. Dicta quoque fuit Josepho Mareone, l. 8. Antiq. c. 7. & Mamortha Plinio, Hist. Nat. l. 5. c. 13. Libet hic quoque ex Josepho de bel. Jud. l. 3. c. 4. territorii conditionem proferre. ἡ Σαμαρείτης, inquit, χώρα μέση μὲν τῆς Ἰουδαίας ἐστὶ, ἐκ τῆς Γαλιλαίας. Ἡ χουδὴν γὰρ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐν τῷ μεγάλῳ πεδίῳ κεκλῶσις γυναίας ὄνομα κώμης, ἐπὶ λήγῃ ἡ ἀκροβατιζῶν ὁπισθιαῖος. Φύσιν δὲ τῆς Ἰουδαίας κατ' ἰδίαν Διαφορὰ. ἀμφὼ ἡ δὲ ὁρεναὶ ἢ πεδιάδες, ὡς ἡ γεωργία μαλθακή, ἐ πολύφορον, καὶ διέσφοροι ἡ κύ ὁπωρὰς ὀρεινῆς ἢ ἡμέρα μεσυῆ. ἀποτασθέντα γὰρ ἰδαμᾶς μὴ φύσι δαψλὲς, ὑσπερ ἡ πλείον. γλυκὺ ἡ νᾶμα πᾶν Διαφέρως ἐν αὐτᾶς,
units.tr: Josephus, Antiquities book 13 chapter 18, teaches that this city was utterly destroyed by Hyrcanus. His words are: "Hyrcanus, having taken the city after a year's siege, was not content to have taken it, but totally destroyed it, flooding it with torrents. For he dug it out and cast it into the channels of the torrent, so that even the traces of the city were wholly removed." [τὴν πόλιν λαβὼν... ἐπηκλύσεν τῆς χαράδρας... ἀλαπαλῶσ δ᾽ αὐτὴν, ὡς εἰς χαράδρας μεταλλάσσειν.] Herod restored it, greatly adorned it, and named it Sebaste in honour of Augustus [τῇ Σεβαστῇ], as stated in book 1 of Wars of the Jews, chapter 16. It was also called Mareone by Josephus, Antiquities book 8 chapter 7, and Mamortha by Pliny, Natural History book 5 chapter 13. Here I will also set out, from Josephus, Wars of the Jews book 3 chapter 4, the condition of the territory. "The region of Samaria," he says, "lies between Judaea and Galilee [ἡ Σαμαρείτις χώρα μέση μέν ἐστι τῆς Ἰουδαίας καὶ τῆς Γαλιλαίας]..." The rest of the passage follows in the context after this point, and is not translated here.

units.la: κή χαὶ Ἀλὰ πλησθῶ. πᾶς ἀγαθὸς, τὸ κλῶν ταλεον, ἡ πρ' ἀλλοις γαλα- λιοφόῳ. μέγιστον γε μὲν πυρίν ἐον ᾧτινες ἐ Ἰδωμίας, τὸ αληθινῶν ἀνδρῶν ἐκαπαυ. id est, Samaritis autem regio, inter Iudaam quidem & Galilaam sita est. incipiens enim à vico in planicie posito, cui nomen est Ginaa, in Acrobatenam definit toparchiam. sed natura nihil à Iudaa discrepat. Amba enim montosa sunt & campestres, agrosque colendo molles atque feraces, nec non arboribus plena: pomisque tam sylvestribus quam mansuetis abundant. etsi enim natura non sint admodum irrigua, compluuntur tamen abunde. dulces autem per eas supra modum aquae sunt, bonique graminis copia, praeter alias earum pecora lactis abundant. quodque maximum virtutis atque opulentia specimen est, utraque viris referta est. Non abs re visum fuit haec referre, quia est ubi vicinitas similitudoque Samariae & Judaeae locis quibusdam lucem adferunt. Nec indignetur lector, si ἐν πρόδῳ hic etiam adferamus, quod Hieronymus in comment. ad Ezech. 9. 4. tradit, Antiquis Hebraeorum literis usque hodie Samaritanos uti. quod quatenus verum sit, alterius loci est examinare. Sed quod addit, extremam Thau literam apud eos habere similitudinem crucis, quae in Christianorum frontibus pingitur, & frequenti manus inscriptione signatur, verum non est, si modo eandem habemus hodie Samaritanorum scripturam, quae fuit tempore Hieronymi. Jam enim Thau sic pingunt Ɲ. At Æthiopes habent quoddam Te, quod pingitur ͳ, & vere crucis figuram repraesentat.
units.tr: Samaria, however, lies between Judaea and Galilee. Beginning from the village called Ginaea, on the plain, it extends to the toparchy of Acrabatene. But in nature it differs in no way from Judaea. Both are mountainous and level, and their soil is soft and fertile for cultivation, and they are full of trees, abounding in fruits both wild and cultivated. Although they are not naturally very well watered, they are nonetheless rained on abundantly. The waters there are exceedingly sweet, the pasture is good and plentiful, and besides, their flocks yield much milk. And the greatest proof of their strength and wealth is that both regions are full of men. It did not seem out of place to report these things, because the nearness and resemblance of Samaria and Judaea clarify certain points. Nor should the reader be annoyed if we also bring in here what Jerome, in his commentary on Ezekiel 9:4, reports: that the Samaritans still use the ancient letters of the Hebrews to this day. How far that is true belongs to another place to examine. But what he adds, that the last letter, Thau, among them has the likeness of a cross, which is painted on the foreheads of Christians and marked by the frequent sign of the hand, is not true, at least if we still have today the same Samaritan script that existed in Jerome's time. For they now draw Thau thus: Ɲ. But the Ethiopians have a certain Te, which is drawn ͳ, and this truly represents the figure of a cross.

units.la: VERS. 6. Προσεῖχον ἡ οἱ ὄχλοι τῆς λεγομένους ἀπὸ φιλίππου ἐμοῦμαδόν. Vulg. & Erasm. Intendebant autem turba iis quae &c. Beza, attendebant ea quae &c. Syrus, Attendebant eum & obediebant omnibus quae dicebat. duabus vocibus expressit illud προσεῖχον, ut docuret, plus eo contineri quam simplicem attentionem. plura de hoc verbo vide infra ad v. 11. Syrus & Arabs omittunt ὁμοῦμαδόν. Vulgatus conjunxit cum sequentibus, quasi legisset, ἐν τῷ ἀκούειν αὐτῆς ὁμοῦμαδόν. sic & Erasmus. quibus tamen exemplaria, quæ penes me sunt, non favent.
units.tr: VERS. 6. "Attended closely to the things said by Philip, all together" [Προσεῖχον δὲ οἱ ὄχλοι τοῖς λεγομένοις ὑπὸ Φιλίππου ὁμοθυμαδόν]. The Vulgate and Erasmus: "The crowds were giving heed to those things which &c." Beza: "they were attending to those things which &c." The Syriac: "They were attending to him and obeying all that he said." By using two words for proseichon, the translator showed that it contains more than simple attention. More on this word may be seen below at verse 11. The Syriac and the Arabic omit homothumadon. The Vulgate joined it to what follows, as if he had read "in hearing them all together," and so did Erasmus. Yet the manuscripts in my possession do not support this.

units.la: VERS. 7. Πολλῶν γὰρ ἐχόντων πνεῦμαῖα ἀκάθαρτα, βοῶντα μεγάλῃ φωνῇ ἐξήρχετο. videantur in locum hunc notæ Cl. Bezæ. quibus addimus, servari posse constructionem, si vertamus, multùm enim habentibus spiritus immundos, clamantes magna voce exibant.
units.tr: VERS. 7. "For many who had unclean spirits, crying with a loud voice, came out" [Πολλῶν γὰρ ἐχόντων πνεύματα ἀκάθαρτα, βοῶντα μεγάλῃ φωνῇ ἐξήρχετο]. The notes of the learned Beza on this passage should be consulted. To them we add that the construction can be kept if we translate: "for many having unclean spirits, crying with a loud voice, came out."

units.la: VERS. 9. Καὶ ἐξιῶν τ᾽ ἐθνῶν ἡ Σαμαρείας. Vulgatus, Syrus, Arabs, & Æthiopicus, & seducens gentem Samariæ, quod Hebraicè diceres, הַשֶּׁ֥ה אֶת־הָעָם שִׁכְרִין. sicut Esa. 28.7. שָׁגּוּ בַּיַּיִן, aberrarunt in vino, LXX verterunt ἐξέστησαν δὲ οἶνον. Beza, & gentem Samariæ obstupefecerat, id est, תִּמָּה, admirabundos, attonitos & obstupefactos reddiderat. id quoque apud LXX est ἐξέστησεν. ut & מִתְמַהֵּר, ἐκστασις. unde etiam Syrus v. 11. ἐξισταντι vertit. Erasmus, dementaverat, id est, הוֹלֵל, sicut Job. 12. 17. יִשְׁוֹלֵל, LXX, κρίνας ἐξέστη ἐπὶ γῆς ἐξέστη, judices terra dementavit. possis etiam vertere, & gentem Samariæ pavidam reddiderat, ita ut quisque eum metueret, Hebraicè חָרֵד. id enim quoque Græci Interpretes per ἐξέστησεν non raro reddunt.
units.tr: VERS. 9. "And he bewitched the people of Samaria" [Καὶ ἐξιῶν τὸ ἔθνος τῆς Σαμαρείας]. The Vulgate, the Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic have "and seducing the nation of Samaria," which in Hebrew would be hishshe et ha-am shichrin. Compare Isaiah 28:7, shagu ba-yayin, "they have erred in wine," which the Seventy rendered exestesan de oinon. Beza has "and had astonished the nation of Samaria," that is, timmah, which made them admiring, amazed and astonished. This too the Seventy render exesteisen, as also mit'ammeh is rendered ekstasis. Hence the Syriac also renders it existanti in verse 11. Erasmus has "had driven them mad," that is, holel, as in Job 12:17, yishollel, where the Seventy have krinas exestē epi gēs, "he made the judges of the earth to go mad." One could also translate, "and had made the nation of Samaria fearful," so that each one feared him, in Hebrew chared. For the Greek interpreters also often render it by exestesen.

units.la: VERS. 10. οὗτός ἐστιν ἡ δύναμις Θεοῦ ἡ μεγάλη. Vulg. hæc est virtus Dei quæ vocatur magna. unde habeat quæ vocatur, nescio. Syrus & Arabs non agnoscunt. Æthiopicus paraphrasticè ut solet vertit, dicentes ei, virtus Dei magna tu vocaris.
units.tr: VERS. 10. "This is the great power of God" [Οὗτός ἐστιν ἡ δύναμις τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡ μεγάλη]. The Vulgate: "This is the power of God which is called great." I do not know where "which is called" comes from. The Syriac and the Arabic do not recognise it. The Ethiopic, as it usually does, paraphrases: "saying to him, you are called the great power of God."

units.la: VERS. 11. ᾧ προσεῖχον. Beza, quem attendebant. Vulg. & Eras. cui auscultabant. Syrus, ܥܒܕܘ ܗܘ ܠܗ ... Trem. & Boder. & acquiescebant illi. verte & obediebant ei. nihil aliud est ܥܒܕ. ponitur passim pro ὑπακοή. inde ܥܒܕܘܬܐ, obedientia. ܠܐ ܥܒܕܘܬܐ, inobedientia. rectè vero Syrus illud [Greek] non tam de aurium quam mentis attentione intellexit. sensus est, mente sua adhærebant ei, dictis fidem habentes, adeoque docenti ac jubenti obediebant ac morem gerebant. ratio additur, quia diu præstigiis suis attonitos eos reddiderat. Arabs eodem prorsus modo intellexit & vertit [Arabic], & erant obedientes ei omnes. Nec aliter phrasin Lucæ intellexit Budæus, qui [Greek] ait interdum significare ausculto, obtempero. & hunc ipsum locum citat: de quo videantur plura apud H.Steph. qui recte addit, verbum hoc etiam de eo dici, qui sic aliquem observat ut spem suam & fiduciam in eo collocet. quod & huic loco optimè quadrat. ut & quod ex Budæo subjungit, [Greek] ]] interdum esse, applicare se ad aliquem, sectatorem ejus se præbere. est sane ubi LXX Interpretes [Hebrew], adhærere, per [Greek] vertunt. quod hic non est aspernandum, ut & quod versu præcedenti Syrus transtulit [Syriac], & inclinati erant versus illum, quod non male Trem. & dediti erant ei.
units.tr: VERS. 11. "to whom they were attending" [ᾧ προσεῖχον]. Beza: "whom they were attending to." The Vulgate and Erasmus: "to whom they were listening." The Syriac: "they served him..." Tremellius and Bode: "and they were acquiescing in him." Render it "and they were obeying him." The Syriac word for "serve" is nothing other than the word for obedience, and it is used everywhere for hypakoē; from it comes the Syriac word for obedience, and "without obedience" for disobedience. The Syriac rightly understood the Greek not so much of attention of the ears as of the mind. The sense is that they clung to him with their minds, giving faith to his words, and so obeyed and complied with his teaching and commands. The reason is added: because for a long time he had struck them with amazement by his sorceries. The Arabic understood and translated it in exactly the same way: "and they were all obedient to him." Budaeus also understood Luke's phrase no differently, saying that proseichō sometimes means "to listen to, to obey," and he cites this very passage. On this, more may be seen in H. Stephanus, who rightly adds that the verb is also used of one who so observes someone that he places his hope and trust in him, which suits this passage very well. Likewise, what he adds from Budaeus, that the verb sometimes means to attach oneself to someone, to make oneself his follower, is also apt. Indeed there are places where the Seventy render the Hebrew dabaq, "to cleave," by this verb. This should not be rejected here, and neither should the rendering of the Syriac in the preceding verse, "and they were inclined towards him," which Tremellius fittingly rendered "and they were devoted to him."

units.la: VERS. 13. [Greek]. Vulg. stupens admirabatur. videtur legisse, [Greek]. ita sane Syrus, Arabs, & Æthiopicus. Etsi Æthiopici exigua hic ratio sit habenda, quia synonymis passim gaudet.
units.tr: VERS. 13. [Greek word]. The Vulgate: "astonished, he marvelled." It seems to have read the verb differently. So indeed the Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic. Yet the Ethiopic is of little weight here, since it everywhere delights in synonyms.

units.la: VERS. 15. [Greek], qui cum descendissent. sic Syr. quoque & Arabs. At Vulgatus, venissent, [Greek]. ut & Æthiopicus.
units.tr: VERS. 15. "who, when they had gone down" [οἵτινες καταβάντες]. So the Syriac also, and the Arabic. But the Vulgate has "had come," which the Ethiopic also has.

units.la: VERS. 16. [Greek]. Vulg. nondum enim in quemquam illorum supervenerat. Eras. & Beza, illapsus fuerat. Æthiopicus, descenderat. Syrus simpliciter erat. Arabs [Arabic], non erat delapsus super quemquam eorum, vel non researcherat aut manserat. utramque enim significationem habet vox Arabica, ut &
units.tr: VERS. 16. "For he had not yet fallen upon any of them" [Οὐδέπω γάρ ἦν ἐπʼ οὐδενὶ αὐτῶν]. The Vulgate: "For he had not yet come upon any of them." Erasmus and Beza: "had fallen upon." The Ethiopic: "had descended." The Syriac simply: "was." The Arabic: "had not fallen upon any of them," or "had not remained" or "had stayed," for the Arabic word has both meanings, as also

units.la: Syrorum [Hebrew], quo de Spiritu S. usus est Syrus pro ἐπιἐπίζ[?], Act. 10. 44. & 11. 15. alibi autem pro σκλωσὶ & κατασκλωσὶν, residere, habitare, Joh. 1. 14. Act. 2. 16. Plane sicut Hebraei de Spiritu S. & gloria Dei interdum utuntur [Hebrew] ἐπιπίζ, ut Ezech. 11. 5. interdum [Hebrew], ἐπισκώζ vel ἐμένε, ut Exod. 24. 16. ubi tamen LXX verterunt κατέλεξη. Adeo ut ex usu Hebraeorum, Syrorum & Arabum, ἐπιπνέων, καταζαίνων, μένων, καταπλωσὶν de Spiritu S. promiscuè usurpentur. Intelligitur autem, non Spiritus communis gratiae salvificae, sed donorum extraordinariorum. quod etsi jam pridem à viris doctis est observatum, illustrare tamen id paucis juvabit.
units.tr: the Syriac word, which the Syriac uses of the Holy Spirit for epipiptō, Acts 10:44 and 11:15, and elsewhere for katascēnoō and katasklōsin, meaning to settle, to dwell, John 1:14 and Acts 2:16. Just as the Hebrews also sometimes use of the Holy Spirit and the glory of God the word nafal, "to fall upon," as in Ezekiel 11:5, and sometimes shakhan or yashav, "to dwell" or "to remain," as in Exodus 24:16, where however the Seventy render katelesē. So that from the usage of the Hebrews, Syrians and Arabs, epipneōn, katoikōn, menōn and katapiptōn are used indiscriminately of the Holy Spirit. It is understood, however, not of the Spirit of common saving grace, but of extraordinary gifts. Although learned men have long observed this, it will help to illustrate it briefly.

units.la: Sciendum itaque ex usitato apud Hebraeos loquendi usu id esse petitum, quibus [Hebrew], Spiritus S. est Spiritus propheticus, qui & [Hebrew], καταπλωσὶς, habitatio ipsis dicebatur, [Hebrew], quia residebat super Prophetas, ut ait Elias in Thisbi ad verbum [Hebrew]. Etsi alii Hebraeorum distinguant [Hebrew] à [Hebrew], per illam intelligentes majestatem Dei sedentem inter Cherubim super arcam, per hunc praesentiam divinae gloriae in Prophetis. Utrumque fatentur cessasse in templo secundo. In fine Gemarae c. 1. in Joma f. 21. sic scribitur, Hagg. 1. 8. scribitur, [Hebrew], & nos legimus, [Hebrew]. defectus [Hebrew] indicat defectum quinque rerum in templo secundo, quae sunt [Hebrew] Arca, propitiatorium & Cherubim: ignis: praesentia majestatis Dei: Spiritus Sanctus: item Vrim & Thummim. Arca, propitiatorium & Cherubim rem unam dicunt. non quievit autem in ea majestas Dei, neque fuit Spiritus S. in Prophetis ab anno secundo Darii, & deinceps. credebant autem fore, ut per Messiam haec omnia restituerentur. Hinc phrases hae, Spiritus S. nondum erat, Joh. 7. 39. ne audivimus quidem an Spiritus S. sit, Act. 19. 2. & hoc loco, nondum in quemquam eorum illapsus fuerat Spiritus S. etsi jam in Christum credidissent, quod sine Spiritus S. praesentia & operatione fieri non poterat. Sed intelligitur Spiritus iste propheticus, qui ab initio templi secundi defecerat inter Judaeos, jam autem,& longe uberius restituebatur per J. Christum. Erat autem Vulgata quoque Hebraeorum sententia, Spiritum istum S. quem diximus non residere nisi in laetis hilaribusque mentibus. quare illud Gen. 45. 27. & revixit Spiritus Iacobi, quum nempe vitam gloriamque Josephi rescivisset, Onkelus interpretatur, & resedit Spiritus S. super Iacobum. in eandem sententiam Jonathan & resedit spiritus prophetiae, qui sublatus fuerat ab eo, quo tempore vendiderant Iosephum, reversusque est super Iacobum. Idem contigit hisce Samaritanis, in quos tum demum Spiritus S. est illapsus, quum jam fide in Christum, & manuum Apostolicarum impositione essent exhilarati.
units.tr: It must therefore be known that this expression is taken from the common usage of speech among the Hebrews, for whom the Holy Spirit is the prophetic Spirit, which was also called for them shekhinah, habitation, because it rested upon the prophets, as Elijah in Tishbi says, in the very words of the Hebrew. Yet some of the Hebrews distinguish shekhinah from yekarah, understanding by the latter the majesty of God sitting between the cherubim above the ark, and by the former the presence of the divine glory in the prophets. Both they confess ceased in the second temple. At the end of the Gemara on Yoma chapter 1, folio 21, it is written thus on Haggai 1:8: "it is written," and "we read," the defect indicates the lack of five things in the second temple: the ark, the mercy seat and the cherubim; the fire; the presence of the majesty of God; the Holy Spirit; likewise the Urim and Thummim. They say the ark, the mercy seat and the cherubim are one thing. Moreover, the majesty of God did not rest in it, nor was the Holy Spirit in the prophets from the second year of Darius onward. They believed, however, that all these things would be restored through the Messiah. Hence these phrases: "the Holy Spirit was not yet," John 7:39; "we have not even heard whether the Holy Spirit is," Acts 19:2; and in this passage, "the Holy Spirit had not yet fallen upon any of them," although they had already believed in Christ, which could not happen without the presence and operation of the Holy Spirit. But that Spirit is understood to be the prophetic Spirit, which had failed among the Jews from the beginning of the second temple, but was now being restored, and far more abundantly, through Jesus Christ. Indeed the common opinion of the Hebrews was also this: that the Spirit we have mentioned rests only in joyful and cheerful minds. Hence in Genesis 45:27, "and the spirit of Jacob revived," when he had learned of the life and glory of Joseph, Onkelos translates, "and the Holy Spirit rested upon Jacob." Jonathan to the same effect: "and the spirit of prophecy, which had been taken from him at the time they sold Joseph, returned and rested upon Jacob." The same happened to these Samaritans, upon whom the Holy Spirit fell only when they had already been gladdened by faith in Christ and by the laying on of the apostles' hands.

units.la: VERS. 18. Quum autem consspexisset Simon &c. Lubet hic referre, quae de Simone hoc tradidit Theodoritus Episcopus Cyri in haereseon Epitome. Verba ejus Latine sic reddidimus. Simon Samaritanus Magus primus haeresεon autor extitit. Hic Gitta oriundus, quod Samaria est oppidum, & praestigiis quammaximè valens, primum quidem miraculis quae edebat persuasit multis se sequi, divinamque quandam potentiam appellare. Ubi vero postea Apostolos vidit vera reapse & divina praestare miracula, suisque affectis spiritus gratiam largiri, eandem postulavit ab ipsis potestatem impetrare. postquam autem magnus Petrus pessimam ejus mentem deprehendisset, & resipiscentia pharmacis sanatu difficillima animi vulnera curare jussisset, protinus ille ad pristinam rerum malarum molitionem rediit. reliqueque, quae jam salutaria femina exceperat, Samariae, ad eos excurrit qui nondum ab Apostolis exculti essent, ut fascinationibus suis captu faciles seducens, suisque alligans fabulis, à suscipiendis S. Apo-
units.tr: VERS. 18. But when Simon saw, &c. It is worth recording here what Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus, handed down about this Simon in his Epitome of Heresies. We have rendered his words into Latin as follows: Simon the Samaritan magician was the first author of heresies. A native of Gitta, which is a town in Samaria, and very powerful in sorcery, he at first persuaded many, by the miracles he performed, to follow him, and he called himself some divine power. But when he afterwards saw the Apostles truly and divinely working miracles, and bestowing the grace of the Spirit on their followers, he asked them to grant him the same power. But after the great Peter had detected his wicked mind, and had ordered that the wounds of his soul, most difficult to heal, be treated with the medicines of repentance, he at once returned to his former evil designs. And he ran off to those in Samaria, and to those who had not yet been trained by the Apostles, to seduce them by his enchantments, capturing the credulous and binding them with his fables, and to turn them away from accepting the holy Apo-

units.la: S. Apostolorum dogmatis averteret. Sed divina gratia magnum Petrum adversus hujus furorem armavit, qui insequens eum, abominandam ejus doctrinam, nebula cujusdam instar & caliginis, dissipavit, verseque lucis radios protulit. Homo tamen infelicissimus, etsi palam convictus, adversari veritati non destitit, donec sub imperio Claudii Caesaris Romam venit, ubi usque adeo Romanos praestigiis suis stupefecit, ut & area columna eum decorarent. At delatus eo D. Petrus denudavit eum rursus aliis sallacia. quum enim ad miraculorum certamen eum tandem provocasset, quidque inter divinam gratiam & praestigias interfit ostendisset, intuentibus omnibus Romanis, ex altissimo eum loco vi precum suarum precipitem egit, ac miraculi spectatores ad salutem adduxit.
units.tr: stles' doctrine. But divine grace armed the great Peter against his madness, and he pursued him and dispersed his abominable teaching as if it were a cloud and a darkness, and brought forth the rays of the true light. The most unhappy man, however, though openly convicted, did not cease to oppose the truth, until under the rule of the Emperor Claudius he came to Rome, where he so astonished the Romans with his sorceries that they even adorned him with a statue in the area. But Peter, having been brought there, stripped him bare of his deceits once more. For when at last he challenged him to a contest of miracles, and had shown what lies between divine grace and sorcery, all the Romans looking on, he cast him headlong from a great height by the power of his prayers, and brought the spectators of the miracle to salvation.

units.la: SIMONIS HAERESIS.
units.tr: SIMON'S HERESY

units.la: Hic, fabulam ejusmodi commentus, infinitam quandam supponebat potentiam, quam Universitatis rerum radicem vocabat, atque Ignem appellabat, cui duplicem inesse operationem ajebat, manifestam unam, alteram latentem. mundum autem esse ingenitum: genitum vero ex manifesta Ignis operatione, ex qua primum tres syzygia sint pramissa, quas etiam radices appellabat. Et primam quidem nominabat, mentem & ingenium. alteram, vocem & intentionem. tertiam, ratiocinationem & cogitationem. seipsum vero infinitam nuncupabat potentiam, qui Iudaeis ut Filius apparuisset, ad Samaritanos ut Pater venisset, inter reliquas Gentes ut Spiritus S. degeret. Aliam porro quandam, in lecto stantem foeminam cognomine Helenam, doniesticam sibi fecit, quam primam suam intentionem esse ajebat, & matrem Universitatis rerum appellabat, per quam & Angelos & Archangelos fecisset. Ab angelis conditum esse mundum, qui postea eum, Helena ipsi invidentes, apud seipsos detinuerint, quod ejus nollent opera vocari. atque idcirco eam in multa muliebria corpora introduxerint, in illam etiam Helenam, ob quam Trojanum contigit bellum, ob hanc eandem se quoque descendisse, ut & illam ab injectis vinculis liberaret, & hominibus per sui cognitionem salutem largiretur. descendisse autem mutata forma, ne ab Angelis res creatas administrantibus agnosceretur. In Iudaea apparuisse ut hominem, quum homo non esset, & passum, quum nequaquam fit passus. Prophetas Angelorum ministros esse factos, quorum affectas esse noluit, quotquot in se crederent, nec legum horrere minas, sed facere tanquam liberos quacunque vellent.non enim per bona opera obtenturos salutem, sed per gratiam. quamobrem hujus sectae homines quamvis audebant petulantiam, variisque utebantur incantationibus, amatorias fabricantes illecebras, aliaque praestigiis propria, veluti divina obeuntes mysteria. Illius imaginem forma Iovis fabricabant, Helena specie Palladis. His suffiebant, & libabant, velutique Deos adorabant, Simonianos seipsos appellantes. Ex amarissima hac radice pullularunt Cleobani, Dositheani, Gortheni, Masbothei, Adrianista, Eutycheta, Kanista. qui tamen exiguas solummodo impia istius haereseos mutationes commenti, pauxillum durarunt, perpetuaque oblivioni sunt traditi.Hactenus ille de monstro isto hominis.
units.tr: Having devised a fable of this kind, he posited an infinite power, which he called the root of the universe, and named Fire, which he said had a twofold operation, one manifest and the other hidden. The world, he said, was unbegotten, but was begotten from the manifest operation of the Fire, from which first three pairs were sent forth, which he also called roots. The first he named mind and understanding; the second, voice and intention; the third, reasoning and thought. He himself he called the infinite power, who had appeared to the Jews as the Son, had come to the Samaritans as the Father, and dwelt among the other nations as the Holy Spirit. He also made for himself a certain woman standing in a brothel, surnamed Helen, whom he said was his first intention, and called the mother of the universe, through whom he had made both angels and archangels. The world, he said, was made by the angels, who afterwards, envying Helen, kept her among themselves, since they did not want his works to be called by his name. For this reason they sent her into many female bodies, including that Helen on whose account the Trojan war came about. For her sake he too had descended, both to free her from the chains that had been put upon her and to grant salvation to men through the knowledge of himself. He had descended, moreover, in a changed form, so that he would not be recognised by the angels who administered created things. He appeared in Judaea as a man, though he was not a man, and suffered, though he by no means suffered. The prophets had become ministers of the angels, whose commands he did not wish to be obeyed by all who believed in him; nor did they need to fear the threats of the laws, but might do as free men whatever they wished, for it is not through good works that they would obtain salvation, but through grace. Therefore the men of this sect, however much they were bold in their wantonness, used various incantations, fashioning love charms and other tricks proper to sorcery, as if performing divine mysteries. They made an image of him in the form of Jupiter, and of Helen in the likeness of Pallas. They burned incense to these and poured libations, and worshipped them as gods, calling themselves Simonians. From this most bitter root sprang the Cleobians, Dositheans, Gortheni, Masbotheans, Adrianists, Eutychetans and Kanists, who, though they devised only small variations of that impious heresy, lasted a little while and were handed down to perpetual oblivion. Thus far that writer concerning this monster of a man.

units.la: VERS. 21.
units.tr: VERS. 21.

units.la: Non est tibi portio neque sors, ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τούτῳ. Syrus & Arabs in hac fide. Æthiopicus, ob hunc sermonem tuum, quasi ἀλλ᾽ ἐν λόγῳ τούτῳ. quod prorsus non laudo. Vulgatus, in hoc sermone. Erasmus, in hac ratione. Beza melius, in hoc negocio. & recte annotat דבר Hebraeis de quavis re dici. Sic λόγῳ pro re, Rom. 9. 28. & alibi. hinc interpretor, in hac re, nempe in dono Spiritus S. Tu potestatem tibi tribui cupis, etiam aliis donandi Spiritum S. Absit. nam ne ipse quidem portionem ullam habes in hac re.
units.tr: Thou hast neither part nor lot in this matter, ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τούτῳ [en tō logō toutō]. The Syriac and Arabic have in this faith; the Ethiopic, because of this word of yours, as if reading ἀλλ᾽ ἐν λόγῳ τούτῳ [all' en logō toutō], which I do not at all approve. The Vulgate has in this word; Erasmus, in this reasoning; Beza more aptly, in this business, and he rightly notes that the Hebrews use דבר [davar] of any matter. So λόγος is used for a thing at Romans 9:28 and elsewhere. Hence I render it in this matter, namely, in the gift of the Holy Spirit. You wish power to be attributed to yourself, to give the Holy Spirit to others also. Far be it. For you do not even have any part in this matter yourself.

units.la: VERS. 22.
units.tr: VERSE 22.

units.la: Ἡ ἐπίνοια τῆς καρδίας σου. Vulg. & Eras. Cogitatio cordis tui. Beza, machinatio. Hezychius, ἐπίνοια, ἐπιμελέτημα, studium. sic recte vertas, ut remittatur tibi studium cordis tui, id est, id quod cor tuum intendit & molitur.Drusius in Praeteritis ait Hebraice dici חשבון, quae Graecis Interpretibus ἐνοια & ἐπίνοια. ἐνοια pro מזמה legō, sed semper in bonum.at per ἐπίνοιαν nusquam ab illis vocem Hebræam redditam invenio. Interim non nego, quin hoc loco vafrum commentum hac voce significetur. unde Syrus ܥܩܪܐ, fraudulentia cordis tui. & eodem sensu Arabs ܡܟܪ. Æthiopicus ܚܠܝܢ, cogitatio cordis tui mala.
units.tr: The Greek ἐπίνοια of your heart. The Vulgate and Erasmus render it the thought of your heart. Beza has contrivance. Hesychius glosses ἐπίνοια as ἐπιμελέτημα, study. So you may rightly translate, that the study of your heart be forgiven you, that is, what your heart intends and plots. Drusius, in his notes on the Prophets, says that the Hebrew is חשבון, which the Greek translators render ἔνοια and ἐπίνοια. I read ἔνοια for מזמה, but always in a good sense. I find nowhere, however, that the Greek translators rendered the Hebrew word by ἐπίνοια. Meanwhile I do not deny that a crafty scheme is meant by this word here. Hence the Syriac has fraudulence of your heart ('iqra d-lbabak), and in the same sense the Arabic has makr. The Ethiopic has the evil thought of your heart (ḥalīn).

units.la: V e r s. 23. Εἰς χάς χολῶ πηγάς. Syrus ܟܠܝܬܐ ܠܒܐ. Trem. & Boder. in Paris. in felle enim amaro. fel Syris ܠܒܐ dicitur Matth. 27. 34. ut & Arab. ܡܪܪܐ, qua voce hic usus est Arabs de Simone. Hebræis etiam מרה. כבד autem Hebræis, ut & ܟܒܕܐ Arabibus hepar est. unde & hoc loco Boder.in Reg. siquidem in hepate amaritudinis. nec aliam significationem exhibet Lexic. Syr. Arab. ubi ܠܒܐ, vertitur ܟܒܕܐ, hepar asini sylvestris. sic & Ferrarius ܟܒܕܐ, jecur, hepar, f. g. & hunc ipsum locum citat. ubi miror scribi per vocalem primam, quum omnes editiones hoc loco habeant vocalem secundam. quæ interpretatio si recta est, videtur Syrus per πικρίας, amaritudinis intellexisse fel, per χολῶ autem receptaculum istius amaritudinis sive fellis, nempe vesiculam & ipsum hepar quo ea continetur. quod non adeo ineptum videri debet.nam & H. Stephanus ex Polluce adfert χολῶ etiam dici τὸ χοληδόχον ἀγγεῖον, vasculum quo bilis aut fel continetur. vel fortassis ܟܒܕܐ, jecur est. at ut hic scribitur ܟܒܕܐ, fel. exspecto ut hic & alibi à doctioribus erudiar. Textus autem Græcus sic habet, εἰς χάς χολῶ πικρίας, ἡ συνδέσμου ἀδικίας ὀρῶ σε ὄντα. Interpretes accipiunt εις pro εν, in. quod fateor alibi necessarium esse. an hic sit, dubito. potest enim εις Hebraismum continere, qualis est Esa. 1. 31. והיה החסן לנעורת ופעלו לניצוץ, & erit fortis in stupam, id est, stupa, & opus ejus in scintillam, id est, scintilla. qualia sunt in N. T. ero tibi εις πατέρα, in patrem, id est, pater, & tu mihi eris εις υἱόν, in filium, id est filius. Sic hoc loco, Fel enim amarissimum, & colligationem iniquitatis video te esse. εἰς φαλλοτέρως sane dicit Lucas, eum esse merum fel amaritudinis, quam in felle: & meram colligationem, quam Vulg. in obligatione, Eras. in colligatione, Beza in nexu iniquitatis. alludi autem arbitror, quoad prius membrum, ad Deut. 32. 32. עַנְבֵי, LXX ἡ χεφυλὴ αὐτῶν χεφυλὴ χολῆς, βότρυς πικρίας αὐτῶν. hinc χολῶ πικρίας junxit Lucas. vel ex Deut. 29. 18. quoad alterum membrum, ad Esa. 58. 6. פתח חרצות רשע, LXX, λύε πᾶσα σύνδεσμον ἀδικίας.
units.tr: VERSE 23. Εἰς χολὴν πικρίας καὶ σύνδεσμον ἀδικίας ὁρῶ σε ὄντα. The Syriac has kelīṯā lebā. Tremellius and Bodin, in the Paris edition, have for in bitter gall. In the Syriac, gall is called lebā, as in Matthew 27:34, and the Arabic has marra, the word the Arabic version uses there of Simon. The Hebrew has מרה (marah). But the Hebrew כבד, like the Arabic kabda, means liver. Hence in this passage Bodin in the Kings has for in the liver of bitterness. Nor does the Syriac-Arabic lexicon give any other meaning, where lebā is rendered kabda, the liver of the wild ass. Ferrarius likewise gives kabda as liver, gall, etc., and cites this very passage. It surprises me that he writes it with the first vowel, since all the editions here have the second. If this interpretation is right, the Syriac seems to have understood by bitterness the gall, and by gall the receptacle of that bitterness or gall, namely the bladder and the liver in which it is contained. That should not seem so absurd. For H. Stephanus, citing Pollux, also notes that χολὴ is used for τὸ χοληδόχον ἀγγεῖον, the little vessel in which bile or gall is held. Or perhaps kabda is the liver, but as it is written here it means gall. I hope to be taught by more learned men here and elsewhere. The Greek text reads, εἰς χολὴν πικρίας, καὶ σύνδεσμον ἀδικίας ὁρῶ σε ὄντα. The translators take εἰς for ἐν, in. I grant that this is necessary elsewhere, but I doubt it is here. For εἰς can carry a Hebraism, such as in Isaiah 1:31, והיה החסן לנעורת ופעלו לניצוץ, and the strong shall be as tow, that is, tow, and his work as a spark, that is, a spark. Such are the New Testament expressions ero tibi εἰς πατέρα, I will be to you a father, that is, a father, and tu mihi eris εἰς υἱόν, you will be to me a son, that is, a son. So here: For I see you to be in bitter gall and in the bond of iniquity. Luke certainly says, in the form εἰς χολὴν πικρίας, that he is pure gall of bitterness, rather than in gall. And he says a bond where the Vulgate has in obligatione, Erasmus in colligatione, and Beza in nexu iniquitatis. I think the first clause alludes to Deuteronomy 32:32, עַנְבֵי, where the Seventy have ἡ χερσαία αὐτῶν χερσαία χολῆς, βότρυς πικρίας αὐτῶν, whence Luke joined χολὴ and πικρία. The second clause may come from Deuteronomy 29:18, or from Isaiah 58:6, פתח חרצות רשע, which the Seventy render λῦε πᾶσα σύνδεσμον ἀδικίας.

units.la: VERS. 26. Surge & vade κατὰ μεσημβρίαν, Vulgatus, Syrus, Eras. Beza, versus Meridiem. Arabs & Æthiopicus, tempore Meridiei. Illi quò, hi quando jubeatur ire doceri existimarunt. καὶ sæpe de tempore usurpari, & respondere quæstioni quando, vide 2 Tim. 4. 1. Apoc. 22. 2. Act. 27. 27.
units.tr: VERSE 26. Arise and go κατὰ μεσημβρίαν: the Vulgate, the Syriac and Erasmus have towards the south, and Beza towards the south. The Arabic and Ethiopic have at the time of noon. The former thought the text taught where he was to go, the latter when he was to go. καὶ is often used of time and answers the question when; see 2 Timothy 4:1, Revelation 22:2, Acts 27:27.

units.la: VERS. 27. Εὐνοῦχος. Hebraicè סריס. etiam uxorato tribuitur, ut Potipharo. itaque non castratum semper designat. non raro à Chaldæo vertitur רבא, magnas, princeps. In plurali רבין, principes. LXX δυνάσται, Jer. 34. 19. Syris sane non à corporis vitio, sed ab officio dicuntur ܪܒܐ, fidi, quorum fidei res principum sive publicæ sive privatæ committebantur. singulare absolutum non est ܗܝܡܢܐ, fidelis qui credit, sed ܗܝܡܢܐ, fidus, cui creditur. Eunucho huic nomen fuisse Indich, testatur apud Damianum à Goes Zaga Zabo regis Æthiopum legatus. verba ejus sunt: Nos Nos ferme prius cateris Christianis omnibus, baptismum ab Eunucho Candacis regina Aethiopia, cui nomen erat Iudith, accepimus. Addit autem Æthiopicus Interpres, quod nulla exemplaria habent, fuisse hunc Eunuchum u הנר לתו מנרה, praefectum urbis Gaza. Plinius l. 6. c. 29. docet, Candacem fuisse nomen reginæ, quod multis annis ad reginas transierit. Huic quidem proprium fuisse nomen Lacasa. Catalogus regum Æthiopiæ, quem Marianus Reatinus Grammaticæ suæ Æthiopicæ subjunxit, asserit. etsi perexigua catalogo isti, quippe fabulis ineptiisque refertissimo, fides adhibenda sit.
units.tr: VERSE 27. Εὐνοῦχος. In Hebrew סריס. It is given even to a married man, as to Potiphar, so it does not always designate a castrated man. Often the Chaldee renders it רבא, great, prince. In the plural it is רבין, princes. The Seventy render it δυνάσται, Jeremiah 34:19. The Syriac word for it, ḥaymānā, is applied not to a bodily defect but to an office: it means faithful, those to whom the affairs of princes, whether public or private, were entrusted. The absolute singular is not faithful who believes, but faithful, to whom trust is given. Zaga Zabo, ambassador of the king of the Ethiopians, testifies in Damian à Goes that this eunuch had the name Indich. His words are: We almost before all other Christians received baptism from the eunuch of Queen Candace of Ethiopia, whose name was Judith. The Ethiopic interpreter adds, though no manuscript has it, that this eunuch was the prefect of the city of Gaza. Pliny, Book 6, chapter 29, teaches that Candace was the name of the queen, which for many years passed to the queens. Marianus Reatinus, in his Ethiopic grammar, asserts that the proper name of this queen was Lacasa. Yet little faith is to be put in that catalogue of kings, which is stuffed full of fables and nonsense.

units.la: VERS. 29. Κολλήθητι τῷ ἀνδρὶ. Vulg. & Eras. adjunge te ad currum istum. Beza, proximè adjungitor. Syrus ܕܒܩ, adhære, quasi affixus & agglutinatus currui. id proprie valet vox Græca. Hebraice דָּבַק לְמַרְכְּבָה. eo nempe sensu, quo Booz dicebat Ruthæ, c. 2. 8. ὥδε κολλήθητι μετὰ τῶν παιδισκῶν μου. quorum sensus non tantum est, adjunge te hic puellis meis, sed adhære eis, maneas adjuncta, ne ab eis discedas. Ita hoc loco sensus est, maneas adjunctus currui, euntem comitare, ne ab eo discedas. malim vertere, sequere currum, quam adjunge te currui. Sicut Ruth. 1. 8. דְּבַק, Ruth autem adhæsit ei, LXX ἐκολλήθη αὐτῇ. At rectissime Syrus & cum eo Arabs ܠܡܩܪܒܐ, adhære currui. sic & Æthiopicus, adhære huic currui, vel sequere hunc currum. alibi enim pro κολλᾶσθαι, ut Luc. 10. 11. de pulvere adhærente pedibus, alibi pro ἀντικολλᾶσθαι usurpatur. ab Hebr. תלה, suspendit, quasi dicas, suspensum adhærere.
units.tr: VERSE 29. Κολλήθητι τῷ ἅρματι. The Vulgate and Erasmus have join yourself to that chariot. Beza has draw near and join yourself. The Syriac has dabbaq, cling, as if fixed and glued to the chariot. That is the proper sense of the Greek word. In Hebrew it is דָּבַק לְמַרְכָּבָה, in the sense in which Boaz said to Ruth (Ruth 2:8), ὧδε κολλήθητι μετὰ τῶν παιδισκῶν μου. Its sense is not merely join yourself here with my maidens, but cling to them, remain joined, and do not leave them. So here the sense is remain joined to the chariot, accompany it as it goes, and do not leave it. I would rather translate follow the chariot than join yourself to the chariot. Compare Ruth 1:8, דְּבַק, Ruth clung to her, which the Seventy render ἐκολλήθη αὐτῇ. The Syriac, and with it the Arabic, render it most accurately as cling to the chariot. So too the Ethiopic, cling to this chariot, or follow this chariot. For elsewhere the Greek κολλᾶσθαι is used, as in Luke 10:11 of dust clinging to the feet, and elsewhere for ἀντικολλᾶσθαι. The Hebrew תלה, hang, is the origin, as if you were to say that a thing hangs and clings.

units.la: VERS. 32. Ἡ ἡ ἀνεωχθεῖσα τῆς γραφῆς. Erasm. Argumentum autem Scripturæ. Melius Vulg. & Beza, locus autem Scripturæ. Quod autem Hebraice id שִׁיר dici velit, non abs re videtur improbare Cl. Drusius, tum quod sectio Prophetica non diceretur שִׁירָה, sed הַמְּשׁוּרָה, tum quod שִׁיר magnam dice- rct. ret sectionem, quales quinquaginta tres universo Pentateucho comprehenduntur. פרשה potius dicerem, quae capitum, minorumque sectionum appellatio est. aut פרשה potius, quo nomine Syrus hic usus est, significatque paucam, non modo quae unum versum finit, sed & quae integram sententiam, ubi certae cujusdam materiae complexio continetur, & ab aliis abscinditur. Estque idem quod Arabs optime vocavit ﺍﻟﻔﺼﻞ ﺍﻟﻜﺘﺎﺏ, sectio Scripturae. Exempli gratia, primum caput Matthaei habet duo ﻓﺼﻞ, sectiones: prima continet genealogiam Christi, altera ejus nativitatem. tales sectiones Euangelium Matthaei Arabicum habet centum & unam. Graeci vocant τμήματα, suntque brevia quaedam capita, secundum materiam distincta.
units.tr: VERSE 32. Ἡ δὲ περιοχὴ τῆς γραφῆς. Erasmus has the argument of Scripture. The Vulgate and Beza render better, the passage of Scripture. As for the Hebrew word that the Greek is meant to render, which is שִׁיר, the learned Drusius seems right to reject it, both because a prophetic section would not be called שִׁירָה but הַמְּשׁוּרָה, and because שִׁיר would mean a large section, such as the fifty-three into which the whole Pentateuch is divided. I would rather say פרשה, which is the name for chapters and smaller sections. Or rather פרשה, the word the Syriac uses here, means a small section, not only one that ends a verse but any complete sentence where a certain matter is contained and separated from others. It is what the Arabic aptly called the section of Scripture (al-faṣl al-kitāb). For example, the first chapter of Matthew has two sections (faṣl): the first contains the genealogy of Christ, the second his birth. The Arabic Gospel of Matthew has one hundred and one such sections. The Greeks call them τμήματα, and they are short chapters, divided according to subject.

units.la: VERS. 33. Ἐν τῇ ταπεινώσει αὐτοῦ ἡ κρίσις αὐτοῦ ἤρθη. Syrus illud ἐν τῇ ταπεινώσει αὐτοῦ junxit praecedenti versui, ut & Aethiopicus pro caeteris habet ܒܬܚܬܝܬܐ ܕܝܢܐ, ex inclusione & ex judicio abductus est. nempe ad verbum expressit illa Prophetae בעיניו משפטו נשא. sed separare non debuit, quae LXX Interpretes, quos ad amussim secutus est Lucas, conjunxere. ταπείνωσις, humilitas, est illa depressio qua in sepulchrum detrusus, veluti in carcere conclusus ac detentus fuit. illud valet Hebraeorum סגר, conclusio, detentio. Variarunt autem constructionem, quasi scriberetur מעצר משפט נלקח. sed nulla sensus variatione: sive enim dicas, sublatus est e judicio, sive judicium ejus sublatum est, idem dicis. Aethiopicus, sublatus est in judicio suo.
units.tr: VERSE 33. Ἐν τῇ ταπεινώσει αὐτοῦ ἡ κρίσις αὐτοῦ ἤρθη. The Syriac joins the words ἐν τῇ ταπεινώσει αὐτοῦ to the preceding verse. The Ethiopic too has, in place of the rest, taken away from confinement and from judgment. It has expressed word for word those words of the prophet, בעיניו משפטו נשא, but it should not have separated what the Seventy translators joined, and which Luke followed exactly. ταπείνωσις, humiliation, is that depression by which he was thrust into the tomb, as if shut up and held in prison. This corresponds to the Hebrew סגר, confinement, detention. They varied the construction, as if it were written מעצר משפט נלקח, but without any change of sense. Whether you say he was taken away from judgment or his judgment was taken away, you say the same thing. The Ethiopic has he was taken away in his judgment.

units.la: VERS. 36. Ἡλθον ἐπὶ τὴν ὕδωρ. Venerunt ad aquam quandam. De hoc loco sic Hieronymus de Locis Hebraicis. Betsur, in tribu Iuda, sive Benjamin, & est hodie Bethsoron vicus euntibus nobis ab Aelia Chebron in vicesimo lapide, juxta quem fons ad radices montis ebulliens ab eadem in qua gignitur sorbetur humo. Et Apostolorum Acta referunt, Eunuchum Candacis Regina in hoc esse baptizatum à Philippo. Hactenus ille. Hebraicè dicitur בית צור, domus rupis. ostenditurque in mapa Judaica inter Jerusalem & sepulchrum Rachelis, Meridiem versus vergens.
units.tr: VERS. 36. They came to a certain water [Ἡλθον ἐπὶ τὴν ὕδωρ]. On this place Jerome writes thus in his Book of Hebrew Places: "Betsur, in the tribe of Judah or of Benjamin, is today Bethsoron, a village on the twentieth milestone as we go from Aelia to Hebron. Beside it a spring bubbles up at the foot of the mountain and is swallowed by the same ground from which it rises. The Acts of the Apostles report that the eunuch of Queen Candace was baptized here by Philip." Thus far Jerome. In Hebrew it is called בית צור, house of rock. It is shown on the Judaean map between Jerusalem and the tomb of Rachel, tending towards the south.

units.la: Εἰς Ἀζώτον. Sic LXX & Josephus vocant אַשְׁדּוֹד, Asdod Philistæorum. de qua Benjamin in Itinerario edit. Leyd. pag. 51. ומשם ב' פרסאות לפלשים היא אשר לפלשתים ... הוא אשר בה יהודים ... inde (nempe à Jafne) sunt duo parasangæ ad Palmis, quæ est ipsa Asdod Philistæorum jam vastata. nec est ibi ullus Judæus. Azoto profectus est Philippus Cæsaream, quæ urbs quoque est ad mare Mediterraneum, ante Turris Stratonis vocata, sed quam Herodes restauratam vehementerque ornatam, in gratiam Cæsaris Cæsaream vocavit. vide Jos. de bell. Jud. l. 1. c. 16. de hac urbe sic Benjamin in Itinerario, ומשם שמה פרסאות לשיריא היא נר אשר לפלשתים ושם כמו עשרה יהודים וסתים כותיים הם היהודים השומרונים הנקראים שמרטניס והיא עיר יפה ... inde sex parasangis abest Sifaria, dicta quondam Gad Philistæorum: ubi decem circiter Judæi, & Cuthæi ducenti. Hi sunt Judæi Schomronita, qui vulgo Samaritani dicuntur. urbs ipsa pulcherrima est ac elegantissima, ad mare sita, structura Imperatoris ac regis Cæsaris, & vocavit nomen ejus Cæsaream. ubi observandum, שיריא, Sifaria corruptam vocem esse ex Cæsarea. deinde errare Benjaminem, quod Cæsari tribuat structuram urbis, quæ Herodi ascribenda. multo autem magis, quod hanc antiquam Philistæorum Gad (pro ר scribendum erat ג) esse asserat. Est enim Gath Philistæorum prope Bethsemes in tribu Dan, quam sequitur Septentrionem versus tribus Ephraim, hanc tribus Manassis, in cujus extremo est Cæsarea. Sic passim solet, etiam turpissimè hallucinari Benjamin. pulcherrimam autem & elegantissimam fuisse, testatur quoque Josephus allato loco. qui & lib. 3. c. 14. ait, esse Judææ maximam civitatem, & quæ majorem incolarum partem Græcos haberet.
units.tr: Into Azotus [Εἰς Ἀζώτον]. The Seventy and Josephus so call אַשְׁדּוֹד, Ashdod of the Philistines. Benjamin, in his Itinerary (Leiden edition, p. 51), speaks of it: "From there (namely from Jaffa) it is two parasangs to Palmis, which is Ashdod of the Philistines, now laid waste. No Jew lives there." (Hebrew: ומשם ב' פרסאות לפלשים היא אשר לפלשתים ... הוא אשר בה יהודים). Philip set out from Azotus to Caesarea, a city also on the Mediterranean, formerly called the Tower of Straton, but which Herod rebuilt and splendidly adorned, and in honour of Caesar named Caesarea. See Josephus, Jewish War 1.16. Of this city Benjamin says in his Itinerary: "From there six parasangs away is Sifaria, once called Gad of the Philistines, where about ten Jews and two hundred Cuthaeans live. These are the Jews of Shomron, commonly called Samaritans. The city itself is most beautiful and elegant, situated by the sea, built by the Emperor and king Caesar, and he called its name Caesarea." (Hebrew: ומשם שמה פרסאות לשיריא היא נר אשר לפלשתים ושם כמו עשרה יהודים וסתים כותיים הם היהודים השומרונים הנקראים שמרטניס והיא עיר יפה). Here it should be noted that שיריא, Sifaria, is a corrupted word from Caesarea. Next, Benjamin errs in ascribing the building of the city to Caesar, when it should be ascribed to Herod. Much more does he err in asserting that this is the ancient Gad of the Philistines (for ר should have been written as ג). Gath of the Philistines lies near Beth-shemesh in the tribe of Dan, which is followed northward by the tribe of Ephraim; then comes the tribe of Manasseh, at whose far end is Caesarea. Benjamin often errs in this way, and even very shamefully. That it was most beautiful and elegant Josephus also attests in the passage cited. In book 3, chapter 14, he says that it was the largest city of Judaea, and that it had a majority of Greek inhabitants.
