units.la: VERS. 1. Saulus autem adhuc, ἐμπνέων ἀπειλῆς καὶ φόνου, Syrus & Arabs, plenus minarum. quasi pro ἐμπνέων legissent ἐμπνέως. aut existimarunt, metaphoram desumtam ab eo qui repletus spirat crebro & anhelat. Est autem ἐμπνέων ἀπειλῆς constructio, qualis Jos. 10. 40. καὶ πᾶν ἐμπνέον ζωῆς ἐξωλόθρευσαν, & omne spirans vitam exterminarunt. Petiit autem literas Damascum ferendas ad synagogas. Quanta Judæorum frequentia Damasci fuerit, ex eo colligi potest, quod Josephus de bel. Jud. l. 2. c. 25. narret, sub Nerone Damascenos in sua urbe decem Judæorum millia, quos in publicis thermis collectos forte habebant, inermes oppressisse & trucidasse. Testatur Benjamin in Itinerario, suo tempore fuisse adhuc Damasci tria ferme Israëlitarum millia, atque inter eos תלמידי חכמים, discipulos sapientum, id est, Pharisæos, qui oralem legem amplectentes, ac sapientum explicationes institutaque tenentes, discipuli sapientum audiebant. præterea ducentos קראים ex Karæis, qui neglectis traditionibus soli Scripturæ adhærebant. itemque Cuthæos sive Samaritanos quadringentos, qui pacem quidem inter se colerent, connubia autem non jungerent. De urbis autem situ conditioneque qui velit, legat eundem Benjaminem. Conditorem ejus fuisse Vsem ע Arami filium, Semi nepotem, testatur Josephus Antiq. l. 1. c. 7. & Hieron. in Quæst. in Genesin, ubi Semi posteritatem enumerat. at paulo post agens de Damasco Eliezere Abrahami verna, addit, Ab hoc ajunt Damascum & conditam, & nuncupatam fuisse. Interpretatur autem דמשק, nunc sanguinis poculum, nunc sanguinem bibens. à □ꞁ sanguis & ִׁ bibit. memoranda ejus sunt, & huc pertinentia verba in Commentar. ad Ezech. cap. 28. Si Damascus, inquit, interpretatur sanguinem bibens, & Hebræorum vera traditio est, campum in quo intersectus est Abel à parricida Cain fuisse in Damasco: unde & locus hoc insignitus vocabulo fit: juste & Paulus post interfectionem Stephani, primi in Christo martyris, perrexit Damascum, ut credentes in Christo duceret vinctos Hierusalem. ut scilicet eodem in loco erga Abelis imitatores Cainis imitaretur opera. alibi autem ait, à quibusdam interpretari sanguinem cilicii, à □ & ִׁ.
units.tr: VERS. 1. Saul, however, still breathing threats and slaughter [ἐμπνέων ἀπειλῆς καὶ φόνου], the Syriac and the Arabic have full of threats, as if they had read ἐμπνέως for ἐμπνέων, or they thought the metaphor was taken from one who, filled up, breathes often and gasps. The construction ἐμπνέων ἀπειλῆς is like that in Joshua 10.40, καὶ πᾶν ἐμπνέον ζωῆς ἐξωλόθρευσαν, and they utterly destroyed everything that breathed life. He asked for letters to be carried to the synagogues at Damascus. How numerous the Jews were at Damascus can be inferred from Josephus, Jewish War 2.25, who relates that under Nero the Damascenes slaughtered ten thousand unarmed Jews in their own city, whom they had perhaps gathered together in the public baths. Benjamin, in his Itinerary, testifies that in his time there were still at Damascus about three thousand Israelites, and among them תלמידי חכמים, disciples of the wise, that is, Pharisees, who embraced the oral law and held to the explanations and institutions of the wise, and heard the teachers. Besides these there were two hundred קראים (Karaites), who, neglecting the traditions, adhered to Scripture alone, and four hundred Cuthaeans or Samaritans, who kept peace among themselves but did not intermarry. Whoever wishes to know about the site and condition of the city may read Benjamin again. Josephus, Antiquities 1.7, and Jerome in the Questions on Genesis, where he lists the posterity of Shem, testify that its founder was Uz (ע), son of Aram and grandson of Shem. But a little later, speaking of Eliezer, Abraham's servant, from Damascus, Jerome adds: "From him, they say, Damascus was both founded and named." The name דמשק is interpreted now as cup of blood and now as drinking blood, from דם blood and שקה drinks. Worth remembering are the words on this subject in his commentary on Ezekiel 28: "If Damascus is interpreted as drinking blood," he says, "and the true tradition of the Hebrews holds that the field in which Abel was slain by the murderer Cain was in Damascus, then the place is marked by this name. Rightly Paul also, after the stoning of Stephen, the first martyr for Christ, went to Damascus to bring the believers in Christ bound to Jerusalem." That is, in that same place he was to imitate the deeds of Cain against the imitators of Abel. Elsewhere he says that some interpret it as blood of sackcloth, from דם and שק.

units.la: VERS. 3. Circumfudit eum lux è cælo. Solus Æthiopicus addit, hoc factum tempore meridiei.
units.tr: VERS. 3. A light from heaven shone around him. The Ethiopic alone adds that this happened at midday.

units.la: VERS. 5. Ego sum Iesus quem tu persequeris. Durum tibi fuerit contra stimulum calcitrare. Hæc & sequentia apud Æthiopicum sic leguntur, Ego sum Iesus Nazarenus. quia tu persequeris justum, tibi ira est. Et quum tremeret, mirati sunt. Ac dixit, Domine quid vis me facere? dixit ei Dominus, surge &c. Addimus hæc notis Cl. Bezæ, ut cum iis conferantur.
units.tr: VERS. 5. I am Jesus whom you persecute. It will be hard for you to kick against the goad. In the Ethiopic, these words and those that follow read thus: I am Jesus the Nazarene. Because you persecute the righteous one, you are under wrath. And as he trembled, they were amazed. And he said, Lord, what do you want me to do? The Lord said to him, Rise, etc. We add these readings to the notes of the illustrious Beza, so that they may be compared with them.

units.la: VERS. 6. Καὶ λαλοῦντες σὺν. Cl. Beza monet, in duobus codicibus legi, καὶ λαλοῦντες. addimus, sic Syrum quoque & Arabem legisse. Æthiopicus habet, & ego oftendam tibi omnia quæ oportebit te facere.
units.tr: VERS. 6. And speaking with him [Καὶ λαλοῦντες σὺν]. The illustrious Beza observes that in two codices it is read καὶ λαλοῦντες. We add that the Syriac and Arabic also seem to have read so. The Ethiopic has: and I will show you all that you must do.

units.la: VERS. 7. οἱ δὲ ἄνδρες οἱ συνοδεύοντες αὐτῷ. Arabs الرجال الذين كانوا معه سائرين في الطريق id est, ad verbum, Viri autem qui erant cum eo ambulantes in via, id est, οἱ συνοδεύοντες αὐτῷ. itaque post συνοδεύοντες non additur in Arabico, morabantur in via, ἱστήκεισαν ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ. fefellit Bezam Junius, quum vertit, viri autem qui erant cum eo, morabantur in via. non opus erat inde subsidium petere, ad concilianda sequentia verba, ἐνεχθέντες ἐνεοὶ, steterunt attoniti, cum Act. 26. 14. ubi omnes dicuntur concidisse. recte enim observavit doctiss. Beza, τὸ ἱστηκέναι opponi τῷ στῆναι, non τῷ καταχκιλδαι. itaque recte vertit, constiterunt, id est, prae stupore non sunt progressi, sed immoti manserunt, quocunque tandem corporis situ ac positione. saepe enim stare usurpatur pro simpliciter manere & non moveri. ut stetit aqua, id est, non fluxit, Gen. 15. 8. stat plaga lepra, id est, non serpit, Lev. 13. 37. ne stes in tota hac planitie, Gen. 19. 17. quid? innocens ne fuisset Loth, si in planitie ista consedisset? nequaquam: sensus enim erat, ne maneas, ne moberis, quocunque tandem corporis situ.
units.tr: VERS. 7. The men who went with him [οἱ δὲ ἄνδρες οἱ συνοδεύοντες αὐτῷ]. The Arabic reads al-rijal alladhina kanu ma'ahu sa'irin fi al-tariq, that is, word for word, the men who were with him walking on the way, that is, οἱ συνοδεύοντες αὐτῷ. Therefore, after συνοδεύοντες the Arabic adds nothing like they stood in the way (ἱστήκεισαν ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ). Junius was mistaken when he translated, the men who were with him stood in the way. There was no need to seek help from that to reconcile the following words, ἐνεχθέντες ἐνεοὶ, stood speechless, with Acts 26.14, where all are said to have fallen down. For the learned Beza rightly observed that τὸ ἱστηκέναι is opposed to τῷ στῆναι, not to τῷ καταχκιλδαι. Therefore he rightly translated it they stood still, that is, for amazement they did not go forward but remained motionless, in whatever bodily position they were. For stand is often used for simply remain and not move: as the water stood, that is, did not flow (Gen. 15.8); the leprous plague stands, that is, does not spread (Lev. 13.37); do not stand in all this plain (Gen. 19.17). What? Would Lot have been innocent if he had settled on that plain? By no means: the sense was, do not remain, do not move, in whatever bodily position.

units.la: IBIDEM. Ἀνέωγεν ... φωνῆς, μηδὲν ἡ ... Videantur notae Cl. Bezae, quibus hunc locum cum Act. 22. 9. conciliat. tandemque Vallam addit, qui hunc locum depravatum exististimans, legendum putat, Ἠκουσαν μὲν τὴν φωνήν, μηδὲν δὲ ἀκούοντες. Addimus, Aethiopicum vertisse ac si legisset, Ἠκουσαν μὲν τὴν φωνήν, τῷ δὲ φωνῇ τῷ λαλοῦντι μὴ ἀκούοντες. sic enim habet viderunt fulgur, vocem autem, quae loquebatur, non viderunt. VERS. 8. Οὐδὲν ἐθεάσατο, neminem vidit. Sic Graeca exemplaria habent, & Chrysost. Vulg. tamen Syrus & Arabs, nihil vidit, οὐδὲν ἐθεάσατο. Aethiopicus, non poterat videre. VERS. 18. Ἀνέβλεψέ τε παραχρῆμα. Vulg. Erasm. Syrus, Arabs & Aethiopicus, non legunt παραχρῆμα. Ut & in Basileensi editione apud Platerum deest, at apud Oporinum legitur. & apud Chrysost. nec annotavit Beza variantem lectionem. VERS. 20. Καὶ εἰσελθὼν εἰς τὴν συναγωγὴν &c. Vulgatus inserit εἰσελθών, ingressus. quod nusquam legimus, nisi apud Aethiopicum. VERS. 21. Ὁ πορθήσας. Syrus & Arabs nimis dilute, qui persequebatur. Vulg. & Erasm. qui expugnabat. Beza, qui perdidit. Malumus, qui vastavit. Glossarium πορθῶ, populo, vasto.
units.tr: IBIDEM. They were hearing the voice, but seeing no one [Ἀνέωγεν ... φωνῆς, μηδὲν ἡ ...]. See the notes of the illustrious Beza, in which he reconciles this passage with Acts 22.9. Finally he adds Valla, who, thinking the passage corrupt, suggests reading Ἠκουσαν μὲν τὴν φωνήν, μηδὲν δὲ ἀκούοντες (they heard the voice, but heard nothing). We add that the Ethiopic translated as if it had read Ἠκουσαν μὲν τὴν φωνήν, τῷ δὲ φωνῇ τῷ λαλοῦντι μὴ ἀκούοντες, for it reads: they saw the lightning, but they did not see the voice that was speaking. VERS. 8. He saw no one [Οὐδὲν ἐθεάσατο]. So the Greek copies read, and Chrysostom. The Vulgate, however, and the Syriac and Arabic, read he saw nothing (οὐδὲν ἐθεάσατο). The Ethiopic has he could not see. VERS. 18. And immediately he regained his sight [Ἀνέβλεψέ τε παραχρῆμα]. The Vulgate, Erasmus, the Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic do not read παραχρῆμα. It is also absent in the Basel edition by Platter, but is read in Oporinus, and in Chrysostom; and Beza did not note the variant reading. VERS. 20. And entering into the synagogue etc. [Καὶ εἰσελθὼν εἰς τὴν συναγωγὴν]. The Vulgate inserts εἰσελθών, entering, which we nowhere read except in the Ethiopic. VERS. 21. He who destroyed [Ὁ πορθήσας]. The Syriac and Arabic, rather loosely, have who pursued. The Vulgate and Erasmus, who ravaged. Beza, who destroyed. I prefer who laid waste. The glossary gives πορθῶ as to plunder, to lay waste.

units.la: VERS. 22. Συμβιβάζων ὅτι κὺς ἐστιν ὁ Χριστός. Vulgat. & Eraf. affirmans. Beza, collatis testimoniis demonstrans. quod doćto commentario illustrat. Lxx tamen Interpretes utuntur simpliciter συμβιβάζειν pro הבין, instruere, facere ut intelligas, Esa. 40. 14. Dan. 9. 22. pro הודיע, notum facere, Ex. 18.16. Deut. 4.9. Esa. 40.13. denique pro הורה, docere, Exod. 4.12.15. Lev. 10. 11. Pf. 32. 10. Syrus itaque simpliciter vertit ܣܡܝܟ ܐܘܢ ܕܡܬܠܡܕܢ, ostendens. Arabs ﻳﻌﻠﻢ, & docens eos. Æthiop. ዘያስተምሮም, docens eos vere, vel certo. Etsi itaque res ipsa ferat, non potuisse Judæos nisi collatis scripturarum testimoniis convinci, non videtur tamen præpositio ουν in συμβιβάζειν ad comportata illa testimonia pertinere, sed potius ad mentes instruendorum, cum quibus argumenta docentis ita comportantur & conjunguntur, ut de rei veritate convinci cogantur. Hinc apud Hezychium, Συμβιβασις, πεισις, διδαχη, πισις, persuasio, doćtrina, fides. Συμβιβάτω, διδάξατω, doceat. Συμβιβασθέντες, διδαχθέντες, συλλεχθέντες, edo-cti, cum quibus differtatio habita est. Συμβιβάζει, εἰς φιλίαν ἀγ-ὴ συνλαλεῖ, in amicitiam inducit, aut colloquitur. vides relationem denotare docentis ad eum qui docetur, qua ambo quasi inter se uniuntur. hinc passim cum Accus. personæ construitur, συμβιβάζειν τινά, qua phrasi actio docentis significari videtur, quâ instruendum ad se allicit, ac persuadendo convincendoque secum quasi compingit ac coagmentat. Huc pertinet illud Apostoli 1 Cor. 2. 16. quis novit mentem Domini, ὃς συμβιβάσει αὐτόν; qui instructurus fit eum? id est, qui rationes suas ita ei sit probaturus, ut eum sibi quasi compingat, & suum esse cogat?
units.tr: VERS. 22. Symbibazōn hoti houtos estin ho Christos [Συμβιβάζων ὅτι κὺς ἐστιν ὁ Χριστός], that is, proving that this is the Christ. The Vulgate and Erasmus have affirming. Beza has demonstrating by comparing testimonies, which he illustrates with a learned commentary. Yet the Seventy use symbibazein simply for [havin] (Hebrew), to instruct, to make one understand, at Isa. 40.14 and Dan. 9.22; for [hodia] (Hebrew), to make known, at Exod. 18.16, Deut. 4.9 and Isa. 40.13; and finally for [horah] (Hebrew), to teach, at Exod. 4.12, 15, Lev. 10.11 and Ps. 32.10. The Syriac therefore translates simply, showing (Syriac, transliterated "hawwi"). The Arabic has "and teaching them." The Ethiopic has "teaching them truly" or certainly. Although the matter itself suggests that the Jews could not have been convinced except by comparing passages of Scripture, the preposition in symbibazein does not seem to refer to those compared testimonies, but rather to the minds of those being instructed. The teacher's arguments are so arranged and joined with them that they are forced to be convinced of the truth of the matter. Hence in Hesychius: symbibasis, persuasion, teaching, faith; symbibazetō, let him teach; symbibasthentes, taught, gathered together, instructed, with whom a discussion was held; symbibazei, eis philian agei ē synlalei, leads into friendship or converses. You see that it denotes the relation of the teacher to the one taught, by which both are as it were united. Hence it is constructed with the accusative of the person, symbibazein tina. In this phrase the action of the teacher seems to be signified, by which he draws the one to be instructed to himself, and by persuading and convincing, as it were fastens and joins him to himself. To this belongs the Apostle's saying at 1 Cor. 2.16: who has known the mind of the Lord, hos symbibasei auton [ὃς συμβιβάσει αὐτόν]; who will instruct him? That is, who will so prove his reasons to him that he binds him to himself and compels him to be his own?

units.la: VERS. 26. Ἐγένετο δὲ Σαοὺλ ἐλθεῖν εἰς Ἱερουσαλήμ.
units.tr: VERS. 26. Egeneto de Saoul elthein eis Ierousalēm [Ἐγένετο δὲ Σαοὺλ ἐλθεῖν εἰς Ἱερουσαλήμ].

units.la: Æthiopicus, & inde profectus est Hierosolymam. quæ versio si recta est, non intercessit triennium, confer cum notis Cl. Bezæ.
units.tr: The Ethiopic: and from there he went to Jerusalem. If this version is correct, no period of three years intervened. Compare the notes of the illustrious Beza.

units.la: VERS. 28. Καὶ ὧ μετ' αὐτῶν εἰσπορευόμενος ἐ εκπορευό- μενος. Beza fatetur in nonnullis codic. deesse ἐ εκπορευόμενος. Eraf. negat se uspiam in Græcis reperisse. Nos tamen in tribus editionibus reperimus. & in textu Chrysostomi. apud Syrum item, Arabem & Æthiopicum, cum quibus consentit Vulgatus. ac res ipsa postulat.
units.tr: VERS. 28. Kai ho met' autōn eisporeuomenos kai ekporeuomenos [Καὶ ὧ μετ' αὐτῶν εἰσπορευόμενος ... ἐκπορευόμενος]. Beza admits that ekporeuomenos is missing in some manuscripts. Erasmus denies that he has found it anywhere in the Greek. We, however, have found it in three editions, and in the text of Chrysostom. It is also found in the Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic, with which the Vulgate agrees, and the matter itself requires it.

units.la: VERS. 29. Ἐλάλει π. Vulgatus, loquebatur quoque Gentibus. Negat Cl. Beza, se in ullis Græcis codicibus reperisse illud πρὸς ἔθνεσι, gentibus. addo, Syrum quoque & Arabem ignorasse. habet autem Æthiopicus. Sequitur, & di- sputabat πρὸς τοὺς Ἑλληνιστάς. Vult doctiss. Interpres, & hic & Act. 6. 1. intelligi proselytos, Græcos origine gentiles, sed per circumcisionem Judæos factos. Assentior potius Syro qui hic vertit [Syriac], cum Iudaeis qui norunt Græcè, id est, qui origine essent Judæi, sed Græcè loquerentur, & Græcanica bibliorum versione uterentur, quia erant τῶν ἀλλογενῶν τ' Ἑλλήνων. Fuisse autem, qui lingua Græca in synagogis administranda esse sacra contenderent, adversus alios qui sola id Hebraea fieri vellent, liquet ex constitutione 146 Justiniani de Hebraeis, qui priorum sententiam decreto stabilivit. videat ibi cui otium & animus.
units.tr: VERS. 29. Elalei p[ros] [Ἐλάλει π]. The Vulgate: he also spoke to the Gentiles. The learned Beza denies that he found the phrase pros ethnesi [πρὸς ἔθνεσι], to the Gentiles, in any Greek manuscripts. I add that the Syriac and the Arabic did not know it either. The Ethiopic does have it. Then follows and disputed pros tous Hellēnistas [πρὸς τοὺς Ἑλληνιστάς]. The most learned translator thinks that here, and at Acts 6.1, proselytes must be understood, Greeks who were Gentiles by origin but made Jews through circumcision. I agree rather with the Syriac, which here renders (Syriac, transliterated "with the Jews who know Greek"): with the Jews who know Greek, that is, who were Jews by origin but spoke Greek and used the Greek version of the Bible, because they were of the other nations, the Greeks [τῶν ἀλλογενῶν τ' Ἑλλήνων]. That there were some who contended that sacred services in the synagogues ought to be conducted in the Greek language, against others who wished them to be conducted in Hebrew alone, is clear from the 146th constitution of Justinian concerning the Hebrews, which by decree confirmed the former opinion. Let whoever has the leisure and the inclination look there.

units.la: VERS. 30. Deduxerunt eum Cæsaream. Solus Syrus addit [Syriac], nocte. Intelligitur autem non maritima illa, quæ & turris Stratonis, de qua supra c. 8, ࿆ f. 40. Sed Cæsarea Philippi, circa montem Libanon ad confluentem Jor & Dan, ubi Jordanes originem ducit. quæ olim Lachis, deinde Dan appellata fuit. de quo Jud. 18. cujus pomœria quum Rex Agrippa protulisset, mutato nomine in honorem Neronis vocavit Neroniada, quæ antea Cæsarea Philippi dicebatur. Josephus l. 20. Antiq. c. 8.
units.tr: VERS. 30. Deduxerunt eum Caesaream. Only the Syriac adds by night. It is not the maritime Caesarea that is meant, which is also the Tower of Strato, of which above in chapter 8, page 40. It is Caesarea Philippi, near Mount Lebanon, at the confluence of the Jor and the Dan, where the Jordan has its source. This place was formerly called Laish and then Dan, concerning which see Judges 18. When King Agrippa had extended its boundaries, he changed its name in honour of Nero and called it Neroniada, which had previously been called Caesarea Philippi. See Josephus, Antiquities, book 20, chapter 8.

units.la: VERS. 31. Εἶχον εἰρλώλω οἰνσδομιμψμα, ὁ προδιόμψαι τῷ φόξῳ ⸿ Κυρίᾳ, ᾧ τῇ ⸿παρακλήσει ⸿ ἀγίᾳ Πνεύματι ⸿ ἐπληθύνοντο. Vulg. Erasm. Syrus, Arabs & Æthiopicus, τῷ φόξῳ κυρίᾳ construxerunt cum προδιόμψαι, sed καὶ τῇ παρακλήσει cum ἐπληθύνοντο. ita ut consolatio Spiritus S. esset id ipsum in quo multiplicabantur vel augebantur. Beza vero utrumque construxit cum προδιόμψαι, adeo ut ratio qua creverint Ecclesiæ sit, quod ambularent in timore Domini & consolatione Spiritus S. Considerent eruditi an non sic etiam construi ac verti hæc possint, Habebant pacem & ædificabantur, ac magis magisque timore Domini & consolatione Spiritus S. crescebant. προδιόμψαι ἐπληθύνοντο, euntes crescebant aut multiplicabantur. Hebr. הלוך וּרְבָה, multiplicatæ sunt eundo & multiplicando, id est, magis magisque sunt multiplicatæ. talia sunt, Gen. 8. 3. καὶ ἐπέστρεψε τὸ ὕδωρ προδιόμψον ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς, & remittebatur aqua magis magisque à terra, Hebr. הלוך וחסור. sic 2 Paral. 17. 12. Iosaphat iens & crescens, id est, magis magisque crescebat. LXX ὡς προδιόμψων ἢ μειζαλωόμψων, quod idem est atque προδιόμψων ἐμειζαλωτέρ. Porro Arabs non vertit in consolatione, sed in obedientia Spiritus S. τῇ παρακλήσει accepit pro hortatione cui obediendum est. utrumque significat. Quod si cui magis placeat, προδιόμψαι τῷ φόξῳ Κυρίᾳ, vertere ambulantes in timore Domini, subaudita præpositione ἐν, monemus constructionem esse, qualis 2 Sam. 15. 11. Καὶ ἐπορεύοντο ἀπλότητι, & ibant in simplicitate, id est, nullius mali conscii, Ps. 81. 14. Ἰσραὴλ τῆς ὁδοῦς μου εἰ ἐπορεύθη, Israël si in viis meis ambulasset, Ps. 89. 31. ἡ τῆς κρίματά μου μὴ προδιόδωσε, & in judiciis meis non ambulaverint. Prov. 28. 26. ὁς ὁ προδιέπα σοφία, σωθήσεται, qui vero ambulat in sapientia, servabitur. videtis omitti ἐν, licet in Hebræo expressum sit.
units.tr: VERS. 31. Eichon eirēnēn, oikodomoumenoi, kai poreuomenoi tōi phobōi Kyriou, kai tēi paraklēsei tou hagiou Pneumatos eplēthynonto [Εἶχον εἰρήνην, οἰκοδομούμενοι, καὶ πορευόμενοι τῷ φόβῳ Κυρίου, καὶ τῇ παρακλήσει τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος ἐπληθύνοντο]. The Vulgate, Erasmus, the Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic construe tōi phobōi Kyriou with poreuomenoi, but kai tēi paraklēsei with eplēthynonto, so that the consolation of the Holy Spirit is that in which they were multiplied or increased. Beza, however, construes both with poreuomenoi, so that the reason the churches grew was that they walked in the fear of the Lord and in the consolation of the Holy Spirit. Let learned readers consider whether these words cannot also be construed and translated thus: they had peace and were built up, and, going on, grew more and more in the fear of the Lord and the consolation of the Holy Spirit. Poreuomenoi eplēthynonto, going on they grew or were multiplied. In Hebrew, [halokh varabah] (Hebrew), they were multiplied by going and multiplying, that is, they were multiplied more and more. There are similar examples: Gen. 8.3, kai epestrepse to hydōr poreuomenon apo tēs gēs, and the water was going back more and more from the earth, Hebrew [halokh vachasor] (Hebrew). So 2 Chron. 17.12: Jehoshaphat going and growing, that is, he grew more and more. The Seventy have hōs proiōn ē megalynomenōn, which is the same as proiōn emegalynthē. Moreover the Arabic does not translate in consolation, but in obedience to the Holy Spirit. It takes paraklēsis as exhortation, which must be obeyed. Both meanings are possible. But if anyone prefers to translate tōi phobōi Kyriou poreuomenoi as walking in the fear of the Lord, with en understood, we note that this is a construction like 2 Sam. 15.11: kai eporeuonto haplotēti, and they went in simplicity, that is, conscious of no wrong; Ps. 81.14: Israēl tēs hodou mou ei eporeuthē, if Israel had walked in my ways; Ps. 89.31: kai en tois krimasi mou mē poreusōsin, and have not walked in my judgments. Prov. 28.26: ho de poreuomenos en sophia sōthēsetai, but he who walks in wisdom shall be saved. You see that en is omitted, although it is expressed in the Hebrew.

units.la: VERS. 34. ἰᾶταί (ὁ Ἰησοῦς), sanat te Iesus. Sic Syrus quoque & Arabs. Vulg. tamen & Erasmus, sanet te, ἰάσθω.
units.tr: VERS. 34. Iatai (ho Iēsous), Jesus heals you. So the Syriac also, and the Arabic. The Vulgate and Erasmus, however, have let him heal you, iasthō [ἰάσθω].

units.la: Sequitur χρώσι στεῖρα, sterne tibi ipsi, grabatum nempe, de quo ꝟ. f. præcedenti. ut autem sternere hic sit colligere, non fit verisimile, quum sint opposita. sternere enim lectum, est in planum extendere. colligere contra, extensum contrahere, & in unum comportare. Syrus ܥܪܣܐ ܐܬܐ, proprie complana, adæqua lectum tuum, id est, complicatum explica & expande. idem est Arabum ﻓﺮﺷﻚ, quo hic Interpres usus est. est Hebræorum פרש, expandere, explicare. & quo Æthiopicus usus est ናሰወ, quod passim significat extendere. unde est Hebræorum משפחה, familia. q. conjugatorum extensio. At quorsum, inquies, apparare lectum ad decubitum, qui surgere jubetur ? respondeo, non juberi surgere & abire, sed ut lectum incompositum & inæqualem, cubantique molestum, ut volutantibus ægris contingere solet, non jam alii, ut fieri consueverat, sed ipsemet surgens componeret, complanaret, æquaret & cubationi aptum redderet. quod penitus restitutæ valetudinis certum erat argumentum.
units.tr: Then follows strōson seautō [στρῶσον σεαυτῷ], spread for yourself, namely the pallet, of which in the preceding verse. That to spread here should mean to gather together is not likely, since they are opposites. To spread a bed is to extend it on a flat surface; to gather, on the contrary, is to draw in what has been extended and bring it together into one. The Syriac word means properly level, make even your bed, that is, fold up what is folded and spread it out. The Arabic word used by this translator is the same. The Hebrew is [paras] (Hebrew), to spread out, to explain. The Ethiopic uses a word which everywhere means to extend. From it comes the Hebrew [mishpachah] (Hebrew), family, that is, the extension of married persons. But why, you will ask, should he prepare his bed for lying down when he is ordered to rise? I answer that he is not ordered to rise and go away, but that, rising himself, he should arrange the bed, which was disordered, uneven and troublesome for the man lying on it, as usually happens with restless sick people. He should not have others do this, as had been customary, but make it level, smooth and fit for lying on himself. This was a sure proof that his health had been fully restored.

units.la: VERS. 35. Οἱ κατοικοῦντες Λύδδαν ἢ τ Σάρωνα. Λύδδα, לוד urbs est tribus Ephraim non procul à mari Mediterraneo, in confinio tribus Dan. Hieronymus de locis Hebraicis Actorum, Lydda, civitas Palæstinæ in littore magni maris sita quæ Diospolis appellatur. eam Ceftius exussit, Josephus de bel. Jud. l. 2. c. 23. Benjamin in Itinerario dicit לוד Lyddam suo tempore לוד, Seguras dictam fuisse. De Σάρων autem vide quid Cl. Drusius in Comment. priore ad voces N. T. annotaverit. quibus addimus, distinguendum esse inter שרון, Σαρῶν, & השרון, ὁ Σαρῶν. prius est nomen urbis ultra Jordanem in tribu Gad ad fluvium Arnon. de qua 1 Chron. 5.16. Alterum est regionis cis Jordanem ad oram maris Mediterranei, à Joppe ad Cæsaream usque, exordiendo infra Lyddam de qua 1 Chron. 27.29 Cant 2.1. Esa. 33.9. & 35. 2. & 65.10. hinc hoc loco ἡ τὴν Σάρωνα, expressō articulo. quod observandum, quia Latina lingua, quæ articulo caret, hæc loca distinguere non potest, & apud doctos etiam viros confundi video, quum neutiquam debeant. Regionis & regni Metropolis dicebatur ישרון, τῷ Σάρωνι, vel ἡ Σάρω-ν@, quæ ad Saronem pertineret. unde Jos. 12. 18. inter Reges à Josua devictos est ישרון הר אחד, Onkelus מלכא דשרון הר. LXX, βασιλεὺς Ασωρῶν ἕνα. Vulgatus & Pagninus, Rex Lazaron unus. recte judicarunt, pertinere ad urbis denominationem. ut & in mappa Judaica ישרון est urbs regia, super montem cui הר שרון, mons Saronis nomen est, in tribu Ephraim. Perperam ergo Cl. Junius vertit, Saronim unus. remittensque lectorem ad 1 Chron. 27. 29. ait, quicquid dicant alii, certum esse Scharonem campestrem regionem esse, Libano subjectam inde à Baschane. error est ex locis non distinctis. Fuit autem regio Σάρων uberrima & feraciissima. mappa Judaica sic eam describit, השרון רשן ושן שר חמר תגן פירה מצין פח תשר בתבצלת, id est, Haffaron pinguis est & oleosa, agros habens desideratissimos & vites frugiferas, florum rosarumque feracissima. Hinc Cant. 2. 1. חבצלת השרון, rosa Haffaronis. Hinc יין השרוני, vinum Haffaroniticum, cui duas partes aquæ admiscebant. Schabbath sol. 77. Midda sol. 19. Audacter scribimus Haffaron. nam & plurimæ editiones pro ἡ Σάρωνα legunt ἡ Α'σαράρωνα, quales sunt Argentorati apud Wolphium an. 1524. Basileæ apud Bryling an. 1546. Ibid. apud Platerum an. 1543. sic Chrysostomus legit. sic Erasmus, qui aliam lectionem non annotavit. Editio Caroli Stephani habet ἡ Α'σαραρωνᾶν. At quatuor aliæ editiones nostræ habent ἡ Σαρωνᾶν. Syrus habet ܫܪܘܢܐ, ܡܐܪܘܢܐ. Vulgatus Saronae. Æthiopicus ሰሮን. Junius ex Arabe nobis dedit Tzekarondæ. Erpeniana editio habet ﺷﺮﻭﻥ, Tsferphondæ, unde sane, nescio. LXX Interpretes ה השרון interdum reddunt nomine proprio, ut 1 Chron. 27. 29. ἐν τῷ Σαρών, Esa. 33. 9. ὾ Σαρών. Interdum appellativo, ut Cant. 2. 1. § מישור, planitiei, Esa. 65. 10. ἐν τῇ δφυμῷ, in nemore.
units.tr: VERS. 35. Hoi katoikountes Lydan kai ton Sarōna [Οἱ κατοικοῦντες Λύδδαν καὶ τὸν Σαρῶνα]. Lydda ([Lod] in Hebrew) is a town of the tribe of Ephraim, not far from the Mediterranean Sea, on the border of the tribe of Dan. Jerome, in his book on the Hebrew places of Acts, says: Lydda, a city of Palestine situated on the shore of the great sea, which is called Diospolis. Cestius burnt it, as Josephus says in The Jewish War, book 2, chapter 23. Benjamin, in his Itinerary, says that Lod was called Lydda in his time, and that it was formerly called Seguras. On Saron, see what the learned Drusius noted in his earlier commentary on the words of the New Testament. To this we add that a distinction must be made between [Sharon] (Hebrew), Sarōn [Σαρῶν], and [ha-Sharon] (Hebrew), ho Sarōn [ὁ Σαρῶν]. The former is the name of a town beyond the Jordan, in the tribe of Gad, by the river Arnon, concerning which see 1 Chron. 5.16. The latter is the region on this side of the Jordan, along the shore of the Mediterranean, from Joppa to Caesarea, beginning below Lydda, concerning which see 1 Chron. 27.29; Song 2.1; Isa. 33.9, 35.2 and 65.10. Hence here hē tēn Sarōna, with the article expressed. This must be observed, because the Latin language, which has no article, cannot distinguish these places, and I see that even learned men confuse them, though they ought not to be confused at all. The metropolis of the region and kingdom was called [Sharon] (Hebrew), that is, the one pertaining to Saron. Hence at Josh. 12.18, among the kings defeated by Joshua, is [melekh Sharon echad] (Hebrew); Onkelos has [malka di-Sharon chad]. The Seventy have basileus Asōrōn hena [βασιλεὺς Ἀσωρῶν ἕνα]. The Vulgate and Pagninus have the king of Lazaron, one. They rightly judged that it pertains to the naming of the city. So too in the Jewish map, Sharon is a royal city, above the mountain which is called [har Sharon] (Hebrew), Mount Saron, in the tribe of Ephraim. Therefore the learned Junius wrongly translates Saronim, one, and referring the reader to 1 Chron. 27.29 he says that, whatever others say, it is certain that Scharon is a flat region under Lebanon, from Bashan onward. This is an error arising from failing to distinguish the places. The region of Saron was very rich and fertile. The Jewish map describes it thus: Haffaron is fat and oily, having most desirable fields and fruitful vines, and most abundant in flowers and roses. Hence Song 2.1 has [chavatzelet ha-Sharon] (Hebrew), the rose of Haffaron. Hence also [yayin ha-Sharoni] (Hebrew), Haffaronitic wine, to which they added two parts of water (Shabbath 77; Midda 19). We boldly write Haffaron. For most editions read for hē Sarōna, hē Asararōna, such as the Strasbourg edition of Wolphius, 1524; the Basel edition of Bryling, 1546; and the Basel edition of Plater, 1543. So Chrysostom read, and so Erasmus, who noted no other reading. The edition of Carolus Stephanus has hē Asararōnan. But our other four editions have hē Saronan. The Syriac has (Syriac, transliterated "Sharona" or "Maronā"). The Vulgate has Saronae. The Ethiopic has Saron. Junius gave us from the Arabic Tzekarondae. The Erpenian edition has (Arabic, transliterated "Tsferphondae"), whence I truly do not know. The Seventy sometimes render [ha-Sharon] by a proper name, as at 1 Chron. 27.29, en tō Saron, and at Isa. 33.9, ho Saron. Sometimes they render it by a common noun, as at Song 2.1, § mishor [Hebrew], of the plain, and at Isa. 65.10, en tē drymō, in the wood.

units.la: VERS. 37. Posuerunt ἐν τῷ ὑπερῴῳ, in cænaculo. Locus erat in editiore ædium parte, ut vel ipsa vox Græca, & Hebræorum, Syrorum, Arabumque עליה indicant, ab עלה, ascendere. miror ergo Æthiopicum, qui plane contra vertit עליה, in infima domo. & ȳ f. 39. ubi Petrum dicuntur duxisse εἰς τὸ ὑπερῷον, in cænaculum, habet ubi erat cadaver.
units.tr: VERSE 37. They laid her in the upper room [ἐν τῷ ὑπερῴῳ], in the upper chamber. The place was in the higher part of the house, as the Greek word itself and the Hebrew, Syriac and Arabic עליה [ʿaliyah] show, from עלה [ʿalah], to ascend. I am surprised, then, at the Ethiopic, which renders עליה quite the opposite, in the lowest house. And in ȳ f. 39, where Peter is said to have been led εἰς τὸ ὑπερῷον, into the upper chamber, it has where the corpse was.

units.la: VERS. 38. Rogantes μὴ ὀκνῆσαι διελθεῖν ἕως αὐτοῦ. Rectè Beza, ne cunctaretur. Sicut Balac Bileamo dici jubebat, ἀξιῶ σε μὴ ὀκνήσῃς ἐλθεῖν πρός με. sic Græci transtulerunt quod in Hebræo est, ne prohibearis quo minus venias ad me, id est, nihil sit quod te retardet & prohibeat, id est, ut habet ibi Vulgatus, ne cunctéris venire ad me. Sic etiam Hebræorum, cui ad amussim respondet ὀκνέω, pigrere, usurpatur. ut Jud. 18. 9. ne sitis pigri ad eundem, LXX, μὴ ὀκνήσητε § παρακλῆσαι. Vulgatus rectè, nolite cessare, eamus.
units.tr: VERSE 38. Asking [μὴ ὀκνῆσαι διελθεῖν ἕως αὐτοῦ], Beza rightly renders that he would not hesitate. Just as Balak bade that Balaam be told, I beg you not to hesitate to come to me [ἀξιῶ σε μὴ ὀκνήσῃς ἐλθεῖν πρός με], so the Greeks rendered what is in the Hebrew, let nothing prevent you from coming to me, that is, let nothing delay or hinder you. This is what the Vulgate has there: do not delay to come to me. The same Hebrew usage is found in the verb ὀκνέω, to be slow, which corresponds exactly to it, as in Judges 18:9, do not be slow to go there, LXX, μὴ ὀκνήσητε [παρακλῆσαι]. The Vulgate rightly has do not hesitate, let us go.

units.la: VERS. 39. Χιτῶνας, tunicas, ἱμάτια, Vulg. & Eraf. vestesque. Beza, & vestimenta. malim & pallia, prout Syrus habet ܠܒܫܐ, pro quo Trem. & Boder. non satis aptè reddiderunt & vestes. ܠܒܫܐ enim pallium est, suprema vestis, quam φελόνιον Græci vocant, quæque ἱμάτιον in N. T. non raro vocatur. Glossarium Syro-Arabicum dicit esse ܣܠܡܐ, vestem plenam, quæ reliquis vestibus circumjecta totum corpus involvit. ea vera descriptio est pallii Orientalium, quod propterea κατ' ἐξοχὴν ἱμάτιον, & Gen. 9. 23. לבוש, vestis, & Pf. 102. 27. לבש, indumentum dicitur, quia præcipua vestis est & plena, plurimosque usus corpori præbens. protinus enim & abjiciunt & assumunt rursus. æstate vim radiorum frangit, hyeme vim frigoris. noctu stragulæ vicem subit, &c. nec aliam vestem intellexit Æthiopicus, quum ܐܪܥܐ vertit, quasi ϲεϰαλύμμαϛ, à ܐܪܥܐ quod pro ϲεϰαλύπτ̈ῳ usurpatur Luc. 22. 64. Additur, ἐσα ἐποίει μετ' αὐτῶν ἔσα ἡ Δορκας, quæ faciebat, dum cum ipsis effet, Dorcas. Sic omnes nostri codices & Chryfoftomus. Vulgatus, Arabs & Æthiopicus, quæ faciebat ipsis Dorcas, ἃ ἐποίει αὐτοῖς. unde Syrus, quæ dederat ipsis Dorcas. Vulgatus tamen & Æthiopicus plane omittunt μετ' αὐτῶν ἔσα. Syrus & Arabs pro eo habent, dum viveret. quod sensu idem est.
units.tr: VERSE 39. Χιτῶνας, tunics, ἱμάτια: the Vulgate and Erasmus have vestesque ("and garments"); Beza has vestimenta. I would prefer pallia ("cloaks"), as the Syriac has lebsha, for which Tremellius and Bodenstein do not render well enough with & vestes. Lebsha is a pallium, the outer garment, which the Greeks call phelonion and which in the New Testament is often called himation. The Syro-Arabic glossary says it is salma, a "full garment," which is wrapped around the body over the other clothes and covers the whole body. That is the true description of the Oriental cloak, which for this reason is called kat' exochen himation ("the cloak par excellence"). In Genesis 9:23 it is called levush (לבוש, "garment"), and in Psalm 102:27 lavash (לבש, "clothing"), because it is the principal and fullest garment and serves the body in many ways. They take it off and put it on again at once. In summer it breaks the force of the rays, in winter the force of the cold; at night it takes the place of a blanket, and so on. The Ethiopic translator also understood nothing else when he rendered it with 'ar'a, as if it were [σεκαλύμμας], a covering, from the word 'ar'a, which is used for the verb meaning "to cover" at Luke 22:64. Then there is the addition [ἃ ἐποίει μετ' αὐτῶν ἦσα ἡ Δορκας], "which Dorcas used to make while she was with them." All our manuscripts and Chrysostom read it this way. The Vulgate, the Arabic and the Ethiopic read quae faciebat ipsis Dorcas ("which Dorcas used to make for them"), [ἃ ἐποίει αὐτοῖς]; hence the Syriac has "which Dorcas had given them." The Vulgate and the Ethiopic, however, omit [μετ' αὐτῶν ἦσα] altogether. The Syriac and the Arabic have "while she was alive" in its place, which means the same thing.

units.la: VERS. 40. Ἐκβαλὼν ἡ ἐξω πεσῖ̈ας. Syrus habet ܐܦܟ̈, quod significat exire fecit, quovis modo, five jussu, five eduͤ ione, five ejectione. Sic & ܥܒܪܝܐ apud Hebræos usurpatur. hinc apud Hellenistas omnia illa verbo ἐκβάλλειν denotantur. primus autem modus hic locum habet.
units.tr: VERSE 40. Ἐκβαλὼν ἔξω πάντας: the Syriac has apaq, which means "made to go out," in whatever way, whether by command, by leading out, or by casting out. The Hebrew word hotsi (הוציא) is used in the same way among the Hebrews, and so among the Hellenists all these senses are expressed by the Greek verb ekballein. The first sense applies here.

units.la: VERS. 43. Apud Simonem quendam βυρσεῦ coriarium. Æthiopicus ܐܪܥܐ ܕܡܕ, instauratorem calceorum. qui σκυτεύς potius vel σκυτοτόμῳ dicitur.
units.tr: VERSE 43. With a certain Simon, a tanner [βυρσεύς]. The Ethiopic has a phrase meaning a restorer of shoes, which is rather to be called σκυτεύς [skyteus] or σκυτοτόμος [skytotomos].

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAP. X.

units.la: VERS. 6. Cui est domus apud mare. pertinere ad Simonem coriarium res ipsa loquitur. itaque ineptissimè hic habet Æthiopicus, & domus Cornelii vicina erat mari. at γ'f.32. rectè. itaque typographicum mendum videtur.
units.tr: VERS. 6. Whose house is by the sea. The matter itself shows that this belongs to Simon the tanner. So the Ethiopic here absurdly has, and Cornelius's house was near the sea. But the reading in γ'f.32 is correct. So this seems to be a typographical error.

units.la: VERS. 7. Et militem pium τ̄ ϲεϑσαχ̈ρ̈ιτ̈ων αὐτ̄ῷ. Syrus ܐܡܪܐ ܕܥܒܕ ܐܦܪܝܢ, quæ Trem. male vertit, quem in pretio habebat. Boderianus melius, qui quidem studiosus erat ipsius. Ferrarius ܥܒܕ ܐܡܪܐ, accessit, appropinquavit. Secundo paruit, præsto fuit. Tertio sustinuit, pertulit, passus est. 2 Cor. 11. 20. de tertia hac significatione agemus ipso loco, quem citat. neque enim rectam putamus. primam communem habet cum lingua Arabica, ubi ﻟﺠﻮ est accedere, appropinquare. Secunda est hujus loci, ex qua vertendum, qui parebat ipsi. ut & Vulgatus Græca vertit. sic Act. 7. 39. pro cui noluerunt ὑπήκοοι ὑπιδῶ, parere, Syrus habet ܐܬܦܠܚ ܩܕܡ ܠܗ. quamvis & ex altera significatione recte verti posset, qui prope ipsum erat, vel, adesse ipsi solebat. atque id primo ac proprie vox Syriaca significat. Glossar. Syro-Arabicum ܐܦܠܣ, id est, ﻗﺮﻳﺐ, prope est, appropinquat. atque ita bene expressit τὰ παρακολουθοῦντα.quod Arabs vertit ﻳﻼﺯﻡ, qui adhærebat ipsi. Æthiopicus ܐܢܐ ܕܥܡܗ, ex iis qui serviebant ipsi.
units.tr: VERS. 7. And a devout soldier of those who attended him [τῶν προσκαρτερούντων αὐτῷ]. The Syriac has amra d-ʿbad afrin, which Tremellius translates badly as whom he held in esteem. Boderianus does better with who was indeed devoted to him. Ferrarius has ʿbad amra, came near, drew close. The second sense is obeyed, was at hand. The third is endured, bore, suffered. We shall deal with this third sense at 2 Cor. 11. 20, the passage he cites, since we do not think it correct. The first sense is shared with the Arabic language, where lajā means to approach, draw near. The second is the sense required here, so it should be rendered who was obedient to him, as the Vulgate also rendered the Greek. So in Acts 7. 39, where the Greek has to whom they would not [ὑπήκοοι], the Syriac has itpalaḥ qadam lah, was subject before him. Yet it could also rightly be rendered from the other sense, who was near him or who was accustomed to be at his side. This is in fact the primary and proper meaning of the Syriac word. The Syro-Arabic glossary gives afals, that is, qarīb, is near, approaches. So it expresses well τὰ παρακολουθοῦντα [those who attended]. The Arab rendered it yalāzim, who clung to him. The Ethiopic has ana d-ʿmah, one of those who served him.

units.la: VERS. 10. Incidit in illum ἔκστασις.
units.tr: VERS. 10. Fell into him [ἔκστασις].

units.la: Syrus ܐܬܬܬ, quod Trem. & Boder. non recte verterunt, mentis excessus. vertendum stupor. est enim ܬܗܪ, stupere, attonitum esse. nec usurpatur fere nisi in admiratione, ut & apud Hebr. תמה, admirari. Luc. 4.36. respondet ei ἐθαύμαζον. cap.5. v.26. ἔκστασις. sed utrumque in admiratione: Videtur ergo Syrus mentem Euangelistæ ita cepisse, quasi admirationis stupor occupasset Apostolum, ob admirandum visum, quod statim narratur. Arabs dixit ﺍﻟﺒﻬﺖ, sopor. id est, sensuum externorum cessatio & stupefactio, qualis in altissimo sopore contingere solet.
units.tr: The Syriac word ʾtt which Tremellius and Boderianus did not translate correctly as excess of mind, should be rendered stupor. For the word tehar means to be stupefied, to be astonished. It is hardly ever used except of wonder, as in Hebrew tmh [תמה], to wonder. At Luke 4. 36 the Greek corresponding is ethaumazon [ἐθαύμαζον], and at Acts 5. 26 it is ekstasis [ἔκστασις]. But both are used of wonder. So the Syriac translator seems to have understood the Evangelist's meaning as though a stupor of wonder had seized the Apostle, because of the marvellous vision that is narrated immediately afterwards. The Arab wrote al-buhtu, deep sleep, that is, the cessation and numbing of the external senses, such as usually occurs in a very deep sleep.

units.la: VERS. 11. Τέσσαρσιν ἀρχαῖς διεσπάρμένον, ἐ κα διεσπαρμένον.
units.tr: VERS. 11. Four corners, let down [Τέσσαρσιν ἀρχαῖς διεσπάρμένον, ἐ κα διεσπαρμένον].

units.la: Vulgat. non legit διεσπαρμένον καί. repugnantibus omnibus quæ vidimus exemplaribus, præterquam Æthiopici, qui similiter ea omittit.
units.tr: The Vulgate did not read διεσπαρμένον καί. All the copies we have seen oppose this, except the Ethiopic, which likewise omits it.

units.la: VERS. 12. Ἐν ᾧ ὑπῆρχε πάντα τὰ πτεράποδα τῆς γῆς, ἐ τὰ θηρία, καὶ τὰ ἑρπετά, ἡ τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ.
units.tr: VERS. 12. In it were all the four-footed creatures of the earth, and the beasts, and the reptiles, and the birds of the air [Ἐν ᾧ ὑπῆρχε πάντα τὰ τετράποδα τῆς γῆς, καὶ τὰ θηρία, καὶ τὰ ἑρπετά, καὶ τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ].

units.la: Vulgatus, Syrus & Arabs non legerunt τὰ θηρία. deinde τῆς γῆς junxerunt post ἑρπετά. Omnes tamen nostri codices receptam lectionem comprobant. Porro Syrus prima verba transtulit [illegible, ~12 letters] [illegible, ~14 letters]
units.tr: The Vulgate, the Syriac and the Arabic did not read τὰ θηρία. Moreover they joined τῆς γῆς after ἑρπετά. Yet all our manuscripts confirm the received reading. As for the Syriac, it translated the first words [illegible].

units.la: [illegible, ~20 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: Trem. & erant in eo omnia viventia, quadrupeda, reptilia &c. qua distinctione effecit, ut Clar. Beza existimarit, Syrum praeposuisse speciebus genus, quasi legisset, πτῶν τὰ ζῶα, πε-τράπoδα, ἑρπετά &c. At vertendus est Syrus ad verbum, & erant in eo omnia animantia quatuor pedum, id est, omnia quadrupeda. In eo ergo convenit cum recepta lectione. Æthiopicus totum hunc versum omittit. fortassis incuria typographi.
units.tr: Tremellius: and there were in it all animals, quadrupeds, reptiles, etc. By this division the illustrious Beza thought that the Syriac had put the genus before the species, as if it had read ta zōa, petrapoda, herpeta, etc. But the Syriac must be rendered word for word: and there were in it all animals of four feet, that is, all quadrupeds. In this it agrees with the received reading. The Ethiopic omits this whole verse, perhaps through the carelessness of the printer.

units.la: VERS. 15. Σὺ μὴ κοίνω. Arabs [illegible, ~10 letters], ne polluito id tu. Junius ergo ad verbum non transtulit, id ne commune dicito. VERS. 21. Τὰς ἁμαρτίας τῶν ἐξ Κορνηλίου πρὸς αὐτόν.
units.tr: VERS. 15. Do not pollute [Σὺ μὴ κοίνω]. The Arabic [illegible], do not pollute that yourself. So Junius did not translate literally, do not call that common. VERS. 21. The reasons of those who came from Cornelius to him [Τὰς ἁμαρτίας τῶν ἐξ Κορνηλίου πρὸς αὐτόν].

units.la: Recte annotavit Beza, haec à Vulgato, Syro & Arabe non fuisse lecta. addo nec ab Æthiopico, nec à Chrysostomo. Reliqui tamen nostri codices habent.
units.tr: The illustrious Beza rightly noted that these words were not read by the Vulgate, the Syriac or the Arabic. I add that they were not read by the Ethiopic either, nor by Chrysostom. Our other manuscripts, however, have them.

units.la: VERS. 22. Καὶ ἀκούσῃ ῥήματα αὐτοῦ σου. Vulgatus & Erasmus, & audiret verba abs te. Longè sane melius quam Beza, & abs te quadam audiret. ῥήματα hic non sunt ῥήματα πράγματα, sed ἐντάλματα, praecepta. sensus est, & audire ex te, τὰ αὐτῶν δὲ ποιεῖν, quid ipsum oportet facere, ut Angelus supra locutus fuerat ψ. 6. sic דבר, verba, LXX Interpretes vertunt ἐντολάς, mandata. Deut. 17. 19. Jer. 19. 15. & sæpe ἀπόστολμα. ut & אמר, dixit, sæpe Hebræis, semper autem Arabibus valet jubere, mandare. quale & illud Luc. 12. 13. Die fratri meo, ut partiatur mecum &c. id est, jube. Syrus, Arabs & Æthiopicus vertunt, & audire verbum ex te. quasi ῥήματα legissent. vel existimarunt verbum Dei ob excellentiam dici pluraliter ῥήματα. sicut sacer codex βιβλία. & λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ pro λόγου, Rom. 3. 1. VERS. 23. Ἐξῆλθε σὺν αὐτοῖς. Vulgat. & Eras. profectus est est cum iis. Beza, abiit. Syrus magis proprie ܝܚܪܓ, exiit.
units.tr: VERS. 22. And hear words from you [Καὶ ἀκούσῃ ῥήματα αὐτοῦ σου]. The Vulgate and Erasmus have and he should hear words from you. This is far better than Beza's and hear certain things from you. Here ῥήματα does not mean things but commands [ἐντάλματα], precepts. The sense is: and to hear from you what he ought to do, as the angel had said above, v. 6. So the Seventy render Hebrew dābār [דבר], word, as entolas [ἐντολάς], commandments, at Deut. 17. 19 and Jer. 19. 15, and often as apostolma. Likewise ʾmr [אמר], said, is often used by the Hebrews, but among the Arabs it always means to order, to command. So too Luke 12. 13: Tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me, that is, order him. The Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic render and hear the word from you, as if they had read rhēma in the singular. Or they thought that the word of God is called rhēmata in the plural because of its excellence, just as the sacred books are called biblia and the oracles of God ta logia tou Theou for logos, Rom. 3. 1. VERS. 23. He went out with them [Ἐξῆλθε σὺν αὐτοῖς]. The Vulgate and Erasmus have he went with them. Beza has he went away. The Syriac uses the more proper word yḥrg, went out.

units.la: VERS. 24. Καὶ σὺν ἀναγκαίως φίλως, & necessarios amicos. Arabs vertit وإصدقاء الخاصين, quæ Junius, & Sanctos necessarios sibi. respexit Hebræorum ישרים, justi, qui iidem sunt qui sancti. fateor apud Arabes الصديق pro justo ac verace usurpari. at الصديق, cujus plurale hoc loco occurrit, amicum significat. صديقا & صديقاء, amicitiam. vertendus Arabs, & amicos suos sibi peculiares. non habuit ergo Cl. Beza, cur in Arabis versionem commentarium faceret.
units.tr: VERS. 24. And his necessary friends [Καὶ σὺν ἀναγκαίοις φίλοις]. The Arabic renders this wa-aṣdiqāʾ al-khāṣṣīn, which Junius rendered holy ones necessary to himself. He had in view the Hebrew yĕšārîm [ישרים], upright, who are the same as the holy ones. I admit that among the Arabs al-ṣadīq is used for the righteous and the true. But al-ṣadīq, whose plural occurs here, means friend, and ṣadīqāʾ means friendship. The Arabic should be rendered and his friends who were peculiar to him. So the illustrious Beza had no reason to comment on the Arabic version.

units.la: VERS. 28. Ostendit mihi Deus, ne quem communem (pollutum) vel impurum hominem dicerem. dixerat nempe Deus ⅟f. 15. quæ Deus purgavit, tu ne polluito. An ergo omnes homines ita purgavit Deus sub Euangelio, ut nemo, ne quidem quoad conscientiam immundus sit dicendus? nequaquam. fides enim demum purificat corda, Act. 15. 9. unde infidelium & mens & conscientia immundæ dicuntur, Tit. 1. 15. An ergo omnes homines sub Euangelio in fœdus suum recepit Deus, ut vel ratione fœderis nemo immundus sit habendus? Neque hoc admittendum. Apostolus enim 1 Cor. 7. 14. docet, viri mulierisque infidelium conjugium adeo esse immundum, ut & liberi eorum sint immundi. Manet ergo etiamnum Ecclesia Dei sic à reliquo distincta mundo, ut ratione fœderis sola sancta, reliqui immundi sint dicendi. qua ratione ergo Ap. Petrus hîc se edoctum à Deo dicit, ut nullum hominem impurum pronunciet? Solutio peti potest è similitudine ciborum Petro in visione lintei oblatorum, quibus vesci intrepidè Petrum jubet, quod antea immundos jam purgassèt. immundi autem fuerant immunditie non naturali,nec morali,sed ceremoniali. pertinebatque ciborum distinctio ad δικαιώματα σαρκὸς, justificationes carnis, Hcb.9.10. ἐπ' κέμου ἐντολῆς σαρκικῆς, Hcb.7.16. purgavit ergo Deus eosdem cibos,quum lege carnalis mandati abolita, liberavit cibos à ceremoniali illa immunditie. Eadem erat ratio inter Judæos & gentes. nam non fœdere tantum, sed & peculiari quadam ceremoniali sanctitate separaverat Deus Judæos à gentibus. ceremonialiter sancti erant Judæi ex aspersione sanguinis taurorum & hircorum, qui mundabat eos πρὸς τὸ τῆς σαρκὸς καθαρότητα, ad carnis puritatem, Hebr. 9. 13. qua carnis puritate destitutæ gentes, immundæ dicebantur. Mundi rursus ceremonialiter erant Judæi per circumcisionem, immundæ contra per præputium gentes, & ceremonialiter carnaliterque detestandæ. unde eas vocat Apostolus ἔθνη ἐν σαρκὶ, gentes in carne, qui dicebantur præputium ab ea quæ dicebatur circumcisio in carne, Eph. 2. 11. ubi in carne notat ceremonialem legis carnalis vim & obligationem, quam legem, ἐν δόγμασι in ritibus sitam, Paulus ibidem vocat τὸ μεσότοιχον τῆς φραγμοῦ, intergerinam sepem, quæ Judæos à gentibus, tanquam mundum quid ab immundo, separaret. ex hac ceremoniali immunditie ortum, quod canes vocentur gentes Matt. 15. 26. quod discipulos suos in viam gentium ire vetet Servator, Matt. 10. 5. quod connubia cum ipsis inire interdixerit Judæis Deus, Deuter. 7. 3. quodque supra Petrus dixerit, ἀκάθαρτον εἶναι, nefas esse Judæo κολλᾶσθαι ἀλλοφύλῳ, agglutinari alienigenæ. Sublatâ itaque lege ceremoniali,sublata quoq; fuit ab omnibus gentibus, ac singulis gentium individuis, ceremonialis illa immundities. nemo exinde ob circumcisionem sanctus, nemo ob præputium immundus dici debuit. hactenus ergo verè offendit Petro Deus, ne quem hominem pollutum deinceps diceret.
units.tr: VERS. 28. God showed me that I should not call any man common or unclean. God had indeed said, at v. 15, what God has cleansed, do not you make unclean. Has God then so cleansed all men under the Gospel that no one may be called unclean, even as to conscience? By no means. For faith alone at last purifies the hearts, Acts 15. 9, whence the minds and consciences of unbelievers are called unclean, Titus 1. 15. Has God then received all men into his covenant under the Gospel, so that by reason of the covenant no one is to be held unclean? This too must not be admitted. For the Apostle teaches at 1 Cor. 7. 14 that the marriage of an unbelieving husband or wife is so unclean that their children are unclean as well. The Church of God therefore remains so distinct from the rest of the world that, by reason of the covenant, only the church is holy and the rest are to be called unclean. On what ground, then, does the Apostle Peter here say that he was taught by God not to pronounce any man impure? A solution may be sought from the likeness of the foods offered to Peter in the vision of the sheet, which he is bidden to eat without fear, because God had already cleansed them. Those foods, however, were unclean with an unclothed uncleanness that was neither natural nor moral but ceremonial. The distinction of foods pertained to the dikaiōmata sarkos, the justifications of the flesh, Heb. 9. 10, and to the entolē sarkikē, the fleshly commandment, Heb. 7. 16. So God cleansed those same foods when, the law of the carnal commandment being abolished, he freed the foods from that ceremonial uncleanness. The same was the case between Jews and Gentiles. For God had separated the Jews from the Gentiles not only by covenant but also by a peculiar ceremonial holiness. The Jews were ceremonially holy through the sprinkling of the blood of bulls and goats, which cleansed them pros to tēs sarkos katharotēta, for the cleansing of the flesh, Heb. 9. 13. Destitute of this cleanness of the flesh, the Gentiles were called unclean. Again, the Jews were ceremonially clean through circumcision, while the Gentiles, on the contrary, were unclean through the foreskin, and were ceremonially and fleshly detestable. Hence the Apostle calls them ethnē en sarki, Gentiles in the flesh, who were called the foreskin by those who were called the circumcision in the flesh, Eph. 2. 11. There in the flesh denotes the ceremonial force and obligation of the carnal law, which law, situated en dogmasin, in ordinances, Paul in the same place calls to mesotoichon tēs phragmou, the middle wall of partition, which separated the Jews from the Gentiles as the clean from the unclean. From this ceremonial uncleanness arises the fact that the Gentiles are called dogs, Matt. 15. 26; that the Saviour forbade his disciples to go into the way of the Gentiles, Matt. 10. 5; that God forbade the Jews to make marriages with them, Deut. 7. 3; and that Peter above said it was unlawful, athemiton, for a Jew to kollāsthai allophylō, be joined to a foreigner. Therefore, with the ceremonial law taken away, that ceremonial uncleanness was also taken away from all the Gentiles and from each individual Gentile. Hence no one ought to be called holy because of circumcision, and no one unclean because of the foreskin. Thus God truly removed from Peter the command that he should call any man unclean from then on.

units.la: VERS.30. A'πò τετάρτης ἡμέρας μέχρι τῆς ὥρας ταύτης, καὶ τὴν ἐνάτην ὥραν προσευχόμενος &c. Primis verbis quidam ad quæstionem quamdiu respondéri autumant, ut sensus sit, eum jam tum per quatuor dies jejunasse. alii ad quæstionem quando, ut sensus sit, quarto abhinc die eum se jejunio dedisse, & ejus diei hora nona contigisse quæ deinceps narrat. posterior hæc sententia verior est, quia cum circumstantiis rei, supra in hoc capite narratæ, quadrat. Postridie enim ejus diei, quo jejunanti ac precanti Cornelio Angelus apparuerat, legati ejus Petrum accesserunt, ⊻f.9. habes duos dies. postridie Petrus discessit cum eis Cæsaream, ⊻f. 23. habes tertium diem. postridie intrarunt Cæsaream, contigitque Petri cum Cornelio colloquium, v. 24. habes quartum. id narrat Cornelius, jam quartum agi diem, quum jejunio se dans, & hora nona precibus vacans Angelum conspexerit. nec alium facile sensum verba ferunt. Si enim mens ejus fuit, quod jam per quatuor jejunaverat dies, quum hora nona Angelus appareret, inepte insersuit μέχρι τῆς ὥρας ταύτης, quæ verba hoc ipsum tempus exprimunt, quo jam loquebatur. at quatriduo ante contigerat visio. Quod si mens est, se jam ea hora, qua alloquebatur Petrum, per quatriduum jejunasse, non intelligetur ex ipsius verbis, cujus diei hora nona, an quarti, an tertii, an secundi Angelus apparuerit. adde quod eo sensu τῆς ὥρας dicendum fuerat, non ἡμέρας τετάρτης. quemadmodum Syrus eam sententiam secutus, vertit, [Syriac text] quatuor dies sunt hunc usque ex quo jejuno. At Cornelius jejunabam dicit, non jejuno. Erasmus itaque alteram sententiam recte secutus, vertit, Die ab hinc quarto usque ad hanc horam sedebam jejunus. Beza, nudius quartus usque ad hanc horam eram jejunus. At non recte videtur Erasmus addidisse abhinc, quod
units.tr: VERSE 30. From the fourth day until this hour, and at the ninth hour I was praying, &c. [ἀπὸ τετάρτης ἡμέρας μέχρι τῆς ὥρας ταύτης, καὶ τὴν ἐνάτην ὥραν προσευχόμενος]. Some authors take the first words to answer the question how long, so that the sense is that he had already been fasting for four days. Others take them to answer the question when, so that the sense is that four days earlier he had given himself to fasting, and that the ninth hour of that day is the time of the events he goes on to narrate. This second view is the truer, because it fits the circumstances of the event related earlier in this chapter. For on the day after the one on which the angel appeared to Cornelius while he was fasting and praying, his messengers came to Peter (verse 9: you have two days). The next day Peter set out with them for Caesarea (verse 23: you have a third day). The next day they entered Caesarea, and Peter's conversation with Cornelius took place (verse 24: you have a fourth). This is what Cornelius reports: it was already the fourth day since, while giving himself to fasting and spending the ninth hour in prayer, he saw the angel. Nor do the words easily bear any other sense. For if his meaning was that he had already fasted for four days when the angel appeared at the ninth hour, he would have inserted, awkwardly, until this hour [μέχρι τῆς ὥρας ταύτης], words which express this very time at which he was now speaking; but the vision had happened four days before. And if his meaning is that he had already been fasting for four days up to the hour in which he was addressing Peter, it would not be clear from his words which day's ninth hour the angel had appeared on: the fourth, the third, or the second. Add that in that sense it should have been of the hour, not of the fourth day. The Syriac translator, following this first view, renders it: four days it is since I began to fast. But Cornelius says I was fasting, not I fast. Erasmus, therefore, rightly followed the second view and translated: Four days ago, up to this hour, I sat fasting. Beza: Three days ago, up to this hour, I was fasting. But Erasmus does not seem to have been right to add abhinc [from this point], since it is not in the Greek, which

units.la: {y} Syriac passage printed in Syriac letters; not transcribed. quod in Græco non est. & neuter videtur recte illud μίχρι τῶν τῆς ἡμέρας retulisse ad ἡμέρ νηστεύων. unde orta est Cl. Bezæ commentatio, hanc loquendi formulam petitam esse è medio. neq; enim horam præsentem declarare, sed duorum diverforum dierum nonam. Existimamus potius horam præsentem indicari, & quidem ejus diei matutinam. quum enim Joppe 9 miliaribus, sive diei itinere distaret Cæsarea, Petrus pridie Joppe profectus, postridie mane Cæsaream intravit, & cum Cornelio sermones miscuit. Ad hanc ipsam, inquit Cornelius, horam quartus dies est elapsus, quo me jejunio dabam (verto enim ἡμέρ νηστεύων, eram jejunans, non jejunus) & ejus diei hora nona precans &c. nec aliter videtur intelligi posse Vulgatus Latinus, A nudiusquarta die usque ad hanc horam orans eram hora nona. id est, à nudiusquarta die usque ad hanc horam tempus fluxit, quo orabam hora nona. obscurior tamen ejus mens est, quia ἡμέρ νηστεύων non legit. ut nec Æthiopicus. Verba Græca satis plana videntur, & hunc mihi habere sensum, si à quarto die ad hanc ipsam horam supputes tempus, habes horam qua me jejunio dabam. exinde hora nona orans vidi &c. quod idem est atque, quarto ab hac hora, vel abhinc, die jejunabam. adeo ut illud Erafmi abhinc in μίχρι τῶν τῆς ἡμέρας comprehensum mihi videatur. neque abit illa Euangelistæ phrasis à Latinorum phrasi, qua quum quis præteritis decem diebus est profectus, à decem diebus profectum dicunt, lapsis scilicet ad hoc ipsum tempus quo id dicitur. Porro nulla Græcarum mearum editionum, quas novem consului, in usitata hujus loci lectione variat. Erafmus in annotationibus legit ἡμέρ, ideoque vertit sedebam. In editione tamen Basilcensi, an. 1546. apud Nicolaum Bryling, cui ipse præfuit, ἡμέρ legitur. quæ vox non adeo est poetica, quin & Paulus ea usus sit Gal. 1. 10. δοῦλος Χριστοῦ ... ἡμέρ, servus Christi non essem. & noster Euangelista infra c. 11. vel ter, nempe v. 5. 11. 17.
units.tr: is not right. Neither of them seems to have rightly referred until the day's [μέχρι τῶν τῆς ἡμέρας] to fasting [ἡμέρα νηστεύων]. From this came the learned Beza's remark that this way of speaking is taken from the middle, and that it does not indicate the present hour but the ninth hour of two different days. I think rather that the present hour is indicated, and specifically the morning of that day. For since Caesarea was nine miles, or a day's journey, from Joppa, Peter set out from Joppa the day before and entered Caesarea the next morning, and spoke with Cornelius. Cornelius says: to this very hour four days have passed, since I was giving myself to fasting (for I translate ἡμέρα νηστεύων as I was fasting, not I was fasted), and at the ninth hour of that day, praying &c. Nor does the Vulgate Latin seem to be understood in any other way: From the day before yesterday's fourth hour until this hour I was praying at the ninth hour; that is, the time from the day before yesterday up to this hour has run its course during which I prayed at the ninth hour. Its meaning is less clear, however, because it does not read fasting [ἡμέρα νηστεύων]. Nor does the Ethiopic. The Greek words seem quite plain and to have this sense: if you reckon the time from the fourth day up to this very hour, you have the hour in which I was giving myself to fasting. From that point, at the ninth hour, while praying, I saw &c. This is the same as saying I was fasting four days ago from this hour, or from now. So that Erasmus's abhinc seems to me to be contained in until the day's [μέχρι τῶν τῆς ἡμέρας]. Nor does this phrase of the Evangelist differ from the Latin idiom by which, when someone has set out ten days before the present, people say he set out from ten days; the days, that is, having elapsed up to the very time at which it is spoken. Moreover, none of the Greek editions I consulted, nine in number, varies in the usual reading of this place. Erasmus in his annotations reads ἡμέρα, and therefore translates I sat. In the Basel edition of 1546, however, printed by Nicolaus Bryling, under his own supervision, ἡμέρα is read. This word is not so poetical that Paul did not also use it, Gal. 1:10: δοῦλος Χριστοῦ ... ἡμέρα, I would not be a servant of Christ; and our Evangelist below in chapter 11 uses it three times, namely verses 5, 11 and 17.

units.la: VERS. 36. Τὸν λόγον ὃν ἀπέστϊλε τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραὴλ. Vulgatus, verbum misit Deus filiis Israël. Laudandus magis Cl: Beza, qui aut intelligendum ait καπὰ, secundum verbum quod misit. aut ϯ λόγον ὃν accipiendum pro ὃν λόγον. sicut Matth. 21. 42. & Act. 13. 2. quem locum tamen aliter construendum putamus: ut ifthic dicemus. Recte autem monet, idem esse quod Hebraicè את־הדבר אשר. quem Hebraismum quum recte examinamus, deprehendimus, particulam את, quae Accusativum format, in hujusmodi constructionibus valere pronomen זה, cum verbo substantivo subintelligendo, & per Nominativum esse reddendum. Exempla fidem facient. Hagg. 2. 5. את־הדבר אשר כרתי אתכם, LXX ad verbum, τὸ ῥῆμα ὃ διέθηκα ὑμᾶς. pro הדבר, זה הדבר, hoc est verbum quod pepigi vobiscum. Zachar. 7. 7. הלא את־הדברים אשר קרא יהוה. pro הלא אלה הדברים, an non illa sunt verba, quae clamavit Dominus? LXX, ταῦτα οἱ λόγοι εἰσὶν, ὡς ἐλάλησε &c. Zachar. 8. 17. כי את־כל אלה, pro כי הנה כל אלה אשר שנאתי, nam haec sunt omnia ea quae odi. 2 Reg. 9 24. אני ואתה את־הרכבים, pro הנה הרכבים, ego & tu sumus illi qui vehebamur. Ita hoc loco, ϯ λόγον ὃν ἀπέστϊλε, idem est quod ὃν τὸ λόγον ὃν ἀπέστϊλε. quod magis etiam confirmat usitatissimus Rabbinis loquendi modus, qui dicturi ὃν τὸ λόγον ὃν ἀπέστϊλε, dicent אותו הדבר אשר שלח. quod ad verbum est, ϯ λόγον ὃν ἀπέστϊλε. אותו enim proprie est eum. sed usurpatur ipsis pro is est. Sic locis ante allatis, Hagg. 2. 5. את־הדבר, אשר כרתי, Rabbinicè est אותו הדבר &c. Zach. 7. 7. הלא את־הדברים, Rabbin. הלא אותם הדברים. Zachar. 9. 17. כי את־כל אלה, Rabb. כי אותם כל אלה. 2 Reg. 9. 24. אני ואתה, Rabb. אני ואתה אותם הרכבים, ad verbum, ego & tu sunt illi qui equitabant.
units.tr: VERSE 36. Τὸν λόγον ὃν ἀπέστειλε τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραήλ. The Vulgate: the word God sent to the sons of Israel. Beza deserves more praise, who says either that κατά [according to] must be understood, according to the word which he sent, or that τὸν λόγον ὃν should be taken for ὃν λόγον, as in Matt. 21:42 and Acts 13:2. We think, however, that this passage should be construed differently, as we shall say there. He rightly observes that it is the same as the Hebrew את־הדבר אשר [eth-haddabar asher]. When we examine this Hebraism carefully, we find that the particle את, which forms the accusative, in constructions of this kind has the force of the pronoun זה [this], with the verb "to be" understood, and must be rendered by the nominative. Examples will confirm this. Hag. 2:5: את־הדבר אשר כרתי אתכם [eth-haddabar asher karoti etkhem], which the LXX render word for word as τὸ ῥῆμα ὃ διέθηκα ὑμᾶς; for הדבר one should read זה הדבר, this is the word which I covenanted with you. Zech. 7:7: הלא את־הדברים אשר קרא יהוה, for הלא אלה הדברים, are not these the words which the Lord cried? The LXX: ταῦτα οἱ λόγοι εἰσὶν, ὡς ἐλάλησε &c. Zech. 8:17: כי את־כל אלה, for כי הנה כל אלה אשר שנאתי, for these are all the things which I hate. 2 Kings 9:24: אני ואתה את־הרכבים, for הנה הרכבים, I and you are those who rode. So in this place τὸν λόγον ὃν ἀπέστειλε is the same as ὃν τὸν λόγον ὃν ἀπέστειλε. This is confirmed even more by the most common idiom of the rabbis, who, where they would say ὃν τὸν λόγον ὃν ἀπέστειλε, say אותו הדבר אשר שלח [oto haddavar asher shalach]. This word for word is τὸν λόγον ὃν ἀπέστειλε, for אותו properly means him, but they use it for this is. So in the passages cited above, Hag. 2:5, את־הדבר, אשר כרתי, in rabbinic usage is אותו הדבר etc.; Zech. 7:7, הלא את־הדברים, rabbinic הלא אותם הדברים; Zech. 8:17, כי את־כל אלה, rabbinic כי אותם כל אלה; 2 Kings 9:24, אני ואתה, rabbinic אני ואתה אותם הרכבים, word for word, I and you are those who were riding.

units.la: Sequitur, Διαγγελίζομαι ὑμῖν εἰρήνην διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. quod verto, quum annunciaret pacem per Iesum Christum. Respici videtur illud Dei apud Esa. 56. 1. Sic dicit Dominus, custodite jus & operamini justitiam: nam propinqua est salus mea ut veniat, & justitia mea ut reveletur. annunciatur ibi pax sive salus quæ instabat per Jesum Christum : sed simul mittitur hoc verbum, id est, mandatum, filiis Israël, ut operentur justitiam. atque ita docentur ipsi filii Israël, eos demum vere esse acceptos Deo, & eos quidem omnes, qui justitiæ studicent. quamobrem statim additur, Beatus vir, qui hoc facit, & filius hominis qui hoc tenebit. quisquis sit, sive ex Judæis, sive ex gentibus, sine ulla personarum acceptione. atque ita vere, id quod v. 35. dixerat, dicit esse eundem illum sermonem quem Deus jam dudum filiis Israël miserat, quum per Esaiam annunciaret pacem, per J. Christum futuram. Quod autem sequitur, ὅτις ἐν πᾶσιν κύριος, recte Cl. Beza ὅτι interpretatur per ὃς, demonstrativum pro relativo, ut & supra 8. 26. sic nos Luc. 18. 7. ὁ μακροθυμῶν ἐν ἀυτοῖς, expositum per ἐφ' οἷς μακροθυμεῖ.
units.tr: There follows: Preaching peace through Jesus Christ [Διαγγελίζομαι ὑμῖν εἰρήνην διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ]. I translate it: while he announced peace through Jesus Christ. There seems to be an allusion to God's words in Isaiah 56.1: Thus says the Lord: keep judgment and do justice, for my salvation is near to come, and my righteousness to be revealed. There peace or salvation, which was at hand, is announced through Jesus Christ; but at the same time this word, that is, this command, is sent to the sons of Israel, that they should do justice. And so the sons of Israel themselves are taught that those are truly accepted by God, and indeed all who strive for righteousness. For this reason it is immediately added: Blessed is the man who does this, and the son of man who holds fast to it, whoever he is, whether of the Jews or of the Gentiles, without any respect of persons. And so truly, what he said at v. 35, that this is the same word which God had long before sent to the sons of Israel, when through Isaiah he announced the peace that would come through Jesus Christ. As to what follows, ὅτις ἐν πᾶσιν κύριος [who is Lord of all], the learned Beza rightly interprets ὅτι as ὃς, a demonstrative for a relative, as also above at 8.26; so we read at Luke 18.7, ὁ μακροθυμῶν ἐν αὐτοῖς, explained by ἐφ' οἷς μακροθυμεῖ.

units.la: VERS. 40. 41. Nulla hic varians lectio est annotata. Miror itaque quam maxime Æthiopicum, qui habet, & dedit eum ut testaretur inter omnes populos, & posuit nos Deus, fecitque nos testes suos, & edimus &c.
units.tr: VERSE 40, 41. No variant reading is noted here. I am therefore greatly surprised by the Ethiopic, which has: "and gave him that he might be witness among all peoples, and God set us, and made us his witnesses, and we ate" etc.

units.la: VERS. 41. Qui comedimus ac bibimus una cum eo, postea quam resurrexit à mortuis. Video quosdam illud postea quam resurrexit à mortuis, conjungere cum ultimis verbis versus præcedentis, dedit eum manifestum fieri, ne cogantur admittere, Christum post resurrectionem bibisse cum discipulis. nusquam enim, inquiunt, ejus fit mentio apud Evangelistas. At edisse memoratur Luc. 24. 43. ut verum se hominem etiam à resurrectione demonstraret. inde colligo, eum etiam bibisse. utrumque enim hominis est, ut vivat. exprimere autem id necesse non fuit, quia potus passim sub cibo comprehenditur, Matt. 15. 2. quando panem comedunt, id est, quum alimentum capiunt, sub quo & potus comprehenditur. Mat. 6. da nobis hodie panem nostrum quotidianum. panis etiam potum comprehendit. Luc. 7. 36. rogavit eum Pharisæus quidam ut ederet secum. ergo, & biberet. Invitat ChristiChristus à resurrectione discipulos suos ad prandium, Joh. 21. 12. Δεῦτε, inquit, Ἰησοῦς. ipse panem distribuit, ac pisces. verisimilene est, pransos discipulos sine potu? quod si & ipsum Servatorem pransum cum illis dicamus, cum alimento potum recte conjungimus. Porro, ut Arabs & vetust. Bezae codex, sic & Æthiopicus subjungit, quadraginta diebus.
units.tr: VERSE 41. "Who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead." I notice that some connect the words "after he rose from the dead" with the last words of the preceding verse, "gave him to be made manifest," so that they need not admit that Christ drank with the disciples after the resurrection. For, they say, there is nowhere any mention of this in the Evangelists. But eating is recorded at Luke 24:43, where he showed himself to be a true man even from the resurrection. From this I conclude that he also drank, for both belong to a man who lives. It was not necessary to express this, because drinking is commonly included under eating, Matt. 15:2: "when they eat bread," that is, when they take nourishment, under which drink is also included. Matt. 6: "give us this day our daily bread." Bread also includes drink. Luke 7:36: "a certain Pharisee asked him that he would eat with him," therefore also drink. Christ, after the resurrection, invites his disciples to breakfast, John 21:12: "Come and eat," he says, "Jesus." He himself distributes the bread and the fish. Is it likely that the disciples had breakfast without drink? And if we say that the Saviour himself had breakfast with them, we rightly join drink with food. Furthermore, as the Arabic and the old codex of Beza, so also the Ethiopic adds "for forty days."

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: Chapter 11.

units.la: VERS. 17. Εἰ οὖν τὴν ἴσην δωρεὰν ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς ὁ Θεὸς &c. ἐγὼ δὲ τίς ἠμην &c.
units.tr: Verse 17. If therefore God gave them the same gift [Εἰ οὖν τὴν ἴσην δωρεὰν ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς ὁ Θεὸς] &c. but who was I [ἐγὼ δὲ τίς ἠμην] &c.

units.la: Expunxit Cl. Beza particulam δὲ. nolim id factum, contra omnium fere Graecorum codicum fidem. Etsi enim discretivam vim hic non habeat, sed otiari videatur, emphasin tamen egregiam habet, ut per sane propemodum exponi queat. ut & Gal. 4. 19. 20. Filii mei, quos iterum parturio, donec formam consequatur Christus in vobis: ἡθέλον παρεῖναι πρὸς ὑμᾶς, vellem sane adesse vobis nunc.
units.tr: Cl. Beza deleted the particle but [δὲ]. I would not have it removed, since almost all Greek manuscripts have it. Although here it has no contrastive force and seems to be idle, it has a fine emphasis, which can almost be expressed by indeed. So also in Gal. 4:19-20: My children, for whom I am again in labour until Christ is formed in you [ἡθέλον παρεῖναι πρὸς ὑμᾶς], I would indeed be present with you now.

units.la: VERS. 19. Qui dispersi fuerant ex afflictione facta, ἐπὶ Στεφάνῳ, Vulgatus sub Stephano. id potius ἐπὶ Στεφάνου diceretur in Genitivo. ut ἐπὶ Ἀβιάθαρ, sub Abiathare pontifice, Marc. 2. 26. ἐπὶ Ἐλισαίου, sub Elisaeo, Luc. 4. 27. ἐπὶ Κλαυδίου, sub Claudio, infra ἐφ. 18. Rectius ergo Eraf. & Beza, ob Stephanum. Hebraice ע, quomodo & Syrus transtulit. quod proprie est super Stephano, quo sensu Latine dicimus, super hac re doleo, id est, ob hanc rem. sic proprie ἐπὶ cum Dativo est super, deinde ob, propter. ut Luc. 1. 29. διεταράχθη ἐπὶ τῷ λόγῳ αὐτοῦ, perturbata fuit super sermone ejus, id est, propter sermonem ejus. VERS. 29. Εἰς διακονίαν πέμψαι τοῖς κατοικοῦσιν ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ ἀδελφοῖς. verto, in submınistrationem (vel, ut recte meo judicio Erasmus, in subsidium) mittere habitantibus &c. Neque enim hic Diaconos respici arbitror, ad quos eleemosynae hae missae fuerint, ut ipsi inde pauperibus subvenirent: sed ipsorum piorum ac liberalium affectum exprimi, qui sua liberalitate ac donis διακονησαν, ministrarunt, id est, subsidio fuerunt fratribus Judaeis. quo sensu dicitur ad Hebr. 6. 10. Διακονησαντες τις αγιοις η Διακονουντες, quum subsidio fuisti sanctis & estis. Sic Διακονια vox pro ipsarum eleemosynarum subsidio, quo pii alii aliis ministrant, accipitur 2 Cor. 8. 4. & 9. 1. 12. *
units.tr: Verse 19. Those who had been scattered by the affliction that arose [ἐπὶ Στεφάνῳ], the Vulgate has under Stephen. It would rather be said in the genitive, ἐπὶ Στεφάνου, as in under Abiathar the high priest [ἐπὶ Ἀβιάθαρ] (Mark 2:26), under Elisha [ἐπὶ Ἐλισαίου] (Luke 4:27), under Claudius [ἐπὶ Κλαυδίου] (below, 18). Erasmus and Beza therefore translate more correctly, on account of Stephen. The Hebrew ע is the same, and the Syriac translated it so as well. Properly it means upon Stephen, in the sense in which we say in Latin I grieve over this matter, that is, on account of this matter. So ἐπὶ with the dative properly means upon, and then on account of, because of. As in Luke 1:29, she was troubled at his word [διεταράχθη ἐπὶ τῷ λόγῳ αὐτοῦ], that is, at his word, because of his word. Verse 29. To send relief to the brethren living in Judea [Εἰς διακονίαν πέμψαι τοῖς κατοικοῦσιν ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ ἀδελφοῖς]. I render it for the support (or, as Erasmus rightly judged, for relief) of the brethren who dwelt &c. For I do not think that deacons are meant here, to whom these alms were sent so that they might in turn help the poor. Rather, the affection of these pious and generous people is expressed, who by their generosity and gifts ministered [διακονησαν], that is, gave help to the Jewish brethren. In this sense it is said in Heb. 6:10, having ministered to the saints, and still ministering [Διακονησαντες τοῖς ἁγίοις ἢ Διακονοῦντες], since you have helped and still help the saints. So the word diakonia is taken for the relief of the alms themselves, by which pious people minister to one another, in 2 Cor. 8:4 and 9:1, 12.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Vers. 1. Τινὰς τ̂ ἐκκλησίας. Vulgatus & Erasmus, quosdam de Ecclesia. Beza, quosdam ex Ecclesia. At Aethiopicus, praepositos domus Dei, id est, Ecclesiae. eam enim nunc per domum Dei, nunc per domum Christianorum effert. ubi porro notandum, eum aut per Ecclesiam intellexisse Synedrium: ut Matt. 18. dic Ecclesiae, id est, Synedrio. ut sensus sit, Herodem apprehendisse quosdam ex Synedrio. aut exiistimasse, aliud esse τινὰς ἐκκλησίας, cui allatae versiones respondent, aliud τινὰς τ̂ ἐκκλησίας. certe οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς στοᾶς significat Stoicos. οἱ ἀπὸ περιπάτου, Peripateticos. οἱ ἀπὸ βήματος, concionatores. sic τ̂ ἀπὸ ἐκκλησίας putaverit esse τ̂ ἐκκλησιαστῶν, ut sensus sit, quosdam Ecclesiastarum, qui nempe Ecclesiae docendae praepositi erant. quales erant Apostoli Jacobus & Petrus, quorum mox fit mentio. non inutile sane fuerit, hoc diligentius perpendere. Arabs vertit ut Beza. Syrus quosdam qui erant in Ecclesia. id est, τινὰς τ̂ ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ.
units.tr: Vers. 1. Τινὰς τῆς ἐκκλησίας [tinas tes ekklesias]. The Vulgate and Erasmus render it some of the Church, Beza some from the Church. But the Ethiopic has the rulers of the house of God, that is, of the Church, for it calls the Church now the house of God, now the house of Christians. It is also worth noting that he may have understood by "the Church" the Sanhedrin, as in Matt. 18, tell it to the Church, that is, to the Sanhedrin. The sense would then be that Herod seized some men from the Sanhedrin. Or he may have thought that τινὰς ἐκκλησίας, which the versions just cited answer to, is one thing, and τινὰς τῆς ἐκκλησίας another. Certainly οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς στοᾶς means the Stoics, οἱ ἀπὸ περιπάτου the Peripatetics, οἱ ἀπὸ βήματος the preachers. So he may have thought that τῆς ἀπὸ ἐκκλησίας means τῶν ἐκκλησιαστῶν, so that the sense is some of the churchmen, namely those set over the teaching of the Church. Such were the apostles James and Peter, who are mentioned shortly after. It would certainly not be useless to weigh this more carefully. The Arabic translates as Beza does. The Syriac has some who were in the Church, that is, τινὰς τῶν ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ.

units.la: Vers. 5. Προσευχῇ ἡ ὧ ἐκλείπει γινομένη. Syrus ἐκτενής, constans. Arabs perdurans. Beza, preces assiduae. Vulg. & Eras. sine intermissione. recte omnes. Hezychius enim ἐκτενίαν esse docet, συνεχῶς ποιεῖν τὸ αὐτό, continuo idem facere. Idem tamen ἐκτενὴς vertit etiam ἀλληλουΐα, intensum. ita recte vertitur etiam intensae preces, id est, vehementes & fervidae. Aethiopicus, precabantur intense. sicut Luc. 22. 44. precabatur ἐκτενέστερον, intensius, Æthiopicus ܐܪܟܐ ܫܪܝܬܐ, intendit precari. sicut cum arcus vi intenditur. id enim proprie est ܬܪܥ. unde permutatis pro more ܐ & apud Hebræos est ܬܪ & ܦܝܬܐ, nervus arcus,ab intendendo sic dictus.
units.tr: Vers. 5. Prayer was made without ceasing [Προσευχῇ ἡ ὧ ἐκλείπει γινομένη]. The Syriac has constant [ekteni], the Arabic enduring, Beza assiduous prayers, the Vulgate and Erasmus without intermission. All of them render it rightly. For Hesychius explains ekteneia as doing the same thing continuously [συνεχῶς ποιεῖν τὸ αὐτό]. Yet the same word ekteneis is also rendered intense in Hallelujah. So intense prayers is also rightly rendered, that is, vehement and fervent. The Ethiopic has they prayed intensely, just as at Luke 22:44 he prayed more intensely [ekteneστερον], and the Ethiopic there is arka sarita, to intend prayer, as when a bow is bent by force. For that is properly tara, and by the usual interchange of letters, among the Hebrews it is tr and pita, the string of a bow, so called from being stretched tight.
