units.la: VERS. 7. Φῶς ἐλαμψεν ἐν τῷ οἰκήματι. Doctiss. Beza vertit in carcere.Sic enim autore Solone carcerem Athenis honestiore vocabulo dictum fuisse, Plutarchum in illius vita testari ait. cui addimus Hezychium, apud quem est, οἴκημα, δεσμωτήριον.
units.tr: VERS. 7. Φῶς ἔλαμψεν ἐν τῷ οἰκήματι. The learned Beza renders it in prison. For, as Plutarch testifies in Solon's life, the prison at Athens was called by a more honourable name. To this we add Hesychius, where οἴκημα means δεσμωτήριον, a prison.

units.la: VERS. 10. Διελθόντες δὲ πρῶτην φυλακὴν καὶ δευτέραν. Syrus vertit, [Syriac text, illegible, ~20 letters] . Trem. & quum praeterita fuisset custodia prima & secunda. sic & Boderianus in interlineari versione. At in Regia, & quum transissent custodiam primam & secundam. Verte, & quum transisset custodia prima & secunda. Mens Syri, ni fallor, est, egressis ipsis e carcere, & versus portam ferream, quae in civitatem ducebat, tendentibus, obviam factas duas custodias, quae ambae non animadversos praeterierunt. quae sententia nec Graeco textui repugnat, nec mira adeo cuiquam videri debet. neque enim porta haec ferrea cum ostio carceris, de quo ɣ C. 6. confundenda. si enim versus iste cum hoc recte conferatur, videtur omnino duplex illa custodia extra ostium carceris, at intra portam ferream versata. Fuit scilicet hic carcer, (si Adrichomio credimus) ἐν τῷ ϙαυνιδῷ, id est, in area, quae Herodis regiam (erat enim hic non civitatis, sed Herodis carcer) undequaque ambiebat, ubi Regii milites excubias agebant. Ab hac area carcereque platea ducebatur, per quam exitus e regia dabatur in civitatem, quam ferrea porta claudebat. Visitatum enim in Oriente (ut in Appendice ad c. 6. Matt. v. 5. antehac annotavimus) majores plateas portis claudi. hanc portam ubi tranfiffet, extra limites regiæ erat, adeoque tutus. intra eam incidit in milites, qui ultro citroque remeantes, plateam istam, qua ad regiam carceremque via erat, observabant & custodiebant. Aut fi Æthiopicum audimus, varia erant inter carcerem portamque ferream atria, quæ Gallice corps des gardes, Belgicè wacht-hupfen dicimus, ubi excubitores agebant. vertit enim, & quum exiissent primum atrium & fecundum.
units.tr: VERS. 10. Διελθόντες δὲ πρώτην φυλακὴν καὶ δευτέραν. The Syriac translates it [illegible Syriac words]. Tremellius: and when the first and second guard had been passed. So also the Bodleian in the interlinear version. But in the Royal (Polyglot) text: and when they had passed the first and second guard. Render it: and when the first and second guard had been passed. The meaning of the Syriac, if I am not mistaken, is that when they had come out of the prison and were heading towards the iron gate which led into the city, two guards met them, and both passed by without being noticed. This view does not conflict with the Greek text, nor should it seem strange to anyone. For this iron gate must not be confused with the door of the prison, which is mentioned in chapter 6. For if this verse is rightly compared with that, it seems that this double guard was entirely outside the prison door, but within the iron gate. The prison was (if we believe Adrichomius) in the Quadrangle, that is, in the courtyard which surrounded Herod's palace on every side (for this was the prison of Herod, not of the city), where the royal soldiers kept watch. From this courtyard and prison a street led out, by which the way from the palace into the city was open, and an iron gate closed it. For it is customary in the East (as I noted earlier in the appendix to chapter 6, Matt. v. 5) for the larger streets to be closed by gates. Once they had passed this gate they were beyond the limits of the palace and so safe. Within it they encountered soldiers, who, moving back and forth, watched and guarded that street, which was the way to the palace and the prison. Or, if we follow the Ethiopic, there were several courtyards between the prison and the iron gate, which we call in French corps des gardes and in Dutch wacht-hupfen, where the sentries kept watch. For it renders it: and when they had passed the first and second courtyard.

units.la: VERS. 13. Accessit puella [Greek: προσῆλθε]. Vulgatus non recte ad videndum. Erafmus & Beza ut subauscultaret. Syrus [Syriac], ut responderet ei. sic & Arabs, [Arabic], quod non prorsus rejiciendum.
units.tr: VERS. 13. The maid came προσῆλθε [prosēlthe]. The Vulgate wrongly has to see. Erasmus and Beza to listen in secret. The Syriac to answer him. So also the Arabic, which is not to be altogether rejected.

units.la: Sæpe enim pro [Greek: ἀποκρίνω], respondere, LXX dicunt [Greek: ἀπεκρίθη]. ut Cant. 5. 7. [Greek: ἐκάλεσα αὐτὴν καὶ οὐχ ὑπήκουσέν], vocavi eum, & non respondit. vide & Esa. 50. 2. & 56. 11. & alibi sæpe, ubi [Greek: ἀπεκρίθη] respondet [Greek: τῷ καλέσαντι], nec est aliud, quam vocanti dicere se adesse, & rogare quid velit. ita exiftimarunt Syrus & Arabs, mentem Euangelistæ esse, accessisse ancillam, ut pulsanti & pulsando vocanti responderet, adesse fe, rogaretque quis effet quidve vellet. idque fecisse liquet ex sequentibus. quum enim Petri vocem dicatur agnovisse, certum est eam non subaufcultando, sed alloquendo pulsantis vocem elicuisse. Et ex Plutarcho liquet, eum qui ad fores accedit daturus pulsanti responsum, dici [Greek: ἀπεκρίθη]. sic enim ille in Sympofio, [Greek: φίλιππος ὁ ἱλαροπρόσωπος ...]. Quin & est ubi pro [Greek: κρούειν] usurpatur [Greek: τὴν φωνὴν]. ut Act. 10. 18. [Greek: καὶ φωνήσαντες ἐπυνθάνοντο], & quum vocassent rogabant, cui sane [Greek: τὸ ἀποκρίνεσθαι] optime quadrat. quin & Æthiopicus reddidit, ut aperiret ei. Quod autem in initio versus Petrus dicitur pulsasse [Greek: τὴν θύραν τοῦ πυλῶνος], Erafmus & Beza verterunt ostium vestibuli. Vulgatus, ostium janua. Melius sane, ex usu LXX Interpretum, qui pro פתח השער, ostium porta aut janua dicunt τὰ θύρα ἡ πυλῶν. vide Jud. 18. 16.17. Ezech. 40. 11. & simpliciter השער, portam vertunt πυλῶνα ibid. & 1 Paral. 26.13. uti & Lucas noster infra ςf. 14. ea significatione dicit, non aperuit τὸν πυλῶνα, sed intro currens annuntiavit stare Petrum, πρὸ ἡ πυλῶν. ubi sane januæ portæque notionem melius quadrare quam vestibuli, res ipsa docet. quod cum Vulgato Syrus quoque hic recte animadvertit. Glossarium πυλών, janua. At inquies, si sic accipiatur πυλών, quid hic differunt θύρα & πυλών? quod apud Hebræos פתח & שער. quorum discrimen sic Kimchi in libro Radicum tradit, ונקרא פתח מה שיש בן השער חוץ לדלתות כי הכל יקרא שער בין מבפנים בין מבחוץ עם הדלתות והאסקופה החיצונה כמו שהיא עם המוחות והמשקוף נקרא פתח לפי שהוא נפתח תמיד אף בהסגר הדלתות הא : פתח נשאר פתח id est, Vocatur פתח, quicquid porta est extra valvas. porta enim, id est, שער vocatur, omne illud quod est introrsum & extrorsum, cum valvis & limine exteriori, quatenus illud junctum est postibus & limini superiori. vocatur autem פתח, quia semper patet, etiam clausis valvis illud patens relinquitur. θύρα autem est à Chaldaico רתת, quod tam pro פתח quam pro שער promiscuè usurpatur.
units.tr: For often the Seventy use ἀπεκρίθη [apekrithe] for to answer, as in Song 5.7, ἐκάλεσα αὐτὴν καὶ οὐχ ὑπήκουσεν [ekalesa autēn kai ouch hypēkousen], I called him, and he did not answer. See also Isa. 50.2, 56.11, and elsewhere often, where ἀπεκρίθη answers τῷ καλέσαντι [tō kalesanti], and means nothing other than to tell the one calling that one is present, and to ask what he wants. The Syriac and the Arabic thought that the evangelist's meaning was that the maid came so that, in answer to the knocking and calling, she might say that she was there, and ask who it was and what he wanted. That this is what she did is clear from what follows. For since it says she recognised Peter's voice, it is certain that she drew out the voice of the one knocking not by listening in secretly, but by speaking to him. And from Plutarch it is clear that the one who goes to the door to give an answer to the knocker is said to ἀπεκρίθη. For so he writes in the Symposium: Philippus the cheerful-faced... Indeed there is also a place where τὴν φωνὴν [tēn phōnēn] is used for κρούειν [krouein], to knock, as in Acts 10.18, καὶ φωνήσαντες ἐπυνθάνοντο [kai phōnēsantes epynthanonto], and having called out, they asked, which certainly fits the sense of answering very well. And the Ethiopic renders it that she might open to him. But as to the statement at the beginning of the verse that Peter knocked at τὴν θύραν τοῦ πυλῶνος [tēn thyran tou pylōnos], Erasmus and Beza translated the door of the vestibule, the Vulgate the door, the gate. More rightly, following the usage of the Septuagint translators, who for פתח השער, the door of the gate, or the gate, say τὰ θύρα or ἡ πυλῶν. See Judg. 18.16–17, Ezek. 40.11, and simply שער, gate, which they render πυλῶνα in the same place and in 1 Chron. 26.13. Our Luke also uses it in this sense below, in verse 14: he did not open the πυλῶνα, but running in announced that Peter stood before the gate, πρὸ ἡ πυλῶν [pro hē pylōn]. Here the fact itself shows that the sense of door or gate fits better than vestibule. The Syriac also rightly notes this here, agreeing with the Vulgate. Glossary: πυλών, gate. But you will say: if πυλών is taken in this way, how do θύρα and πυλών differ here? Among the Hebrews they are פתח and שער. Kimchi in his book of Roots gives this distinction: petach is called whatever is the gate outside the doors; for all is called shaar, whether inside or outside, with the doors and the outer threshold, as far as it is joined to the posts and the upper lintel. It is called petach because it is always open; even when the doors are shut, that opening remains petach. Thyra, however, comes from the Chaldean word deleth, which is used indiscriminately for both petach and shaar.

units.la: VERS. 15. Μαίνη, insanus.
units.tr: VERS. 15. Μαίνη [mainē], insane.

units.la: Syrus habet ܡܐܢܝܐ ܕܫܠܝ. Tremell. omnino turbata es tibi. Boder. in Reg. terrore conturbata es. in Parif. turbando perturbaris tibi. verto, commovendo commotum est tibi. id est, mota tibi mens est, ut ea tibi non constet. quod idem est atque, insanis. Est mihi autem ܡܐܢܝܐ tertia præteriti fœminini generis, formæ ܕܪܥܐ, dolet mihi: sed cum Jod prosthetico, quod quamvis raro huic personæ addatur, addi tamen potest. sicut è contra, tertiæ futuri ܢܬܪܥܐ adest plerumque illud Jod, sed abesse potest, & non raro abest. alioqui in secunda præteriti fœminina dicendum fuerat ܡܐܢܝܐ.
units.tr: The Syriac has mānyā dashlī. Tremellius renders it you are wholly troubled. Boderianus on the Kings renders it you are struck with terror; in the Paris edition it is you are troubled by troubling. I render it moved by moving, it has been moved for you, that is, your mind has been stirred so that it holds together for you no longer, which is the same as you are mad. The form mānyā is the third person feminine singular of the past tense, of the pattern ra'ā, it grieves me, but with a prosthetic yod, which, though it is rarely added to this person, can still be added. Conversely, the third person of the future, netra'ā, usually has that yod, but it can be absent and often is. Otherwise, in the second person feminine of the past, one would have had to say mānyā.

units.la: P 3 ܡܐܢܝܐ una tantum vocali. In benoni dicendum fuerat ﻝ per usitatam contractionem pro ﻝ Æthiopicus legit per interrogationem, insanis ne?
units.tr: P 3: mānyā with only one vowel. In the participle the form should have been written by the usual contraction, in the manner of the Arabic. The Ethiopic reads it as a question: are you mad?

units.la: VERS. 21. Ταχὺ ἡμέρᾳ. Vulgatus, Erasmus & Beza, statuto autem die.
units.tr: VERS. 21. Ταχὺ ἡμέρᾳ [tachy hēmera]. The Vulgate, Erasmus and Beza: but on an appointed day.

units.la: fortasse festus aliquis dies intelligitur ab ipso Deo statutus, & conventui publico destinatus, qui מועד Hebraeis dicitur, à יעד, tempus locumque indicere & statuere, quod per προτάξασθαι interpretantur LXX Exod. 29.43. 2 Reg. 20. 5. ut & מועד, χρόνοι τακτοί, Job. 12. 5. ita Syrus verti poterit ﻝ die celebri vel solenni. quomodo etiam ἡμέρᾳ ἐορτῆς interpretatus est Marc. 6. 21. ita Sacra solennitas intelligeretur, quae in magna populi frequentia dicendi publice occasionem Herodi dedit. nec obstat, quod sacro festo repugnare videatur, quod pro tribunali consedisse rex dicatur. Lege Rabbi Mikotsi ad praeceptum negativum 75. ubi opera quae in מועד licita sunt recenseт, videbis expresse dici, Aguntur judicia capitalia & pecuniaria in solennitate. מועד autem esse dicit, septimum diem post panes fermentatos, qui חג vocatur, item novilunia, festum dedicationis, & Purim. Moneo tamen, Tremellium non male ﻝ vertisse, certo die, id est, simpliciter quodam die. ea enim phrasi Syros uti, quum innominatus quidam dies designatur, patet ex Act. 16. 12. ubi pro ἡμέρας τινὰς Syrus dixit ﻝ, diebus notis, certis, id est, quibusdam. Sic quoque ταχτῇ ἡμέρᾳ hic accipi potest, sive enim statuto die dicas, sive certo idem dicis. ut non necesse sit celebriorem aliquem diem intelligere, qui edicto sit praestitutus, sed certum aliquem, qui quamvis non nominetur, suum tamen in reliquorum dierum serie habuerit ordinem, atque
units.tr: Perhaps some festal day is meant, appointed by God himself and fixed for a public assembly, which the Hebrews call מועד [moed], from יעד [yā'ad], to appoint and fix a time and place, which the Seventy render by προτάξασθαι [protaxasthai] at Exodus 29:43 and 2 Kings 20:5, and moed as χρόνοι τακτοί [chronoi taktoi] at Job 12:5. So the Syriac could be rendered, on a famous or solemn day. In the same way it also rendered ἡμέρᾳ ἐορτῆς [hēmera heortēs] at Mark 6:21, so that the sacred solemnity would be understood, which gave Herod the occasion of speaking publicly before a great crowd of the people. Nor does it count against this that a sacred feast seems to be at odds with the king being said to have sat on the tribunal. Read Rabbi Mikotsi on the negative precept 75, where he lists the works that are lawful on a moed, and you will see it expressly stated: capital and monetary judgments are conducted during the solemnity. He says that the moed is the seventh day after the unleavened bread, which is called the chag, likewise the new moons, the feast of dedication, and Purim. I note, however, that Tremellius did not translate badly with on a certain day, that is, simply on a particular day. That the Syriac uses this phrase when some unnamed day is designated is clear from Acts 16:12, where for ἡμέρας τινὰς [hēmeras tinas] the Syriac has on known, fixed days, that is, on certain ones. So too ταχτῇ ἡμέρᾳ [taktē hēmera] can be taken here: whether you say on an appointed day or on a fixed day, you mean the same thing. So it is not necessary to understand some more famous day, fixed by an edict, but some definite day which, though it is not named, nevertheless had its own place in the series of the other days, and

units.la: Sed hoc ut Hebraeum est, sic et textus Graecus. atque in eo reperiri queat. nec aliud voluit Arabs quum dixit ‎ﻓﻠﻮﻡ ‎يوم ‎, die noto, id est, certo. Clarissime autem Æthiopicus ‎אחת יום‎, uno die, id est, uno quodam die.
units.tr: But this is as the Hebrew has it, and so also the Greek text, and it can be found in it. Nor did the Arab mean anything else when he said fulān yawm, on a certain day, that is, a fixed one. Most clearly the Ethiopic has ahat yom, on one day, that is, on one particular day.

units.la: V E R S. 25. Πληρώσαντες τὸν διακονίαν, quum explevissent ministerium. Syrus, Arabs & Æthiopicus addunt suum, id est, officium sibi demandatum, deferendi Hierosolymam eleemosynas inter gentes collectas. Existimo tamen ut supra c.11.29. ita & hic per διακονίαν intelligi posse subsidium, seu id quod gentes subministrarant, ut sensus sit, quum complevissent, id est, plene tradidissent, subministrationem, id est, subministratas à gentibus eleemosynas. qualis est phrasis 1 Sam. 18.27. ‎ויממלא למלך‎, LXX ἐπλήρωσεν αὐτὰς τῷ βασιλεῖ, & complevit ea regi, id est, plene regi injuncta præputia tradidit.
units.tr: VERS. 25. Πληρώσαντες τὸν διακονίαν [plērōsantes tēn diakonian], when they had completed the ministry. The Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic add their own, that is, the office entrusted to them of carrying to Jerusalem the alms collected among the Gentiles. Yet I think that, as above at chapter 11:29, διακονίαν [diakonian] here too can be understood as the aid, or what the Gentiles had supplied, so that the sense is: when they had completed, that is, fully handed over, the supply, that is, the alms supplied by the Gentiles. Such is the phrase at 1 Samuel 18:27, [ויממלא למלך], the Seventy [ἐπλήρωσεν αὐτὰς τῷ βασιλεῖ], and he filled them up for the king, that is, he fully handed over to the king the foreskins that had been enjoined.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: V E R S. 1. Mavaluˊ. Sic & Arabs ‎مناين‎, Manain. at Syrus ‎מנאיל‎, Manail. non mirum. Nunc enim & Lamed literæ linguales, adeoque ejusdem organi, facile permutantur. hinc in Hebræa lingua idem est ‎לשכה‎ & ‎נשכה‎, cubiculum. in plur. ‎לשכות‎ & ‎נשכות‎, cubicula. In Targum ‎נשה‎ & ‎לשה‎, vagina. pro Hebræo ‎צלם‎, imago, idolum, Arabes dicunt ‎צם‎. pro Hebræo ‎ויתן‎, dedit, Syri ‎נתל‎ in futuro dabit. Hinc & apud Danielem & Esdram sunt ‎להוא‎ pro ‎נהוא‎. ‎להן‎ pro ‎נהון‎. ‎להתן‎ pro ‎נהתן‎. de quo in Notis nostris ad Esdr. 4. 12. pluribus agemus, divino afflante numine. dubito itaque an recte Cl. Drusius Manahen emendaverit in Manahem, ut sit Hebræum ‎מנחם‎, consolator. omnia enim exemplaria conspirant in Nun finale. quod si, ex sententia Syri, pro Lamed positum dicamus, ‎מנאיל‎ valet quid est Deus? Æthiopicus scribit ‎מנאי‎, quod in Benoni Piel à ‎מנא‎, duxit, posset significare ducem, ductorem. Græcè μαναὴ. & addito Nun μαναλὼ, ut
units.tr: VERSE 1. Mavaluˊ. So also the Arab has Manain, and the Syrian Manail. This is not surprising. The liquid letters Lamed and Nun, being of the same organ, are easily interchanged. Hence in Hebrew lishkah and nishkah [לשכה, נשכה] are the same word, "chamber"; in the plural lishkot and nishkot are "chambers." In the Targum nesha and lesha [נשה, לשה] mean "sheath." For the Hebrew tzelem [צלם], "image, idol," the Arabs say tsam. For the Hebrew vayiten [ויתן], "he gave," the Syrians say netal in the future, "he will give." So too in Daniel and Ezra we find lehu for nehu, lehun for nehun, and lehtan for nehtan. We shall deal with this at greater length in our Notes on Ezra 4:12, God willing. I therefore doubt whether the learned Drusius was right to emend Manahen into Manahem, so that it would be the Hebrew menachem [מנחם], "comforter." For all the copies agree on a final Nun. But if, following the Syrian, we say that Lamed is put for Nun, then Manail would mean "what is God?" The Ethiopic writes manai, which, in the Benoni of Piel from mana [מנא], "he led," could signify "leader, guide." In Greek it is manaē [μαναὴ], and with Nun added, manalō [μαναλὼ], as in

units.la: pro שלום , αυλωμών, & alia plura. Porro συνηγορῶ ἡμῶν vertit Syrus ܐܬܝܘܢܝ ܐܘܠܐ ܕܒܝܬܐ ܕܝܢ. Tremel. Filius educationum Herodis. Boderianus in Parisiensi, Filius educationis. Malim educatorum, vel nutritiorum Herodis. concreta enim vox est, non abstracta, derivata à participio secundae conjugationis ܠܐܘܠܦ, educans, forma emphatica ܐܘܠܦܐ, unde nomen ܠܐܘܠܦ, educator. estque filius educatorum Herodis, qui sub iisdem cum Herode fuit educatoribus. ubi observandum, ܒܢܝ, filium in compositione apud Syros consortium saepe & communionem designare. sic ܒܢܝ ܒܢܝ ܒܢܝ, filii civitatis sanctorum,id est, concives sanctorum, Eph.2.19. ܒܢܝ ܒܢܝ ܒܢܝ, filii jugi, id est, ejusdem jugi participes. 2 Cor. 6.14. ܒܢܝ ܒܢܝ ܒܢܝ, filii annorum meorum, id est, coaetanei mei, Gal. 1. 14.
units.tr: for shalom [שלום], aulomon [αυλωμών], and many others. Further, the Syrian renders synēgorō hēmōn as 'atyoni ola d-bayta din (Tremellius: "son of Herod's upbringings"). The Parisian Boderian has "son of upbringing." I would prefer "son of Herod's foster-fathers" or "nurses." The word is a concrete noun, not an abstract one, derived from the participle of the second conjugation meaning "rearing," in its emphatic form, whence the noun "foster-parent." So it means "son of the foster-parents of Herod," that is, one who was brought up under the same foster-parents as Herod. Here it should be noted that among the Syrians "son" in compounds often denotes companionship and fellowship. Thus bnay madinta d-qaddishe, "sons of the city of the saints," that is, fellow citizens of the saints (Eph. 2:19); bnay yuga, "sons of the yoke," that is, sharers in the same yoke (2 Cor. 6:14); and bnay shnay, "sons of my years," that is, my contemporaries (Gal. 1:14).

units.la: VERS. 2. Εἰς τὸ ἔχειν ὁ προσκληθεὶς αὐτός. Nihil necesse videtur repetere εἰς ante ὁ, ut plena sit constructio.
units.tr: VERSE 2. "To have him who was called" [Εἰς τὸ ἔχειν ὁ προσκληθεὶς αὐτός]. There seems to be no need to repeat εἰς before ὁ, so that the construction is complete.

units.la: plena omnino est, quia ὁ regitur à sequente προσ, resolvique potest in προσ ὁ κλῆσιν αὐτοῦ. sicut infra ἡf. 31. τὴς ἀναβᾶσιν αὐτῷ, pro τὴς ἀναβᾶσιν ἐν αὐτῷ.
units.tr: It is indeed complete, because ho is governed by the following pros, and it can be resolved into pros ho klēsin autou [προσ ὁ κλῆσιν αὐτοῦ]. Just as below, at verse 31, tēs anabasin autō [τὴς ἀναβᾶσιν αὐτῷ] stands for tēs anabasin en autō [τὴς ἀναβᾶσιν ἐν αὐτῷ].

units.la: VERS. 6.
units.tr: VERSE 6.

units.la: Cujus nomen erat Bar Suma. Boder. explicat, filius nominis. à Chaldaico ܒܪ pro Hebr. בן, nomen. at Syri Vau illud eo sensu non adhibent. dicunt enim ܫܡܐ vel ܒܪܫܡܐ, nomen. Junius ergo maluit vertere, filius tumoris vel inflationis, qui enunciandis suis divinationibus intumescit, tanquam si e ventre creparet oracula, ἐνσαρξιμύθῳ. certum est ܒܪܫܡܐ, Syris esse cicatricem, livorem, vibicem. item ulcus, plagam tumentem. ut & in Targ. macula, nota, tumor. In Græco est Βαρίησες. id credit Junius esse à Syro ܐܪ quod scientiam veram denotet: adeoque esse filium scientiæ, divinum, divina quadam scientia præditum. Vnde id habeat nescio. nusquam enim apud Syros nec ܐܪ, nec affine aliquid reperio, quod veram scientiam denotet. apud Hebræos à verbo substantivo ܐܪ fit nomen ܪܐܝܐ, quod interdum veram ac realem sapientiam & prudentiam designat, sed id neque Syriacum est, neque huc facit. quid si ex Arabica lingua derivetur? vertitur hoc loco ab Arabe ܒܐܪ ܝܫܘܥ, ubi primo observandum, alterius plane originis & significationis hoc loco esse Ἰησᾶς, quam quum de Servatore dicitur. tum enim Arabs scribit ܝܫܘܥ, ܐܪ. deinde quum Interpres scripsit ܝܫܘܥ, reliquisse eum Jod quod erat in Ἰησᾶς, quia nomen proprium hîc est. alioqui primam radicalem Jod mutari plerumque apud Arabes in Vau, quod & hîc faciendum. tertio ܐܘܬ, ܝܫܘܥ in Alcor. Sura ult. significare suggessit, sufurravit, de diabolo dictum. & nomen ܝܫܘܥ, ܝܫܘܥ, instinctus, susurrus diaboli. Ibid. unde & 2 Cor. 2. 11. pro ὁσ ἀγνοῦμεν τὰ νοήματα αὐτοῦ, Arabs dixit ܢܘܪ, nos novimus instinctus ejus, vel suggestiones ejus. Hinc idem verbum, in passivo nisi fallor, significat insanire, furere, ut scilicet solent qui dæmonis instinctu correpti vaticinantur. quare & apud Græcos ὁ ἐνθουσιασμὸς à furendo dicitur μάντις vates. Sic Act.26.24. ܝܫܘܥ ponitur pro μαίνεσθαι. & ܝܫܘܥ pro μανία. mutato ergo solummodo Vau Arabum in Jod Syrorum & Græcorum, ܝܫܘܥ, Βαρίησες erit filius divini instinctus vel furoris, qui à dæmone correptus furit & vaticinatur. quod non tantum cum munere ejus rectè congruit (dixit enim Lucas fuisse μάγοι ψιλοδοξοφιλῶ) sed & cum interpretatione Syriaca. erit enim idem fere quod ܐܪ ܪܐܝܐ, filius inflationis, qui scilicet instinctu daemonis inflatus, & ut supra dixit Junius, ἐνσαρξιμυθ factus, vaticinatur. scrupulum tamen movet, quod ברpro filio non fit Arabum, qui אבdicunt. nec scripsit hic ברb, sed באר, quod justum denotat Arabibus. videtur ergo potius Arabs suo באר ישוס ad literam expressisse Graecum Βαρηρσέ. Aliunde ergo arcessenda videtur ejus notio. quid si fit Hebraicae derivationis בר ישוע, Βαρηρσά, & exigua mutatione Βαρηρσέ, filius salutis, qui salutis sanitatisque conferendae artem profitetur? Sic Syriacum ברשומא, filius ulcerum, erit Medicus qui ulcerum curationem prositetur. שומא certe non inflationem tumoremve quemvis, sed eum qui cicatricum ulcerumque est, denotat. Aethiopicus scribit ברשעא praestat ex lingua Hebraea vocis hujus etymon depromere, quia Magus iste dicitur Judaeus fuisse.
units.tr: Whose name was Bar Suma. Boder explains it as "son of the name," taking the Chaldee bar for the Hebrew ben [בן], "son," and the word for "name." But the Syrians do not use that word in that sense. They say shuma or bar-shuma for "name." Junius therefore preferred to render it "son of swelling or inflation," one who puffs himself up when he utters his divinations, as if his oracles burst out of his belly [ἐνσαρξιμύθῳ]. It is certain that in Syriac bar-shuma means a scar, a bruise, or a weal, also an ulcer or a swelling wound, as in the Targum too: a spot, a mark, a swelling. In Greek it is Βαρίησες [Bariēsēs]. Junius believes this comes from the Syriac word which denotes true knowledge, so that it means "son of knowledge," endowed with some divine knowledge. I do not know where he got that. Nowhere among the Syrians do I find that word, or anything akin to it, meaning true knowledge. Among the Hebrews the noun from the substantive verb is used, which sometimes denotes true and real wisdom and prudence, but that is neither Syriac nor relevant here. What if it is derived from the Arabic language? Here it is rendered by the Arab as bar Yeshu', and here we must first observe that the Yeshu' in this place is of quite a different origin and meaning from Iēsas [Ἰησᾶς], which is used of the Saviour. For there the Arab writes Yeshu' with the same letters. Second, since the translator wrote Yeshu', he kept the yod that was in Iēsas, because here it is a proper name. Otherwise the first radical yod is mostly changed to waw among the Arabs, and that should be done here too. Third, the root in the last sura of the Qur'an means to have suggested or whispered, said of the devil, and the noun means an instinct or whisper of the devil. In the same place, at 2 Corinthians 2.11, where the Greek has "we are not ignorant of his devices" [ὁσ ἀγνοῦμεν τὰ νοήματα αὐτοῦ], the Arab says "we know his instincts" or "his suggestions." Hence the same verb in the passive, unless I am mistaken, means to be insane or to rave, as those do who prophesy when seized by the instinct of a demon. Wherefore among the Greeks too, enthusiasm [ὁ ἐνθουσιασμὸς] is named from raving, and a seer [μάντις] is a prophet. So at Acts 26.24 the word is used for "to be mad" [μαίνεσθαι], and the noun for "madness" [μανία]. So if only the Arabic waw is changed to the yod of the Syrians and Greeks, the name Bariēsēs will mean son of divine instinct or fury, one who, seized by a demon, raves and prophesies. This agrees well not only with his office (for Luke called him a magus, "a lover of vainglory" [μάγοι ψιλοδοξοφιλῶ]), but also with the Syriac interpretation. It will be almost the same as "son of swelling," that is, one who, puffed up by the instigation of a demon and, as Junius said above, made ensarximythos, prophesies. There is a difficulty, however, because bar for "son" is not Arabic, which says ab [אב]. Nor does the Arab write bar here, but ba'r, which to the Arabs means "just." It seems therefore that the Arab has rather expressed the Greek Bariēsē literally with his bar Yeshu'. Its meaning must therefore be sought elsewhere. What if it is of Hebrew derivation, bar Yeshua [בר ישוע], Baryēsa, and by a slight change Bariēsē, "son of salvation," one who professes the art of bringing salvation and health? Then the Syriac bar-shuma, "son of ulcers," will be a physician who professes the cure of ulcers. Shuma certainly does not denote swelling or any tumour, but what belongs to scars and ulcers. The Ethiopian writes bar-sha'a. It is better to draw the etymology of this word from the Hebrew language, since this magus is said to have been a Jew.

units.la: Vers. 8.
units.tr: Verse 8.

units.la: ܒܪ ܫܘܡܐ ܕܐܠܝܡܐ ܣܡ ܪܫܝܡܐ. Resistebat autem ipsis iste magus Bar-Schuma, cujus nomen exponitur Elumas. Sentit Doctiss. Drusius, Ἐλύμας esse Arabicum עלים, עלם, sapiens. quia id convenit cum interpretamento ejus μάγος. sic enim apud Persas sapientes dicebantur. confirmat eam sententiam Cl. Beza ex Arab. interpretatione Pentateuchi a R. Saadia facta, ubi pro Hebr. חרטם fit עלמא. Gen. 41. 8. Exod. 8. 19. in quibus locis editio Cl. Erpenii, pro חרטם habet ܥܠܝܡ, pro חכמים vero ܥܠܡ, ܥܠܡܐ. fateor tamen Exod. 7. 11. כהאין usurpari pro מכשפים, עלמא autem pro חכמים & חרטים. quod quidem me adegit antehac ut crederem Ἐλύμας esse Arabum עלים, atque idem esse quod μάγος. prout ad Mat. 2. 1. observavimus. sed jam rursus haeremus, quia Syrus non scribit per Ain sed per Aleph. ut & Arabs atque Aethiopicus, qui legunt الماس. praesertim vero, quia ex mente Syri Ἐλύμας non exponitur per μάγος, neque μάγος per Ἐλύμας. sed Ἐλύμας est interpretamentum nominis Βαριησοῦς, seu ut Syrus vertit ברשושא. quod aperte Lucas indicat. dicit enim, ἀνθίςτατο ὃ αὐτῆς Ἐλύμας ὁ μάγος, ἔτω γὰρ μεθερμηνευόμενον τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ: at quodnam erat τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ? Id. γ. 6. dixit, ὦ ὄνομα Βαριησοῦς. ergo Βαριησοῦς exponitur per Ἐλύμας. nec immerito rejicit Junius sententiam Tremellii, qui dictum vult quasi ישׁ אלי, id est, divinum consilium. an ad verbum, Deus meus consilium? non videtur literis ac rei satis aptum. nec scio ubi ישׁ pro עצה, consilium denotet. minus tamen placet Junii sententia, qui ab Arabico אלאם derivat, quod illis, inquit, est mussitare. utinam quam verbi formam intellexerit sciremus. non video enim cujus id conjugationis esse queat, nisi quartæ, à themate לאם, reprehendit, culpavit. quod hic plane est alienum. nobis potius Ἐλύμας videtur esse Hebræum vel Chaldæum הלימא, sanator, curator, à חלם, sanare, quo sensu non apud Hebræos tantum, sed & apud Syros frequenter obtinet. nec discrepat à בר ישועה, filius salutis, & בר שומא, filius ulcerum, de quibus supra γ. 6. nec insolens est, durissimæ aspirationis ה per Ε reddi. talia sunt חנוך, Ἐνὼχ, Ἐξηρὶν, Ἐξεὼν. neque terminationem א in ας mutari. talia sunt תאמא, Θωμᾶς, ברנאא, Βαρναβᾶς. ברואא, Βαρξεβᾶς. Etsi autem de etymo vocis μάγος in notis nostris, ad Matt. 2. 1. quædam diximus, quia tamen hic rursus occurrit, non pigebit, quæ Rabbi David de Pomis in Lexico suo suggerit, addere. Radicem dat פנש, quam exponit רמא, innuit. inde nomen אמנישא pro רמא, nutus. inde מנוש pro כשוף, præstigiator, לפי שהמעשים בשעת סעדתם עותקין ואין מתיאין רבר בפיהם, אלא מתיאין קול שאינו מחותך בנעויות והנעיומות בלבן, id est, quia magi ubi cibum capiunt, silent neque quicquam ore proferunt, præter vocem nulla elegantia distinctam, qua tota in corde ipsorum est. fit penes authorem fides. Fuit sane Magorum genus Judæis apprime invisum. unde lex apud ipsos הלופר רבר מן המעש חייב הויה מינו , qui discit quicquam à Mago , rcus est mortûs.
units.tr: Bar-Shuma d-Elima sam reshima. But this magician Bar-Shuma, whose name is interpreted as Elumas, withstood them. The learned Drusius holds that Elumas is the Arabic 'alim, 'alam, meaning wise, since this agrees with the rendering magos, for among the Persians the wise were called by that name. The illustrious Beza confirms this view from the Arabic translation of the Pentateuch made by R. Saadia, where 'alama stands for the Hebrew chartummim (חרטם) at Gen. 41. 8 and Exod. 8. 19. In those passages the edition of the illustrious Erpenius has 'alim for chartum, and 'alam or 'alama for chakhamim. I admit, however, that in Exod. 7. 11 kahhaʾin is used for mekhashshephim (מכשפים), and 'alma for chakhamim and chartummim. This indeed led me formerly to believe that Elumas is the Arabic 'alim and the same as magos, as I noted at Matt. 2. 1. But now we hesitate again, because the Syriac writes not with Ain but with Aleph, as the Arab and the Ethiopian do, who read al-mas. Above all, because in the Syriac's sense Elumas is not explained by magos, nor magos by Elumas. Rather, Elumas is the interpretation of the name Bariesous, or as the Syriac renders it, Bar-Shusha. Luke plainly indicates this: "Elymas the magician withstood them, for so his name is translated" [ἀνθίστατο αὐτοῖς Ἐλύμας ὁ μάγος, οὕτω γὰρ μεθερμηνευόμενον τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ]. But what was his name? In Acts 13. 6 it is said: "whose name was Bariesous" [ᾧ ὄνομα Βαριησοῦς]. Therefore Bariesous is explained by Elumas. Nor without reason does Junius reject the view of Tremellius, who wants the word to be as if it were divine counsel, that is, yesh eli (ישׁ אלי). Would that is mean, word for word, my God counsel? That does not seem sufficiently suited to the letters or to the matter, and I do not know where yesh denotes counsel (ʿetsah, עצה). Yet Junius's view, which derives it from the Arabic alam, which he says means to mutter, pleases me less. I wish we knew what conjugation of the verb he had in mind, for I cannot see which conjugation it could be except the fourth, from the root lam, to reprove, to blame, which here is plainly out of place. To me it seems rather that Elumas is the Hebrew or Chaldee halima, healer, curer, from chalam, to heal, a sense that is common not only among the Hebrews but also among the Syrians. It does not differ from bar yeshua, son of salvation, and bar shuma, son of ulcers, of which we spoke above at chapter 6. Nor is it unusual for the very harsh aspirate ה to be rendered by Ε; such are Chanoch, Enoch, Ezriun and Exeon. Nor is it unusual for the ending א to be changed into ας; such are Thoma, Thomas, Barnaa, Barnabas, and Barsaba, Barsabas. Although we have said some things about the etymology of the word magos in our notes on Matt. 2. 1, because it occurs again here, it will not be tedious to add what Rabbi David de Pomis suggests in his Lexicon. He gives the root pnsh, which he explains as ramaʾ, to beckon. From this comes the noun amnisha for ramaʾ, a nod. From this comes manush for kashuf (כשוף), a sorcerer, because magicians, when they take their meal, keep silent and utter nothing with the mouth, but only make a sound not distinguished by any clear articulation, all of which is in their heart [לפי שהמעשים בשעת סעדתם עותקין ואין מתיאין דבר בפיהם, אלא מתיאין קול שאינו מחותך בנעימות והנעימות בלבן]. The credit for this rests with the author. Certainly the race of the Magi was especially hateful to the Jews, whence the law among them: whoever learns anything from a magus is guilty of death [הלומד דבר מן המכשף חייב מיתה].

units.la: VERS. 10. Οὐ πωύστῃ Ἀλαςφίφων τὰς ἰδὰς Κυρίω τὰς ἀϑέαςς.Manifestum est Ἀλαςφίφῳ opponi τῷ ἀϑέως πιῶν. At utJoan.1.23 non laudavimus ἀζυνεν vel ἀϑέως ποιῶν verti complanare,ita hic non videtur nobis Ἀλαςφίφων recte accipi pro suffodere viam,ut iter non fit pervium. viæ planæ, λᾶϛ dicuntur Luc. 3.5. בקעה Esa.40.4 cui opponuntur αἱ τεαχεῖαι,aspera,salebrosa, הרים Prophetæ,quasi elevata dicas,quales sunt viæ suffossæ. at ἀϑέως מישר dicuntur, id est, rectitudo, cui opponitur ibidem עקש, tortuosum, deflexum, τὰ σκολιά apud Lucam. ergo Ἀλαςφίφων τὰς ἰδὰς hic est σκολιὰς πιῶν. sensus est, cur tu vias Domini rectas,quæ ambages nullas, nullos curvitatum flexus habent,à rectitudine pervertis,tortuosas reddis, & fraudibus tuis in varios anfractus deflectis? Syrus recte vertit [illegible, ~12 letters] torquere, detorquere,ea enim propria est vocis significatio. quo sensu & ἡ ἑλιὰ διεσπαμμένη à Syro redditur [illegible, ~14 letters] gens detorta,tortuosa,Belgicè een verdraept geslachte. Velim ergo hic transferre, an non cessabis divertere vias Domini rectas ? id est, in diversum vertere, ut à rectitudine sua aliorsum deflectant. sicut supra ϒf. 8. ζητῶν Ἀλαςφίψαι τ ἀνϑρωπῶν ἀνὰ τ πίστως, quarens divertere propratorem à fide.ubi & Syrus [illegible, ~12 letters] detorquere. ut & Tit.3.11. ἐξίςρεψαι ἀπ' vertit [illegible, ~10 letters] detortus est.
units.tr: VERSE 10. Οὐ παύσῃ διαστρέφων τὰς ὁδοὺς Κυρίου τὰς εὐθείας; [Will you not cease to pervert the straight ways of the Lord?] It is clear that διαστρέφων [perverting] is set against εὐθεῖα [straight]. But just as we did not approve of rendering ἰσοῦν [to level] or εὐθύνειν [to make straight] at John 1:23 as "to level," so here it does not seem to us that διαστρέφειν [to pervert] should rightly be taken to mean "to dig up the road so that the way is not passable." Level roads are called λεῖα [smooth] at Luke 3:5, Hebrew בקעה [biq'ah] at Isa. 40:4, and they are set against αἱ τραχεῖαι [the rough ways], rough and stony, Hebrew הרים [harim, mountains], as the Prophet says, as one might say, raised places, like dug-up roads. But εὐθεῖα [straight] is called מישר [mishor], that is, uprightness, to which is set against it in the same place עקש ['iqqesh], crooked, bent, τὰ σκολιά [the crooked things] in Luke. Therefore διαστρέφων τὰς ὁδούς [perverting the ways] here means σκολιὰς ποιῶν [making crooked]. The sense is: why do you pervert the straight ways of the Lord, which have no windings and no bends of curvature, from their uprightness, making them crooked, and turning them aside by your frauds into various twists? The Syrian rightly renders it [illegible] to twist, to distort, for that is the proper meaning of the word. In the same sense the γενεὰ διεστραμμένη [crooked generation] is rendered by the Syrian [illegible] a distorted, twisted race, in Dutch een verdraept geslachte. I would therefore like to translate here, "will you not cease to turn aside the straight ways of the Lord?" that is, to turn them to the opposite, so that they are bent away from their straightness, as above at 13:8, ζητῶν διαστρέψαι τὸν ἀνθύπατον ἀπὸ τῆς πίστεως [seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith], where the Syrian also has [illegible] to twist. So also at Titus 3:11, ἐξέστραπται [is perverted], the Syrian renders [illegible] is twisted.

units.la: VERS. 14. Τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τ σαββάτων, pro ἡ σαββάτῳ. σάββατα enim in plurali, significatione singulari dicere in more est Euangelistis ex usu LXX Interpretum, qui Exod. 20.10. Die septimo erit שבת sabbathum Domino Deo tuo, dixerunt σάββατα Κυρίῳ. & sic passim.
units.tr: VERSE 14. Τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῶν σαββάτων [on the day of the sabbaths], for τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ σαββάτου [on the day of the sabbath]. For it is the habit of the Evangelists, following the usage of the Septuagint, to use the plural σάββατα [sabbaths] with a singular meaning. The Seventy, at Exod. 20:10, where it says "the seventh day is the sabbath (Hebrew שבת [shabbat]) of the Lord your God," wrote σάββατα Κυρίῳ [sabbaths to the Lord]. And so throughout.

units.la: VERS. 15. Post lectionem legis & Prophetarum. Notum est Veteris Testamenti libros in tres classes fuisse disperti-tos, tos, in תורה נביאים וכתובים Legem, Prophetas, & Hagiographa. Harum tertia in publicis coetibus ordinarie non legebatur. Lex & Prophetæ legebantur, divisis in eum finem libris legis in 54 sectiones, quæ פרשיות dicuntur, lectaque singulis septimanis sectione una (nisi quod bis duas minores conjungunt) quotannis legem absolvunt. His totidem selectæ hinc inde ex Prophetis sectiones respondent, quæ הפטורות dicuntur. de quibus vide Eliam in Thisbi in voce פטר. ubi Prophetarum lectionem post Antiochi demum Epiphanis tempora, quum legis lectio palam & severe esset interdicta, ortam docet. retentam vero deinceps. Causam autem, cur sermones prophetici non vocentur דברי תורה, verba legis, sed solis libris Mosis ea appellatio competat, assignat author הליכות שלם, quia libri Mosis dati sunt omnibus seculis: At Prophetarum sermones sunt דברי הקבלה, quia quamque prophetiam acceperunt a Spiritu S. secundum temporis necessitatem, aut seculi istius, aut alicujus facti. quod non omnino est spernendum.
units.tr: VERSE 15. After the reading of the law and the Prophets. It is known that the books of the Old Testament were divided into three classes, into תורה, נביאים, וכתובים [Torah, Nevi'im, and Ketuvim], the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa. The third of these was not ordinarily read in public assemblies. The Law and the Prophets were read. For this purpose the books of the Law were divided into 54 sections, called פרשיות [parashiyyot], and one section was read each week (except that they join two smaller ones twice), so that the Law was finished each year. To these correspond the same number of sections chosen from the Prophets here and there, called הפטורות [haftarot]. On these see Elijah in the Tishbi under the word פטר. He teaches that the reading of the Prophets arose only after the time of Antiochus Epiphanes, when reading the Law was openly and severely forbidden, and was afterwards retained. The author gives the reason why the prophetic sermons are not called דברי תורה [words of the Law], the words of the Law, but that name belongs only to the books of Moses: he says in הליכות עולם [Halikhot Olam] that the books of Moses were given to all ages, whereas the sermons of the Prophets are דברי הקבלה [words of tradition], because each prophet received his prophecy from the Holy Spirit according to the need of the time, either of that age or of some event. This is not to be altogether despised.

units.la: I B I D. Miserunt ad eos οἱ ἑξαποστάλωσι, præfecti synagogæ. inepte hic habet Æthiopicus ליקן כהנאת, id est, οἱ ἐχθεῖς. pro מנאת סרבר. sic enim præfectos synagogæ alibi vocat.
units.tr: IBID. They sent to them οἱ ἀρχισυνάγωγοι [the rulers of the synagogue]. Here the Ethiopian foolishly has ליקן כהנאת [the priests], that is, οἱ ἱερεῖς [the priests], for מנאת סרבר [the rulers of the synagogue]. For he calls the rulers of the synagogue by this name elsewhere too.

units.la: V E R S. 17. Εν τῇ παροικίᾳ ἐν γῇ Αἰγύπτου. Hebraicè בהיותם אורחים, indigenæ, sed accolæ tantum & inquilini. μὴ βεβαιωσ ὑψηλῇ. id Exod.14.7. dicitur בני רמה, ἐν χειρὶ ὑψηλῇ.
units.tr: VERSE 17. Ἐν τῇ παροικίᾳ ἐν γῇ Αἰγύπτου [in the sojourning in the land of Egypt]. In Hebrew בהיותם גרים [while they were strangers], not natives but only sojourners and resident aliens. μετὰ βραχίονος ὑψηλοῦ [with an uplifted arm]. This is said at Exod. 14:7 as בני רמה [with a high hand], ἐν χειρὶ ὑψηλῇ.

units.la: V E R S. 18. ⟨Syriac⟩ O, & nutrivit eos. In Græco est, ἐτροποφόρησεν ὡς τὴς. ad quam vocem D. Drusius annotat ex Hezychio, ἐτροποφέρησεν, ἐτεψεν. lapsus est. nam apud Hezych. scribitur ἐτροφοφόρησε. atque ita textum Lucæ à Syro lectum probabiliter admodum conjectat doctiss. Beza. Addo quoque ab Arabe, qui similiter vertit, ⟨Arabic⟩, deinde nutrivit eos in deserto. male Junius, qui-que que eum secutus est Beza duxit. Jle enim non duxit, sed nutrivit denotat. Æthiopicus quoque habet שיזמ, aluit eos. quod si legatur ἐτροφοφόρησα (quæ vox educandi significatione extat, 2 Mach.7.27. quasi dicas τροφὼ φίρε cibum adferre, vel δίxλω τ τροφῆς φέρειν instar nutricis gestare) recte observavit doctiss. Beza respici illud Mosis Num. 11. 12. באשר ישא האמן את הינק. sicut portabit nutricius fugentem. At ἐτροπροφόρησε petitum est ex Deut. 1. 31. ubi נשאך יהוה אלהיך כאשר ישא איש את בנו, tulit te Dominus Deus tuus, sicut ferret vir filium suum, LXX verterunt ἐτροποφόρησέ σε κύριος ὁ Θεός σου, ὡς εἴτις τροποφορήσει ἄνθρωπος τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ.
units.tr: VERSE 18. ⟨Syriac⟩ And he nourished them. In the Greek it is ἐτροποφόρησεν ὡς τροφός [he bore them as a nurse]. On this word Dr. Drusius notes from Hesychius, ἐτροποφέρησεν, ἔθρεψεν [he nourished]. He has slipped, for in Hesychius it is written ἐτροφοφόρησε, and the most learned Beza fairly probably conjectures that the text of Luke was read in this way by the Syrian. I add also the Arabic, who similarly translates, ⟨Arabic⟩, then he nourished them in the desert. Junius, and Beza who followed him, were wrong to render it led, for the word denotes not led but nourished. The Ethiopian also has שיזמ [he fed them]. If one reads ἐτροφοφόρησα (a word that exists in the sense of bringing up, 2 Macc. 7:27, as if you said τροφὼ φέρειν [to bring food], or like a nurse carrying a child in her arms), the most learned Beza rightly observed that the passage of Moses in Num. 11:12 is in view, באשר ישא האמן את הינק [as a nurse carries the suckling]: as a nurse carries the nursling. But ἐτροποφόρησε is taken from Deut. 1:31, where it reads נשאך יהוה אלהיך כאשר ישא איש את בנו [the Lord your God bore you, as a man bears his son]: the Seventy rendered it ἐτροποφόρησέ σε κύριος ὁ Θεός σου, ὡς εἴ τις τροποφορήσει ἄνθρωπος τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ.

units.la: VERS. 20. Καὶ μὴ τῶν τὰ ὡς ἔτη πεντακοσίοις ἐ πνήκοντα ἰδωκε κριτὰς ἕως Σαμουὴλ. omnino assentior iis, qui hic annos, quibus rexerunt judices, supputari nolunt (sic enim annos hosce 450 cum 480 qui ab exitu ex Ægypto ad templi Salomonici initium effluxisse dicuntur 1 Reg. 6.5. conciliare impossibile videtur) sed qui à nato Isaaco usque ad Judices fluxere. quasi scriptum sit, καὶ μὴ τῶν τῶν ὡς ἔτη πεντακοσίους ἐ πνήκοντα πεντηκοντα, ἰδωκε κριτὰς. ut non quamdiu rexerint Judices, sed quando eos Deus dederit, indicetur: nempe post ea quæ v. 17.18.19. narrata fuerant, quæ 450 circiter annis gesta fuere. convenit computus. Nam à nato Isaaco ad natum Jacobum sunt 60 anni. inde ad introitum in Ægyptum, 130 inde ad exitum, 210. inde ad introitum in terram Canaan, 40. inde ad distributionem terræ, anni 7. qui simul faciunt 447 annos, id est, circiter 450. desunt enim solummodo tres. Recte autem ad nati Isaaci tempus refertur illud versus 17, elegit Deus patres nostros. tum enim Deus, qui jam Abrahamum elegerat ex omnibus terræ populis, ex omnibus Abrahami liberis elegit Isaacum, in cujus familia fœdus consisteret, dicens, in Isaaco vocabitur semen tum. Quia autem Cl. Junius novam hic ex Arabica translatione sententiam adfert, visum nobis est, sincere Arabem & verbotenus reddere. sic is habet, v.20. Et dedit ipsis Iudices 450 annis ad Samuelem Prophetam. Ϛf. 21. Tum petierunt regem, deditque ipsis Deus Saulem filium Kis virum è tribu Benjamin, 40 annis. Ϛf. 22. Deinde amovit eum, & post eum suscitavit ipsis Davidem regem, &c. quæ ut cum Syro plane conveniunt, ita à Junii & interpretatione & quam inde eruit sententia longe sunt aliena. Sententiam ejus, qui vult, videat in Actis Apostolicis ex Arabica translatione Latine ab ipso redditis.
units.tr: VERS. 20. Καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα ὡς ἔτη τετρακόσια πεντήκοντα ἔδωκε κριτὰς ἕως Σαμουήλ. I entirely agree with those who do not want the years during which the judges ruled to be counted here. For that reading makes the years come to 450, and it seems impossible to reconcile them with the 480 years said to have run from the exodus from Egypt to the beginning of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:1). Instead, the count should run from the birth of Isaac. It is as if the text read: καὶ μετὰ τῶν ὡς ἔτη τετρακόσια πεντήκοντα, ἔδωκε κριτάς, so that what is indicated is not how long the judges ruled, but when God gave them: namely, after the events narrated in verses 17, 18 and 19, which took place about 450 years later. The reckoning fits. From the birth of Isaac to the birth of Jacob are 60 years; from there to the entry into Egypt, 130; from there to the exodus, 210; from there to the entry into the land of Canaan, 40; and from there to the distribution of the land, 7. Together these make 447 years, that is, about 450; only three are missing. Verse 17, God chose our fathers, is rightly referred to the time of Isaac's birth. For then God, who had already chosen Abraham from all the peoples of the earth, chose Isaac from all Abraham's children, in whose family the covenant would stand, saying, in Isaac shall thy seed be called. Since the learned Junius here brings forward a new interpretation from the Arabic translation, I have thought it right to render the Arabic faithfully and word for word. It reads thus in verse 20: And he gave them judges for 450 years, until Samuel the prophet. Verse 21: Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul, son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for 40 years. Verse 22: Then he removed him, and after him he raised up for them David as king, and so on. These agree entirely with the Syriac, but both Junius's rendering and the sense he draws from it are far from it. Whoever wishes may see his interpretation in the Acts of the Apostles, rendered into Latin by himself from the Arabic translation.

units.la: VERS. 24. Πρὸ προσώπου τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ. Vulgatus & Eras. ad verbum, ante faciem adventus ejus. Beza, coram eo jam adventante. Arabs inter manus ejus (id est, coram eo. sic enim loquuntur passim Arabes) in adventu ejus. Syrus simpliciter ante adventum ejus. quod rectum est, modo ante non ad tempus referatur (sic enim cæteris etiam prophetis, quantumvis à Christo remotis, id tribui posse, rectè sensit doctissimè Beza) sed ad locum situmve. quæ ambiguitas quoque est in Hebraeo מִלִּפְנֵי. verti enim poterit, vel antequam veniret, vel coram adventu ejus. Ambiguitatem eam non habet πρὸ προσώπου τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ. id enim, ut rectè loquitur Cl. Beza, non tam præcedens tempus declarat, quam præsentiam illius, cui aliquis præeat, quique jam in adventu est. imo nequaquam præcedens tempus declarat. est enim πρὸ προσώπου, in conspectu ipsius rei, ita sitæ, ut faciem suam veluti obvertat nobis. sensus itaque est, prædicasse quidem Johannem paulo ante Christum, sed tamen quum jam adesset Christus, adventusque ejus homines jam respiceret, faciemque suam ipsis obverteret. habent ergo ipsa verba textus, etiam Latinè ἐξ πόδα reddita, miram quandam emphasin, quæ obscuritatem, si qua in iis est, facile compensat. sic Num. 19.4. וְהוּא אֶל נִכְחֵי פְּנֵי אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד, LXX ἐ ῥανῶ ἀπέναντι ᾿Ἰ προσώ-που [Greek and Syriac phrase, ending with] σωτηρίας ⸗ ... sufficiebat אַחֵר ... ante tabernaculum. Sed emphasis insignem habet, ante faciem tabernaculi, id est, sic constitutus ante tabernaculum, ut id eum quasi respiciat faciemque ei obvertat.
units.tr: VERS. 24. Πρὸ προσώπου τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ. The Vulgate and Erasmus render it word for word: before the face of his coming. Beza: in his presence, while he was already coming. The Arabic has between his hands (that is, in his presence; for Arabs commonly speak this way), at his coming. The Syriac simply has before his coming. This is correct, provided that before is not taken as referring to time (for, as the learned Beza rightly saw, this can be said of the other prophets too, however far they lived from Christ), but to place or position. The same ambiguity is found in the Hebrew מִלִּפְנֵי, which may be rendered either before he came or in the presence of his coming. The Greek πρὸ προσώπου τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ does not have this ambiguity. For, as the learned Beza rightly says, it declares not so much a preceding time as the presence of one to whom someone goes before, and who is already at hand. Indeed it does not express a preceding time at all. πρὸ προσώπου means in the sight of the thing itself, situated so that it, as it were, turns its face toward us. The sense, then, is that John indeed preached shortly before Christ, but when Christ was already present, and John looked upon his coming and turned his face toward the people. The words of the text, even when rendered in Latin as ante faciem, therefore carry a remarkable emphasis, which easily makes up for any obscurity in them. So in Numbers 19:4, the Hebrew וְהוּא אֶל נִכְחֵי פְּנֵי אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד, the Septuagint has ἀπέναντι τοῦ προσώπου, and the Hebrew word אַחֵר would have sufficed as before the tabernacle. But the emphasis is remarkable: before the face of the tabernacle, that is, placed so directly before the tabernacle that it, as it were, looks at him and turns its face toward him.

units.la: VERS. 27. τῆσν ἀγνοήσαντες. Beza, quum hunc ignorarent, incertum est, ad personam Christi referat, de qua v. 25. an ad λόγον σωτηρίας, de quo v. 26. vertit enim masculino genere, sermonem salutis. At Vulgatus neutro genere, verbum salutis. quum ergo hîc dixit, hunc ignorantes, certum est, cum τῆσν non ad λόγον, sed ad personam Christi retulisse. Contra Syrus ad λόγον vertit enim τῆσν foeminino genere, ob ܟܠܡܐ, verbum, quod foemineum sexum sequitur. ἀγνοήσαντες autem vertit ܐܬܝ ܐܢܫܝ, Boderianus, non consenserunt ei. Tremel. rectius, non senserunt eum sermonem. ܫܡܥ proprie est sensit. deinde experimento quasi personsum cognovit, certam alicujus rei notitiam habuit. ut Marc. 5. 29. ... ἤγνω τῷ σώματι. Act. 5. 2. ... quum & ipsa cognitionem rei habueret. Hebr. 13. 2. Quidam Angelos hospitio exceperunt ... insciì, nescientes. 1 Joan. 2. 3. ... ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν. ita & hoc loco, τῆσν ἀγνοήσαντες vertit ... non cognoverunt illud verbum, id est, non habuerunt ejus veram & experimentalem cognitionem, sic ut conscii sibi fuissent veritatis, ejusque vim in animis sensissent. Sequitur, ἡ τῆς φωνῆς τῶν ... ἀκουσάντων ... κείμενα ... ἐναγνωστόμενα ... ἐνσωμάτων. Syrus, Arabs, & Beza, ἐπὶ τῆς φωνῆς construunt cum ἀγνοήσαντες, satis commode. possis tamen etiam cum ἐνσωμάτων πωτω construere, si modo κῆ vertas etiam, hoc modo: Qui enim habitabant Hierosolymis & primores eorum, quum hunc ignorarent, etiam voces Prophetarum &c. judicando (vel damnando) impleverunt. & inducor, ut τῶν rectius ad personam, quam ad sermonem referri credam, quia κ̔ράιλες coquoque referri debet.
units.tr: VERS. 27. τὸν ἀγνοήσαντες. Beza's since they did not know him leaves it uncertain whether the pronoun refers to the person of Christ, mentioned in verse 25, or to the word of salvation, mentioned in verse 26; for he renders the word in the masculine, the message of salvation. The Vulgate, however, uses the neuter, the word of salvation. Since it says here not knowing him, it is certain that the translator referred τὸν to the person of Christ and not to the word. The Syriac, by contrast, refers it to the word, for it renders τὸν in the feminine gender, on account of word, which takes the feminine. It renders ἀγνοήσαντες by the Syriac ithi anshi, which the Boderian text gives as they did not agree with him. Tremellius more correctly has they did not perceive that word. The verb shama properly means to perceive, and then, as it were by experience, to know a thing personally, to have a certain knowledge of something. Compare Mark 5:29, where the woman felt in her body (ἔγνω τῷ σώματι). Acts 5:2: and she herself was aware of the matter. Hebrews 13:2: some have entertained angels in their house … unawares, not knowing. 1 John 2:3: by this we know (ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν). So also here, τὸν ἀγνοήσαντες is to be rendered: they did not know that word, that is, they had no true and experiential knowledge of it, so that they would have been conscious of its truth and would have felt its power in their minds. There follows: ἡ τῆς φωνῆς τῶν ... ἀκουσάντων ... κείμενα ... ἐναγνωστόμενα ... ἐνσωμάτων. The Syriac, the Arabic and Beza construe ἐπὶ τῆς φωνῆς with ἀγνοήσαντες, which is reasonably suitable. Yet one could also construe it with ἐκπληρώσαντες, if only one renders καὶ as also, thus: For those who lived in Jerusalem, and their rulers, since they did not know him, also fulfilled the voices of the prophets, read every sabbath, by judging (or condemning). I am inclined to think that τῶν refers more correctly to the person than to the word, since the phrase the rulers must also be referred to the same.

units.la: VERS. 32. Et nos vobis euangelizamus eam promissionem quae patribus facta est, ὅτι πωτῶ ὁ Θεὸς ἐκπεπλήρωκε τοῖς τέκνοις αὐτῶν ἡμῖν. Erasmus, Beza & Syrus ὅτι accipiunt ἐκπεπληρωκώς, quod expleverit, vel explevisse eam Deum &c. Vulgatus ἀπεπληρωκώς, quoniam hanc Deus adimplevit. etsi fortassis & illud quoniam, ex peculiari huic interpreti usu ἐκπεπληρωκώς accipi queat. Potest autem ὅτι non inepte ita sumi, ut causam reddat Paulus, cur promissionem patribus factam ipse ipsis jam annunciet, quia, inquit, Deus jam eam nobis, qui patrum filii sumus, explevit. tempus itaque suadet & urget, ut quod explevit nobis, nos vobis annunciemus. τοῖς τέκνοις αὐτῶν ἡμῖν, Syrus transposuit ἡμῖν τοῖς τέκνοις αὐτῶν, ne necesse sit particulam exegeticam nempe aut scilicet aut id est inferere. quod fecerunt Erasmus & Beza, filiis illorum, id est, nobis. planius est, nobis filiis illorum.
units.tr: VERS. 32. And we bring you good news of the promise made to the fathers, that God has fulfilled the same to us their children. Erasmus, Beza and the Syriac take ὅτι as having fulfilled (ἐκπεπληρωκώς), that is, that God has fulfilled it, or has fulfilled that promise, and so on. The Vulgate reads having fulfilled (ἐκπεπληρωκώς) as since God has fulfilled this; though perhaps the word since may also be understood as ἐκπεπληρωκώς in that translator's peculiar usage. ὅτι may not unsuitably be taken so that Paul gives the reason why he now announces to them the promise made to the fathers: because, he says, God has already fulfilled it for us, who are the sons of the fathers. The time therefore urges and requires that we announce to you what he has fulfilled for us. The Syriac transposed τοῖς τέκνοις αὐτῶν ἡμῖν to to us, their children, so that there is no need to insert an explanatory particle such as namely, that is or id est. Erasmus and Beza did insert one: to their sons, that is, to us. It is plainer to say to us, the sons of them.

units.la: VERS. 33. Ὡς ἐν τῷ Ψαλμῷ τῷ δευτέρῳ γέγραπται. Syrus, Arabs & Æthiopicus legerunt quoque τῷ δευτέρῳ. Vide porro notas Clar. Bezae, ubi quum mentio fiat Davidis Kimchii, visum est Commentarium ejus in Psalmi istius initium adferre, & quia non recte à doct. Paulo Fagio translatus est, accuratius interpretari. sic ait magister, זה המזמור השני כן מציאנו אותו בכל הספרים המדוקים שהוא ראש מזמור ובחשבן כתבין אותו, id est, Hic psalmus est psalmus secundus. & sic reperimus eum in omnibus correctis libris, quod nempe sit caput Psalmi. atque in suppputatione scribunt eum secundum. Cave vertas, quod sit caput Psalmorum. Sic enim non tantum ad primum pertineret, sed & primi initium faceret. quum contra mens magistri sit, ex correctissimis exemplaribus probare, hunc Psalmum secundum esse. Mens ergo istorum verborum est, correctissima exemplaria non exhibere hæc verba הַיּוֹם בְּנִי אַתָּה tanquam uno tenore annexa Psalmo primo, sed tanquam separata, & מִזְמוֹר שִׁיר caput psalmi, id est, novi psalmi initium constituentia. quæ libenter huc attulimus, quia usitatam in hoc Actorum loco lectionem approbant & firmant. Addit quidem Magister, quosdam Magistros dicere, Beatus vir &c. & quare fremuerunt gentes, psalmum unum esse. idque quia quotiescunque David sectionem aliquam charam habuerit, inchoavit eam ab יאשרי, beatus, & finiverit per יאשרי, beatus. verum refragantur emendatissimi libri, & ratio ea vere frivola est, nec perpetua. vide Psalmos 32. 112. 119. qui incipiunt ab אשרי, sed sic non desinunt. Locus qui ex Psal. 2. citatur est, Tu es filius meus, ego hodie genui te. Christum non ex æterna e Patre generatione, sed ex novæ per resurrectionem vitæ collatione, filium Dei vocari, resurrectionis tempore genitum, ex isto loco colligunt Divinitatis Christi hostes. Enervant argumentum viri magni, quod quamvis ego hodie genui te referatur ab Apostolo ad resurrectionem, non tamen recens Christi generatio, sed æternæ generationis manifestatio, per resurrectionem facta, de qua Rom. 1. 4. indicetur. prout passim fieri gignique in scriptura dicuntur, quæ esse manifestantur. vide Prov. 17. 17. ut sensus sit, ego hodie per resurrectionem manifestavi, te filium meum esse, ex me genitum. Nescio autem an opus sit admittere, Apostolum ex Hodie genui te voluisse resurrectionem colligere. Malo ea verba, ut apud Prophetam, sic apud Apostolum & hic & Heb. 1. 5. referre ad divinitatem Christi, æternamque ejus generationem. mentemque Apostoli non esse, ex iis verbis inferre resurrectionem, sed proferre promissionem patribus factam, & ex resurrectione impletionem ejus demonstrare. Sic enim ϒἭ præeedenti dixerat, se Euangelizare ipsis, Deum promissionem patribus factam implevisse, quum Jesum suscitavit. quæ est illa promissio? patet ex Ps. 2. ubi Deus Ecclesiæ promittit, fore ut talem super eam regem ungat, qui filius suus esset, hodie (id est, ab æterno in æternum: nam apud Deum perpetuum est hodie) ex se genitus. Id jam, inquit Apostolus Deus nobis præstitit in Jesu Christo. patet ex ejus resurrectione, quæ irrefragabile est æternæ ejus filiationis documentum. quia enim filius Dei erat, cujus generatio æternum haberet hodie, impossibile fuit eum à morte detineri. mortis itaque dolores cum solvit, palam fecit jam missum esse istum promissum filium, ab æterno genitum, qui regnum Ecclesiæ occuparet. Non ergo ea proprie verba spectat Apostolus, ego hodie genui te, quasi iis resurrectio contineretur, & hodie diem resurrectionis denotaret, sed ex toto loco infert Apostolus, promissum fuisse patribus Messiam, qui filius Dei esset, de quo jam Davidis tempore dixerit Deus, ego hodie genui te. quiq; adeo æternæ generationis existens, mortis dominio subjici non potuerit. hoc, inquit, implevit Deus, quum Jesum hunc dedit quem è mortuis suscitavit. Quod autem ipsam etiam resurrectionem Messiæ prædixerit Deus, pergit probare v. 34. & 35. quos propterea hac præfatione inchoat, ὅτι ἀνέστησεν αὐτὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν. Vnde liquet, eum v. 33. non tam resurrectionem ipsam, quam ex resurrectione jam factâ promissionis Psalmo secundo factæ impletionem probare voluisse. siquidem promissio ea talis erat, ut quamvis resurrectionem Messiæ verbis non exprimeret, ex rei tamen necessitate & consequentia eam in se contineret, siquidem impossibile esset filium Dei, ab æterno in æternum ex ipso genitum, mortuum non resurgere. Argumentum ergo Apostoli, ni fallor, tale est. Qui mortem devincendo ostensurus se esset filium Dei, hodie id est ab æterno in æternum è Deo genitum, is debebat esse rex Ecclesiæ. patet ex Pf. 2. At hic Iesus quem prædicamus, is est qui morte devincendo oftendit se esse filium Dei &c. Ergo is est promissus rex Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: VERS. 33. As it is written in the second Psalm [Ὡς ἐν τῷ Ψαλμῷ τῷ δευτέρῳ γέγραπται]. The Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic also read "the second" [τῷ δευτέρῳ]. See further the notes of the distinguished Beza, where, since mention is made of David Kimchi, I have thought fit to bring forward his commentary on the beginning of this Psalm, and, because it was not correctly translated by the learned Paul Fagius, to interpret it more accurately. The master says: [זה המזמור השני כן מציאנו אותו בכל הספרים המדוקים שהוא ראש מזמור ובחשבן כתבין אותו] that is, This psalm is the second psalm. And so we find it in all the correct books, that it is the head of a psalm, and in the reckoning they write it as second. Take care not to translate it that it is the head of the Psalms. For so it would pertain not only to the first psalm but would also make the beginning of the first. Whereas the master's intention is to prove from the most correct copies that this Psalm is the second. The meaning of these words, therefore, is that the most correct copies do not present the words "Today I have begotten you" [הַיּוֹם בְּנִי אַתָּה] as joined in one continuous line to the first Psalm, but as separate, and forming the head of the psalm [מִזְמוֹר שִׁיר], that is, the beginning of a new psalm. We have gladly brought these things forward here because they approve and confirm the customary reading in this passage of Acts. The master indeed adds that some masters say that "Blessed is the man" etc. and "Why did the nations rage" are one psalm, because whenever David had some section dear to him he began it with "blessed" [אשרי] and ended it with "blessed" [אשרי]. But the most accurate books refute this, and the reason is truly frivolous and not constant. See Psalms 32, 112 and 119, which begin with "blessed" but do not end so. The passage cited from Psalm 2 is You are my son, today I have begotten you. The enemies of Christ's divinity gather from this place that Christ is called the Son of God not from his eternal generation from the Father, but from the conferring of a new life through the resurrection, and that he was begotten at the time of the resurrection. They weaken the argument of a great man, who, although today I have begotten you is referred by the Apostle to the resurrection, holds that it is not a recent generation of Christ but a manifestation of his eternal generation, made through the resurrection, of which Romans 1:4 gives indication, just as in Scripture things are said to be generated and begotten everywhere when they are made manifest. See Proverbs 17:17. So the sense is: today, by the resurrection, I have shown that you are my son, begotten of me. I do not know, however, whether it is necessary to admit that the Apostle wished to infer the resurrection from Today I have begotten you. I prefer that these words, as in the Prophet, so in the Apostle both here and at Hebrews 1:5, be referred to the divinity of Christ and his eternal generation; and that it is not the Apostle's intention to infer the resurrection from these words, but to set out the promise made to the fathers, and from the resurrection to demonstrate its fulfilment. For he had said in the preceding verse that he was announcing to them that God had fulfilled the promise made to the fathers when he raised up Jesus. What is that promise? It is clear from Psalm 2, where God promises the Church that he will anoint over it such a king, who would be his son, begotten from himself today (that is, from eternity to eternity, for with God "today" is perpetual). This, says the Apostle, God has now performed for us in Jesus Christ. It is clear from his resurrection, which is an irrefutable proof of his eternal sonship. For since he was the Son of God, whose generation has an eternal today, it was impossible for him to be held by death. Therefore, when he loosed the pains of death, he made plain that this promised son, begotten from eternity, who was to occupy the kingdom of the Church, had now been sent. The Apostle therefore does not look to those words, today I have begotten you, as if the resurrection were contained in them, and today denoted the day of the resurrection; rather, from the whole passage the Apostle infers that the Messiah was promised to the fathers, who would be the Son of God, of whom God had already said in David's time, today I have begotten you; and who, existing in such eternal generation, could not be subject to the dominion of death. This, he says, God has fulfilled, when he raised up this Jesus whom he gave. That God also foretold the resurrection of the Messiah itself he goes on to prove in verses 34 and 35, which he therefore introduces with this preface, that he raised him from the dead [ὅτι ἀνέστησεν αὐτὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν]. Whence it is clear that in verse 33 he wished to prove not so much the resurrection itself as the fulfilment, by the resurrection now accomplished, of the promise made in the second Psalm. For the promise was such that, although it did not express the resurrection of the Messiah in words, it nevertheless contained it by the necessity of the matter and by consequence, since it would be impossible for the Son of God, begotten of him from eternity to eternity, not to rise when dead. The Apostle's argument, then, if I am not mistaken, is this: he who, by overcoming death, was to show himself to be the Son of God, today, that is, begotten of God from eternity to eternity, ought to be the king of the Church. This is clear from Psalm 2. But this Jesus whom we preach is he who, by overcoming death, showed himself to be the Son of God, etc. Therefore he is the promised king of the Church.

units.la: VERS. 34. Dabo vobis <bl>τὰ ὅσια Δαβίδ τὰ πιστά</bl>. Nihil habeo addendum ad ea quæ Calvinus, Beza, Drusius aliique ad hæc verba annotarunt. Nisi quod הסדי־דוד, quod Esa. 55.
units.tr: VERSE 34. Dabo vobis τὰ ὅσια Δαβίδ τὰ πιστά [I will give you the holy things of David, the sure ones]. I have nothing to add to what Calvin, Beza, Drusius and others have noted on these words, except that חסדי דוד [the mercies of David], which is in Isa. 55.

units.la: 3. LXX verterunt τὰ ὅσια Δαῦίδ, 2 Par. 6. 42. verterint τὰ ἐλέη Δαῦίδ. idem ergo τὰ ὅσια & τὰ ἐλέη. intelliguntur utrobique gratuitæ Dei promissiones Davidi factæ. pro quibus τὰ ὅσια dixisse Hellenistas non mirabitur, qui noverit eos Deum etiam, quum הסד, benignum dicere volunt, ὁσιότης dicere, Pf. 18. 28. & הסד, benignitatem promisisse per ἔλεος & δικαιοσύνην reddere. & nequis aliud eos ibi per δικαιοσύνην intelligere autumet, quam per ἔλεος, ipsum etiam πρᾶς quod proprie δικαιοσύνην denotat, per ἔλεος & ἐλεημοσύνην reddunt frequenter. sicut & apud Arabes justitia, frequens est pro beneficentia. idem ergo ex Hellenistarum usu τὰ ὅσια, τὰ δικαια, & τὰ ἐλέη. quod quum nec Apostolus nec alii linguæ Hellenisticæ assueti ignorarint, recte hic Paulum LXX Interpretum verba retinuisse malim afferere, quam cum incomparabili viro Joh. Calvino dicere, eum id rudibus & infirmis concessisse, qui Græcæ lectioni magis assueti essent. At quomodo ex Dabo vobis sancta David fidelia, colligit Apostolus resurrectionem Christi, & vitam ejus nulli amplius corruptioni obnoxiam? Ipse Apostolus altero, quem ex Pf. 16. citat, loco priorem firmat & explicat. quum enim τὰ ὅσια Δαβίδ sint benignæ Dei promissiones Davidi factæ, Davidi autem promissum esset, ut ex semine ejus oriretur Messias, qui tanquam Sanctus Dei non videret corruptionem, recte colligit Apostolus, non potuisse Deum sancta Davidis fidelia dare, quin & sancto suo, Davidi promisso, incorruptibilem per resurrectionem vitam largiretur. Deprecor autem veniam, ne quis vitio vertat, si occasione vocis πηγὴ addam hîc, quamvis non suo loco, quædam quæ Commentario nostro in Marc. 14.3. ubi de ῥάφῳ πηγῆς egimus, addi velim. Abulfeda præstantissimus Arabum Geographus tradit, ﻓﻴﺴﻰ, Bift sive Pift (pro p enim Arabes semper b usurpant) esse urbem Metropolim Caramaniæ cis Indum fluvium. At Jakutus Hamawæus dicit esse ex regione Cabul in ipsa India. ex qua regione pleraque aromata Indica peti, & ipse testatur, & usus seculi nostri docet. Ptolomæus eodem ubi hodie Cabul est loco habet Pisca. quod procul dubio legendum Pista. Inde Nardus Pistica, id est, Indica ex urbe Pista in regione Cabul ubi optima nascitur, & unde plurima adfertur. atque ita laudandus Interpres Æthiopicus Joan.12.3. ubi pro nomine proprio id habens vertit ܢܪܕܝܢ. etsi Marc. 14.3. reddiderit ܢܪܕܝ, Nardi optima.
units.tr: The Seventy translated τὰ ὅσια Δαβίδ [the holy things of David] in 2 Chron. 6:42, where they rendered τὰ ἐλέη Δαβίδ [the mercies of David]. So τὰ ὅσια and τὰ ἐλέη are the same. In both places the gratuitous promises of God made to David are meant. No one will be surprised that the Hellenists said τὰ ὅσια for these, if he knows that they also render God's benignity, when הסד [hesed, kindness] is used of God, as ὁσιότης [holiness] in Ps. 18:28, and that they render הסד [hesed] by ἔλεος [mercy] and δικαιοσύνη [righteousness]. And lest anyone think that they understand δικαιοσύνη there in a different sense from ἔλεος, note that they often translate צדקה [tsedaqah] itself, which properly denotes righteousness, by ἔλεος and ἐλεημοσύνη [almsgiving]. Likewise among the Arabs justice is often used for beneficence. So by the usage of the Hellenists τὰ ὅσια, τὰ δίκαια and τὰ ἐλέη are the same. Since neither the Apostle nor others accustomed to the Hellenistic language could have been ignorant of this, I would rather maintain that Paul rightly retained the words of the Septuagint here than, with the incomparable John Calvin, say that he conceded this to the untutored and weak who were more used to the Greek reading. But how does the Apostle infer the resurrection of Christ and His life no longer subject to corruption from I will give you the holy and sure things of David? The Apostle himself confirms and explains the first by the other passage, which he cites from Psalm 16. For since the ὅσια Δαβίδ are the kindly promises of God made to David, and it had been promised to David that the Messiah would arise from his seed, who, as the Holy One of God, would not see corruption, the Apostle rightly concludes that God could not give the holy things of David without also granting to His Holy One, the one promised to David, a life incorruptible through resurrection. I beg pardon, however, lest anyone blame me if, on the occasion of the word πηγή [spring, fountain], I add here, though not in its proper place, some matters which I would wish to add to our commentary on Mark 14:3, where we dealt with the ῥάφος πηγῆς [the flask of spikenard]. The most distinguished Arab geographer Abulfeda reports that Fisi, written Bift or Pift (for the Arabs always use b for p), is the metropolis of Caramania on this side of the river Indus. But Yaqut al-Hamawi says it lies in the region of Kabul, in India itself, a region from which most Indian aromatics are sought, as he himself attests and as the practice of our own age teaches. Ptolemy, in the very place where Kabul now is, has Pisca, which without doubt should be read Pista. Hence Pistic nard, that is, Indian nard from the city of Pista in the region of Kabul, where the best grows and whence very much is brought. And so the Ethiopic translator is to be commended at John 12:3, where, having this as a proper name, he renders it nardin, although at Mark 14:3 he rendered it nardi optima [best nard].

units.la: VERS. 41. ἴδετε οἱ καταφρονηταί.
units.tr: VERSE 41. Behold, you despisers [ἴδετε οἱ καταφρονηταί].

units.la: Desumtus locus ex Habac. 1.5. ubi legitur הַבִּיטוּ בַגּוֹיִם, aspicite Gentes. Rectè conjiciunt viri eruditi, LXX Interpretes legisse בגוים, errore orto ex affinitate literarum ו & ד. solent enim בגוים & alibi vertere καταφρονηταί. ut & verbum בג καταφρονεῖν. Non est autem quod turbetur quisquam, quod errorem hunc non emendaverit Euangelista noster. etsi enim in verbis, in re tamen ipsa nullus error, nulla varietas. ubi quidem Apostoli receptam in Ecclesiis Græci textus lectionem mutare, nec operæ pretium, nec utile duxere. Nullum autem hic esse sensus errorem, ex ipsa Prophetæ mente liquet. quum enim Gentes aspicere jubet, καταφρονηταί facit Judæos, eosque aperti contemtus arguit, quòd ad Gentium scholam ablegari, & à Gentibus discere merERentur, qui ex Sacro ipsius Dei ore discere hactenus recusarant, & fidelem sedulamque Prophetarum operam flocci fecerant. Hoc dico, contemtores arguuntur Judæi, quum Gentes magistros aspicere jubentur. Sensus itaque recte constat, imo mentem Prophetæ quasi per commentarium explicat. Sequitur, & admiramini, ἡ ἀφανισθῆτε, Vulgatus, & dispersdimini.
units.tr: The passage is taken from Habakkuk 1:5, where the Hebrew reads "Look among the nations" [הַבִּיטוּ בַגּוֹיִם]. Learned men rightly conjecture that the Septuagint translators read בגוים, the error arising from the similarity of the letters ו and ד. They also usually render בגוים elsewhere as "despisers" [καταφρονηταί], just as the verb בג means "to despise" [καταφρονεῖν]. Nor should anyone be troubled that our Evangelist did not correct this error. Although the words differ, the matter itself contains no error and no variation. Indeed, the Apostles judged it neither worthwhile nor useful to change the reading of the Greek text that was received in the Churches. That there is no error in sense here is clear from the Prophet's own mind. When he bids them look to the Gentiles, he makes the Jews "despisers" and rebukes them for open contempt. They deserved to be sent off to the school of the Gentiles and to learn from the Gentiles, since they had refused to learn from the sacred mouth of God himself and had made light of the faithful and diligent labour of the Prophets. I say this: the Jews are rebuked as despisers when the Gentiles are ordered to be looked upon as teachers. The sense is therefore rightly established, and indeed the Prophet's meaning is explained, as it were, by a commentary. There follows "and be amazed, ἠ ἀφανισθῆτε" [and be astonished]; the Vulgate has "and be scattered."

units.la: Syrus ܐܘܕܝܢ, & corrumpamini. Arabs omittit. Erasmus & Beza, & evanescite. LXX usi sunt pro תִּשָּׁמֵמוּ, & stupescite. Est & alibi, ubi pro stupore, terrore & desolatione animi verbo hoc usi sunt. ut Osee 5. 15. Ibo & revertar in locum meum, ἕως ἂν ἀφανισθῶσιν ἐν ζητήσει τῶν προσώπων μου, donec mente desolati quærant faciem meam. Ezech. 12. 19. τὸ ὕδωρ αὐτῶν μετ’ ἀφανισμοῦ πίονται, aquam suam cum stupore bibent. Sensus ergo est, stupescite animo, sic ut mens vobis ac consilia pereant atque evanescant.
units.tr: The Syriac has "’wdyn" [and be corrupted]. The Arabic omits the word. Erasmus and Beza have "and vanish." The Septuagint used "and be astonished" for the Hebrew תִּשָּׁמֵמוּ. The same word is used elsewhere where they mean stupor, terror and desolation of mind, as in Hosea 5:15: "I will go and return to my place, ἕως ἂν ἀφανισθῶσιν ἐν ζητήσει τῶν προσώπων μου" [until they are left desolate in mind and seek my face]. And in Ezekiel 12:19: "τὸ ὕδωρ αὐτῶν μετ’ ἀφανισμοῦ πίονται" [they shall drink their water with astonishment]. The sense, then, is: be stunned in mind, so that your judgment and counsels perish and vanish away.

units.la: VERS. 42.
units.tr: VERSE 42.

units.la: Ut Vulgatus Latinus legit, sic Syrus quoque & Arabs. item Chrysostomus. Apud Æthiopicum versus hic sic habet, & rogarunt ut loquerentur sibi hoc verbum sequenti Sabbatho. tum versus 43. Quumque exivissent è synagoga, secuti sunt eos multi Iudæi &c. quæ lectio etsi facilis sit & expedita, nulla tamen nititur authoritate.
units.tr: The Latin Vulgate reads this, and so do the Syriac and the Arabic, as does Chrysostom. In the Ethiopic this verse reads: "and they asked that these words be spoken to them on the following Sabbath," and then verse 43: "And when they had come out of the synagogue, many Jews followed them, etc." This reading, though it is easy and smooth, has no authority behind it.

units.la: IBID. Εἰς τὴν μεταξὺ σάββατον. Beza vertit, intra sequens Sabbathum, id est, profectis diebus inter duo sabbatha intercedentibus. quod & Scaliger de Emend. temporum sensit, qui legendum putabat ἐν τῷ μεταξὺ σαββάτων. Sed recte illud in spicilegio suo confutat doctiss. Lud. Capellus, ac nodum solvit ex Josepho de bello Judaico l. 6. c. 6. ubi μεταξὺ pro μετὰ ταῦτα, post usurpatur. dicit enim Δαυὶδ τῆς Σολομῶνος, ἐν ᾗ τ' μεταξὺ τούτων βασιλέων, hoc est, τ' μὴ τούτους βασιλέων, qui hos secuti sunt reges. nulli enim inter Davidem & Salomonem fuerunt, sed multi secuti sunt reges. Itaque & εἰς τὴν μεταξὺ σάββατον recta est locutio, & Syrus, Arabs, Æthiopicus, Vulgatus atque Erasmus recte interpretati sunt sequente Sabbatho, ut idem sit quod Ἰσ. 44. ἐχομένῳ σαββάτῳ.
units.tr: Εἰς τὴν μεταξὺ σάββατον. Beza renders this "within the following Sabbath," that is, with the intervening days having passed between two Sabbaths. Scaliger, in his De emendatione temporum, also took it this way, and thought the text should read ἐν τῷ μεταξὺ σαββάτων. But the most learned Ludovicus Cappellus rightly refutes this in his Spicilegium, and solves the knot from Josephus, Jewish War book 6, chapter 6, where μεταξὺ is used for μετὰ ταῦτα, "after." For there Josephus says of David and Solomon, "ἐν ᾗ τ' μεταξὺ τούτων βασιλέων" [in which, among these kings], that is, "τ' μὴ τούτους βασιλέων" [the kings who followed these]. For no kings came between David and Solomon, but many followed them. So the phrase εἰς τὴν μεταξὺ σάββατον is a correct expression, and the Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopic, Vulgate and Erasmus have translated it rightly as "the following Sabbath," so that it means the same as ἐχομένῳ σαββάτῳ [the next Sabbath], as in Acts 13:44.
