units.la: Addo Josepho Clementis Romani locum ex Epistola ejus ad Corinthios, nuper admodum è Magnæ Britanniæ Regis Bibliotheca à doctiss. viro Patricio Junio edita, qui sic habet, Καὶ οἱ Ἀπόστολοι ἡμῶν ἔγνωσαν Δι᾽ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χρι-στῶ, ὅτι ἐξ ἐκ ἐχει ἀπ᾽ ἑνὸς μέσου ἀ [...] ἐπισκοπῆς, Διὰ ταύτην εως τὸ αὐτὸ ἀπεγνωσαν ἀληθῶς πλείαν, καλέσαντος αὐτῶν ἐπισκοπῆς, ἐ μεταξὺ Ἀποστόλων διδάξαντες, ὅπως ἐὰν κοιμηθῶσιν, Διαδέξωνται ἐπὶ διδάσκαλοι ἀνδρες τῷ λειτουργίᾳ αὐτῶν. id est, Et Apostoli nostri cognoverunt per Dominum nostrum I. Christum, sive ut de nomine Episcopatus contenderetur, itaque omnimodâ in se curâ susceptâ constituerunt prædictos. Deinde autem ordinationem instituerunt, ut defunctis illis succederent alii probati viri, qui ministerium eorum capesserent. vides & hic μεταξύ non inter, sed post significare, vel deinceps, idem quod ἐπὶ πᾶσι aut καθεξῆς. Similiter in proximè sequentibus, Τὴς ἐως καθαιρεθέντας ὑπ᾽ ἐκείνων, ἢ μεταξὺ ὑφ᾽ ἑτέρων εὐλογίμων ἀνδρῶν, συνεδοκησάντων τῆς ἐκκλησίας πάσης &c. id est, Constitutos itaque ab illis, aut deinceps ab aliis legitimè viris, consentiente universa Ecclesia &c.
units.tr: To Josephus I add a passage from Clement of Rome's Epistle to the Corinthians, lately published from the library of the King of Great Britain by the most learned Patricius Junius. It reads: "Καὶ οἱ Ἀπόστολοι ἡμῶν ἔγνωσαν διὰ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ὅτι ἔρις ἔσται ἐπὶ τοῦ ὀνόματος τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς" [And our Apostles knew through our Lord Jesus Christ that there would be strife over the name of the episcopate]. And so, having received complete foreknowledge, they appointed those already mentioned, and then gave instructions that when they had died, other approved men should succeed them and take up their ministry. You see here too that μεταξύ means not "between" but "after," or "afterwards," the same as ἐπὶ πᾶσι or καθεξῆς [in order]. Similarly in what follows: "Τοὺς ἐκ ἐκείνων καθαιρεθέντας... ἢ μεταξὺ ὑφ᾽ ἑτέρων εὐλογίμων ἀνδρῶν, συνευδοκησάντων τῆς ἐκκλησίας πάσης" [those put down by them, or afterwards by other reputable men, with the consent of the whole Church], that is, "Those therefore appointed by them, or afterwards by other lawful men, with the whole Church consenting," and so on.

units.la: VERS. 45. Ἀντέλεγον τῆς ὑπὸ Παύλου λεγομένοις, ἀντιλέγοντες ἡ βλασφημοῦντες. Annotat Cl. Beza, nec Vulgatam Latinam, nec Syram nec Arabicam editionem legere ἀντιλέγοντες καὶ, atque etiam videri id redundare. Addo, neque Æthiopicum legere. non quod à Græcis exemplaribus ea abfuerint (constanter enim omnia habent) sed quod omiserint quæ redundare putarent. Erasmus quoque ad Vulgati lectionem commentans ait, Graeci addunt verbum unum, haud scio an rectè, ἀντιλέγοντες ἐ βλασφημοῦντες, contradicentes ac blasphemantes. rectissimè inquam. insignis enim & ἐμφατικώτατον huic phrasi inest Hebraismus, qualem habes 1 Sam. 6. 12. הלך הלך ולא, LXX ἐπορεύοντο πορευόμενοι ἐ βοῶντες, ibant euntes & mugientes, id est, perpetuo mugitu euntes comitante. sic, contradicebant, contradicentes & blasphemantes, id est, perpetua blasphemia contradictionem comitante.
units.tr: Verse 45: "Ἀντέλεγον τοῖς ὑπὸ Παύλου λεγομένοις, ἀντιλέγοντες ἢ βλασφημοῦντες" [They contradicted what was said by Paul, contradicting and blaspheming]. The learned Beza notes that neither the Latin Vulgate, nor the Syriac, nor the Arabic edition reads "ἀντιλέγοντες καὶ" [contradicting and], and that it seems to be superfluous. I add that the Ethiopic does not read it either. This is not because the Greek manuscripts lack it (they all have it without exception), but because the translators omitted what they thought superfluous. Erasmus, too, commenting on the Vulgate reading, says: "The Greeks add one word, I know not whether rightly: ἀντιλέγοντες ἢ βλασφημοῦντες, contradicting and blaspheming." Most rightly, I say. For this phrase contains a striking and most emphatic Hebraism, like the one you have in 1 Samuel 6:12: הלך הלך ולא [going and going, and not], which the Septuagint render "ἐπορεύοντο πορευόμενοι καὶ ἐβόων" [they went along going and lowing], that is, going with continual lowing accompanying them. So too "contradicting, contradicting and blaspheming" means contradiction accompanied by continual blasphemy.

units.la: VERS. 46. Παρρηναοαμένοι ἡ ὁ Παῦλ@· ⁊ ὁ Βαρνάβας. Vulgatus, Erasmus & Beza δὲ vertunt tunc. Syrus autem & Arabs propria retenta significatione vertunt sed. recte, ni fallor. ut sensus sit, sperabant quidem Judæi, se blasphemis suis contradictionibus Paulum Barnabamque deterrituros, sed hi libertate usi, nec quicquam fracti, dixerunt &c.
units.tr: Verse 46: "Παρρησιασάμενοι δὲ ὁ Παῦλος καὶ ὁ Βαρνάβας" [And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly]. The Vulgate, Erasmus and Beza render δὲ as "then." The Syriac and Arabic, keeping its proper meaning, render it "but," which is correct, unless I am mistaken. The sense is this: the Jews hoped that by their blasphemous contradictions they would frighten Paul and Barnabas away, but these men, using their freedom and not broken in the least, said, etc.

units.la: VERS. 48. Quotquot erant τεταγμένοι ad vitam æter- nam.
units.tr: VERS. 48. As many as were τεταγμένοι to eternal life.

units.la: Syrus [illegible, ~6 letters] positi. ignoravit enim quod hodierni hæretici somniarunt, per τεταγμένος intelligi, qui in seipsis apti essent, ac seipsos disponerent ad vitam æternam.
units.tr: The Syriac has [illegible, about six letters] "placed" (positi). For he did not know what the present-day heretics have dreamed up, that by τεταγμένος is meant those who were fit in themselves and who disposed themselves to eternal life.

units.la: VERS. 50. Τὰς σεμνὰς γυναικας, ἢ τὰς εὐχημονας, καὶ τῶν πρώτως τῆς πόλεως. Syrus τὰς εὐχήμονας vertit divites. non arbitror recte. Beza, honoratas. dubito an & hoc satis bene. Malim cum Vulgato honestas. εὐχήμων enim vel de decentibus honestisque moribus dicitur, vel de decenti specie ac forma. prius elegit Vulgatus, alterum Arabs, qui vertit [illegible, ~5 letters], & pulchras forma. Æthiopicus omissis viris qui hic πρῶτοι τῆς πόλεως dicuntur, dixit mulieres maximas civitatis, & probissimas regionis. præstat prius. eodem sumo sensu, quo Marc. 15. 43. εὐχήμων βουλευτής, honestus senator. & infra Act. 17. 12. Ἑλληνίδων γυναικῶν τῶν εὐχημόνων, Gracarum mulierum honestarum.
units.tr: VERS. 50. Τὰς σεμνὰς γυναικας, ἢ τὰς εὐχημονας, καὶ τῶν πρώτως τῆς πόλεως [the honourable women, or the well-reputed ones, and the chief men of the city]. The Syriac renders τὰς εὐχήμονας as "the rich"; I do not think this is right. Beza has "honoured"; I doubt whether this is quite good either. I would prefer, with the Vulgate, "honest". For εὐχήμων is said either of decent and honest conduct or of a comely appearance and form. The Vulgate chose the former, the Arabic the latter, which renders it [illegible, about five letters], "and beautiful in form". The Ethiopic, omitting the men who are here called οἱ πρῶτοι τῆς πόλεως, has "the greatest women of the city and the most upright of the region". The former is preferable. I take it in the same sense as Mark 15.43, εὐχήμων βουλευτής, "an honest senator", and below, Acts 17.12, Ἑλληνίδων γυναικῶν τῶν εὐχημόνων, "of honourable Greek women".

units.la: VERS. 52. οἱ μαθηταί. Arabs hoc nomen, & sequens verbum ἐπληρώθησαν duali numero (quem Arabes, ut Græci, habent) interpretatus est, existimans ad Paulum & Barnabam hæc referri, qui ejecti Antiochia non tantum non desponderint animum, sed gaudio etiam ac spiritu S. fuerint repleti. Æthiopicus οἱ μαθηταί per Apostolos est interpretatus, intelligens fortassis & ipse Paulum ac Barnabam, qui ambo Apostoli vocantur infra c. 14. 14. facius est generalius sumere.
units.tr: VERS. 52. οἱ μαθηταί. The Arabic translated this noun, and the following verb ἐπληρώθησαν, in the dual number (which Arabic, like Greek, has), supposing that these things refer to Paul and Barnabas, who, though cast out of Antioch, did not lose heart at all but were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit. The Ethiopic translated οἱ μαθηταί as "the Apostles", perhaps understanding, as it does, Paul and Barnabas, who are both called apostles below in chapter 14.14. It is safer to take it more generally.

units.la: C A P. XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: VERS. 1. Ἐγένετο δὲ ἐν Ἰκονίῳ κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ εἰσελθεῖν αὐτοὺς &c. Syrus ἐν Ἰκονίῳ κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ omittit. Arabs transtulit, & Iconii etiam fecerunt similiter, ingressi sunt &c. nempe ut fecerant Antiochiæ. quo sensu Beza etiam κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ vertit itidem. Vulgatus & Erasmus simul. quod non est aspernandum. LXX enim Interpretes ῾ּ‎ו & ֵּ‎ו, simul, una, pariter non tantum reddunt ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ, sed & κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ. vide 1 Sam. 30.24. & 31.6. 2 Sam. 2.16. Exod. 26.24. & 36.23. & alibi.
units.tr: VERSE 1. Now it came to pass in Iconium that they went in together, and so on. The Syriac omits "in Iconium, at the same time." The Arab renders it, "and in Iconium too they did likewise, they entered," and so on, namely as they had done at Antioch. In this sense Beza also renders κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ in the same way. The Vulgate and Erasmus have "together" (simul), which is not to be scorned. For the Seventy, when they render the Hebrew words for "together," "as one," and "alike," use not only ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ but also κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ. See 1 Sam. 30:24, 31:6; 2 Sam. 2:16; Exod. 26:24, 36:23, and elsewhere.

units.la: VERS. 2. Οἱ δὲ ἀπειθοῦντες Ἰουδαῖοι ἐπήγειραν τὰς ψυχὰς τῶν ἐθνῶν κατὰ τῶν ἀδελφῶν. Vulgatus, exacerbaverunt ad iracundiam concitaverunt. Beza, male affectos reddiderunt. Erasmus, corruperunt. Inusitata haec hujus verbi significatio itaque fecit Syrum & Arabem, ut verterint quasi legissent, ἐπήγειραν τὰς ψυχὰς τῶν ἐθνῶν κατὰ τῶν ἀδελφῶν. Æthiopicus etiam longe aliter, & reliqui Iudæi qui renuerunt, contenderunt cum gentibus & cum Apostolis, & afflixerunt animas ipsorum. quæ lectio procul dubio pessima est. nulla in Græco difficultas videtur. ad verbum verto, concitarunt & afflixerunt (vel pressterunt, urserunt) animas gentium contra fratres, Hebraicè ῾ּ‎ו, impulerunt & afflixerunt, id est, cum afflictione impulerunt, tam importunè scilicet instantes, urgentes & premenres ad hoc facinus, ut Gentibus non usquequaque adeo ad id pronis ac facilibus molesti etiam fuerint. Quod autem Beda monuerit, in codicibus Græcis post τῶν ἀδελφῶν addi, ὁ δὲ Θεὸς ἐποίησεν, addo notis Cl. Bezæ, Syrum, Arabem atque Æthiopicum hæc ignorasse. & in Correctionibus Romanis moneri, non esse addendum Deus autem pacem fecit.
units.tr: VERS. 2. But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the minds of the Gentiles against the brethren [Οἱ δὲ ἀπειθοῦντες Ἰουδαῖοι ἐπήγειραν τὰς ψυχὰς τῶν ἐθνῶν κατὰ τῶν ἀδελφῶν]. The Vulgate: embittered them and roused them to anger. Beza: made them ill-disposed. Erasmus: corrupted them. This unusual sense of the verb has led the Syriac and Arabic translators to render it as though they had read [ἐπήγειραν τὰς ψυχὰς τῶν ἐθνῶν κατὰ τῶν ἀδελφῶν]. The Ethiopic differs widely as well, and the other Jews who refused, "contended with the Gentiles and with the Apostles, and afflicted their souls." That reading is doubtless very poor. In the Greek there seems to be no difficulty. Word for word, I render it: "they stirred up and afflicted the souls of the Gentiles against the brethren," where the Hebrew [ו] would be "they impelled and afflicted," that is, they impelled with affliction, pressing and urging so importunately and insistently to this deed that they were troublesome to the Gentiles, who were not everywhere so inclined or so ready for it. As for Bede's remark that the Greek codices add after "the brethren" the words [ὁ δὲ Θεὸς ἐποίησεν], I add, on the notes of the illustrious Beza, that the Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic translators were ignorant of these words; and it is noted in the Roman Corrections that "But God made peace" is not to be added.

units.la: VERS. 10. Addimus notis Bezæ, Æthiopicum quoque Interpretem non legisse ea quæ in quibusdam exemplaribus se reperisse ait, & approbat.
units.tr: VERSE 10. I add, following Beza's notes, that the Ethiopic interpreter also did not read those things which he says he found in some copies, and he approves of this.

units.la: - VERS. 12. Εκάλεῖ τὴ τ μῷ Βαρναβᾶ Δία, τ ᾗ Παῦλον Ἐρ-μλῷ. Æthiopicus Græca hæc Deorum nomina retinuit. Deinde autem addit אשם יה כהיל פרקרי כהיל בנר רום, quia Iovis dicitur, Mercurius dicitur sermone Romano. monet Δία, Iovem, Ἐρμλῆ, Mercurium dici Latinè. quod quum quis in margine in gratiam Latini Interpretis annotasseт, indein textum irrepsit.
units.tr: VERSE 12. They called Barnabas Zeus [Δία], and Paul Hermes [Ἑρμῆν]. The Ethiopic retained these Greek names of the gods. It then adds, "because he is called Jupiter, Paul is called Mercury in the Roman language." The author observes that Δία means Jupiter and Ἑρμῆς means Mercury in Latin. When someone had noted this in the margin for the sake of the Latin translator, it crept into the text.

units.la: VERS. 13. Ταύρως ἐ σἰμμαῖα ἀπὸ τὴν πυλῶνας ἐνίγκας. Quum templum Jovis initio hujus versus dicatur à Luca fuisse ante urbem, quæritur quid per τὴν πυλῶνας intellexerit, quò sacerdos victimas adduxit. Æthiopicus vertit ad portas urbis.quod rectum est, si in portis urbis concionem habuit Paulus. Cl. Beza ait, plerosque ἀπὸ τὴν πυλῶνας exponere, ad ipsius templi suburbani porticus: at suo judicio esse fortassis enallagen numeri, pro ἀπὸ τὴν πυλῶν, ut earum ædium vestibulum intelligatur, in quas diverterant Apostoli. quod non exístimamus esse necessarium. etsi enim ad diversorium Pauli Syrus hæc retulerit, retinet tamen τὴν πυλῶνας plurali numero. vertit enim ... ad portas (male Trem. portam) atrii ubi commorabantur. hæc enim apud omnes Orientales ædium est structura, ut aperta prima domus janua, quæ plateam spectat, mox in aliam incidas, quæ velo, quod tegumentum Arabes vocant, obducitur, ne intranti introspicere in conclave detur, ubi paterfamilias degit. Itaque & nos hic, non cum D. Beza ad vestibula, sed cum Syro ad portas aut januas vertimus. de quo pluribus supra c. 12. 14.
units.tr: VERSE 13. Here the Greek reads "bringing oxen and garlands to the gates." Since Luke says that the temple of Jupiter stood before the city, at the beginning of this verse, the question is what he meant by "the gates," to which the priest brought the victims. The Ethiopic renders it "to the gates of the city," which is correct if Paul preached in the city gates. Beza says that most interpreters explain "to the gates" as the porticoes of the suburban temple itself. But in his judgment there is perhaps a change of number, for "to the gate," so that the vestibule of the houses where the Apostles lodged is understood. We do not think this necessary. For although the Syriac refers these words to Paul's lodging, it still keeps "the gates" in the plural: it renders "to the gates (Tremellius wrongly has 'gate') of the court where they stayed." For in all Eastern lands the structure of a house is such that, after the first outer door, which faces the street, you come at once to another, which is covered with a curtain (the Arabs call this a covering), so that a person entering cannot look into the room where the master of the household lives. So we too translate here, not with Beza "to the vestibules," but with the Syriac "to the gates" or "doors." More on this above, at chapter 12:14.

units.la: VERS. 15. ὀμοιοπαθῆς ὑμῖν.non improbamus Erasmum, qui vertit, iisdem obnoxii malis quibus vos. sicut Sapient. 6. 3. ἐπὶ τὸ ὁμοιοπαθῆ κατέπεσον γῆν, in terram iisdem malis (vel incommodis) obnoxiam incidi.
units.tr: VERSE 15. We do not disapprove of Erasmus, who renders ὁμοιοπαθῆς ὑμῖν as "subject to the same evils as you," as in Wisdom 6:3, "I fell upon a land subject to the same evils (or hardships)" [ἐπὶ τὸ ὁμοιοπαθῆ κατέπεσον γῆν].

units.la: VERS. 19. Ex illis additamentis quæ Cl.Beza hic profert, solus Arabs habet, & dum illic docerent.
units.tr: VERSE 19. Of those additions which Beza presents here, only the Arab has "and while they were teaching there."

units.la: VERS. 22. Καὶ ὅν ἀπὸ πολλῶν ... &c. Annotat Junius, Arabem legere sine copula, quocirca vertit nam. Erpeniana editio exhibet copulam ﻭ, quod vertendum & quod. Æthiopicus legit sine copula ܕܝܢ, quia.
units.tr: VERS. 22. And who from many ... [Καὶ ὅν ἀπὸ πολλῶν ...] &c. Junius observes that the Arab reads without a conjunction, and so translates it as for. The Erpenius edition gives the conjunction wa, which should be rendered and or which. The Ethiopic reads without a conjunction, d'yn, because.

units.la: VERS. 27. Annunciarunt quanta fecisset Deus μετ' αὐτῶν, Beza per ipsos. Insolens illa est significatio præpositionis μετὰ. nec video cur jure culpari queant Vulgatus & Erasmus, cum quibus facit Syrus, qui ad verbum reddunt cum illis. Etsi enim sensus ejus sit, ipsis cooperantibus, non magis id gloriæ divinæ obstat, quàm quum 2 Cor. 6. 1. vocantur Dei συνεργοὶ. & 1 Cor. 3. 9. Θεοῦ γάρ ἐσμεν συνεργοί. Sed aliam interpretationem submin istrat Arabs, qui μετ' αὐτῶν accepit pro αὐτοῖς. vertit enim ... , Junius, quicquid fecerat Deus per ipsos, id Arabes dicerent ... at vertendum ipsis. optimè, ex Hebraismo, ubi נעשה, fecit construitur cum עם vel את, cum, pro Dativo personæ. ut Deut. 10. 21. אשר עשה אתך את־הגדלות, qui fecit tecum magna, id est, tibi: pro multis sic locus Jud. 8. 35. ubi Hebraismum sequentes LXX, habent, καὶ οὐκ ἐποίησαν ἔλεος μετ' ἐμοῦ ... pro τῷ οἴκῳ Ιερομβάαλ, & τῷ Ιερομβαάλ. sic alibi passim. quam phrasin in Novo T. habes Luc. 1. 72. & 10. 37. sic hoc loco, & infra c. 15. 4. ὅσα ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς μετ' αὐτῶν, sensus est, quanta fecisset Deus ipsis, quanta ipsos gratia & honore esset dignatus, quanto in prædicando Euangelio, convertendis hominibus, edendisque miraculis auxilio & robore ipsis præsto fuisset. similiter Æthiopicus ... & narrarunt omnia quæ fecerat ipsis Deus. Etsi autem non hoc loco, alibi tamen eandem phrasin imitatur Æthiopicus, ut infra c. 15. 3. pro ἐξ ἐποίησε χαρὰν μεγάλην πᾶσι τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς, φοῖς, habet ... & fecerunt magnum gaudium cum omnibus sociis suis; id est, omnibus sociis suis.
units.tr: VERSE 27. They reported how much God had done "with them" [μετ' αὐτῶν]. Beza takes this as "through them." That sense of the preposition μετά is unusual, and I do not see why the Vulgate and Erasmus, with whom the Syriac agrees, can rightly be blamed, since they render it word for word as "with them." For although its sense is "with them, cooperating," this is no more an obstacle to divine glory than when they are called God's fellow-workers [συνεργοί] at 2 Cor. 6:1, and at 1 Cor. 3:9, "for we are God's fellow-workers" [Θεοῦ γάρ ἐσμεν συνεργοί]. But the Arab offers another interpretation: he took "with them" as "to them." Junius renders it, "whatever God had done through them, the Arabs would say," but it should be rendered "to them." This is best, following the Hebrew idiom, where "to do" [נעשה / עשה] is construed with "with" (עם or את) for the dative of the person, as in Deut. 10:21, "who did with you great things" [אשר עשה אתך את־הגדלות], that is, for you. Many passages do the same; for example, Judges 8:35, where the Seventy, following the Hebrew, have "and they did not show mercy with me" (for "to the house of Jerubbaal" and "to Jerubbaal"), and so elsewhere throughout. You find this phrase in the New Testament at Luke 1:72 and 10:37. So here, and at 15:4, "as much as God had done with them," the sense is: how much God had done for them, how much grace and honour he had deigned to give them, how much he had stood by them with help and strength in preaching the gospel, converting people, and working miracles. Similarly the Ethiopic: "and they related all that God had done for them." Although not in this place, the Ethiopic imitates the same phrase elsewhere: at 15:3, where the Greek has "he caused great joy to all the brothers," it has "and they made great joy with all their companions," that is, for all their companions.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAP. XV.

units.la: VERS. 2. Τεταμένης οὖ φάσεως ἐ συζητήσεως οὐκ ἐλίγης &c. Vulgatus non legit συζητήσεως, quod tamen Syrus, Arabs, Æthiopicus, Chrysostomus & Græca exemplaria legerunt, nisi quod apud Chrysostomum sit ζητήσεως. Porro φάσεως, quod Vulgatus & Erasmus seditione, Syrus & Arabs tumultu verterunt, Cl. Beza non male repugnantia vertit: quum enim, teste Suida, φάσις sit ἐμφύλιος μάχη, intestina pugna, intelligi ea voce hic potest religiosa pugna, quam Paulus & Barnabas in Circumcisionis patronos sanctè susceperunt. posset simpliciter pro lite & controversia sumi.
units.tr: VERSE 2. Τεταμένης οὖ φάσεως ἐ συζητήσεως οὐκ ἐλίγης &c. The Vulgate did not read συζητήσεως, though the Syrian, the Arabic, the Ethiopic, Chrysostom and the Greek copies all read it, except that Chrysostom has ζητήσεως. Further, φάσεως, which the Vulgate and Erasmus rendered sedition and the Syrian and Arabic tumult, Beza not badly rendered opposition. For since, according to Suidas, φάσις is ἐμφύλιος μάχη, civil strife, one can understand here the religious contest which Paul and Barnabas faithfully undertook against the defenders of circumcision. It could also simply be taken as dispute and controversy.

units.la: VERS. 6. Συνῆχθησαν δὲ οἱ ἀπόστολοι &c. Vulgatus & Erasm. convenerunt que. Beza, convenerunt igitur. Syrus retinuit propriam significationem τὰ δὲ, autem.
units.tr: VERSE 6. Συνῆχθησαν δὲ οἱ ἀπόστολοι &c. The Vulgate and Erasmus have convenerunt que, that is, and they came together. Beza has convenerunt igitur, so they came together. The Syrian kept the proper meaning of τὰ δὲ, but or and.

units.la: VERS. 7. Ἀφ' ἡμερῶν ἀρχαίων. Vulgatus & Eras. à diebus antiquis. Beza, jam pridem. Syrus quod verti potest, vel à diebus antiquis, vel à diebus primis. utrumque enim significat. posterioris significationis loca vide Luc. 2: 2. Matth. 27. 64. Joh. 2. 11. & passim. posteriori quoque ista significatione τῶν ἀρχαίων accepit Arabs, qui vertit à diebus primis. & Æthiopicus à principio, quum nempe primum ad divulgandum ubique locorum Euangelium Apostoli mitterentur. respicit Petrus historiam Cornelii Act. 10. quæ non ita diu post illapsum in Apostolos Spiritum S. contigit, itaque à primis Apostolicæ missionis diebus. & ἀρχαίων quidem non modo antiquum, sed & πρῶτον, primum significare testis est Hezychius. ἀπ' ἀρχαίων usurusurpatur pro ab initio. & dicitur medicus aegrum is ἡ ἀρχαίου ἀπαλλ..., quando eum è morbo in priorem statum restituit. Est & ubi apud LXX Interpretes ἀρχαῖῳ pro ראשון, primum usurpatur, diciturque simpliciter de eo quod praecesserit, sive à multis seculis sive non ita pridem. ut Psal. 79. 8. ne memineris nobis עונות ראשונים, iniquitatum primarum, LXX ἀνομιῶν ἀρχαίων iniquitatum praeteritarum, sive antiquarum sive recentium.
units.tr: VERSE 7. Ἀφ' ἡμερῶν ἀρχαίων. The Vulgate and Erasmus have à diebus antiquis, from ancient days. Beza has jam pridem, long ago. The Syrian, which can be rendered either vel à diebus antiquis or vel à diebus primis, or from the first days, since it means both. For places where the later sense occurs, see Luke 2:2, Matt. 27:64, John 2:11, and passim. In this later sense the Arabic also took τῶν ἀρχαίων, rendering it à diebus primis, from the first days, and the Ethiopic à principio, from the beginning, since the apostles were sent first to spread the Gospel everywhere. Peter refers to the history of Cornelius in Acts 10, which happened not long after the Holy Spirit fell upon the apostles, and so it belongs to the first days of the apostolic mission. Hesychius bears witness that ἀρχαίων means not only ancient but also πρῶτον, first. ἀπ' ἀρχαίων is used for from the beginning, and a physician is said to restore a sick man ἀπ' ἀρχαίου when he brings him back from disease to his earlier state. Also in the Septuagint ἀρχαῖῳ is sometimes used for ראשון, first, and is said simply of what has gone before, whether many centuries ago or not so long ago. So in Psalm 79:8, ne memineris nobis עונות ראשונים, iniquitatum primarum, the Septuagint has ἀνομιῶν ἀρχαίων, iniquitatum praeteritarum, that is, past iniquities, whether ancient or recent.

units.la: IBID. ὁ Θεὸς ἐν ἡμῖν ἐξελέξατο, Alij δὲ σύματα μὲ ἀνέωσε &c. Syrus ἐν ἡμῖν non legit, neque Æthiopicus, Arabs legit ἐν ὑμῖν, quod vertit ex vobis. Cl. Beza post ἐξελέξατο, elegit, supplevit me, ut & Æthiopicus, non item Arabs, etsi Junius in versione sua expresserit. abstinuerunt quoque ab eo supplemento Syrus, Vulgatus & Erasmus. & recte meo judicio, sensus enim esse videtur, Deus inter vos omnes acceptum habuit, ut ex meo ore &c. saepe hoc verbum ad rem refertur, & acceptum habere significat. ut Ef. 58. 5. οὐ τοῦτο τὸ νηστείαν ἐξελεξάμην, non hoc jejunium elegi, id est, acceptum habeo. quamvis non negem semper aliquid eligendi significationis adesse, etiam hoc loco.
units.tr: IBID. ὁ Θεὸς ἐν ἡμῖν ἐξελέξατο, Alij δὲ σύματα μὲ ἀνέωσε &c. The Syrian and the Ethiopic do not read ἐν ἡμῖν, and the Arabic reads ἐν ὑμῖν, which it renders ex vobis, from among you. After ἐξελέξατο, chose, Beza supplied elegit and me, as does the Ethiopic, though not the Arabic, although Junius expressed it in his version. The Syrian, the Vulgate and Erasmus also abstained from that supplement, and rightly so in my judgment. For the sense seems to be: God among you all held it acceptable that by my mouth &c. This verb is often applied to a thing, and means to hold as acceptable. So Isaiah 58:5, οὐ τοῦτο τὸ νηστείαν ἐξελεξάμην, non hoc jejunium elegi, I have not chosen this fast, that is, I do not hold it acceptable. Yet I do not deny that a sense of choosing is always present, even in this place.

units.la: VERS. 8. ὁ Θεὸς ἐμαρτύρησεν αὐτοῖς, Deus dedit ipsis testimonium. qua re? quum dedit ipsis Spir. Sanctum sicut & nobis. spiritum nempe donorum extraordinariorum, seu propheticum, qui datus erat Apostolis, datus & Cornelio cum suis Act. 10. hinc recte colligitur, Deum palam testatum esse, Gentes quoque pertinere ad Christum. nam ἡ μαρτυρία ἐστὶν τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς προφητείας, Apoc. 19. 10. de quo qui plura cupit, videat in Spicilegio Lud. Capelli ad dictum locum Apocal. doctissimum Commentarium. cui hoc solummodo confirmationis gratia addo, quod de spiritu hoc ipse Servator dicit Joan. 15. 26. ἐκεῖνος μαρτυρήσει περὶ ἐμοῦ, ipse testabitur de me. nam ἐκ τῆς ἐμῆς λήψεται, de meo meo accipiet, & annunciabit vobis, qui ergo hunc Spiritum habent, testimonio Christi sunt obsignati.
units.tr: VERSE 8. ὁ Θεὸς ἐμαρτύρησεν αὐτοῖς, Deus dedit ipsis testimonium, God gave them testimony. On what ground? quum dedit ipsis Spir. Sanctum sicut & nobis, since he gave them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us. That is, the Spirit of extraordinary gifts, or prophetic gifts, which was given to the apostles and also to Cornelius with his people (Acts 10). From this it is rightly inferred that God openly testified that the Gentiles also belong to Christ. For ἡ μαρτυρία ἐστὶν τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς προφητείας, the testimony is the spirit of prophecy (Rev. 19:10). Whoever wants more on this should see the most learned commentary of Ludovicus Cappellus on that passage of Revelation in his Spicilegium. To this I add, only for confirmation, what the Saviour himself says of this Spirit in John 15:26: ἐκεῖνος μαρτυρήσει περὶ ἐμοῦ, ipse testabitur de me, he will testify of me. For ἐκ τῆς ἐμῆς λήψεται, de meo, from what is mine, he will receive, and will declare it to you. Therefore those who have this Spirit are sealed by the testimony of Christ.

units.la: VERS. 10. Nunc autem quid tentatis Deum, ‹Greek›&c. Syrus & Arabs recte intellexerunt, subintelligi ἐπὶ quamobrem verterunt ut imponatis. quum enim circumcisionis ac legis patroni in publico isto Concilio adversus Paulum disceptarent, hoc agebant, ut publica Concilii istius Apostolici, adeoque ipsius Dei authoritate, servandae legis Mosaicae necessitas gentibus injungeretur. hac ratione Deum tentari recte agnoscit Petrus, quippe qui periculum secerant, an lex Moïs, quae solis olim Judaeis fuerat data, quaque illi a reliquis gentibus tanquam pariete intergerino fuerant distincti, non posset divina authoritate in gentes etiam transferri, non alium in finem quam ut jugum collo discipulorum imponatur. hoc pacto non in discipulos modo, sed in Deum quoque ipsum peccari, qui quum nunquam gentes, sed solos Israelitas lege Moïs obstrinxerit, nunc vero dato Spiritu S. & purificatis fide earum cordibus, parem cum credentibus Judaeis, ipsisque Apostolis gratiam eis sit largitus, acquiescendum esse in hac Dei gratia, nec ulterius eum tentandum, ut antiquum illud patrum jugum in gentes protendatur. Aethiopicus illam interrogativam orationem, quid tentatis Deum? paraphrastice satis bene expositi per prohibitivam, & nunc ne tentate Deum, & ne imponite jugum gentibus super collum ipsarum.
units.tr: VERSE 10. Nunc autem quid tentatis Deum, &c. The Syrian and the Arabic rightly understood that ἐπὶ is to be supplied, and so rendered it ut imponatis, that you may impose. For when the defenders of circumcision and the law disputed against Paul in this public council, they were aiming at this: that the necessity of keeping the Mosaic law should be imposed on the Gentiles by the public authority of that apostolic council, and so by the authority of God himself. Peter rightly recognises that God is being tested in this way, since they were making an experiment of whether the law of Moses, which had once been given to the Jews alone, and by which they had been separated from the other nations as by a dividing wall, could be extended to the Gentiles by divine authority, with no other purpose than that a yoke be placed on the disciples' necks. In this way sin is committed not only against the disciples but against God himself, who, although he never bound the Gentiles but only the Israelites by the law of Moses, has now, by giving the Holy Spirit and purifying their hearts by faith, bestowed on them the same grace as on the believing Jews and on the apostles themselves. Therefore we must rest in this grace of God, and not test him further by extending that old yoke of the fathers over the Gentiles. The Ethiopic has expounded that interrogative sentence, quid tentatis Deum? why do you tempt God?, fairly well in paraphrase by a prohibition: and now do not tempt God, and do not put a yoke on the necks of the Gentiles.

units.la: VERS. 11. Ἀλλὰ διὰ τῆς χάριτος. Beza, imo per gratiam, ad verbum sed per gratiam, quod Syrus, Arabs, Aethiopicus, Vulgatus & Erasmus recte retinuerunt. Optime enim gratia Christi per adversativam opponitur legis jugo.
units.tr: VERSE 11. Ἀλλὰ διὰ τῆς χάριτος. Beza has imo per gratiam, nay, through grace, but the literal is sed per gratiam, but through grace, which the Syrian, the Arabic, the Ethiopic, the Vulgate and Erasmus rightly kept. For the grace of Christ is set over against the yoke of the law very well by the adversative.

units.la: VERS 14. Καθὼς πρῶτον ὁ Θεὸς ἐπεσκέψατο λαβεῖν ἐξ ἐθνῶν λαὸν. Vulgatus, quemadmodum Deus primum visitavit sumere ex gentibus populum. Erasm. visitavit, ut sumeret. Beza, resperespexerit gentes, ut sumeret ex ipsis. Arabs, [Arabic], vidit ut sumeret ex gentibus. quod nos secuti vertimus, dispexit sumere ex gentibus, quo sensu dicimur dispicere de re aliqua, quum providemus & curamus ut ea fiat. qua significatione usurpatum est hoc verbum supra c. 6. 3. Επισκεψασθαι ανδρας εξ υμων, dispicite viros ex vobis. nisi forte Hebraismum hic agnoscamus, qui in verbo פקד, visitavit saepe reperitur, quando Deo tributum significat, cum promissionum minarumve suarum recordari, ut, quae diu ante denunciavit, praestet. ut 1 Sam. 15. 2. פקדתי את אשר שם עמלק, visitavi (id est, recordatus sum) quae fecerit Amalec. atque ita R. Nathan in Concordantiis, ubi verbum פקד dixisset in quatuor significationum capita dispescit, addit, primum esse שזכר ונזכר, cujus interpretatio sit recordatio. Sic hoc loco, navigavit Simeon, quomodo primum Deus visitaverit (id est, secundum promissiones dudum in Prophetis datas, sed per multas aetates dilatas, tandem recordatus sit) sumere ex gentibus populum. Syrus πρῶτον ἐπεσκέψατο unico verbo vertit [Syriac], incepit. quod non omnino aspernandum. nam primum recordatus est sumere, idem est atque incepit sumere. estque rei, de qua hic agitur, convenientissimum. Ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι αὐτοῦ, nomini suo. ad verbum, pro nomine suo, id est, qui suus esset.
units.tr: VERSE 14. Καθὼς πρῶτον ὁ Θεὸς ἐπεσκέψατο λαβεῖν ἐξ ἐθνῶν λαὸν. The Vulgate: quemadmodum Deus primum visitavit sumere ex gentibus populum, as God first visited to take from the Gentiles a people. Erasmus: visitavit, ut sumeret, visited, that he might take. Beza: respe(xerit gentes), respexerit gentes, ut sumeret ex ipsis, looked upon the Gentiles, that he might take from them. The Arabic, [Arabic], vidit ut sumeret ex gentibus, saw that he might take from the Gentiles. We, following these, rendered it dispexit sumere ex gentibus, took thought to take from the Gentiles, in the sense in which we say that we look out for something when we provide for it and take care that it is done. This verb is used in that sense above in chapter 6:3: Επισκεψασθαι ανδρας εξ υμων, look out from among you men. Unless perhaps we recognise a Hebraism here, since the verb פקד, to visit, is often found when it is said of God, denoting that he remembers his promises or threats, so as to perform what he declared long before. As in 1 Samuel 15:2, פקדתי את אשר שם עמלק, I visited (that is, I remembered) what Amalek did. So also R. Nathan in his Concordances, when he had divided the verb פקד into four heads of meaning, adds that the first is שזכר ונזכר, whose interpretation is remembrance. So in this place, as Simeon relates, how God first visited (that is, according to the promises long ago made through the prophets but deferred through many ages, at last remembered) to take a people from the Gentiles. The Syrian rendered πρῶτον ἐπεσκέψατο with a single word, [Syriac], incepit, began, which is not entirely to be despised. For primum recordatus est sumere, first remembered to take, is the same as incepit sumere, began to take, and it is most suitable to the matter discussed here. Ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι αὐτοῦ, nomini suo, for his name; literally pro nomine suo, for his name, that is, who was his own.

units.la: VERS. 17. Ὅπως ἂν ἐκζητήσωσιν οἱ κατάλοιποι τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὸν Κύριον, &c. Petita haec sunt ex Amos 9. 12. ubi textus Hebraeus sic habet, למען ירשו את שארית אדום, &c. quae verti solent, ut possideant reliquias Edom, & omnes gentes &c. quam versionem fateor difficillimam mihi videri, quae cum loco hoc Actorum concilietur. non item, si nx non Accusativi, sed, ut alibi saepe, Nominativi casus notam dixerimus, vertamusque, Ut possideant (nempe restauratum Davidis Tabernaculum, de quo Vf. praecedenti) relireliquiæ Edom, & omnes gentes super quas invocatum fuerit nomen meum. Nec dubium mihi est, quin LXX Interpretes sic acceperint. Sic enim transferunt, ὅπως ἐκζητήσωσιν οἱ κατάλοιποι τῶν ἀνθρώπων, καὶ πάντα τὰ ἔθνη &c. ut requirant ceteri homines, & omnes gentes &c. quæ verba nullam habent sensum, nisi subintelligas quidnam sint requisituri, nempe id quod jam jam dixerat, dirutum instauratumque tabernaculum Davidis. Pro quo Jacobus non male substituit τὴν σκηνὴν sive enim eos instauratum tabernaculum, sive Dominum, istius tabernaculi instauratorem, ejusdemque herum requirere dicas, idem dicis. Adde quod tabernaculum istud non propter ipsum, sed propter Dominum essent requisituræ Gentes. Indagandum hic quoque, cur pro יִרְשׁוּ, possideant, dixerint LXX ἐκζητήσωσιν, requirant. an quod legerint יִדְרְשׁוּ? sic existimatur vulgo. Licet tamen aliud conjectare. Tenendum apud omnes fermè Orientales verba, quæ significant esse, sæpe etiam significare fieri, id est, moveri ad esse. ut פתח, aperire & solvere, quia solutio motus est ad apertionem. קנה, possidere & emere, quia emtio est motus ad possessionem, aliaque sexcenta. Sic ירש non tantum est possidere, sed etiam movere se ad possidendum. Exemplo sit illud Deut. 2. 24. הַחֵל רֵשׁ לְהִתְיָרֵשׁ, incipe possidere (id est, possessionem adi) & confligere cum eo bello. non poterant incipere actu possidere, antequam conflixissent & ejecissent hostem. Sensus ergo est, incipe adire possessionem. Et clarius etiam Ψ.f. 32; הַחֵל יֵשׁ לָרֶשֶׁת אֶת־הָאָרֶץ, quæ si vertas cum Pagnino, incipe possidere, ut possideas terram ejus, tautologia mera est, nequaquam vero, si vertas, incipe adire possessionem. Ita & hoc loco לִירְשׁוּ, ut possideant, non tam ipsam possessionem, quam possidendi studium denotare existimarunt LXX ἐκζητήσωσιν, quod requirendi verbo satis feliciter expresserunt. Neque mirum, quod יֵשְׁאֲרוּ אָדָם verterint οἱ κατάλοιποι τῶν ἀνθρώπων, fortassis enim legerunt אָדָם, aut potius ut alibi sæpe, hic quoque Edom latius quam de proprie sic dicto populo accipiendum sunt arbitrati. sicut enim duorum Rebeccæ filiorum minimus Ifaac Ecclesiam, sic maximus natu Esau sive Edom omnes reliquos homines ab Ecclesia alienos adumbrabat. quamobrem in scriptis Rabbinorum Imperium Romanum, præsertim quum longè lateque per universum fere orbem pateret, מלכות אדום fuit nuncupatum, atque etiamnum per בני אדום Christiani omnes ipsis intelliguntur. quum itaque hic à Propheta Tabernaculo Davidis, id est, Reipublicæ Israëlis, opponantur reliquiæ Edom, satis commodè per eas reliquos homines intellexerunt. Quod autem diximus םא interdum nominativum designare, si quis fortassis id post verba passiva fateatur, alibi vero neget, videat loca 2 Reg. 9, 25. Nehem. 9. 32. 1 Sam. 17. 34. 2 Reg. 6. 5. Ezech. 43. 7. Jer. 33. 5. ubi cum verbis neutris construitur. Est & ubi cum transitivis, ut Nehem. 9. 34. Jerem. 38. 16. Ezech. 39. 14. unde factum ut, ואת quod alioqui Accusativi casus est, apud Rabbinos cum omnibus promiscue verbis Nominativum faciat, ut אתו ואת, ipse fecit.
units.tr: VERSE 17. Ὅπως ἂν ἐκζητήσωσιν οἱ κατάλοιποι τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὸν Κύριον, &c. These words are taken from Amos 9:12, where the Hebrew text reads למען ירשו את שארית אדום, &c., which is usually rendered ut possideant reliquias Edom, & omnes gentes &c., that they may possess the remnant of Edom, and all the nations &c. I confess this version seems to me very hard to reconcile with this passage of Acts. It is otherwise if we say that the particle את marks not the accusative but, as often elsewhere, the nominative case, and render it: Ut possideant (namely the restored tabernacle of David, of which the preceding verse speaks) reliquiæ Edom, & omnes gentes super quas invocatum fuerit nomen meum, that the remnant of Edom and all the nations over which my name has been called may possess it. Nor do I doubt that the Septuagint understood it in this way. For they translate: ὅπως ἐκζητήσωσιν οἱ κατάλοιποι τῶν ἀνθρώπων, καὶ πάντα τὰ ἔθνη &c., ut requirant ceteri homines, & omnes gentes &c., that the rest of men and all the nations may seek &c. These words have no sense unless you supply what they are to seek, namely that which had just been mentioned, the fallen and restored tabernacle of David. For this James rightly substituted τὴν σκηνὴν, the tabernacle. For whether you say they are to seek the restored tabernacle or the Lord, the restorer of that tabernacle and its master, you say the same thing. Add that the nations were to seek not for the tabernacle itself but for the Lord on account of it. Here one must also inquire why the Septuagint said ἐκζητήσωσιν, they may seek, for יִרְשׁוּ, they may possess. Did they read יִדְרְשׁוּ? That is the common opinion. Yet one may conjecture something else. It must be held that among almost all Orientals verbs which mean to be often also mean to become, that is, to move towards being. As פתח means to open and to loosen, because loosening is a movement towards opening; קנה means to possess and to buy, because buying is a movement towards possession; and six hundred other examples. So ירש does not only mean to possess but also to move oneself to possess. Let Deuteronomy 2:24 serve as an example: הַחֵל רֵשׁ לְהִתְיָרֵשׁ, begin to possess (that is, approach the possession) and engage that enemy in war. They could not actually begin to possess before they had fought and driven out the enemy. The sense therefore is: begin to approach the possession. Even more clearly in Psalm 32 (הַחֵל יֵשׁ לָרֶשֶׁת אֶת־הָאָרֶץ): if you render it with Pagninus, incipe possidere, ut possideas terram ejus, begin to possess, that you may possess its land, it is sheer tautology; but not at all if you render it incipe adire possessionem, begin to approach possession. So also in this place, the Septuagint thought that לִירְשׁוּ, that they may possess, denotes not so much the possession itself as the desire to possess, and they expressed it fairly happily with the verb ἐκζητήσωσιν, to seek. Nor is it surprising that they rendered יֵשְׁאֲרוּ אָדָם as οἱ κατάλοιποι τῶν ἀνθρώπων, the remnant of men, for perhaps they read אָדָם, or rather, as often elsewhere, they judged that Edom here too should be taken more broadly than of the people properly so called. For just as Isaac, the younger of Rebecca's two sons, prefigured the Church, so Esau or Edom, the elder, prefigured all other men alien to the Church. Therefore in the writings of the rabbis the Roman Empire, especially since it extended far and wide over almost the whole world, was called מלכות אדום, the kingdom of Edom, and even now all Christians are understood by בני אדום, the sons of Edom. Since, then, here the remnant of Edom is set by the prophet over against the tabernacle of David, that is, the commonwealth of Israel, they fairly well understood by it the rest of men. As for what we said, that את sometimes designates the nominative, if anyone admits this after passive verbs but denies it elsewhere, let him see the passages 2 Kings 9:25, Nehemiah 9:32, 1 Samuel 17:34, 2 Kings 6:5, Ezekiel 43:7, Jeremiah 33:5, where it is construed with neuter verbs. It is also found with transitive verbs, as in Nehemiah 9:34, Jeremiah 38:16, Ezekiel 39:14. Hence it comes about that את, which otherwise is a sign of the accusative, among the rabbis makes the nominative with all verbs indiscriminately, as אתו ואת, he himself did.

units.la: VERS. 18. Γιωσκὰ ἀπ' αἰῶνός ἐστι τῷ Θεῷ πάντα ἔργα αὐτοῦ. Variis lectionibus quas hic annotavit Beza addo, Syrum legere, γνωσταὶ ἐστιν ἀπ' αἰῶνος ἔργα ἡ Θεοῦ. Arabem, γνωστὸν ἐστι τῷ Κυρίῳ ἀπ' αἰῶνος. Æthiopicum, ἃ γνωσταὶ ἐστιν ἀπ' αἰῶνος. vel ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου.
units.tr: VERS. 18. Known to God from the beginning are all his works [Γνωστά ἐστι τῷ Θεῷ ἀπ' αἰῶνός πάντα τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ]. To the variant readings Beza notes here I add the following. The Syriac reads, "Known from the beginning are the works of God" [γνωσταί ἐστιν ἀπ' αἰῶνος τὰ ἔργα τοῦ Θεοῦ]. The Arabic reads, "It is known to the Lord from the beginning" [γνωστὸν ἐστι τῷ Κυρίῳ ἀπ' αἰῶνος]. The Ethiopic reads, "Known are, from the beginning," [ἃ γνωσταί ἐστιν ἀπ' αἰῶνος], or perhaps "from the foundation of the world" [ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου].

units.la: VERS. 19. Μὴ παρενοχλεῖν &c. ἐνοχλεῖν dicuntur qui ab immundis spiritibus vexantur, Luc. 6. 18. Act. 5. 16. ἐνοχλεῖν, turbas dare dicitur radix amaritudinis sursum enascens, Hebr. 12. 15. Παρενοχλεῖν usurpatur à LXX Interpretibus pro פיק, affligere, arctare, Jud. 14. 17. pro הרם, commovere, inquietare, 1 Sam. 28. 15. pro ילע, molestare, Jud. 16. 16. pro הרה, pavefacere, perturbare, Jer. 46. 26. pro תלא, fatigationem ac molestiam parere, Mich. 6. 3. quæ omnes significationes satis bene hic quadrant. usurpant autem nunc cum Accusativo, nunc cum Dativo. posterius secutus est Lucas.
units.tr: VERS. 19. "Not to trouble" [Μὴ παρενοχλεῖν] and so on. The verb "to trouble" [ἐνοχλεῖν] is used of those who are vexed by unclean spirits (Luke 6:18; Acts 5:16). It is used of the root of bitterness springing up and causing trouble (Heb. 12:15). The Septuagint use "to trouble" [παρενοχλεῖν] for several Hebrew verbs: for פיק, to afflict or straiten (Judg. 14:17); for הרם, to stir up or disquiet (1 Sam. 28:15); for ילע, to harass (Judg. 16:16); for הרה, to terrify or perturb (Jer. 46:26); and for תלא, to cause weariness and annoyance (Mic. 6:3). All these meanings fit this place quite well. They use the verb sometimes with the accusative and sometimes with the dative. Luke followed the latter construction.

units.la: VERS. 20. Æthiopicus non facit hîc mentionem τῆς προφητείας. infra autem γ′. 29. in epistola, eam cum cæteris commemorat. utroque in loco addit, & quod non vultis fieri vobis, ne facite proximo vestro. de quo vide notas Bezæ. Eadem autem quæ hîc sacra Synodus, vetuit etiam suis Impostor Mahomed, nisi quod loco scortationis carnem porcinam nominet. verba ejus sunt in Surata Bacara, حُرِّمَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْمَيْتَةُ وَالدَّمُ وَلَحْمُ الْخِنْزِيرِ وَمَا أُهِلَّ لِغَيْرِ اللَّهِ بِهِ
units.tr: VERSE 20. The Ethiopic version does not mention τῆς προφητείας ("of the prophecy") here, but at verse 29 in the epistle it lists it with the others. In both places it adds "and what you do not want done to you, do not do to your neighbour." On this see Beza's notes. The same things this holy Synod forbids here were also forbidden to his followers by the impostor Muhammad, except that in place of fornication he names the flesh of swine. His words in the Sura al-Baqara are: ḥurrima ʿalaykumu l-maytatu wa-d-damu wa-laḥmu l-khinzīri wa-mā ahilla li-ghayri llāhi bihi.

units.la: prohibuit vobis morticinia, sanguinem, carnem porcinam, & super quod laudes dicta sunt aliis quam Deo, id est, ἀδωλόθυτα. solent enim in Oriente omnes bestias quas mactant sanctificare per بِسْمِ اللَّهِ, in nomine Dei. quæ verba qui proferret, dicebatur أَهِلَّ, laudem dicere.
units.tr: "He has forbidden you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which praises have been spoken for anyone other than God," that is, ἀδωλόθυτα [things sacrificed to idols]. For in the East they usually consecrate all the beasts they slaughter by saying bismillah, "in the name of God." The one who pronounced those words was said to ahalla, "to speak praise."

units.la: VERS. 24. Ἐπιστῆσαι ὑμᾶς. Syrus ﻋﻠﻴﻜﻢ؟. lege in plurali ﻋﻠﻴﻜﻢ؟, perturbarunt vos. etsi omnes editiones in mendosa ista lectione consentiant. Ἀναστάτοῦντες τὰς ψυχὰς ὑμῶν. Vulgatus, evertentes animas vestras. ut & Arabs يقلبون, prosternentes. Erasmus & Beza labefactantes. Fortassis & rectè vertatur, transferentes, Belgicè verstettende. sicut Apostolus ad Gal.1.6. Miror quod tam cito μετατίθεσθε transferimini,nempe per eosdem de quibus hîc agitur, qui jungentes Christo circumcisionem reliquasque legis ceremonias, in aliud Euangelium Christianos transferebant. Hezychius ἀναστατῶν, μεταπηδῶντες. in quam sententiam Budæus docet, ἀναστατῶντος proprië de iis dici, qui collectis vasis alio migrant.unde & apud Hezychium ἀνασκευάζομενοι, μεταιικιζόμενοι. Æthiopicus hæc non legit. ut nec quæ sequuntur, λέγοντες περιτμηθῆναι, ἐὰν μὴ περιτμηθῆτε τῷ ἔθει τῷ Μωϋσέως, quæ posteriora Vulgatus quoque non legit. Syrus & Arabs legerunt omnia, verterunt〈que〉 hæc posteriora dicentes ut circumcideremini. Beza, dicentes oportere vos circumcidi. Vertimus cum Erasmo, jubentes circumcidi & servare legem. λέγω & ἄπου pro jubeo non est insolens. vide Luc. 12. 13. Mat. 4. 3. Marc. 5. verf. ult. ut & ܐܡܪ apud Hebræos 1 Reg. 11. 18. Esth. 1. 10. 11. 1 Paral. 20. 17. & alibi. unde apud Arabes nihil aliud est quam mandare.
units.tr: VERSE 24. Ἐπιστῆσαι ὑμᾶς ("to trouble you"). The Syriac has ʿalaykum, which should be read in the plural, ʿalaykum, "they troubled you," although all the editions agree in this faulty reading. Ἀναστατοῦντες τὰς ψυχὰς ὑμῶν ("unsettling your souls"): the Vulgate has "subverting your souls," and the Arabic yuqalliboona likewise means "overturning." Erasmus and Beza have "shaking." Perhaps it may also be rightly rendered "transferring" (Dutch verstettende). So the Apostle says in Gal. 1:6, "I marvel that you are so quickly transferring [μετατίθεσθε]," namely through the same people of whom he speaks here, who, joining circumcision and the other ceremonies of the law to Christ, were transferring Christians to another gospel. Hesychius explains ἀναστατῶν as μεταπηδῶντες [leaping from one place to another]. Budaeus teaches to this effect that ἀναστατοῦντος is properly said of those who, having packed up their vessels, migrate elsewhere; hence also in Hesychius ἀνασκευάζομενοι is explained as μεταικιζόμενοι [being moved from their dwelling]. The Ethiopic does not read these words, nor does it read what follows, λέγοντες περιτμηθῆναι, ἐὰν μὴ περιτμηθῆτε τῷ ἔθει τῷ Μωϋσέως ("saying that you must be circumcised, unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses"); the Vulgate also omits these latter words. The Syriac and the Arabic read everything, and they render these latter words as "saying that you should be circumcised." Beza has "saying that you ought to be circumcised." We translate, with Erasmus, "commanding that you be circumcised and keep the law." Using λέγω and ἄπου for "to command" is not unusual; see Luke 12:13, Matt. 4:3, Mark 5 (last verse). So too the Syriac ʾamar among the Hebrews, 1 Kings 11:18, Esth. 1:10, 11, 1 Chron. 20:17, and elsewhere. Hence among the Arabs it means nothing other than "to command."

units.la: VERS. 25. Visum est nobis ἐλθόντας ὁμοθυμαδὸν, Erasmus, unanimiter congregatis. Beza, concorditer coactis. Vulgatus, collectis in unum. sufficiebat cum Syro simpliciter dixisse, collectis, vel congregatis. ad verbum, factis simul. ὁμοθυμαδὸν enim pro simplici ἅμα usitatissimum esse LXX Interpretibus, docuimus supra c. 2. 1.
units.tr: VERS. 25. "It has seemed good to us, being come together with one accord" [ἐλθόντας ὁμοθυμαδόν]. Erasmus has "gathered together unanimously," Beza "gathered together in agreement," the Vulgate "gathered into one." It would have been enough to say simply, with the Syriac, "gathered," or "assembled," literally "made together." For I have shown above, on chapter 2:1, that ὁμοθυμαδόν is a very common equivalent of the simple ἅμα in the Septuagint.

units.la: VERS. 29. Μηδὲν πλέον ἐπιτίθεσθαι ὑμῖν βάρος. Vulgatus, nihil ultra vobis imponere oneris. Arabs, Æthiopicus, Eras. & Beza, ne quod amplius imponeremus vobis onus. Malim tamen generalius vertere cum Syro passive, ne quod amplius imponatur vobis onus, scilicet nec à nobis, nec à quopiam alio.
units.tr: VERS. 29. "To lay upon you no greater burden" [Μηδὲν πλέον ἐπιτίθεσθαι ὑμῖν βάρος]. The Vulgate has, "to impose on you no burden beyond these things." The Arabic, Ethiopic, Erasmus and Beza have, "that we should not impose on you any greater burden." I would prefer, however, to render it more generally and in the passive, with the Syriac: "that no greater burden be laid upon you," namely neither by us nor by anyone else.

units.la: VERS. 32. Syrus hic habet ܐܚܝܢ ܕܝܢ ܗܘ ܠܗܘܢ ܡܬܘܒܢ ܠܐܝܢ. Tremel. & Boder. in Regiis, & confirmarunt domesticos Judas & Silas. Domesticos, inquit Tremel. appellat fideles ipsos, qui in Ecclesiam Dei tanquam ipsius familiam cooptati fuerant. At primò, Apostolus eos qui roborabantur & confirmabantur vocat ἀδελφούς, quos Syrus præcedentibus verbis transtulit ܐܚܘܗܝ, fratres, nec quicquam præterea in Græco est, quod domesticos ullatenus indigeret: Secundo, videntur viri illi eruditi ܐܚܝܢ ܐܠܐ accepisse pro periphrasi domesticorum, quasi dicas eos qui domus, sup. sunt, ut ad verbum habet Boder. in Parisiensi. At vero ܩܠܐ quod sciam nunquam post se habet ܕ; ad formandum pron. relat. qui, id enim Syri efferunt per ܕ ܩܠܐ vel per ܕ ܐܠܐ. Sed ܩܠܐ aut verbum valet substantivum sunt, aut demonstrativum est, & quidem Accusativi casus, eos. Tertio ܐܠܐ ܕ quod hic absque vocalibus scribitur, non est in statu absoluto legendum, ut per se significet domesticos, sed in constructo ܕܝܡ, & referendum ad sequentia unde regitur. adeo ut ܩܠܐ separatim sumtum sit Accusativus patiens, ܐܠܐ ܕ Nominativus agens. atque ita, si hic domesticorum notio locum sit habitura, vertere oportet, & confirmarunt eos domestici Iuda & Sila. quae periphrasis mihi videtur ipsius Judae & Silae, ut sensus sit, & confirmarunt eos Iudas & Silas. sicut & Graeci periphrasin illam imitantur, οἱ τῶν Παῦλον, id est, Paulus, Act. 13. 13. τὰς τῶν Μαρίας Martham & Mariam, Joan. 11. 19. & frequens est in Thargum, ut pro ܝܗܘܕܝ dicatur ܝܗܘܕܝ, id est, Iudai. pro ܣܢܝܢ, ܝܗܘܕܝ. vide Jud. 1. ܝܕ. 4. & 27. Similiter capio Marc. 5. 35. ܐܠܐ ܕ ܐܠܐ, Boder. venerunt a domo principis synagogae. non recte. nam eo sensu redundaret ܕ, & suffecisset dixisse, ܐܠܐ ܕ. Trem. itaque, venerunt ex domesticis principis synagogae. non repugno. malim tamen statuere sensum simpliciter esse, venerunt a principe synagogae. sicut in Graeco est, ἐκ τοῦ ἀρχισυναγώγου. adeo ut ܐܠܐ ܕ periphrasis sit ipsius ἀρχισυναγώγου. quod cum Actorum loco plane conveniret. sic Luc. 4. 25. multæ viduæ erant [Syriac] pro ἐν τῷ Ιστρῄλ. præsertim vero notari volo locum ad Hebr. 8. 8. [Syriac] [Syriac] [Syriac] [Syriac] [Syriac], Καὶ συνελίσω ἐπὶ τὸν οἶκον Ισραὴλ καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν οἶκον Ιούδα. [Syriac] est ἐπὶ τὸν οἶκον. ergo [Syriac] [Syriac] & [Syriac] simpliciter est Ισραὴλ & Ιούδα. nemo enim hic vertat, super domum domus Israël, & super domum domus Iuda. multo minus, super domum domesticorum Israëlis &c. nec cum propriis tantum, sed & cum appellativis nominibus [Syriac] sæpe pleonasticum est. ut Luc. 14. 23. [Syriac] [Syriac] nihil est nisi [Syriac]. φεγμὸς, sepes.
units.tr: VERS. 32. The Syriac here reads "ahin dain hu lahon mtubhan l'ahin." Tremellius and Boderianus (in the Royal text) render it: "and Judas and Silas confirmed the domestics." Tremellius says that "domestics" refers to the believers themselves, who had been admitted into the Church of God as its household. But first, the Apostle calls those who were being strengthened and confirmed "brethren" (adelphous), which the Syriac rendered in the preceding words as "ahuhi," brothers. Nothing else in the Greek requires the word "domestics" in any way. Second, those learned men seem to have taken "ahin" as a periphrasis for "of the domestics," as if one said "those who are of the house," as Boderianus renders it word for word in the Parisian text. But so far as I know, the Syriac "la" is never followed by "d" to form the relative pronoun "who." The Syrians express that by "d" with "la" or "d" with "ala." Here "la" is either the verb "are" or a demonstrative, and indeed in the accusative case, "them." Third, the word written here without vowels ("ahin d") is not to be read in the absolute state, so as to mean "domestics" by itself, but in the construct state, and it must be referred to what follows, by which it is governed. So taken separately, "la" is the accusative object, and "ahin d" is the nominative subject. If the notion of "domestics" is to stand here, one must therefore translate, "and the domestics of Judas and Silas confirmed them." This seems to me rather a periphrasis for Judas and Silas themselves, so that the sense is "and Judas and Silas confirmed them." The Greeks likewise imitate this periphrasis: "those of Paul" [οἱ τοῦ Παύλου], that is, Paul, Acts 13:13; "the things of Mary," that is, Martha and Mary, John 11:19. It is also frequent in the Targum, where for "Jehudi" is said "Jehudi," that is, Jews, and for "Sinai," "Jehudi," see Judges 1 and 4 and 27. I take Mark 5:35 in the same way, "ahin d ahin," which Boderianus renders "they came from the house of the ruler of the synagogue." This is not right, for in that sense "d" would be redundant and it would have sufficed to say "ahin d." Tremellius's rendering, "they came from the domestics of the ruler of the synagogue," I do not oppose. Yet I would rather hold that the sense is simply "they came from the ruler of the synagogue," as in the Greek, ek tou archisynagogou [ἐκ τοῦ ἀρχισυναγώγου], so that "ahin d" is a periphrasis for archisynagogos itself. This agrees plainly with the passage in Acts. So in Luke 4:25, "many widows were" [Syriac] stands for "in Israel" [ἐν τῷ Ἰσραήλ]. Above all, I want the passage at Hebrews 8:8 to be noted, where the Syriac has, following the Greek, "And I will make a covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah" [Καὶ συνελῶ ἐπὶ τὸν οἶκον Ισραὴλ καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν οἶκον Ιούδα]. The Syriac for "upon the house" is "ahin d" in the Greek "ἐπὶ τὸν οἶκον"; so the Syriac for "Israel" and "Judah" is simply Israel and Judah. Nobody here should render it "upon the house of the house of Israel, and upon the house of the house of Judah," much less "upon the house of the domestics of Israel," and so on. Nor is such pleonasm frequent only with proper names, but also with common nouns, as at Luke 14:23, where the Syriac is nothing but "fence" [φραγμός, sepes].

units.la: VERS. 33. 34. Ποιήσαντες ἡ χρόνον. de hac phrasi egimus Matt. 20. 12. occurrit & infra Act. 18. 23. & 20. 3. usitatissima Syris est hæc phrasis. unde Act. 20. 16. pro festinavit ut die Pentecostes esset Hierosolymis, Syrus habet, ut diem Pentecostes [Syriac], faceret, id est, transigeret, Hierosolymis. Sequitur in fine versus, ὥστε ἂν ἐπὶ Ἰσραὴλ. sic & Syrus legit. Arabs addit & seniores qui erant Hierosolymis. Vulgatus & Æthiopicus vertunt ad eos qui miserant illos, q. ὥστε ἂν ἐπὶ Ἰσραὴλ αὐτούς. vide notas Bezæ. Variat autem & hic & ψ. 34. Æthiopicus. hic habet, & quum morati essent, dimiserunt in pace fratres ad eos qui miserant ipsos. Deinde ψ. 34. (quem Vulgatus & Arabs legerunt, Syrus non legit) pro ἔδοξε ἡ τῷ Σιλᾶ ἐπιμεῖναι αὐτοῖ, habet Æthiopicus, & statuit Paulus manere. Tum subjungit ψ. 35. & Paulus & Barnabas haserunt Antiochiæ.
units.tr: VERS. 33, 34. "Having spent some time" [Ποιήσαντες δὲ χρόνον]. We discussed this phrase at Matt. 20:12. It also occurs below at Acts 18:23 and 20:3. The phrase is very common among the Syriac. Hence in Acts 20:16, for "he hastened to be at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost," the Syriac has, "that he might make the day of Pentecost at Jerusalem," that is, that he might pass it at Jerusalem. At the end of the verse follows, "to those who had sent them" [ὥστε ἂν ἐπὶ Ἰσραὴλ]. So also the Syriac reads. The Arabic adds, "and the elders who were in Jerusalem." The Vulgate and the Ethiopic translate, "to those who had sent them," reading ὥστε ἂν ἐπὶ Ἰσραὴλ αὐτούς. See Beza's notes. Here and at verse 34 the Ethiopic varies. Here it has, "and when they had stayed, they dismissed the brothers in peace to those who had sent them." Then at verse 34 (which the Vulgate and the Arabic read, but the Syriac does not), in place of "it seemed good to Silas to remain there" [ἔδοξε δὲ τῷ Σιλᾶ ἐπιμεῖναι αὐτοῖς], the Ethiopic has, "and Paul decided to remain." Then it adds at verse 35, "and Paul and Barnabas remained at Antioch."

units.la: VERS. 36. [Syriac/Arabic script, illegible] . Boder. & Trem. & videamus quid faciant. id diceretur potius [Syriac/Arabic script, illegible], malim ergo passive, ut solet in Peil, & videamus quid factii sint. [Greek: τῶς ἐχῶσι], quomodo se habeant. fateor tamen Peil nunc activè, nunc passivè sumi. adeo ut utraque interpretatio hic locum habere queat. vide quæ annotamus ad Rom. 15. 18.
units.tr: Verse 36. The Syriac word (illegible in the transcription) is rendered by Boderianus and Tremellius as "and let us see what they do." The word would more naturally be passive, as it usually is in Peil, so I prefer "and let us see how they have fared" [τὰ ἔχουσι], that is, how they are doing. I admit, however, that Peil is sometimes taken actively and sometimes passively, so that either rendering can stand here. See what we note on Romans 15:18.

units.la: VERS. 38. [Greek: παῶλ@ ὁ ἀξίως μὴ συμπερελαβὼν τὴν]. Syrus & Arabs, Paulus autem nolebat assumere hunc secum. sic & Erasmus. est enim ἀξιῶν, volo, Act. 28. 22. Beza, æquum censebat eum non simul assumere. & recte reprehendit Vulgatum, quod barbarè & obscurè verterit, rogabat eum non debere recipi. sed planius Æthiopicus, rogavit Paulus Barnabam ut non assumeret Marcum. ἀξιῶν pro rogare, orare usitatum est apud bonos authores. Glossarium ἀξιῶ, Desidero, oro, postulo, posco.
units.tr: Verse 38. The Greek reads: "Paul, however, did not think it right to take him with them" [Παῦλος δὲ ἠξίου μὴ συμπαραλαμβάνειν τὸν]. The Syriac and Arabic have, "But Paul was unwilling to take this man with him," and Erasmus agrees. Indeed ἀξιῶν means "I wish," as in Acts 28:22. Beza has, "he thought it fair not to take him along." He rightly criticises the Vulgate, which translated barbarously and obscurely, "he asked that he should not be received." The Ethiopic is plainer: "Paul asked Barnabas not to take Mark." The use of ἀξιῶν to mean "to request, beg" is common among good authors. The glossary gives ἀξιῶ: I desire, beg, request, demand, ask.

units.la: VERS. 40. [Greek: Παῶλ@ ὁ ἐκλεξάμενος Σίλαν.] Erasmus & Beza, Paulus autem allecto Sila. Vulgatus autem Syrus, Arabs & Æthiopicus electo. Glossarium [Greek: ἐκλίγομαι, opto, deligo, eligo.] [Greek: ἐκλεκτός, electus, lectus.] nec aliam significationem tradunt Lexicographi, dicunt enim idem esse quod [Greek: ἐκλέγειν].
units.tr: Verse 40. The Greek reads: "Paul, having chosen Silas" [Παῦλος ἐκλεξάμενος Σίλαν]. Erasmus and Beza have, "Paul, however, having been enlisted, Silas." The Vulgate, the Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic have "chosen" (in the ablative absolute). The glossary gives ἐκλέγομαι: I choose, select, pick out, elect; and ἐκλεκτός: chosen, picked out. The lexicographers give no other meaning, for they say that the word is the same as ἐκλέγειν.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: VERS. 10. [Greek: Συμβιβάζοντες]. Vulgatus & Erasm. certi facti, pro quo Cl. Beza non male docet dicendum potius fuisse [Greek: συμβιβασθέντες]. quod etiam de Syri, Arabisque versione judicandum. quorum ille intelligentes, hic scientes. Beza, collatis testimoniis colligentes. verbum hoc, fateor, conferre significat. sed an collatis testimoniis colligere & inferre dubito. pluribus de hoc verbo egimus Act. 9. 22. ubi & illud Hezychii protulimus, συμβιβάζῃ, εἰς φιλίαν ἀγὰπ, συμλαλεῖ. quorum posterius potest esse hujus loci, ut συμβιβάζοντες sit συλλαλῶντες, colloquentes, conferentes inter nos, alter alteri dicentes, Dominum nos vocasse &c. Monere tamen oportet, συμβιβάζειν non tantum transitivè sumi pro εἰς φιλίαν ἀγάπν, coire, facere, in amorem & consensum agere, unde apud Thucyd. συνεβιβάσθησαν, convenerunt, pacti sunt: sed & ipsummet intransitivè sumi eadem significatione. ut apud Plat. de Rep. l. 6. συνεβιβάζουσι δικαιοσύνης πρὸς σωφροσύνης, convenit inter nos de justitia & temperantia, interprete Budæo. συμβιβασμὸς, transactio, concordia. hinc rectè vertas hoc loco, Consentientes, pariter hoc statuentes, Deum nos vocasse &c.
units.tr: VERS. 10. [συμβιβάζοντες]. The Vulgate and Erasmus render it certi facti, "made certain." Beza rightly observes that it should rather have been [συμβιβασθέντες], and the same judgment should be made of the Syriac and Arabic versions: the Syriac has intelligentes ("understanding") and the Arabic scientes ("knowing"). Beza has collatis testimoniis colligentes ("gathering together by comparing the testimonies"). I admit the verb means "to compare," but I doubt that it means "to gather by comparing testimonies and to infer." We have discussed this verb at length at Acts 9:22, where we also cited Hesychius's gloss, συμβιβάζῃ, εἰς φιλίαν ἀγάπῃ, συλλαλεῖ ["he brings together into friendship and love, he talks with"]. The latter part of that gloss may fit this place, so that συμβιβάζοντες means συλλαλοῦντες, "conversing," "conferring among ourselves," each saying to the other that the Lord had called us, and so on. We should note, however, that συμβιβάζειν is used not only transitively, in the sense of εἰς φιλίαν ἀγάπην ["into friendship and love"], to bring together, to make, to bring about harmony and agreement, whence in Thucydides συνεβιβάσθησαν ["they came together, they made terms"]. It is also used intransitively in the same sense, as in Plato, Republic book 6: συνεβιβάζουσι δικαιοσύνης πρὸς σωφροσύνης ["they agree concerning justice and temperance"], as Budaeus translates it. From this the noun συμβιβασμός means "agreement" or "concord." Hence in this place I would rightly render it, "agreeing together, resolving in common" that God had called us, and so on.

units.la: VERS. II. Εἰς Νεάπολιν. Æthiopicus, ad novam urbem, cui nomen est Neapolis.
units.tr: VERS. 11. Εἰς Νεάπολιν. The Ethiopic has ad novam urbem, cui nomen est Neapolis ("to the new city, whose name is Neapolis").

units.la: ea enim nominis hujus est interpretatio. Est enim civitas Campaniæ à Chalcidensibus olim condita, quæ quum, jubente id Apollinis oraculo, à Cumanis ob ingruentem immanissimam pestem, esset eversa, ab iisdem splendidius est restituta, & ad differentiam veteris urbis, Neapolis appellata.
units.tr: For that is the interpretation of the name. It is a city of Campania, once founded by the Chalcidians. When it was overthrown by the Cumaeans, by the command of an oracle of Apollo because of a dreadful and monstrous plague, it was restored by the same people more splendidly, and, to distinguish it from the old city, it was called Neapolis.

units.la: VERS. 13. Egressi sumus ex urbe ad flumen, ὃ ἐνομίζετο προσευχὴ εἶναι.
units.tr: VERS. 13. We went out of the city to the river, ὃ ἐνομίζετο προσευχὴ εἶναι ["where a place of prayer was thought to be"].

units.la: Vulgatus obscurè, ubi videbatur oratio esse. Erasmus & Beza, ubi solebat oratio esse, quod & ipsum clarius esset, si legeretur ὑπελέγειν fieri. Syrus, quia ibi conspiciebatur domus orationis. Arabs, locus orationis. Ad hunc modum non gravatè verterem, ubi fama erat proseucham esse. νομίζειν enim pro in fama & existimatione esse aliquando usurpari, docet ex Platone Budæus. vel, ubi putabatur proseucha esse. putabatur, scilicet à nobis, id est, putabamus, ut vertit Æthiopicus. Proseuchas autem non preces tantum, sed & precationum loca atque ædificia dicta fuisse, eaque extra urbes esse solere, in Commentariis Drusii abundè probatum reperiet qui volet. quibus hoc tantum addimus, ritus istius originem fortassis è facto patris sui Isaaci petiisse Judæos, qui Gen. 24. 62. 63. dicitur exivisse in agrum, & quidem ad puteum sive fontem, בְּאֵר, ad orandum, interprete Chaldæo, quem sequitur Pagninus. hinc ritus videtur ortus, ut proseuchæ extra urbes in agris, & fere ad flumina, fontes, torrentes, aliosque aquarum rivos erigerentur. Quod & idololatræ sunt imitati, quos torrentibus delectatos fuisse, ibique Deos suos coluisse, quin & ipsofinet torrentes tanquam Deos, Esaias c. 57. 6. his verbis abundè testatur, in divisionibus torrentis portio tua, illa sunt sors tua, etiam illis sudisti libamen, obtulisti munus.
units.tr: The Vulgate, obscurely, has ubi videbatur oratio esse ("where prayer seemed to be"). Erasmus and Beza have ubi solebat oratio esse ("where prayer used to be"), which would itself be clearer if it were read as ὑπελέγειν [a different verb] taking effect. The Syriac has quia ibi conspiciebatur domus orationis ("because there was seen a house of prayer"). The Arabic has locus orationis ("a place of prayer"). In this manner I would not hesitate to translate: "where it was reported that there was a proseucha" (a prayer-house). That νομίζειν can be used for to be in report and opinion Budaeus shows from Plato. Or: "where a proseucha was thought to be," with "thought" meaning "by us," that is, "we thought," as the Ethiopic translates. That proseuchae were not only places of prayer but also places and buildings for prayer, and that these were usually outside the cities, anyone who wishes can find abundantly proved in the commentaries of Drusius. To these we add only this: perhaps the Jews derived this custom from the act of their father Isaac, who according to Gen. 24:62–63 went out into the field, and indeed to a well or spring, בְּאֵר ["to meditate" or "to pray"], as the Chaldee interpreter renders it, whom Pagninus follows. From this the custom seems to have arisen, that proseuchae were built outside the cities in the fields, and nearly always by rivers, springs, torrents, and other channels of water. The idolaters imitated this, who took delight in torrents and worshipped their gods there; indeed, Isaiah 57:6 clearly bears witness to their worship of the torrents themselves as gods, in these words: "Among the smooth stones of the torrent is your portion; they are your lot; to them you have poured a drink offering and offered a gift."

units.la: VERS. 14. Πεῤῥυρόπωλις πόλεως Θυατείρων, Boza, qua purpuram vendebat in urbe Thyatirorum. habitasse eam tamen cum familia sua Philippis non Thyatitis, ex seq. versu liquet. malim itaque cum Vulgato & Erafmo ad verbum transferre, urbis Thyatirorum, atque intelligere eam inde oriundam fuisse. unde Syrus & Arabs, ex urbe Thyatira.
units.tr: VERS. 14. Πορφυρόπωλις πόλεως Θυατείρων ["a seller of purple of the city of Thyatira"]. Beza: qua purpuram vendebat in urbe Thyatirorum ("who sold purple in the city of the Thyatirans"). That she lived with her household at Philippi and not at Thyatira is clear from the following verse. I would therefore prefer, with the Vulgate and Erasmus, to translate word for word, "of the city of the Thyatirans," and to understand that she was originally from there. Hence the Syriac and Arabic have "from the city of Thyatira."

units.la: VERS. 16. Πνεῦμα πύθωνος, Spiritum Pythonis. Hunc non à πνεῦμα, sed ab Hebræo יִדְּעֹנִי, serpens, aspis, quippe qui sacer esset Apollini, & per quem divinationes olim instituerentur, sic dictum, eruditissimè, ut omnia, summus Heinsius docuit & evicit Aristarchi sui p. 18. 19. ubi plurima ad hanc rem scitu dignissima. Syrus vertit spiritum divinationis. idem est quod Hebræorum טוֹפ, permutatis ף & ד, quia apud Orientales sunt ejusdem pronunciationis.
units.tr: VERS. 16. Πνεῦμα πύθωνος ["a spirit of Python"]. This is named not from πνεῦμα but from the Hebrew יִדְּעֹנִי [yidde'oni], "serpent" or "asp," since it was sacred to Apollo and through it divinations were once practised. Heinsius, the most learned of men, has taught and proved this, as he does everything, in his Aristarchus, pp. 18–19, where there is much that is most worth knowing about this matter. The Syriac renders it spiritum divinationis ("a spirit of divination"). It is the same as the Hebrew טוֹפ [tof], with ף and ד exchanged, because among Orientals they have the same pronunciation.

units.la: VERS. 18. Πνεῦμα ἔτι. perperam Æthiopicus accepit Πνεῦμα Ablat. casu. vertit enim, dixit per Spiritum Sanctum. intelligitur Spiritus Pythonis, quem increpuit Paulus.
units.tr: VERS. 18. Πνεῦμα ἔτι ["the spirit still"]. The Ethiopic wrongly took Πνεύματι as an ablative case. It renders it "he said through the Holy Spirit." What is meant is the spirit of Python, whom Paul rebuked.

units.la: VERS. 19. Οὐκ ἐξῆλθεν ἡ ἐλπὶς τῆς ἐργασίας αὐτῶν. non dixit ἀπῆλθεν, abiit. sed ἐξῆλθεν, exiit. itaque Syrus & Arabs addiderunt, ex ea. atque ita spes lucri sui, est Spiritus Pythonis, qui erat spes lucri per Metonymiam.
units.tr: VERS. 19. Οὐκ ἐξῆλθεν ἡ ἐλπὶς τῆς ἐργασίας αὐτῶν ["the hope of their gain went not out"]. Luke did not write ἀπῆλθεν ("departed"), but ἐξῆλθεν ("went out"). Therefore the Syriac and Arabic added "from her" ("from it"). And so "the hope of their gain" is the spirit of Python, which by metonymy was the hope of gain.

units.la: IBID. E'ν τῇ ἀγχοῦλας. Syrus & Arabs non omiserunt, sed sequentibus immiscuerunt, hoc modo, & literunt eos coram strategis (Arabs prefectis satellitum) & coram primatibus urbis. primi sunt οἱ στρατηγοί, alii οἱ ἀρχοντες. Videntur ineptum existimasse, eos primum ad ἀρχοντας dici perductos, deinde adductos ad στρατηγούς. itaque utrosque conjunxerunt. Sed Cl. Bezæ ἐν τῇ ἀρχοντας redundare videtur. conveniens tamen judico, ut primum ad magistratus sive praefectos urbis, quippe pacis publicæ tutores, & fontium judices, deinde ad praetores sive satellitum praefectos, quippe quibus, praeeunte τῶν ἐχθρῶν judicio, capiendorum, incarcerandorum & puniendorum fontium cura incumberet, deducerentur.
units.tr: IBID. Ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ["in the marketplace"]. The Syriac and Arabic did not omit these words but mixed them into what follows, in this way: "and they dragged them before the generals" (the Arabic says "prefects of the guards") "and before the chief men of the city." The generals are οἱ στρατηγοί, the others οἱ ἄρχοντες ["the rulers"]. They seem to have thought it absurd that they were first brought to the rulers and then led on to the generals, and so they joined the two together. But Beza's ἐν τῇ ἀρχοντας seems to be redundant. I nevertheless judge it fitting that they were first led to the magistrates or prefects of the city, as guardians of the public peace and judges of the crimes, and then to the praetors or prefects of the guards, to whom, under the guidance of the judgment of the enemies, the care of seizing, imprisoning, and punishing the offenders would fall.

units.la: VERS. 21. ἐˇ ἡ ἀ αυ ἐξεστι &c.
units.tr: VERSE 21. οὐκ ἔξεστιν &c.

units.la: Sic quoque legit Arabs. Vulgatus autem & Æthiop. in singulari, morem quem non licet &c. Syri quoque editiones omnes habent in singulari [Arabic], quod tamen in plurali legendum esse [Arabic], suadet sequens pronomen [Arabic], quod pluralis est numeri. in singulari enim dicendum fuerat [Arabic] οὐ.
units.tr: The Arab also reads it this way. The Vulgate and the Ethiopic, however, have the singular, the custom which it is not lawful &c. All the Syriac editions also have the singular, which, however, ought to be read in the plural, as the following pronoun, which is plural, shows. For in the singular the Syriac word should have been used for "which" [οὐ].

units.la: VERS. 22. Καὶ συνεπῆσθη ὁ ὄχλος κατ' αὐτῶν.
units.tr: VERSE 22. Καὶ συνεπῆσθη ὁ ὄχλος κατ' αὐτῶν.

units.la: Beza, una autem insurrexit turba. Erasmus non male, concurrit turba. quod Syrus & Arabs dixerunt, multa turba congregata est. ouerunt multitudinem significare. ἐπέστη autem, advenit, adfuit, convenit. ut Luc. 20. 1. ἐπέστησαν οἱ Ἀρχιερεῖς, Vulg. & Eras. convenerunt. Beza, supervenerunt. vide & Luc. 2. 9. 38. & 21. 34. & alibi, eodem sensu.
units.tr: Beza has a crowd rose up together against them. Erasmus has, not badly, the crowd ran together. The Syrian and the Arab have a great crowd gathered. They meant that a multitude is signified. The word ἐπέστη means came, was present, assembled, as in Luke 20:1, ἐπέστησαν οἱ Ἀρχιερεῖς, which the Vulgate and Erasmus render assembled, and Beza came upon. See also Luke 2:9, 38, 21:34 and elsewhere, in the same sense.

units.la: Sequitur, καὶ οἱ στρατηγοί. Vulgatus & Erasmus supra γ f. 2q. & hic vertunt magistratus. Beza illic praetores, hic praefectos. Optime autem Arabs utrobique [Arabic], praefectos satellitum, vel ministrorum, vel lictorum, id est, eorum qui ad supplicia de fontibus sumenda adhibebantur. quam interpretationem res ipsa evincit. Ϲεἶρρήξαυτες αὐτὴν τὰ ἱμάτια. Syrus ܣܘܪܝܐ ambigue; quia lingua sua aliter non poterat. ut & Hebraicè שמלותיהם, vestimenta sua, vel vestimenta eorum. posterius huc pertinere, res ipsa docet. quamobrem Arabs usus est affixo dualis num. ut ad Paulum & Silam pertinere intelligeremus. Porro rectè dixit ϲεἶρρήξαυτες, quum dirupissent: thoracem enim flagellandorum non exuebant, sed lacerabant. ut legitur in Mischna libro כנרו ... cap.3. ... id est; quomodo autem flagellatur, alligantur amba manus ejus columna utrimque. tum minister synagoga apprehendit vestes ejus, nihil morans lacerenturne an dissuantur, donec pectus ejus discooperuerit.
units.tr: There follows καὶ οἱ στρατηγοί. The Vulgate and Erasmus, above at γ f. 2q, and here too, render it magistrates. Beza there has praetors, here prefects. The Arab, however, renders it excellently in both places as prefects of the guards, or of the attendants, or of the lictors, that is, of those who were used to take punishments from the prisoners. The thing itself proves this interpretation. Having torn their garments [ϲεἶρρήξαυτες αὐτὴν τὰ ἱμάτια]. The Syriac word is ambiguous, because their language could not express it otherwise, as also the Hebrew שמלותיהם means their garments or the garments of them. That the latter applies here, the thing itself teaches. For this reason the Arab used the dual suffix, so that we would understand it to refer to Paul and Silas. Moreover, he rightly said having torn, when they had torn, for they did not strip off the tunic for the scourging, but tore it. As is read in the Mishnah, in the book כנרו, chapter 3, that is: now, how one is flogged: both his hands are tied to a pillar on either side. Then the minister of the synagogue seizes his garments, not pausing whether they are torn or ripped apart, until his breast is uncovered.

units.la: VERS. 24.
units.tr: VERSE 24.

units.la: Pedes eorum ἠσφαλίσαντο εἰς τὸ ξύλον. Vulg. & Erasm. strinxit ligno. Beza, adstrinxit. Syrus & Arabs, ligavit. Æthiopicus rectè munivit. quo modo & illud Matt. 27.65. verterat, ἀσφαλίσασθε τὸ μνημεῖον, munite sepulchrum. Belgicè hp verseeckerde hacre boeten inden stock.
units.tr: Their feet [ἠσφαλίσαντο εἰς τὸ ξύλον]. The Vulgate and Erasmus have bound them with a wooden fetter. Beza has fastened. The Syriac and the Arab have bound. The Ethiopic rightly has secured, as he had also rendered Matthew 27:65, ἀσφαλίσασθε τὸ μνημεῖον, as secure the sepulchre. In Dutch: they were made fast in the stocks.

units.la: VERS. 26.
units.tr: VERSE 26.

units.la: Καὶ πάντων τὰ δεσμὰ αὐτῶν. Syrus ܟܠ ܐܣܘܪܐ. Tremel. & vincula omnium eorum soluta sunt. dele eorum. phrasis enim Syriaca non fert, nec est in Græco. sensus est, omnium captivorum vincula esse soluta, non Pauli tantum & Silæ.
units.tr: And the bonds of all of them [Καὶ πάντων τὰ δεσμὰ αὐτῶν]. The Syriac has all. Tremellius and the bonds of all of them were loosed. Delete of them, for the Syriac idiom does not bear it, nor is it in the Greek. The sense is that the bonds of all the prisoners were loosed, not only those of Paul and Silas.

units.la: VERS. 28.
units.tr: VERSE 28.

units.la: Ἐφώνησε &c. Vulg. Erasm. & Beza, clamavit. id est, ἐκραύγασε. Syrus, Arabs & Æthiopicus vocandi significatione acceperunt. ideoque addito pronomine verterunt vocavit eum. est tamen ubi φωνεῖν pro κεάζειν usurpatur apud lxx Interpretes. ut Dan. 4.11.
units.tr: He called out [Ἐφώνησε] &c. The Vulgate, Erasmus and Beza have he cried out, that is, ἐκραύγασε. The Syriac, the Arab and the Ethiopic took it in the sense of calling, and so, by adding a pronoun, rendered it he called him. Yet there are places where φωνεῖν is used for κεάζειν (to split) in the Septuagint, as in Daniel 4:11.

units.la: VERS. 34.
units.tr: VERSE 34.

units.la: Ἀναγαγὼν τὰ αὐτοῖς εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτῶν. Vulg. & Erasm. quumque perduxisset eos domum suam. Beza, & ipsis deductis. Syrus, Arabs & Æthiop. ascendere fecit eos in domum suam. quo sensu ἀναγὼν sumitur Luc. 4. 5. Act. 9. 39. & alibi passim. respondet Hebræorum הלה.
units.tr: Having brought them up into his house [Ἀναγαγὼν τὰ αὐτοῖς εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτῶν]. The Vulgate and Erasmus have and when he had led them into his house. Beza has and they were led in to them. The Syriac, the Arab and the Ethiopic have he caused them to go up into his house. ἀναγὼν is used in this sense in Luke 4:5, Acts 9:39 and elsewhere throughout; it corresponds to the Hebrew הלה.

units.la: VERS. 37. Paulus autem dixit πρὸς αὐτὸς ad eos. vide Bezæ commentarium. Syrus singulari numero ܘܠ, ei. male Tremellius eis. Arabs quoque ܐܠ, ei. Sequitur, cæsos nos publice ἀκαταχθήτως; Vulg. indemnatos. Erasm. & Beza, indicta causa. Syrus ܥܠܐ ܕܐܠ, sine delicto. Arabs ܐܠܐ ܕܥܠܐ sine crimine. Æthiop. ܐܠܐ ܕܥܠܐ, non habentes maleficium. voluisse videntur, ἀκαταχθήτως esse indemnabiles, id est insontes, innoxios, qui damnari non essent meriti.
