units.tr: VERSE 37. But Paul said to them [πρὸς αὐτὸς]. See Beza's commentary. The Syriac has the singular dative, to him. Tremellius badly has to them. The Arab too has to him. There follows beaten openly, uncondemned [ἀκαταχθήτως]. The Vulgate has uncondemned. Erasmus and Beza have without a hearing of the cause. The Syriac has without fault. The Arab has without crime. The Ethiopic has not having any wrongdoing. They seem to have wished ἀκαταχθήτως to mean not liable to condemnation, that is, innocent and blameless, men who did not deserve to be condemned.

units.la: VERS. 39. Καὶ ἐλθόντες παρεκάλεσαν αὐτὸς, ἐξαγαγόντες ἡμῶν ἐξελθεῖν ἀπὸ τῆς πόλεως. Syrus, Arabs & Æthiop. omiserunt ἐξαγαγόντες ἡμῶν, quia redundare videbatur. cur enim bis dicantur orasse eos? attamen dici possunt primum orasse, ne indignè ferrent, quod per tumultum contigisset. Deinde rursus orasse, ut è civitate exirent, ad novos tumultus vitandos. posset etiam παρεκάλεσαν verti, consolati sunt eos. sicut ܐܦ seq. id est, blandis verbis compellarunt, ut missa omni ira solarentur se de acceptis verberibus, & illata ignominia.
units.tr: VERSE 39. And they came and begged them, and led them out, and asked them to leave the city [Καὶ ἐλθόντες παρεκάλεσαν αὐτὸς, ἐξαγαγόντες ἡμῶν ἐξελθεῖν ἀπὸ τῆς πόλεως]. The Syriac, the Arab and the Ethiopic omitted ἐξαγαγόντες ἡμῶν, since it seemed superfluous. For why are they said to have begged them twice? Yet they can be said to have begged them first, so that they would not take it badly that it had happened in the tumult, and then again to have begged them to leave the city, in order to avoid new tumults. παρεκάλεσαν could also be translated they comforted them, as the Syriac in the following word does, that is, they addressed them with gentle words, so that, with all anger set aside, they might console them for the beatings received and the disgrace inflicted.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 17.

units.la: VERS. 5. Ζηλώσαντες δὲ οἱ ἀπειθοῦντες Ἰουδαῖοι. Vulgatus, Syrus & Arabs non habent ἀπειθοῦντες. Æthiopicus autem præterea etiam omittit Ἰουδαῖοι: quod manifestum mendum habet, quia hoc pacto pessima hæc actio piis illis ascribenda esset, qui v. præced. dicuntur credidisse & Paulo adhæsisse. Sequitur, ἐπισπασάμενοι τὸ ἀγοραίων ὄχλον ἀνδρας πονη-ρούς. Syrus ܘܠܗ ܐܠܗ ܕܥܠܐ ܐܠܐ ܕܥܠ Tremel. & Boder. & adjunxerunt se illis viri mali &c. id in
units.tr: VERSE 5. But the unbelieving Jews, moved by envy [Ζηλώσαντες δὲ οἱ ἀπειθοῦντες Ἰουδαῖοι]. The Vulgate, the Syriac and the Arab do not have ἀπειθοῦντες. The Ethiopic, moreover, also omits Ἰουδαῖοι, which is an obvious error, because in this way this wicked action would be ascribed to those pious people who, in the preceding verse, are said to have believed and attached themselves to Paul. There follows having drawn to themselves a crowd of the market-place, wicked men [ἐπισπασάμενοι τὸ ἀγοραίων ὄχλον ἀνδρας πονηρούς]. The Syriac has the Syriac phrase; Tremellius and Beza have and wicked men joined themselves to them, &c.

units.la: Kat dicendum fuisset Syriac word. Sed in Aphel Syriac word duo significat. 1. Incipere. quod non est huius loci. 2. facere ut quis sequatur, adjungere. verte ergo, & adjunxerunt sibi viros malos e foro civitatis.
units.tr: The verb ought to have been the Syriac form. But in the Aphel the Syriac word has two meanings: (1) to begin, which does not fit this place; (2) to cause someone to follow, to join to oneself. So translate: and they joined to themselves wicked men from the marketplace of the city.

units.la: VERS. 6. Traxerunt Iafonem, κ᾽ τινὰς ἀδελφὰς & quos- dam fratres.
units.tr: VERSE 6. They dragged Jason, and certain brethren [καὶ τινὰς ἀδελφούς].

units.la: Monet Cl. Beza, Syrum & Arabem praeterea legisse Greek, qui erant ibi. Sentio potius, eos periphrastice interpretatos esse vocem τινάς, quae apud eos non legitur. & quosdam fratres, id est, & fratres qui erant ibi.
units.tr: Beza observes that the Syriac and Arabic also read who were there. I think rather that they paraphrased the word certain [τινάς], which is not found in their text. And certain brethren means and the brethren who were there.

units.la: VERS. 9. Greek ad verbum, & cum accepissent fatus a Iafone. sive apologia satisfecerit, sive cautionem dederit. posteriori sensu accepit Syrus, qui vertit Syriac, & acceperunt fidejussores a Iafone. eodem modo Arabs, Arabic, quod recte vertit Cl. Junius, & acceptis sponsoribus. sed non satis recte ad marginem annotavit, Arab. duplis, quasi dicas, secundis reis, ut Iurecoss. veteres nominarunt. respexit Hebr. Hebrew, duplicavit, geminavit. at Arabice id non significat, ut recte adversus Raphelengium observavit doctiss. Erpenius. significat Arabic, in tutelam recipere, hinc custodire, educare, spondere. quae omnia tutelae speciem habent. significat & congregare. Arabic, sponsor. unde plurale, quod hic occurrit Arabic, sponsores. VERS. 10. Εἰς Βέροιαν. Arabs reddidit, Arabic, ad urbem Haleb. constat autem ex Geographo Nubiensi, Haleb esse urbem in ea parte Asiae sitam, ubi est fluvius Euphrates. docetque quomodo Antiochia per Haleb Racecam eatur. est celebre istud emporium, quod nunc Aleppo dicitur, non procul a Damasco. Et hanc eandem urbem bem Berœam olim fuisse dictam, ex Plinio liquet, qui Natur. Hist. l. 5. c. 23. Berœenses collocat in cava Syria, & c. 26. Berœam infra Palmyræ solitudines. At ista non est hæc Berœa, de qua hoc loco Lucas, quæ Macedoniæ urbs est, non procul à Thessalonica. de qua idem Plinius Natur. Hist. l. 4. c. 10. hanc tamen quoque nostri Arabs [illegible, ~3 letters], חלב, Haleb, id est, lac vocat, ob puritatem fortassis & munditiem, ob quam procul dubio utraque urbs Berœa dicta, ab Arabico [illegible, ~3 letters], mundus fuit. [illegible, ~3 letters], munditiæ. [illegible, ~3 letters], mundus. Æthiopicus [illegible, ~4 letters] Βίρωα scribit [illegible, ~3 letters].
units.tr: VERSE 9. Literally, and when they had received satisfaction from Jason [λαβόντες τὸ ἱκανὸν παρὰ τοῦ Ἰάσονος], whether he had made satisfaction by an apology or had given security. The Syriac took the latter sense, rendering and they received sureties from Jason. The Arabic does the same, and Junius rightly translates it and having taken sponsors. But in the margin he did not annotate quite correctly: the Arabic has "doubled", as if you were to say "second defendants", as the old Jurisconsults called them. He had in view the Hebrew word meaning doubled, multiplied. But in Arabic the word does not mean that, as the learned Erpenius rightly observed against Raphelengius. In Arabic it means to take into guardianship, hence to guard, to bring up, to stand surety. All of these have the look of guardianship. It also means to gather together. The Arabic word for sponsor gives the plural that occurs here, sponsors. VERSE 10. Εἰς Βέροιαν. The Arab rendered it to the city of Haleb. It is clear from the Nubian geographer that Haleb is a city in that part of Asia where the river Euphrates is, and he shows how one goes from Antioch to Racca by way of Haleb. This famous market town, now called Aleppo, is not far from Damascus. From Pliny (Nat. Hist. 5.23) it is clear that this same city was once called Berœa, for he places the Berœenses in Hollow Syria, and at 5.26 places Berœa beyond the deserts of Palmyra. But this is not the Berœa of which Luke speaks here, which is a city of Macedonia, not far from Thessalonica, of which the same Pliny speaks (Nat. Hist. 4.10). Nevertheless our Arab also calls this one Haleb, which in Hebrew is חלב, that is, milk, perhaps on account of its purity and cleanliness, and doubtless for this reason both cities were called Berœa, from the Arabic word meaning was clean, cleanliness, clean. The Ethiopic writes Βίρωα.

units.la: VERS. 11.
units.tr: VERSE 11.

units.la: Οὗτοι δὲ ἦσαν εὐγενέστεροι τῶν ἐν Θεσσαλονίκῃ. Laudo Cl. Bezam, quod εὐγενέστεροι comparativè potius quam superlativè acceperit, & de animo potius, quam genere aut prosapia. Secus quam Vulg. & Erasm. fecerunt. Quod autem Syrum & Arabem manifestè sententiam suam confirmare affirmat, de Syro dubium est. ait enim [illegible, ~5 letters]
units.tr: Οὗτοι δὲ ἦσαν εὐγενέστεροι τῶν ἐν Θεσσαλονίκῃ. I commend Beza for taking εὐγενέστεροι as comparative rather than superlative, and as referring to disposition rather than to birth or lineage. The Vulgate and Erasmus did otherwise. That the Syriac and Arabic clearly confirm his view is doubtful in the case of the Syriac. For it says:

units.la: nobiliores enim erant illi Iudai qui erant ibi, Iudæis &c. quod tam ad genus, quam ad animum referri poterit. Arabs autem manifestè ad genus retulit. verba ejus sunt [illegible, ~12 letters] hi autem ipsi Iudai qui erant ibi, fuerunt genitores illius Iudæis qui &c. Sed vertere oportet idque quia illi Iudai qui erant ibi, fuerunt nobiliores genere iis Iudæis qui &c.
units.tr: For those Jews who were there were nobler, the Jews etc. This could refer to both birth and disposition. The Arab, however, clearly refers it to birth. His words are these same Jews who were there were the progenitors of those Jews who etc. But one ought to render it: and that because those Jews who were there were nobler by birth than those Jews who etc.

units.la: VERS. 12. Γυναικῶν ἐλλημένων, mulierum honestarum
units.tr: VERSE 12. Γυναικῶν εὐσχημόνων [of honourable women].

units.la: Vulgatus. honoratarum Beza. Syrus [illegible, ~5 letters], Trem. mulieres celebres. dubito an non aliud voluerit Syrus. Glossarium Syro Arabicum [illegible, ~6 letters] vertit [illegible, ~4 letters] scitus, scitus, notus, vel nobilis, idem sane est Syris ܢܒܝܠ quod Arabibus novit. idem itaque illis quod his ܡܥܪܘܦ At moneo sæpe Arabibus usurpari pro honesto, bono, justo & æquo, quippe quod præcæteris sit nobile. frequens hoc sensu est in Alcorano Surata Bacara, ex. gr.
units.tr: The Vulgate has honoured, Beza honourable. The Syriac word, according to Tremellius, means famous women. I doubt whether the Syriac meant something else. The Syriac–Arabic glossary renders the word as skilled, known, or noble. Certainly in Syriac the word for knowing is the same as the Arabic word for knowing, so the word means for them what the other means for these. But I note that Arabs often use it for honest, good, just and fair, since such a thing is noble above all others. This sense is frequent in the Qur'an, in the Surah al-Baqara, for example:

units.la: [illegible, ~12 letters]verbum bonum (proprie nobile) & condonatio, melior est eleemosyna quam sequitur injuria. Ita hic quod dixit Syrus [illegible, ~6 letters] mulieres nobiles, intelligi arbitror bonas & honestas, quas Εὐχήμονας dixit Lucas. Atque eodem fortassis sensu Vulgatus Marc. 15. 43. Εὐχήμων βουλευτής vertit nobilis decurio, pro honestus seu bonus decurio, justus & æquus. fateor tamen supra sf. 4. Syrum sic vertisse γυναικῶν πρώτων. Arabem quoque & ibi & hic, [illegible, ~4 letters]. ita Εὐχήμονων idem esset quod πρώτων, ac significaret primarias, nobiliores, æstimatiores atque honoratiores fœminas. Æthiopicus vertit bona, honesta.
units.tr: a good word (properly, a noble one) and forgiveness; better is a charity followed by injury. So here I take it that what the Syriac says, noble women, is to be understood as good and honest women, whom Luke called well-reputed [Εὐσχήμονας]. Perhaps with the same sense the Vulgate at Mark 15.43 renders εὐσχήμων βουλευτής as noble decurion, that is, honest or good decurion, just and fair. I admit, however, that above (in section 4) the Syriac translated γυναικῶν πρώτων [of the leading women], and the Arab likewise both there and here. In that case εὐσχημόνων would be the same as πρώτων, and would signify leading, noble, most esteemed and most honoured women. The Ethiopic renders it good, honest.

units.la: VERS 14. Τὸν παῖδον ἐξαπέςτειλαν.
units.tr: VERSE 14. Τὸν παῖδον ἐξαπέςτειλαν [they sent away Paul].

units.la: Sæpe dimittere, à LXX-vertitur, ἐξαπέστειλεν. ut Gen. 25. 6. & 26. 29. 31. &c. πορεύεσθαι ὡς ἐπὶ τὴν θάλασσαν. Eraf. & Beza, ut iret velut ad mare. Vulgatus, ut iret usque ad mare. quasi ὡς pro ἐως. Syrus, Arabs & Æthiopicus simpliciter habent ad mare. vacante vel ὡς vel ἐπὶ. nam ὡς θάλασσαν Atticè rectè dicitur pro ἐπὶ θάλασσαν, ad mare. sicut ὡς βασιλέα, ad regem. ὡς ἐμέ, ad me. passim apud Aristophanem, Xenophontem, Demosthenem, Æschinem, aliosque scriptores Atticos, etiam apud Homerum, qui Odysseæ ρ dixit, ὡς αἰεὶ τ' ὁμοῖον ἀγὰ Θεὸς ὡς τ' ὁμοῖον, quàm semper similem adducit Deus ad similem! neque desunt alia exempla, ubi ὡς aliis particulis sic jungitur, ut alterutrum vacet. ut ὡς ὅπ μάλιστα, quam maximè, apud Platonem, quum sufficeret ὡς μάλιστα, vel ὅπ μάλιστα. apud eundem ὡς ὅπ βέλτιον, quam optimum.apud Galenum, ὡς ὅπ μαλακώτατα, quam mollissima. sic ὡς ἀληθῶς, pro simplici ἀληθῶς, verè, apud Demosth. Platonem & alios. & ad illud Homeri Iliad. β, ὡς ἐπ' σ' ἀφρικὴν ... ὡς νύπε ὦδε, Eusthatius annotat, oratores saepe ponere ὡς tanquam πεπλέκον, redundans, ut πᾶγμα δὴ ἐ ὡς ἐπίπως ἔχον, pro ἐπί-ῳ; ἔχον.
units.tr: The word to send away is often rendered by the Seventy as ἐξαπέστειλεν, as at Gen. 25.6, 26.29, 31, etc. πορεύεσθαι ὡς ἐπὶ τὴν θάλασσαν: Erasmus and Beza, that he should go as if to the sea. The Vulgate, that he should go as far as the sea, as if ὡς stood for ἕως. The Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic simply have to the sea, with neither ὡς nor ἐπί. For ὡς θάλασσαν is rightly used in Attic Greek for ἐπὶ θάλασσαν, to the sea, just as ὡς βασιλέα is to the king and ὡς ἐμέ is to me. This occurs frequently in Aristophanes, Xenophon, Demosthenes, Aeschines and other Attic writers, and also in Homer, who in the Odyssey (ρ) says ὡς αἰεὶ τ' ὁμοῖον ἄγει Θεὸς ὡς τ' ὁμοῖον, how God always brings like to like! Nor are there lacking other examples where ὡς is joined with other particles in such a way that one of them is superfluous. For instance ὡς ὅπ μάλιστα, as far as possible, in Plato, where ὡς μάλιστα or ὅπ μάλιστα would have sufficed; in the same author ὡς ὅπ βέλτιον, as best possible; in Galen ὡς ὅπ μαλακώτατα, as softest possible. So too ὡς ἀληθῶς for simple ἀληθῶς, truly, in Demosthenes, Plato and others. And on that line of Homer, Iliad 2, ὡς ἐπ' σ' ἀφρικὴν ... ὡς νύπε ὦδε, Eustathius notes that the orators often put ὡς as a redundant word, as in πᾶγμα δὴ ἐ ὡς ἐπίπως ἔχον, for ἐπί-ῳ ἔχον.

units.la: VERS. 16. Κατείδωλον. rectè Cl. Beza ex Cafaubono, idolis refertam. sic Syrus ﻣﻠﺌﻴﻦ. & Arabs ﻣﻠﺊ اﺻﻨﺎم. VERS. 18. Τῆς ἡ τ' Ἐπικουρείων ἢ τ' Σπικῶν φιλοσόφων συνέβαλλον αὐτῷ. Arabs habet, والفلاسفة ايضا الذين مرن تعليم افيقوروس واخرون يسمون الرواقيين quæ Junius valde perperam vertit, Ac philosophi etiam qui erant ex disciplina Epicuri, aliique, auditis pronunciatis ejus, magnificabant eum. putavit الرواقين significare dicta, pronunciata. atque ideo pro يسمون, vocantur, legendum يسمعون, audiunt. at vero الرواقين sunt stoici. à رواق, porticus.
units.tr: VERSE 16. Κατείδωλον [full of idols]. Beza rightly, following Casaubon, renders full of idols. So the Syriac has a word meaning full, and the Arabic full of idols. VERSE 18. Τῆς ἡ τ' Ἐπικουρείων ἢ τ' Σπικῶν φιλοσόφων συνέβαλλον αὐτῷ. The Arabic has wa-l-falasifa aydan alladhina min ta'lim Ifiqurus wa-akharun yusammuna al-riwaqiyin, which Junius translated very wrongly: and the philosophers also who were of the teaching of Epicurus, and others, having heard his pronouncements, magnified him. He thought that al-riwaqin meant sayings, pronouncements, and so for yusammuna, are called, one should read yasma'una, they hear. But al-riwaqin are the Stoics, from riwaq, porch.

units.la: deinde significationem verbi جادلوا derivavit ab Hebraeo גדל, magnum esse, in Piel magnificare. At apud Arabes significat in prima conjugatione torquere, contorquere. in tertia, quæ hic occurrit, torquere adversus alium, controvertere, disputare. vertendus ergo Arabs, & philosophi etiam qui erant de doctrina Epicuri, & alii qui vocantur Stoici, disceptabant cum eo, hinc emendandæ notæ Cl. Bezæ.
units.tr: Next, he derived the meaning of the verb jadalu from the Hebrew גדל, to be great, in Piel to magnify. But in Arabic, in the first conjugation, it means to twist, to twist about; in the third, which occurs here, to turn against another, to contend, to dispute. So the Arabic must be rendered: and the philosophers also who were of the teaching of Epicurus, and others who are called Stoics, disputed with him. Hence Beza's note must be corrected.

units.la: Sequitur, τί οἱ ἄλλοι ὁ σπερμολόγος ἂν τοῦτο. Syrus, ﻣﻠﻘﻂ ﻋﻠﻴﻪ ﻣﻠﻘﻂ, quid vult hic collector verborum? verbum σπερμολόγος, Hebraeis, Syris & Arabibus significat res in terram effusas separatim tollere & colligere, ut pauperes spicas à messe in arvo sparsim relictas, & columbæ semina per arvum sparsa. atque ejusmodi aves proprie ἀντεμολόγως dictas fuisse, ex auctoribus constat. inde apud Atticos ad homines translatum fuisse docet Eustathius, οἷον ἀπὸ ἰμπέλια ἐ ἀγρῶν ἀλλαγίζοντας, ἀλλὰ τὰ ἀναλίσκοντα τὰ ἐκ τ Φαλίων ἀπηρίσουσα, ἢ ἀλαξὴν ἐκ τάτων, qui circa mercatus & fora versantur, ut quæ ex saccis defluunt colligant, atque inde vivant. eo viles & contempti homines describuntur. quid impedit autem, cur non alia metaphora vani homines eodem describantur, qui fora perreptantes dicta aliorum captant, & quæ ex ore cujusque, velut grana e sacco, excidunt, colligunt, ut animum suum istis pascant, & habeant quod fabulentur & garriant? certè si hoc non voluit Syrus, nescio quid voluerit. Nec à re ipsa abludit. quum enim Paulum per forum oberrantem viderent, & obvios quosque compellantem, non aliter eum sermones qui serebantur colligere, quam aves quasdam sata semina, autumabant. Arabs vertit يقول هذا الذي هو الكلام, quod non satis aptè reddidit Junius, quid narras ipse fator verborum? verto, quid cupit hic effatitor sermonis? est enim ﻝﺍ, pronunciare, proferre, effutire. quod si puncta mutes, & scribas ﻝﻝ, eadem vox est, qua usus est Syrus, & idem significans. Vulgatus vertit, seminator verborum, quod Æthiopicus dixit ܐܡܪܐ ܕܡܠܝܐ. de quo vide doctas notas Cl. Bezæ, qui vertit garrulus. pro eo facit Hezychius; apud quem ἀντεμολόγος, φλυαρέας, nugator, garrulus. & apud Plutarchum ἀντεμολόγος ῥήματα, nugatoria verba. Monuit me doctissimus, mihiquo intimus, D. Joh. Cloppenburgius, Bruchthonum ex auctoritate Vlpiani apud Demosthenem interpretari sacrilegum. existimatque vir doctiss. frigere apud Demosthenem pro corona orationem, nisi sacrilegium dicatur auctori Æschini exprobrare Demosthenes, quo Amphissenses, sacras Apollinis segetes depasti erant. judicent eruditi. mihi Syrus vehementer arridet. Sequitur, quia Euangelizabat Iesum ἐν τῇ ἀνάστασιν & resurrectionem. Syrus & Arabs, & resurrectionem ejus.
units.tr: There follows τί ὁ σπερμολόγος οὗτος ἂν θέλοι λέγειν; The Syriac has a phrase meaning what does this collector of words want? In Hebrew, Syriac and Arabic the word σπερμολόγος signifies one who picks up separately things scattered on the ground, as poor people gather ears of corn left scattered in the field from the harvest, or as doves pick up seeds scattered over a field. From the authors it is clear that such birds were properly called σπερμολόγοι. Eustathius shows that the Attics transferred the term to men: like those who wander about markets and fora, gathering up what falls from the sacks, and living on that. By this image worthless and contemptible men are described. But what prevents vain men from being described by another metaphor, those who roam the fora seizing on the sayings of others and gather up whatever falls from each mouth, like grain from a sack, so as to feed their minds on these and have something to babble and chatter about? Certainly if the Syriac did not mean this, I do not know what it meant. Nor does it differ from the facts. For when they saw Paul wandering through the forum and addressing whomever he met, they supposed that he gathered up the words that were scattered, no differently than certain birds gather scattered seeds. The Arab renders it yaqulu hadha alladhi huwa al-kalam, which Junius did not translate aptly as what do you say, yourself the collector of words? I translate: what does this speaker of words want? For the word is qala, to pronounce, to utter, to babble. If you change the points and write it differently, it is the same word the Syriac used, with the same meaning. The Vulgate renders sower of words, which the Ethiopic rendered as a phrase meaning one who speaks idle words. On this see the learned notes of Beza, who renders babbler. Hesychius agrees: there ἀντεμολόγος means trifler, babbler, and in Plutarch ἀντεμολόγος ῥήματα means trifling words. The very learned Johann Cloppenburg, my close friend, reminded me that on the authority of Ulpian, Bruchthonus in Demosthenes should be interpreted as sacrilegious. And that learned man thinks the oration against Aeschines falls flat unless Demosthenes is saying that the author of the sacrilege was the Amphissians, who had grazed the sacred crops of Apollo. Let the learned judge. For my part the Syriac pleases me greatly. There follows because he preached Jesus and the resurrection [ἐν τῇ ἀναστάσει]. The Syriac and Arabic have and the resurrection of him.

units.la: VERS. 19. Ἐπὶ τὸ Ἄρειον πάγον. Syrus & Arabs, in domum judicii quæ dicitur Areopagus. recte. inde enim Judices Areopagitæ dicti. & Areum judicium, apud Tacit. I. 2. Æthiopicus, deduxerunt eum in domum Dei sui. erat enim Areopagus, teste Stephano, vicus Athenis à templo Martis sic dictus, ubi Mars, quum Halirrhotium Neptuni filium, qui vim Alcippæ filiæ suæ intulerat, occidisset, & à Neptuno homicidii reus ageretur, causa à 12 Diis in Areopago cognita, sex sententiis est absolutus. In templo Martis Areopagitæ quoque judicabant.
units.tr: VERS. 19. Ἐπὶ τὸ Ἄρειον πάγον. The Syriac and Arabic have into the house of judgement which is called the Areopagus. Rightly so, for the judges were called Areopagites from it, and the Areian court appears in Tacitus, Annals 1.2. The Ethiopic has they brought him into the house of his God. For the Areopagus, as Stephanus tells us, was a district of Athens named after the temple of Mars. There Mars, when he had killed Halirrhothius, son of Neptune, who had violated his daughter Alcippe, was tried for murder by Neptune. The case was heard before the twelve gods on the Areopagus, and he was acquitted by six votes. The Areopagites also sat in judgement in the temple of Mars.

units.la: VERS. 23. Contemplans τὰ σέβασματα ὑμῶν. Syrus ܐܠܗܐ. Trem. domum religionum vestrarum, vel ut ad verbum Boderianus in Parisiensi, domum formidinum vestrarum. quasi certum aliquod & singulare templum innueret. quum mens Syri fuerit, plur. num. dicere, domos religionis vestræ, id est, templa vestra. quod quum recte intelligeret Arabs, vertit pl. num. Junius, loca simulachrorum vestrorum, verte cultuum vestrorum. est enim cultus religiosus. pl. ritus & officia religionis. Libet hic docere Syriasmi amantes, solere Syros in ejusmodi compositionibus singulare vertere in plurale, mutato posterioris membri numero. ut locus collectionis, id est, horreum. at locus collectionum, id est, horrea. locus sepelitionis, id est, sepulchrum. locus sepelitionum, id est, sepulchra. domus. nus inimicitia, id est, inimicus. [Syriac word], dominus inimicitiarum, id est, inimici. ita hoc loco [Syriac word] locus religionum vestrarum, id est, templa vestra. quum in singulari esset [Syriac word], locus religionis vestrae, id est, templum vestrum. Non laudo autem, quod Syrus & Arabs σέβασμα templa verterint. Beza, sacra vestra. Vulgatus & Æthiopicus non male simulachra vestra. viderunt enim σέβασμα proprie esse id ipsum quod colitur, quæ quidem apud Athenienses erant simulachra. malim tamen numina vestra reddere. ut in libro Sapientiæ Salom. c. 14. 20. τὴν τῶν ἐλίγυ τιμηθέντα ἀιθρωπον, τὸν σέβασμα ἰλογίσωντο, qui paulo ante homo honorabatur, eum nunc numen reputarunt. & c. 15. 17. dicit, Idolorum fabricatorem esse χρύσεον τὸ σέβασμάτων αὐτὸ, præstantiorem suis numinibus, ὅτι αὐτὸς ζῆσιν, ἐκεῖνα ἡ ἀδύνατα, quia ipse quidem vivit, illa autem nunquam. Et in historia Draconis, dirupto idolo dicit Daniel, ἰδοὺ τὰ σέβασματα ὑμῶν, vide numina vestra. sic Paulus 2 Thess. 2. 4. ἐπὶ πάντα λεγόμενον Θεὸν ἢ σέβασμα, super omnem qui dicitur Deus aut numen.
units.tr: VERS. 23. Contemplans τὰ σέβασματα ὑμῶν. The Syriac has alaha, and the Tremellius version has the house of your religions, or, to translate word for word, as Boderianus has it in the Parisian text, the house of your terrors. This would seem to point to some one particular and unique temple. But the Syriac intends the plural, the houses of your religion, that is, your temples. The Arab rightly understood this, and Junius translates the plural the places of your images. Translate instead your worship. For cultus means religious worship, in the plural the rites and duties of religion. I would like to point out to those who love Syriasms that the Syrians commonly turn a singular into a plural in such compounds, changing the number of the second member. Thus locus collectionis, a place of gathering, that is, a granary; but locus collectionum, places of gathering, that is, granaries. Locus sepelitionis, a place of burial, that is, a tomb; locus sepelitionum, places of burial, that is, tombs. Dominus inimicitiae, that is, an enemy; dominus inimicitiarum, that is, enemies. So here the Syriac place of your religions means your temples, whereas in the singular it would be place of your religion, that is, your temple. I do not, however, praise the Syriac and Arabic for rendering σέβασμα as temples. Beza has your sacred things. The Vulgate and the Ethiopic rightly have your images, for they saw that σέβασμα properly means the very thing that is worshipped, which among the Athenians were images. I would still prefer to render it your deities, as in the Wisdom of Solomon 14.20, τὸν ἐλίγου τιμηθέντα ἄνθρωπον, τὸ σέβασμα ἐλογίσαντο, the man who had been honoured a little while before they reckoned a deity; and 15.17 says that the maker of idols is χρείαν ἔχων τῶν σεβασμάτων αὐτοῦ, more excellent than his deities, because he himself lives, while those never do. And in the story of the Dragon, when the idol is broken, Daniel says, ἰδοὺ τὰ σέβασματα ὑμῶν, see your deities. So Paul too, 2 Thess. 2.4, ἐπὶ πάντα λεγόμενον Θεὸν ἢ σέβασμα, against everything that is called God or deity.

units.la: Sequitur, inveni βωμὸν aram. Syrus, omnibus consentientibus editionibus, pro eo habet [Syriac word], quod causam, occasionem, pratextum significat, habetque plur. [Syriac word]. at quod hujus loci est ara, scribendum [Syriac word]. ejus plur. [Syriac word]. Huic arae inscriptum erat, ignoto Deo. vide Drusii praeterita, & Bezae notas. quae sequuntur, οὐ ὢν ἀγνοῦντες εὐσεβεῖτε, τοῦτο ἐγὼ καταγγέλλω ὑμῖν. ὁ Θεὸς ὁ ποιήσας τὸν κόσμον ἡ πάντα τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ, Æthiopicus nescio qua paraphrasi interpolavit potius, quam interpretatus est. sic enim habet, [Hebrew text], mundate vos ipsos, ecce videte ut cognoscatis quid quid colatis. & ego doceo vos, ut colatis Deum qui fecit mundum & quicquid in eo est.
units.tr: The text continues, I found an altar, βωμόν, ara. The Syriac, in all the editions agreed, has for this a word that means cause, occasion, pretext, with a plural. But where the sense requires altar, it should be written with the plural of that word. An inscription on this altar read to the unknown God. See the notes of Drusius and Beza. The words that follow, ὃν οὖν ἀγνοοῦντες εὐσεβεῖτε, τοῦτο ἐγὼ καταγγέλλω ὑμῖν· ὁ Θεὸς ὁ ποιήσας τὸν κόσμον καὶ πάντα τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ, the Ethiopic has expanded with some paraphrase rather than translated. For it reads: purify yourselves; see, so that you may know what you worship. And I teach you to worship the God who made the world and all that is in it.

units.la: VERS. 25. Neque à manibus hominum θεραπεύεται, Vulg. Eras. & Beza, colitur. malim, ministratur. colere enim honoris potius est, qui hîc non respicitur, quippe qui Deo debetur & ab ipso admittitur. ministrare autem proprie utilitatis est, quam quenquam Deo adferre, merito negatur. neque satis aptè videntur manus dici colere, ministrare autem, rectè. quod quum annoto, mens est, pronunciationis emphasin, non in ὧν χερσὶν ponere, quasi hîc describatur verus Dei cultus, qui cordis sit, non manuum: sed in θεραπεύεται, ut sensus sit, quando homines cultum suum manibus Deo quasi offerunt, non ministratur inde, id est, nullum inde ministerium capit, quod usui ipsi sit, ut servorum heris. ideo additur, ipsum non tantum nullius rei esse egentem, sed & omnibus dare omnia. ita quivis cultus rejicitur, sive externus sit sive internus, qui eo animo datur, quasi is ministerio & usui esse possit, unde aliquid ad Deum accedat. atque ita versu praecedenti Dei incomprehensibilitas & infinitas, hîc ejus perfectio & αὐτάρκεια asseritur. quod si autem manus animo opponi quis velit, & ibi emphasin constitui, tum rectè θεραπεύεται per colitur vertitur. tribuiturque Deo, sicut Esa. 54. 17. ubi pro ... LXX habent, ἡ κληρονομία τῆς θεραπείας τοῦ Κυρίου, hereditas est colentibus Deum. Æthiopicus videtur sanandi significatione accepisse illud θεραπεύει. vertit enim ..., sanatur. nisi forte ..., sanare, etiam ministrare ipsis significet, ut apud Græcos θεραπεύει. quod sequitur, ... omittit, contra fidem omnium Græcorum exemplarium, quæ Vulgatus, Syrus & Arabs etiam sunt secuti. quumque additur, ... ineptissimo commentario pro ... dixit ..., ei qui rogaverit ipsum. apti scilicet sunt homines petere à Deo vitam, quum eâ ab ipso donantur. quod annoto, ut oculis quisque cernat, quanta audacia Interpretes quidam, quos impudentissimos potius interpolatores dicas, divinas literas tractent. ζωὴ δ πνοὴ ἡ πνεῦμα. pro πνοὴ, quod inspirationem Vulgatus, halitum verterunt Eras.& Beza, Syrus & Arabs dixerunt ܢܦܫܐ, animam. ut & LXX, Proverb. 24. ורוח נשמה vertunt, ὁ πλάσσας πνοὴν πᾶσι. At καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα Syrus, Arabs & Æthiopicus non legunt.
units.tr: VERS. 25. Neque à manibus hominum θεραπεύεται. The Vulgate, Erasmus and Beza have is worshipped. I would prefer is ministered to. For to worship belongs rather to honour, which is not what is in view here, since honour is owed to God and is accepted by him. To minister, however, properly belongs to usefulness, and it is rightly denied that anyone can bring anything of use to God. Nor does it seem quite apt to say that hands worship, whereas minister fits well. When I note this, the point is that the emphasis of the statement lies not on by human hands, as if the passage described the true worship of God, which is of the heart and not of the hands; the emphasis lies on is ministered to, so that the sense is: when people offer their worship to God with their hands, as if to give it to him, he is not ministered to by it, that is, he gains no service from it as a master gains from his servants. That is why it is added that he not only lacks nothing, but gives all things to all. So every kind of worship is rejected, whether external or internal, if it is given with the idea that it can serve God or be of use to him, so that something might be added to God. Thus in the preceding verse the incomprehensibility and infinity of God are asserted, and here his perfection and self-sufficiency (αὐτάρκεια). But if anyone wishes to set hands against the mind, and to place the emphasis there, then it is right to translate θεραπεύεται as is worshipped, and it is ascribed to God, as in Isaiah 54.17, where the Seventy have for the Hebrew the inheritance of the service of the Lord, that is, an inheritance for those who worship God. The Ethiopic seems to have taken the verb in the sense of healing, for it renders it is healed. Unless perhaps the verb can also mean to serve, as θεραπεύει does among the Greeks. What follows, τὰ πάντα, the Ethiopic omits, against the agreement of all the Greek copies, which the Vulgate, Syriac and Arabic have followed. And where αὐτὸς διδοὺς is added, the Ethiopic has rendered it, by a most absurd commentary, to him who has asked him. Evidently people are fit to ask God for life when it is given to them by him! I note this so that everyone can see with their own eyes how great the audacity is of certain interpreters, who should rather be called most shameless corrupters, in handling the divine letters. ζωὴ καὶ πνοή, or πνεῦμα. For πνοή, the Vulgate has inspiration, Erasmus and Beza breath. The Syriac and Arabic have soul, as the Seventy also do in Proverbs 24, where they render the Hebrew and the spirit of breath as the one who has formed breath for all. But the Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic do not read and the spirit.

units.la: VERS. 26. Ἐποίησά τε ἐξ ἑνὸς αἵματος, &c. sic Syrus etiam legit. Arabs ܐܕܡ ܘܚܕ, & ex homine vel Adamo uno. apud Orientales unius tantum literæ discrimen est inter דם, sanguis, & אדם, homo. & res hîc eadem est. Vulgatus tantum dicit, ex uno. Æthiopicus narrat tantum, Deum fecisse omne genus hominum, nulla facta mentione unde fecerit.
units.tr: VERS. 26. Ἐποίησέ τε ἐξ ἑνὸς αἵματος, &c. The Syriac also reads it this way. The Arabic has Adam one, and from one man or from one Adam. Among the Orientals there is only a difference of one letter between dam, blood, and adam, man, and the thing is the same here. The Vulgate has only from one. The Ethiopic merely says that God made every kind of man, with no mention of the material from which he made them.

units.la: Sequitur, κατοικεῖν ut habitarent super universa superficie terra, ὁρίσας πρ᾽ αὐτοῖς πρ̄ ἡ ὁρισμένα καιρὸς καὶ τὰς ὁροθεσίας τῆς κατοικίας αὐτῶν. verto ad verbum, quum definivisset praordinata tempora, & terminos statutos habitationis ipsorum. quæ non sic capio, quasi definivisset Deus tempora, ante definitionem istam præordinata, sed, antequam ipsa illa tempora aut res in temporibus contingant, præordinata. Solent autem Commentatores πρ᾽ αὐτοῖς προτεταγμένους καιρούς, & τὰς ὁροθεσίας τῆς κατοικίας sic distinguere, ut per primum præfixa tempora quando & quamdiu, per alterum præfixi regionum limites, ubi quisque populus esset habitaturus, designentur. quod recte & vere dicitur. dubito tamen, an ὁροθεσίαι τῆς κατοικίας non sint positi limites vitæ uniuscujusque, ad quos pertingit, nec ulterius. sicut paulo ante, fecit totam gentem hominum κατοικεῖν ut habitaret, id est, viveret, ætatem ageret super terram. sæpe enim hæc vox nihil aliud quam durationem significat. ut quum Hebraei dicunt אלהים לעולם ישב ובן אדם לא לעולם ישב, Deus in aeternum durat, filius autem hominis non in aeternum durat, ad verbum κατοικῶ, habitat. sic à יש, habitare, fit ר׳ ætas, generatio, duratio ætatis quamdiu homo in vita habitat. & apud Arabes ab عمر, habitavit, fit عمر tempus vitæ, quamdiu quis in mundo habitat & perdurat. ut in historia Elmacini, dicitur mater Mahomedis mortua, [illegible, ~8 letters] quum habitatio ejus, id est, vitæ ætas, essetsex annorum. paulo post dicitur avus ejus mortuus, [illegible, ~6 letters] cum habitatio, id est, ætas, ejus esset annorum centum & decem. secundum hanc sententiam Apostolus hic uno verbo decidit controversiam, quæ tanto molimine nunc agitatur, de Termino vitæ, fixus ne sit an mobilis. sensus enim esset, definivisse Deum omnibus hominibus tempora & constitutos vitæ limites, intra quos duratio sive habitatio ejus in hoc mundo consistat, quos nec antevertere nec superare posset. Sic Æthiopicus intellexit, quum vertit [illegible, ~6 letters], & ordinavit tempora sua & annos suos, quamdiu habitarent.
units.tr: The text continues, to dwell upon the whole face of the earth, κατοικεῖν, having determined the appointed times and the bounds of their habitation, ὁρίσας προστεταγμένους καιροὺς καὶ τὰς ὁροθεσίας τῆς κατοικίας αὐτῶν. I render it word for word: when he had defined the appointed times beforehand, and the fixed boundaries of their habitation. I do not take this to mean that God first defined the times, and that these were appointed before that definition, but that they were appointed before the times themselves, or the events that occur in them, came about. Commentators usually divide the words the times appointed beforehand and the bounds of their habitation in such a way that the first designates the fixed times, when and how long, and the second the fixed limits of the regions where each people was to dwell. This is correct and true. I doubt, however, whether the bounds of their habitation may not be the set limits of each person's life, beyond which it does not extend. Just as a little earlier, he made the whole race of men to dwell, that is, to live, to pass their lifetime upon the earth. For this word often means nothing other than duration. So when the Hebrews say, God endures for ever, but the son of man does not endure for ever, the verb is literally dwells. Thus from the verb to dwell, there comes the noun age, generation, the duration of a lifetime, as long as a man dwells in life. And among the Arabs, from the verb he dwelt, comes the time of life, as long as someone dwells and lasts in the world. So in the history of Elmacin, it is said that the mother of Muhammad died when her habitation, that is, the span of her life, was six years. A little later it is said that his grandfather died when his habitation, that is, his age, was one hundred and ten years. In this sense the Apostle here settles with a single word a controversy that is now pursued with so much effort, concerning the term of life, whether it is fixed or movable. For the sense would be that God had determined for all men their times and fixed limits of life, within which their duration or habitation in this world should lie, and which they could neither anticipate nor exceed. The Ethiopic also understood it so, when it renders and he ordained their times and their years, for as long as they should dwell.

units.la: VERS. 27. Ut quaererent Dominum, si forte ψηλαφήσαιαὐτὸν ... Vulgatus, attrectent eum & inveniant.
units.tr: VERSE 27. That they should seek the Lord, if perhaps they might feel after him [ψηλαφήσαι αὐτόν] ... The Vulgate has that they should handle him and find him.

units.la: quod improbat Cl. Beza, quoniam Attrectare eorum est qui invenerunt. maluit ergo, palpando eum invenirent. ambiguum sane est ψηλαφάω. interdum enim tangere & contrectare significat, interdum palpare, id est, conari tangere, & manu vestigare cæcorum instar. ac metaphorice, scrutari, rimari. posterius etiam Syrus & Arabs secuti sunt. verterunt enim, ut essent quarentes Deum, & investigantes, & ex creaturis ejus invenientes eum. addiderunt ex creaturis ejus, per modum commentarii. Ego tamen malim illam investigandi seu palpandi actionem in præcedenti ζητῶν comprehendere, & per ψηλαφήσαι ipsam contrectandi actionem intelligere. neque impedit quod sequitur, & inveniant eum. qui enim palpando quærunt, non tam attrectant ubi invenerunt, nerunt, quam inveniunt ubi attrectant. attrectando inveniunt, sic ut attrectatio ordine naturæ inventionem, tanquam causa effectum, antecedat, etsi tempore simul sint. sic Deus in creaturis invenitur, quando post diligentem inquisitionem & scrutationem actu contrectatur, id est, æternitas, omnisciencia, omnipotentia ac bonitas ejus quasi tanguntur.
units.tr: Beza rejects this, since attrectare belongs to those who have already found. He therefore preferred that they might find him by groping. The word ψηλαφάω is certainly ambiguous. Sometimes it means to touch and handle, and sometimes to grope, that is, to try to touch and feel about with the hand, as the blind do. Metaphorically it means to search out and examine. The Syrian and the Arab later followed this sense. They render it: that they might be seeking God and investigating, and finding him from his creatures. They added from his creatures by way of commentary. I would nonetheless prefer to take the act of searching or groping within the preceding word ζητῶν, and to understand ψηλαφήσαι as the act of touching itself. Nor is the following and find him an obstacle. Those who seek by groping do not so much handle what they have found as find what they handle. By handling they find, so that the handling precedes the finding in the order of nature, as cause precedes effect, even though they are simultaneous in time. So God is found in his creatures when, after diligent inquiry and searching, he is actually touched, that is, when his eternity, omniscience, omnipotence and goodness are, as it were, felt.

units.la: IBID. Καύτηγε ὐ μαχεῳ &c. Vulgat. Eraf. & Beza vertunt per Adversativam quamvis. Syrus & Arabs per causale quia. sic ut causa reddatur, cur facile Deus in creaturis suis attrectari & inveniri queat: quia non procul est ab unoquoque nostrum. quod ut recte quadrat, ita non est spernendum. καί enim non tantum quamvis, verum etiam, sed, sed & & quidem, imo nam significat. vide Lexic. Constantini, & Comment. Budæi. & huic etiam loco quadrant, sed & non procul est &c. vel, & quidem non procul est &c.
units.tr: IBID. [καίγε οὐ μακράν] &c. The Vulgate, Erasmus and Beza render this by an adversative, although. The Syrian and the Arab render it by a causal, because, so that the reason is given why God can easily be touched and found in his creatures: because he is not far from each one of us. This fits well, and so should not be scorned. For καί means not only although but also indeed, yes, and indeed, even for. See the Lexicon of Constantinus and the Commentary of Budé. And to this passage also fit yet indeed he is not far &c., or and indeed he is not far &c.

units.la: VERS. 30. Τὰς ὀλὼ οὖ χείνας ἡ ἀγνοίας ὑπερεῖδων ὁ Θεὸς, ταῦτ &c. Eraf. & tempora quidem hujus ignorantia quum dissimularit Deus. Beza, conniventia dissimularit. Syrus transfire fecit. quod eodem sensu dixit Arabs. placet præ cæteris Vulgatus, & tempora quidem hujus ignorantiæ despiciens Deus. vel, quum despexisset, sprevisset, neglexisset. hoc enim proprie verbum significat. rectèque huic loco quadrat. non minus enim providentiæ Dei id convenit, quam quum omnia sibi adversa, etiam populum suum rebellem despicere dicitur. usurpant LXX pro indignari, detestari, reprobare, irascii, ut Deut 3.26. & iratus est Iehovah mihi, LXX καὶ ὑπερεῖδε με Κύριος. Ps. 78.59. audivit Dominus & iratus est, LXX ἤκουσεν ὁ Κύριος ὁ ὑπερεῖδε. & Ps. 62. & haereditati sua iratus fuit, LXX ἐν τῇ κληρονομίᾳ αὐτοῦ ὑπερεῖδε. Hinc locum hunc Lucæ Hebraicè vertas, & quum & quum irasceretur Deus temporibus ignorantia hujus. est & ubi pro םולע sequente ִּ usurpatur. ut Deut.21.1. התעלמ םתמ, abscondas te ab illis. LXX ἀπεκρύψατο αὐτῷ. sic ψξ. 3. & 4. Hinc verba Lucæ Hebraicè versas, ךי התעלם אלהים מטחות השנה, & quum absconderit se Deus à temporibus ignorantia. nempe causam dat, curjam hisce, sub Euangelio, lucis, non autem istis, sub lege, ignorantiæ temporibus resipiscentiam omnibus hominibus prædicari voluerit Deus. quia ista, quippe ignorantiæ tempora, sprevit Deus ac contempsit, iratus illis fuit, seque ab iis abscondidit, non dignatus ea isthac gratia.
units.tr: VERSE 30. [Τοὺς μὲν οὖν χρόνους τῆς ἀγνοίας ὑπεριδὼν ὁ Θεός, ταῦτα] &c. Erasmus: and indeed when God had overlooked the times of this ignorance. Beza: God overlooked them with forbearance. The Syrian: caused to pass over, which the Arab also said in the same sense. Above the rest the Vulgate pleases me: God, despising the times of this ignorance, or when he had despised, scorned, neglected them. For this is the proper meaning of the word, and it fits the passage well. It belongs no less to the providence of God than when he is said to despise all adversity, even his rebellious people. The Seventy use it for to be angry, to detest, to reject, to be wrathful, as in Deut. 3.26, and the LORD was angry with me, where the Seventy have [καὶ ὑπερεῖδέ με Κύριος]. In Ps. 78.59, the LORD heard and was wroth, the Seventy have [ἤκουσεν ὁ Κύριος ὁ ὑπερεῖδε]. And in Ps. 62, and he was wroth with his inheritance, the Seventy have [ἐν τῇ κληρονομίᾳ αὐτοῦ ὑπερεῖδε]. Hence you may render this passage of Luke into Hebrew thus: and when God was angry in the times of this ignorance. The word is also used where it takes the following from (מ) instead, as in Deut. 21.1, hide yourself from them (התעלם מהם), which the Seventy render [ἀπεκρύψατο αὐτῷ]; so also in Ps. 3 and 4. Hence the words of Luke may be rendered into Hebrew thus: [כי התעלם אלהים מעתות השגה], when God had hidden himself from the times of ignorance. He gives, namely, the reason why God willed that repentance should now be preached to all men under the Gospel, with its light, and not in those times of ignorance under the law. For God overlooked and despised those times, was angry with them, and hid himself from them, not deigning to grant them this grace.

units.la: Sequitur, τοῖς ἀνθρώποις πᾶσι. Vulg. & Erasm. annunciat. Beza, denunciat. Syrus, Arabs & Æthiop. præcipit. rectè, eo enim sensu passim in N. T. usurpatur, imo fere semper, & majorem hic habet emphasin.
units.tr: There follows [τοῖς ἀνθρώποις πᾶσι]. The Vulgate and Erasmus have announces. Beza has declares. The Syrian, the Arab and the Ethiopian have commands. Rightly so, for the word is used in this sense throughout the New Testament, indeed almost always, and here it carries greater emphasis.

units.la: VERS. 31. Quia constituit diem, in quo judicaturus est totam terram in justitia, per virum quem determinavit. πίστιν πεῖς ἀναστάσεως ἀυτὸν &c. Beza rectè, fidepalam factam omnibus. Vulgatus, fidem præbens omnibus. quod non ita capio, ac si voluisset, factam esse universo mundo potestatem, Christum per fidem amplectendi; sed præbens, mihi est faciens, ut mens sit, eum certo & fide digno argumento probasse, Christum fore judicem, quum eum è mortuis suscitavit. nec aliter Syrum capio, & Arabem. Syrus, [Syriac text] . Trem. & converti fecit omnem hominem ad fidem ejus, quum excitavit eum à mortuis. Boder. in Parisf. & convertit omnem hominem. In Reg. & restituit. At veritas non patitur, ut Deus dicatur omnes homines convertisse aut restituisse ad fidem Christi. neque cum mente Lucæ quadrat, quæ est, certo credendum futurum judicium, quia Deus fidem ejus rei fecit omnibus per resurrectionem ἀionem ctionem Christi. Itaque Syrum verto, & obvertit omni homini fidem suam, quum suscitavit eum ex mortuis. eo sensu quo Matt. 5. 39. [Arabic], obverte ei etiam alteram. sensus est, per resurrectionem Christi, Deus fidem suam, id est, certitudinem consilii de futuro judicio initi, obvertit omnibus, id est, effecit ut ea coram omnium vultu ac facie versetur. Arabs [Arabic] , & certum reddidit omnem hominem de fide sua, per suscitationem ejus e mortuis.
units.tr: VERSE 31. Because he has appointed a day in which he will judge the whole earth in righteousness, by the man whom he has determined [πίστιν παρασχὼν πᾶσιν ἀναστήσας αὐτὸν] &c. Beza rightly renders faith made plain to all. The Vulgate has offering faith to all. I do not take this as if it meant that the power of embracing Christ through faith had been made available to the whole world. Rather, offering for me means making, so that the sense is that by raising him from the dead he proved, by a certain and trustworthy argument, that Christ would be judge. I take the Syrian and the Arab in the same way. The Syrian: and turned every man to his faith, when he raised him from the dead. Boderianus in the Parisian edition: and turned every man. In the Regius: and restored. But the truth does not allow that God is said to have turned or restored all men to the faith of Christ. Nor does it agree with the mind of Luke, which is that the future judgment is to be believed with certainty, because God made proof of this matter to all men through the resurrection of Christ. Therefore I render the Syrian: and turned his faith toward every man, when he raised him from the dead, in the same sense as Matt. 5.39, turn to him the other also. The meaning is that through the resurrection of Christ God turned his faith, that is, the certainty of his decided counsel concerning the future judgment, toward all men, so that it is set before the face and sight of everyone. The Arab: and made every man certain of his faith, through his raising from the dead.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CHAP. XVIII.

units.la: VERS. 3. [Greek] Syrus, [Syriac]. Trem. artificio autem suo conficientes tabernacula erant. Boder. opifices conopeorum erant. Ferrarius, hunc ipsum locum citans, scribit [Syriac], & vertit, artifex conopeorum, textor aulaeorum, scenofactor. At in appendice vertit ephippium. nec aliam ejus significationem invenio in Lex. Syr. Arab. ubi [Syriac] vertitur [Arabic], id est, ephippia, clitellae. subdit deinde [Syriac] quod Syriacè vertit [Syriac]. ubi fateor, me quid [Syriac] fit, non intelligere. at Arabicè exponit per [Arabic] quod opifices ephippiorum significat. ergo [Syriac], ephippia.
units.tr: VERS. 3. The Syriac word here (Tremellius): but by their craft they were makers of tents. Boderianus: they were makers of canopies. Ferrarius, citing this same place, writes the Syriac word and translates it maker of canopies, weaver of hangings, scene-builder. But in the appendix he translates it saddle. I find no other meaning for it in the Syriac-Arabic lexicon, where it is rendered by words meaning saddles, pack-saddles. Ferrarius then adds another Syriac word, which he renders as the Syriac equivalent of the first. Here I confess I do not understand what that word means. But the Arabic explains it by a word meaning makers of saddles. Therefore the sense is saddles.

units.la: VERS. 4. Quod hic interserit Vulgatus, interponens nomen Domini Iesu, Syrus, Arabs & Aethiopicus non agnoscunt.
units.tr: VERS. 4. The Vulgate's insertion here, interposing the name of the Lord Jesus, is not recognized by the Syriac, the Arabic or the Ethiopic.

units.la: VERS. 5. [Greek]. Beza, pergens testificari. ut exprimeret vim praepos. [Greek]. at plurima sunt loca N.T. ubi vim illam habere nequit. Ex. gr. Hebr. 2. 6. [Greek] [Greek]. ubi ipse Beza simpliciter, & bene, Testatus est autem quidam alicubi, & apud LXX pro הַיִּר passim usurpatur.
units.tr: VERS. 5. Beza renders continuing to testify, to bring out the force of the preposition. But there are very many places in the New Testament where that force cannot apply. For example Heb. 2.6, where Beza himself simply and rightly renders someone testified somewhere. And in the Septuagint the same verb is used constantly for a Hebrew verb.

units.la: VERS. 7. In domum cujusdam οἰκίαν Ἰδρς nomine Iusti. Vulg. Titi Iusti. Syrus & Arabs tantum, Titi. Æthiopicus tantum, Iusti.
units.tr: VERS. 7. In the house of a certain man named Justus. The Vulgate: of Titus Justus. The Syriac and the Arabic have only Titus; the Ethiopic has only Justus.

units.la: VERS. 10. οὐδὲς ζημιώσει σοι, ἢ κακῶσαί σε. Vulgatus, Syrus & Arabs, nullus poterit nocere tibi. Non rectè enim Arabem interpretatus est Junius, neque aggredietur quisquam nocere tibi. verba sunt, ولن يقدر احد ... ad verbum, & nequaquam poterit aliquis super lesione tui, id est, ex peculiari quadam constructione, quam habet verbum يقدر, nequaquam poterit quis nocere tibi. Erasmus ἐπιθήσεται σοι vertit, adorietur te. Beza, invadet te. rectè. ad verbum, imponet tibi, vel ponet supra te, sup. χεῖρας, manus. Hebraicè id eadem prorsus phrasi dixero, איש לא ירות עליך להרע. occurrit ea Ps. 3. 7. עלי, אשר סביב שתו, LXX τῶν κύκλῳ συνεπιλήμπτει μοι, qui circumcirca simul imponunt mihi, vel ponunt supra me, sup. manus, id est, invadunt & adoriuntur me, quasi injectis in me manibus.
units.tr: VERS. 10. No one shall harm you [οὐδεὶς ζημιώσει σοι, ἢ κακῶσαί σε]. The Vulgate, the Syriac and the Arabic have no one will be able to harm you. Junius did not render the Arabic correctly when he gave nor will anyone attack to harm you. The words are wa-lan yaqdiru aḥad, word for word and no one will be able against the injury of you, that is, by a special construction that the verb yaqdiru has, no one at all will be able to harm you. Erasmus translated ἐπιθήσεται σοι as will attack you, and Beza as will invade you, rightly. Literally it is will lay upon you or will put upon you, with χεῖρας, hands, understood. In Hebrew I would say exactly the same phrase: ʾîsh lōʾ yārûṭ ʿālêkh lehāraʿ [איש לא ירות עליך להרע]. It occurs in Ps. 3.7: [עלי, אשר סביב שתו], which the LXX render who all round together lay hold of me, or lay upon me, that is, supply hands: they attack and assault me, as if hands had been thrown upon me.

units.la: VERS. 14. Εἰ μὲν οὖν ἦν ἀδίκημά τι, ἢ ῥᾳδιούργημα πονηρόν, ὦ Ἰουδαῖοι, κατὰ λόγον ἂν ἠνεχόμην ὑμῶν. si quidem esset iniquum aliquid, aut facinus malum, ô Iudai, nempe de quo accusationem instituere velletis. ideo Syrus per modum commentarii hoc supplens, vertit, si de aliqua re mala, aut fraudulenta aut exosa accusaretis ô Iudai, convenienter susciperem vos. pro ῥᾳδιούργημα πονηρόν, videtur legisse ῥᾳδιούργημα ἢ πνηρόν. Arabs pro πονηρόν non legit φαυλόν, neque ut ait Junius δήλον. sed κατ' ἀδα secutus Syrum vertit, لن كنتم على شي ردي او ... قبيح كنتم تسعون بالواجب والكنت اقبلكم quæ Junius inconvenientissimè reddidit, si de aliquo consilio aut injuria aut maleficii referretis, ô Iudai, manifesti, equidem acciperem vos. verto, si de re mala aut fraudulenta aut turpi accusaretis ô Iudai, conveniens esset, & acciperem vos, id est, conveniens essFet ut acciperem, vel admitterem vos. atque id omnino arbitror voluisse Lucam,per ξ' λόγον αὐ ἡμεχόμεν ὑμῶν, ad verbum, secundum rationem ferrem vos, id est, rationi consentaneum esset ut vos ferrem.
units.tr: VERS. 14. The Greek: "If indeed there were some wrong or wicked villainy, O Jews, I would reasonably endure you" (Εἰ μὲν οὖν ἦν ἀδίκημά τι, ἢ ῥᾳδιούργημα πονηρόν, ὦ Ἰουδαῖοι, κατὰ λόγον ἂν ἠνεχόμην ὑμῶν). If indeed there were some iniquity, or wicked crime, O Jews, namely one about which you wished to bring an accusation. So the Syriac, supplying this by way of commentary, renders: if you were to accuse me, O Jews, of some evil, fraudulent or shameful matter, I would receive you fittingly. For πονηρόν it seems to have read ῥᾳδιούργημα ἢ πνηρόν. The Arabic did not read φαῦλον for πονηρόν, nor δῆλον, as Junius says. But following the Syriac, it renders what Junius most unsuitably translated as if you were speaking of some plan, or injury, or evil, O manifest Jews, I would indeed accept you. I translate: if you accused me of an evil, fraudulent or base matter, O Jews, it would be fitting, and I would accept you, that is, it would be fitting for me to receive or admit you. And I am quite sure this is what Luke meant by κατὰ λόγον ἂν ἠνεχόμην ὑμῶν, literally I would bear you according to reason, that is, it would be consistent with reason that I should bear with you.

units.la: VERS. 15. Si vero quaestio est περὶ λόγυ ἐ ὀνομάτων, ἢ νόμυ ἢ καθ' ὑμᾶς, de verbo & nominibus & lege quam habetis. Per verbum potest absolute intelligi verbum Dei. & per nomina, nomina Dei, quae absolute שמות, Nomina dicuntur Hebraeis. vocantur & שמות, commemorationes. vide Eliam in Thisbi. Æthiopicus habet ... & de nominibus hominum.
units.tr: VERS. 15. The Greek: "But if the question concerns a word and names and the law which you have" (περὶ λόγου καὶ ὀνομάτων καὶ νόμου τοῦ καθ' ὑμᾶς). By word can be understood, absolutely, the word of God; and by names, the names of God, which the Hebrews call absolutely Names (שמות). They are also called שמות, commemorations. See Elijah in Thisbi. The Ethiopic has and concerning the names of men.

units.la: VERS. 18. Κατεχόμενοι τῷ κτ... Æthiopicus, & totonderunt caput suum: habebant enim votum. addo id notis Cl. Bezae. non habet ἐν Κυγχεαῖς.
units.tr: VERS. 18. The Greek begins "Κατεχόμενοι τῷ κτ..." The Ethiopic: and they shaved their head, for they had a vow. I add this to the notes of the distinguished Beza. The Greek does not have ἐν Κεγχρεαῖς (in Cenchreae).

units.la: VERS. 19. Κατῳκήσεν εἰς Ἐφεσον, καὶ εὑρόντες κατελίπον αὐτήν. Sic & Æthiopicus legit. At Syrus, quem sequitur Arabs, pro κατῳκήσεν legit κατῳκησαν, pervenerunt. & καὶ εὑρόντες κατελίπον αὐτὴν, non hic, sed infra sub finem γ' cf. 21. legerunt. ibi enim pro ἡ ἀνήχθη καὶ εἰς Ἐφεσον, habent, & Aquilam & Priscillam reliquerunt Ephesi: & ipse iter fecit per mare, & venit Caesaream. quae lectio mihi valde bene quadrare videtur. Rectius enim illic, ubi Ephesio discedit, Aquilam & Priscillam reliquisse ibi dicitur, quam hic ubi primum intrat.
units.tr: VERS. 19. The Greek: "He dwelt at Ephesus, and having found them, he left her there" (Κατῴκησεν εἰς Ἔφεσον, καὶ εὑρόντες κατέλιπον αὐτήν). The Ethiopic also reads it thus. But the Syriac, which the Arabic follows, reads κατῴκησαν for κατῴκησεν, they arrived. And the words καὶ εὑρόντες κατέλιπον αὐτήν they read not here but further on, near the end, see verse 21. For there, in place of and he also sailed to Ephesus, they have: and they left Aquila and Priscilla at Ephesus, and he himself made the journey by sea and came to Caesarea. This reading seems to me to fit very well. For it is more correct to say there, where he departs from Ephesus, that they left Aquila and Priscilla there, than here, where he first enters the city.

units.la: VERS. 21. Δεῖ μὲ πάντως τὴν ἑορτὴν τὴν ἐχομένην ποιῆσαι εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα. annotat Cl. Beza Vulgatum nihil horum legisse. Addo, nec Æthiopicum. Syrus & Arabs legerunt. in Syro notandum quod πάντως verterit ..., Tremell. & Boder. in Parif. sedulo. verte certo sive constanter. id est, sic ut de sententia ista nihil mutem. Arabs autem, ... Junius, oportet me agere venturum diem festum in loco sancto. non assecutus est mentem Interpretis, qui vertendus est, oportet ut ut incipiam facere festum sequens Hierosolyma. non construxit πάντως cum δὲ, sed cum τοιῆσαι, & τοιήσας τῷ ἑορτῷ πάντως ipsi fuit, non festi dies quosdam, sed à primo initio omnes celebrare. ideo dixit, oportet ut incipiam facere &c.
units.tr: VERS. 21. The Greek: "It is necessary by all means to keep the coming feast at Jerusalem" (Δεῖ με πάντως τὴν ἑορτὴν τὴν ἐρχομένην ποιῆσαι εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα). Cl. Beza notes that the Vulgate read none of these words. I add that the Ethiopic did not read them either. The Syriac and the Arabic did. In the Syriac it should be noted that Tremellius and Boderianus in Paris rendered πάντως as diligently; translate it certainly or constantly, that is, so that I change nothing of this sentiment. The Arabic, as Junius rendered it, it behoves me to celebrate the coming feast in the holy place, did not grasp the mind of the translator, who should be rendered: it behoves me to begin to keep the following feast at Jerusalem. He did not construe πάντως with δέ, but with ποιῆσαι; and to keep the feast by all means meant for him not certain days of the feast but to celebrate all of them from the very beginning. Therefore he said: it behoves me that I begin to keep etc.

units.la: VERS. 22.
units.tr: VERS. 22.

units.la: Quumque descendisset Cæsaream, ἀναβὰς καὶ ἀσπασάμενος τὴν ἐκκλησίαν. Beza post ἀναβὰς subintelligit ἱεροσολύμαν, Hierosolymam. dicitque in Syra interpretatione exprimi. fefellit virum doctiss. Tremellius, qui quum locum id postulare existimaret, supplevit, neque diverso charactere ab ipso textu Syri distinxit. Editiones Syriacæ non habent. nec sensus postulat, qui omnino esse videtur, cum Cæsaream ingressum, ad Ecclesiam illius loci ascendisse, eamque salutasse. Nec est quod ascendendi vox quenquam offendat. ea enim non semper ex depressiori loco in altiorem conscendere, sed saepe simpliciter loco se movere significat. ut ostendimus ad Luc. 5. 2. neque inepte sentiet quis, in editiori urbis loco conventum Ecclesiæ fuisse habitum, ad quem ascendere Paulus necesse habuerit. in elevatioribus enim locis strui templa solebant. Æthiopicus non aliter accepit, quum vertit, & descendit Cæsaream, & ascendit in domum Christianorum (id est, Ecclesiam) & salutavit eos, & abiit Antiochiam.
units.tr: And when he had come down to Caesarea, going up [ἀναβὰς] and saluting the church [ἀσπασάμενος τὴν ἐκκλησίαν]. After ἀναβὰς, Beza understands to Jerusalem and says that the Syriac version expresses it. The learned Tremellius was misled: thinking the place required it, he supplied the words, and he did not mark them with a different character from the text of the Syriac. The Syriac printed editions do not have them. Nor does the sense require them, which seems to be simply that, having entered Caesarea, he went up to the church of that place and greeted it. Nor should the word going up trouble anyone. It does not always mean climbing from a lower place to a higher one, but often means simply moving to a place, as I have shown at Luke 5:2. Nor would anyone reasonably think that the assembly of the church was held in a higher part of the city, to which Paul had to go up. Temples were in fact commonly built on higher ground. The Ethiopic version understands it no differently when it renders: and he came down to Caesarea, and went up into the house of the Christians (that is, the church) and greeted them, and went away to Antioch.

units.la: VERS. 24.
units.tr: VERS. 24.

units.la: Ἀνὴρ λόγιος, vir eloquens. Sic omnes interpretes præter Æthiopicum, qui habet איש נבון, vir prudens, vel sapiens. Lexic. Constant. λόγιος, eloquens, prudens, doctus, verbosus. Hezychius vertit, ὁ σοφὸς ἱστορίας ἐμπειρος, ἱστοριῶν πεπαιδευμένος, historiarum peritus, eruditus. peritia historiarum prudentiam parit.
units.tr: A learned man [Ἀνὴρ λόγιος], an eloquent man. So all the interpreters, except the Ethiopic, which has ish nabon [איש נבון], a prudent or wise man. The Constantinople lexicon: logios means eloquent, prudent, learned, verbose. Hesychius glosses it as one wise in history, instructed in histories, skilled and learned in history. Skill in history produces prudence.

units.la: VERS. 27.
units.tr: VERS. 27.

units.la: Quum autem vellet transire in Achaiam, προτρεψάμενοι οἱ ἀδελφοί, exhortati eum fratres. Syrus, ܠܒܪ ܡܢ Tremel. anteverterunt eum, Boderianus in Parisiensi, prævenerunt eum fratres. unde Cl. Beza ait, Syrum nova & Græcis prorsus inusitata significatione vertisse. Sed Syriacum verbum valet rapuerunt eum fratres. neque enim ܐܬܚܛܦ Syris, ut & הֵפְיִ Hebræis, aliud quam rapere significat. sensus est, incitarunt eum ut, quod facere volebat, raptim faceret, quasi ipsi eum ad iter illud abriperent. nisi forte mendum in textu Syro statuamus, & transpositis solum literis legendum dicamus ܐܬܝܚܕܬܐ, incitarunt eum. ita sane legit Ferrarius, qui probaturus ܐܬܝܚܕ significare suasit, hortatus est, incitavit, hunc ipsum locum citat. significat proprie diligentem, studiosum & concitatum ad rem aliquam reddere. Arabs vertit gavisi sunt de eo. antecedens dixit pro consequente. ideo enim hortati sunt ut proficisceretur, quia gaudebant eum id propositum esse. Æthiopicus permiserunt ei, potestatem ei fecerunt, quasi Συνεχώρησαν legisset, aut Συνεχώρησαν id ipsum significare voluisset.
units.tr: When he wished to pass over into Achaia, the brethren exhorted him [προτρεψάμενοι οἱ ἀδελφοί]. The Syriac [lbr mn], in Tremellius, has "they went before him"; the Parisian Boderianus has "the brethren forestalled him." Whence Beza says that the Syrian has rendered it in a new sense, wholly unusual among the Greeks. But the Syriac word means "they seized him" or "they snatched him away," for [ithchatheph] in Syriac, like [hephi] in Hebrew, means nothing other than "to snatch." The sense is that they urged him on, so that he would do quickly what he was wishing to do, as if they themselves were hurrying him away on that journey. Unless perhaps we suppose a fault in the Syriac text, and say that by transposing the letters one should read [ithichadatha], "they urged him on." Ferrarius indeed reads it so, and, wishing to prove that [ithichad] means "to persuade, exhort, incite," he cites this very passage. Properly it signifies "to make someone diligent, eager and stirred up to some matter." The Arabic translates "they rejoiced over him," putting the consequent for the antecedent: they urged him to set out because they were glad that this was his purpose. The Ethiopic has "they allowed him, gave him leave," as if it had read [Συνεχώρησαν], or as if [Συνεχώρησαν] was meant to signify that very thing.

units.la: IBID. Οὐς συνεβάλετο πολὺ τῆς πίστεως αὐτοῦ διὰ τὴν χάριν. Vulgatus, Eras. Beza, Syrus & Arabs acceperunt συνεβάλετο significatione commodi. Solus Æthiopicus, significatione collationis per sermonem. vertit enim, וידברו עמהם, & cum advenisset, locutus est multum iis qui crediderant per gratiam Dei. eodem sensu quo apud Euripidem est συμβάλλω σοι λόγως, colloquor tecum. prior tamen significatio usitatior, præsertim in medio συμβάλλομαι. & huic loco convenientior, quia ἐπεὶ seq. ratio additur, cur multum profuerit credentibus: quia nempe vehementer redarguebat Judæos.
units.tr: Who greatly helped those who had believed through grace [Οὐς συνεβάλετο πολὺ τῆς πίστεως αὐτοῦ διὰ τὴν χάριν]. The Vulgate, Erasmus, Beza, the Syriac and the Arabic have taken synebaleto in the sense of being of service. Only the Ethiopic takes it in the sense of conferring by speech. For it renders: wayedabberu 'immahem [וידברו עמהם], and when he had arrived, he spoke much with those who had believed through the grace of God. It is the same sense as in Euripides, symballō soi logous, I converse with you. Still, the former meaning is more common, especially in the middle symballomai, and it fits this passage better, because the following clause, introduced by epei, gives the reason why he was very helpful to the believers: namely, because he powerfully refuted the Jews.

units.la: VERS. 28. Εὐτόνως γὰρ τῆς Ἰουδαίοις διαχατηλέγχετο. Vulgatus εὐτόνως, vehementer. Beza, magna contentione. Syrus ܥܠܚܕ, fortiter. Hezychius, εὐτόνως, ἰσχυρῶς, ἰλαφρῶς, valide, levi negocio. Idem, εὐτόνῳ, εὐμενῶς, ἡ φρονίμως, animoanimosus, generosus. hinc non inepte vertas, animosè, generosè. Idem, Ζηλία, ἀνεξικακία, καρτερία, ὑπομονή, malorum tolerantia, fortitudo, perseverantia. neque hinc male vertas, constanter, perseveranter. Cætera Vulgat. & Erasm. verterunt, Iudæos revincebat. Beza, magis magisque redarguebat. ut vim præpositionis ἀνά, qua augeri significationem vult, exprimeret. sed vis potius præpositionis κατά attendenda, quæ ut verbo, cum quo componitur, dat ut construatur cum Dativo τῆς Ἰουδαίοις, ita eidem actionis significationem dare videtur, qua agebat Apollos adversus Judæos. adeo ut non gravatè verterem, adversus Iudæos arguebat. ita sane Syrus [Syriac text] disputabat contra Iudæos. & Arabs [Arabic text] disputabat cum Iudæis coram turbis disputatione valida.
units.tr: VERS. 28. For he powerfully refuted the Jews publicly [Εὐτόνως γὰρ τῆς Ἰουδαίοις διαχατηλέγχετο]. The Vulgate renders eutonōs as vehemently. Beza: with great contention. The Syriac: strongly. Hesychius: eutonōs, vigorously, strongly, lightly, with ease. The same: eutonō, kindly, or wisely; spirited, noble. Hence one might fairly render it spiritedly, nobly. The same: zēlia, anexikakia, karteria, hupomonē, endurance of evils, fortitude, perseverance. Nor would it be wrong to render it here steadily, perseveringly. The rest the Vulgate and Erasmus render he refuted the Jews, and Beza he refuted them more and more, so as to express the force of the preposition ana, which is meant to increase the sense. But the force of the preposition kata deserves more attention. As it gives the compound verb the construction with the dative tēs Ioudaiois, so it seems also to give the verb the sense of the action that Apollos was carrying on against the Jews. So much so that I would not hesitate to render it he argued against the Jews. Thus the Syriac, he disputed against the Jews [Syriac, transliterated: wa-hwa mtnaṣṣeḥ, not reproduced], and the Arabic, he disputed with the Jews before the crowds in a vigorous debate.

units.la: IBID. Εἶναι τὸν Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν. Ambiguum est, utrum sit subjectum, utrum prædicatum. ambiguitatem reliquerunt Vulgatus & Æthiopicus, esse Christum Iesum. At Syrus, Arabs, Erasm. & Beza Ἰησοῦν faciunt subjectum, τὸν Χριστὸν prædicatum. si tamen mutes in ὅτι ὁ Χριστὸς ἐστὶ Ἰησοῦς, subjectum potius est ὁ Χριστός, ac sensus, cum qui dicitur Christus, esse verum mundi Servatorem. fateor tamen id non omnino esse necessarium, quia articulus ὁ, etsi non frequenter, interdum tamen etiam prædicato apponitur. ut Joan. 1. 4. & 8. 44. Jac. 3. 6.
units.tr: Ibid. That Christ Jesus is [Εἶναι τὸν Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν]. It is ambiguous which is the subject and which the predicate. The Vulgate and the Ethiopic leave the ambiguity, rendering that Christ Jesus is. But the Syriac, the Arabic, Erasmus and Beza make Jesus the subject and the Christ the predicate. If, however, you change it to hoti ho Christos esti Iēsous, then ho Christos is rather the subject, and the sense is that he who is called Christ is the true Saviour of the world. I admit, though, that this is not entirely necessary, since the article ho, though not frequently, is sometimes also placed before a predicate, as in John 1:4, 8:44, and James 3:6.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CAP. XIX.

units.la: VERS. 3. Εἰς τί οὖν ἐβαπτίσθητε; οἱ δὲ εἶπαν, εἰς τὸ Ἰωάννου βάπτισμα. Vulgatus, Syrus, Arabs & Æthiopicus εἰς pro ἐν acceperunt, quod passim in N. T. usitatum. in quo baptizati estis? id est, in qua doctrinâ? in baptismate Iohannis, id est, in doctrina quam Johannes baptismate obsignauit. sicut
units.tr: VERSE 3. "Into what then were you baptized?" [Εἰς τί οὖν ἐβαπτίσθητε;] They said, "Into John's baptism" [εἰς τὸ Ἰωάννου βάπτισμα]. The Vulgate, the Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic take "into" [εἰς] in place of "in" [ἐν], which is common throughout the New Testament. In what were you baptized? that is, in what doctrine? In John's baptism, that is, in the doctrine which John sealed with baptism. So also

units.la: 1 Cor. 10. 2. εἰς τ̄ Μωϋσᾶ ἐβαπτίσθησαν, in Mose, id est, in doctrina Mosis, baptizati sunt.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 10. 2: They were baptized into Moses [εἰς τὸν Μωϋσῆν ἐβαπτίσθησαν], that is, into the doctrine of Moses.

units.la: VERS. 9. Ἐν τῇ χώλῃ Τυρίων πηγῇ. Syrus & Arabs nomen proprium viri cujusdam esse voluerunt. Arabs autem, non in editione Erpeniana tantum, sed & in alio M. S. habet Turadius. Æthiopicus vertit coram praetorio & praesidibus, seu principibus. vult χώλῃ Τυρίων fuisse praetorium, ubi praesides convenirent, apud summum scilicet tyrannum & urbis principem.
units.tr: VERSE 9. "In the hall [χώλῃ] of Tyrannus" [ἐν τῇ χώλῃ Τυρίων πηγῇ]. The Syriac and the Arabic wanted this to be the proper name of a certain man. The Arabic, however, reads "Turadius", not only in the Erpenius edition but also in another manuscript. The Ethiopic renders it before the praetorium and the governors, or chiefs. He holds that the χώλῃ Τυρίων was the praetorium, where the governors met, namely at the house of the chief tyrant and ruler of the city.

units.la: VERS. 12. Σωδάρια ἡ σμικίνθια. Sunt qui duas hasce voces idem significare volunt. Suidas, σμικίνθιον, φαξιόλιον ἢ σωδάριον. quid autem φαξιόλιον? idem Suidas ait esse, τὸ τῆς κεφαλῆς σκεπέλημα, ὃ φᾶσι Κυπρίοις Κορδύλη, πας' Ἀθηναίοις Κρώβυλον, φᾶσι δὲ Περσαῖς Νιδάριον καλεῖσθαι, capitis velamen, quod Cyprius Cordyle, Atheniensibus Crobylum, Persis autem Nidarium dicitur. Hezychius quoque σμικίνθια vertit φαξιόλια. Sed addit, ζωσάρια ὠφάρια τ̄ ἱερέων, Cingula horaria sacerdotum. Cingula intelligo, quibus se accingerent cum sacra facerent. cum enim talaribus induerentur vestibus, non nisi succinctos solere sacris vacare, liquet ex Exod. 39. 29. Levit. 14. 6.
units.tr: VERS. 12. Sudaria or semicinctia. Some hold that these two words mean the same thing. Suidas: smikinthion, a little veil or sudarion [σμικίνθιον, φαξιόλιον ἢ σωδάριον]. What then is a phaxiolion? The same Suidas says it is the covering of the head, which the Cypriots call kordyle, the Athenians krobylos, and the Persians call nidarion [τὸ τῆς κεφαλῆς σκεπέλημα, ὃ φᾶσι Κυπρίοις Κορδύλη, παρ' Ἀθηναίοις Κρώβυλον, φᾶσι δὲ Περσαῖς Νιδάριον καλεῖσθαι]: a head-cloth. Hesychius too renders smikinthia as phaxolia. But he adds: zosaria, the linen cloths of priests [ζωσάρια ὠφάρια τ̄ ἱερέων], that is, hour-girdles of priests. I understand these to be the girdles with which they girded themselves when they performed sacred duties. For that the priests, when clothed in long robes, were not accustomed to serve in the sacred offices unless girded up, is clear from Exod. 39. 29. Levit. 14. 6.

units.la: 1 Sam. 2. 18. Talibus quoque cingulis, quo expeditius & inciderent & sua peragerent, usus procul dubio fuit Paulus. quæ semicinctia recte dicuntur, quia in medio corporis medium vestis accingunt. At Syrus vertit, [Syriac] Arabs [Arabic], lacinias. sunt autem laciniæ, in vestimento extremæ partes, ejusque segmenta quædam vestem dividentia, unde & à lacerando Latinis, Syris & Arabibus dictæ sunt. quarum etiam in abstergendis sudoribus usus erat. Plaut. Merc. Ac tu adepol fume laciniam, atque abstergesudorem tibi. hæ quia ad medium corporis scissæ erant, atque ibi accingebantur, recte ob id semicinctia dicantur. quo videtur respexisse Æthiopicus quum vertit [Hebrew], & tulerunt. runt de extremitatibus vestis ejus, & sudaria ejus. ܐܪܒ quo utitur Æthiopicus, etiam in Targum pro lacinia & extremitate vestis usurpatur. Hebraei ܐܫܪ dicunt, cujus duale ܬܪܝܢ observetur non de avibus tantum, sed & de vestibus dici, Jer. 2. 34. ut sciamus, sicut avium, ita & vestium duas fuisse alas, quæ quia jam ad medium corporis erant scissæ, ubi cingebantur, facile porro à reliqua veste abscindi & separari potuerunt. quod uni alæ vestis Regis Saulis à Davide contigit 1 Sam. 24. Ut itaque hæ alæ per σμικρότητα hic intelligantur, plane non repugno.
units.tr: 1 Sam. 2. 18. Paul also surely used such girdles, so that he could work and carry out his tasks more readily. These are rightly called half-girdles, because they gird the middle part of the body with the middle part of the garment. But the Syriac renders the word as [Syriac] and the Arabic as [Arabic], lacinias, that is, flaps. Flaps are the outermost parts of a garment, certain segments of it that divide the garment; hence they are called lacinia by the Latins, and by the Syrians and Arabs from tearing. They were also used for wiping away sweat. Plautus, Merc.: And you, by Pollux, take a flap and wipe the sweat from yourself. Since these were cut at the middle of the body and girded there, they are rightly called half-girdles for this reason. The Ethiopic seems to have had this in mind when it translates [Hebrew] as and they took: they took from the extremities of his garment, and his handkerchiefs. The word the Ethiopic uses is also used in the Targum for flap and the extremity of a garment. The Hebrews use the word [Hebrew: kanaf], whose dual, kenafayim, is found not only of birds but also of garments (Jer. 2. 34). So we may know that, as birds have wings, so garments had two wings, which, since they were already cut at the middle of the body where they were girded, could easily be cut off and separated from the rest of the garment. This happened to one wing of King Saul's robe, which David cut off (1 Sam. 24). So I am not at all opposed to understanding these wings here by way of diminutive.

units.la: VERS. 13. In fine versus, Solus Arabs addit ܕܪܫܢ, & sanabantur.
units.tr: VERSE 13. At the end of the verse, only the Arabic adds [Arabic: wa-yabra'ūn], and they were healed.

units.la: VERS. 16. Καὶ καταχυνόμενος αὐτῶν. Sic Syrus, Arabs & Æthiopicus quoque legerunt. non ut Vulgatus, dominatus amborum. In fine versus pro γυμνὸς ἢ πεζωμαλισμένος, Syrus habet ܐܪܒܕܫܒ ܕܫܒ. Trem. nudati ac vulnerati. Boder. nudati sauciique. Ferrarius ܒܐܪܒܕܫܒ, contritus, contusus, comminutus. ܒܐܪܒܕܫܒ & ܒܐܪܒܕܫܒ, contritio, contusio, comminutio. ܐܪܒܕܫܒ, contrivit, contudit, comminuit.
units.tr: VERSE 16. "And falling upon them" [καταχυνόμενος αὐτῶν]. The Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic also read it so. Not as the Vulgate has it, overpowering both of them. At the end of the verse, for "naked or wounded" [γυμνὸς ἢ πεζωμαλισμένος] the Syriac has [Syriac], and wounded. Tremellius: stripped and wounded. Beza: stripped and bloodied. Ferrarius renders the Syriac as crushed, bruised, broken in pieces; the nouns as crushing, bruising, breaking in pieces; and the verb as crushed, bruised, broke in pieces.

units.la: VERS. 19. Εὗρον ἀργύριον μυριάδας πέντε. Vulgatus, invenerunt pecuniam denariorum 50 millia. Beza quoque ἀργύριον per denarios vertit. Arabs per ܕܪܗܡ, drachmas, quae tantundem fere valebant atque denarii. Syrus ܟܣܦܐ, sicut LXX plerumque pro ܟܣܦ ponunt ἀργύριον. interdum δίδραχμα ἀργύριον ut Deut. 22. 29. interdum δίδραχμα absolute. ut Gen. 20. 16. aliquando οἰκλῶν, siclus. ut Num. 7. 85. Deut. 22. 19. 2 Reg. 15. 20. Esa. 7. 23. Jer. 32. 9. intelligitur autem siclus communis, valens δίδραχμον duas drachmas. quomodo & Chaldaeus pro ܫܩܠ solet dicere ܟܣܦܐ, siclus. ex hac supputatione, summa esset, siclorum quinquaginta millia. altero major quam denariorum. siclus enim communis duos denarios comprehendit.
units.tr: VERSE 19. "They found silver, fifty thousand [μυριάδας πέντε]." The Vulgate: they found money of fifty thousand denarii. Beza also translates argyrion as denarii. The Arabic renders it by [Arabic: dirham], drachmas, which were worth almost the same as denarii. The Syriac has [Syriac: kaspa], silver, as the Seventy usually render [Hebrew: kesef] by argyrion. Sometimes they have argyrion didrachmon, as in Deut. 22. 29; sometimes simply didrachma, as in Gen. 20. 16; and sometimes siclus, as in Num. 7. 85, Deut. 22. 19, 2 Kings 15. 20, Isa. 7. 23, Jer. 32. 9. The ordinary shekel is meant, which was worth a didrachmon, two drachmas. In the same way the Chaldee paraphrast usually says [Aramaic: kaspa], silver, for [Hebrew: shekel], shekel. By this reckoning the sum would be fifty thousand shekels, which is greater than fifty thousand denarii by a factor of two, since an ordinary shekel comprises two denarii.

units.la: VERS. 22. Καὶ Ἐ͂ρχησιν. Consentiunt in hac lectione Vulg. Syr. & Arabs. Solus Æthiopicus mendose legit, & Aristarchum. qui quomodo potuit missus dici in Macedoniam, quum infra ꝟ. 29. dicatur cum Gajo comprehensus Ephesi. & in fine versus, solus legit Ephesi, quum reliqui omnes constanter habeant in Asia.
units.tr: VERSE 22. "And Erastus [Ἐ͂ρχησιν]." The Vulgate, the Syriac and the Arabic agree in this reading. Only the Ethiopic reads wrongly, and Aristarchus. But how could he be said to be sent into Macedonia, when below, in verse 29, he is said to have been seized with Gaius at Ephesus? And at the end of the verse, only he reads at Ephesus, whereas all the others consistently have in Asia.

units.la: VERS 23. Περὶ τῆς ὁδῶς. Syrus, Arabs & Beza, ob viam Dei. Æthiopicus ob hanc doctrinam. τῆς pro τωνῆς.
units.tr: VERSE 23. "Concerning the Way [περὶ τῆς ὁδοῦ]." The Syriac, the Arabic and Beza have on account of the way of God. The Ethiopic has on account of this teaching. [The Greek] τῆς is read for τωνῆς.

units.la: VERS. 24. Ναὸς Ἀργυρᾶς. Arabs & Æthiop. habent imagines argenteas.
units.tr: VERSE 24. "Silver shrines [ναοὺς ἀργυροῦς]." The Arabic and the Ethiopic have silver images.

units.la: VERS. 25. Οὓς συναθροίσας ἐ σὺν σὺ τὰ πιαῦτα ἐργάτας. Syrum sic quoque legisse, non autem ut habebat vetustissimus Bezæ codex, clarum est. habet enim, [Syriac text illegible] . [Syriac text illegible] o, hic congregavit istos coartifices suos omnes, & qui operabantur cum illis. ubi quoque manifeste distinguit inter τεχνίτας & reliquos ἐργάτας. per istos intelligens, qui sicut Demetrius magistri artis erant, & aliis operas præscribebant, per hos vero, inferiores operarios, quibus à magistris artificibus operæ præscribebantur.
units.tr: VERSE 25. "Whom he gathered together, with the workmen of such things [σὺν τοὺς τοιούτους ἐργάτας]." That the Syriac also read it thus, and not as the very ancient codex of Beza had it, is clear.
