For it reads [Syriac text illegible]: he gathered these, all his fellow craftsmen, and those who worked with them. Here too it plainly distinguishes between technitai and the other ergatai. By the former it means those who, like Demetrius, were masters of the craft and assigned work to others; by the latter, the lower workmen, to whom work was assigned by the master craftsmen.

units.la: VERS. 27. Οὐ μόνον ἡ τῶν κινδυνῶν ἡμῖν τὸ μέρος ὡς ἀπιλεγμὸν ἐλθὼν. Vulgatus τῶν τὸ μέρος vertit ad verbum hæc pars. Beza, illud quod nobis est peculiare: cui longè præfero quod Syrus & Arabs verterunt, hæc res, vel hoc negocium. quo sensu idem nomen capiendum nobis videtur 2 Cor. 9. 3. ne gloriatio nostra de vobis inanis fiat ἐν τῷ μέρει τῶν, hac in re. Col. 2. 16. ne quis vos damnet in cibo aut in potu, ἢ ἐν μέρει ἑορτῆς, aut in negocio festi. 1 Pet. 4. 16. glorificet autem Deum ἐν τῷ μέρει τούτῳ, in hac re. Belgicè ad verbum recte dicimus, in desen deele, in hac parte, id est, in eo quod ad hanc rem spectat. Sic, nemo damnet vos in parte festi, id est, in eo quod ad festum spectat. Ne gloriatio nostra de vobis inanis fiat in hac parte, id est, in eo quod hanc rem, nempe subsidium pauperum, spectat. Sic hoc loco, periclitatur nobis hac pars, id est, hoc quod ad hanc rem, nempe artificium & quastum nostrum, spectat. Porro, κινδυνεύει εἰς ἀπολογίαν ἐλθεῖν, Vulg. vertit, periclitatur in redargutionem venire. Beza, periculum est ne nobis probrosum evadat. laudo. sed examinandum quod addit, Syrum & Arabem vel hunc locum non intellexisse, vel diversum quidpiam in Græcis codicibus legisse. neutrum necesse videtur. Syrus habet ܐܝܬ ܠܘܬ ܥܒܕܐ ܕܐܢܫܐ ܐܚܪܢܐ ܕܥܠܡܐ Trem. & non hac res tantum innotescit. correxit Junius, & non hoc studium tantummodo infamatur. Boder. & non hoc placitum tantum diffamatur. ܠܐ ܥܒܕܐ non est proprie placitum, nec studium. etsi sit à ܐܬܐ, voluit. sed rem, negocium denotat. nec quicquam amplius. voluntas, placitum ܪܨܘܢܐ dicitur. sicut & Arab. à ܐܬܐ, voluit, fit ܨܒܐ, voluntas, & ܐܢܐ quod nihil nisi rem, negocium significat. Porro Syr. ܡܫܬܥܠܐ significat publicè ignominia exponere, ut ad Matt. 1. 19. pluribus tradidimus. Verto ergo, & non hac res tantum (nempe ars quam profitemur) publicè ignominia exponetur & cessabit. optimè mentem textus videtur assecutus, qui habet εἰς ἀπολογίαν ἐλθεῖν. malui autem participia Syriaca per futura vertere, quia non tantum frequenter eum usum habent, sed & hoc loco melius explicant mentem Euangelistæ, qui dixit, κινδυνεύει ἡμῖν τῶν τὸ μέρος εἰς ἀπολογίαν ἐλθεῖν. quid futurum sit proponit. Arabs Syrum secutus reddit [illegible, ~12 letters] & non utique prabrosa reddetur res haec tantum & cessabit. Junius aliter, sed male.
units.tr: VERSE 27. "Not only is this part of ours in danger of coming into disrepute [οὐ μόνον ἡ τῶν κινδυνῶν ἡμῖν τὸ μέρος εἰς ἀπολογισμὸν ἐλθεῖν]." The Vulgate translates tōn to meros word for word as this part. Beza: that which is peculiar to us. Far better is what the Syriac and the Arabic rendered: this matter, or this business. In this sense the same word seems to me to be taken at 2 Cor. 9. 3: lest our boasting about you be made empty in this respect [ἐν τῷ μέρει τούτῳ]. Col. 2. 16: let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a feast [ἐν μέρει ἑορτῆς], or of a new moon, that is, in the business of a feast. 1 Pet. 4. 16: let him glorify God in this respect [ἐν τῷ μέρει τούτῳ]. In Dutch we rightly say word for word in desen deele, in this part, that is, in what concerns this matter. So, let no one condemn you in a part of the feast, that is, in what concerns the feast. Lest our boasting about you be vain in this part, that is, in what concerns this matter, namely the relief of the poor. So here, this part of ours is in danger, that is, what concerns this matter, namely our craft and our gain. Further, kindynenei eis apologian elthein the Vulgate renders is in danger of coming into refutation. Beza: there is danger that it will turn out shameful for us. I praise this. But what he adds needs examination: that the Syriac and the Arabic either did not understand this passage here, or read something different in the Greek manuscripts. Neither seems necessary. The Syriac has [Syriac: ith lewath 'abda d'enasha 'ahrana d'alma]. Tremellius: and not only this matter becomes known. Junius corrected it: and not this study alone is defamed. Boderianus: and not this purpose alone is defamed. The word ['abda] is not properly purpose nor study, although it derives from [Syriac: ith], he wished. It denotes matter, business, and nothing more. [Syriac: retzona] is called will, purpose; just as the Arabic, from [Arabic: ataa], he wished, makes [Arabic: sabiyya], will, and [Arabic: amr], which signifies nothing but matter, business. Further, the Syriac [Syriac: mashta'la] means to expose publicly to disgrace, as I have shown at more length on Matt. 1. 19. So I translate: and not this matter alone (namely the craft we profess) will be publicly exposed to disgrace and will cease. The Syriac seems to have grasped the sense of the text very well, which has eis apologian elthein. But I preferred to render the Syriac participles by futures, because they not only often have that use, but in this place also better express the mind of the Evangelist, who said kindynei hēmin ... eis apologian elthein, setting out what will be. The Arabic, following the Syriac, renders [Arabic text illegible] and not this matter alone will be made disreputable, and it will cease. Junius differently, but wrongly.

units.la: Sequitur in fine versus apud Syrum [illegible, ~30 letters]. Trem. & etiam ipsa Dea totius Asia,& quam omnes gentes adorant,despectui habetur. Inseruit pronomen relat. quam, utpote quod in Syro deesse putabat. similiter fere Boder. in Reg. at in Parisf. pro הלהן legit הלהן contra omnium codicum fidem,& absque copula vertit, & etiam ipsa Dea totius Asia, quam omnes gentes adorant, ludibrio habebitur. nempe quia cum Tremellio ʔ in [illegible, ~10 letters] acciperet pro nota Gen. caf. nec alibi reperiret pronomen relat. quod hic tamen omnino erat necessarium, mutavit copulam ו in relat. ו. nihil id necesse. Sic enim vertendum, & etiam ipsa Dea, quam tota Asia & omnes populi adorant, contemnetur. ὡς ὅλη ἡ Ἀσία ἡ οἰκουμένη σέβεται. Neque mirum, quod pro ἡ μεγαλειότης αὐτῆς, Syrus dixerit, ipsa Dea. est enim μεγαλειότης Θεᾶ, quae μεγαλοπρεπῆς δόξα dicitur 2 Pet. 1. 17. ipsa divinitas. quamobrem hic Æthiopicus habet [illegible, ~8 letters], & destruetur divinitas ejus.
units.tr: The verse continues at the end in the Syriac [illegible]. Tremellius: "and even the goddess herself, whom all the nations worship, is held in contempt." He inserted the relative pronoun "whom", since he thought it was missing in the Syriac. Boderianus does much the same in the Regius manuscript, but in the Parisian he reads הלהן [hlhn] for הלהן, against the testimony of all the manuscripts, and translates without the conjunction: "and even the goddess herself, whom all the nations worship, will be held in ridicule." Evidently, because with Tremellius he took the ʔ as the sign of the genitive and found no relative pronoun elsewhere, though one was entirely necessary here, he changed the conjunction ו into the relative ו. That change is unnecessary. The passage should be rendered: "and even the goddess herself, whom all Asia and all peoples worship, will be despised." [ὡς ὅλη ἡ Ἀσία ἡ οἰκουμένη σέβεται] Nor is it surprising that the Syriac says "the goddess herself" for "her majesty" (ἡ μεγαλειότης αὐτῆς). For the word is μεγαλειότης, which is called "majestic glory" [μεγαλοπρεπῆς δόξα] at 2 Pet. 1:17, that is, divinity itself. Hence the Ethiopic here has [illegible], "and her divinity will be destroyed."

units.la: VERS. 35. Καταςρέλας ὁ γραμματεὺς τ ἰσχύν. Vulgatus, Æthiopicus & Beza vertunt γραμματεὺς ad verbum Scriba. Syrus & Arabs, primarius civitatis. quod non rejicio. Glossarium, γραμματεὺς, Scriba, Tesserarius. est autem tesserarius, qui tesseras tribuit, & militibus symbola dat. quod apud nos in urbibus praesidiariis Gubernatoris est, in ceteris primarii consulis. Papias: Tesserarius praepositus currunt, qui bellum nunciat. Plutarchus, Τεσσερακόντα καλοῦντες, οἱ δὲ ἀγγέλων ἡ διοπήρων ὑπηρεσίας πλανῆς, Tesserarii vocantur, qui per nuncios & speculatores ministeria peragunt.quum ergo hîc in urbe Ephesò designatur aliquis qui absolutè vocatur ò γραμματεὺς, merito intelligitur præfectus, qui militibus symbola & munia præscribit.
units.tr: VERS. 35. "Who is the scribe [γραμματεὺς] of the city?" [Καταστέλλας ὁ γραμματεὺς τὸν ὄχλον]. The Vulgate, the Ethiopic and Beza translate γραμματεύς literally as "scribe." The Syriac and the Arabic have "chief man of the city," which I do not reject. The glossary has γραμματεύς: "scribe, tesserarius." A tesserarius is one who distributes the tesserae and gives the watchword [symbola] to the soldiers. Among us, in garrison towns this is the business of the governor, and in other places of the chief magistrate. Papias: "A tesserarius is a officer set over the runners, who announces war." Plutarch: "Those called tesserarii, who carry out the services of messengers or scouts, are called tesserarii [Τεσσερακόντα καλοῦντες...]." Since here in the city of Ephesus someone is designated absolutely as ὁ γραμματεύς, he is rightly understood to be the prefect, who sets the watchword and duties for the soldiers.

units.la: VERS. 38. [Hebrew and Arabic text, illegible, ~12 letters] . Non recte Trem. ecce proconsul est in civitate, & fasti dies sunt. rectè vero Boder.ecce proconsul est in urbe, artifices sunt. In Græco est, ἀγοραῖοι ἄγονται, ἐ ἀνθυπατοί εἰσί. ubi primum Syrus invertit ordinem. deinde legit in singulari ἀνθύπατός ἐστι. Tertio, Syro ἀγοραῖοι non sunt forenses conventus ubi jus dicitur, nec forenses judices, nec fasti dies, sed accepit eodem sensu quo capitur Act. 17-4. συνεπλακέμενοι τῶν ἀγοραίων τινὰς ἀνδρὰς πονηρὰς. sunt enim ἀγοραῖοι plebei, qui manu victum quærunt, suaqi manuficia in foro venum exponunt. quæ autem in hac interpretatione mens Syri fuerit, ex Arabica versione clarius liquet, quæ habet [Arabic text, illegible, ~8 letters], & ecce judex est in civitate, tantummodo illi operarii sunt. Id est, peccarunt Demetrius ejusque sodales, quod adversus hos viros tantas turbas dederint. si quid enim deliquerunt, non ipsorum est hîc jus dicere, quippe qui operarii tantum sint & artifices. proconsul est in civitate, ad quem hoc pertinet. Eo sensu ἀγοραῖοι ἄγονται vertendum esset, circumforanei vel forenses habentur. nam ut Latinis duco, sic & ἄγω Græcis aliquando pro existimo, habeo usurpatur. ut ἄγω ὑμᾶς ἐν ἴσῃ τιμῇ, habeo vos in pari honore. ἀξῶ ὀδαμῶς μείζονας ὑμῶν, nullos habebo majores vobis.
units.tr: VERS. 38. [Hebrew and Arabic text, illegible]. Tremellius is wrong: "Behold, there is a proconsul in the city, and there are court days." Boderianus is right: "Behold, there is a proconsul in the city; there are craftsmen." The Greek is ἀγοραῖοι ἄγονται, ἀνθύπατοί εἰσί, where the Syriac first reverses the order, and then reads the verb in the singular, "there is a proconsul." Third, the Syriac word for ἀγοραῖοι does not mean the courts where law is pronounced, nor court judges, nor court days, but is taken in the same sense as at Acts 17:5, συναγαγόντες τῶν ἀγοραίων τινὰς ἀνδρας πονηρούς, "gathering some lewd fellows of the baser sort." For ἀγοραῖοι are the common people, who seek their living by manual work and sell their handiwork in the market. What the Syriac meant by this rendering is clearer from the Arabic version, which reads [illegible]: "and behold, there is a judge in the city; only those workmen are there." That is, Demetrius and his fellows did wrong in stirring up such great disturbance against these men. For if they had committed any offence, it is not for these men, who are only workers and craftsmen, to pronounce judgement here. "There is a proconsul in the city" to whom this belongs. In this sense ἀγοραῖοι ἄγονται should be rendered "they are regarded as the rabble, or as men of the market." For, as in Latin duco, so the Greek ἄγω is sometimes used for "I think, I hold." Thus ἄγω ὑμᾶς ἐν ἴσῃ τιμῇ means "I hold you in equal honour," and ἀξῶ οὐδαμῶς μείζονας ὑμῶν means "I will hold no one greater than you."

units.la: VERS. 40. Possimus reddere rationem τῆς συστροφῆς ταύτης, Vulg. Eras. & Beza, concursus hujus. Arabs bene [Arabic word, illegible], seditio. tumultuarium enim & seditiosum concursum significat. ut συστρέφειν est συναλιχῶς συνάγειν, populum factiosè cogere: sic συςροφὴ est factiosus cætus. Hezychius reddit, ἰλιγξ ὕδατ@, σχολασμὸς, vortex, obtenebratio. ubi per obtenebrationem intelligo capitis vertiginem, quæ spirituum in cerebro tumultuantium ac sursum deorsum conversorum ac convolutorum vortex quidam est, tenebras oculis inducens. ita se habet יערות דבש, examen apum, quod propterea συςροφὴ μελισσῶν, LXX Interpretibus dicitur Jud. 14.8. nec aliter se habet συςροφὴ ἓ λαῶν. seditiosa coitio populi. LXX etiam pro רגש, conjuratione utuntur. 2 Reg. 15. 15. Amos 7. 10. & alibi. sic verti potest Ps. 64. 3. σκέπασόν με ἀπὸ συςροφῆς πονηρευομένων, protege me à conjuratione maleficorum. Suidas vult, intelligi ibi τὸν ὄχλον καὶ συμφωνίαν. in Hebraeo est, סוד, à concilio, vel à consilio. concilia enim & consilia improborum factiosa sunt & conjuratoria.
units.tr: VERS. 40. "We are in danger of being called in question for this uproar [τῆς συστροφῆς ταύτης]," so the Vulgate, Erasmus and Beza: "for this concourse." The Arab rightly has [Arabic word, illegible], "sedition." For it signifies a tumultuous and seditious assembly. As συστρέφειν is to gather together in a factious way, to muster the people in a faction, so συστροφή is a factious gathering. Hesychius gives it as "whirlpool, dizziness, vortex, darkening." By "darkening" I understand the dizziness of the head, which is a kind of whirl of spirits stirring in the brain, turned and rolled up and down, bringing darkness before the eyes. So the Hebrew יערות דבש [yaʿărôt debash], "a swarm of bees," is called συστροφὴ μελισσῶν by the Seventy at Judg. 14:8. Nor is συστροφὴ λαῶν, "a seditious gathering of the people," any different. The Seventy also use "conspiracy" for the Hebrew רגש [rgsh] at 2 Kings 15:15, Amos 7:10 and elsewhere. So it may be rendered at Ps. 64:3, "σκέπασόν με ἀπὸ συστροφῆς πονηρευομένων," "protect me from the conspiracy of evildoers." Suidas wishes this to be understood as "the crowd and agreement." In the Hebrew it is סוד [sôd], "from the council" or "from the counsel." For the councils and counsels of the wicked are factious and conspiratorial.

units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: VERS. 4. Ἀχεὶ ᵻ Ἀσίας. Vulgatus, Arabs & Æthiop. non legerunt. Σώπατρος. Arabs Sosipatrus. Quod autem Vulgatus addit Pyrrhi, Syrus, Arabs, & Æthiop. non legerunt. Et in fine versus post ᵻ Τιμόθεος, Syrus & Arabs addunt, qui erat ex Lystra.
units.tr: VERSE 4. Asia [Ἀσίας]. The Vulgate, the Arabic and the Ethiopic did not read this. Sopater [Σώπατρος]. The Arabic has Sosipatrus. The Vulgate adds of Pyrrhus, but the Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic did not read this. At the end of the verse, the Syriac and Arabic add after Timothy the words who was from Lystra.

units.la: VERS. 7. Τῆ κλάσει ἄρτον. Syrus [Syriac text], ut frangeremus eucharistiam. Arabs [Arabic text], ut distribueremus corpus Christi. Æthiopicus [Ethiopic text], ad benedicendum mensæ. omnes de S. Coena intellexerunt.
units.tr: VERSE 7. To break bread [Τῆ κλάσει ἄρτον]. The Syriac has "that we might break the eucharist." The Arabic has "that we might distribute the body of Christ." The Ethiopic has "for blessing the table." All of them understood this of the Holy Supper.

units.la: VERS. 8. οὗ ἦσαν συνηγμένοι. ubi erant congregati. sic & Æthiopicus. At Vulg. Syrus & Arabs, ubi eramus congregati.
units.tr: VERSE 8. Where they were gathered [οὗ ἦσαν συνηγμένοι]. The Ethiopic also has this. But the Vulgate, the Syriac and the Arabic have "where we were gathered."

units.la: VERS. 9. Ἀπὸ ᵻ τρικλίνων. Syrus [Syriac text], ex tribus contignationibus, id est, à tertia contignatione. Moneo tantum, male à Boderiano legi מדירים. lege, מדירים. quod manifesto liquet ex secunda vocali sub Mem. Ferrarius [Syriac text]. ﬠ ... contignatio superior, tabulatum, cænaculum. sic Pf. 104. 3. ... fecit in aquis cænacula sua, הַמְּקֵרֶה בַּמַּיִם עֲלִיּוֹתָיו.
units.tr: VERSE 9. From the three-storeyed rooms [Ἀπὸ τῶν τρικλίνων]. The Syriac means "from three storeys", that is, from the third storey. I only note that Boderianus wrongly read the Hebrew word as מדירים; it should be read as מדירים with the vowel, as is clear from the second vowel under the Mem. Ferrarius gives the sense "upper storey, floor, upper room." So Psalm 104:3: "who lays the beams of his chambers in the waters" [הַמְּקֵרֶה בַּמַּיִם עֲלִיּוֹתָיו].

units.la: VERS. 11. Οὕτως ἐξῆλθεν. ita exiit. ἵτως interdum non similitudinis esse particulam, sed quæ consequens antecedenti subjungat, diximus supra c. 7. 8. & Joan. 4. 6. Syrus & Arabs hic vertunt tum. nec aliter בֵּן usurpatur Pf. 61. 9. בֵּן אֹמְרָה שְׁמֶךָ, LXX, ἵτως ψαλῶ τῷ ὀνόματί σου. sic, id est, tum, quum res se sic habebit, canam nomini tuo. Porro quum Paulus hic dicitur exire, sensus est, eum pedestri itinere profectum esse, cæteris navi iturjs, ut ex γ′ f.13. apparet. quamobrem Syrus & Arabs, explicationis gratia, verterunt, tunc exiit utrèret per aridam, id est, terrâ.
units.tr: VERSE 11. So he departed [Οὕτως ἐξῆλθεν]. I have said above, at Acts 7:8 and John 4:6, that ἵτως is sometimes not a particle of comparison but one that attaches what follows to what has gone before. The Syriac and Arabic translate it here as "then." So too בֵּן is used in Psalm 61:9, "so will I sing to your name" [בֵּן אֹמְרָה שְׁמֶךָ], where the LXX have "so will I sing to your name" [ἵτως ψαλῶ τῷ ὀνόματί σου]. That is, "then, when things are so, I will sing to your name." Moreover, since Paul is said here to have departed, the sense is that he set out on foot while the others went by ship, as appears from verse 13. For this reason the Syriac and Arabic, to make the sense clear, rendered it "then he departed to go by land", that is, overland.

units.la: VERS. 13. Ἀνήχθημεν εἰς τὴν Ἄσσον. Syrus ... Trem. & Boder. in Parif. & iter fecimus ad cœtum Thesus. In Reg. ad congregationem Thesus. respexerunt Hebr. נִיעַ, congregari, convenire. unde est קְהִלָּה congregatio, cætus. & apud Rabbinos idem. בֵּית הַוַּעַד, domus conventus, schola, synagoga. at id hoc loco non habet locum. verte, & navigavimus ad portum Thesos. Habemus enim ex Gloss. Syro-Arab. ... significare ..., λιμένα, Arabicè ..., portum. ... Arab. ..., & pactum. sic quoque Ferrarius, ..., portus, refugium, pactum. Explicat ergo Syrus, urbem Asson fuisse maritimam, aptumque portum navibus. Plin. lib.5. cap.30. in litore Troadis eam collocat, eandemque Apolloniam quoque dici ait. Strabo lib. 13. tradit, qua parte mare spectat, esse natura ac arte munitissimam. Annotavit autem D. Beza, pro Ἄσσον quædam exemplaria legere Θάσσον. talé fuit quo Syrus noster est usus. At Arabs & Æthiopicus legerunt Ἄσσον.
units.tr: VERSE 13. We sailed to Assos [Ἀνήχθημεν εἰς τὴν Ἄσσον]. The Syriac, as in Tremellius and Boderianus in Paris, has "and we made the journey to the assembly of Thesus." The Regius has "to the congregation of Thesus." They looked to the Hebrew verb meaning "to gather, to come together", from which comes קְהִלָּה "congregation, assembly." Among the rabbis the same idea appears in בֵּית הַוַּעַד "house of assembly, school, synagogue." But that has no place here. Translate instead "and we sailed to the harbour of Thesos." The Syro-Arabic glossary gives the sense of the Greek λιμένα "harbour," and in Arabic "port" and also "covenant." Ferrarius likewise gives "port, refuge, agreement." So the Syriac explains that the city Asson was on the coast and had a harbour suitable for ships. Pliny (book 5, chapter 30) places it on the shore of the Troad and says it was also called Apollonia. Strabo (book 13) relates that on the side facing the sea it was very strongly fortified by nature and by art. Beza noted that some copies read Θάσσον [Thasson] instead of Ἄσσον, and this is the reading our Syriac followed. But the Arabic and Ethiopic read Ἄσσον.

units.la: VERS. 16. Festinabat, si fieri posset, τῷ ἡμέρᾳ τῆς Πεντηκοστῆς ἡμέρᾳ ὡς ἱεροσόλυμα. Vulg. Syr. & Arabs, ut diem Pentecostes faceret Ierosolymis. videntur pro ἡμέρᾳ legisse ὡσιαν. de qua phrasi vide supra Act. 15.33. & 18.23. & Mat.20.12.
units.tr: VERSE 16. He hastened, if it were possible, to be at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost [τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῆς Πεντηκοστῆς ἡμέρᾳ ὡς ἱεροσόλυμα]. The Vulgate, Syriac and Arabic have "that he might keep Pentecost at Jerusalem." They seem to have read ὡσιαν instead of ἡμέρᾳ. On this phrase see above at Acts 15:33, 18:23, and Matthew 20:12.

units.la: VERS. 18. Ὡς ἡ παρεγένοντο πρὸς αὐτὸν. quum autem venissent ad eum. Vulgatus addit, & simul essent. quod Syrus, Arabs, & Æthiopicus non agnoverunt.
units.tr: VERSE 18. When they had come to him [Ὡς δὲ παρεγένοντο πρὸς αὐτόν]. The Vulgate adds "and were together", which the Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic did not recognise.

units.la: VERS. 20. Δημοσίᾳ ἕκαστ' οἴκας. Eras. publicè & per singulas domos. Beza, & domatim. Malim cum Vulgato, & per domos. sive ut habent Syrus & Arabs & in domibus, id est privatim. nulla hic distributio indicatur, sed publicè & privatim opponuntur. vide quæ supra diximus, Act. 2.46. Æthiopicus rectè ܒܒܝܬ ܐܢܫܐ, foris & intus.
units.tr: VERSE 20. Publicly and from house to house [δημοσίᾳ ἕκαστ' οἴκας]. Erasmus has "publicly and through single houses", and Beza "and from house to house." I would prefer, with the Vulgate, "and through the houses", or as the Syriac and Arabic have it, "and in houses", that is, privately. No distribution is indicated here; rather "publicly" and "privately" are set against each other. See what I said above at Acts 2:46. The Ethiopic rightly has "outside and inside."

units.la: VERS. 21. Testans Iudaeis [Syriac] & Gentilibus. annotat hic F. Junius, Syr. & Aramæis, id est, Syris, pro eo quod est gentibus, σνγεξθνικῶς. at vero [Syriac], ut hoc loco legendum, non sunt Syri. tum enim scribitur [Syriac]. vide Luc. 4. 27. [Syriac]. Ethnicum denotat, & non usurpatur nisi oppositè ad Judæos, ut & [Syriac], gentiliter Gal. 2.14. [Syriac] autem est Syriacè.Neque tamen inficior illud ex hoc esse natum.Quum enim populus Judæorum in Babylonia degeret, inter Chaldæos, qui & Aramæi dicebantur, ipsorumque lingua Aramæa, unde Dan. 2. 4. dicuntur Regem allocuti [Hebrew] Aramæ,adeoq; populi Chaldæae aut Aramæi tum essent aut Judæi, factum ut præ cæteris gentibus hi Judæis opponerentur, quumque quis Aramæus diceretur, gentilis sive Ethnicus intelligeretur, qui non esset è populo Judaico. Deinde vero discriminis causa, [Syriac] dictus qui natione esset Syrus, [Syriac] autem qui origine & religione ethnicus, quam vocem & Æthiopicus passim pro ἐΓΛΛω usurpat.
units.tr: VERSE 21. Testifying to Jews and Gentiles. F. Junius notes here that the Syriac means "Syrians" or "Aramaeans" in place of "Gentiles" (ἐθνικῶς). But the word in the Syriac text, as it should be read here, does not mean Syrians; otherwise it would be written differently. See Luke 4:27. The word denotes "Gentile" and is used only in contrast to Jews, as also the adverb "in the manner of Gentiles" in Galatians 2:14. The word for "in Syriac" is different. I do not deny, however, that the one meaning arose from the other. When the Jewish people lived in Babylon among the Chaldeans, who were also called Aramaeans, and whose language was Aramaic, they are said in Daniel 2:4 to have addressed the king in Aramaic [אֲרָמִית]. So the people of Chaldea or the Aramaeans were either Jews, and for this reason the Jews were set against them before the other nations; and when someone was called an Aramaean he was understood to be a Gentile, that is, one not of the Jewish people. Later, however, for the sake of distinction, the term was used for one who was a Syrian by nation, while the word for one who was Gentile by origin and religion is also used by the Ethiopic everywhere for the Greek Hellene [Ἕλλην].

units.la: V E R S. 24. Vt peragam cursum meum μετὰ χαρᾶς cum gaudio. Syrus, Arabs, Æthiop. & Vulgatus non legerunt μετὰ χαρᾶς. Omnia tamen Græca nostra exemplaria, ut & Chrysostomus legunt.
units.tr: VERSE 24. That I may finish my course with joy [μετὰ χαρᾶς]. The Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopic and Vulgate did not read "with joy." Yet all our Greek copies read it, as did Chrysostom.

units.la: V E R S. 28. Spiritus S. constituit vos Episcopos. Æthiopicus pro Ἐπισκόπους habet ܐܦܣܩܘܦܐ, quod plur. est à singul. ܐܦܣܩܘܦܐ, episcopus. quod proculdubio corruptum est è Græco, sicut apud Arabes ܐܦܣܩܘܦ pro Ἀλεξάνδρε. omissis enim quatuor literis, & priori p juncto posteriori, ex Ἐπισκοπῷ fit ܐܦܩܘ. estque hoc ipsum quod Angli dicunt pope, Muscovitæ pop, Latini papa, non tantum de summo Pontifice, sed & de omnibus pastoribus atque inspectoribus Ecclesiæ, quos Belgicè Papen dicimus.
units.tr: VERSE 28. The Holy Spirit has made you bishops. The Ethiopic, for Ἐπισκόπους, has a word which is the plural of the singular "bishop." It is without doubt corrupted from the Greek, just as among the Arabs the word for "Alexander" is corrupted. For when four letters are dropped and the earlier p is joined to the later, Ἐπισκοπῷ becomes a shorter form. This is the very word that the English call "pope", the Muscovites "pop", and the Latins "papa", and it refers not only to the supreme Pontiff but also to all the pastors and overseers of the Church, whom we in Dutch call Papen.

units.la: V E R S. 29. Μετὰ τὴν ἀφίξιν μου, post discessum meum. Notat Cl. Beza, novam esse significationem, quum ἀφίξις, adventum declaret. Generalius tamen in Glossar. redditur ἀφίξις, adventus, profectio. hinc verte, post profectionem meam. sicut apud Demosthenem, ἀφίξιν εἰς Σικυῶνα πλεμίας ἐποιήσατο, profectionem in hostes instituit. nec diverso sensu Gen. 38. 1. pro ויט ער איש שלמי, declinavit ad virum Adullamitam, LXX habent, ἀφίκετο εἰς ἄνθρωπον &c.
units.tr: VERSE 29. After my departure [Μετὰ τὴν ἀφίξιν μου]. Beza notes that this is a new meaning, since ἀφίξις denotes "arrival." But in the Glossary ἀφίξις is rendered more generally as "arrival, departure." So translate "after my departure", as in Demosthenes, where ἀφίξιν εἰς Σικυῶνα πλεμίας ἐποιήσατο means "he set out on an expedition against the enemy." The sense is no different in Genesis 38:1, where for "he turned aside to the Adullamite man" the LXX have "he came to a man" and so on.

units.la: V E R S. 32. Τῷ Θεῷ Ϲ τῷ λόγῳ τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ, τῷ δυναμένῳ ἐποικοδομῆσαι &c. Erasmus, Syr. & Arabs construxerunt τῷ δυναμένῳ cum propinquiori λόγῳ. Vulgatus & Beza cum remotiori Θεῷ. utrumque consistere potest. & quocunque modo construatur, Deus & verbum ejus hîc concurrunt. verbum gratiæ à Deo ædificat, & Deus per verbum.
units.tr: VERSE 32. To God and the word of his grace, which is able to build up [Τῷ Θεῷ καὶ τῷ λόγῳ τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ, τῷ δυναμένῳ ἐποικοδομῆσαι]. Erasmus, the Syriac and the Arabic construe "which is able" with the nearer word, "word." The Vulgate and Beza construe it with the more remote word, "God." Both are possible. However it is construed, God and his word meet here: the word of grace builds up, from God, and God builds up through the word.

units.la: V E R S. 35. Μνημονεύειν τῶν λόγων τοῦ Κυρίου. Syrus, ܕܡܚܝ ܠܝ ܡܢ ܒܗ ܕܐܡܪ ܝܗܘܢܘ. Trem. & Beder. & meminisse verborum Domini nostri. Id nisi fallor in Kal dicerent ϑοῖ ... ο. at in Aphel transitivum est, ac vertendum, & commonefacere verba Domini nostri. scribendum autem est ὀϑοῖ ... ο.
units.tr: VERSE 35. To remember the words of the Lord [Μνημονεύειν τῶν λόγων τοῦ Κυρίου]. The Syriac has a phrase meaning "that he said." Tremellius and Boderianus have "and to remember the words of our Lord." Unless I am mistaken, they would say this in the Kal, but in the Aphel the verb is transitive and should be rendered "and to remind them of the words of our Lord." The verb should also be written with the correct pointing.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CAP. XXI.

units.la: VERS. 3. Ἀναφανέντες ἡ τῷ Κυπρῳ. Antiquissima haec est & vulgatissima lectio, quam Chrysostomus, Vulgatus & pleraque nostra Graeca exemplaria habent. quia tamen insolens videbatur constructio, nec satis evidens sensus, audaculi quidam immutare eam nonnihil sunt ausi. Hinc duo ex nostris codicibus legunt ἀναφάνειλες, quum aperuissemus vel detexissemus. non satis Grammatice. dicendum enim in aor. 1. fuerat ἀναφλωαλες. in aor. 2 ἀναφανέντες. alii duo codices habent ἀναφανέντ@ ἡ τ' Κύπρε, quum apparuisset Cyprus. solœcismo manifesto. dicendum enim fuerat ἀναφανέντος ἡ τ' Κύπρε. nos antiquiorem lectionem rectam putamus, quae ad verbum sonat, quum autem ostensi essemus Cyprum, id est, ostensa nobis esset Cyprus. sicut πιστεύθηναι τὸ λόγια ἡ Θεῖ, creditii sunt verba Dei, id est, credita sunt ipsis verba Dei. Rom. 3. & πιστεύθηναι τὸ Ευαγγέλιον, pro, creditum est mihi.
units.tr: VERS. 3. "Having appeared at Cyprus" [Ἀναφανέντες ἡ τῷ Κυπρῳ]. This is the oldest and most widely attested reading, found in Chrysostom, the Vulgate, and most of our Greek manuscripts. Because the construction seemed odd and the sense not clear enough, some over-bold men have ventured to alter it somewhat. Two of our manuscripts accordingly read [ἀναφάνειλες], "when we had opened up" or "had sighted". This is not sound grammar: in the first aorist it should have been [ἀναφλωαλες], and in the second aorist [ἀναφανέντες]. Two other manuscripts have [ἀναφανέντ@ ἡ τ' Κύπρε], "when Cyprus had appeared", which is a plain solecism; it should have been [ἀναφανέντος ἡ τ' Κύπρε]. We think the older reading is correct, and it means word for word "when we had been shown Cyprus", that is, "when Cyprus had been shown to us". Compare [πιστεύθηναι τὸ λόγια ἡ Θεῖ], "the words of God were entrusted", that is, "the words of God were entrusted to them" (Rom. 3), and [πιστεύθηναι τὸ Ευαγγέλιον], "the gospel was entrusted to me".

units.la: VERS. 15. Ἀπροσδιασάμενοι. Eraf. sublatis sarcinis. Beza, collectis sarcinis, quasi ἀναπροσδιασάμενοι. Vulgatus, Syr. & Arabs, praeparati, quasi προσπροσδιασάμενοι. Sed & προσπροσδιάζειν significat interdum remotis impedimentis praeparare. hoc sensu LXX Interpretes usurpant pro Hebr. רְפָא, Lev. 14. 36. quod alibi per ἐπιμάζειν reddunt, ut Gen. 24. 31. Esa. 40. 3. Ita hoc loco sensus esse potest, quum sublatis omnibus obstaculis parassemus nos. sed tacendum non est, LXX Interpretibus ἀναπροσδιάζω frequenter usurpari pro רָכַשׁ, supellectile seu substantia quam quis acquisivit, sive apparatu cujusvis rei familiaris. vide Gen. 14. 12, & 15. 14. 2 Paral. 32. 29. & alibi sæpe. hinc χαροκλαύμοι recte vertas, apparatu facto.
units.tr: VERS. 15. "Having made ready" [Ἀπροσδιασάμενοι]. Erasmus has "with the baggage removed" [sublatis sarcinis]. Beza has "with the baggage gathered together", as if the word were [ἀναπροσδιασάμενοι]. The Vulgate, the Syriac and the Arabic have "prepared", as if the word were [προσπροσδιασάμενοι]. But [προσπροσδιάζειν] sometimes means "to prepare after the hindrances have been removed". In this sense the Seventy use it for the Hebrew [רְפָא], Lev. 14:36, which they elsewhere render by [ἐπιμάζειν], as in Gen. 24:31 and Isa. 40:3. So here the sense may be, "when we had removed every obstacle and got ready". But it must not be passed over that the Seventy often use [ἀναπροσδιάζω] for the Hebrew [רָכַשׁ], meaning household goods or property that someone has acquired, or the equipment of any household business. See Gen. 14:12 and 15:14, 2 Chron. 32:29, and often elsewhere. Hence the Greek [χαροκλαύμοι] may rightly be rendered "having made the preparations".

units.la: VERS. 22. Tí οὖν ἐστι; πάντως δεῖ συνελθεῖν. hæc Syrus, Arabs, & Æthiop. non legerunt. Quod sequitur, ἀκούσονται γὰρ ὅτι ἐληλύθασι verterunt, quasi legissent, ἐπειδὴ οὖν ἀκούσονται ὅτι ἐληλύθασι, & conjungunt cum verf. sequenti. Non laudo autem Tremell. qui participium præsens per præteritum vertit, auditum est. malim consueto more per futurum, audietur. sic Arabs. Æthiopicus necesse est ut audiant, id est, non poterunt non audire.
units.tr: VERS. 22. "What then is to be done? They must certainly come together" [Tí οὖν ἐστι; πάντως δεῖ συνελθεῖν]. The Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic did not read this. What follows, "for they will hear that they have come" [ἀκούσονται γὰρ ὅτι ἐληλύθασι], they have rendered as though they had read "since therefore they will hear that they have come", and they join it to the following verse. I do not commend Tremellius, who renders the present participle by a past, "has been heard". I would prefer the usual future, "will be heard", as the Arabic does. The Ethiopic has "it is necessary that they hear", that is, they will not be able not to hear.

units.la: VERS. 24. Ἀλλὰ φυλάσσων ἐκ τῆς τοῦ νόμου φυλάσσων. Syrus [Syriac], Trem. tuque legem perficias & serves, Boder. teque legem adimplere & confervare. Nunquam [Syriac] in Kal sumitur transitive, sed intransit. compleri, absolvi, expirare. item concordare, consentire. posterior significatio est hujus loci, & tu legi consentis, & observas. quod Arabs dixit [Arabic], & tu consentis legi, observans eam. quod idem valet atque Græca, incedis & ipse legem observans. sic cap. 22. 10. [Syriac]. Trem. & complebam. Boder. & adimplebam voluntatem eorum. verte, & consentiebam voluntati eorum.
units.tr: VERS. 24. "But keeping the law" [Ἀλλὰ φυλάσσων ἐκ τῆς τοῦ νόμου φυλάσσων]. The Syriac, Tremellius has "and you may fulfil and keep the law", and Beza has "and that you keep and observe the law". The Syriac verb is never used transitively in the Kal, but intransitively: "to be completed, finished, come to an end", and likewise "to agree, consent". The second meaning fits this place: "you consent to the law and observe it". The Arabic says "you consent to the law, observing it", which means the same as the Greek, "you walk yourself also observing the law". So also in chapter 22:10. Tremellius has "and I fulfilled", and Beza "and I fulfilled their will". Translate it "and I consented to their will".

units.la: VERS. 34. Ἄλλοι δὲ ἄλλο τι ἔκραζον ἐν τῷ ὄχλῳ. Syrus, [Syriac]. Trem. & clamabant adversus eum homines è turba quisque aliquid. Boder. in Reg. alii aliud. In Parif. ad verbum aliquid aliquid, id est, varium quid, nunc hoc nunc illud. sicut Act. 25. 19. [Syriac], quæstiones autem varia. Sæpe enim repetitio illa varietatem
units.tr: VERS. 34. "Some cried one thing and some another in the crowd" [Ἄλλοι δὲ ἄλλο τι ἔκραζον ἐν τῷ ὄχλῳ]. The Syriac has the same. Tremellius has "and men in the crowd each cried out something against him". Beza in the Regius edition has "some one thing, others another". In the Paris edition the Greek is rendered word for word as "something something", that is, something varied, now this, now that. Compare Acts 25:19, where the Greek has "questions of various kinds". Such repetition often denotes variety.

units.la: A a denotat. ut [Hebrew/Arabic-script words] varиis linguis. [Arabic-script words] , varii homines. alibi universalitatem.
units.tr: A a denotes this: as in the Hebrew phrase meaning "in various languages", and the Arabic phrase meaning "various men". Elsewhere it denotes universality.

units.la: I B I D. Iussit eum duci iς τὸν παρεμβολὴν. Vulgatus, Erasmus & Beza, in castra. rectè tamen Cl. Beza observat, intelligi arcem Antoniam. malim ergo vertere, in castrum. hæc enim sic differunt, ut in singulari castrum sit locus muris munitus, alias castellum vel arx dictus. in plur. autem castra, locus in quo milites tentoria fixere, vel ipsa tentoria in quibus milites diversantur. utrumque παρεμβολὴ significat. Glossarium παρεμβολὴ, phalanx, castrum. Hezychius, παρεμ-βολὴ, τεγκὴ πλῆθος, ὀλιγὴ πλῆξις, ὑφ᾽ τεγκὰς ἢ ἀληθῶν, ἢ οἰκήσης, ἢ κώμης, castra, acies, cuneus, exercitus aut multitudo, aut habitaculum, aut castrum. Sic Esa. 21. 8. pro [Hebrew text] LXX habent, [Greek text] idem est quod eodem versu, [Hebrew text], in specula ego sto. intelligitur castrum, arx, locus editus & munitus, ubi quis tutò hostes speculatur & observat. talis παρεμβολὴ fuit arx Antonia, ad quam per ἀναβαθμὸς, gradus, de quibus ff. sequenti, & 40. Paulo ascendendum fuit, quia in edito erat collocata.
units.tr: IBID. "He commanded him to be led into the barracks" [Iussit eum duci εἰς τὴν παρεμβολήν]. The Vulgate, Erasmus and Beza have "into the camp". Yet Beza rightly observes that the Antonia fortress is meant. I would therefore prefer to render it "into the fortress". The two words differ in this way: in the singular, "castrum" means a place fortified with walls, otherwise called a castle or citadel; in the plural, "castra" means the place where soldiers have pitched their tents, or the tents themselves in which soldiers lodge. [Παρεμβολή] means both. The Glossary gives [παρεμβολή] as "phalanx, camp". Hesychius gives [παρεμβολή] as "a band of men, a marching column, a mass, an army or multitude, or a dwelling, or a village, or a fortress". So in Isa. 21:8 the Seventy have [Greek] for the Hebrew, which is the same as the Hebrew in the same verse, "I stand upon the watchtower". Here is meant a fortress, a raised and fortified place from which one can safely watch and observe the enemy. Such a [παρεμβολή] was the Antonia fortress, to which Paul had to go up by the steps, the "gradus" mentioned below in verse 40, because it was built on high ground.

units.la: V E R S. 38. Σικαρίων, Sicariorum. Ægyptius addit, cujus interpretatio est, latronum. quod ex margine irrepsisse, cuivis liquet.
units.tr: VERS. 38. "Of the Sicarii" [Σικαρίων, Sicariorum]. The Egyptian version adds, "whose interpretation is 'of robbers'". Anyone can see that this crept in from a marginal note.

units.la: C A P. XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 22.

units.la: V E R S. 3. Educatus ad pedes Gamalielis. Sedebat enim Magister in loco editiore. At [Hebrew], discipulus dicebatur [Hebrew], prostratus sive jacens in solo, ad pedes magistri. tamdiu dicebatur [Hebrew], parvus, & tempus illud [Hebrew], parvitas. tum erat [Hebrew], juvenis, neque vocabatur nisi nomine patris, ex. gr. [Hebrew] filius Simeonis. At postea [Hebrew], impositionem manuum, qua ad Rabbinatum promovebatur, suo nomine appellabatur, Rabbi David filius Simeonis. hic, dum esset [Hebrew] הבר הרב, socius magistri, non amplius jacebat in solo, at nec sedebat sedente magistro, sed erat משה, inclinatus sive in latus recumbens. At quum factus esset מורה הוראה, doctor legis, vocareturque מורי הרב, doctor noster Rabbi, sedebat quum alios juniores aut imperitiores doceret, at stabat coram alio Rabbi sene.
units.tr: VERS. 3. Brought up at the feet of Gamaliel. For the teacher sat in a higher place, while the disciple was called [talmid], one who lay prostrate or reclining on the ground at the teacher's feet. As long as he was a boy he was called [katan], little, and that period was called [qetanut], littleness. Then he was [na'ar], a youth, and was called only by his father's name, for example [ben Shim'on], son of Simeon. Later, when he was promoted to the rabbinate by the laying on of hands, he was called by his own name, Rabbi David son of Simeon. While he was [chaver harav], a colleague of the teacher, he no longer lay on the ground, but neither did he sit while the teacher sat; he was [mesubb], inclined or reclining on his side. But when he had become [morah horaah], a teacher of the law, and was called [morai harav], our teacher Rabbi, he sat while he taught the younger or less learned, but he stood before another elderly Rabbi.

units.la: I B I D. Πεπαιδευμένος κατὰ ἀκρίβειαν τοῦ πατρῴου νόμου. Vulgatus, eruditus juxta veritatem paterna legis. ἀκριβὴς accepit, sicut apud LXX. Dan. 7. 16. καὶ τῶν ἀκριβῶν ἱστῶν παρ' αὐτοῦ, Chaldaice מרע אלמא, & veritatem quaerebam abeo. est enim קשט, verum, certum, firmum. per ἀληθείαν alibi exponunt, ut Dan. 2. 8. 45. & alibi. Erasmus vertit, quasi scriptum esset, πεπαιδευμένος κατ' ἀκρίβειαν ἐν τῷ πατρῴῳ νόμῳ, institutus accurate in paterna lege. Sic Syrus quoque & Arabs. nisi quod pro accurate dixerunt perfecte. His omnibus praefero Cl. Bezae versionem, institutus ad exquisitam formam patriae legis. ubi per patriam legem non intelligo simpliciter, quam patres à Deo per Mosen acceperant, sed πατρογονικὸν, quam ipsi à patribus acceperant. Pharisaeorum religionem denotat, quae πατρικῆς ἀγωγῆς magnam partem constabat, quarum ζηλωτὴς se fuisse olim ait ad Gal. 1. 14. quumque ἀκριβῶς ei religioni tribuit, idem dicit quod infra Act. 26. 5. κατὰ τὴν ἀκριβεστάτην αἵρεσιν τῆς ἡμετέρας θρησκείας ἔζησα Φαρισαῖος. Sensus ergo est, se institutum fuisse in Pharisaismo, quae accuratissima est patriae legis forma.
units.tr: IBID. Πεπαιδευμένος κατὰ ἀκρίβειαν τοῦ πατρῴου νόμου. The Vulgate: instructed according to the truth of the paternal law. He took ἀκριβής as the Septuagint does, Dan. 7:16: καὶ τῶν ἀκριβῶν ἱστῶν παρ' αὐτοῦ [kai tōn akribōn histōn par' autou], Chaldee [min'ah 'ala'ma], and I sought the truth from him. For the word is [qeshot], true, certain, firm. Elsewhere they render it by ἀλήθεια, as in Dan. 2:8, 45 and elsewhere. Erasmus translated as if the text read πεπαιδευμένος κατ' ἀκρίβειαν ἐν τῷ πατρῴῳ νόμῳ [pepaideumenos kat' akribeian en tō patrōiō nomō], trained accurately in the paternal law. The Syriac and the Arabic do the same, except that for accurately they said perfectly. Of all these I prefer the version of the distinguished Beza: trained to the exact form of the ancestral law. Here I do not understand the ancestral law simply as the law which the fathers received from God through Moses, but as the law πατρογονικόν [patrogonikon], which they themselves had received from their fathers. It denotes the religion of the Pharisees, which consisted largely of the traditions of the fathers, and of which Paul says he was once a zealot, Gal. 1:14. When he ascribes ἀκρίβεια [akribeia] to that religion, he says the same thing as below, Acts 26:5: κατὰ τὴν ἀκριβεστάτην αἵρεσιν τῆς ἡμετέρας θρησκείας ἔζησα Φαρισαῖος [kata tēn akribestatēn hairesin tēs hēmeteras thrēskeias ezēsa Pharisaios]. The sense therefore is that he had been trained in Pharisaism, which is the most exact form of the ancestral law.

units.la: Addit, zelo accensus & Θεοῦ Dei. Sic Syrus, Arabs & Aethiopicus quoque legerunt. sic Chrysostomus, & omnia Graeca exemplaria quaevidere contigit. itaque non est germana habenda lectio Vulgati, qui legis habet. ζηλωτὴς Θεοῦ se fuisse ait Paulus, eodem sensu quo de Judaeis dicit Rom. 10. 2. μαρτυρῶ γὰρ αὐτοῖς ὅτι ζῆλον Θεοῦ ἔχουσι.
units.tr: He adds, zealous and for God. So the Syriac, the Arabic and the Ethiopic also read. So Chrysostom reads, and so do all the Greek manuscripts I have been able to see. Therefore the reading of the Vulgate, which has of the law, should not be regarded as genuine. Paul says he was a zealot of God, in the same sense in which he says of the Jews, Rom. 10:2: μαρτυρῶ γὰρ αὐτοῖς ὅτι ζῆλον Θεοῦ ἔχουσι [martyrō gar autois hoti zēlon Theou echousi], for I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God.

units.la: V E R S. 5. A quibus etiam literis acceptis &c. Aethiopicus explicat cujusmodi fuerint literae, כתבה, litera potestatis, quibus nempe senatus eum potestate sua & authoritate muniebat.
units.tr: VERS. 5. And from whom also, having received letters, etc. The Ethiopic explains what kind of letters they were: [ktbh], a letter of authority, by which the council confirmed him with its power and authority.

units.la: VERS. 9. Καὶ ἐμφοβοι ἐγὼ... Æthiopicus legit.
units.tr: VERS. 9. Καὶ ἐμφοβοι ἐγὼ... [Kai emphoboi ego...]. The Ethiopic reads it so.

units.la: VERS. 10. Ὢν τί ποιῆσαι σοι ποιῆσαι. Vulg. quae oportet te facere. Eras. quae ordinata sunt tibi ut facias. Beza, quae constitutum est tibi ut facias. Syrus, quod jubetur tibi ut facias. τάσσω interdum pro ἐντέλλομαι mando, jubeo. ut Matt. 28. 16. non male ergo vertas quae jussa sunt tibi ut facias. Deus enim jusserat Ananiae, quae ipse jussurus esset Paulo. & haec jussa facienda erant Paulo.
units.tr: VERS. 10. Ὢν τί ποιῆσαι σοι ποιῆσαι [Hōn ti poiēsai soi poiēsai]. The Vulgate: what it behoves you to do. Erasmus: what has been ordered for you to do. Beza: what has been appointed for you to do. The Syriac: what is commanded you to do. τάσσω [tassō] sometimes means ἐντέλλομαι [entellomai], to command or order, as in Matt. 28:16. So it is not wrong to translate: what has been commanded you to do. For God had commanded Ananias what he himself was about to command Paul, and these commands were to be carried out by Paul.

units.la: VERS. 14. Deus patrum nostrorum προεχειρίσατό σε γνῶναι &c. Vulg. praeordinavit te. Erasmus, praeparavit te. Beza, designavit te. Syrus, Arabs & Æthiop. constituit te. non gravate verto, sumsit te ut cognoscas voluntatem ejus. proprie enim προχειρίζεσθαι est pra manibus sumere id quo uti velis, sive ad rem, sive ad personam referatur. hinc pro ṇḥ, capere, sumere, recte usurpatur. Josh. 3. 12. קחו לכם שני אנשים, sumite vobis 12 viros. LXX, προχειρισάμενος ὑμῖν δώδεκα ἀνδρας. sic 2 Machab. 3. 7. ὁ δὲ προχειρισάμενος Ἡλιόδωρον τὸν ταμίαν τῶν χρημάτων, ἀπέστειλε &c. hic autem sumens Heliodorum aerarii praefectum, misit eum &c. eodem modo cap. 8. 9.
units.tr: VERS. 14. The God of our fathers προεχειρίσατό σε γνῶναι [proecheirisato se gnōnai], etc. The Vulgate: has predestined you. Erasmus: has prepared you. Beza: has designated you. The Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic: has appointed you. I do not hesitate to render it: has taken you up, that you may know his will. For προχειρίζεσθαι [procheirizesthai] properly means to take into one's hands what one wishes to use, whether the reference is to a thing or to a person. Hence it is rightly used for [laqach], to take, to grasp. Josh. 3:12: [qachu lakhem sheneh anashim], take for yourselves twelve men. The Septuagint: προχειρισάμενος ὑμῖν δώδεκα ἄνδρας [procheirisamenos hymin dōdeka andras]. So 2 Macc. 3:7: ὁ δὲ προχειρισάμενος Ἡλιόδωρον τὸν ταμίαν τῶν χρημάτων, ἀπέστειλε κτλ. [ho de procheirisamenos Hēliodōron ton tamian tōn chrēmatōn apesteilen ktl.], and he, taking Heliodorus, the treasurer, sent him, etc. In the same way in chapter 8:9.

units.la: VERS. 22. Ἡκουσον ὃ αὐτὸς ἀκεῖ τῆς τοῦ λόγου. Æthiopicus, & audivi eum sic loquentem mihi. ἤκουσον accepit pro prima singul. atque αὐτὸς ad Deum retulit. alii Interpretes longe melius ἤκουσον acceperunt pro 3 plurali, & αὐτὸς ad Paulum retulerunt.
units.tr: VERS. 22. Ἤκουσον ὃ αὐτὸς ἀκεῖ τῆς τοῦ λόγου [Ēkouson ho autos akei tēs tou logou]. The Ethiopic: and I heard him speaking thus to me. It took ἤκουσον as the first person singular and referred αὐτὸς to God. Other interpreters, much better, took ἤκουσον as the third person plural and referred αὐτὸς to Paul.

units.la: VERS. 25. Ὡς ἢ προεῖταναι αὐτὸν τῆς ἰμᾶσιν &c. Beza, quum autem eum distendissent loris caedendum. ubi loris construit, non cum distendissent, sed cum subaudito caedendum, ut significari sciamus per ἰμάντας, non vincula quibus adstringeretur verberandus, sed taureas scuticas quibus caederetur. Dura illa est & insolens constructio. rectius reliqui interpretes intellexerunt vincula quibus adstringeretur verberandus. In Talmud lib. מכות, cap. 3. in Mifna, ubi ritus describuntur, erga flagellandum usurpandi, legitur, כתר פלקין אותו׳ כופת כתי ידיו על העמוד היליך ואילך quomodo flagellatur ille? ligantur amba manus ejus ad columnam hinc inde. ubi columnam, & alligationem ad eam non oportet ex noftratium ritu, quo fures publicè flagellantur, concipere. columna ifta erat lignum terræ infixum, altitudinis fefquicubiti, ut reus ipfi incumbere poffet inclinatus. fic enim habet Mifna, ואינו מכה אותו לא עומד ולא יושב אלא מוטה שנאמר והפיל הושמט id eft, neque percutiet eum minifter aut ftantem aut fedentem, fed inclinatum. quia fcriptum eft Deut. 25. 2. profternet illum judex. & ut ita pofitum aptius cæderet lictor, האכן נתתה מאחרי חן הכונסת שמר עלי lapis pofitus erat poft reum, in quo minifter fynagoga ftabat. ob hunc ritum dixit fortaffis Lucas ἐπεὶ πέτραν αὐτῷ, ut præpofitio ἐπί indicet, cum fic fuiffe tenfum, ut fuperiori corporis parte pronus columnæ incumberet. Arabs alium videtur ritum refpexiffe, etiamnum Orientalibus ufitatum, apud quos reus proftratus ita extenditur, ut utrinque lictores caput & pedes contineant, ne ictus flagellantis evadere aut declinare poffit. hinc vertit, وابلـ ... & quum extendiffent ipfum inter lictores, quorum nempe alii ad caput, alii ad pedes reum loris continerent. nec inde abluditÆthiopicus, וכ אסירומ כחנו אתרו, & quum vincto eo traheren pedes ejus.
units.tr: VERS. 25. "As they stretched him out with the thongs" (ὡς δὲ προέτειναν αὐτὸν τοῖς ἱμᾶσιν). Beza renders it: "when they had stretched him out with thongs to be beaten." Here Beza construes "with thongs" not with "stretched" but with the understood "to be beaten", so that by "thongs" we are to understand not the bonds by which the man to be beaten was tied, but the leather scourges with which he was beaten. That construction is harsh and unusual. The other translators have rightly understood the thongs as the bonds by which the man to be beaten was fastened. In the Talmud, tractate Makkoth, chapter 3, in the Mishnah where the rites of flogging are described, we read: כיצד מלקין אותו? קושרין שתי ידיו על העמוד מכאן ומכאן [how is he flogged? His two hands are bound to the column on either side]. Here we should not picture the column and the binding to it as in our own custom, by which thieves are flogged in public. That column was a piece of wood fixed in the ground, about a cubit and a half high, so that the guilty man could lean forward on it. The Mishnah says so: ואינו מכה אותו לא עומד ולא יושב אלא מוטה, שנאמר והפילו השופט [the minister does not strike him either standing or sitting, but while he is bent over, as it is written: "the judge shall cause him to lie down", Deut. 25.2]. So that the lictor could strike more conveniently when the man was placed in this way, there was a stone set behind the guilty man, on which the minister of the synagogue stood (האבן הזאת נתונה מאחורי החייב, והשמש עומד עליה). Perhaps for this reason Luke wrote ἐπὶ πέτραν αὐτῷ, the preposition ἐπί showing that the man was so stretched that his upper body lay prone upon the column. The Arab seems to have had in mind another custom, still in use among the Orientals, in which the guilty man is stretched out flat, with lictors on each side holding his head and feet, so that he cannot escape or dodge the blows of the one beating him. Hence he translates: wa-lamma madadūhu bayna al-lāḥinīn [and when they had stretched him out between the lictors], meaning that some of them held the man's head and others his feet with the thongs. The Ethiopic version is not far from this: וכ אסירומ כחנו אתרו [and when they had bound him, they dragged his feet].

units.la: VERS. 28. Ἐγὼ προῖκα κεφαλαίω, ego multa fumma civitatem hanc emi.
units.tr: VERS. 28. Ἐγὼ προῖκα κεφαλαίῳ [Egō polloū kephalaiō], I bought this city for a great sum.

units.la: Nqvè, inquit Cl. Beza. nec enim κεφάλαιον in re nummaria, fed in oratione pro fumma dici confuevit. At inquam, de numero proprie dicitur, quando plures numeri in unam fummam contrahuntur, quæ ראש, caput Hebræis dicitur. unde LXX Num. 4. 2. ἀνάξει τὸ κεφάλαιον τῶν υἱῶν Καὰθ, cape fummam filiorum Caath. fic c. 5. 7. & 31. 26. quid ni ergo & de multis nummis in unam fummam collectis ufitatè dicatur? Glofsariùm, κεφάλαιον, ἀπὸ δαπάνης. fors, summa. Vult, in usura sortem quae usurae exponitur, quam ṗ Hebraei vocant, κεφάλαιον dici.
units.tr: No, says the distinguished Beza. For κεφάλαιον [kephalaion] is not commonly used of money but of a sum in speech. But I say that it is properly used of number, when several numbers are gathered into one sum, which the Hebrews call [rosh], head. Hence the Septuagint, Num. 4:2: ἀνάξει τὸ κεφάλαιον τῶν υἱῶν Καὰθ [anaxei to kephalaion tōn huiōn Kaath], take the sum of the sons of Kohath. So also in chapters 5:7 and 31:26. Why, then, should it not be commonly said of many coins collected into one sum? The glossary has κεφάλαιον, ἀπὸ δαπάνης [apo dapanēs], perhaps, sum. He means that in usury the principal which is exacted as interest, which the Hebrews call [ribbit], is called κεφάλαιον.

units.la: VERS. 30. Volens scire τὴν ἀσφαλείᾳ certum. Annotat Cl. Beza, nove id dici pro τὴν ἀληθείας. Reperio tamen etiam in lib. Sap. Salom. c. 18. 6. ἵνα ἀσφαλῶς εἰδῶσι οἷς ἐπίστευσαν ὅρκοις, ἐπιγνόντες, ut vere, vel certo, scientes quibus credidissent iuramentis, bono esset animo. Sic ἀσφαλῶς supra quoque usurpatum fuit, Act. cap. 2: 36. & τὴν ἀσφαλείς supra cap. 21.34. & infra c. 25.26, & ἀσφάλεια pro certitudine, aut certa veritate, Luc. 1. 4.
units.tr: VERS. 30. Wishing to know the certainty τὴν ἀσφάλειαν [tēn asphaleian]. Beza notes that this word is used new for τὴν ἀληθείαν [tēn alētheian]. I find, however, that it is also used in the book of Wisdom of Solomon, ch. 18:6: ἵνα ἀσφαλῶς εἰδῶσι οἷς ἐπίστευσαν ὅρκοις, ἐπιγνόντες [hina asphalōs eidōsi hois episteusan horkois, epignontes], that they might know surely, or with certainty, the oaths in which they had believed, and so be of good courage. So ἀσφαλῶς [asphalōs] was also used above, Acts 2:36, and τὴν ἀσφάλειαν above in chapter 21:34 and below in 25:26, and ἀσφάλεια [asphaleia] for certainty or sure truth, Luke 1:4.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: VERS. 1. Ego omni bona conscientia πεπολιτεύμαι τῷ Θεῷ. Syrus & Vulg. conversatus sum coram Deo. laudarem, si constructio cum Dat. id ferret, magis recessit Arabs, quum vertit ܐܠܗܐ ܟܠܝܪܐ ... institutus & educatus sum coram Deo. Budaeus, manere meo functus sum Deo. Beza, servivi Deo. Malim, vixi Deo. sicut Phil. 1. 27. digne Evangelio Christi πολιτεύεσθε vivite. 2 Machab. 6. 1. τῆς νόμοις ἡ Θεῷ μὴ πολιτεύεσθαι, legibus Dei non vivere. & c. 11. 25. καὶ πολιτεύεσθαι ἐν τῇ ἀρχαίᾳ αὐτῶν ἐθνῶν, & vivere secundum majorum suorum instituta. hoc sensu apud alios etiam probatos auctores usurpari, ex Lexicographis discet qui volet.
units.tr: VERS. 1. I have lived before God in all good conscience [πεπολιτεύμαι τῷ Θεῷ]. The Syriac and the Vulgate have I have conducted myself before God. I would praise this if the construction with the dative allowed it. The Arab departs further when he renders it Alaha kalira, I was instructed and brought up before God. Budaeus has I have served God in my own station. Beza has I have served God. I would prefer I have lived for God, as in Phil. 1:27, conduct yourselves worthily of the Gospel of Christ [πολιτεύεσθε]. In 2 Macc. 6:1 we find not to live according to the laws of God [τῆς νόμοις ἡ Θεῷ μὴ πολιτεύεσθαι], and in ch. 11:25, and to live according to their ancestral customs [καὶ πολιτεύεσθαι ἐν τῇ ἀρχαίᾳ αὐτῶν ἐθνῶν]. Anyone who wishes may learn from the lexicographers that the word is used in this sense also by other authors of good standing.

units.la: VERS. 6. Ego Pharisaeus sum, filius Φαρισαίων Pharisaei. Sic Chrysostomus quoque legit & omnes nostrae editiones, nisi quod earum duae ad marginem annotent variantem lectionem τῶν Φαρισαίων. Sic Syrus ܒܢܝ ܦܪܝܫܝܐ filius Pharisaeorum. certe ita Viennensis & Cothenensis editiones habent. at in Reg. ܒܪ ܦܪܝܫܝ filius Pharisaei. sic Trem. quoque legit. nec aliter Arabs & Aethiopicus. si Pharisaeorum legimus, docet non patrem tantum, sed & majores fuisse Pharisaeos. cui confirmando Drusius adfert, Pharisaeus ex Pharisaeus. quod nusquam reperimus. sed quidem Ebraeus ex Ebraeus, Philip. 3. 5.
units.tr: VERS. 6. I am a Pharisee, the son of Pharisees [Φαρισαίων]. Chrysostom also reads it thus, and all our printed editions do, except that two of them note in the margin a variant reading, of the Pharisees [τῶν Φαρισαίων]. The Syriac has bnai p'rishaiya, sons of the Pharisees, and the Viennese and Cothenian editions certainly read so. But in the Regius manuscript it is bar p'rishai, son of a Pharisee, and Tremellius also reads so. The Arab and the Ethiopic do not differ. If we read of the Pharisees, it shows that not only the father but also the ancestors were Pharisees. To confirm this, Drusius cites a Pharisee from a Pharisee, which we nowhere find. But we do find a Hebrew from Hebrews, Phil. 3:5.

units.la: VERS. 8. Neque Angelum, neque Spiritum. Æthiop. ܘܠܐ ܪܘܚܐ, neque Spiritus sanctus.
units.tr: VERS. 8. Neither angel nor spirit. The Ethiopic has and not spirit, nor the Holy Spirit.

units.la: VERS. 9. Καὶ ἀναστάντες οἱ γραμματεῖς τοῦ μέρους τοῦ Φαρισαίων. Syrus, [Syriac]. Trem. & surrexerunt quidam Legisperiti ex lectissimis Pharisaeorum. Boder. ex delectis Perischaeorum. acceperunt [Syriac] pro [Syriac] malè: plurale est à [Syriac]. quod passim latus significat. addit Ferrarius etiam partem denotare 1 Reg. 23. 26. vertendum ergo, & surrexerunt quidam Scriba ex lateribus (id est, ex partibus) Pharisaeorum. sicut & Belgicè dicimus, hp is aen mijn spde, à latere meo est, id est, à partibus meis stat. Arabs [Arabic], Scriba ex sectà Pharisaeorum. Æthiopicus, Scriba & Pharisaei.
units.tr: VERS. 9. And some of the scribes of the party of the Pharisees arose [Καὶ ἀναστάντες οἱ γραμματεῖς τοῦ μέρους τοῦ Φαρισαίων]. The Syriac [Syriac]. Tremellius: and there arose certain learned men out of the choicest of the Pharisees. Bodmer: out of the chosen Pharisees. They have wrongly taken [Syriac] for [Syriac]; the plural comes from [Syriac], which commonly means side. Ferrarius adds that it also denotes part, as in 1 Kings 23:26. It should therefore be rendered and there arose certain scribes from the sides (that is, from the parties) of the Pharisees. Just as we say in Dutch, hp is aen mijn zijde, it is at my side, that is, it stands on my side. The Arab has a scribe from the sect of the Pharisees. The Ethiopic has a scribe and Pharisees.

units.la: IBID. Εἰ δὲ πνεῦμα ἐλάλησεν αὐτῷ ἢ ἄγγελος, μὴ θεομαχῶμεν. Vide notas Erasmi & Bezae. Syrus pro μὴ θεομαχῶμεν (quod è margine in textum, tanquam sensus supplementum irrepsisse videtur) habet [Syriac], Trem. quid malì est in hoc? verte, quid est in hoc? Eodem modo Arabs, tam ab Erpenio editus, quam alius M. S. habet enim, [Arabic], quæ male admodum vertit Junius, si Spiritus aut Angelus insidet ei, esto sane in eo. verte, si Spiritus aut Angelus allocutus est eum, quæ res, id est quid, est in hoc? Æthiopicus, Quod si Spiritus sanctus allocutus est eum, aut angelus? nihil supplet. plane ut Vulgatus. quæ genuina videtur esse lectio.
units.tr: IBID. But if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him, let us not fight against God [Εἰ δὲ πνεῦμα ἐλάλησεν αὐτῷ ἢ ἄγγελος, μὴ θεομαχῶμεν]. See the notes of Erasmus and Beza. In place of let us not fight against God [μὴ θεομαχῶμεν], which seems to have crept from the margin into the text as a supplement to the sense, the Syriac has [Syriac], and Tremellius renders what harm is there in this? Say, what is there in this? The Arab, both as edited by Erpenius and in another manuscript, has the same, though Junius translates it very badly: if a spirit or an angel dwells in him, let it be so. Render it: if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him, what matter is it, that is, what is there in this? The Ethiopic, But if the Holy Spirit or an angel has spoken to him?, adds nothing to the sense. It agrees simply with the Vulgate, which seems to be the genuine reading.

units.la: VERS. 12. Ποιήσαντες συσπολῶ. verto, facta conspiratione. vide quæ supra annotavimus ad c. 19. 40.
units.tr: VERS. 12. Having made a conspiracy [Ποιήσαντες συσπολῶ]. I render it having made a conspiracy. See what we noted above on ch. 19:40.

units.la: VERS. 15. Νῦν οὖν ὑμᾶς ἐμφανίσαι τῷ Χιλιάρχῳ σὺν τῷ συνεδρίῳ, ὅπως αὔριον αὐτὸν καταγάγῃ &c. Eras. σὺν τῷ συνεδρίῳ vertit, & concilio. sic & Æthiopicus, qui porro etiam pro καζαγάγῃ dixit pluraliter, ut eras adducant. malè. neque enim à tribuno & concilio,sed à tribuno ad concilium produci debebat. ut ÿf. 20. expressè dicitur. laudo prorsus Syrum & Arabem, qui αὐτ τῷ συνεδρίῳ conjunxerunt cum ὑμᾶς. vos & concilium indicate Chiliarcho.
units.tr: VERS. 15. Now therefore, signify to the tribune, together with the council, that he bring him down tomorrow [Νῦν οὖν ὑμᾶς ἐμφανίσαι τῷ Χιλιάρχῳ σὺν τῷ συνεδρίῳ, ὅπως αὔριον αὐτὸν καταγάγῃ]. Erasmus renders σὺν τῷ συνεδρίῳ as and with the council. The Ethiopic also does so, but it further renders καταγάγῃ in the plural, that they bring him down, which is wrong. For he was to be brought from the tribune to the council, not from the tribune and the council, as is expressly said in v. 20. I entirely commend the Syriac and the Arab, who joined σὺν τῷ συνεδρίῳ with ὑμᾶς: you and the council signify to the chiliarch.

units.la: VERS. 23. Καὶ δεξιολάβας Αλαφσπάς. Recte doctiff. Beza, & stipatores ducentos. ad cujus notas nihil addo, nisi quod Æthiopicus vertit ducentos viros lancea, vel gladii. enim pro λόγχη usurpat, Joan. 19. 34. & Matt. 17. 50. quò totum quoque illum versum de latere Christi lancea transfosso ex Johanne transtulit. pro μαχαίρας, Luc. 21. 24. pro ῥομφαία; Luc. 2. 35. estque idem quod Vulgatus dixit, & lancearios ducentos. Arabs ... & octoginta jaculatores. ubi miror tantam numeri diversitatem. quum omnia Græca exemplaria, aliique Interpretes conveniant in ducentos. convenit tamen hic cum editione Erpeniana exemplar M. S. quod ex Bibliotheca Boreliana Academia nostra sibi comparavit, Epistolas cum Actis Apoftolorum subnexis continens. VERS. 24. Κτλών τι ... Beza, & ut jumenta praberent. Malim cum Vulgato, Erafmo,& Syro per Imperat. vertere, & jumenta parate, vel præbete.- quod non tantum non est durum, sed & uficatiffimum. vide Mat. 5. 34. 39. & passim. Arabs quoque omnino hæc legit, consentiente M. S. habet enim & parate jumentum ad imponendum Paulum. singulari numero dixit jumentum, ut & Syrus. qua voce Arabes quoque utuntur, & speciatim pro camelo, jumento portandis oneribus aptissimo, atque in Oriente usitatissimo. VERS. 30. Μλωνθείσης δὲ μοι ... Ait Cl. Beza, se sane non videre quomodo hæc cohæreant. Nulla tamen hîc videtur esse syntaxeos anomalia, quum ad verbum vertere liceat, Indicatis autem mihi insidiis in hunc virum, fore ut fierent à Iudæis. nec aliter hæc vertenda censeo: Indicatæ enim ipsi fuere, quum mente conceptæ solum, nondum factæ essent, quippe postridie demum effectui dandæ. Observandum quoque μέλλω, etsi futuri significationem in se contineat, adeoque non nisi cum præsenti, aut aoristo præsentis significationem habente, construi, eique futuri vim dare solet, hîc tamen cum futuro construi. quod alibi in hisce libris non observavimus. & in hoc quidem libro cum solo ἐσται, nempe hîc, & Act. 11.28. & 24.15.16. & 27.10. Apud alios tamen authores cum aliis etiam verbis interdum contingit. ut apud Demosth. pro Cor. τί ἐμελλον καλεῖν ἢ τί συμβαλεῖν αὐτῇ ποιεῖν; quid jussurus essem aut quid consulturus ei facere? alia exempla ex Synesio & Thucidide vide apud Lexicographos.
units.tr: VERS. 23. And two hundred bodyguards [Καὶ δεξιολάβας]. Beza rightly renders it two hundred bodyguards. I add nothing to his notes, except that the Ethiopic renders it two hundred men with spears, or swords. For it uses the word for spear [λόγχη] in John 19:34 and Matt. 17:50, and it has transferred that whole verse about Christ's side pierced with a spear from John. It renders μαχαίρας in Luke 21:24 and ῥομφαία in Luke 2:35 in the same way, and it is the same as the Vulgate, which has two hundred spearmen. The Arab has and eighty javelin-men, where I wonder at so great a difference in number, since all the Greek copies and the other translators agree on two hundred. Yet here the manuscript that our university obtained for itself from the Borel library, containing the Epistles together with the Acts of the Apostles, agrees with the Erpenius edition. VERS. 24. And provide beasts [Κτλών τι]. Beza has that they might provide beasts. I would prefer, with the Vulgate, Erasmus and the Syriac, to render it in the imperative, provide beasts, or set out, which is not only not harsh but very usual; see Matt. 5:34, 39 and passim. The Arab also reads it entirely in this way, and the manuscript agrees, for it has and prepare a beast to set Paul upon. It uses the word beast in the singular, as does the Syriac. The Arabs also use this word, and especially for camel, a beast most suited to carrying burdens and most common in the East. VERS. 30. And when it was revealed to me [Μλωνθείσης δὲ μοι]. The illustrious Beza says that he does not see how these words cohere. Yet there seems to be no anomaly of syntax here, since it is permissible to render word for word: and the plot against this man having been revealed to me, that they were going to be done by the Jews. Nor do I think it should be rendered otherwise. For the plot was revealed to him when it had only been conceived in mind and was not yet carried out, since it was to be put into effect only the next day. It should also be noted that μέλλω, although it contains the sense of the future in itself and so is usually construed only with a present or aorist having the sense of the present, and gives it the force of the future, here is construed with the future. This we have not observed elsewhere in these books. In this book it is found only with ἔσται, namely here, and in Acts 11:28, 24:15–16 and 27:10. Among other authors, however, it sometimes occurs with other verbs too, as in Demosthenes, Pro Corona: τί ἐμελλον καλεῖν ἢ τί συμβαλεῖν αὐτῇ ποιεῖν, what was I going to call her, or what was I about to do to her in return? For other examples from Synesius and Thucydides, see the lexicographers.

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: CHAP. XXIV.

units.la: VERS. 3. Πολλῆς εἰρήνης τυγχάνοντες ἀξία σῶ. Syrus
units.tr: VERS. 3. Obtaining much peace [Πολλῆς εἰρήνης τυγχάνοντες ἀξία σῶ]. The Syriac version has:

units.la: Sic habent omnes editiones Syriacæ. quod vertendum, in multitudine annorum habitamus propter te, id est, quod per multos annos subsistamus & habitemus, id tibi debemus. Trem. tamen & Boder. verterunt, in magnitudine, aut multitudine tranquillitatis habitamus propter te. eo sensu legendum esset ..., ablatis primo punctis plur. num. deinde translata vocali à secunda radicali in primam, ac transpositis tandem Nun & Jod. Nec dubito, quin ea sit recta lectio, quam verbotenus expressit Arabs, في جربل السلام, in abundantia pacis habitamus propter te.
units.tr: All the Syriac editions have it thus. It ought to be rendered "we dwell for many years because of you," that is, we continue and live on for many years, and we owe this to you. Tremellius and Boderianus, however, rendered it "we dwell in the greatness or multitude of tranquillity because of you." On that sense the text would have to be read differently: first the plural points removed, then the vowel moved from the second radical to the first, and finally the Nun and Yod transposed. I do not doubt that this is the correct reading, which the Arab rendered word for word as "fī jarbal al-salām" ("in abundance of peace we dwell because of you").

units.la: Sequitur, καὶ καταρθωμάτων γνωμψίων τῷ ἰθιά τάτω ἀλλ' ὃ ὃς. Syrus, ܒܘܪܟܐ ܕܥܡܐ ܗܢܐ ܫܪܝܐ ܕܡܠܟܐ ܘܒܪ ܥܡܐ. Trem. & emendationes multa fiunt moderamine iudicii tui in populo hoc. Boder. in Reg. multaque directiones fiunt genti huic pondere rationis tuae. in Parif. per libramen rationis tuae. videntur accepisse quasi ܐܪܘܗܡ, ab Hebr. ברר, quod ibi non gustum tantum ac saporem, sed & rationem ac consilium significat. at ܐܠܚܘܢ Syris nihil aliud quod sciam quam onus significat. verto itaque, & emendationes multa facta sunt populo huic per portationem oneris tui. id est, te onus portante, per tuam curam & sollicitudinem. Ferrarius ܐܒܝܪܐ, gestatio sarcina, sollicitudo, anxietas, labor. idem fere quod καταρθωσις. Porro Beza vertit, & ea quae recte ac feliciter in hac gente prudentia tua gesta sunt. id est, γνωμψίων. at legitur in praesenti γνωμψίων. Erasmus itaque, & multa recte gerantur in populo hoc &c. At multa non est in textu. neque legitur ἐν τῷ ἰθιά τάτω, sed τῷ ἰθιά τάτω. Ut itaque & nostram sententiam dicamus, καταρθῶ proprie est dirigere, & à LXX Interpretibus usurpatur saepe pro ܝܫܪ. hinc non dubitem vertere, & directiones fiant populo huic per tuam providentiam. sed magis placet, quod saepius ab iisdem Interpretibus usurpetur pro ܟܘܢ, confirmare, stabilire. ut Ps. 96. 10. κατωρθωσε τὴν οἰκουμένην ἧς ἡ σαλευθήσεται, firmavit terram, quae non commovebitur. vide & 1 Paral. 16. 30. Prov. 12. 19. & passive pro stabiliri, firmari, Prov. 4. 19. & 12. 3. & alibi. hinc verto, & stabilimenta fiant genti huic per &c. Nec rejiciendus qui vertat, & correctiones fiant genti huic per &c. Gloss. καταρθῶ, corrigo. nec ea significatione insolens est τῆς. LXX. Tres has postremas significationes fere ܐܠܝܬܗܘܢ, quo Syrus noster usus est. significat enim directiones, correctiones, stabilimenta. ut & verbum [illegible, ~6 letters], direxit, correxit seu instauravit, & firmavit, stabilivit.
units.tr: There follows "καὶ καταρθωμάτων γνωμψίων τῷ ἔθνει τούτῳ" (kai katarthōmatōn gnōmpsiōn tō ethnei toutō). The Syriac reads "burkhā d-ʿammā hānā sharyā d-malkā wa-bar ʿammā," which is hard to pin down. Tremellius has "and corrections are made to this people by the measure of your judgement." Boderianus, in the Regius text, has "and many directions are given to this nation by the weight of your reasoning," and in the Paris text "by the balance of your reasoning." They seem to have taken the Syriac word as if it came from the Hebrew בר[ר], which means not only "taste" or "savour" but also "reason" or "counsel." But the Syrians, so far as I know, use the word ʾalḥōnā for nothing other than "burden." I therefore translate: "and many amendments are made to this people through the bearing of your burden," that is, while you bear the burden, through your care and concern. Ferrarius renders the Syriac ʾabîrā as "bearing, burden, concern, anxiety, labour," which is nearly the same as καταρθώσεις. Beza translates: "and those things which are done rightly and happily among this people by your prudence," which corresponds to γνωμψίων. But the Greek of the present text reads γνωμψίων, and Erasmus has "let many things be done rightly among this people," etc. Yet "many" is not in the text, nor is the reading ἐν τῷ ἔθνει τούτῳ; it is τῷ ἔθνει τούτῳ. To give our own opinion as well: καταρθῶ properly means "to direct," and the Seventy often use it for [ישר]. So I would not hesitate to render "directions are made for this people through your providence." But it seems better to take the sense more often given by the same translators for [כון], "to confirm, to establish," as in Ps. 96.10: "κατώρθωσε τὴν οἰκουμένην, ἥτις οὐ σαλευθήσεται," "he established the world, which shall not be moved." See also 1 Chron. 16.30 and Prov. 12.19, and in the passive, "to be established, to be confirmed," Prov. 4.19, 12.3 and elsewhere. Hence I render: "establishments are made for this people through" etc. Nor should one reject the rendering "corrections are made for this people through" etc. The gloss gives καταρθῶ as "I correct," and this meaning is not unusual for the Seventy. Our Syriac translator used the Syriac word that covers these three last meanings, for it signifies "directions, corrections, establishments," as does the verb [illegible], "he directed, he corrected," or "he restored, and he confirmed, and he established."

units.la: Sequitur denique, πάντη π Ê ὠασ[?] ἀποδεχόμεθα, ᾧ κ ε ν φήλιξ, μ πάσης ἀχαρισίας. Syrus, [illegible, ~5 letters] [illegible, ~8 letters]. Trem. & nos omnes in omni loco accipimus gratiam tuam. Boder. recipimus. Nos sensum exprimentes vertimus, gratias tibi agimus. Syris enim accipere alicujus gratiam, est gratias alicui agere. sicut & gratiarum actio dicitur [illegible, ~8 letters], acceptio gratia. sic & Arabs, [illegible, ~12 letters]. & nos omnes in omni loco laudamus gratiam tuam. In Graeco est, πάντῃ πι ἡ ϖαυζαχῶ ἀπoδεχόμεϑα, quod Beza recte, prorsus & ubique agnoscimus. itaque miror quod Syrum Interpretem diversam hic lectionem secutum fuisse dicat, quum ad amussim omnia expresserit. imo ex Syriasmo petitum videatur, quod ἀπoδέχεσϑαι, accipere, sumatur pro agnoscere & gratias agere.
units.tr: Finally there follows πάντη π Ê ὠασ[?] ἀποδεχόμεθα, ᾧ κ ε ν φήλιξ, μ πάσης ἀχαρισίας. The Syriac has [illegible, about five letters] [illegible, about eight letters]. Tremellius gives and we all in every place receive your grace. Boderianus has we receive. In expressing the sense, I translate we give you thanks. For in Syriac to receive someone's grace means to give someone thanks, just as the act of giving thanks is called [illegible, about eight letters], the receiving of grace. So too the Arab: [illegible, about twelve letters]: and we all in every place praise your grace. In the Greek it is πάντῃ πι ἡ ϖαυζαχῶ ἀπoδεχόμεϑα, which Beza rightly renders we acknowledge altogether and everywhere. So I am surprised that he says the Syriac translator followed a different reading here, since he has rendered everything exactly. Indeed the Syriac usage seems to be drawn on here, so that ἀπoδέχεσϑαι, to receive, is taken to mean to acknowledge and to give thanks.

units.la: VERS. 5. Comperimus enim virum hunc λοιμὸν pestem.
units.tr: VERS. 5. For we have found this man to be a pest [λοιμὸν].

units.la: Syrus [Syriac]. Trem. quod sit sicarius. respexit Hebr. [Hebrew], mactavit, jugulavit. Boder. perniciosus. Ferrarius, [Syriac], corrupit, vitiavit, devirginavit: dicitur de moribus, de maribus & virginibus. [Syriac], corruptio, vitiatio, devirginatio. refertur ad morum, ad marium & ad virginum vitiationem. [Syriac], devirginatio; vitiatio.
units.tr: The Syriac word [Syriac] is rendered by Tremellius as that he is a murderer, which reflects the Hebrew word [Hebrew], he slew, he cut the throat of. Boderianus has pernicious. Ferrarius gives the Syriac word as he corrupted, he defiled, he deflowered, said of morals, of males and of virgins; corruption, defilement, deflowering. It refers to the corrupting of morals, of men, and of virgins. The Syriac noun means deflowering, defilement.

units.la: IBID. Πρωτοστάτην τῆς τῶν Ναζωραίων αἱρέσεως. Eras. πρωτοστάτην, authorem vertit. Vulg. authorem seditionis. nempe πρωτοστάτης ipsi fuit, quasi πρῶτ@ς ἡ ϛάσεως. Melius Beza prinprincipem. quod Syrus [?] dixit. Glossarium πρωτοστάτης, princeps. Hezychius, πρωτοστάτης, ὁ πρῶτ@ ... ἡ κάεμς τ' ... τάξεως πεγραφόμενος, qui primus ad frontem aciei constitutus est. Porro quod Nαζωραῖος sive Nαζαρῶς dictus fuerit Christus, ejusque asseclæ Nαζωραῖοι, non ex errore vulgi, Nazarethæ natum eum opinantis, neque ex impiorum ludibrio, id ipsi contumeliæ esse existimantium, originem primam traxit, sed ex ipsius Dei consilio & voluntate, ipsorumque piorum usu. consilium Dei patet Mat.2. ꝑs.ult. ubi Joseph cum puero Jesu ex Ægypto reversus, jubetur Nazarethæ habitationis sedem figere, ut, secundum monita Prophetarum, Nazaræus diceretur. & placuisse piis nominis istius usum, liquet ex Joan. 1. 45. Act. 2. 22. & 3. 6. & 4. 10. Quin & ipse Christus se ita nuncupat, Act. 22. 8. Gloriosissimum scilicet ipsi hoc erat nomen, quo declarabatur esse נצר, surculus ille, per Prophetas promissus, qui in urbe נצר, surculus dicta educatus, atque inde ad muneris functionem productus, multos נצרים, Nazaræos, id est, è furculo oriundos protulit. nec est quod dicas, ζ in Nαζωραῖος postulare ut à נצר deducatur, potius quam à נץ. usitatum enim est ꝓ in ꝑ permutare. ut pro Hebr. נצר, justus, dicunt Syri נצר. pro נצר, unde נצרה, viaticum, Syri נצר, viaticum dedit. נצרה, viaticum. pro נצר, parvus, Syri נצרא idem.
units.tr: IBID. The ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes [Πρωτοστάτην τῆς τῶν Ναζωραίων αἱρέσεως]. Erasmus translates πρωτοστάτην as author, and the Vulgate has author of the sedition. But πρωτοστάτης means the leader in front, as if from πρῶτ@ς ἡ ϛάσεως. Beza better renders it the chief, as the Syriac also does. The gloss gives πρωτοστάτης as leader. Hesychius explains πρωτοστάτης as one who is set first at the front of the line, who stands first at the front of the battle line. As for why Christ was called Nazarene (Ναζωραῖος or Ναζαρῶς) and his followers Nazarenes, the name did not arise from the error of the common people, who thought he was born at Nazareth, nor from the mockery of the impious, who regarded it as an insult. It arose from God's own counsel and will, and from the usage of the godly themselves. God's purpose is clear from Matt. 2, last verse, where Joseph, returning with the child Jesus from Egypt, is commanded to settle in Nazareth, so that, according to the words of the prophets, he should be called a Nazarene. That the godly liked this name is clear from John 1. 45, Acts 2. 22, 3. 6, and 4. 10. Christ himself also calls himself so, Acts 22. 8. The name was indeed most glorious to him, because by it he was declared to be נצר, that branch promised through the prophets, who, reared in the city called נצר, branch, and from there brought forth to his office, produced many נצרים, Nazarenes, that is, those springing from a branch. Nor can one object that the ζ in Ναζωραῖος requires derivation from נצר rather than from נץ. For it is common to exchange ꝓ and ꝑ. Thus the Syriac uses נצר for the Hebrew נצר, just*; and from נצר, whence נצרה, provision for a journey, the Syriac has נצר, gave provision for a journey. נצרה, provision for a journey. And for נצר, small, the Syriac has the same נצרא.

units.la: VERS. 7. Ἐκ τ̃ χαρῶν ἡμῶν ἀπήχαχα. Notat Cl. Beza, in quibusdam codicibus addi, ἡ ἀρῆς σε ἀπίςλε. Monemus, Syrum quoque & Arabem ea addere. Æthiopicum, non. Quodque totus hic versus, cum parte præcedentis & sequentis, in quibusdam Vulgatæ editionis codicibus non legatur, monent Correctores Romani, non esse ista omittenda. Syrus, Arabs & Æthiopicus habent. VERS. 14. Κατὰ τὸν λόγον, ὧ λέγεται ἀρτον. Syrus & Arabs non legunt ἀρτον. ἰδὸν verterunt doctrinam. Æthiopicus picus habet, verum confiteor tibi, quod ad id quod dicunt de me, docet harefin, ego servio &c.
units.tr: VERS. 7. Ἐκ τ̃ χαρῶν ἡμῶν ἀπήχαχα. The learned Beza notes that some manuscripts add ἡ ἀρῆς σε ἀπίςλε. We note that the Syriac and the Arab also add these words; the Ethiopic does not. And since the whole of this verse, together with the part before and after it, is not read in some codices of the Vulgate edition, the Roman correctors warn that these words should not be omitted. The Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic have them. VERS. 14. Κατὰ τὸν λόγον, ὧ λέγεται ἀρτον. The Syriac and the Arab do not read ἀρτον. They rendered ἰδὸν as doctrine. The Ethiopic has: I confess to you the truth, that according to what they say of me, he teaches heresy; I serve, etc.

units.la: V E R S. 16. E᾽ν τάτῳ ἢ ἀνὴς ἀσκῶ. Vulgatus & Eraf. in hoc, id est, in hac re, ἐν τύτῳ πρᾶγμα. Beza, interea, ἐν τύτῳ χρόνῳ. Æthiopicus, sic, ἐν τύτῳ τόπῳ. Syrus & Arabs, propterea, ᾿Δ ἐν τῇ. sicut, putant exaudiri in τῇ πολυλογίᾳ αὐτῶν, pro ᾿Δ τῷ πολυλογίαν, propter multiloquium suum, Mat. 6.7. ne segnescite in τάις ϑλίψεσι μου, propter afflictiones meas, Eph. 3. 13. nemo judicet vos in βρώσει propter cibum, Col. 2. 16. Hebraismus est, ubi ב in sæpe valet propter. vide Gen. 18. 28. propter quinque. & alibi passim.
units.tr: VERS. 16. E᾽ν τάτῳ ἢ ἀνὴς ἀσκῶ. The Vulgate and Erasmus have in this, that is, in this matter, reading ἐν τύτῳ πρᾶγμα. Beza has meanwhile, reading ἐν τύτῳ χρόνῳ. The Ethiopic has thus, reading ἐν τύτῳ τόπῳ. The Syriac and Arabic have therefore, with ᾿Δ ἐν τῇ. Similarly, they think it is heard in their much speaking, for ᾿Δ τῷ πολυλογίαν, because of their much speaking, Matt. 6. 7; do not be weary in my afflictions, because of my afflictions, Eph. 3. 13; let no one judge you in eating, because of food, Col. 2. 16.
