It is a Hebraism, where ב, in, often means because of. See Gen. 18. 28, because of the five, and elsewhere throughout.

units.la: I B I D. Ἀσκῶ sæpe intransitivè sumitur. ut ἀσκῶ ποιεῖν, studeo facere, apud Xenoph. Hezychius, ἀσκέω, μελετῶ, γυμνάζω, φιλοπονεῖ, meditatur, exercet se, allaborat.
units.tr: IBID. Ἀσκῶ is often used intransitively, as ἀσκῶ ποιεῖν, to strive to do, in Xenophon. Hesychius: ἀσκέω, μελετῶ, γυμνάζω, φιλοπονεῖ, he practises, trains himself, labours at.

units.la: V E R S. 17. Καὶ προσφορὰς, & oblationes. quod Vulg. addit, & vota, Græci codices non agnoscunt, ut nec Syrus, Arabs aut Æthiop.
units.tr: VERS. 17. Καὶ προσφορὰς, and oblations. The Vulgate adds and vows, which the Greek manuscripts do not recognise, nor do the Syriac, Arabic or Ethiopic.

units.la: V E R S. 18. Et invenerunt me illi in templo purificatum, non cum turba neque in tumultu, [Syriac text] . Trem. & Boder. in Reg. nisi quod tumultuati sint illi Iudaï qui venerunt ex Asia.
units.tr: VERS. 18. "And they found me purified in the temple, not with a crowd nor in a tumult," [Syriac]. Tremellius and Boderie, in the Regia, read: "except that certain Jews who came from Asia stirred up a tumult."

units.la: [Syriac text] acceperunt pro [Syriac text], & quidem in Nominat. casu, quum hic sit fœminin. & in utroque genere non nisi pro Accusativo usurpentur. excipe quum verbum substantivum valent. quæ difficultas tanta visa fuit, ut Boder. in Parif. ausus fuerit scribere [Hebrew text], homines Iudaï, vel quidam Iudaï. Miror & apud Plantinum ita legi. quum & Tremellius & omnes Syriacæ editiones primam lectionem constanter retineant: in qua nos nihil videmus difficultatis.
units.tr: The Syriac takes the word as a nominative, although it is feminine, and these forms are used in both genders only as accusatives, except where they serve as the substantive verb. This difficulty seemed so great to Boderie in the Paris edition that he dared to write the Hebrew, "men, Jews," or "certain Jews." I am surprised that this reading also appears in Plantin's edition, since Tremellius and all the Syriac editions consistently keep the first reading, and I see no difficulty in it.

units.la: [Syriac text] habemus pro pronomine relativo plur. fœm. Accusativi casus, ac referimus ad duo præcedentia substantiva tiva [Syriac] & [Syriac], quibus plur. fœm. pro neutro, quo Syri carent, recte respondet. vertimus, non cum turba & tumultu, nisi quod excitarunt ea Judæi qui venerunt ex Asia. ubi simul notandum, [Syriac] in Kal non tantum intransitivè, sed & transitivè sumi ut [Syriac]. vide Act. 14. 19. Jac. 1. 6. Arabs vertit [Arabic], nisi quod quidam Judæi, qui venerant ex Asia, tumultuati sint contra me. Græca lectio, quam Vulgatus & Erasmus sunt secuti, quamque in octo meis diversis editionibus reperio, habet, Ἐν οἷς δέ ποτε μὴ γνωσμένον ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ, ἃ μὴ ὄχλα, ἀλλ᾽ μὴ ἰουδαῖοι. hic punctum. Deinde additur, Τινὲς ἦ ὄντ᾽ ἐκ τῆς Ἀσίας Ἰουδαῖοι, ᾧς εἶδεν σε πειράσαι. Beza autem ex tribus M. S. codicibus hanc dedit lectionem, Ἐν οἷς δέ ποτε μὴ γνωσμένον ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ, ἃ μὴ ὄχλα, ἀλλὰ μὴ ἰουδαῖοι, τινὲς ὄντ᾽ ἐκ τῆς Ἀσίας Ἰουδαῖοι. deinde novo versu, ᾧς εἶδεν &c. nec aliter Chrysostomum ait legisse. cui editio Etonensis refragatur, quippe quæ antiquam illam & lectionem & distinctionem habet. nec aliter Chrysostomum legisse, ex adjuncta ejus paraphrasi colligi poterit. Nec dubito quin Syrus & Arabs eodem modo legerint. qui quum sensum hiare viderent, nisi suppleretur, hoc modo supplevLerunt, τινὲς ἦ ὄντ᾽ ἐκ τῆς Ἀσίας Ἰουδαῖοι, ἐξηρύξησαν. plane ut Erasmus in notis suis, ut & Æthiopicus, qui habet [Ethiopic], qui commoverunt turbas fuerunt Judæi qui venerunt ex Asia. Quicquid sit, non tantam hic reperio difficultatem, ut ab antiqua & maximè recepta lectione recedendum putem, præsertim quum expeditum & planum satis sit, subintelligere ἂν. Quidam autem ex Asia Judæi sunt, quos oportebat apud te adesse. Quod si liceret Encliticum τινές mutare in Interrogativum τίνες, sic legerem, τίνες δὲ ὄντ᾽ ἐκ τῆς Ἀσίας Ἰουδαῖοι &c Invenerunt me &c. Quinam autem? ex Asia Judæi, quos oportuit adesse.
units.tr: The Syriac has, as a relative pronoun, the feminine plural accusative, and it refers to the two preceding nouns, [Syriac] and [Syriac]. The plural feminine answers correctly to a neuter, which Syriac lacks. We translate: "not with a crowd and tumult, except that Jews who came from Asia stirred them up." Here it should also be noted that the verb in the Kal stem is taken not only intransitively but also transitively, as in [Syriac]; see Acts 14:19 and James 1:6. The Arabic translates: "except that certain Jews who had come from Asia rose in tumult against me." The Greek reading, which the Vulgate translator and Erasmus followed, and which I find in my eight different editions, has: "Among whom they found me purified in the temple, not with a crowd, but not Jews [ἐν οἷς δέ ποτε μὴ γνωσμένον ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ, ἃ μὴ ὄχλα, ἀλλ᾽ μὴ ἰουδαῖοι]." Here there is a full stop. Then it adds: "Certain Jews from Asia, whom it was right for them to have been before you [Τινὲς ἦ ὄντ᾽ ἐκ τῆς Ἀσίας Ἰουδαῖοι, ᾧς εἶδεν σε πειράσαι]." Beza, however, from three manuscripts, gave this reading: "Among whom they found me purified in the temple, not with a crowd, but certain Jews from Asia [Ἐν οἷς δέ ποτε μὴ γνωσμένον ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ, ἃ μὴ ὄχλα, ἀλλὰ μὴ ἰουδαῖοι, τινὲς ὄντ᾽ ἐκ τῆς Ἀσίας Ἰουδαῖοι]," and then, with a new verse, "whom it was right" etc. He says that Chrysostom read it in the same way, but the Eton edition contradicts this, since it has that older reading and punctuation. Nor can it be gathered from the paraphrase attached to Chrysostom that he read it otherwise. I do not doubt that the Syriac and the Arabic read it in the same way. Seeing that the sense gapes unless it is supplied, they supplied it in this way: "Certain Jews from Asia stirred them up [τινὲς ἦ ὄντ᾽ ἐκ τῆς Ἀσίας Ἰουδαῖοι, ἐξηρύξησαν]," just as Erasmus does in his notes, and as does the Ethiopic, which has: "The Jews who came from Asia were those who stirred up the crowds." Whatever the case, I find no difficulty here so great that I think we should depart from the ancient and most widely received reading, especially since it is quite simple and clear to supply ἂν: "Certain Jews from Asia there are, whom it was right to be present before you." If one could change the enclitic τινές into the interrogative τίνες, I would read it thus: "Who then are the Jews from Asia" etc., "who found me" etc. "Who then? Jews from Asia, whom it was right to be present."

units.la: VERS. 25. Disseruit Paulus nominatim τῆ ἐγκρατείας, de castitate, sive continentia, quia hic summi sceleris rei erant Felix & Drusilla, quippe quae alterius mariti, nempe Azizi Emesenorum regis, uxor, ad Felicem turpiter transierat. Joseph. Ant. l. 20.
units.tr: VERS. 25. Paul discussed by name "the self-control [τῆ ἐγκρατείας]," that is, concerning chastity or continence, because Felix and Drusilla were guilty of the greatest wickedness here: she, the wife of another husband, namely Azizus, king of the Emesenes, had shamefully passed over to Felix. Josephus, Antiquities, book 20.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: VERS. 5. Οἱ οὖν δυνατοὶ ἐν ὑμῖν. Ad verbum puto sonare, Qui ergo possibiles sunt inter vos, id est, οἱς οὖν δυνατὸν ἐν ὑμῖν, quibus ergo possibile est inter vos. affine est illud Act. 12. 18. τί ἂν ἐγένετο ὁ Πέτρος, quid Petrus factus esset, pro quid Petro factum esset.
units.tr: VERSE 5. Οἱ οὖν δυνατοὶ ἐν ὑμῖν ["Those then who are able among you"]. Word for word, I think, it reads "Who then are possible among you", that is, οἷς οὖν δυνατὸν ἐν ὑμῖν ["to whom then it is possible among you"]. Similar is Acts 12:18, τί ἂν ἐγένετο ὁ Πέτρος ["what would Peter have become"], for "what had been done to Peter".

units.la: VERS. 6. Διατρίψας ἡ ἐν αὐτοῖς ἡμέρας ἢ πλείους ἢ δέκα. Sic Beza legit, ex tribus Graecis codicibus. Vulgatus quoque negantem particulam habet. & porro ante decem habet octo aut. quod & in tribus Graecis codicibus reperiri testatur Cl. Beza. Reliqui codices Graeci habent πλείους ἢ δέκα, omisso ἢ. quomodo & Chrysostomus legit. Syrus autem, Arabs & Aethiopicus nec ἢ nec πλείους legunt, sed pro eo habent octo. hoc modo, & quum mansisset ibi dies octo aut decem. quae commodissima est lectio.
units.tr: VERSE 6. Διατρίψας ἡ ἐν αὐτοῖς ἡμέρας ἢ πλείους ἢ δέκα ["Having stayed among them not more than eight or ten days"]. Beza reads it so, from three Greek manuscripts. The Vulgate also has the negating particle, and before "ten" it has "eight or". Beza testifies that this too is found in three Greek manuscripts. The other Greek manuscripts have πλείους ἢ δέκα ["more than ten"], without the ἢ, as Chrysostom also reads. The Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic versions read neither the ἢ nor πλείους, but have "eight" in its place, so that the sense is "and when he had stayed there eight or ten days". This is by far the most suitable reading.

units.la: VERS. 9. Ὁ Φῆστος ἠθέλησε τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις χάριν καταθέσθαι. Syrus [Syriac text, illegible, ~40 letters]. Trem. & Beder. Festus autem, quia volebat fenerari beneficium Iudaeis. Chaldaismum secuti sunt, ubi ישׁא significat mutuare, mutuo dare, fenerari. apud Syros in Kal significat culpare, objurgare, reprehendere. In Pael interprete Ferrario dedit, obtulit. in Aphel interprete eodem, incepit, inchoavit. praeterea reprehendit, objurgavit. addenda fuit & hic significatio quam in Pael dederat, exigente id necessario hoc loco quem tractamus, quemque vertimus, Festus autem, propterea quod volebat gratiam offerre Iudaïs,vel dare Iudaïs. convenit cum Arab. [Syriac], munera dare. [Syriac] idem quod [Hebrew], munus. In lingua Æthiopica [Ethiopic] est facere. vide Matt. 4 19. & alibi. unde & [Hebrew] Esdr. 3. 7. facultas, faciendi potestas.quod hic à significatione Syriaca non multum abit. & præced. cap. [Syriac] ult. pro [Syriac] dixit [Syriac] facere gratiam Iudaïs.
units.tr: VERSE 9. Ὁ Φῆστος ἠθέλησε τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις χάριν καταθέσθαι ["Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favour"]. The Syriac text here is illegible. Tremellius and Beza render it, "Festus, because he wished to lend a benefit to the Jews". They followed the Chaldee idiom, in which ישׁא means to lend, to lend at interest, to borrow. In Syriac, in the Kal, it means to blame, to rebuke, to reprove. In the Pael, according to Ferrarius, it means to give, to offer; in the Aphel, by the same authority, to begin, to initiate; and besides, to reprove and rebuke. The meaning it has in the Pael must also be added here, as the passage we are treating requires, and as we translate it: "Festus, because he wished to offer favour to the Jews", or "to give to the Jews". This agrees with the Arabic, "to give gifts". The Syriac equivalent of the Hebrew munus ["gift"] is the same word. In Ethiopic it means "to do"; see Matt. 4:19 and elsewhere. Whence also the Hebrew in Ezra 3:7 means "ability, power of doing", which here does not differ much from the Syriac meaning. In the preceding chapter the Syriac, in the last verse, for the Greek, says "to do favour to the Jews".

units.la: VERS. II. Οὐδὲς μὲ δώσατη αὐτῆς χαρίσασθαι· Καίσαρα ἐπικαλέσμαι. Syrus, [Syriac] [Syriac] [Syriac] Tremel. nemo daturus est me eius dono, protectiones Cæsaris appello. Ἀδόσαλο forma constructa accipitur hic adverbialiter, dono. sicut [Syriac], postremò. [Syriac], primò. [Syriac], vivè. de quo Gram. nostræ p. 400. Quod autem Tremel. ut & Boder. in Parif. [Syriac] vertant protectiones, perperam est. melius in Reg. Cæsaris provocationes appello est enim verbum [Syriac], clamavit, vociferatus est. imploravit, provocavit ad judicem. inde teste Ferrario, [Syriac], appellatio, provocatio ad majorem judicem. Act. 25. 11. & 12. in singulari vix reperias. in plur. solum cum affixis, hæc ille. ubi observandum, utroque in loco scribi per ר ad [Syriac]. pro quo Ferrarius habet -. & [Syriac] quidem 12. extat in singul. [Syriac] appellationem Cæsaris inclamasti. ut & Act. 26.32. pro quo in Lex.Syr.Arab. habetur [Syriac], qua punctatione
units.tr: VERSE 11. Οὐδεὶς με δύναται αὐτοῖς χαρίσασθαι· Καίσαρα ἐπικαλοῦμαι ["No one can give me to them as a favour; I appeal to Caesar"]. The Syriac, as Tremellius renders it: "no one is going to give me up as a gift; I appeal to Caesar's protections". The Syriac form in the construct state is here taken adverbially, "as a gift", just as the Syriac for "finally", "first", "alive" are used adverbially; on which see our Grammar, p. 400. But that Tremellius, and Boderianus in the Paris edition, render it "protections" is wrong; the Regius edition is better: "I appeal to Caesar's appeals", for the word means to cry out, to shout, to implore, to appeal to a judge. Hence, according to Ferrarius, it means "appeal, appeal to a higher judge". In Acts 25:11, 12 one can scarcely find it in the singular; in the plural it occurs only with suffixes, so far Ferrarius. Here it should be noted that in both places it is written with ר, for which Ferrarius has another letter. The singular does occur in Acts 12 ("you have invoked Caesar's appeal"), as also in Acts 26:32, for which the Syriac-Arabic lexicon gives a form read with that pointing in Acts 28:19.

units.la: legitur Act. 28. 19. video in his & similibus non raro confundi inter se vocales ʼ & ̊. ut, quod Amira scribit ܐܣܛܐ, stagnum. Ferrarius scribit ܐܣܛܐ. sic quod jam scribunt ܐܣܛܐ, licet etiam legere ܐܣܛܐ, ager. unde ἀκίλδαμα Act. 1. nec id mirum. nam & Arabes, qui tres tantum vocalium notas habent, pathach suum efferunt jam per a, jam per e. & Hebraei segol vocant pathach parvum. Hinc est quod βεφίκη Syr. scribatur per pathach ܐܣܛܐ Act. 25. 23. similia multa.
units.tr: I see that in these and similar words the vowel signs are not rarely confused with one another, as when Amira writes one form for "pond" and Ferrarius writes another; so what they now write, though one may also read it differently, means "field". Whence Akeldama in Acts 1, and this is no surprise. For the Arabs too, who have only three vowel signs, pronounce their pathach sometimes as "a", sometimes as "e"; and the Hebrews call the pathach the little segol. Hence it is that the Syriac for Berenice is written with a pathach in Acts 25:23, and there are many similar cases.

units.la: VERS. 16. Quod hic Festus de jure Romanorum tradit, idem erat juris Hebraeorum. In פנהרים enim legitur, אסור לרין שישפט דברי בעל רין קדם שינא בלל רין חבר vetitum est Iudici audire partem accusantem, antequam adsit pars altera defendens.
units.tr: VERSE 16. What Festus here reports of Roman law was also the law of the Hebrews. In the book the text cites, it reads that it is forbidden for a judge to hear the words of the accusing party before the other party, the defender, is present.

units.la: VERS. 20. Ἀπροσῶπων δὲ ἐγὼ εἰς τὸ αὐτὸ τῶν ζητῶν. Vulg. Hasitans autem ego de hujusmodi quaestione. Beza, Dubitans autem ego super hujusmodi inquisitione. Malim verbotenus magis reddere, Inops autem consilii ego ad quaestionem de hac re, solvendam nempe & expediendam.
units.tr: VERSE 20. Ἀπορούμενος δὲ ἐγὼ περὶ τὴν περὶ τούτων ζήτησιν ["But I, being at a loss about the inquiry into these matters"]. The Vulgate: "But I, hesitating about this kind of question." Beza: "But I, doubting about this kind of inquiry." I would rather render it more literally: "But I, at a loss what to do about the question concerning this matter", namely how it is to be resolved and settled.

units.la: VERS. 24. Θεωρῶν τῶν τοῦ ἐν πᾶν τὸ αὐλῆθ Τ Ἰουδαίων ἐπένχον μοι. Syrus, ܣܝܪܘܣ ܕܚܡܢ ܠܫܡܥܐ. Trem. de hoc homine quem videtis, universus populus Iudaeorum interpellavit me. Boder. adversus hunc virum quem videtis, universa gens Iudaeorum compellavit me. Quid ܩܢܛ sit in Pael satis constat, nempe accipere, recipere. at quid ܩܢܛ in Kal, non conveniunt Interpretes, nec Lexicographi. tribus in locis N. T. reperitur, quorum primus hic est, ubi per interpellare aut compellare vertunt. Secundus Rom. 8.33.
units.tr: VERSE 24. Θεωρεῖτε τοῦτον ὃν ... ἐντυγχάνον μοι ["You see this man ... who has appealed to me"]. The Syriac text here is illegible. Tremellius: "concerning this man whom you see, the whole multitude of Jews interpellated me." Boderianus: "against this man whom you see, the whole nation of the Jews cried out to me." What the Syriac word means in the Pael is clear enough, namely to receive, to accept. But what it means in the Kal the interpreters and lexicographers do not agree on. It occurs in three places in the New Testament, of which the first is this one, where they translate it "interpellate" or "compellate". The second is Rom. 8:33.

units.la: [illegible, ~12 letters] Trem. & Boder. quùs se opponet electis Dei? Tertius Rom. 11. 2.
units.tr: [Syriac text illegible] Tremellius and Boderianus: "who will oppose the elect of God?" The third is Rom. 11:2.

units.la: [illegible, ~12 letters] Trem. & Boder. in Parif. cum clamaret ad Deum adversus Israël. In reg. quomodo invocet Deum adversus Israel. In Thargum frequenter usurpatur pro clamare, vociferari. At Ferrarius [illegible, ~3 letters] solummodo vertit accusavit. Sic Lex. Syr. Arab. [illegible, ~8 letters], accusat & culpat. Masius vertit, ἐντυγχάνειν, interpellare aliquem, adire, aggredi. Id vehementer arridet. proprie enim denotare arbitror id quod Graeci dicunt ἐντυγχάνειν, occurrere alicui, sicut & apud Arabes in 4 conjug. [illegible, ~3 letters], & in 10 [illegible, ~4 letters], accedere, occurrere, sistere se ante, coram, ex adverso alicujus. est enim apud Hebr. [illegible, ~2 letters], Chaldaeos [illegible, ~2 letters], Syros [illegible, ~5 letters], Arab. [illegible, ~2 letters], ante, coram, ex adverso. Hinc [illegible, ~3 letters], non simpliciter, sed sequente praepos. [illegible, ~3 letters] significat occurrere contra aliquem, id est, accusare. ut Rom. 8. 33. quis occurret contra electos Dei? id est, quis accusabit eos? Rom. 11. 2. quum occurreret Deo contra Israelem, id est, quum accusaret apud Deum Israelem. Ω's ἐντυγχάνει τῷ Θεῷ κατ' ἐμοῦ Ἰσραήλ. Ita hoc loco, contra hunc virum quem videtis, totus populus Iudaeorum occurrit mihi, id est, hunc virum accusavit apud me. quod si ergo verbum [illegible, ~3 letters] semper construitur cum [illegible, ~3 letters] ut sane in tribus hisce locis fit, fieri potest ut ubique significet accusare. ut & in tribus dictis locis Arabs reddidit per [illegible, ~4 letters], accusare.
units.tr: [Syriac text illegible] Tremellius and Boderianus in the Paris edition: "when he cried out to God against Israel." In the Regius edition: "how he calls upon God against Israel." In the Targum it is frequently used for to cry out, to shout. But Ferrarius translates it only as "accused". So the Syriac-Arabic lexicon: "accuses and blames". Masius renders it ἐντυγχάνειν ["to approach, to petition, to address someone"], and this pleases me greatly. For I think it properly denotes what the Greeks mean by ἐντυγχάνειν, "to meet someone", just as also among the Arabs in the fourth and tenth conjugations it means to approach, to meet, to present oneself before, in front of, face to face with someone. For the word meaning "before, in front of, opposite" is found in Hebrew, Chaldee, Syriac and Arabic. Hence, not simply but with a following preposition, it signifies "to meet against someone", that is, to accuse. So Rom. 8:33: "who will meet against God's elect?", that is, who will accuse them? Rom. 11:2: "when he met God against Israel", that is, when he accused Israel before God. So in this place: "against this man whom you see, the whole Jewish people met me", that is, accused this man before me. If therefore the verb is always construed with the preposition, as indeed it is in these three places, it may be that everywhere it signifies "to accuse". So also in the three said places the Arab rendered it by a word meaning "to accuse".

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: VERS. 3. Μάλισα γινώσκω ὅτι σε εἰδὼς πάντων &c. Cl. Beza ex uno codice pervetusto addidit ἀδὼς, quum reliqui codices Græci id non agnoscant, nec Vulg. legerit, nec Erasmus, nec Chrysostomus. alius codex legit Ϡησάμψ. unde clarè colligitur, audaculos aliquos, quum constructionem Græcam hiare arbitrarentur, addidisse in alio codice ἀδὼς, in alio Ϡησάμψ. Syrus quoque & Arabs addiderunt, quod peregrina constructio videretur, quæ supplementum tale postularet. quod & Erasmum adegit, ut solutionem se videre negaret, nisi subaudiatur ἀδὼς. At nihil periculi, quum Accusativi absoluti esse possint pro Genitivis. γνώσῳ ὀντα pro γνώσῳ ὀντος. sicut apud Halicarnassæum, ὡς δὴ ἀκινδύνως αὐτῆς τὸ ἔργον ἐπιμέλον, pro ὡς ἀκινδύνῳ αὐτῆς ἔργα ἐπιμέλε, quasi res illùs sine periculo esset futura. & apud Aristot. ὥσπερ γὰρ αὐτῷ χώρᾳ τινὰ ἴσως, quasi ei non esset aliqua regio. sic rectè capi potest illud Eph.1. 18. πεφωτισμένους ὀφθαλμοὺς τῆς διανοίας ὑμῶν, illuminatis oculis mentis vestræ. ut rectè ibi explicuit Cl. Beza.
units.tr: VERSE 3. Μάλιστα γινώσκω ὅτι σε εἰδὼς πάντων [Especially since I know you to be acquainted with all] &c. Cl. Beza added ἀδὼς [expert] on the authority of one very old codex, although the other Greek codices do not have it, nor did the Vulgate translator read it, nor Erasmus, nor Chrysostom. Another codex reads Ϡησάμψ. From this it is clearly gathered that some bold people, thinking the Greek construction incomplete, added ἀδὼς in one codex and Ϡησάμψ in another. The Syriac and the Arabic version also added something, because the construction seemed foreign and needed such a supplement. This also drove Erasmus to say that he could not see a solution unless ἀδὼς is understood. But there is no danger here, since accusatives absolute can stand in place of genitives, γνώσῳ ὀντα for γνώσῳ ὀντος, as in Halicarnassaeus, ὡς δὴ ἀκινδύνως αὐτῆς τὸ ἔργον ἐπιμέλον, for ὡς ἀκινδύνῳ αὐτῆς ἔργα ἐπιμέλε, as if that matter were going to be without danger. And in Aristotle, ὥσπερ γὰρ αὐτῷ χώρᾳ τινὰ ἴσως, as if there were not some region for him. So too the words in Eph. 1:18, πεφωτισμένους ὀφθαλμοὺς τῆς διανοίας ὑμῶν, may be rightly taken as "the eyes of your mind being illuminated," as Cl. Beza there rightly explained.

units.la: VERS. 5.
units.tr: VERSE 5.

units.la: Προγινώσκοντές με ἀνωθὲν, (ἐὰν θέλωσι μαρτυρῆν) ὅτι κατὰ τὴν ἀκριβεστάτην αἵρεσιν ἔζησα Φαρισαῖος. Syrus & Arabs parenthesin istam non hic, sed in medio versus præcedentis legunt. Æthiopicus hic legit. omnes autem ἀνωθὲν construunt cum προγινωσκόντες, non cum ἔζησα, quod D. Bezæ visum est. optimè autem Syrus & Arabs vertisse videntur, à longo tempore. Hezychius, ἀνω, ἀνωτέρω τινα ἐν χρόνῳ τῇ Φιλίππῳ ἑαυτοῦ, de superiori loco & tempore hoc adverbium usurpatur. proprie ergo est, à superiori tempore, van voozt« eden tijden, id est, à multis hinc retro elapsis annis. Cur autem ἀκριβεστάτη dicatur Pharisæorum secta, videatur Myrothecium Cameronis in hunc locum.
units.tr: Προγινώσκοντές με ἀνωθὲν, (ἐὰν θέλωσι μαρτυρεῖν) ὅτι κατὰ τὴν ἀκριβεστάτην αἵρεσιν ἔζησα Φαρισαῖος [They knew me from the beginning, (if they are willing to testify) that according to the strictest sect I lived as a Pharisee]. The Syriac and the Arabic read this parenthesis not here but in the middle of the preceding verse. The Ethiopic reads it here. All, however, construe ἀνωθὲν with προγινώσκοντες, not with ἔζησα, which seemed right to D. Beza. The Syriac and Arabic seem to have translated it very well, as from a long time. Hesychius says, ἀνω, ἀνωτέρω τινα ἐν χρόνῳ τῇ Φιλίππῳ ἑαυτοῦ, that this adverb is used of a higher place and time. Properly, then, it means from an earlier time, van voozt« eden tijden, that is, from many years long past. Why the sect of the Pharisees is called ἀκριβεστάτη [strictest] may be seen in Cameron's Myrothecium on this passage.

units.la: VERS. 7.
units.tr: VERSE 7.

units.la: E'v ἐκλεία νύκτα καὶ ἡμέραν λατρεύον. Syrus, [Syriac line illegible, ~20 letters] Trem. & Boder. precibus assiduis dei & noctu. verto studiofis, vel incitatis, vel intensis. ἐν ἐκλυσίᾳ non ad temporis extensionem, sed ardoris intensionem retulit. deinde τὸ προσεύχεσθαι speciatim precibus applicavit.
units.tr: Ἐν ἐκλυσίᾳ νύκτα καὶ ἡμέραν λατρεύον [serving God night and day]. The Syriac, [Syriac, transliterated approximately] Tremellius and Boderianus render it with assiduous prayers to God and by night. I translate it eager, or urgent, or intense. He referred ἐν ἐκλυσίᾳ not to the extension of time but to the intensity of zeal. Then he applied τὸ προσεύχεσθαι specifically to prayers.

units.la: V e r s. 9. Ἐγὼ μὲν οὖν εἶδοξα ἐμαυτῷ ωρὸς τὴν ὀνομα Γησῦν Ναζωραίου δὲν ωολλὰ ἐνωλία πεδήσαι. Syrus Arabs & Clar. Beza ἐμαυτῷ construunt cum εἶδοξα, quasi pro πρὸς ἐμαυτῷ ponatur. Vulgatus autem & Erasmus cum δὲν. quod non omnino spernendum. etsi enim usitatius diceretur, εἶδοξα ἐμαυτὸν δὲν πεδήσαι, est tamen ubi Dativus usurpatur, etiam apud probatissimos autores. Arist. in Problem. δὲ τῷ πνεῖ διελθεῖν οὖν ἄλλως, necesse est ignem subire sales.
units.tr: Verse 9. Ἐγὼ μὲν οὖν εἶδοξα ἐμαυτῷ πρὸς τὸ ὄνομα Ἰησοῦ Ναζωραίου δεῖ πολλὰ ἐναντία πρᾶξαι [I therefore indeed thought with myself that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth]. The Syriac, the Arabic and Cl. Beza construe ἐμαυτῷ with εἶδοξα, as if it stood for πρὸς ἐμαυτῷ. The Vulgate and Erasmus, however, construe it with δεῖ, which is not to be wholly rejected. For although it would more commonly be said εἶδοξα ἐμαυτὸν δεῖν πράξαι, the dative is nonetheless found in places, even among the most approved authors. Aristotle, in the Problems: δὲ τῷ πνεῖ διελθεῖν οὖν ἄλλως, it is necessary for the fire to pass through the salts.

units.la: V e r s. 10. Et quum interimerentur, καταλυοντα ψηφον. Vulg. & Eras. detuli sententiam, ut minister qui Judicum decretum defert. At id ἀναφέρειν dicunt Graeci, non καταφέρειν, quod deferre quidem significat, sed alio sensu, nempe pro κάτω φέρειν, deorsum ferre, dejicere, ut ἀναφέρειν pro ἄνω φέρειν, sursum ferre. Beza itaque καταφέρειν sumpsit pro simplici φέρειν, adeoque vertit, tuli suffragium. quid si καταφέρειν hic convenientiam significet, quasi dixisset κατ' αὐτὴν ἡνεγκα ψῆφον, secundum id ipsum tuli suffragium, id est, confirmavi suffragium. quod Syrus & Arabs dixerunt, associavi me iis qui condemnarunt eos.
units.tr: Verse 10. Et quum interimerentur, καταφέρων ψῆφον [and when they were put to death, I cast my vote]. The Vulgate and Erasmus render I delivered sentence, like a minister who conveys the judges' decree. But the Greeks say ἀναφέρειν for this, not καταφέρειν, which does mean to deliver, but in another sense, namely for κάτω φέρειν, to carry down, to cast down, as ἀναφέρειν is for ἄνω φέρειν, to carry up. Beza therefore took καταφέρειν for the simple φέρειν, and so translated it I gave my vote. But what if καταφέρειν here signifies agreement, as if he had said κατ' αὐτὴν ἤνεγκα ψῆφον, I cast my vote in accordance with it, that is, I confirmed the vote? This is what the Syriac and the Arabic meant when they said, I associated myself with those who condemned them.

units.la: V e r s. 11. Καὶ κὴ πόσας συναγωγὰς πολλάκις τιμωρῶν αὐτὰς. Syrus, ܠܐܠܐ ܕܡܢ ܩܛܝܠܐ ܪܕܦܐ ܗܘܘ ܠܗܘܢ. Trem. & in omni synagoga agitabam eos. Melius Boder saeviebam in eos. Lex. Syr. Arab. ܟܠ ܡܢ, paravit in eos & miseros eos fecit. ܝܠܝ, cruciatus. Hebr. 11. 35. ܝܠܝ, cruciavit, torsit. teste Ferrario. Arabs legit ܝܚܝܢ, quod Junius non recte vertit, etiam in synagogis omnibus coegi eos blasphe- blasphemare, unde Cl. Beza annotat, Arabem totum hoc πολλάκις πραωσῶν αὐτὰς non legisse. verto Arabem, & in omni synagoga fui puniens eos ut blasphemarent. idem sensus est qui in Græco, puniens eos coëgi blasphemare. πολλάκις non legit. ut nec Syrus.
units.tr: Verse 11. Καὶ κατὰ πάσας συναγωγὰς πολλάκις τιμωρῶν αὐτοὺς [and in every synagogue, often punishing them]. The Syriac, [Syriac, transliterated approximately: la' d-min qatila radfa hawu lahun], Tremellius: and in every synagogue I harassed them. Boderianus is better: I raged against them. In the Syriac and Arabic lexicon, the word means prepared against them and made them miserable; the root means torment. In Heb. 11:35 it means tortured, racked, according to Ferrarius. The Arabic reads [Arabic, transliterated approximately], which Junius does not translate correctly as I even compelled them in all synagogues blasphe- blasphemare. Hence Cl. Beza notes that the Arabic did not read the whole phrase πολλάκις [often] ... αὐτοὺς. I translate the Arabic: I was punishing them in every synagogue so that they would blaspheme. The sense is the same as in the Greek: punishing them, I compelled them to blaspheme. It does not read πολλάκις, nor does the Syriac.

units.la: VERS. 12. Ἐν οἷς προσεδόμεθα. Syrus & Arabs hic tursus & acceperunt pro ⟨ʿal⟩, propter. ut supra c.24. 18. ubi notas nostras vide.
units.tr: VERSE 12. Ἐν οἷς προσεπορευόμην [in which I was going]. The Syriac and the Arabic here take the word tursus [and] as ʿal, meaning on account of, as above in chapter 24:18, where see our notes.

units.la: IBID. Μετ' ἐξουσίας τῆς ἀρχιερέων τῶν ἐξ ἑαυτῶν. Syrus, [Syriac] Boder. in Reg cum potestate & procuratione principum sacerdotum. At in Parif. ut & Trem. cum potestate & permissione princ. &c. qua significatione derivarunt, ut & nonnulli Lexicographi, ipse quoque Masius, ab [Syriac], permisit. quod est ex defectivis secunda. unde est [Syriac], licitus, permissus, At salva doctorum virorum pace, non permittit id analogia Grammatices: nam à [Syriac], Emphat. [Syriac] fit [Syriac], quod recte à Ferrario vertitur concessio, permissio, venia. At [Syriac] non potest derivari nisi à quiescentibus secunda, à partic. [Syriac], persuasus, peritus, plenè sciens. ab [Syriac], persuasit, fecit ut quis penitus cognosceret. inde apud Ferrar. est [Syriac], cognitio, peritia. & in Lex. Syr. Arab. vertitur [Arabic], cognitio, scientia. Idem puto esse [Syriac], ut sensus sit, cum potestate. & cognitione principum sacerdotum. nisi forte perperam vocales hic adhibitæ sint pro [Syriac]. Arabs enim etiam habet [Arabic], cum potestate & per-missu missu maximorum sacerdotum. In priori tamen lectione concordant editiones.
units.tr: IBID. Μετ' ἐξουσίας τῆς παρὰ τῶν ἀρχιερέων [with authority from the chief priests]. The Syriac, [Syriac, transliterated approximately], Boderianus in the Royal edition: with the power and procuration of the chief priests. But in the Paris edition, as also Tremellius, with the power and permission of the chief priests, &c. Some lexicographers, and Masius himself, derived the word in this sense from [Syriac, transliterated approximately], he permitted, which belongs to the second class of defective verbs, whence comes [Syriac], licit, permitted. But with all due respect to learned men, the analogy of grammar does not allow this. For from [Syriac], in the emphatic form [Syriac], comes [Syriac], which Ferrarius rightly translates concession, permission, pardon. But [Syriac] can only be derived from verbs with a middle weak radical, from the participle [Syriac], persuaded, skilled, fully knowing, from [Syriac], he persuaded, he caused someone to know thoroughly. Hence in Ferrarius is [Syriac], knowledge, skill, and in the Syriac and Arabic lexicon it is rendered [Arabic], knowledge, science. I think the same word is meant here, so that the sense is with the power and knowledge of the chief priests, unless perhaps the vowels were wrongly applied here in place of [Syriac]. For the Arabic also has [Arabic], with the power and permission of the chief priests. In the former reading, however, the editions agree.

units.la: V E R S. 18. -Vt aperias oculos eorum; ᾧ ἀνοιξεις αὐτῶν. Beza, & convertas eos. transitivè accepit, prout accipiendum Luc. 1. 16. 17. Jac. 5. 19. 20. In reliquis omnibus N. T. locis intransitivè accipitur pro reverti, converti, convertere se. atque ita Syrus, Arabs, Vulg. & Eras. quos sequor, ne ellipsin statuere sit opus.
units.tr: VERSE 18. That you may open their eyes; ὥστε ἐπιστρέψαι αὐτῶν [that they may turn]. Beza took it transitively, and convert them, as it should be taken in Luke 1:16-17 and James 5:19-20. In all the other places of the New Testament it is taken intransitively, for to return, to be converted, to turn oneself. So too the Syriac, the Arabic, the Vulgate and Erasmus, whom I follow, so that no ellipsis need be assumed.

units.la: V E R S. 33. Εἰ πνεῦμά ὁ Χριστὸς, ἡ πεῖρα ἐξ ἀναστάσεως &c. ei pro ὅτι quod, apud probatos etiam autores usurpari, Budaeus & H. Stephanus abundè docent. sic Syrus & Arabs verterunt. Porro ei πνεῦμα ὁ Χριστὸς mihi poni videtur pro ei πνεῦμα τῷ Χριστῷ, quod patiendum esset Christo. sicut supra c. 25. 5. οἱ δυνατοὶ ἐν ὑμῖν, pro οἷς δυνατὸν ἐν ὑμῖν, quibus possibile est inter vos. vide ibi.
units.tr: VERSE 23. Εἰ πάσχων ὁ Χριστὸς, εἰ πρῶτος ἐξ ἀναστάσεως &c. [if Christ is to suffer, if he would be the first from the resurrection]. That ei may stand for ὅτι [that], as is used even by approved authors, Budaeus and H. Stephanus show abundantly. So the Syriac and the Arabic translated it. Moreover, εἰ πάσχων ὁ Χριστός seems to me to stand for εἰ πάσχων τῷ Χριστῷ, which would be fitting for Christ to suffer. Just as above in chapter 25:5, οἱ δυνατοὶ ἐν ὑμῖν, stands for οἷς δυνατὸν ἐν ὑμῖν, to whom it is possible among you. See there.

units.la: V E R S. 26. Ἐπίσταται γὰρ περὶ τούτων ὁ Βασιλεύς. Syrus, [Syriac text illegible, ~20 letters] . Recte Boderianus in Parif. vertit, & etiam rex Agrippa maximè novit de his ipsis. in Regiis autem addit, quod sint ejusmodi. Tremel. quod ita habeant. haesitarunt quid sit [Syriac text illegible, ~6 letters]. idem est quod sine affixo [Syriac text illegible, ~6 letters], de his. ut enim in gratiam Syriasmi amantium hoc doceamus, sunt praepositiones quae cum nomine construuntur, in modum duorum substantivorum in regimine Genitivi. Sicut ergo Ex. gr. domus Davidis dicitur [Syriac text illegible, ~6 letters], & [Syriac text illegible, ~4 letters] vestis patris, [Syriac text illegible, ~6 letters], & [Syriac text illegible, ~4 letters]: ita supra c. 23. 6. habuimus [Syriac text illegible, ~6 letters], pro [Syriac text illegible, ~6 letters]; quod ex populo, id est, quod pars populi. & & 2 Joan: ÿf. 12. dicitur Demetrius habere testimonium [illegible, ~12 letters] ab Ecclesia & à ve-ritate, idem quod [illegible, ~10 letters]. Rursus, sicut scripta Prophetarum dicitur [illegible, ~8 letters], & simpliciter [illegible, ~8 letters], ita quod hîc legitur [illegible, ~10 letters], idem est quod [illegible, ~6 letters] de hisce.
units.tr: VERSE 26. Ἐπίσταται γὰρ περὶ τούτων ὁ Βασιλεύς [for the king knows of these things]. The Syriac, [Syriac text illegible]. Boderianus in the Paris edition rightly translates it and King Agrippa knows very well about these very things. In the Royal edition he adds that they are of this kind. Tremellius: that they are so. They hesitated over what [Syriac] means. It is the same as without the suffix [Syriac], concerning these. For, to oblige those who love Syriac idiom, we should note that there are prepositions which are construed with a noun in the manner of two substantives in the genitive case. Thus, for example, the house of David is said [Syriac], and [Syriac], the garment of the father [Syriac] and [Syriac]. So above in chapter 23:6 we had [Syriac] for [Syriac], which is of the people, that is, which is part of the people. And in 2 John, verse 12, Demetrius is said to have testimony [illegible] from the Church and from the truth, the same as [illegible]. Again, just as the writings of the prophets is said [illegible], and simply [illegible], so what is read here as [illegible] is the same as [illegible], concerning these things.

units.la: VERS. 29. Καὶ ἐν ὀλίγῳ ἐ̔ν πολλῷ. Non desunt hæc apud Arabem in edit. Erpen. neque in M. S. legit [illegible, ~6 letters], in pauco & in multo.
units.tr: VERSE 29. Καὶ ἐν ὀλίγῳ ἐν πολλῷ [both in little and in much]. These words are not lacking in the Arabic in the Erpenius edition, nor does the manuscript read [illegible], in little and in much.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 27.

units.la: VERS. 1. Versum hunc & sequentem Æthiopicus sic reddidit, Tunc judicarunt & præceperunt ut abiret Paulus cum aliis qui custodiebantur, ad centurionem nomine Iulium, qui ex cohorte Augusta erat, ut irent in Italiam ad Cæsarem. Tunc ascenderunt in navem Adramuttenam quæ ibat versus Asiam, & solvimus ex eo loco, & direximus iter, & Aristarchus Macedonius Thessalonicensis, qui semper mansit nobiscum, adhærens nobis. Addimus hæc notis Cl. Bezæ. Arabs verbotenus sequitur Syrum.
units.tr: VERSE 1. The Ethiopic renders this verse and the next thus: "Then they judged and commanded that Paul, with the other prisoners, should be handed over to a centurion named Julius, who was of the Augustan cohort, to go to Caesar in Italy. Then they went up into a ship of Adramyttium which was sailing towards Asia, and we set out from that place and held our course, and Aristarchus the Macedonian of Thessalonica, who always stayed with us, adhering to us." We add these words from the notes of the famous Beza. The Arabic follows the Syriac word for word.

units.la: VERS. 4. Τ᾽παραλλάξαμεν τὴν Κύπρον. Vulg. subnavigavimus Cyprum. Eras. subnavigamus juxta Cyprum. juxta non est in Græco. Beza, sublegimus Cyprum. nos vertimus, na-vigavimus infra Cyprum. ὑπό, sub, id est, infra. Si ventus tulisset, direxissent iter recto fere cursu Sidone Myram supra insulam Cyprum, relicta insula ad dextram. jam vero obliquare cursum, & infra insulam declinare debuerunt, relictâ ea ad sinistram, adeoque insulam quodammodo cir-cuire. hinc Syrus, [illegible, ~8 letters], circircuivimus juxta Cyprum. Arabs similiter quod & planius explicat Syrus ȳf. 7. ubi pro μὴ προσπλεύντων ἡμᾶς ἐν ἀνέμῳ, ἐπλέομεν τὴν Κρήτην, Syrus habet [illegible, ~12 letters] Syriac [illegible, ~30 letters]
units.tr: VERSE 4. [Παρηλλάξαμεν] τὴν Κύπρον. The Vulgate has "we sailed under Cyprus." Erasmus has "we sail past Cyprus," though "past" is not in the Greek. Beza has "we sailed under Cyprus," and we have rendered it "we sailed below Cyprus." [ὑπό] means "under," that is, below. If the wind had allowed, they would have made a nearly straight course from Sidon to Myra, passing above the island of Cyprus, leaving it on the right hand. But now they had to alter their course and bear away below the island, leaving it on the left, and so in a way go round the island. Hence the Syriac has "we went round near Cyprus." The Arabic does likewise, and the Syriac, which explains it more plainly, does so at verse 7, where for "since the wind did not allow us to approach, we sailed under Crete" it has [illegible].

units.la: & quia non permittebat ventus ut iremus recta, circuivimus juxta Cretam, id est, quum ab insula Cnido in mare Adriaticum recta via supra Cretam, relicta eâ ad sinistram, tendere per ventum non liceret, declinavimus infra eam, atque ita capientes eam ad dextram, circuivimus. quod certe Vulgatus non rectè vertit, adnavigavimus Cretæ. Phrases illæ etiamnum nautis usitatæ sunt, ut rem in mari objectam præternavigaturi, dicantur supra eam navigare quum recta via prætervehuntur, infra eam, quum declinare & circuitu uti coguntur. prius ὑπερπλεῖν, alterum ὑπερπλεῖν Græcis dicitur. adeoque laudamus Cl. Bezam, qui infra ȳf. 16. ὑποπλεύσαντες, vertit, & infra parvam quandam insulam cursu delati.
units.tr: And because the wind did not allow them to go straight, they went round near Crete. That is, since from the island of Cnidus they could not sail straight across towards the Adriatic Sea over Crete, leaving it on the left, because the wind would not permit it, they bore away below it, and so, keeping it on the right, went round it. The Vulgate certainly does not translate this correctly when it renders it "we sailed to Crete." These phrases are still used by sailors: when they are about to pass some object at sea, they are said to sail above it when they pass it on a straight course, and below it when they are compelled to bear away and go round. The Greeks use [ὑπερπλεῖν] for the first, and [ὑποπλεῖν] for the second. So we commend Beza, who, at verse 16, renders [ὑποπλεύσαντες] as "and, carried along by the current, below a certain small island."

units.la: VERS. 5.
units.tr: VERSE 5.

units.la: Κατήλθομεν εἰς Μύρα τῆς Λυκίας. Syrus quoque legit Myra. At Vulgatus & Æthiopicus Lystra.
units.tr: "They came down to Myra in Lycia." The Syriac also reads "Myra." But the Vulgate and the Ethiopic read "Lystra."

units.la: VERS. 8.
units.tr: VERSE 8.

units.la: πόλις Λασαία. Sic Syrus & Arabs quoque legerunt. At Vulg. & Æthiop. civitas Thalassa.
units.tr: "A city called Lasea." The Syriac and the Arabic also read it so. But the Vulgate and the Ethiopic read "a city called Thalassa."

units.la: VERS. 9.
units.tr: VERSE 9.

units.la: Καὶ ὀντῶν ἡδη ἠπορεῖς ἢ πλοῦς. Syrus, [illegible, ~20 letters] Trem. & erat in ea vitandum unicuique, quominus iter faceret mari. Boder. in Parif. & erat sibi vitandum, ut pergeret homo per mare. recte [illegible, ~3 letters] vertit sibi, quod hic, ut alibi sæpe pleonasticè redundat. At [illegible, ~6 letters], vitandi significationem non habet. etsi hoc loco, & 2 Cor. 8. 20. ita vertant. In Regiis melius, ita ut periculosum esset aliquem sulcare mare. Ferrarius in Lex. Syr. [illegible, ~6 letters], metus. Masius in Pecul. Syro, terror, horror. unde [illegible, ~6 letters] locus terribilis, qualis est infernus, ut mihi est interpretatus per Epistolam Moses Mardenus.& ut etiam Barcepha usurpat. haec ille. Mihi anxietatem eam significare videtur quae est in metu, quae animum affligit & pungit. fortasse à Graeco κεντέω pungo. ut manifeste liquet ex 1 Joan. 4. 18. ubi extat [illegible, ~8 letters]. Tremel. quia metus in irritatione est. Boderianus in utraque verf. melius, quia metus in perturbatione est. Ego verto, quia metus cum anxietate est, καλαον ἐχί, inquit Apostolus, id est, habet anxium quid, quo hominis animus affligitur, & quasi punitur. Ita hoc loco ad verbum, & erat sibi anxietas, ut iter faceret quisquam per mare. id est, res erat anxietate & metu plena, adeoque periculosissima. Sic eodem hoc cap. ϛ. 38. hodie est quadragesimus dies, [illegible, ~10 letters] Trem. à concitatione nihil gustatum est vobis. Boder. in Parif. à commotione. In Reg. pra periculo. Ego, pra anxietate. nec aliter verto 2 Cor. 8. 20. [illegible, ~4 letters] quam anxii fumus, timidi fumus & solliciti. quod alii, devitamus. vide quae ibi annotavimus. Arabs quoque primo Actorum loco habet timoris significationem. vertit enim [illegible, ~12 letters], & erat tempus timoris, ut iret quisquam in mare. sic & altero loco, [illegible, ~4 letters], ex metu non editus quicquam. Haec in gratiam Syriacae linguae studiosorum.
units.tr: "And since the fast was now past, sailing was dangerous." The Syriac has [illegible], Tremellius has "and in it each one had to avoid making the journey by sea," and the Bodleian in Paris has "and it was for him to avoid, that the man should go through the sea." He rightly renders the word as "for him," which here, as often elsewhere, is a redundant pleonasm. But the word [illegible] does not have the sense of "avoiding," although in this place and at 2 Cor. 8:20 they translate it so. In the Royal manuscripts it is better: "so that it was dangerous for anyone to plough the sea." Ferrarius in his Syriac lexicon gives [illegible] as "fear," and Masius in the Syriac Peculium as "terror, horror," whence [illegible] is a "terrible place," such as hell, as Moses Mardenus has translated it for me in a letter, and as Barhebraeus also uses it. So far he. To me it seems to signify that anxiety which lies in fear, which afflicts and pricks the mind. Perhaps it comes from the Greek [κεντέω], to prick, as is clear from 1 John 4:18, where the Syriac has [illegible]. Tremellius has "because fear is in irritation." The Bodleian version in both places reads better: "because fear is in perturbation." I render it, "because fear was with anxiety," [κακὸν ἔχει], as the Apostle says, that is, it holds something anxious by which the mind of a man is afflicted and as it were pricked. So in this place, word for word: "and there was anxiety for them, so that anyone should make the journey by sea," that is, the matter was full of anxiety and fear, and so most perilous. Likewise in this same chapter, verse 38: "today is the fortieth day," [illegible]. Tremellius: "from agitation you have tasted nothing." The Bodleian in Paris: "from commotion." In the Royal manuscripts: "from danger." I render it "from anxiety." Nor do I translate 2 Cor. 8:20 otherwise, [illegible] than "we are anxious, timid and solicitous." Others have "we avoid." See what we have noted there. The Arabic also in the first place in Acts has the sense of fear: for it renders, "and it was a time of fear, so that anyone should go out on the sea." So too in the other place [illegible], "by fear nothing was given out." These remarks are for the benefit of students of the Syriac language.

units.la: VERS. 10. Θεωρῶ ὅτι &c. μέλλειν ἔσεσθαι τ πλεῖν. pro μέλλ ἔσεσθαι ὁ πλεῖς. ad quod Erasmus & Beza non animadverterunt, quum manifestum habeat soloecismum, nisi excusetur. Dico ergo, ὅτι non esse hic ex Graecismo accipiendum ἀδικῶς, pro Latino quod, ut ad verbum vertas, video quod futura sit navigatio. sic enim procul dubio dicendum fuisset ὅπ μέλλ{ι} ἱσᾶσθαι ὁ πλοῦς. sed ex Hellenismo ἀμφιβολικῶς, sicut Graecè & Latinè redundet. Vsitatissimum est ex Hebraismo Hellenistis, post verba dicendi, audiendi, videndi &c. adhibere pleonastice ὅτι, ad designandum solummodo id quod dictum, audirum, & visum est. & posset verti nempe. ut Matt. 26. 72. & rursus juravit cum juramento, ὅτι οὐκ οἶδα τὸν ἄνθρωπον, nempe non novi hominem. indicat tantum quid juraverit Petrus. Accipe exemplum vicinius ex Marc. 12. 19. Μωϋσῆς ἔγραψε, ὅτι ἐὰν τινὸς ἀδελφὸς ἀποθάνῃ &c. ἵνα λάβῃ ὁ ἀδελφὸς αὐτοῦ. constructio est, ἔγραψε ἵνα λάβῃ, pro quo rectè etiam dicas ἔγραψε λαβεῖν, intervenit ὅτι ad innuendum quid scripserit. Ita quoque hoc loco, Ἰκαρῷ ὅτι μέλλει ἱσᾶσθαι τὸ πλοῦν. cohaerent constructione Ἰκαρῷ μέλλει ἱσᾶσθαι. intervenit tantum ὅτι, ad indicandum quid viderit, nempe futuram navigationem. Vel ὅτι, ut saepe ה apud Hebraeos, particula est affirmativa, valens οὕτως, ut 1 Joan. 3. 20. ὅτι μείζων ἐστὶν ὁ Θεὸς τῆς καρδίας ἡμῶν, utique major est Deus corde nostro. sic hoc loco, video utique futuram navigationem &c. id maximè arridet.
units.tr: VERSE 10. "I see that [the voyage] ... is about to be" [μέλλειν ἔσεσθαι τὸν πλοῦν], instead of [μέλλ... ἔσεσθαι ὁ πλοῦς], over which Erasmus and Beza did not notice, since it has a manifest solecism unless it is excused. I say, then, that [ὅτι] here is not to be taken in the Greek sense of "because," so that you would translate it word for word as the Latin "that": "I see that the voyage is about to be." For in that case it would undoubtedly have been said [ὅτι μέλλει ἔσεσθαι ὁ πλοῦς]. But it is used in the Hellenistic manner, ambiguously, as it redundates in both Greek and Latin. It is very common, from the Hebraism of the Hellenists, after verbs of saying, hearing, seeing and so on, to use [ὅτι] pleonastically, to designate only that which was said, heard or seen. It may be translated "namely." As in Matt. 26:72, "and again he swore with an oath, [ὅτι] I do not know the man," namely, I do not know the man. It only indicates what Peter swore. Take a closer example from Mark 12:19: "Moses wrote [ὅτι] if any man's brother dies, etc., that his brother may take her." The construction is "he wrote that he may take," for which you may also rightly say "he wrote to take," and [ὅτι] is inserted to indicate what he wrote. So too in this place, "I see [ὅτι] the voyage is about to be," the words cohere in the construction "I see [that the voyage] is about to be." Only [ὅτι] is inserted, to show what he saw, namely the future voyage. Or [ὅτι], as often the Hebrew [ה] is an affirmative particle, meaning "thus," as in 1 John 3:20: "[ὅτι] God is greater than our heart," that is, surely God is greater than our heart. So in this place: "I see, surely, that the voyage will be..." This pleases me most.

units.la: VERS. 12. Βλέπων ζ ἀλλ Αἴβα ἐξ Χῶρον. Cl.Beza, secutus Junium, ait Arabem haec omisisse. At si editioni Erpeniae, & M. S. exemplari fidem habemus, legit ut Syrus, respicientem ad Meridem. Si enim mappis credimus, erat portus iste in ea Cretae parte, quae recta Africam, adeoque Meridiem respiciebat. Quomodo ergo respexit Ἀίβα ἐξ Χῶρον, Africum & Corum, qui duo venti sunt Occidentales, Africus ad occasum Meridionalem, Corus ad Borealem? Respondeo, portum fuisse sinuosum ac flexuosum, qui, si totum in se spectes, Meridiem recta respiciebat: sin sinus & usum ejus, spectabat Africum, id est, illud Occidentis meridionalis punctum, ubi Africus Coro in recta linea opponitur. adeoque opportunissimus huic navigationi erat portus. illac enim in mare Adriaticum rectum erat iter.
units.tr: VERSE 12. "Looking towards Africus and Caurus, the harbour of Phoenix in Crete." Beza, following Junius, says that the Arabic omitted this. But if we trust the Royal edition and the manuscript, it reads as the Syriac does, "looking towards the South." For if we believe the maps, that harbour lay in that part of Crete which faced Africa straight, and so faced south. How then did it look towards Africus and Corus, which are two western winds, Africus toward the south-west and Corus toward the north-west? I answer that the harbour was sinuous and winding, so that if you regard the whole of it, it faced directly south, but if you regard its opening and its use, it faced Africus, that is, that point of the south-west where Africus lies in a straight line opposite to Corus. And so the harbour was most suitable for this voyage, for the straight course to the Adriatic Sea lay that way.

units.la: VERS. 13. Ἀ̔ρας Ἀ̔οτον πωρελίγιο. Vulgatus, quum sustulissent de Assón. eodem modo Æthiopicus. Syrus & Arabs omiserunt Ἀ̔οτον.aureus hic est Bezæ commentarius, cui nihil addo. nisi quod omnes Græcæ editiones, præter Bezæ, etiam Chrysostomus, Ἀ̔οτον jungant cum ἀρας, & per comma distinguant à sequentibus.
units.tr: VERSE 13. "[When they had weighed anchor] they sailed close to Assos." The Vulgate has "when they had raised anchor from Assos." The Ethiopic does the same. The Syriac and the Arabic omitted [Ἄσσον]. This is the golden commentary of Beza, to which I add nothing, except that all the Greek editions, apart from Beza's, and also Chrysostom, join [Ἄσσον] with [ἄραντες] and separate it by a comma from what follows.

units.la: VERS. 15. Ἐπιδόντες ἐφερόμεθα. tradentes, sup. navem ventis ac fluctibus,ferebamur. Syrus [Syriac] Boder. in Paris. & dati sumus in manum illius. male activum [Syriac] accepit pro passi. [Syriac]. Trem. & dedimus in manum illius, nempe [Syriac] venti. verto, & dedimus manum illius, nempe [Syriac], navis. eo sensu quo manum dare dicimus, pro victum se tradere. sensus est, victam eam tradidimus.
units.tr: VERSE 15. "[Having given ourselves up], we were carried along." That is, having given up the ship to the winds and waves, we were carried along. The Syriac, in the Bodleian in Paris, has "we were given into his hand," wrongly taking the active [illegible] for the passive. Tremellius has "we gave into his hand," namely [illegible], the wind. I translate "we gave the ship into his hand," namely [illegible], the ship, in the sense in which we say we give our hand, that is, surrender ourselves as vanquished. The sense is that we surrendered the ship as conquered.

units.la: VERS. 16. Καλαμψὶν κλαῦδιν. sic Vulgatus quoque & Arabs. Syrus [Syriac], Caura. Æthiopicus Cauda. nisi forte incuria typographi (est enim editio ista mendosissima) litera l neglecta sit. quod doctiss. & diligentiss. vir Josephus Scal. in margine annotavit.
units.tr: VERS. 16. Καλαμψὶν κλαῦδιν. The Vulgate and the Arabic read it the same way. The Syriac has Caura, and the Ethiopic Cauda, unless perhaps the letter l was dropped through the printer's carelessness (this edition is very full of errors). The most learned and diligent Joseph Scaliger noted this in the margin.

units.la: VERS. 17. Ἡν ἀρας, βοηθέαις ἐχρῶντο, ὑποζωννύντες τὸ σκεῦος. Syrus, [Syriac]. Trem. quumque sustulissemus eam,extrinsecus succingebamus remedia, & muniebamus ipsam navim. Boder.ea vero sublata,cingebamus & dirigebamus navim. Ferrarius [Syriac], cinxit, pracinxit. Lex. Syr. Arab. [Syriac], constringit, ligat. significat ergo cingulis constringere & ligare. Deinde [Syriac] à Ferrario vertitur, firmavit, stabilivit, composuit, aptavit, disposuit. In Lex. Syr. Arab. [Arabic], paravit & emen-davit. verto ergo, & quum sustulissemus eam (scapham) cingulis constringebamus & firmabamus navim. Arabs habet [Arabic], & quum accepissemus eam, cœpimus ligare navim & ducere eam. Sequitur in eodem versu,& quia timebamus ne incideremus [Syriac], Tremel. & Boder. in Syrtim maris. Ferrarius [Syriac], descensus, vorago. [Syriac], Syrtis. ad verbum ergo vertendum, in descensum vel vorag« ginem maris. descriptio Syrtis est, ubi aquæ maris quasi in voraginem descendunt. sic & Arabs [Arabic], in des-scensum maris. Sequitur [Syriac]. Trem.& Boder.submisimus antenam. Ferrarius [Syriac] per quartam vocalem scribit in fine, quia peregrina vox est, deducta procul dubio ab [Greek]. vertit, velum navis, antenna. sic [Syriac] 40. [Syriac] vertit artemon, parvum velum addititicum dirigendæ navis causa. Lucas hoc loco dixit, [Greek] recte Syrus [Syriac] pro velo sumsit. Beza,summissis velis.sic & Arabs [Arabic] demisimus velum. sunt enim [Arabic], vela.
units.tr: VERS. 17. Ἡν ἀρας, βοηθέαις ἐχρῶντο, ὑποζωννύντες τὸ σκεῦος. The Syriac has the same sense. Tremellius: when we had hoisted her up, we girded the ship from outside with aids, and secured it. Boderianus: when she was taken up, we girded and steered the ship. Ferrarius renders the Syriac verb as girded, pre-girded. The Syriac-Arabic lexicon gives binds tight, ties. So the word means to bind with girdles and to tie fast. The Syriac verb that follows Ferrarius renders as made firm, established, put in order, fitted, arranged. The Syriac-Arabic lexicon gives prepared and mended. I therefore translate: when we had hoisted up the boat, we bound the ship fast with girdles and made it firm. The Arabic has when we had taken her in, we began to tie the ship and to draw it along. The next words in the same verse are and because we feared we would fall (Tremellius and Boderianus: into the Syrtis of the sea). Ferrarius renders the Syriac as descent, abyss, and the Syriac for Syrtis as Syrtis. So the word should be rendered literally as into the descent or abyss of the sea. This describes the Syrtis, where the waters of the sea sink as if into a whirlpool. The Arabic also has into the descent of the sea. Next comes the word for sail-yard. Tremellius and Boderianus render it we lowered the sail. Ferrarius writes it with a fourth vowel at the end, since it is a foreign word, doubtless derived from the Greek. He renders it sail of the ship, sail-yard. The Syriac artemon in the Seventy's usage is rendered by him a small additional sail for steering the ship. Luke used the Greek word here, and the Syriac rightly takes it to mean sail. Beza: with the sails lowered. The Arabic likewise has we lowered the sail, for the Arabic word means sails.

units.la: VERS. 18.
units.tr: VERS. 18.

units.la: [Syriac]. Trem. quumque staret contra nos tempestas dura. Boder. eodem sensu. Ferrarius, [Syriac], procella, tempestas. [Greek] Græcorum.
units.tr: The Syriac word. Tremellius: and while the hard tempest lay against us. Boderianus in the same sense. Ferrarius: storm, tempest. The Greek word is of the Greeks.

units.la: VERS. 20.
units.tr: VERS. 20.

units.la: Syrus [Syriac] [Syriac].
units.tr: The Syriac reads as follows.

units.la: [illegible, ~8 letters] . Boder. in Reg. quumque tempestas corripuisset eam per dies complures. In Parif. & quum teneret eam tempestas dies complures. malè [illegible, ~6 letters] retulit ad [illegible, ~8 letters], navim. sic enim dicendum fuerat [illegible, ~5 letters] in fœmin.gen.ut vel ex præced. ỷf. apparet. ad verbum verto, & quum haberet sibi tempestas dies multos, id est, ut rectè Trem. quumque duraret tempestas dies multos. Sed non probo, quod in notis tradat, ad verbum esse teneret se hiems. malo, teneret vel haberet sibi hiems, cui subjungo dies multos per Accusat. patientem. phrasis Syriaca est, habere multos dies, vel multum temporis, pro diu durare. quam imitatus est Joannes c. 5. 6. τὴν ἰδὼν Ἰησοῦς καταχαμόνον, ἡ γνὼς ὅτι πολλὼ ἤδη χρόνον ἔχει. Syrus, [illegible, ~12 letters] hunc vidit Iesus decumbentem, & scivit quod tempus multum esset ei, vel haberet. id est, quod diu ipsi duraret morbus. In Græco est, χειμῶν ἡ πνεῦμα ολί- γη ἀπλοήσα. quæ Syrus non intellexit de tempestate imminente, quæ adhuc expectaretur & timeretur, sed de præsenti, quæque jam super ipsos, ut sic dicam, jaceret, & actu premeret. sicut Luc. 5. ỷf. 1. dicitur turba Christo ἐπικεῖσθαι. & lapis sepulchro Lazari, Joan. 11.38. & piscis prunæ Joh. 21. 9. quomodo & infra c. 28. 2. ἀφ' ἡ ὑπὲρ τὴν ἐφεστῶσαν, non significat imminentem, sed præsenter prementem pluviam. porro Syrus, quem sequitur Arabs, invertit ordinem, quasi legisset, χειμῶν ἡ ἐπικεῖσθαι ἡ πλέον ἡμέρας, καὶ μὴ ἡλίου, μὴ σελήνης μὴ ἄστρων ἐπιφαινόντων, &c. addit μὴ σελήνης, quæ Græci codices & Vulg. non habent.
units.tr: [illegible] Boderianus in the Regius text: and while the tempest beat upon her for many days. In the Parisian text: and while the tempest held her for many days. The [illegible] has been badly referred to [illegible], the ship; for it should have been rendered in the feminine gender, as is clear from the preceding verse. Word for word, I translate: and while the tempest had many days for itself, that is, as Tremellius rightly renders it: while the tempest lasted many days. But I do not approve what he gives in his notes, that the word means literally the winter held itself. I prefer the winter held or had for itself, to which I add many days in the accusative of extent. The Syriac idiom is to have many days, or much time, meaning to last a long time. John imitates it in chapter 5, verse 6: τὴν ἰδὼν Ἰησοῦς καταχαμόνον, ἡ γνὼς ὅτι πολλὼ ἤδη χρόνον ἔχει [when Jesus saw him lying there, and knew that he already had a long time]. The Syriac: Jesus saw him lying, and knew that it was a long time for him, or that he had it, that is, that his sickness had lasted long. In the Greek the text reads: χειμῶν ἡ πνεῦμα ὀλίγη ἀπλοήσα [a storm, and no small tempest]. The Syriac did not understand this of an approaching storm, which was still expected and feared, but of the present storm, which already lay, so to speak, upon them and pressed them. So in Luke 5:1 the crowd is said ἐπικεῖσθαι [to press upon] Christ, and the stone lay on the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:38), and fish lay on the coals (John 21:9). So also in chapter 28, verse 2, the phrase ἀφ' ἡ ὑπὲρ τὴν ἐφεστῶσαν does not mean an impending rain, but a rain that is already pressing down. Further, the Syriac, which the Arabic follows, inverts the order, as if it had read: χειμῶν ἡ ἐπικεῖσθαι ἡ πλέον ἡμέρας, καὶ μὴ ἡλίου, μὴ σελήνης, μὴ ἄστρων ἐπιφαινόντων, etc. It adds nor of the moon, which the Greek manuscripts and the Vulgate do not have.

units.la: VERS. 21.
units.tr: VERS. 21.

units.la: Κιρδηνεῖ ἡ τὸν ὕδωρ πώτον ἡ τὸν ζημίαν. Vulg. ad verbum, lucrique facere injuriam hanc & jacturam. Beza, vitare. præstat evitare, effugere, evadere. qui enim evadit malum, habet cur id in lucro deputet. ut est apud Comicum. hinc Syrus [Syriac] , & prohibiti fuissemus, id est, immunes ab hoc damno & afflictione. ὑβρίζειν etiam supra vertit [Syriac], afflictionem.
units.tr: Κερδῆσαι τὴν ὕβριν ταύτην καὶ τὴν ζημίαν. The Vulgate, word for word: and to gain this injury and loss. Beza: to avoid. It is better to render it to escape, to get away from, to be spared. For whoever escapes an evil has reason to count it a gain, as the comic writer has it. Hence the Syriac has and we would have been spared, that is, free from this loss and affliction. The Syriac also renders ὑβρίζειν, above, as affliction.

units.la: VERS. 27. Et post 14 dies, quibus erraveramus, addit
units.tr: VERS. 27. And after the fourteen days in which we had been drifting, he adds

units.la: Syrus, [Syriac], Boder. & ferremur in Adriaticum mare. Trem. & abrepti fueramus in Adriaticum mare. respexit Hebr. דָּחַף, rapuit, abripuit. quam significationem apud Syros nondum invenimus. [Syriac] in Kal sumitur pro τύπτειν Luc. 18.13. & 23. 48. unde à Ferrario vertitur, allisit, contudit, quassiit. In Pael [Syriac] Ferrarius, turbavit, perturbavit, repulit, excussit. Ps. 135. 15. Praeterea angore affecit, tutudit, pulsavit, plausit, supplosit. Isa. 3.16. hinc in paff. [Syriac] ponitur pro καταχράομαι, Heb. 11.37. pro ὑποπτάομαι 2 Cor. 4.8. significat eos, qui perculsi & perturbati animo quò se vertant nescisunt. hinc de navigatione dictum verto, & jactati fuimus in Adriatico mari, id est, ventis flustibusque pulsi, concussi & huc illuc disjecti fuimus in Adriatico mari. rectè expressit quod Lucas dixit, διαφερόμενοι ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ Ἀδρίᾳ, quod optimè Beza, & jactaremur in Adria.
units.tr: The Syriac: and we were driven into the Adriatic sea. Boderianus: and we were driven into the Adriatic sea. Tremellius: and we had been swept away into the Adriatic sea. The Syriac verb corresponds to the Hebrew דָּחַף [dachaph], snatched away, carried off. We have not yet found this meaning among the Syriac writers. The verb in the Pe'al is used for τύπτειν [to strike] in Luke 18:13 and 23:48, whence Ferrarius renders it dashed, battered, shattered. In the Pa'el Ferrarius gives disturbed, troubled, drove back, shook out. Psalm 135:15. Besides, it means to afflict with anguish, to beat, strike, smite. Isaiah 3:16. Hence in the passive it is used for καταχράομαι [to misuse], Hebrews 11:37, and for ὑποπτάομαι [to be fearful], 2 Corinthians 4:8. It signifies those who, struck and disturbed in mind, do not know where to turn. Hence, of the voyage, I translate: and we were tossed about in the Adriatic sea, that is, driven, shaken and scattered hither and thither by the winds and waves in the Adriatic sea. The Syriac expresses rightly what Luke said, διαφερόμενοι ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ Ἀδρίᾳ [we were driven up and down in the Adriatic], which Beza rendered very well: and we were tossed about in Adria.

units.la: VERS. 28. Εὗρον ἐργυιὰς εἴκοσι. Syrus, [Syriac], Boder. & invenerunt passus viginti. Trem. ulnas viginti, quod magis probo. ad verbum statuc viginti. est enim [Syriac], statura, erecti hominis longitudo, & Hebr. קומה dicitur. ponitur hoc loco pro ἐργυιά, quae teste Hezychio est ἡ τῶν ἀμφοτέρων χειρῶν ἔκτασις. παστς. Eustat. ἡ ὡς πλάτ@ ἐκζασις ἀμφοῖν τῶν χειρῶν. Suid. τὸ μ᾿ τιδίων χαρῶν μέτρον, mensura quæ inter expansas manus continetur. Latinis ulna dicitur. & staturam hominis longitudine prorsus æquat. definitur enim ulna, mensura tam longa atque est spatium duorum brachiorum utrinque extensorum. potest quoque passus verti, quatenus pro intervallo passorum brachiorum, non passorum inter deambulandum pedum accipitur. Arabs quoque vertit ﻋﻠﻰ ﻳﺪﻳﻪ, viginti staturas. Æthiopicus, quantitatem viginti staturarum viri.
units.tr: VERS. 28. Εὗρον ἐργυιὰς εἴκοσι. The Syriac and Boderianus: and they found passus twenty. Tremellius: twenty ulnae, which I prefer. Word for word, the Syriac is twenty statures, for the Syriac word means the stature, the length of an upright man, and in Hebrew it is called קומה [qomah]. Here it stands for ἐργυιά [fathom], which according to Hesychius is ἡ τῶν ἀμφοτέρων χειρῶν ἔκτασις [the stretch of both hands]. Eustathius: ἡ ὡς πλάτος ἔκτασις ἀμφοῖν τῶν χειρῶν [the extension of both hands as in breadth]. Suidas: τὸ μεταξὺ τῶν ἐκτεταμένων χειρῶν μέτρον [the measure between the outstretched hands]. In Latin it is called ulna (a fathom), and it exactly equals a man's height, for the ulna is defined as a measure as long as the space of two arms stretched out on either side. Passus may also be rendered, insofar as it is taken for the span of the arms, not for the paces of feet in walking. The Arabic also renders it twenty statures on his hands. The Ethiopic: the quantity of twenty statures of a man.

units.la: VERS. 29.
units.tr: VERSE 29.

units.la: φοβούμενοί π μήπως εἰς τραχεῖς τόπους ἐκπέσωσι. Syrus, [Syriac text, illegible, ~20 letters] Trem. Quumque metueremus ne nos inveniremus esse in loco quo essent saxa. Boder. in Reg. ne forte nos ipsos nancisceremur loca scopulosa. [Syriac text, illegible, ~6 letters] acceperunt activè. ac propterea [Syriac text, illegible, ~3 letters] in Accusativo. utrumque malè. In Paris. posterius emendatum, sed non prius. ne inveniremus nobis in locis ubi &c. verte, ne inveniremur nobis, per pleonasmum pronominis, Syris familiarissimum.
units.tr: Fearing lest they should fall upon rough places [φοβούμενοι μήπως εἰς τραχεῖς τόπους ἐκπέσωσι]. The Syriac [Syriac text, illegible]. Tremellius: And when we feared that we should find ourselves in a place where there were rocks. Boderianus in the Regius edition: lest perhaps we should light upon rocky places. The Syriac [Syriac text, illegible] was taken actively, and so [Syriac text, illegible] is put in the accusative. Both are wrong. In the Parisian edition the latter was corrected, but not the former. Translate: lest we should be found in places where etc. The pleonastic use of the pronoun, lest we should be found ourselves, is very common in Syriac.

units.la: VERS. 30.
units.tr: VERSE 30.

units.la: Ὡς ἐκ πεῶρας μελλόντων ἀγκύρας ἐκτείνειν. Merito hîc Cl. Beza versionem Syri traducit. Sed non magis excusari potest Arabs, quippe qui ne latum quidem unguem à Syro recedit. verba ejus sunt, consentiente etiam M. S. [Arabic text, illegible, ~8 letters], Junius, ut fugerent ea in terram, dimissa nave. verte, ut abirent in eam, & alligarent navem terra. [Arabic text, illegible, ~2 letters] non dimittere, sed ligare & firmare significat.
units.tr: As those who were about to stretch out anchors from the prow [Ὡς ἐκ πρῴρας μελλόντων ἀγκύρας ἐκτείνειν]. Rightly here Cl. Beza renders the Syriac version. But the Arabic cannot be excused in the same way, since it does not depart a single nail's breadth from the Syriac. Its words, with the agreement of the manuscript [Arabic text, illegible], are, according to Junius: that they might flee to the land, the ship having been let go. Render: that they might go off to it, and tie the ship to the land. The Arabic [Arabic text, illegible] means not to let go but to tie fast and secure.

units.la: VERS. 40.
units.tr: VERSE 40.

units.la: Καὶ τὰς ἀγκύρας ἐκπεταλόντες. Vulg. & Eras. & quum anchoras sustulissent. Beza, anchoris igitur sublatis.
units.tr: And having cast off the anchors [Καὶ τὰς ἀγκύρας ἐκπεταλόντες]. The Vulgate and Erasmus: and when they had taken up the anchors. Beza: therefore the anchors having been taken up.

units.la: ambiguum est. sensus videri posset, sublatis e mari in navem, quod Belgice dicimus ophalen. Melius Syrus ܐܘܦܠܝܢ ܘ & amputarunt anchoras à navi. eo sensu quo apud Xenoph. dicitur ἀφειλκυσμένη ἀγκύρα, amputata vitis. est enim ἀφειλκυσμένη, separando rem auferre. vide Act. 27. 20. 2 Cor. 3.16. Sequitur, ἐαν εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν, Vulg. & Erasm. committebant se mari. Beza, permiserunt eam mari. melius, ni fallor, Syrus ad amputatas anchoras referens vertit ܐܢܫܝܢ ܘܐܬܘ ܘ. Trem. & Boder. & laxaverunt eas in mare. anchorae fundo maris infixae, ubi à navi resecto fune abscinduntur, non laxantur, sed relinquuntur ubi sunt. verto ergo, & reliquerunt eas in mari. sicut enim apud Hebraeos הניח non tantum est laxavit, remisit, sed & dimisit, sivit, reliquit, unde usitatum הניח, sine. similiter & apud Syros. Exempli gratia, 1 Cor. 10. 13. ܠܐ ܢܣܝܢ ܕܝܢ ܘ, non sinet vos tentari. eo sensu εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν ponetur pro ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ, quo nihil usitatius.
units.tr: The expression is ambiguous. It could seem to mean taken up from the sea into the ship, which we in Dutch call ophalen. The Syriac [Syriac text, illegible] is better: and they cut off the anchors from the ship, in the sense in which Xenophon uses ἀφειλκυσμένη ἀγκύρα, a vine cut away. For ἀφειλκυσμένη means to carry off a thing by separating it. See Acts 27:20; 2 Cor. 3:16. There follows ἐαν εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν, which the Vulgate and Erasmus render they committed themselves to the sea, and Beza they permitted it to the sea. The Syriac, referring it to the cut anchors, more fittingly, I think, renders [Syriac text, illegible]. Tremellius and Boderianus: and let them go into the sea. But anchors fixed in the bottom of the sea, when the rope is cut through from the ship, are not let go; they are left where they are. I therefore translate: and they left them in the sea. For just as among the Hebrews הניח means not only to let go, to slacken but also to dismiss, to allow, to leave, whence the common הניח, let alone, so too among the Syrians. For example, 1 Cor. 10:13: [Syriac text, illegible], he will not allow you to be tempted. In this sense εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν stands for ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ, than which nothing is more usual.

units.la: Sequitur, ἁμα ἀνιῆς τὰς ξλκυσμένας τ' ἀγκύρας. simul laxatis junctuaris gubernaculorum. Consentiunt in num. plur. omnes lectiones. Annotat itaque Cl. Beza, gubernacula plurali num. dici pro singulari, quum unius navis plura non sint gubernacula. Respondere etiam possumus, non respici hic singulare illud istius navis gubernaculum, sed quum plures res, etiam in navibus, habeant suas junctiuras, additum fuisse discriminis gratia gubernaculorum, ut intelligerentur ejusmodi junctiurae, quae gubernaculis continendis & firmandis adhiberi solebant. Belgice uno vocabulo recte dicimus, de toeverbanden, quod ad totam clavorum speciem universim pertinet.
units.tr: There follows: ἅμα ἀνιῆς τὰς ζευχθείσας τῶν πηδαλίων ζευκτηρίας, at the same time loosing the bands of the rudders. All the readings agree in the plural number. Cl. Beza therefore notes that gubernacula (rudders) is put in the plural for the singular, since one ship has not several rudders. We may answer that the author does not here refer to the single rudder of that ship; rather, since many things, even in ships, have their own fastenings, gubernaculorum was added for the sake of distinction, so that the fastenings of the kind used to hold and secure the rudders would be understood. In Dutch we properly say it in one word, de toeverbanden, which applies generally to the whole class of ropes and fastenings.

units.la: VERS. 41. Πεϱιπεσόντες δὲ εἰς τόπον διϑάλασσον. Syrus ܐܕܘܠܐ ܘ
units.tr: VERSE 41. But falling into a place where two seas met [Πεϱιπεσόντες δὲ εἰς τόπον διϑάλασσον]. The Syriac [Syriac text, illegible].

units.la: [illegible, ~20 letters]. Trem. & Boder. in Parif. & pervenit navis in locum jacentem inter duas profunditates maris. In Reg. & impegit navis &c. verto, & tetigit navis locum excelsum, inter duas profunditates maris. [illegible, ~6 letters] non significat pervenire, sed tangere. miror autem quod [illegible, ~8 letters] verterint jacentem. nisi forte existimarint esse à [illegible, ~8 letters] , projecit. & locum projectum inter duo maria, esse locum jacentem inter ea. quo sensu dicendum fuisset [illegible, ~8 letters]. at quod hîc habemus [illegible, ~8 letters] est à [illegible, ~4 letters], altus fuit. sic & Arabs [illegible, ~12 letters] & tetigit navis locum altum (ascendentem) inter duas profunditates maris. secuti autem sumus exemplar M.S. nam in Erpeniana editione per errorem unius literæ omissæ, legitur [illegible, ~4 letters] terra pro [illegible, ~4 letters], maris. Exprimere voluit Syrus periphrastice, quid sit π῾π῾ᾰ δ῾ι᾽ ᾰ ᾱ ᾱ, nempe locus inter duas profunditates maris eminens instar scopuli, qui utrinque fluctibus petitur.
units.tr: [Syriac text, illegible]. Tremellius and Boderianus in the Parisian edition: and the ship came to a place lying between two depths of the sea. In the Regius edition: and the ship struck, etc. I translate: and the ship touched upon a high place between two depths of the sea. The Syriac [Syriac text, illegible] does not mean to arrive but to touch. I am surprised, however, that they rendered it lying, unless perhaps they thought it came from [Syriac text, illegible], to throw, and took the thrown place between the two seas to be a place lying between them. In that sense it should have been rendered [Syriac text, illegible]. But what we have here, [Syriac text, illegible], comes from [Syriac text, illegible], was high. So also the Arabic [Arabic text, illegible]: and the ship touched a high (rising) place between two depths of the sea. I have followed the manuscript copy, for in the Erpenian edition, through the error of one omitted letter, the word reads [Syriac text, illegible], earth, instead of [Syriac text, illegible], of the sea. The Syriac wished to express periphrastically what the Greek means, namely a place between two depths of the sea rising like a reef, which is struck by the waves on either side.

units.la: V E R S. 24. Μὴ πις ἐκ πλυμβήσως. Syrus [illegible, ~8 letters], Tremel. ne injicerent se natatu. Boder. in Parif. ne committerent se natatui. ad verbum est, ne jacerent natationem, id est simpliciter ne natarent. phrasis est Syriaca, à jactu brachiorum inter natandum desumta. quod ex v.seq. plane liquet, ubi eadem phrasis per injicere se natatu, aut committere se natatui incommodè exponitur.
units.tr: VERSE 24. Lest anyone should leap out of the water with swimming [Μὴ τις ἐκ πλυμβήσως]. The Syriac [Syriac text, illegible]; Tremellius: lest they should cast themselves into swimming. Boderianus in the Parisian edition: lest they should commit themselves to swimming. Literally it is lest they should throw swimming, that is, simply lest they should swim. The phrase is Syriac, taken from the throwing of the arms in swimming. This is quite clear from the following verse, where the same phrase is awkwardly explained as to cast oneself into swimming or to commit oneself to swimming.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII.

units.la: V E R S. I. Μελίτη. Syrus, Militi. Arabs, Maltia, quod cum hodierno nomine Maltha congruit. Scribit autem Cl.
units.tr: VERSE 1. Melite [Μελίτη]. The Syriac, Militi. The Arabic, Maltia, which agrees with the modern name Malta. Moreover, Cl.

units.la: Beza, esse & aliam Melitam insulam in mari Adriatico, quam Ptolomæus Militinem appellat. Sic legisse videri posset Æthiopicus. habet enim ܡܠܛܝܢ.
units.tr: Beza writes that there is also another island Melita in the Adriatic Sea, which Ptolemy calls Militine. The Ethiopic might seem to have read it so, for it has Malṭīn.

units.la: VERS. 3. Et Paulus fustulit. Syrus, ܥܒܕ ܕܢܫܐ ܐܡܝܪ ܒܐܪܘܡܐ. Trem. & Boder. in Parif. multitudinem ramorum. In Reg. multa farmenta Ferrarius ܐܪܡܐ, farmentum. Lucas dixit φρυγάνων ξηρῶν. Glossarium φρύγανον, fomes. Stephanus, Cremium. vel, virgultum aridum, sive furculus aridus. continet omnia sarmentosa ligna arida, ignisque fomenta, sive ad cremandum facilia. ἀ φρύγω, torreo. idem plane est ܐܪܡܐ, à verbo geminanti secundam ܐܪܡܐ accensus est, exarsit. Arabs ܐܠܢܪ ܡܢ ܡܐܪ, multitudinem stipularum. materiæ sunt crematu faciles.
units.tr: VERS. 3. "And Paul gathered a bundle of sticks" (fustulit). The Syriac has ʿbd dnšʾ ʾmyr bʾrwmʾ. Tremellius and Boderianus in Paris have "a multitude of branches." In the Regius edition it is "many sticks." Ferrarius gives ʾrmʾ, "twig" or "brushwood." Luke wrote [φρυγάνων ξηρῶν], "dry sticks." The Glossary gives [φρύγανον] as "kindling." Stephanus gives "dry brushwood" or "a dry twig." It denotes all dry, twiggy wood and the fuel of fire, or wood that is easy to burn, from [φρύγω], "I roast." The Syriac ʾrmʾ is plainly the same word, from a verb that doubles its second letter, meaning "was kindled, blazed up." The Arabic has "a multitude of stubble." These are materials that catch fire easily.

units.la: VERS. 5. Ἀ'πολυάξας τὴν ϑηρίον εἰς τὸ πῦρ. Syrus, ܐܢܐ ܕܐܝܬ ܠܗ ܐܝܬܝܪ ܡܢ ܟܠ. Trem. ipse vero Paulus extulit manum suam & injecit viperam in ignem. Boder. in Reg. Ipse vero Paulus sublata manu sua dejecit &c. Melius in Parif. movit manum suam. verto agitavit manum suam. id enim proprie est ܐܝܬܝܪ. ficut & Hebr. הניף.
units.tr: VERS. 5. "Having shaken off the beast into the fire" [ἀποτινάξας τὴν θηρίον εἰς τὸ πῦρ]. The Syriac has ʾnʾ d-ʾyt lh ʾytyr mn kl. Tremellius: "But Paul himself lifted up his hand and threw the viper into the fire." Boderianus in the Regius edition: "Paul himself, having lifted his hand, cast it off," etc. The Paris edition is better, with "moved his hand," which I render "shook his hand." For the Syriac ʾytyr is the proper word, just as the Hebrew has [הניף], "to wave."

units.la: VERS. 6. οἱ δὲ προσδόκων αὐτὸν μέλλειν πίμπρασθαι. Vulg. & Beza πίμπρασθαι pro intumescere acceperunt. Erasm. & Æthiop. pro incendi & uri. utrumque significat. Syrus, ܐܬܢܦܚ, Tremel. confumeretur. Boder. Intumesceret. apud Hebr. נפח & נפח, liquefcere, diffolvi. fic apud Syros ܐܬܢܦܚ teste Ferrario fætere fecit, mucefcere fecit, putrefecit. ܐܬܢܦܚ, mucuit, fætuit, putruit, tabuit, Efa. 34. 4. fic in Lex. Syr. Arab. dicitur esse à ܐܬܢܦܚ, quod fœtorem, mucorem significat. & vertitur ⟨Arab.⟩ quod Arab. est computrescere, tabescere. verto ergo, putabant autem barbari quod statim tabesceret. id est, quod vi veneni statim colliquesceret & dissolveretur. ea enim, ut ex Hebraismo patet, primaria est huius verbi significatio. sic Arabs ⟨Arabic⟩, quod statim dissolveretur.
units.tr: VERS. 6. "But they expected that he would swell up or be inflamed" [οἱ δὲ προσδόκων αὐτὸν μέλλειν πίμπρασθαι]. The Vulgate and Beza took [πίμπρασθαι] to mean "swell up." Erasmus and the Ethiopic took it to mean "be burned and inflamed." The word means both. The Syriac has ʾtnpḥ; Tremellius has "would be consumed," and Boderianus "would swell up." In Hebrew, [נפח] and [נפח] mean "to melt, to dissolve." So too among the Syrians ʾtnpḥ, as Ferrarius testifies, means "made to stink, made to mould, made to rot." ʾtnpḥ means "moulded, stank, rotted, decayed" (Isa. 34:4). So too the Syriac lexicon says the word derives from a root meaning "stench, mould," and the Arabic word means "to rot, to waste away." I therefore translate: "The barbarians thought that he would at once waste away," that is, that by the force of the poison he would at once melt and dissolve. For this is the primary meaning of the verb, as the Hebraism makes clear. So too the Arabic, "that he would at once dissolve."

units.la: IBID. Μηδὲν ἀπῖτον ὡς αὐτὸν γινόμενον. Vulg. nihil mali in eo fieri. Beza, nihil incommodi ei accidere. ἄπτον de malo morali sive culpæ usitatè dicitur, ut Luc. 23.41. 2 Thess. 3.2. apud LXX Interpretes pro ⟨Hebrew⟩, iniquitas, ⟨Hebrew⟩, improbitas, ⟨Hebrew⟩, vanitas, malitia usurpatur. de malo autem physico sive poenæ, raro. citant Lexicographi Theophrastum, qui pro incommodo usurparit. At est ubi pro re turpi, infami, & ignominiosa accipiatur, quæ ipsa sua turpitudine, vitii & criminis notam habet, ut apud Platonem, ἀπτῳ ἐ αἰχρᾶ νίκῃ νικᾶν, infami ac turpi victoria vincere. Ita Syrus hoc loco accepisse videtur, cum vertit ⟨Syriac⟩, nihil odibile ipsi factum esse. eâdem omnino phrasi, quâ τὸ ἄπτον in vitio positum verterat Luc. 23.41. Mentem ejus explicat Arabs, ⟨Arabic⟩, non evenisse ei quicquam turpe, id est, ullum incommodum turpe & ignominiosum, unde criminis alicujus, prout suspicati fuerant, reus haberi posset. Hezychius & Suidas reddunt etiam per ⟨Greek⟩, quod insolens, novum & admirandum est. apud Thucyd. lib. 3. opponuntur τὰ ἄπτα ἐ τὰ ἐωθότα, insolita & solita. hinc rectè vertas, nihil ipsi novi contingere, vel insoliti, vel inexpectati.
