units.tr: IBID. "That no harm was happening to him" [μηδὲν ἄτοπον εἰς αὐτὸν γινόμενον]. The Vulgate has "that nothing evil happened to him in it," and Beza "that nothing inconvenient befell him." [ἄτοπον] is commonly used of moral evil or fault, as in Luke 23:41 and 2 Thess. 3:2. In the Septuagint it stands for "iniquity," "wickedness," "vanity," and "malice." It is used of physical evil or punishment rarely. The lexicographers cite Theophrastus, who uses it for "inconvenience." But sometimes it means a shameful, disgraceful and ignominious thing, which by its very shame carries the mark of vice and crime, as in Plato: "to win an unseemly and shameful victory." The Syriac seems to have taken it this way when it renders "nothing hateful happened to him," using exactly the same phrase by which it had rendered [τὸ ἄτοπον] as a fault in Luke 23:41. The Arabic explains the author's meaning: "nothing shameful happened to him," that is, no disgraceful harm by which he could be held guilty of some crime, as they had suspected. Hesychius and Suidas also render it by [something] "unusual, new and wonderful." In Thucydides, book 3, [τὰ ἄτοπα] is opposed to [τὰ εἰωθότα], "the unusual and the customary." So one may rightly translate, "nothing new happened to him," either unusual or unexpected.

units.la: VERS. 7. Ἐν ᾗ τῆς ἐξ ἐ πόλον ἐκεῖνον. Vulg. & Eras. & Arabs, in locis autem illis. Beza, caterum circa locum illum. ad verbum est, in iis quæ erant circa locum ipsum. ubi τῆς ἐξ ἐ πόλον ἐκεῖνον, ponitur pro τῷ πόλῳ ἐκείνῳ, sicut eleganti Græcorum phrasi ἐι ἐξ τὴν Παῦλον dicitur pro ὁ Παῦλ@-
units.tr: VERS. 7. "Now in those places around that place" [Ἐν δὲ τοῖς περὶ τὸν τόπον ἐκεῖνον]. The Vulgate, Erasmus and the Arabic have "in those places." Beza has "but around that place." Literally it is "in those things which were around that place," where the genitive article phrase stands for the dative [τῷ πόλῳ ἐκείνῳ], just as in the elegant Greek idiom the phrase is used for [ὁ Παῦλος].

units.la: Act. 13. 13. præpositá præpos. ἐν, simpliciter valet, in loco autem illo. ut rectè Syrus vertit. vel in regione illa. ⌐ ⌐ enim locum & regionem significat.
units.tr: Acts 13:13. With the preposition [ἐν] prefixed, it simply means "in that place," as the Syriac rightly renders it, or "in that region." For the word means both place and region.

units.la: IBID. ὁ'ς ἀναδιξάμεν ἡμᾶς τῆς ἡμέρας φιλοφρόνως ἰδί-ξαλο. Vulg. & Erasm. φιλοφρόνως, benignè. Beza, peramicè. Syrus Δ.]_ , libenter, vel ut vim vocis Syriacæ exprimam, gaudenter, quod Arabs ... dixit. non male. nam & apud Hezych. φιλοφροντίσμα exponitur, δεξιῶς ἐ ... dextro & prompto animo excipio.
units.tr: IBID. "Who received us kindly in the day" [ὃς ἀναδεξάμενος ἡμᾶς τῆς ἡμέρας φιλοφρόνως]. The Vulgate and Erasmus have "kindly" for [φιλοφρόνως]. Beza has "most kindly." The Syriac has "gladly," or, to express the force of the Syriac word, "joyfully," which the Arabic also says. Not badly so, for Hesychius explains [φιλοφροντίσμα] as "I receive with a ready and cheerful mind."

units.la: VERS. 14. ἐπ' αὐτῆς ... apud ipsos permanere. rarum est ἐπὶ pro ... apud. non tamen omnino insolens. ut ἐπὶ ταῖς θύραις, adfores, apud januam, omnibus fere scriptoribus usitatum. & apud Thucid. l. 3. ὧ ἐπὶ ... situs erat apud fluvium. quod si quis hoc non velit, ἐπὶ frequentissime valet propter, causâ, gratiâ. ut cum dicunt, ἐπὶ τῷ κέρδει, lucri causa hoc fecit. ita hic, rogati sumus ut ipsorum causa maneremus septem dies.
units.tr: VERS. 14. "To remain with them" [ἐπ' αὐτοῖς]. It is rare for [ἐπὶ] to mean "with" or "at," but it is not wholly unusual, as in [ἐπὶ ταῖς θύραις], "at the doors, by the door," a usage found in almost all writers. And in Thucydides, book 3, [ἐπὶ τοῦ ποταμοῦ] means "situated by the river." If anyone does not want this sense, [ἐπὶ] very often means "on account of, for the sake of, for the benefit of," as when they say [ἐπὶ τῷ κέρδει], "he did it for the sake of gain." So here: "we were asked to stay seven days for their sake."

units.la: VERS. 16. ὁ ἐκαλέσαςχ ... πεπίδωκε τὴν διαμίνης τῷ σπλο-πάδεχη. Vulgatus, Syrus & Arabs hoc membrum non legerunt, ut nec Chrysostomus. reliquæ editiones Græcæ constanter legunt. legit & Æthiopicus.
units.tr: VERS. 16. The Vulgate, the Syriac and the Arabic did not read this clause, nor did Chrysostom. The other Greek editions consistently read it. The Ethiopic reads it too.

units.la: IBID. Permisit Paulo habitare καθ' ἑαυτὸν, Vulgatus sibi. Eras. solus. Beza, seorsim. Glossarium, καθ' ἑαυτὸν, in se, secum. Hezychius, αὐτῆς δ' ἑαυτοῦ, ipse per se. Belgicè dicimus, op hem selben woonen. Aliter tamen Syrus, Arabs & Æthiopicus, qui verterunt, ubi vellet. καθ' ἑαυτὸν acceperunt pro secundum se, id est secundum animi sui sententiam, καθ' ἑαυτὸ γνώμην. Quæ hic Cl. Beza subjungit, Deest autem totum hoc membrum in recepta editione Latina, quod tamen abundare non puto, & non tantum in Græcis codicibus, sed etiam in Syra & Arab. interpretatione reperi, nescio quid sibi velint. si enim proximum hoc membrum intelligit, in quo de privato Pauli domicilio agitur, extat in Vulgata Latina editione. si praecedens, ubi Centurio dictus est vinctos tradidisse praefecto exercituum, jam ante monuit, id deesse in Latinis codicibus, nec verum est id in Syra & Arabica interpretatione reperiri.
units.tr: IBID. "Paul was permitted to dwell [καθ' ἑαυτὸν]." The Vulgate has "by himself," Erasmus "alone," and Beza "apart." The Glossary gives [καθ' ἑαυτὸν] as "in himself, with himself," and Hesychius gives "by himself, on his own." In Dutch we say "op hem selven woonen," "to live by himself." The Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic, however, rendered it differently, "wherever he wished." They took [καθ' ἑαυτὸν] to mean "according to himself," that is, according to his own judgment, [κατὰ ἑαυτοῦ γνώμην]. Beza here adds: "This whole clause is missing from the received Latin edition, which I do not think is superfluous, and I have found it not only in the Greek manuscripts but also in the Syriac and Arabic translation." I do not know what he means by this. If he means the following clause, in which Paul's private lodging is discussed, it is found in the Latin Vulgate. If he means the preceding clause, where the centurion is said to have handed the prisoners over to the commander of the army, he has already noted that this is lacking in the Latin codices, and it is not true that it is found in the Syriac and Arabic translation.

units.la: VERS. 28. Vobis ergo sit notum, Gentibus missum esse salutare Dei, αὐτοὶ ἀκούσονται. Vulg. & Eras. & illi audient. Beza, & illos audituros. At data opera videtur mihi Euangelista, majoris emphaseos gratia, ἐκ postposuisse. quod servandum arbitror, ac vertendum, illi etiam audient. Syrus efficaciter, illi enim etiam audient. Arabs habet ... quae vertenda sunt. Scitote igitur nunc hoc, quod ad gentes missa est haec salus, salus Dei, ut illi obediant ei. id emphasin valde imminuit.
units.tr: VERS. 28. "Be it known to you therefore that the salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they [αὐτοὶ ἀκούσονται] will also hear." The Vulgate and Erasmus have "and they will hear." Beza has "and they will hear it." But I think the evangelist deliberately put [αὐτοὶ] last, for greater emphasis, and this should be kept and rendered "they too will hear." The Syriac powerfully says, "for they too will hear." The Arabic has words that must be rendered: "Know therefore now that this salvation, the salvation of God, has been sent to the nations, so that they may obey him." This greatly weakens the emphasis.

units.la: VERS. 29. Hunc totum versum Syrus & Arabs non legerunt. ut vere annotavit Cl. Beza. Æthiopicus legit.
units.tr: VERS. 29. The Syriac and the Arabic did not read this whole verse, as the learned Beza rightly noted. The Ethiopic reads it.

units.la: VERS. 30. Syrus, [Syriac text]. Trem. & mercede conduxit sibi Paulus de suo domum. sic fere Boder. si autem recta est punctatio in [Syriac], ut in eo editiones consentiunt, vertendum erit, & traxit sibi Paulus e suo domum. est enim [Syriac] Aphel a [Syriac], traxit. Sin autem legendum [Syriac] recte verterunt viri doctissimi. nec dubium quin sic legerit Arabs, qui vertit [Arabic], & conduxit sibi Paulus ex opibus suis domum. id est, quod dixit Lucas, εν ἰδίῳ μισθώματι.
units.tr: VERS. 30. The Syriac, in the pointing which Tremellius renders, "and Paul hired a house for himself from his own means," and Boderianus much the same. But if the pointing of the Syriac word is correct, as the editions agree, it must be rendered "and Paul drew a house to himself from his own." For the Syriac verb is the causative form of the verb meaning "to draw." But if the other reading is intended, the most learned men have translated rightly. Nor is there any doubt that the Arabic read it so, for it renders "and Paul hired a house for himself from his own resources," which is what Luke says: [ἐν ἰδίῳ μισθώματι], "in his own rented lodging."
